en: The Laws of Manu,
accompanied by the *Manvarthamuktāvalī* commentary composed by Kullūkabhaṭṭa;
the First Chapter.
Approaching Manu as he sat with a one-pointed mind, the great seers honored him according to custom and spoke these words.

Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One Vāsudeva! In the venerable lineage of Varendra, in the family known as Nandanavāsin, honored by virtuous men, there lived Kullūkabhaṭṭa, the son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Divākara.
In Kāśī, on the northern bank of the daughter of Jahnu (the Gaṅgā), this *Manvarthamuktāvalī* is composed by him together with learned scholars for the benefit of the wise. (1)
Although I am not omniscient, I shall explain the verbal corpus of the Omniscient Man;

for this has been extensively expounded by many excellent sages through reasoning. Thus, it is only right that I should speak in favor of this explanation, even though it was composed by those of the present day.
Through devotion to him who is composed of human speech and who destroys worldly existence, may he become the Lord of all. ||2||

I have served you, Mīmāṃsā, extensively; you, Tarka, have been my friends; you, Vyākaraṇa, have been my constant companions; and you, the teachers of the realization of the Supreme Self, have been worshipped by me in solitude.
Since childhood, we have grown up together as friends; therefore, I entreat you all.
This moment has arrived; let assistance be provided for this commentary on the words of Manu. ||3||
Although I am free from defects such as hatred and am striving here for the benefit of the virtuous and to explain the true meaning of the *Manu-śāstra*,
should there nevertheless be some lapse on my part due to fate, [may it be forgiven].
May the Inner Soul of the universe be my deliverer. ||4||
In this *Mānavavṛtti*, a new commentary distinct from previous ones should be understood; yet it is also pleasing to all ancient commentators. (5)

“Manu, seated with one-pointed attention,” and so forth. Here, in response to the great sages’ inquiry regarding the subject of *dharma*, Manu provides an answer through these four introductory verses beginning with “Listen” (*śrūyatām*); by means of them, he establishes the subject matter (*viṣaya*), the connection (*saṃbandha*), and the purpose (*prayojana*) of this treatise, which are necessary for the engagement of discerning persons. In this context, *dharma* alone is the subject matter. The connection between that *dharma* and the Mānava-śāstra—which consists of a composition of words—is characterized as that of the expressed and the expresser (*pratipādyapratipādaka*). This is because *dharma*, which is not accessible through other means of knowledge and which is the means to attaining heaven, liberation, and so forth, is cognizable solely through the scripture. The purpose, however, is heaven, liberation, and the like, since these are dependent upon *dharma*. Although desire (*kāma*), such as approaching one’s wife, is also mentioned here, nevertheless, because it is governed by rules such as “one should approach [one’s wife] during her season, always devoted to one’s own wife” (3.45), even that is indeed *dharma*. Likewise, it should be understood that the acquisition of wealth (*artha*) is also *dharma* when governed by rules such as “one should live by the true and the untrue” (4.4). Since the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*), taught as a means to liberation, is also a form of *dharma*, it is logically established that this scripture has *dharma* as its subject matter and serves as an instruction on liberation. Even though the words of Manu are of human origin (*pauruṣeya*), they possess authority because they are accepted by great people of unimpeachable character and because they are supported by the Veda (*śruti*). Thus, it is heard in the Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa: “Whatever Manu said was medicine, by virtue of its being medicine. Bṛhaspati also says: [text follows].
Because it is based upon the meaning of the Vedas, the Smṛti of Manu is considered preeminent;
however, any Smṛti that contradicts the meaning of Manu is not commended.
Treatises on logic and grammar remain splendid only so long as Manu,
the instructor of dharma, artha, and mokṣa, is not seen.
It is also stated in the Mahābhārata:
"The Purāṇas, the Dharma of Manu, the Veda with its auxiliary limbs, and medical science—
these four are established by authority and must not be undermined by reasoning."

They must not be destroyed by contradictory reasoning (*tarka*) such as that of the Buddhists and others; however, favorable reasoning such as that of the Mīmāṃsakas should certainly be employed. For this very reason, he will say (12.106):
"He who investigates the traditional teaching of Dharma with reasoning that does not contradict the Vedic scriptures knows Dharma, and no other."

Because he reflects upon the meaning of the entire Veda and so forth, the great seers spoke this word—consisting of the words of the second verse—as "Manu. The mention of Manu at the beginning of the verse is for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). This is because the Supreme Self himself has manifested in a form corresponding to his nature, endowed with omniscience, sovereignty, and other qualities, for the sake of the maintenance of the world; thus, the naming of him constitutes a supreme auspiciousness. For he will say later (12.123): "Some call him Agni, others Manu, and others Prajāpati."

"Single-minded" means with a mind not distracted by other objects. "Seated" means comfortably settled, for only one in such a state is fit to provide answers to the questions of a great seer (*maharṣi*). "Having approached" means having gone before him. "Great seers" refers to those who are both great and seers. "Having honored" means having paid homage; or rather, it is inferred from the word "having honored" that he performed the same honor as was previously shown by Manu through welcoming, offering a seat, and so forth. "In accordance with propriety" means by whatever method or rule a question is fittingly made, such as through prostration, devotion, and an excess of faith. And he will say later (2.110):

"One should not speak to anyone unless asked, nor to one who asks improperly. In this passage, "Manu" is the object of all three actions—"having approached," "having honored," and "not speaking. In the phrase "not speaking," Manu functions as an *akathita-karman* (an unexpressed object), because the verbal root *brū* (to speak) is transitive with two objects.
In response to the expectation of what they said, he says:
"O Blessed One, you ought to speak to us of the Dharma for all the social classes (varṇas) in their proper order, as well as for those born of intermediate castes. (1.2)

"Bhagavan," and so forth. The word *bhaga* is a designation for sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) and the other [perfections]. As it is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "The term *bhaga* is the name for these six: complete sovereignty, valor, fame, splendor, knowledge, and dispassion."

The address "O Blessed One" (*bhagavan*) is formed with the suffix *matup*. "Castes" (*varṇāḥ*) refers to the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras. "All those castes" (*sarvavarṇāḥ*) includes them all; furthermore, there are those born from the intermediate [castes] (*antaraprabhavāḥ*), that is, those of mixed origin (*saṃkīrṇajāti*) produced through the direct (*anuloma*) or inverse (*pratiloma*) order, such as the Ambaṣṭhas, Kṣattṛs, Karṇas, and so forth. Because these are produced from sexual union between different castes—just as a mule is produced from the contact of a donkey and a mare—and because they constitute a distinct species (*jātyantara*) not included under the term "caste," they are asked about separately. By this, the universal utility of this treatise is demonstrated. By the phrase "whatever dharma belongs to whichever caste and in whatever manner it is appropriate," there is also an inquiry regarding the duties of the stages of life (*āśramadharma*) and so forth. "In due order" (*anupūrvaśaḥ*) means sequentially: first the birth-rite (*jātakarma*), then the naming ceremony (*nāmadheya*), and so on. "You ought to tell us our duties" (*dharmān no vaktum arhasi*); since you are capable of declaring all duties, the request "therefore, please speak" is to be supplied. As for the mention here of non-dharma (unrighteousness) in the form of killing a Brahmin and so forth, that is intended as a subject for the rules of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), and not as an independent topic. 2.
He states the reason for his fitness to designate all phenomena:
"O Lord, you alone are the knower of the true meaning of the purpose of the activity of this entire self-existent ordinance, which is inconceivable and immeasurable. (1.3)

By the words "You alone," etc., the word *hi* indicates the reason (*hetu*). Because you alone are without a second (*advitīya*) with respect to this entire *vidhāna*—which is directly heard in the Śruti and inferred from Smṛti and other sources; which is called *vidhāna* because by it actions such as the Agnihotra are enjoined; which is the Veda, self-existent (*svayaṃbhū*), not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), and inconceivable; which, due to being divided into many branches, is incapable of being delimited by a finite measure; which is immeasurable (*aprameya*), its objects of knowledge (*prameya*) not being understood through dependence on logic such as Mīmāṃsā; and which has for its object the *kārya*, i.e., the duty to be performed such as the Agniṣṭoma—you know that *tattva*, the Brahman known through the Vedānta in passages such as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (Taitt. Up. 2.1.1). That very [Brahman] is the *artha*, the portion to be established; thus, you are a knower of the reality of the object of duty (*kāryatattvārthavit*). Medhātithi, however, under the influence of his training in Karma-mīmāṃsā, explains it as: "The Veda’s object, in the form of reality, is only the duty (*kārya*); he knows that, therefore he is a knower of the reality of the object of duty (*kāryatattvārthavid*). The address "O Lord" (*prabho*) is used because of your capacity to establish the distinction between dharma and adharma. (Verse 3)
Thus questioned by those great-souled ones, he of immeasurable luster duly honored all those great seers and replied, "Listen. 1.4.

"Thus questioned by them, [he replied] correctly," and so forth. That Manu, being questioned by those great seers (*maharṣi*) in that manner—by means of the previously mentioned method consisting of prostration, devotion, and an excess of faith and so on—replied to them correctly, according to the truth, beginning with the words "Listen! He was one whose immeasurable and unlimited power (*ojas*), that is, capacity, existed in the exposition of the principles of knowledge and other matters. For this very reason, by virtue of his omniscience and omnipotence, he was a fit subject for the questions even of the great seers. Having honored—that is, having worshipped—those high-souled ones of great majesty; this is the form of the root *arc* preceded by the prefix *ā*, ending in a gerundive suffix (*lyap*). By this, it is established that even the exposition of the Dharma must be performed preceded by worship.

Now, if this treatise were composed by Manu, it would not be appropriate for it to say, "Being questioned, he replied"; rather, it would be more fitting to say, "Being questioned, I speak. Furthermore, if it were composed by someone else, how could it be called the *Mānavī Saṃhitā* (the collection belonging to Manu)?

It is said: It is generally the style of the teachers (*ācāryas*) that they describe even their own intended meaning as if it were the instruction of another. For this very reason, "Jaimini [says] that ritual acts also [are to be performed], because they are for the sake of the fruit" (Jaimini’s *Nyāyasūtra* 3.1.4) is indeed Jaimini’s own *sūtra*. For this very reason, "Bādarāyaṇa [says] that there is also [the possibility of gods attaining liberation] above that, because of the possibility" (Brahmasūtra 1.3.26) is indeed Bādarāyaṇa’s own *Śārīrakasūtra*. Alternatively, the duties (*dharmas*) taught by Manu were compiled by his disciple Bhṛgu at his command. For this very reason, he will say (1.59): "This Bhṛgu will recite this scripture to you in its entirety. Therefore, it is entirely appropriate that he, being questioned, provides an answer. And because it is a compilation of the duties taught by Manu, it is designated as the *Mānavī Saṃhitā*. || 4 ||
Having introduced the subject with the words "Let it be heard," he states the matter:
"In the beginning, this was enveloped in darkness, unperceived, without distinguishing marks, beyond reasoning, unknowable, as if entirely asleep. (1.5)

"This was so. Now, it might be argued that when the sages asked a question concerning *dharma*, it would have been more appropriate to give an answer on that very subject. Why, then, this introduction of a topic irrelevant to the context—the process of creation of the universe which was dissolved into its cause during the state of dissolution? On this point, Medhātithi provides the following resolution: "The entire purpose of this treatise is established by all of this; here, the various states of transmigratory existence, from Brahmā down to the stationary beings, are explained as being caused by *dharma* and *adharma*."
"Enveloped by manifold darkness caused by their past actions"—thus [it is said].
And he will further state:
"But having observed these destinies of the living being with his own mind..."
"One should always fix the mind upon dharma and indeed upon adharma" (MDh 12.23).

Therefore, since dharma is the cause of unsurpassed sovereignty and adharma is its opposite, this scripture—which serves the purpose of fully understanding their nature—is of great utility and must be studied; such is the purport of this chapter. (Medh. transcription, p. 10)

[This concludes] up to that point. Govindarāja also offers this same resolution. However, this is not compelling. To mention the fruit of dharma when the question concerns the essential nature of dharma is likewise irrelevant; for the scripture is purposeful merely by the statement of dharma itself.

Furthermore, since the great sages asked, "Please describe the production of the fruits of actions," it is not appropriate to speak of that [production] at the outset, as it will be discussed in the twelfth chapter.

To this we reply: regarding the question of the sages concerning the Dharma, the exposition of Brahman as the cause of the world is indeed a discourse on Dharma, and thus it is not an irrelevant statement; for even the knowledge of the Self is of the nature of Dharma. As Manu himself [states] (6.92): "Fortitude, forbearance, self-restraint, non-stealing, purity, control of the senses, wisdom, learning, truthfulness, and freedom from anger—this is the tenfold characteristic of Dharma."

Thus, in the exposition of the tenfold dharma, self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*), which is denoted by the term "knowledge" (*vidyā*), is stated to be a form of dharma. In the *Mahābhārata* as well, it is stated that self-knowledge and forbearance are the common dharma for all: "Self-knowledge and forbearance, O King, are the common dharma. However, that which was described by Yājñavalkya as the supreme dharma—
Of the acts of sacrifice, ritual conduct, self-restraint, non-violence, charity, and Vedic study, this indeed is the supreme dharma: that one perceives the Self through yoga. (YDh 1.8)

Furthermore, being the cause of the world is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman. For this very reason, immediately after the first aphorism of the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*, "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (*atha ato brahma-jijñāsā*), the venerable Bādarāyaṇa composed the second aphorism, "From which the origin, etc., of this [world]" (*janmādy asya yataḥ*). The meaning of the aphorism is: "That from which there is the origin and so forth—namely the creation, maintenance, and dissolution—of this world. Accordingly, the Śruti (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1) teaches that Brahman is primarily the instrumental and material cause of the world's origin, maintenance, and dissolution: "That from which indeed these beings are born; that by which, once born, they live; that into which they enter at their departure—that you should seek to know; that is Brahman. There is no contradiction whatsoever in the fact that, having composed the first chapter for the purpose of understanding the supreme Dharma, which is the nature of the knowledge of the Self, he will subsequently explain in the second chapter and following, in due order, the Dharma consisting of ritual purification (*saṃskāra*) and so forth as a subordinate limb (*aṅga*) of that [knowledge]. Moreover, this meaning stated by me is obtained precisely from the natural force (*svārasya*) of the questions and answers in the text. To illustrate: [The text continues with the dialogue.]
When asked about dharma, Manu, declaring Brahman to be the cause of the world, spoke thus in order to say:
"Know that the supreme dharma is the knowledge of the Self."
Because of its preeminence, it was rightly proclaimed in the first chapter;
however, since other forms of dharma are subordinate to it, they are appropriately discussed immediately thereafter.

The word "this" (*idam*) refers to the world, because everything appears before the perceiver (*adhyakṣa*). This world was "consisting of darkness" (*tamobhūtam*), meaning it was situated in, or dissolved within, darkness. By the term "darkness," *prakṛti* is indicated through a metaphorical application of a quality (*guṇavṛttyā*). It is called "darkness" because it is like darkness. Just as objects dissolved in darkness are not manifested by the perceiver, so too the entities dissolved in *prakṛti* are not perceived; this is the connection with the quality [of darkness]. The meaning is that at the time of dissolution, it existed dissolved in *prakṛti* in a subtle form. And thus says the Śruti (RV 8.7.17): "In the beginning, there was darkness, hidden by darkness. Even *prakṛti* existed in an unmanifest state with Brahman as its self. For this very reason, it was "unknowable" (*aprajñātam*) and imperceptible. That which is within the range of perception is called "known" (*prajñāta*) because perception is the best among all means of knowledge; since this was not so, it was "unknowable. It was "without characteristics" (*alakṣaṇam*), meaning it could not be inferred. A "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) is a mark (*liṅga*)—that by which something is characterized—and because such a mark did not exist, it was "without characteristics. It was "inconceivable" (*apratarkyam*), meaning it was impossible to conceive of it then, and because of the absence of gross words capable of denoting it, it was also unknowable even through speech. This very triad of means of knowledge along with inference is accepted by Manu in the twelfth chapter; therefore, it is "unknowable" in the sense that it is beyond the scope of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) and the rest. This has also been explained by Dharaṇīdhara. Nor should it be said that it simply did not exist, for it was established by Śruti at that time. Thus it is heard in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (1.4.7): "This, indeed, was then unmanifest. And the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (6.2.1): "Being alone, my dear, this was in the beginning. This world was indeed Being; the meaning is that it existed as the Self of Brahman. The word "Being" (*sat*) is a synonym for Brahman. For this very reason, it was "as if asleep on all sides. The suffix *-tasi* is used here in the sense of the first case (*prathamārthe*). The meaning is that it was incapable of producing its own effects. || 5 ||
To answer the question "What then happened?", he says:
Then the self-existent Lord, unmanifest, making this manifest—the primordial elements and so forth—appeared, his power having been awakened, the dispeller of darkness. (1.6)

Then the Blessed Self-Existent One, and so forth. "Then," meaning immediately after the conclusion of the dissolution (*pralaya*), the Self-Existent One—the Supreme Self—comes into being; by His own will He assumes a body, but unlike other living beings, His body is not dependent upon karma. And thus says the Śruti (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.2): "He becomes one-fold, He becomes two-fold. The Blessed One is endowed with sovereignty and other such attributes. "Unmanifest" (*avyakta*) means beyond the reach of the external senses; that is to say, He is to be realized through the practice of yoga. "This [universe] beginning with the great elements": the great elements are ether and the rest. By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the principles beginning with *mahat* are also included. Manifesting them while in the state of the unmanifest—first in a subtle form and then in a gross form—[He acts]. "Of perfected vigor" (*vṛttaujas*): "perfected" (*vṛtta*) means unimpeded. For this very reason, in the rule "In the sense of 'vṛtti', 'creation' (*sarga'), and 'extension' (*tāyana'), the suffix *krama* is used" (Pāṇini 1.3.38), Jayāditya has explained that "vṛtti" means non-obstruction. Thus, He is one whose "vigor" (*ojas*)—meaning the power of creation—is "perfected," i.e., unimpeded. "Dispeller of darkness" (*tamonuda*): the impeller of primordial nature (*prakṛti*). As it is said in the Bhagavad Gītā (9.10):
"Under my supervision, Nature brings forth the moving and the unmoving.
Thus [it is said]. "Prādurāsīt" means he became manifest; "tamonudaḥ" means the destroyer of the state of dissolution—so say Medhātithi and Govindarāja. (6)
He who is beyond the grasp of the senses, subtle, unmanifest, eternal, consisting of all beings, and inconceivable—he himself manifested forth. 1.7.

"Who is he?"—by these two pronouns (*sarvanāman*), he points to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) as renowned throughout all the worlds, the Vedas, the Purāṇas, the Itihāsas, and so forth. "Perceptible by that which transcends the senses": since it exists beyond the senses, it is "transcendental" (*atīndriya*); the meaning is that it is to be grasped by the mind (*manas*). As Vyāsa said:
"He is not to be grasped by the eye, nor even by the other remaining senses;
however, by the mind with effort, He is grasped by those who perceive the subtle."

Subtle (*sūkṣma*), it is beyond the range of the external senses. Unmanifest (*avyakta*), it is devoid of manifest parts (*vyakti*). Eternal (*sanātana*), it is permanent. Consisting of all beings (*sarvabhūtamaya*), it is the self of all beings (*sarvabhūtātmā*). For this very reason, it is inconceivable (*acintya*), impossible to be delimited by measure. It itself arose (*udbabau*)—it became manifest—in the form of effects such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest. The root *bhāti* preceded by the prefix *ut* denotes manifestation, since verbal roots have multiple meanings. (1.7)
Desiring to emit various creatures from his own body, he first created the waters alone; into them he cast the seed. (1.8)

"He meditated" (*so ’bhidhyāya*): that Supreme Self (*paramātman*), desiring to emit various kinds of creatures, meditated; by mere meditation—thinking "Let the waters be born"—He created the waters themselves. For one who asserts that creation is preceded by meditation, the position that primordial matter (*prakṛti*) alone, being insentient and independent, undergoes transformation, is not accepted; rather, it appears that the very conclusion of the Tri-daṇḍin Vedānta—that Brahman alone, in the form of unmanifest power (*avyākṛta-śakti*), is the cause of the world—is intended. Thus says the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (6.2.3): "It [Brahman] thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate. Therefore, the author of the Śārīraka-sūtras, Vyāsa, established the final doctrine: "On account of seeing, [the cause] is not that which is not based on scripture" (Br. Sū. 1.1.5). The meaning of the sūtra is: because of the hearing of "seeing" (*īkṣati*), the Pradhāna is not the cause of the world; "not based on scripture" (*aśabdam*) means that for which there is no scriptural word (*śabda*) or revelation (*śruti*). In the Bhagavad-Bhāskara’s Vedānta system, the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) itself is the primordial matter (*prakṛti*), and that alone is His body. By the term "unmanifest," the five elements, the organs of perception, the organs of action, the vital breaths, the mind, karma, ignorance (*avidyā*), and latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are designated as existing in a subtle form as power (*śakti*). Because both difference and non-difference between the unmanifest and Brahman are admitted, the non-duality of Brahman (*brahmādvaita*) is maintained, and it is thus logically consistent that Brahman transforms into the form of the world through its aspect as power. "In the beginning" (*ādau*) means prior to the creation of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), which is its own effect. This creation of the waters is to be understood as proceeding through the sequence of the Great Principle (*mahat*), the Ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), because of the previous mention in verse 1.6 of "manifesting the great elements, etc.," and because the subsequent creation of the Great Principle and so forth will be described later. He placed the seed—the form of power—within those waters. (1.8)
That egg became golden, possessing a radiance equal to the thousand-rayed sun;
within it was born Brahmā himself, the grandfather of all the worlds.

"That egg became golden" (1.9). By the will of the Supreme Lord, that seed became a golden egg (*haimam aṇḍam*). It is "golden" (*haima*) because of its association with the quality of purity, but it is not literally made of gold, since it will be stated later that the earth was fashioned from one of its shells. Furthermore, the metaphorical designation is used because the earth's golden nature is perceived through direct observation. The "thousand-rayed one" is the sun; [the egg] possessed a luster equal to his. Within that egg, Hiraṇyagarbha was born. Having entered the individual soul (*jīva*) limited by the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*) of him who, in a previous birth, had performed the worship of the Supreme Lord with the contemplation of both difference and non-difference—thinking, "I am Hiraṇyagarbha"—the Supreme Self himself manifested in the form of Hiraṇyagarbha. He is the grandfather and progenitor of all worlds; or rather, "Grandfather of All Worlds" (*sarvaloka-pitāmaha*) is his name. (1.9)
Now, by providing an etymological explanation of the word *Nārāyaṇa* well-known in the scriptures, he confirms the very point already stated:
"Water is called *nārāḥ*; water, indeed, is the offspring of *nara*.
Since that [water] was his primordial abode (*ayana*), for that reason he is remembered as *Nārāyaṇa*. (1.10)

"Water is called *nārāḥ*, etc. Water is expressed by the word *nārāḥ*. Since the word *nārāḥ* is not well-known in the sense of "water," he says [the following] for that purpose: because those [waters] are the sons, i.e., the offspring (*apatya*), of the Supreme Self known as *Nara*. The suffix *aṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.3.120 (*asyedam*). Although the suffix *ṅīp* would have been required once *aṇ* is applied, nevertheless, because the usage of even Vedic grammatical rules is found in the Smṛtis—according to the principle "all rules are optional in the Veda" (Pariśiṣṭa 26)—there is optionally the suffix *ṅīp*. In the case where *ṅīp* is absent, the form *nārāḥ* is established by applying the general suffix *ṭāp*. It is recorded in the Āgamas that this [Supreme Self], who existed previously in the form of Brahmā, had water as his *ayana* (course or support), and thus he is *Nārāyaṇa*. Govindarāja, however, reads and explains it as "āpo nārāḥ" [sic], stating that when *nārāyaṇa* is reached, the form *nārāyaṇa* arises through lengthening according to Pāṇini 6.3.137 (*anyeṣām api dṛśyate*). Others, however, read "āpo nārāḥ."
That cause which is unmanifest, eternal, and composed of both being and non-being—from that he was emitted; that Puruṣa is celebrated in the world as Brahmā. 1.11.

"That which is the unmanifest cause"—by the two pronouns "that" and "which," he points to the Supreme Self, who is well-known in all the worlds, the Vedas, and so forth. It is the "cause" of all things that have an origin. It is "unmanifest" (avyakta), being beyond the range of the external senses. It is "eternal," being devoid of birth and destruction. Because it is established by the Vedānta, its nature is existent; yet, because it is not an object of perception and other such means of knowledge, its nature appears as if non-existent. Alternatively, "existence" refers to the collection of all existing things, and "non-existence" is that which constitutes their very self. Thus says the Śruti (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7): "All this has that as its self. "Created by Him," meaning produced by Him—that Puruṣa is celebrated everywhere as Brahman. (1.11)
Having dwelt within that egg for a full year, the Blessed One himself,
through his own meditative concentration, split that egg in two.

"In that egg, that Blessed One," and so forth. In that aforementioned egg, that Brahmā, having dwelt for a year according to the measurement of time to be described for Brahmā, made that egg split into two halves by the mere power of his own meditation, thinking, "May the egg become divided in two by itself. (1.12)
From those two fragments, he fashioned heaven and earth;
in between, the intermediate space, the eight directions, and the eternal abode of the waters.

"By those two shells," and so forth. A *śakala* is a fragment; by means of those two egg-shells, he fashioned above [the shell] the sky, the world of *svar*, and below the world of *bhūr*; between the two, the ether together with the directions—including the intermediate directions—and the stable abode of the waters known as the ocean. (1.13)
Now, in order to demonstrate that the creation of the world proceeds precisely through the sequence beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), he describes each stage of that creation:
"And from the Self alone, he drew forth the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent;
and from the mind, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), the ruler who is the conceiving subject. (1.14)

"From himself indeed he drew forth," and so on. Brahmā drew forth the mind from himself—that is, from the Supreme Self—in that form. This is because, according to the Vedānta philosophy, the mind was produced from the Supreme Self alone in the form of Brahmā, and the creation of the mind proceeds from the Supreme Self alone, not from *pradhāna* (primordial matter). Thus says the Śruti (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.3): "From this [Self] are born breath, mind, and all the senses;
ether, air, light, water, and the earth which supports the universe."

The mind (manas) exists because it is established by scripture and because its existence is inferred from the fact that cognitions do not arise simultaneously; yet, because it is not directly perceived, it is as if non-existent. Prior to this is the principle of ego (ahaṃkāra-tattva), which is endowed with the effect called self-conceit (abhimāna)—the notion "I am"—and is the Lord capable of performing its own functions through its instruments. 1.14.
And [he perceives] the Self as truly great, as well as all the five sense organs, which consist of the three qualities and are the perceivers of objects, [all of which he views] gradually. 1.15.

"Indeed, the Great Self," and so forth. "The Great" refers to the principle known as *mahat*, which was extracted from the Supreme Self together with *prakṛti* in the form of unmanifest power (*avyākṛta-śakti*) prior to *ahaṃkāra*. Because they have arisen from the Self, or because they are beneficial to the Self, all those things already mentioned and those yet to be mentioned are produced; they are all endowed with the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and they are the perceivers of the objects—sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. These include, in due order, the five sense organs (*buddhīndriya*) beginning with the ear, as established in the Vedānta and to be discussed in the second chapter; by the word "and" (*ca*), the five organs of action (*karmendriya*) beginning with the feet are included; and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) beginning with sound were likewise produced.

But was it not previously stated that because creation is described as being preceded by meditation (*abhidhyāna*), the view of Manu is indeed identical to the established doctrine of the Vedānta? That [previous statement] does not now hold together. For at present, creation is described according to the sequence beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*), whereas in the Vedāntic system, creation from the Supreme Self alone is said to proceed through the sequence beginning with space (*ākāśa*). Thus, the Taittirīya Upaniṣad (2.1.1) states: "From this very Self, space was produced; from space, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth."

It is said: those who know the system explain that in the philosophy of the venerable Bhāskara, it is accepted that creation proceeds from *prakṛti* through the sequence beginning with the *mahat*. *Prakṛti* is held to be the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) itself; its state of being oriented toward creation—consisting in its connection with the initial moment of creation—is precisely the principle of *mahat*. Then, the unmanifest’s connection with the moment of the creative vision consisting of the conceit "May I become many" is the principle of *ahaṃkāra*. From that, the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*)—ether and the rest—are produced in succession; and from those very [subtle elements], the five gross elements are produced. Since the emergence of effects is observed to follow the sequence of the subtle and the gross, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, even though the qualities (*guṇas*) of the unmanifest are *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, it is logical that all things consist of the three *guṇas*. Or, let the primordial *prakṛti* be simply the state of equilibrium among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; and let the *mahat*, *ahaṃkāra*, and *tanmātras* be indeed distinct principles (*tattvas*). Nevertheless, the inherent intention of Manu is that *prakṛti* is non-different from Brahman, since he will say (12.91): [text follows].
"In all beings one sees oneself, and in oneself all beings.
Likewise (12.125):
"Thus, he who by means of his own self perceives the Self in all beings..."
Having attained universal equanimity, he follows Brahman to the supreme state. Thus [it is said].
Having combined the subtle components of those six [great elements], each possessing immeasurable power, with their own respective portions, he fashioned all beings.

"But their subtle components," and so forth. Having joined those subtle components of the six previously mentioned—the ego (ahaṃkāra) and the subtle elements (tanmātra)—with the individual measures (ātmamātrā) within their own respective transformations, the Supreme Self fashioned all beings, such as humans, animals, and stationary objects. In that process, the transformation of the subtle elements is the five gross elements, and that of the ego is the sense organs. Once the earth and other elements have evolved into the form of bodies, the joining of the subtle elements and the ego is performed; thus occurs the creation of the entire aggregate of effects. For this very reason, they are said to possess "immeasurable luster" (amitaujas), being endowed with supreme vigor through the fashioning of infinite effects. (1.16)
The six subtle components of form resort to this [body];
therefore, the wise call that form of his "the body" (śarīra). 1.17

Regarding the passage beginning with "the subtle parts of the form," etc.: because the *mūrti* is the body, its constituent parts are subtle, consisting of the *tanmātras*, the *ahaṃkāra*, and so forth—these six [categories] serve as the substratum for the effects of that Brahman together with *prakṛti*, namely the elements (*bhūtas*) which will be described hereafter, and the sense organs (*indriyas*) mentioned previously; for the elements arise from the *tanmātras*, and the sense organs arise from the *ahaṃkāra*. Thus they recite (Sāṃkhya Kārikā 22): "From *prakṛti* arises the Great One (*mahat*); from that, the *ahaṃkāra*; and from that, the group of sixteen."
From those five among the sixteen, the five gross elements arise.

Therefore, that form which belongs to that Brahman—its very nature—which has thus evolved and is endowed with the senses and so forth, people call the "body" (śarīra). By this etymological definition of the body as "that which the six [elements] resort to," the previously stated order of evolution is further confirmed. (1.17)
Then the great elements, together with their functions, enter that immutable creator of all beings, along with the mind and its subtle components. 1.18.

“They enter that, O Bhūtas,” and so forth. In the preceding verse, the word *tasya* (of that) referred to Brahman; here, that same Brahman is referred to by the pronoun *tat*. That Brahman, abiding in the form of the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*) such as sound and the rest, enters the great elements (*mahābhūtas*)—namely ether and the others—and arises from them. Together with their functions (*karmas*), which are their own effects: therein, the function of ether is to provide space; that of air is expansion, in the form of arrangement; that of fire is digestion; that of water is cohesion, in the form of congealing; and that of earth is support. Abiding in the form of ego (*ahaṃkāra*), Brahman enters the mind (*manas*). The meaning is that [Brahman] arises from ego. By its parts—which are its own effects consisting of pure and impure volitions, pleasure, pain, and so forth, which are subtle and beyond the range of the external senses—it is the creator of all beings, the cause of the origin of everything, because the world originates from the pure and impure actions produced by the mind. It is imperishable (*avyaya*), indestructible. (1.18)
From the subtle constituent elements of form of these seven immensely powerful beings, this perishable world arises from the imperishable.

"Of these seven," and so forth. Because these seven—namely the Great Principle (mahat), ego-consciousness (ahaṃkāra), and the subtle elements (tanmātra)—have arisen from the Person, the Self (ātman), and because they are the objects of perception for that Person, this perishable world arises from those subtle material portions (mūrtimātrāḥ) which constitute the parts that produce bodies for those Persons of great power who are vigorous in accomplishing their own effects. Whatever effect is non-perishable, that [effect] is perishable and dissolves back into its own cause; however, the cause is stable relative to the effect. This restatement is intended to demonstrate that the Supreme Cause, Brahman, is eternal and worthy of worship. 1.19.
Each subsequent one among these acquires the quality of each preceding one;
whichever among them occupies which position, it is traditionally held to possess that many qualities. (1.20)

“Of these, however, each subsequent one acquires the quality of each preceding one,” and so forth. The word “of these” (*eṣām*) refers back to the elements (*bhūtāni*) mentioned in the previous verse (1.18): “The elements enter into that. Their order of origination—beginning with ether (*ākāśa*)—as well as their possession of qualities such as sound, will be explained later. Among them, each subsequent element, beginning with air (*vāyu*), acquires the quality of each preceding one, beginning with ether, such as sound and so on. He clarifies this very point with the words “whichever... whichever”: among these, whichever occupies a particular position—as indicated by the ordinal number formed according to Pāṇini 5.2.53 (*vator ithuk*)—that element, being the second and so on, is remembered by Manu and others to possess double, triple, and so forth, the qualities [of its predecessors]. By this, the following is stated: sound is the quality of ether; sound and touch of air; sound, touch, and form of fire; sound, touch, form, and taste of water; and sound, touch, form, taste, and smell of earth. Although the form *ādyādyasya* would have been expected through reduplication according to Pāṇini 8.1.4 (*nityavīpsayoḥ*), nevertheless, because the Smṛtis share the same domain as Vedic meters (*chandas*), the case-ending of the first *ādyasya* is elided according to Pāṇini 7.1.39 (*supāṃ suluk*), thereby establishing the form *ādyādyasya*. 1.20.
But he, at the beginning, fashioned the individual names and actions of all beings, as well as their distinct social orders, from the words of the Veda itself.

"But he [created] the names of all," and so forth. That Supreme Self, existing in the form of Hiraṇyagarbha, created the names of all things—the name "cow" for the bovine species, "horse" for the equine species—and their respective functions, such as Vedic study for the Brāhmaṇa and the protection of subjects for the Kṣatriya. Having understood these individually from the very words of the Veda at the beginning of creation in a previous Kalpa, He fashioned them. Even by the venerable Vyāsa, in the Vedānta inquiry (*Vedamīmāṃsā*), the creation of the world was demonstrated as being preceded by the Veda. Thus, the *Śārīraka-sūtra* (1.3.28) states: "If it be argued that there is a contradiction because of the word [of the Veda], no, because of its origin from Him, according to both perception and inference. The meaning of this is as follows: If it be argued that there would be a contradiction regarding the corporeal nature of deities in the case of Vedic words like "Vasu" which denote deities—since that would entail the consequence of the Veda having a beginning—[the reply is] there is no contradiction. Why? Because of the very word "from Him" (*ataḥ*); because of the origin of the world, the mass of the Vedas remains in the Supreme Self in a subtle form even at the time of dissolution. At the beginning of this Kalpa, it manifests in the mind of Hiraṇyagarbha—the first embodied form of the Supreme Self—without undergoing any change of state, just as one does upon waking from sleep. By means of that [Veda], which stands in the place of a lamp, He creates the world, divided into gods, humans, animals, and so forth, which constitutes the objects of denotation. How is this known? "By perception and inference"; the meaning is: by Śruti and Smṛti. Śruti is "perception" because it is independent; Smṛti is "inference" because it depends on an inferred Śruti. And thus says the Śruti:

With the word *eta* (come), Prajāpati created the gods; with *asṛgram* (they have flowed forth), human beings; with *indavaḥ* (drops), the ancestors; with *tiraḥpavitram* (through the filter), the cups; with *āśavaḥ* (swift ones), the hymn of praise (*stotra*); with *viśvāni* (all things), the recitation (*śastra*); and with *abhi saubhaga* (toward good fortune), other creatures.

As for the traditional teaching, however, such as "He [gave] names to all," it was indeed composed by Manu and others. And as for the phrase "and separately the established forms," he created worldly arrangements according to their respective divisions, such as the potter’s making of pots and the weaver’s making of cloth. 1.21.
The Lord created the gods whose nature is action, as well as living beings;
he also created the subtle host of the Sādhyas and the eternal sacrifice.

"And of the gods whose nature is action," and so forth. He, Brahmā, created the host of gods: those beings whose very selves—that is, their inherent nature—are their actions, such as Indra and the others; and of non-beings, such as the pressing-stones and other divine objects; and of the Sādhyas, a specific class of gods; and the sacrifice, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others, which is eternal because it is inferred even in other Kalpas. The Sādhyas are mentioned separately from the general "host of gods" because of their subtlety. (1.22)
From fire, wind, and the sun, he milked forth the threefold eternal Brahman—
characterized as the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman— for the sake of accomplishing sacrifice.

"From fire, wind, and the sun," and so forth. Brahmā drew forth from fire, wind, and the sun the three Vedas known as Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman. This is eternal and constant. It is precisely the position that the Vedas are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*) that is intended by Manu. Those very Vedas which existed in the previous *kalpa* were present in the memory of Brahmā—the omniscient embodiment of the Supreme Self—and at the beginning of the current *kalpa*, he drew them forth from fire, wind, and the sun. This scriptural meaning is not to be doubted; for thus says the Śruti: "The Ṛgveda from Agni, the Yajurveda from Vāyu, and the Sāmaveda from Āditya. Because the root *duh* (to milk) signifies drawing forth, fire, wind, and the sun do not function here as "unspecified objects" (*akathita-karman*), but rather as the "ablative source" (*apādāna*). Since sacrifices are accomplished through the three Vedas, the verb *duh* is used figuratively to denote "drawing forth" in order to show the manifestation of the Vedas—which already exist like milk in a full udder—for the sake of the success of sacrifice. (1.23)
Time and the divisions of time, as well as the lunar mansions and the planets;
the rivers, the oceans, and the mountains; and the level and uneven terrains.

“Time, the divisions of time,” and so forth. Here, the verb “he created,” which occurs in the following verse, is connected [to these objects]. Time, which consists of a collection of activities such as those of the sun and other celestial bodies; the divisions of time, such as months, seasons, and solstices; the constellations, beginning with Kṛttikā; the planets, beginning with the Sun; the rivers, that is, streams; the oceans, that is, seas; the mountains, that is, peaks; the level places, that is, even terrains; and the uneven places, consisting of high and low ground. (1.24)
Desiring to bring forth these creatures at the beginning of creation, he [created] austerity, speech, pleasure, desire, and anger, as well as this very process of creation. || 1.25 ||

"Asceticism, speech," and so forth. He created asceticism (tapas), such as the *prājāpatya* penance; speech (vāc), which is the organ of voice; delight (rati), which is the satisfaction of the mind; desire (kāma), which is longing; and anger (krodha), which is a modification of the mind. He brought forth this creation (*sṛṣṭi*)—namely, that which is mentioned in this verse and that mentioned in the preceding verse. It is called "creation" because it is created (*sṛjyate*); the suffix *ktin* is used here in the passive sense. Desiring to bring these creatures (*prajā*) about to be described, beginning with the gods, he performed this act. || 1.25 ||
For the sake of distinguishing between karmas, he separated dharma and adharma;
and he joined these creatures with pairs of opposites, such as pleasure and pain.

"And of actions" (karmaṇām): Dharma consists of sacrifice and so forth, and that is to be performed; adharma consists of the killing of Brahmins and so forth, and that is not to be performed. Thus, for the sake of distinguishing between actions, he "discriminated" (vyavecayat)—that is, he declared them separately—as dharma and adharma. The fruit of dharma is happiness; the fruit of adharma is suffering. By means of the pairs of opposites (dvandva) consisting of the fruits of dharma and adharma—such as pleasure and pain, which are mutually contradictory—he joined these creatures. By the inclusion of the word "etc. (ādi), [the pairs] such as desire and anger, attachment and aversion, hunger and thirst, grief and delusion, and so forth, are also included. (1.26)
The minute, perishable particles which are said to constitute the five elements—along with these, all this [universe] comes into being in successive order. (1.27)

"Subtle particles (aṇvyo mātrāḥ)": those which are the five subtle elements (tanmātras) of the five great elements (mahābhūtas), which are minute, subject to destruction, and transformable into the form of the five great elements—with these, all this that has been said and will be said arises. "Successively" means in order: from the subtle to the gross, and from the gross to the grosser. By this, [the author], wishing to dispel the doubt that the mental creation of the omnipotent Brahman might sometimes be independent of the [evolutive] principles (tattvas), has reminded us of what was stated previously—that this creation proceeds through those very principles. (1.27)
Whatever task the Lord first appointed him to perform,
that very same task he himself undertook again and again as he was being created.

Regarding the phrase "which [he assigned] to action": that particular species—such as a tiger or the like—which Prajāpati assigned at the beginning of creation to a specific activity, such as the killing of deer, performed that very same action again and again as it was being created, under the influence of its own past karma. By this, it is shown that Prajāpati’s creation of superior and inferior species depends upon the karma of living beings and is not governed by passion or hatred. For this very reason, he will say later (1.41): "The stationary and moving world was created according to their karma through the power of austerity. || 1.28 ||
He elaborates on this very point:
"The violent and the non-violent, the mild and the cruel, merit and demerit, truth and falsehood—whatever each deposited at the beginning of creation, that entered into him of its own accord. (1.29)

"Violent and non-violent," and so forth. Violent action (*hiṃsra*) is that of lions and the like, such as the killing of elephants; non-violent (*ahiṃsra*) is that of deer and the like. Mild (*mṛdu*), characterized by compassion, is that of Brahmins and the like; cruel (*krūra*) is that of Kṣatriyas and the like. Righteousness (*dharma*) is, for example, the service to one's teacher and so forth for a celibate student (*brahmacārin*); unrighteousness (*adharma*) is, for example, the consumption of meat and indulgence in sexual intercourse for that same person. Truth (*ṛta*) is the real; that belongs mostly to the gods. Untruth (*anṛta*) is the unreal; that also belongs mostly to humans. Thus says the Śruti: "The gods are speakers of truth, humans are speakers of untruth. Among these, whatever action Prajāpati assigned to each at the beginning of creation, even after the time of creation, he himself performed that very same action due to the power of his prior unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). (1.29)
Regarding this, he states an illustration:
"Just as the seasons themselves, at the change of seasons, assume their own respective characteristics, so too do embodied beings [assume] their respective actions. (1.30)

"Just as the seasons," etc. Just as the seasons, such as spring and so forth, and their characteristic signs, such as mango blossoms and the like, arrive of their own accord at the turn of the season when it is time for their respective effects, so too do the embodied beings [attain] their actions, such as violence and so forth. (1.30)
For the sake of the increase of the worlds, he brought forth from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.

"Of the worlds," etc. For the sake of the abundance of the worlds beginning with *bhūr*, He fashioned from His mouth, arms, thighs, and feet the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras respectively. When an oblation is cast into the fire by the Brāhmaṇas and others in the evening and morning, it reaches the Sun; from the Sun comes rain; from rain, food; and from food, the abundance of progeny. And He will say: "The oblation properly cast into the fire [reaches] the Sun," and so forth (3.76). Furthermore, the creation of the Brāhmaṇas and others from the mouth and other limbs was effected through divine power. A Brāhmaṇa is not to be doubted, because this is established by the Śruti. Thus says the Śruti: "The Brāhmaṇa was His mouth," and so forth (RV 8.4.19). 1.31.
Dividing his own body into two parts, he became a man with one half and a woman with the other; in her, the Lord created Virāj.

"Having divided into two" means that Brahmā, having split his own body into two parts, created a woman from one half; through her, by means of sexual union, he produced the person known as Virāj. And the Śruti (RV 8.4.17) says: "From that, Virāj was born. (1.32)
O best of the twice-born, know me to be that Virāj, the Supreme Person himself, whom he created after performing austerities; I am the creator of all this.

"Having performed austerities... [means: O best of the twice-born, know me—that whom the Virāj, having stored up his austerity, created—to be Manu, the creator of this entire world. By this, he has declared the excellence of his own birth and the preeminence of his power, for the sake of inspiring confidence in the people. 1.33.
Desiring to create offspring, I performed most difficult austerities and first created ten great seers as the lords of creatures.
"I am. Desiring to create progeny, I performed most difficult austerities and first created the ten Prajāpatis, since even by them progeny was to be created. (1.34)
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada. || 1.35 ||
"Marīci," and so forth; these ten Prajāpatis have been indicated by name. (1.35)
These [Manus], possessing great splendor, created seven other Manus,
as well as the gods, the classes of gods, and the great seers of immeasurable power.

"These Manus... [The commentary explains: These ten, beginning with Marīci, possessed great splendor—that is, they were of immense luster—and they created other seven Manus of immeasurable brilliance, as well as the gods created by Brahmā, the celestial abodes such as heaven, and the great seers (*maharṣi*). This word "Manu" denotes an office. Among the fourteen *manvantaras*, whichever one has the authority for creation and so forth in a particular period is designated as "Manu" in that *manvantara* by names such as Svāyaṃbhuva, Ārociṣa, and others. (1.36)
And [he saw] the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas; the gandharvas, apsarases, and asuras;
the nāgas, sarpas, and suparṇas; and the various hosts of the ancestors (pitṛs). || 1.37 ||

Regarding the term *yakṣarakṣa*: the phrase "he created these" (*ete ’sṛjat*) from the preceding verse is to be supplied here and in the two subsequent verses. *Yakṣas* refers to Vaiśravaṇa and his followers. *Rākṣasas* refers to Rāvaṇa and others. *Piśācas* are inferior to them, dwelling in impure regions and windy places. *Gandharvas* are Citraratha and others. *Apsarases* are Urvaśī and others. *Asuras* are Garuḍa and others. *Nāgas* are Vāsuki and others. *Sarpas* (snakes) are inferior to those, such as the *alagarda* and so forth. *Suparṇas* are Garuḍa and others. The "host" (*gaṇa*) of the *Pitṛs* (ancestors), such as the Ājyapās and others, refers to their collective assembly. The distinctions among these are well-known from the *Itihāsas* and other traditional sources; they are not objects of direct perception (*adhyakṣa*) or other ordinary means of knowledge. (1.37)
Lightnings, thunderbolts, and clouds; red-hued portents and Indra’s bows; meteors, atmospheric crashes, and comets; and celestial lights of various kinds.

"Lightning," etc. Lightning (*vidyut*) is the elongated light seen in the clouds. That light which issues from the cloud itself and destroys trees and other things is the thunderbolt (*aśani*). Clouds are well known. The red, staff-shaped [light] is the rainbow (*indradhanus*), that very light of various colors seen in the sky. A meteor (*ulkā*) is a light shaped like a streak falling from the atmosphere. A thunderclap (*nirghāta*) is an ominous sound occurring on the earth or in the atmosphere. Comets (*ketavaḥ*) are crested lights appearing as portents. Other lights are the various kinds such as Dhruva, Agastya, and so forth. (1.38)
Kinnaras, monkeys, fish, and various birds;
domestic animals, wild beasts, humans, and fanged predators.

Regarding "kinnaras": kinnaras are a class of divine beings with the faces of horses and the bodies of humans. Monkeys are well known. Fish are the rohita and other such species. Birds are winged creatures. Domestic animals are cows and the like. Wild beasts are deer and the like. Beasts of prey are lions and the like. "Those with two rows of teeth" refers to those who possess two sets of teeth, one upper and one lower. (1.39)
And worms, insects, and moths; lice, flies, and bedbugs; all gadflies and mosquitoes; and various kinds of stationary beings. 1.40.

Regarding the phrase "worms, insects," etc.: insects (*kīṭāḥ*) are slightly larger than worms (*kṛmayaḥ*). Moths (*pataṅgāḥ*) are locusts. Lice and so forth are well known. The singular collective form is used according to Pāṇini 2.4.8, *kṣudrajantavaḥ*. The stationary (*sthāvaram*) consists of various types, distinguished as trees, creepers, and so on. || 1.40 ||
Thus, by my command, all this— both the stationary and the moving— was created by those high-souled ones through the power of their asceticism, each according to their own karma.

"Thus by these": "thus" means in the manner described; by these [sages] beginning with Marīci, all this—both the stationary and the moving—was created. "According to action" means in accordance with whatever kind of action belongs to a particular being, the production of that being in the wombs of gods, humans, animals, and so forth, occurred "by my direction," that is, by my command. "By the power of austerity" means having performed great austerity. This demonstrates that all sovereignty is dependent upon austerity. (1.41)
But whatever kind of karma is proclaimed here for these beings,
that I shall describe to you accordingly, as well as the sequence of their births.

"Of whom," and so forth. Furthermore, I shall describe to you exactly what kind of karma has been taught here in this cycle of existence by the former teachers—for example: "Plants, which are endowed with many flowers and fruits, end with the ripening of their fruit" (1.46)—as well as the duties such as Vedic study for the Brahmins and other castes, and the sequence of birth and so forth. || 1.42 ||
Domestic animals and wild beasts, as well as fanged predators, and *rakṣas* and *piśācas*, and humans—these are all born from the womb. (1.43)

"And the beasts. *Jarāyu* is the skin that covers the embryo; therein humans and others appear, and subsequently they are born released from it. The sequence of birth for these very beings has been previously stated and explained. The word *daccha*, which has the same meaning as the word *danta*, exists immediately after *prakṛti*; this is its form in the nominative plural: *ubhayatodataḥ*. 1.43.
Birds born from eggs, snakes, crocodiles, fish, and tortoises—whatever other such creatures there are, whether terrestrial or aquatic. (1.44)

"Oviparous" refers to birds; their order of birth is that they first exist as eggs and are born from them thereafter. "Aquatic reptiles" refers to crocodiles and *kumbhīras*. "Terrestrial" refers to chameleons and the like. "Aqueous" refers to conchs and the like. || 1.44 ||
Gnats, mosquitoes, lice, flies, and bedbugs are born from moisture;
whatever else is of this kind arises from heat.

Regarding the term "born from moisture" (*svedaja*): moisture (*sveda*) is the dampening of earthly substances through heat; from that, gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like are born. Furthermore, from heat—which is a cause of moisture—there are also born other creatures similar to gadflies and the like, such as gnats and ants. || 1.45 ||
All stationary beings are born from sprouts, growing from seeds or stems;
they are plants that perish after the ripening of their fruit and are endowed with many flowers and fruits. (1.46)

Regarding the term *udbhijjāḥ*: *udbhid* means "breaking forth" (*udbhedana*), derived from the root with the suffix *kvip* in the sense of an action (*bhāve*). Those which are born by breaking through the seed and the earth upwards are called *udbhijjāḥ*, namely trees. These are of two kinds: some are born from the seed alone, while others, such as branches planted from a stem, attain the state of a tree. Now, their respective karmas are described—[the category of] *oṣadhyaḥ*. *Oṣadhyaḥ* refers to rice, barley, and so forth; they perish only upon the ripening of their fruit and are endowed with many flowers and fruits. From the word *oṣadhi* itself, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule “*kṛdikārādaktinaḥ*” (Pāṇini 4.1.45), resulting in the form *oṣadhyaḥ*. (1.46)
Those which bear fruit without flowers are known as *vanaspatis*;
those which bear both flowers and fruit are known as *vṛkṣas*. || 1.47 ||

Regarding the phrase "without flowers": this verse does not aim to establish a relationship between a name and its referent, as is the case with a lexicon (*abhidhānakośa*), because such a topic is not under discussion here. Rather, since "the sequence of birth" (1.42) was previously introduced, this is stated for that purpose. For those which are forest trees (*vanaspati*), the production of fruit occurs even without flowers; for others, however, flowers are produced first, and from them the fruits arise. Thus, trees are of both types. The suffix *tasi* is used after a word ending in the nominative case. (1.47)

Furthermore, there are various kinds of shrubs and clusters, as well as species of grasses; likewise, there are those that grow from seeds or from stems, as well as spreading creepers and climbing vines.

Regarding the phrase *gucchagulmam tu*: where a cluster of creepers arises from the very root and does not have distinct trunks, those are *gucchāḥ*, such as the *mallikā* and others. *Gulmāḥ* are those that grow from a single root in a mass, such as reeds (*śara*) and sugarcanes (*ikṣu*). The various kinds of grasses are *ulapā* and so forth. *Pratānāḥ* are those provided with tendrils, such as cucumbers (*trapuṣa*) and bottle gourds (*alābu*). *Vallayaḥ* are those like *guḍūcī* and others which climb from the ground to a tree. These too are produced from seeds or from cuttings (*kāṇḍa*). The neuter gender is used according to Pāṇini 1.2.69: "A neuter [word] followed by a non-neuter [word] may optionally become singular. || 1.48 ||
Enveloped by manifold darkness caused by their past actions,
these beings possess internal consciousness and are endowed with pleasure and pain.

Regarding the phrase "by tamas": these trees and other such beings are pervaded by the quality of *tamas*, which results in manifold suffering and is caused by unrighteous action (*adharma-karma*); thus, they possess consciousness only internally. Although all of them indeed perceive within, they are designated in that way because they lack external activities and other such effects. For this very reason, they are endowed with pleasure and pain; since the quality of *sattva* is also present, a slight trace of pleasure sometimes arises for them through contact with water produced by the clouds. (1.49)
These destinies, beginning with that of Brahmā, are declared to end here within this terrible cycle of existence for living beings, which is constantly and perpetually moving.

"Ending with this": the destinies and births, beginning with Brahmā and ending with the stationary beings, have been described; [destinies] which, in the continuous succession of birth and death of living beings—the knowers of the field (kṣetrajña)—are terrifying due to their abundance of suffering and are ever-perishing. (1.50)
Having thus described creation, he speaks of the state of dissolution:
"Having thus created all this and me as well, he of inconceivable prowess again withdrew into himself, subduing time with time. (1.51)

"Thus all": in this manner, having created this entire world of the moving and the stationary, that Prajāpati, whose peace is inconceivable, brought about his own disappearance within himself in the form of casting off the body. The meaning is that, destroying the period of creation by means of the period of dissolution, he repeatedly effects creation and dissolution according to the karma of living beings.
He states the reason for this:
"When that god is awake, then this world moves;
when he sleeps, his self being at peace, then everything closes its eyes. (1.52)

Regarding the phrase "when": when that Prajāpati is awake—that is, when he desires creation and maintenance—then this world obtains its activities such as inhalation, exhalation, and eating. When he sleeps—that is, when his desire has ceased, his self is at peace, and his mind is intent on withdrawal—then this world dissolves.

He clarifies what was previously stated: "But when that [Self] is well-established in its own state, embodied beings whose nature is action desist from their own actions, and the mind falls into exhaustion. (1.53)

"In him he sleeps": when that Prajāpati has ceased from desire and is established in well-being, with the activities of body and mind withdrawn, the knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas), who have obtained bodies through their karma, desist from their respective actions such as the assumption of bodies; the mind, together with all the senses, becomes devoid of its functions. 1.53.
Now he describes the great dissolution:
"But when they dissolve simultaneously into that Great Self, then this Self of all beings sleeps happily and at peace. (1.54)

Regarding the phrase "simultaneously" (*yugapat*): when all beings go to dissolution within that Supreme Self at one and the same time, then this Self of all beings, being *nirvṛta*—meaning its activities of waking and dreaming have ceased—sleeps happily, as if in deep sleep (*suṣupta*). Although there is no sleeping in the Supreme Self, whose nature is eternal knowledge and bliss, nevertheless, this [state] is metaphorically attributed to it as a property of the individual soul (*jīva*). (1.54)
Now, in connection with the topic of dissolution, he describes the departure of the individual soul (*jīva*) in two verses:
"Having resorted to this darkness (*tamas*), the soul remains for a long time endowed with its senses;
yet it does not perform its own functions, and then it departs from the body. (1.55)

"This is darkness" means that this *jīva*, having reached the state of darkness—the cessation of knowledge—remains for a long time accompanied by the senses and other faculties. It does not perform its own functions, such as inhalation and exhalation; at that time, it departs from the previous body in its material form and goes elsewhere. Since the *jīva* is delimited by the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), its departure is also logically established. Thus it is said in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* (4.4.2): "As he departs, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) departs after him; as the vital breath departs, all the vital breaths depart after it. Here, "vital breaths" refers to the senses. 1.55
To the question "When does it take on another body?", he says: "When, having become minute in size, it enters—united with it—the seed, whether stationary or moving, then it abandons its form. (1.56)

Regarding the phrase "consisting of atoms" (*aṇumātrika*): he whose "atoms" (*mātrā*) are the subtle bodies (*puryaṣṭaka*) is "one consisting of atoms. By the word *puryaṣṭaka*, the eight [constituents] beginning with the elements are denoted. As it was said by Sananda:

"The elements, the senses, the mind, the intellect, the latent impressions (*vāsanā*), karma, the vital breaths (*vāyu*), and ignorance—this group of eight is declared by the best of sages to be the *puryaṣṭaka*."
It is also stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"He is joined with the subtle body (*liṅga*), the eightfold city consisting of the vital breaths and so forth;
for one bound by that, there is bondage, and for one liberated from it, there is liberation."

When, having become minute in size and having entered—that is, presiding over—the seed which is the cause of stationary things such as trees and the cause of moving things such as humans, then, conjoined with the *puryaṣṭaka*, it casts off and takes up a form, that is, another gross body, in accordance with its karma. || 1.56 ||
Having incidentally described the departure of the individual soul (jīva), he concludes the subject at hand:
"Thus, by means of waking and dreaming, that imperishable one incessantly brings to life and causes to perish all this world of the moving and the unmoving. (1.57)

"Thus, by means of waking and dreaming": that Brahmā, in this manner, through his own states of waking and dreaming, brings to life and causes the death of this entire world of moving and non-moving beings. "Ajasaṃ" means constantly; "avyayaḥ" means imperishable. (1.57)
Having composed this treatise himself, he first caused me alone to receive it according to the prescribed rule; I, in turn, [taught] Marīci and the other sages.

Regarding the phrase "this treatise": at the beginning of creation, that Brahmā, having composed this treatise, duly taught it to me alone through the performance of the bodily rites prescribed in the scripture. I, in turn, taught it to Marīci and the others. Now, one might ask: if this treatise was composed by Brahmā, how can it be designated as "Mānava" (of Manu)? On this point, Medhātithi states: "By the word 'śāstra' (treatise), the meaning of the scripture—the collection of injunctions and prohibitions—is intended. Brahmā caused Manu to grasp that [meaning]; however, Manu then composed the text that expounds it. Thus, there is no contradiction.

Others, however, maintain that although this work was composed by Brahmā, it is designated as "Mānava" because Manu first revealed its form and meaning to Marīci and the others; thus, even though the Veda is not of human origin, it bears designations such as "Kāṭhaka. This is what is being said: Brahmā, having composed this Dharmaśāstra consisting of one hundred thousand verses, taught it to Manu, who then condensed it with his own words and transmitted it to his disciples; therefore, there is no contradiction. Accordingly, Nārada records in his Smṛti: "This text consists of one hundred thousand [verses]. (1.58)
This Bhṛgu will proclaim this scripture to you in its entirety;
for this sage has learned all of it from me without exception.
"This to you," and so forth. This scripture and this Bhṛgu will relate everything to you, because he has learned this in its entirety from me. (1.59)
Then, having been addressed in that manner by Manu, the great seer Bhṛgu, with a joyful soul, spoke to all those sages: "Listen! (1.60)

Then, having been told "So be it" by Manu with the words, "He shall cause this to be heard," and because he had been addressed as "one who has studied [this]," Bhṛgu, immediately thereafter, with a mind gladdened by his reverence for his teacher in the presence of many sages, replied to those ṛṣis, "Listen! (1.60).
Of this Svāyaṃbhuva Manu, there were six other high-souled and greatly powerful Manus in his lineage who each created their own respective progeny.

Regarding the phrase "of Svāyambhuva": from this Manu, the son of Brahmā, six other Manus have arisen as his progeny. Thus acting as agents, they were each authorized in their own time for the creation, protection, and so forth of the world, and they produced their respective offspring. (1.61)
Svārociṣa, Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata,
the highly resplendent Cākṣuṣa, and the son of Vivasvat as well.
"And Svarociṣ. Thus, these six Manus have been specified by name individually. (1.62)
These seven Manus, beginning with Svāyambhuva, possessed immense splendor;
each, within his own interval (antara), produced and protected this entire world of moving and non-moving beings.

Regarding the word "svāyaṃbhuva": these seven Manus, beginning with Svāyaṃbhuva, having produced this world of moving and non-moving beings during their respective periods of authority, have protected it. 1.63.
Now, in order to fully understand the measurement of time regarding the creation and dissolution of the manvantaras that have been described, he says:
Eighteen nimeṣas (twinklings of an eye) make one kāṣṭhā; thirty of those make one kalā;
thirty kalās make one muhūrta; and a day and night consists of as many [muhūrtas]. (1.64)

"Eighteen *nimeṣas* [make one *kāṣṭhā*]. A *nimeṣa* is that which assists the natural opening of the eyelids. Eighteen of those constitute the time known as a *kāṣṭhā*. Thirty *kāṣṭhās* are designated as a *kalā*. Thirty *kalās* are the time called a *muhūrta*. One should know that thirty such *muhūrtas* constitute the time of a day and night (*ahorātra*). Because of the use of the accusative case in the word "tāvat," the verb "vidyāt" (one should know) is to be supplied. 1.64.
The sun divides day and night for both human beings and gods:
night is for the sleep of living beings, and day is for the performance of actions.

Regarding "day and night": the sun divides the periods of day and night belonging to both humans and the gods. Between those two, night exists for the sleep of living beings, and day for the performance of actions. (1.65)
Among the ancestors, a month constitutes a night and a day; its division consists of two fortnights.
For active duties, the dark fortnight is their day, while the bright fortnight is their night for sleep.

Regarding the phrase "in the ancestral [realm]": a month of human beings constitutes a day and night for the ancestors (*pitṛs*). Therein, the division is made by two fortnights: the dark fortnight is the day for the performance of rituals, and the bright fortnight is the night for sleep. (1.66)
For the gods, a year constitutes day and night; their division is as follows:
the northern course (udagayana) is their day, and the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) is their night. 1.67.

"Day and night for the gods constitute a year. A human year becomes a day and a night for the gods. Furthermore, this is their division: the northern course of the sun (*udagayana*) is the day for the gods, during which the performance of divine rites generally takes place; the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*), however, is their night. (1.67)
Now learn, in brief and in their proper order, the measure of each individual Yuga within a day and night of Brahmā. 1.68.

Regarding the phrase "of Brahmā": listen now to a brief summary, in due order, of the measure of a single day-and-night of Brahmā and of the individual Yugas, beginning with Kṛta. Even though the division of time is the subject at hand, the separate mention of Brahmā’s day-and-night is for the purpose of knowing the meritorious fruit of that knowledge. For it will be said (1.73): "They know the day of Brahmā to be meritorious. The meaning is that merit arises from knowing that [division]. (1.68)
They say that four thousand years constitute the Kṛta Yuga;
its morning twilight lasts as many hundreds of years, and its evening twilight is of the same duration.

Regarding the phrase "they say there are four": Manu and others state that the duration of the Kṛtayuga is four thousand years; its *saṃdhyā* (dawn) and *saṃdhyāṃśa* (twilight) each consist of as many hundreds of years. The *saṃdhyā* is the beginning of the age, and the *saṃdhyāṃśa* is its end. As it is stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "The preceding *saṃdhyā* is said to be of a magnitude equal to one hundred of those [thousand-year units], and the subsequent *saṃdhyāṃśa* is likewise equal to that, occurring immediately after the age."

O best of sages, that period of time which lies between the twilight (saṃdhyā) and the twilight-fraction (saṃdhyāṃśa) is to be known as the "yuga," designated by such names as Kṛta, Tretā, and so forth.
And this number of years is according to the divine measure, because that alone was the subject immediately preceding;
"The four ages, known as Kṛta, Tretā, and so forth, consist of twelve thousand divine years. Learn from me their division."
And this is also from the statement in the Viṣṇupurāṇa: 1.69.
In the other three [ages], together with their twilights and twilight-interims,
the thousands and hundreds decrease by one.

"In the others" means: in the other ages—Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali—together with their junctions (*saṃdhyā*) and sub-junctions (*saṃdhyāṃśa*), there are thousands and hundreds reduced by one [respectively]. Thus it is established: Tretā-yuga consists of three thousand years; its junction and sub-junction consist of three hundred years each. Likewise, Dvāpara consists of two thousand years; its junction and sub-junction consist of two hundred years each. Likewise, Kali consists of one thousand years; its junction and sub-junction consist of one hundred years each. (1.70)
This cycle of four ages, which has been enumerated at the very beginning,
consisting of twelve thousand [years], is called a yuga of the gods.

Regarding the phrase "that which is this": at the beginning of this verse, it is stated that what has been calculated as this human *caturyuga* (four-age cycle) is called a *yuga* of the gods. When there is a doubt regarding the non-inclusion of the *saṃdhyā* and *saṃdhyāṃśa* (twilight and transitional periods) by the term *caturyuga*, he says: "this [is] twelve-thousand-fold" (*etad dvādaśasāhasram*). The suffix *aṇ* is used here in its own sense (without changing the meaning). However, the error of Medhātithi—who claimed that "by twelve *caturyugas* alone, a divine *yuga* [is formed]"—is not to be respected, because Manu subsequently describes a day of Brahmā as consisting of a thousand divine *yugas*. Furthermore, since the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* proclaims a day of Brahmā as consisting of a thousand human *caturyugas*, it follows that a divine *yuga* corresponds precisely to a human *caturyuga*. And so says the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: [The *Viṣṇupurāṇa* continues: "A thousand times four ages is said to be a day of Brahmā; his night is of the same duration. Thus, the calculation of a day of Brahmā is established by means of a thousand human *caturyugas*. Therefore, the statement that "a divine *yuga* consists of twelve *caturyugas*" is merely a figurative expression based on the fact that twelve human *caturyugas* constitute one divine *yuga*. Otherwise, the mention of a thousand divine *yugas* for a day of Brahmā would be inconsistent with the definition of a divine *yuga*. Consequently, the view of Medhātithi is untenable. As for the statement in the *Mahābhārata*—"O King, a divine *yuga* consists of twelve human *caturyugas*"—that too must be understood in the same way. For even there, the context concerns the measurement of a day of Brahmā, and thus it is established that a divine *yuga* is measured by a human *caturyuga*. The same applies to the *Bhāgavatapurāṇa*, where it is stated: "Twelve times four ages is a divine *yuga*. This is also consistent with the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*, which says: "A thousand times four ages is a day of Brahmā. Therefore, the calculation of a day of Brahmā is indeed by means of a thousand human *caturyugas*. Thus, the view of Medhātithi is rejected. As for the *Matsyapurāṇa*, which states: "A thousand times four ages is a day of Brahmā," this too is consistent with the aforementioned calculation. The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali constitute the four yugas;
O Sage, a thousand such cycles is said to be one day of Brahmā.
