A thousand divine yugas, by calculation, should be known as one day of Brahmā, and his night is of the same duration. (1.72)

Regarding the phrase "of the divine": a thousand divine yugas should be known as one day of Brahmā; the night is likewise a thousand [yugas]. The expression "by way of enumeration" is a restatement of the meaning for the purpose of completing the verse. (1.71)
Those people who know day and night understand that the holy day of Brahmā lasts for a thousand yugas, and his night is of exactly the same duration. 1.73.

"That indeed is called an age (yuga)"—that which has its completion at the end of a thousand ages is the day of Brahmā; those who know his night to be of the same duration are "knowers of day and night. This is a praise. And by means of this praise, an injunction is implied that the day and night of Brahmā must be known. Therefore, the qualification "meritorious" is applied because this [knowledge] is a cause of merit. (1.73)
At the end of that day and night, he who was asleep awakens;
having awakened, he creates the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent. (1.74)

Regarding the word "tasya" (of him): that Brahmā, upon the completion of his aforementioned day-and-night (*ahorātra*), becomes awakened. Having awakened, he creates his own mind—that is, he employs it for the creation of the triad beginning with the *bhūrloka*, but he does not produce [the mind anew]. This is because the mind has not perished, having been produced after the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*); and since only the triad beginning with the *bhūrloka* is destroyed during an intermediate dissolution (*avāntarapralaya*), the "creation of the mind" consists simply in the employment of the mind for the purpose of creation. Thus it is heard in the Purāṇa: "The mind, joined with the desire to create, was again directed toward the act of creation."

Alternatively, this word *manas* refers exclusively to the principle of *mahat*. Although that [principle] arises immediately after the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), and its creation has also been described by the passage beginning with "and indeed the Great One" (1.18), nevertheless, in order to explain the unmentioned sequence of the origin of the elements and their qualities, [the author] reiterates the creation of *mahat* and so forth, as well as the creation of the elements, as occurring immediately after the great dissolution; for since Hiraṇyagarbha is also ultimately real, he is the agent of that [creation]. By this, the following is stated: at the beginning of the creation following the great dissolution, Brahmā, in the form of the Supreme Self, creates the principles of *mahat* and so forth for the purpose of creating the world. For this very reason, he will state later (1.78): "Thus is this creation from the beginning. However, regarding the creation of the mind and so forth following an intermediate dissolution (*avāntarapralaya*), the attainment of primacy would occur simply through the order of naming; thus, [if the former were not meant], the statement "thus is this creation from the beginning" would be a redundant reiteration. (1.74)
Impelled by the desire to create, the mind undergoes transformation and brings about creation;
from it, space is born, and they know sound to be its quality. (1.75)

Regarding the phrase "the mind creates": the mind, which is the Great Principle (mahat), performs the act of creation. Impelled by the desire of the Supreme Self to create, space (ākāśa) arises from it. And following the sequence previously mentioned—namely, through the stages of ego (ahaṃkāra) and the subtle elements (tanmātra)—Manu and others understand sound to be the quality of space. 1.75.
From ether, undergoing transformation, there arises the pure and powerful wind, which carries all fragrances; it is indeed considered to have touch as its quality.

"From space" means that from space, which produces modifications, there arises wind—carrying fragrant and foul odors, pure, and powerful—and this wind, possessing the quality called touch, is the one accepted by Manu and others. (1.76)
From the air as well, undergoing transformation, there arises luminous light that dispels darkness; it is radiant and is said to have the quality of form (rūpa). 1.77.
"Also from air": fire is also produced from air. It is radiant, illuminating others, the destroyer of darkness, and luminous; and that is designated as having the nature of a quality. || 1.77 ||
And from light, undergoing transformation, water is said to arise with the quality of taste;
from water, earth arises with the quality of smell—such is the creation from the beginning.

"And from light [comes water]. From fire (tejas), water is produced; and that is endowed with the quality of taste (rasa). From water comes earth, endowed with the quality of smell (gandha). This is the creation of the elements at the beginning of creation following the great dissolution (mahāpralaya). By those very same elements, the construction of the three worlds, beginning with Bhūr, also occurs after an intermediate dissolution (avāntarapralaya). 1.79.
That divine age (yuga) which was previously stated to consist of twelve thousand [years],
multiplied by seventy-one, is here called a Manvantara.

Regarding the phrase "that which was before": that period of four *yugas* for humans, previously stated to have a duration of twelve thousand years including the *sandhyās* and *sandhyāṃśas*, and which constitutes one *yuga* of the gods—when multiplied by seventy-one, it is designated here in this treatise as the time called a *manvantara*. In that period, one *Manu* holds the authority over creation and so forth. (1.79)
Countless Manvantaras, as well as creation and dissolution, the Supreme Lord performs again and again, as if in play. (1.80)

Regarding the phrase "the Manvantaras": although fourteen Manvantaras are enumerated in the Purāṇas, they are nevertheless innumerable because of the infinity of creations and dissolutions. Through repetition, creation and withdrawal are countless. Prajāpati performs all this again and again as if in play. For activity is play for the sake of pleasure; however, since his desires are already fulfilled, he has no need for pleasure—thus the word "as if" (*iva*) is employed. He who stands in the supreme station, characterized by non-reversion, is the Parameṣṭhin. If it is asked how the Supreme Self engages in creation and so forth without a purpose, the answer is: simply out of play (*līlā*), meaning that such is His very nature. It is like the clapping of hands and so on by a storyteller; likewise, the Śārīraka Sūtra (Brahma Sūtra 2.1.33) states: "But it is like the world, for play is the sole motive. (1.80)
In the Kṛta age, Dharma was complete with all four feet, as was Truth;
no acquisition whatsoever occurred for humans through unrighteousness.

"Law was four-footed in its entirety. In the Age of Truth (*satyayuga*), the entire Law (*dharma*) was four-footed, complete in all its limbs. Since the primary "feet" of Dharma cannot exist as separate entities, and because he is celebrated as a bull in such scriptural passages as, "The Blessed Lord Dharma is indeed a bull" (8.16), and because he is complete with four feet, this term "four-footed" refers to the completeness of the Laws through all their constituent parts even in the Age of Truth. Alternatively, since Manu himself mentions these four—penance, knowledge, sacrifice, and charity—in the verse, "Penance is supreme" (1.86), and because Dharma is complete with these four feet, the meaning is that they were present in their entirety in the Age of Truth as its constituent parts. Likewise, the Age of Truth was characterized by truthfulness. Truth is mentioned separately because of its preeminence among all aspects of Dharma. Furthermore, in that age, the acquisition or birth of wealth, knowledge, and so forth for human beings did not occur through the transgression of the scriptures. (1.81)
In the other [ages], dharma exists by means of tradition (āgama), but it is diminished quarter by quarter; through theft, falsehood, and deceit, dharma likewise departs quarter by quarter. (1.82)

"In the others" means in the *tretā* and subsequent ages other than the *satya-yuga*. Because of *āgama*—meaning through unrighteous means (*adharmeṇa*)—wealth, knowledge, and so forth are acquired; for that [unrighteousness] was the subject under discussion in the preceding verse. However, Govindarāja and Medhātithi interpret *āgama* as the Veda. Dharma, such as sacrifice and the like, is "degraded"—that is, diminished—by one quarter in each successive age. Likewise, even that dharma which is practiced when wealth and knowledge have been acquired also vanishes, because it declines quarter by quarter in each age due to theft, falsehood, and deceit. There is no one-to-one correspondence between the *tretā* and following ages and theft, falsehood, and deceit, since all of these are observed in every age.
In the Kṛta age, people are free from disease, all their aims are accomplished, and their lifespan is four hundred years;
however, in the Tretā and subsequent ages, their lifespan decreases by one quarter in each.

"Free from disease" means that they are free from disease because of the absence of unrighteousness (*adharma*), which is the cause of disease; they possess all desired fruits of accomplishment, and their lifespan of four hundred years is natural due to the absence of obstructing *adharma*. However, by the power of merit (*dharma*) that procures a longer life, they may also have a longer lifespan;
for instance, Rāma ruled the kingdom for ten thousand years.

Thus, there is no contradiction with such [scriptural passages]. As for the Śruti statement, "Man has a lifespan of a hundred years" (śatāyur vai puruṣaḥ), the word "hundred" (śata) refers to a large number or pertains to the Kṛta age. Humans of this kind exist during the Kṛta; however, in the Tretā and subsequent ages, the lifespan becomes progressively diminished by one quarter in each. || 1.83 ||
The lifespan declared for mortals in the Vedas, as well as the fruits of ritual actions and the powers of embodied beings, bear fruit in the world according to the respective age. 1.84.

“Life span as declared by the Vedas”: the life span declared in the Vedas, such as “Man indeed lives for a hundred years,” and the prayers directed toward the fruits of optional (*kāmya*) actions, as well as the powers of Brahmins and others—such as their capacity for cursing or bestowing grace—bear fruit in accordance with the specific age (*yuga*). 1.84.
The duties of men in the Kṛta age are of one kind, those in the Tretā and Dvāpara ages are different,
and those in the Kali age are yet another, in accordance with the decline of the ages.
"Others" means that in the Kṛta Yuga, other dharmas prevail; likewise, in the Tretā and subsequent ages, there is a distinct variation in dharma corresponding to the decline of the ages. || 1.85 ||
In the Kṛta age, austerity is supreme; in the Tretā age, knowledge is said to be so;
in the Dvāpara age, they say sacrifice alone is supreme; and in the Kali age, charity is the one thing of importance.

"Asceticism is supreme": although all practices beginning with asceticism are to be performed in all ages, it is nevertheless made known that in the Kṛta age, asceticism is preeminent and yields great fruit. Likewise, self-knowledge [is preeminent] in the Tretā age, sacrifice in the Dvāpara, and charity in the Kali age. (1.86)
But for the sake of protecting this entire creation, that one of great splendor assigned distinct duties to those born from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet.

"Of all this": that Brahmā, possessed of great splendor, for the sake of protecting this entire creation, created by means of division the duties—having both visible and invisible purposes—for the Brāhmaṇas and other classes born from his mouth and the other [parts of his body], according to the principle stated in the verse, "The oblation cast into the fire... (3.76). || 1.87 ||
He ordained for the Brāhmaṇas teaching, studying, performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices, as well as giving gifts and receiving them. (1.88)

Regarding "teaching": the mention of teaching and the other [duties] here in this section on creation is for the purpose of designating them as specific aspects of creation; their detailed treatment will occur later. He ordained these six duties, beginning with teaching, for the Brāhmaṇas. 1.88.
The protection of subjects, giving, sacrifice, and study, as well as non-attachment to sensual objects, constitute the duty of a Kṣatriya in brief. 1.89.

"Of the subjects" means that he ordained the protection of the subjects and so forth as the duties of the Kṣatriya. "Non-attachment to sense objects"—namely, singing, dancing, women, and the like—and their non-recurrence; "in brief," that is, in summary. (1.89)
The protection of cattle, giving, sacrifice, study, trade, money-lending, and agriculture are the duties of the Vaiśya. (1.90)
"Of cattle" means that he ordained for the Vaiśya the protection of cattle and so forth, as well as trade by land and water, and usury, which is the lending of money at interest. || 1.90 ||
But the Lord assigned only one duty for the Śūdra: to serve these very same classes without malice. (1.91)

"But only one," [it says]. The Lord Brahmā created for the Śūdra a duty consisting of service to the three varṇas beginning with the Brāhmaṇa. The phrase "only one" is intended to show its preeminence, since giving and other duties are also prescribed for him. "Without envy" means without disparaging the virtues [of others]. (1.91)
Now, because this treatise primarily aims at the protection of creation and begins with the exposition of the duties of the Brāhmaṇa, the author states a praise of the Brāhmaṇa:
"A man is declared to be more pure above the navel;
therefore, his mouth has been called the most pure by the Self-existent One. (1.92)
"Upwards": a person is pure in every respect, but above the navel he is especially pure; even more than that, the mouth is declared by Brahmā to be the most pure of all. 1.92.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
"Because of his birth from the highest limb, because of his seniority, and because he upholds the Veda, the Brāhmaṇa is by right the lord of this entire creation. (1.93)

Regarding the phrase "because of birth from the highest limb": the highest limb is the head; because he was born from that, and because he was produced before the Kṣatriyas and others, the Brāhmaṇa is the lord of this entire world through his instruction in Dharma by means of teaching, exposition, and so forth, and through his superior retention of the Veda.
Furthermore, due to the distinction of his sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*), the Brāhmaṇa is the lord of the social classes (*varṇas*).
From whose head did he emerge? To this he says:

"For the Self-Existent One, having performed austerities from the beginning, created him from his own mouth for the purpose of conveying the offerings to the gods and ancestors, and for the protection of all this world. (1.94)

Regarding the phrase "for he is the Self-Existent One" (svayaṃbhū): Brahmā, having performed austerities, first created that Brāhmaṇa from his own mouth for the purpose of conveying the sacrificial offerings to the gods and ancestors (haviḥ-kavya), and for the protection of the entire world, [placing him] before the Kṣatriyas and the other castes. 1.94.

He clarifies the aforementioned offering of *havya* and *kavya*: "That being by whose mouth the dwellers of heaven always eat the *havyas*, and the ancestors eat the *kavyas*—what being could be greater than that? (1.95)

"By whose mouth... means: what other being could be more excellent than that brahmin, by whose mouth the gods always consume the *havya* offerings and the ancestors the *kavya* offerings at the *śrāddha* and other rites? (1.95)
Among beings, those with breath are the best; among those with breath, those who live by intelligence;
among the intelligent, men are the best; and among men, Brāhmaṇas are traditionally held to be the best.

Regarding the phrase "of beings" (*bhūtānām*): among beings—both stationary and moving—which are composed of the elements, living creatures such as insects and the like are superior because they occasionally experience a trace of happiness. Even among them, animals and the like are superior, for they live by means of intelligence and are capable of approaching or withdrawing from places that are beneficial or useless respectively. Superior even to them are human beings, due to their connection with preeminent knowledge. Superior even to them are Brahmins, because they are worthy of universal veneration and are fit for the qualification toward liberation (*apavarga*). 1.96.

Among Brahmins, those who are learned; among the learned, those whose intellects are perfected; among those of perfected intellect, those who perform their duties; and among those who perform their duties, those who know Brahman.

"And among the Brāhmaṇas": among the Brāhmaṇas, however, the learned are superior because they possess the qualification for performing rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, which yield great fruit. Even more so than them are those of "perfected intellect" (*kṛtabuddhi*), meaning those who possess the conviction "it has been done by me" even regarding what is yet to come—the sense being that they have developed the sense of duty toward the performance of what is prescribed in the scriptures. Even more so than them are the practitioners (*anuṣṭhātāraḥ*), because they partake in the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful. Even more so than them are the knowers of Brahman (*brahmavidaḥ*), because of their attainment of liberation. (1.97)
The very birth of a Brahmin is the eternal embodiment of Dharma; for he is born for the sake of Dharma and is fit for becoming one with Brahman. 1.98.

"Birth alone" means that the mere birth of a Brahmin body is the indestructible body of dharma. This is because he is born for the sake of dharma, and through self-knowledge supported by dharma, he attains liberation. || 1.98 ||
For when a Brāhmaṇa is born, he is indeed born preeminent upon the earth;
he is the lord of all beings for the protection of the treasury of Dharma. 1.99.

Regarding the word "brāhmaṇa": because a brāhmaṇa, upon being born, exists above (adhi) upon the earth; that is to say, he is the most excellent. He is the lord for the protection of the entire collection of dharma among all living beings, since all dharmas have been taught by the brāhmaṇa. 1.99.
"Everything belongs to the Brāhmaṇa, whatever exists within the world;
by virtue of his preeminence and noble birth, the Brāhmaṇa indeed deserves all this. (1.100)

"Everything is his own. Whatever wealth exists in the world, that is said to be the Brāhmaṇa’s own; this is stated by way of praise. It is "his own as it were," but not his own in the absolute sense, because theft from a Brāhmaṇa will also be mentioned by Manu. Therefore, due to his noble lineage—having originated from the mouth of Brahmā—the Brāhmaṇa is preeminent; he truly deserves everything and is fit to receive all things. The particle *vai* is used for emphasis. 1.100
A Brahmin eats only his own, wears his own, and gives away his own; it is through the Brahmin’s compassion that other people eat at all. 1.101.

"His own indeed": even that food which a Brāhmaṇa eats belonging to another, the garment of another which he wears, or what he takes from another and gives to someone else—that too is the Brāhmaṇa’s own. This is a praise, as before. This being so, others perform acts such as feeding him out of compassion for the Brāhmaṇa. 1.101.
Now begins the praise of the treatise by way of describing the preeminent duties of the Brāhmaṇa:
"For the sake of discerning those duties, the wise Manu, son of the Self-existent, composed this treatise in due order for the rest [of the social classes]. (1.102)

"For the sake of discerning his duties" means that for the sake of knowing the duties of the Brāhmaṇa and of the others—the Kṣatriyas and so forth—the wise Manu, the son of Brahmā, born of the Self-Existent, who possesses knowledge of all subjects, composed this treatise.
This should be studied with diligence by a learned Brahmin, and it should be correctly expounded to disciples by someone according to the proper method. (1.103)

Regarding the word *viduṣā*: by a Brāhmaṇa who knows the fruit of studying this treatise, a diligent study of this work—suitable for its exposition and teaching—must be performed, and it must be explained to pupils; it is not [to be studied] by anyone else, such as a Kṣatriya or the like. However, mere study, devoid of exposition and teaching, will be prescribed even for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas in the passage beginning with "from conception until the cremation ground" (2.16). Medhātithi’s opinion is that this [verse] is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). That is not convincing, because from it one does not obtain the rule that study is for the twice-born [in general] while exposition and teaching are for the Brāhmaṇa alone. As for the passage "the three castes may study" (10.1), he will state that it refers to the Vedas. Since the rule that teaching belongs to the Brāhmaṇa alone is already established, this [present verse] could indeed be a restatement; thus, Medhātithi’s adherence to his view is futile. (1.103)
A Brahmin who studies this treatise and whose vows are well-praised is never tainted by the defects of action arising from mind, speech, or body. (1.104)

"This is the treatise": one who recites this treatise, having understood its meaning and being one whose vows are praised—that is, whose vows are properly observed—is not bound by the sins arising from mind, speech, and body. (1.104)
He purifies his lineage, seven ancestors and seven descendants;
indeed, even a single such person merits this entire earth.

Regarding the word *punāti* (“purifies”): the phrase “one who studies this treatise” (*idaṃ śāstram adhīyāna*) is understood to carry over from the previous verse. He purifies the assembly (*paṅkti*)—a group of people seated in succession—who has been deemed unfit for the company (*apāṅkta*). Furthermore, he purifies seven ancestors above him, beginning with his father, and seven descendants below him, beginning with his son. Moreover, by virtue of knowing all dharmas, he becomes worthy of receiving the entire earth as a fit recipient. (1.105)
This is the most excellent means of securing well-being; this increases the intellect;
this brings fame and long life; this is the supreme state of ultimate bliss.

"Idam" (this): "Svasti" is the non-destruction of the intended object; its "ayana" is that which leads to it. This study of the treatise is a "svastyayana"; and because it makes known [the means of] recitation, oblation, and so forth, it is the most excellent "svastyayana," superior to those following it, and an enhancer of the intellect, since through the practice of this treatise one gains a thorough understanding of all injunctions and prohibitions. It is "yaśasya" (conducive to fame), as it brings about the attainment of self-respect through scholarship, and it is "niḥśreyasa" (leading to the supreme good), because it teaches the means to liberation (*mokṣa*). (1.106)
In this [work], the Dharma has been declared in its entirety, as well as the merits and faults of actions, and the eternal conduct of all four social classes. 1.107

"In this [work] is Dharma": this is a praise of the treatise, meaning that Dharma has been expounded here in its entirety. Furthermore, regarding the desired and undesired fruits of actions—both prescribed and prohibited—the conduct (*ācāra*) consisting of the duties of men for the four castes is eternal and handed down through tradition. Although conduct is itself a form of Dharma, it is mentioned separately in order to emphasize its preeminence. (1.107)
He clarifies its very preeminence: "Conduct is the supreme dharma, whether declared in the Śruti or prescribed in the Smṛti.
Therefore, a self-possessed twice-born man should always be constantly devoted to it. (1.108)

Regarding the term "conduct" (ācāra): it refers to one who is disciplined, diligent, and desirous of his own welfare. Since everyone possesses a self, the word "self" here indicates the desire for one's own welfare.
A Brahmin who has fallen away from right conduct does not enjoy the fruit of the Vedas;
however, one who is endowed with right conduct shall partake of the full fruit. 1.109

Regarding the phrase "from conduct": A Brahmin who has fallen away from right conduct does not obtain the fruit of the Vedas; however, one endowed with right conduct becomes a partaker of the full fruit. 1.109.
Having thus observed the course of Dharma through conduct, the sages adopted right conduct as the supreme root of all austerity. 1.110

"Thus": having understood that the attainment of Dharma results from conduct in the manner described, the sages accepted conduct—such as the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances—as the cause for the fulfillment of all asceticism (tapas) and took it up as something to be practiced. The praise of conduct mentioned here is for the purpose of praising the scripture, which will be discussed further below. 1.110.

Now, for the easy comprehension of the disciple, he states the table of contents of the subjects to be explained: "The origin of the world, the very procedure for the ritual refinements (saṃskāra), the practice and observance of vows, and the supreme rite of bathing. (1.111)

"And the origin of the world" (*jagataś ca samutpattim*): the origin of the world is described as stated [in the verses] ending with "and the doctrines of the heretical sects" (*pāṣaṇḍagaṇadharmāṃś ca*, 1.118). Furthermore, the praise of the Brāhmaṇa is for the purpose of protecting the creation (*sarga*). The praise of the Brāhmaṇa’s authority and so forth is also included within the account of creation itself. This is the subject matter of the first chapter. The performance of the *saṃskāras*—the rites such as the birth-ceremony (*jātakarma*) and others; the observance of vows by the religious student (*brahmacārin*); and the respectful service toward teachers and others, such as salutation and attendance. The singular form [of the compound] is according to the rule: "Every *dvandva* compound may optionally be treated as a singular" (*sarvo dvando vibhāṣaikavad bhavati*, Patañjali I: 476–77). This is the subject matter of the second chapter. "Bathing" (*snāna*) refers to a specific *saṃskāra* for one returning from the teacher's house (*gurukula*); its prescription is the topic here. (1.111)
The acquisition of a wife, the characteristics of marriages, the rules for the great sacrifices, and the eternal ritual for ancestral offerings (śrāddha). || 1.112 ||

"Acquisition of a wife" means marriage; it also includes the definition of its specific forms, such as the *brāhma* and others. The "great sacrifices" (*mahāyajña*) are the five, beginning with the *vaiśvadeva*. The "eternal rule for the *śrāddha*" is perpetual, being constant through the beginningless flow of successive world-creations. This is the subject matter of the third chapter. 1.112
The characteristics of the modes of livelihood, the vows of the Snātaka, the edible and non-edible, purification, and the cleansing of substances. (1.113)

"Of the modes of livelihood" (vṛttīnām) means the definition of the means of subsistence, such as agriculture and the like. "Vows" (vratāni) are the observances of a *snātaka* householder. This is the subject matter of the fourth chapter. "Edible" refers to curd and so forth; "inedible" refers to garlic and so forth. "Purification" refers to the ten-day period of impurity for Brahmins and others following a death or birth. "Purification of substances" refers to cleansing with water and the like. (1.113)
The application of the duties of women, asceticism, liberation, and renunciation itself;
the entire duty of kings and the legal adjudication of lawsuits.

"Regarding the application of the duties of women": this [chapter] concerning the fifth [topic] is the application of duty (*dharmayoga*), that is, the means for attaining duty (*dharmopāya*) for women. "Asceticism" (*tāpasya*) refers to the duty of one who is fit for the forest-dweller stage (*vānaprastha*) for the sake of austerity. "Liberation" (*mokṣa*) refers to the duty of the ascetic (*yatidharma*), because it is the cause of liberation. Although renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is indeed included within the duties of an ascetic, its separate instruction is for the purpose of making known its preeminence. This is the subject matter of the sixth chapter. "The duty of the consecrated king" refers to all the duties of a king who has been anointed, whether their purpose is visible (*dṛṣṭa*) or invisible (*adṛṣṭa*). This is the subject matter of the seventh chapter. "The decision on legal cases" (*kāryanirṇaya*) refers to the determination of the truth after deliberation regarding matters such as debts and the like, which have been presented by the plaintiff and the defendant. (1.114)
The rules for examining witnesses, the law concerning husband and wife, the law of partition, gambling, and the removal of thorns [criminals]. 1.115.

"Regarding witnesses": as for the rule concerning the interrogation of witnesses, although the interrogation of witnesses is a constituent part of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), it is mentioned separately because it is the means for determining the application of the rule. This belongs to the eighth chapter. "The performance of religious duties by a woman and a man"—that is, by wife and husband—both when they are together and when they are apart; and "the law regarding the division of inheritance. Although the division of inheritance is already included by the phrase "and the decision of cases" (1.114), it is nevertheless mentioned separately due to the distinction between chapters. "The rule concerning gambling" is expressed by the word *dyūta*. And "the clearing away of thorns," that is, the removal of thieves and other such pests. (1.115)
The conduct of Vaiśyas and Śūdras, the origin of the mixed castes, the duties of the social orders in times of distress, and likewise the rules for expiation; 1.116.

"And the conduct of Vaiśyas and Śūdras. The conduct of Vaiśyas and Śūdras refers to the performance of their own specific duties; this is treated in the ninth [chapter]. Likewise, in the tenth [chapter], there is the account of the origin of those born from mixed unions—both in the direct (anuloma) and inverse (pratiloma) orders—as well as the instruction on livelihoods in times of distress, which constitutes the law for times of adversity (*āpaddharma*). In the eleventh [chapter], the rules for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) are set forth. 1.116.
The journey through saṃsāra, which arises from the threefold karma, as well as the supreme good resulting from actions and the examination of their virtues and defects. || 1.117 ||

Regarding "the wandering in saṃsāra": wandering in saṃsāra consists in the attainment of various bodies; it is threefold—superior, middling, and inferior—and has virtuous and non-virtuous karma as its cause. "The highest good" (niḥśreyasa) is the knowledge of the Self, because it is the cause of the highest excellence characterized by liberation. Furthermore, there is the examination of the merits and defects of actions, both those prescribed and those prohibited. (1.117)
In this treatise, Manu has declared the eternal laws of regions, the laws of castes, the laws of families, and the laws of heretical sects and assemblies. (1.118)

Regarding "the laws of regions" (*deśadharma*): regional laws (*deśadharma*) are those practiced in a specific locality; caste-laws (*jātidharma*) are those fixed by birth, such as that of the Brāhmaṇas and others; family-laws (*kuladharma*) are those based on particular lineages; heresy (*pāṣaṇḍa*) refers to the practice of prohibited vows based on scriptures outside the Veda; because of association with that, a person is also called a heretic, and the laws pertaining to them—such as "those who follow heretical paths and stand in improper occupations" (4.30)—are not mentioned separately [from the preceding categories]. A "group" (*gaṇa*) is a collection of merchants and the like. 1.118.
Just as Manu formerly spoke this scripture when questioned by me, so now do you also learn it from me. 1.119
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Mānava Dharmaśāstra*, in the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu.

Regarding the words "yathedam" (as this): the repetition is for the sake of increasing the reverence of the sages, signifying that "listen from me exactly as Manu, when previously questioned by me, declared this scripture—neither deficient nor redundant. (1.119)
Thus ends the first chapter of the *Manvarthamuktāvalī* composed by the illustrious Kullūkabhaṭṭa.
The Second Chapter.

Having established Brahman as the cause of the world for the sake of knowing Dharma—which consists of the knowledge of the supreme Self—[the author], now desiring to explain Dharma in the form of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and so forth which constitute an auxiliary to the knowledge of Brahman, first states the general definition of Dharma:
"That which is practiced by the wise, by the virtuous, and constantly by those free from hatred and passion..."
Learn that dharma which has been approved by my heart.

Regarding the phrase "by the learned": by the learned (*vidvadbhiḥ*)—that is, by those who know the Vedas, who are virtuous, righteous, and free from passion and hatred—who have practiced [it] and understood it directly with their hearts; by this, the means to the highest good (*śreyas-sādhana*) is stated. For it is therein that the mind becomes inclined of its own accord. By the force of employing the qualification "known by those who know the Vedas," it is intended that the Veda itself, once known, is the cause for knowing the means to the highest good. Just as when it is said, "He was killed by a sword-wielder," the primary agency in the act of killing belongs specifically to the one holding the sword. Therefore, it has been stated: "Dharma is the means to the highest good, having the Veda as its authority. Learn that Dharma which is of such a nature. Here are the summary verses on the meaning thus explained:
By employing the qualification "known by those who know the Vedas," Manu has stated that Dharma is understood from the Veda alone.
Pointing out that it is known through the heart—that is, by way of direct orientation—he says it is the means to the highest good; for in that state, the mind is oriented toward it.
Since dharma is that which is established by the Veda as the means for attaining the highest good,
the sages have formulated the definition of dharma exactly as stated by Manu.

For this very reason, Hārīta says: “Now, therefore, we shall explain Dharma. Dharma has the Śruti as its authority. And the Śruti is of two kinds: Vedic and Tantric. In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: “Dharma is declared to be the highest good (śreyas); the highest good is characterized by worldly prosperity (abhyudaya). That [Dharma] is said to be fivefold, eternal, and rooted in the Veda.”
From its correct performance, O Lord of Birds, heaven and liberation arise,
as well as incomparable happiness and sovereignty in this world.

The meaning is: that which is a means to the highest good (*śreyas*). Jaimini also formulated this definition of *dharma* in his aphorism: "Dharma is a purposeful object characterized by Vedic injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇo ’rtho dharmaḥ*, Jai. Sū. 1.1.2). By means of an injunction (*codanā*), two things are characterized: a purposeful object, such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice which is a means to the highest good; and a non-purposeful object, such as the *Śyena* sacrifice which is a means to sin (*pratyavāya*). The meaning of the aphorism is that *dharma* is a means to the highest good, such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, which has the Veda as its authority. We shall demonstrate later that the *Smṛtis* and other sources are also authorities regarding *dharma* only because they are rooted in the Veda. Govindarāja, however, explained that "authorized by the heart" means being free from the hesitation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-vicikitsā-śūnya*). According to his view, the definition of *dharma* would be: that which is performed by those learned in the Veda and is free from doubt. However, wise men do not place their trust in such a definition of *dharma*, as it would apply equally to worldly activities with visible purposes, such as going to a village. Medhātithi, on the other hand, explained "authorized by the heart" as "that toward which the mind inclines," or alternatively, he stated that "the heart" refers to the Veda; for when it is studied, it resides in the heart in the form of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and thus it is called the "heart. (2.1)
To have desire as one's sole motive is not praised, yet here there is no such thing as being without desire;
for the study of the Vedas and the performance of Vedic ritual action are themselves objects of desire.

Regarding the phrase "having desire as one's nature" (*kāmātmatā*): a person’s disposition characterized by longing for results is "having desire as one's nature. That is not praiseworthy, because it is a cause of bondage. Ritual actions performed with the longing for fruits such as heaven become the cause for rebirth. However, obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, when acting as auxiliaries to the knowledge of the Self, lead to liberation. Yet, mere desire itself is not prohibited by this; as it is said: "And indeed, there is no absence of desire here in this world," since the acquisition of the Vedas and the connection with all Vedic duties are themselves objects of desire. (2.2)
Regarding this, he states the reasoning: "Desire indeed has its root in volition; sacrifices originate from volition;
vows, restraints, and duties—all are traditionally held to be born of volition. (2.3)

"Saṃkalpa is the root": by this [term], *saṃkalpa* is defined as the cognition whose object is the thought, "By this action, this desired fruit is to be accomplished. Immediately after that, once the action is understood as a means to the desired end, desire arises for it, and one exerts effort toward it. Thus, sacrifices (*yajña*), vows (*vrata*), and the duties consisting of restraints (*yama*)—which will be described in the fourth chapter—all originate from *saṃkalpa*. By the word "all," it is meant that other purposes of the scriptures (*śāstrārtha*) also arise solely from *saṃkalpa*; the meaning is that even those do not occur without desire. Govindarāja, however, says that vows are of the nature of things to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*), while the duties of restraint are prohibitory in nature (*pratiṣedhārthaka*). 2.3.
Right here he demonstrates the worldly rule:
"No action whatsoever is ever seen here to be performed by one who is free from desire;
for whatever one does, all that is the movement of desire. (2.4)

Regarding the phrase "of one who is without desire": in the world, no action whatsoever—such as eating, walking, or the like—is ever seen to occur in one who lacks desire. Therefore, whatever action a person performs, whether worldly or Vedic, each and every one of them is the product of desire. (2.4)
Now he establishes the prohibition of desire for rewards mentioned previously:
"One who conducts oneself rightly toward these goes to the world of the immortals;
and here, one enjoys all desires exactly as they were intended. (2.5)

"Acting rightly in those [duties]" means that here desire is not prohibited; rather, right conduct in the actions prescribed by the scriptures is enjoined. Performing scriptural duties without longing for the results that cause bondage is "acting rightly in them. Acting rightly in this way, he goes to the state of the immortal world—the nature of Brahman—and attains liberation; this is the meaning. Furthermore, being such a one, because he is the Lord of all, he obtains all desired things even in this world. Thus it is said in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (8.2.1): "If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers, by his mere will the fathers arise for him," and so forth. || 2.5 ||

Now he states the authorities for dharma: "The entire Veda is the root of dharma, as are the tradition (smṛti) and conduct (śīla) of those who know it, the practice of the virtuous, and also self-satisfaction. (2.6)

"The Veda is the entirety [of knowledge]; it is the root of Dharma. The Veda—characterized by the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, *Sāman*, and *Atharva*—is in its entirety, consisting of injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and mantras, the root and authority for Dharma. Even the explanatory passages possess authority regarding Dharma by virtue of being laudatory and forming a single syntactical unit with an injunction. As Jaimini stated (Jai. Sū. 1.2.7): "But because they form a single syntactical unit with the injunction, they exist for the purpose of praising the injunctions. Mantras and explanatory passages also possess authority regarding Dharma solely by forming a single syntactical unit with injunctive sentences; furthermore, at the time of performance, they serve as reminders of what is to be practiced. And the authority of the Veda regarding Dharma—which consists in its being the instrument for direct experience—is established through reasoning (*nyāya*). This [definition] is restated in order to demonstrate that the authority of the *Smṛtis* and other sources also derives solely from their having the Veda as their root. Furthermore, the *Smṛti* of Manu and others who know the Veda is an authority for Dharma. By employing the qualification "of those who know the Veda," it is intended that the authority of the *Smṛtis* and so forth rests precisely upon their Vedic foundation. "Character" (*śīla*) consists of qualities such as devotion to Brahman and the like. Regarding this, Hārīta says:

Reverence for Brahmins, devotion to the gods and ancestors, gentleness, not causing pain to others, freedom from envy, mildness, absence of harshness, friendliness, pleasant speech, gratitude, providing refuge, compassion, and tranquility—these constitute the thirteenfold conduct (*śīla*). Govindarāja, however, states that the conduct of the righteous and the self-satisfaction regarding optional matters are the authorities (*pramāṇa*) concerning dharma. As Garga said: "In matters of option, self-satisfaction is the authority. (2.6)

Although it has been stated that the authority of other [scriptures] besides the Veda is based on their being rooted in the Veda, [the author] specifically declares the Vedic foundation of the *Manusmṛti* in order to demonstrate its preeminence over all:
"Whatever dharma has been proclaimed by Manu for anyone, all that is declared in the Veda, for he is the embodiment of all knowledge. (2.7)

"Whoever" means: whatever dharma has been declared by Manu for anyone—such as for a Brāhmaṇa or others—all of that is established in the Veda. For this Manu is omniscient; and being omniscient, he has correctly understood the meaning of the Veda—which, though lost, scattered, or currently being recited—and has composed [this work] for the welfare of the world. Govindarāja, however, explains the phrase "consisting of all knowledge" (*sarvajñānamaya*) as an epithet of the Veda, stating: "The Veda is, as it were, composed of all knowledge. (2.7)
Having examined all this entirely with the eye of knowledge,
the learned man, guided by the Veda, should indeed be established in his own duty.

"But all," [it says]. All the collection of treatises—knowledge such as Mīmāṃsā, grammar, and so forth, which is appropriate for understanding the meaning of the Veda—is indeed the eye of knowledge. Having scrutinized everything through that [eye] in its particulars, and having understood what is to be practiced by means of the authority of the Veda, one should remain steadfast in one's own duty (svadharma). 2.8.
For a human being who practices the dharma declared in the Śruti and Smṛti attains fame in this world and unsurpassed happiness after death. (2.9)

"Enjoined by the Śruti and Smṛti. By practicing the dharma enjoined by the Śruti and Smṛti, a human being attains in this world the incidental fame of being righteous, and in the next world the excellent fruit of dharma, consisting of happiness such as heaven and liberation. Through this statement of its actual qualities, an injunction is inferred: "One should practice the dharma enjoined by the Śruti and Smṛti. (2.9)
The Veda is to be known as Śruti, while the Dharmaśāstra is indeed Smṛti;
these two are not to be questioned in any matter, for from them Dharma has shone forth.

"But the *śruti*... This is a restatement of the relationship between a name and the thing named (*saṃjñā-saṃjñi-sambandha*) as established in common worldly usage, intended for the purpose of enjoining that [the *smṛti*] must not be scrutinized by counter-arguments (*pratikūla-tarka*), and for the purpose of establishing the superior authority of the *smṛti* over custom (*ācāra*) and the like by demonstrating its equality with the *śruti*. Consequently, the practical result is that conduct contrary to the *smṛti* is to be abandoned. *Śruti* is the Veda; *smṛti* is the treatise of Manu and others. Both of these are not to be investigated through counter-arguments, because by means of them, Dharma has shone forth—that is, attained complete manifestation—without exception. (2.10)

Any twice-born man who, relying on the treatises of logic, would show contempt for these two roots [the Veda and the Smṛti], should be excluded by the virtuous as an atheist and a reviler of the Veda. (2.11)

"Whoever would despise them": furthermore, that twice-born man who would despise those two—the Śruti and the Smṛti—should be expelled by the learned from the duties such as study and so forth which are to be performed by the twice-born. Lest there be the delusion that because of the prohibition of *mīmāṃsā* (speculative inquiry) in the preceding verse with the words "not to be investigated," even favorable *mīmāṃsā* should not be undertaken, he specifies [the reason for exclusion]: "by resorting to the science of logic" (*hetuśāstra*). One who, like a nihilist such as a Cārvāka, relies on adverse reasoning—such as "Vedic statements are not authoritative because they are statements, like the speech of a deceiver"—is a nihilist (*nāstika*) because he is a reviler of the Veda. (1.11)

Now, since conduct (*ācāra*) alone can be included within virtuous character (*śīla*), [the author] states that the fourfold means of knowing dharma (*dharmapramāṇa*) in order to show that its basis is solely the Veda, and not a restrictive rule regarding the specific types such as Smṛti and *śīla*:
"The Veda, Smṛti, the conduct of the virtuous, and what is pleasing to oneself—these they declare to be the fourfold direct definition of dharma. (2.12)

"Veda" means that the Veda is the authority for dharma; its purport is simply that it is sometimes directly perceived and sometimes inferred through Smṛti, not that it is being enumerated as a distinct source of knowledge. For this very reason, in the verse "dharma declared by Śruti and Smṛti" (2.9), he mentioned only these two. "Sadācāra" is the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭas). "One's own pleasure" (ātmatuṣṭi) is what is dear to oneself. (2.12)
For those who are unattached to wealth and sensual desires, the knowledge of Dharma is prescribed;
for those seeking to understand Dharma, the Śruti is the supreme authority. (2.13)

Regarding the phrase "in matters of wealth and desire": this is an instruction on Dharma for those who are unattached to wealth and desire, being devoid of any longing for them. The meaning is that the fruit of action does not accrue to those who practice Dharma merely out of a pursuit of wealth and desire for the sake of worldly reputation. Furthermore, for those who wish to know Dharma, the Veda (*śruti*) is the supreme authority (*pramāṇa*). By emphasizing its preeminence, the intention is that in case of conflict between the Veda and the Smṛti, the meaning of the Smṛti is not to be respected. For this very reason, Jābāla says: "But in the case of a conflict between Śruti and Smṛti, the Śruti alone is more authoritative."
When there is no conflict, the virtuous should always perform the Smārta rites just as they do the Vaidika ones.
It is also stated in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
"But when there is a contradiction with Śruti, [Smṛti] is sublated, except for its specific subject matter."

Jaimini also says (Jaimini Nyāya Sūtra 1.3.3): "But in case of contradiction, it should be disregarded; for when there is no [contradiction], there is inference. The meaning is that when there is a contradiction with Śruti, a Smṛti statement is to be disregarded, being non-authoritative and not to be accepted; whereas in the absence of contradiction, it serves as an inference for its source in the Veda. 2.13.
But where there may be a conflict between two Vedic texts, both are traditionally held to be Dharma;
for both of those are rightly declared to be Dharma by the wise. (2.14)

Regarding the phrase "but where there is a conflict of Śrutis": where, however, there is a conflict between two Śrutis themselves—that is, where they set forth mutually contradictory meanings—there both rules are recorded by Manu as Dharma. Because they possess equal force, there is no contradiction, as the performance of either is prescribed as an option (*vikalpa*). This is because even scholars who lived earlier than Manu and others declared both those Dharmas to be perfectly correct. The application to the present subject is that, due to the equality of their reasoning, when there is a conflict between two Smṛtis as well, there is an option; for there is no distinction in their equal force. Thus says Gautama: "In the case of a conflict between those of equal force, there is an option. (2.14)
Regarding this, he states an illustration:
"Whether the sun has risen, or has not yet risen, or likewise at the time of dawn—sacrifice proceeds in every way; such is the Vedic revelation. (2.15)

"Whether at sunrise or even before sunrise": the time devoid of both the sun and the stars is expressed by the term *samyādhyuṣita*. The period prior to sunrise, characterized by the presence of the first rays of dawn and still possessing sparse stars, is the "pre-sunrise time" (*anudita-kāla*). Although two mutually contradictory times are heard in the scriptures, the Agnihotra oblation proceeds in every case as an option. Here, the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) is used figuratively because of its association with the quality of relinquishing a substance for the sake of a deity. "The offering should be made when the sun has risen," and so forth, is the Vedic revelation (*śruti*). (2.15)

He for whom the ritual procedure beginning with the impregnation and ending at the cremation ground has been prescribed by means of mantras—only he should be known as qualified for this scripture, and no one else whatsoever. (2.16)

"Niṣekādi" means that for which the entire collection of rites, beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*) and ending with the funeral (*antyeṣṭi*), is prescribed by means of mantras for the twice-born caste; this is the meaning. Only such a person has the right (*adhikāra*) to study and hear this *Mānava-dharma-śāstra*, and not anyone else, such as a Śūdra. Furthermore, the performance of the injunctions of this treatise must be carried out by all according to their respective eligibility. However, its "exposition"—meaning teaching and commentary—is to be performed solely by Brāhmaṇas, as explained under verse 1.103: "by a learned Brāhmaṇa. (2.16)
Having stated the essential nature, the means of knowledge, and the technical definitions of Dharma, [the author] now describes the regions suitable for the performance of Dharma:
"The region situated between the two divine rivers, the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī, that land created by the gods is called Brahmāvarta. (2.17)

Regarding the term *Sarasvatī*: they call the region between the two rivers, the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī, the land of Brahmāvarta. The words "river of the gods" (*devanadī*) and "created by the gods" (*devanirmita*) are intended to express the excellence of the river and the region. (2.18)
Whatever custom has been handed down through a continuous tradition in that region for the social classes (varṇas) and the intermediate castes (antarālas), that is called right conduct (sadācāra).

"In that country" means: because the learned (śiṣṭas) generally exist in that country, the conduct of those belonging to the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas and extending down to the mixed castes—which has come down through a traditional succession and is not merely contemporary—is designated as "good conduct" (sadācāra). || 2.18 ||
Kurukṣetra, Matsya, Pañcāla, and Śūrasena—
this is indeed the land of the Brahman-sages (brahmarṣi), which follows immediately after Brahmāvarta.

Regarding "Kurukṣetra": words such as *matsya* and others, when used in the plural, denote regions and sub-regions. The Pañcālas are the region of Kānyakubja; the Śūrasenakas are the region of Mathurā. This is the land of the Brahman-sages (*brahmarṣideśa*), which is slightly inferior to Brahmāvarta.
From the presence of a twice-born man born in this region, all men on earth should learn their respective duties. (2.20)
"Regarding 'this region': all men should learn their respective customs from a Brāhmaṇa born in a region such as Kurukṣetra. (2.20)
The region situated between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains,
to the east of Vinaśana and to the west of Prayāga, is proclaimed as Madhyadeśa.

Regarding the term "Himavat": the mountains Himavat and Vindhya are situated in the northern and southern directions respectively; the region between them—east of Vinaśana, the place where the Sarasvatī disappears, and west of Prayāga—is declared to be the land named Madhyadeśa (the Middle Country). || 2.21 ||
From the eastern ocean to the western ocean, and between those very two mountains, the wise know the land to be Āryāvarta. (2.22)

"From the ocean," it is said. The learned know that the region of Āryāvarta is that which lies between the eastern ocean and the western ocean, and between the Himavat and the Vindhya mountains. Here, the prefix *ā* denotes a limit (*maryādā*), not an inclusive extent (*abhividhi*). Therefore, islands situated within the ocean do not belong to Āryāvarta. It is called Āryāvarta because the noble ones (*āryāḥ*) turn toward (*āvartante*) it, arising there again and again. (2.22)
That land where the black antelope roams by its own nature is to be known as a land fit for sacrifice; beyond that is the land of the Mlecchas. 2.23.

"But [the land] where the black antelope roams": that region where the black antelope (kṛṣṇasāra) naturally dwells, and not one brought there by force, is to be known as a land fit for sacrifice; the meaning is that any other land is a barbarian territory (mlecchadeśa) and unfit for sacrifice. || 2.23 ||
The twice-born should diligently seek refuge in these countries;
however, a Śūdra who is distressed for a livelihood may dwell in any place whatsoever. (2.24)

"Regarding these": even twice-born men born in other lands should diligently resort to these regions for the sake of performing sacrifices and because it serves an invisible (transcendental) purpose. However, a Śūdra, when oppressed by lack of livelihood, may resort to another land for the sake of subsistence. || 2.24 ||
This origin of dharma has been proclaimed to you in brief, as well as the source of all this; now learn the duties of the social classes.

"This is the source of Dharma. This has been stated briefly as the source (*yoni*) of Dharma for you. "Source" means the cause of its cognition; the meaning is that it was stated [in verse 2.6] as "the entire Veda is the root of Dharma," and so forth. Govindarāja, however, explained: "In this context, the word 'Dharma' refers to Dharma consisting of the *apūrva* (unseen potency). In the phrase 'practiced by the wise' (2.1), it is the source of that cause—the *apūrva*-type Dharma—such as the *iṣṭakā* [sacrificial bricks], and so on. Furthermore, the "origin" (*saṃbhava*) of the world has been described as its production. Now, listen to the duties of the social classes (*varṇadharma*). And the term "duties of the social classes" (*varṇadharma*) is indicative of the duties of the social classes, the duties of the stages of life (*āśramadharma*), the duties of both social class and stage of life (*varṇāśramadharma*), the duties based on specific qualities (*guṇadharma*), and the occasional duties (*naimittikadharma*). These are also mentioned in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*.

The duty of the social classes (varṇadharma) is traditionally taught first; after that, the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-dharma). Third is the duty of both class and stage (varṇāśrama-dharma), as well as the secondary (gauṇa) and occasional (naimittika) duties.
O King, that dharma which proceeds by relying upon a single caste is called the dharma of caste, such as the initiation ceremony (upanayana).
But that which, having taken recourse to a stage of life (āśrama), proceeds as a specific qualification—
that indeed is the duty of the stage of life (āśramadharma), such as the alms-bowl and the staff, and so forth.
That which functions by taking both caste and stage of life as its basis is the dharma of caste and stage (varṇāśramadharma), just as the girdle made of muñja grass is for the student.
That which proceeds by virtue of a quality is called a "quality-dharma," such as the protection of subjects by one who has been consecrated as a king.
Whatever phenomenon proceeds by depending upon a single cause is to be known as "causally produced," just like the rule for penance.

For the twice-born, the purifying refinement of the body—beginning with the rite of impregnation and performed through meritorious Vedic rituals—must be carried out for the sake of sanctification both in this world and after death. (2.26)

"By Vedic [rites]" means that, because they are rooted in the Vedas, the purification of the body for the twice-born—beginning with the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*)—must be performed by means of meritorious and auspicious Vedic rites such as the application of mantras. It is "purifying," meaning it is the cause for the destruction of sin. This is because one who has been purified is connected to the fruits of sacrifices and other rites in the next world (*pretya*), and possesses the qualification for the study of the Vedas and so forth in this world. (2.26)
From where does the origin of sin arise, such that these [rites] serve as the cause for the destruction of sin? To this he says:

"By means of the oblations performed in the womb, and by the birth-rite, the tonsure, and the tying of the girdle, the taint born of seed and the taint born of the womb are wiped away from the twice-born. (2.27)

Regarding the term "gārbhaiḥ": those rites performed for the purification of the embryo are called *gārbha*. The mention of *homa* (fire-offerings) is illustrative, since rites such as *garbhādhāna* (conception) do not take the form of a fire-oblation. That rite which, for one who has been born, consists of the consumption of clarified butter (*sarpiḥprāśana*) and so forth accompanied by mantras, is the *jātakarman* (birth-rite). *Cauḍa* is the rite of tonsure (*cūḍākaraṇa*). *Mauñjīnibandhana* is the initiation (*upanayana*). By means of these, whatever sin of the twice-born arises from the paternal seed—due to prohibited sexual intent and the like—and whatever sin is *gārbhika*, born from dwelling in the womb of an impure mother, is wiped away. (2.27)

Through private study of the Vedas, through vows, through burnt offerings, through the knowledge of the three Vedas, through sacrifices, through sons, and through the great sacrifices and other rites, this body is made fit for Brahman. (2.28)

"By study" means by the study of the Vedas. "By vows" refers to the observances such as the avoidance of honey and meat; "by oblations" refers to the *sāvitra-caru* oblations and others, as well as the morning and evening fire-sacrifices (*sāyaṃprātar-homa*). It is mentioned separately because it is not the primary element among the vows. "By sacrifice" refers to the rites consisting of the libations to gods, sages, and ancestors during the stage of studenthood (*brahmacarya*), and by the procreation of sons during the householder stage. "By the great sacrifices" refers to the five, beginning with the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*). "By sacrifices" refers to the *jyotiṣṭoma* and other such rituals. This body—meaning the self (*ātman*) as delimited by the body—is made fit for Brahman, that is, capable of attaining Brahman; for liberation is attained through the knowledge of Brahman assisted by ritual action. (2.28)
For a male child, the birth-rite (jātakarma) is ordained before the cutting of the umbilical cord;
it includes the ceremonial feeding of him with gold, honey, and clarified butter, accompanied by sacred mantras.

"Before" means that before the cutting of the umbilical cord, the sacramental rite called *jātakarman* (birth-rite) is performed for the person. At that time, he is made to consume gold, honey, and clarified butter with the mantras prescribed in his own *Gṛhya-sūtra*. (2.29)
One should have his naming ceremony performed on the tenth or the twelfth day,
or on an auspicious lunar day, at a favorable moment, or under a constellation endowed with excellent qualities.

Regarding the term "name-giving" (*nāmadheya*): since birth was introduced in the preceding verse as "the birth-rite" (*jātakarma*), it is with reference to that birth that one should personally give this infant a name on the tenth or twelfth day; or, in one's own absence, have another do so.
Alternatively, the rite of naming (*nāmakarma*) is prescribed once the period of ritual impurity (*āśauca*) has passed. (Śaṅkha 2.2)

According to this statement of Śaṅkha, it should be explained that when the tenth day has passed, it is the "eleventh day" (ekādaśāha). Even in that case, if the rite is not performed, it must be carried out on an auspicious lunar day (tithi), at an auspicious moment (muhūrta), and under a virtuous constellation (nakṣatra) as determined by astrology. The word "or" (vā) is used in the sense of restriction. 2.30.
The name of a Brāhmaṇa should be auspicious; that of a Kṣatriya, endowed with power;
that of a Vaiśya, connected with wealth; but that of a Śūdra, contemptible. (2.31)

Regarding the term "auspicious" (*maṅgalyam*): names such as *śubha*, *bala*, *vasu*, and *dīna*, which respectively signify auspiciousness, strength, wealth, and humility, should be given to Brahmins and the other castes in their proper order. (2.31)

Now he speaks for the purpose of defining the specific suffixes: "The name of a Brāhmaṇa should end in a word meaning 'happiness' (śarman); that of a Kṣatriya should be endowed with a word meaning 'protection' (rakṣā); that of a Vaiśya should be joined with a word meaning 'prosperity' (puṣṭi); and that of a Śūdra should be joined with a word meaning 'service' (preṣya). (2.32)

Regarding the rule "like [the suffixes] for a Śramaṇa and a Brāhmaṇa": for these [classes], in their respective order, the suffixes *śarman*, *rakṣā*, *puṣṭi*, and *dāsa* should be applied as secondary designations (*upapada*), such as *śarman*, *varman*, *bhūti*, and *dāsa*. Examples are: Śubhaśarman, Balavarman, Vasubhūti, and Dīnadāsa. And so says Yama: "Śarman and Deva should be used for a Brāhmaṇa; Varman and Trātṛ for a King (Kṣatriya); Bhūti and Datta for a Vaiśya; and one should cause Dāsa to be used for a Śūdra."
It is also stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"A name for a Brāhmaṇa is said to end in *śarman*, one for a Kṣatriya to be joined with *varman*,
while names ending in *gupta* or *dāsa* are recommended for Vaiśyas and Śūdras."
For women, [names] should be easy to pronounce, gentle, clear in meaning, captivating, auspicious, ending in long vowels, and containing words of benediction. (2.33)

Regarding the names of women: the name of women should be easy to pronounce, not signifying anything cruel, clearly expressive of its meaning, producing joy in the mind, auspicious in sound, ending in a long vowel, and accompanied by a word that expresses a blessing. For example: "Queen Yaśodā. (2.33)
In the fourth month, the child's first outing from the house should be performed;
in the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana), or whatever auspicious rite is desired in the family.

"In the fourth month" means that in the fourth month after the child's birth, the ceremony of going out (*niṣkramaṇa*) should be performed for the purpose of seeing the sun. Furthermore, the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*) should take place in the sixth month; or else, whatever auspicious rite is desired according to family custom should be performed, and thus the *niṣkramaṇa* may occur at a time other than the one specified. Likewise, Yama states: "Then, in the third month, the sight of the sun should be performed.

And this [rule] applies as a supplement to all remaining sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*). Therefore, the suffixes such as *śarman* for names should also be applied according to family tradition. (2.34)
The tonsure ceremony for all twice-born classes must be performed according to the dharma in either the first or the third year, as enjoined by the sacred revelation. (2.35)

Regarding the *cūḍākarma*: the performance of the tonsure ceremony (*cūdākaraṇa*) for the twice-born should, according to the law, be performed for the sake of dharma in either the first or the third year, because of the injunction of the Śruti. This is based on the indicative mark of the mantra: "Where the arrows fly together like boys with shorn hair. Thus, this is an optional alternative determined according to family custom. For this very reason, the *Āśvalāyana-gṛhya-sūtra* (1.17) states: "The tonsure ceremony is performed in the third year, or according to family custom. (2.35)
One should perform the initiation ceremony for a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception;
for a Kṣatriya, in the eleventh year from conception; and for a Vaiśya, in the twelfth year from conception. (2.36)

"Regarding the phrase *garbhāṣṭame*: the initiation (*upanayana*) of a Brāhmaṇa should be performed in the eighth year from conception. The term *upanāyana* is simply another form of *upanayana*, with the lengthening of the vowel according to Pāṇini 6.3.137 (*anyeṣām api dṛśyate*). For a Kṣatriya, it is in the eleventh year from conception; for a Vaiśya, in the twelfth year from conception. (2.36)
For a Brahmin desiring the glory of sacred knowledge, the [ceremony] should be performed in the fifth year;
for a King seeking power, in the sixth; and for a Vaiśya seeking prosperity in this world, in the eighth.

"Of one desiring *brahmavarcasa*": *Brahmavarcasa* is the splendor produced by excellence in the study of the Vedas and the knowledge of their meaning; for a Brāhmaṇa desiring that, the initiation (*upanayana*) should be performed in the fifth year from conception. For a Kṣatriya seeking the power of sovereignty such as elephants and horses, it should be in the sixth year from conception. For a Vaiśya seeking extensive activities such as agriculture, it should be in the eighth year from conception, because it is the years from conception that are under discussion here. Although a desire is not possible for a child, nevertheless, the father's own desire for the fruit residing in the child is figuratively attributed to the child himself. (2.37)
The Sāvitrī does not expire for a Brāhmaṇa until the sixteenth year;
for a Kṣatriya until the twenty-second; and for a Vaiśya until the twenty-fourth. (2.38)

"Up to the sixteenth year"—here the prefix *āṅ* denotes inclusion (*abhividhi*). Since it is intended that for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, the doubling of the previously stated ages of eight, eleven, and twelve years respectively should apply, the initiation (*upanayana*) for the sake of the *Sāvitrī* does not exceed its prescribed time for a Brāhmaṇa until the end of the sixteenth year, for a Kṣatriya until the end of the twenty-second year, and for a Vaiśya until the end of the twenty-fourth year. Here, the prefix *āṅ* denotes a limit (*maryādā*). Some explain this by reference to the statement of Yama; and thus says Yama:
He for whom the Sāvitrī has fallen for fifteen years—
specifically in the case of a Brāhmaṇa, and likewise for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya— is an outcast.
The glorious Yama, the son of Vivasvat, the best among speakers and knower of the true principles of dharma and worldly affairs, declared the expiation for these.
Having performed a tonsure including the top-knot, he should observe the vow with a concentrated mind;
he should feed seven or five Brahmins food consisting of sacrificial oblations (haviṣya).
Beyond this time, all three of these, having failed to perform the consecration at the proper time, become Vrātyas fallen from the Sāvitrī, despised by the Āryas. (2.39)

"Beyond this" means as follows: these [classes], beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, have specific secondary (*anukalpika*) times for initiation (*upanayana*) prescribed according to their respective periods, extending up to the age of sixteen and so forth. Those who remain uninitiated beyond that time become fallen from the *Sāvitrī*, deprived of initiation, and despised by the learned; they are designated as *vrātyas*. The purpose of this designation is to establish legal status through such rules as, "Having performed a sacrifice for *vrātyas*... (11.197). || 2.39 ||
A Brāhmaṇa should never, even in times of distress, enter into spiritual or matrimonial alliances with those who have not been purified according to the prescribed rules. (2.40)

"Not with these" means that a Brāhmaṇa should never perform social connections—such as teaching, giving a daughter in marriage, and so forth—even in times of distress, with these impure Vrātyas who have not performed the penance according to the rule. (2.40)
The students of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin) shall wear, in their respective order, skins of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, and the goat, as well as garments made of hemp, flax, and wool. 2.41.

Regarding the phrase "clothes made of the skins of black antelope, Ruru deer, and goat": although the term *kārṣṇa* (black) does not specify a particular species, the black antelope (*kṛṣṇamṛga*) is understood here because of its association with the Ruru deer and because of the statement of Āpastamba: "The upper garment of a Brāhmaṇa should be that of a black antelope, a Ruru deer, or a deer. Thus, the skins of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, and the goat are to be worn as upper garments by the religious student (*brahmacārin*), according to the Gṛhya rule: "The skins are the upper garments. Likewise, the Brāhmaṇas and the other classes shall respectively wear lower garments made of hemp, flax, and sheep’s wool. || 2.41 ||
The girdle of a Brahmin should be made of muñja grass, triple-stranded, even, and smooth;
that of a Kṣatriya, however, should be a bowstring made of mūrvā fiber; and that of a Vaiśya, a cord woven from hemp.

Regarding the *mauñjī*: a girdle made of *muñja* grass, consisting of three equal strands (*triguṇā*) woven from three equal threads and pleasant to the touch, should be made for a Brāhmaṇa. For a Kṣatriya, the girdle is made of *mūrvā* fiber, in the form of a bowstring (*jyā*). Because it would lose its status as a string if it were not so, Medhātithi and Govindarāja maintain that it does not possess the quality of being "threefold" (*trivṛt*). For a Vaiśya, it is made of hemp thread (*śaṇasūtra*). Here, the requirement of being threefold certainly persists, because Pracetas has stated generally: "The girdles are threefold and twisted to the right. (2.42)
If muñja grass is unavailable, however, they should be made from kuśa, aśmantaka, or balvaja;
they should have three strands and a single knot, or three, or even five. (2.43)

Regarding the phrase "in the absence of muñja grass": because of the use of the plural number in the word *kartavyāḥ* ("should be made") and because three types of religious students (*brahmacārin*) are under discussion, it should be understood that since the requirement [for a girdle] is equal for all three in the event of the primary material being unavailable, the injunctions for the three alternatives beginning with *kauśa* apply when muñja is not found. Thus, the plural form *kartavyāḥ* is more appropriate. Medhātithi, who explains [the girdles] as being connected to different castes, also accepts the reading in the plural. In the absence of muñja and the others, the three classes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa should respectively make their girdles from specific types of grass beginning with *kuśa*. These should be triple-stranded and provided with one knot, or else with three or five knots. Here, because of the mention of the word "or" (*vā*), the knots are not to be associated with the Brāhmaṇas and the other classes in a fixed order; rather, there is an option (*vikalpa*) in every case according to family custom. This distinction regarding the number of knots should be understood as depending on whether the primary or secondary materials are available. (2.43)
The sacred thread of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of cotton, twisted upward and triple-stranded;
that of a Kṣatriya should be made of hempen threads, and that of a Vaiśya of woolen threads.

"Made of cotton" (*kārpāsam*): that whose specific arrangement he will later call by the name *upavīta*—that [thread] belonging to the Brāhmaṇa as its substrate is made of cotton; for the Kṣatriya it is made of hemp fibers; for the Vaiśya it is made from the wool of sheep. "Threefold" (*trivṛt*): having made it three-stranded, it is wound upwards, turned to the right. And this [term] is connected with everything [that follows]. Although Manu has stated that the three strands themselves are wound upwards, nevertheless, having tripled those [strands], they should be made threefold by being wound downwards. This is stated in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*:
The upper part should be made triple, with three threads wound downward;
the sacred thread (upavīta) should be tripled, and for it, a single knot is prescribed.
Devala also said:
"One should make the sacrificial thread (yajñopavīta) with nine threads as its strands."
According to the law, a Brāhmaṇa deserves staffs made of Bilva or Palāśa wood; a Kṣatriya, of Vaṭa or Khadira; and a Vaiśya, of Pīlu or Udumbara. (2.45)

Regarding the term "Brāhmaṇa": although it might be understood from the use of a copulative compound (*dvandva*) that the carrying [of the staff] must also be performed in combination, nevertheless—because singularity is intended in the injunctions such as "the Brāhmaṇa’s staff should be made to reach the hairline" (2.46) and likewise "having taken the desired staff" (2.48), and because the *Vasiṣṭha-smṛti* shows an option with the words "the staff may be of *bilva* or *pālāśa* wood"—only a single staff is connected to one Brāhmaṇa through its being split or unsplit; thus, the combination is restated by means of the copulative compound. The Brāhmaṇas and others are entitled to perform the duties to be described using two staves each, according to their respective options. (2.45)
The staff of a Brāhmaṇa should be made according to the measurement reaching to the hairline; that of a Kṣatriya should reach the forehead, and that of a Vaiśya should reach the nose. (2.46)
"Reaching the hair" means that the staffs of the Brahmins and others should be made according to the sequence of measurements ending at the hair, the forehead, and the nose.
All of them should be straight, without blemishes, and pleasant to behold;
they should not cause alarm to men, possessing their bark intact and being undamaged by fire. (2.47)
"Upright" means that those staffs should be without blemishes, uninjured, of beautiful appearance, covered with bark, and free from burns by fire. || 2.47 ||
And he says that they must not cause distress to living beings:
"Having taken up his desired staff and having stood before the sun, and having circumambulated the fire clockwise, he should go about for alms according to the rule. (2.48)

"Having accepted what is desired": having taken up the staff characterized as previously described and which is desired for attainment, and having stood facing the sun and circumambulated the fire, he should beg for alms according to the rule. 2.48.
An initiated man of the highest twice-born class should go for alms using "bhavat" at the beginning;
a Kṣatriya, however, should place it in the middle; and a Vaiśya, at the end. (2.49)

Regarding the word *bhavat*: a Brāhmaṇa should utter the sentence for begging alms preceded by the word *bhavat*, as in, "O sir (*bhavati*), give alms. A Kṣatriya [should use] the word *bhavat* in the middle, as in, "Sir, give alms (*bhikṣāṃ bhavati dehi*). A Vaiśya [should use] the word *bhavat* at the end, as in, "Give alms, sir (*bhikṣāṃ dehi bhavati*)" (2.49).
One should first beg for alms from one's mother, or a sister, or one's own maternal aunt—whichever among these would not treat him with contempt. (2.50)

"Or from his mother": for the alms that constitute a limb of the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), he should first beg from his mother, or his sister, or his mother’s sister born of the same womb—whichever does not treat this religious student (*brahmacārin*) with contempt by refusing him. In the absence of the former, the latter is to be accepted. 2.50.
Having collected that alms-food, as much as there is of food, without guile, he should offer it to his teacher; then, having sipped water, being pure and facing the east, he should eat. 2.51.

Regarding the phrase "having brought together": having brought that food from many sources, and having offered to the teacher as much food as is appropriate for his satisfaction, he should do so without guile—that is, not concealing inferior food with superior food under the thought, "The teacher will accept this. Having been permitted by him and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), being pure, he should eat facing the east.
Now he describes eating for specific desires:
"One who eats facing east gains long life; one facing south gains fame;
one facing west gains prosperity; and indeed, one facing north eats according to truth. (2.52)

"Conducive to long life" (āyuṣyam): one who desires long life eats facing the east, for food is beneficial for longevity; the meaning is that one who desires long life eats facing the east. That which is conducive to fame, he eats facing the south. Desiring prosperity, he faces west. Desiring *ṛta*—that is, truth—and its fruit, he should eat facing north. (2.52)
Having sipped water, a twice-born man should always eat his food with a concentrated mind;
having eaten, he should likewise sip water properly and touch the cavities of his head with water.
