Regarding the phrase "having touched": although sipping water (*ācamana*) before eating is prescribed by the rule, "Having offered [the food] to the teacher, one should eat after sipping water" (2.51), the statement "he should touch the apertures with water" is a restatement for the purpose of enjoining an ancillary detail (*guṇavidhāna*). A twice-born man should always eat his food after sipping water, even when it follows immediately upon the period of studenthood (*brahmacarya*). Being composed, meaning single-minded, he should sip water after eating. "Properly" means according to the scriptures. By that [rule], having washed both hands and feet, he should drink water three times that has been inspected.

This also includes what has been stated by Dakṣa and others: one should touch with water the cavities, the sense organs, and the six apertures; and these should be understood as being located in the head, such as the nose, eyes, ears, and so forth, according to the statement of Gautama: "And one should touch the apertures situated in the head. Since there is a separate injunction stating that after performing the *upasparśana* (sipping) one should touch the cavities, it is shown that *ācamana* consists merely of drinking water three times, while the touching of the cavities and so forth constitutes the specific procedure (*itikartavyatā*). 2.53.
One should always honor one's food and eat it without disparaging it;
upon seeing it, one should rejoice, be gracious, and welcome it in every way. (2.54)

"One should worship food": one should always worship food and meditate upon it as being for the sake of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). This has been stated in the *Ādipurāṇa*, following the verse "Viṣṇu himself declared that food [is me]," in the passage: "One should always meditate on me as being for the sake of the vital breaths; he who does so would always be worshipping me.
Without disparaging it, one should eat this, and having seen it, one should rejoice and be gracious."

One should also abandon weariness upon seeing food. One should always offer a greeting by saying, "May this be for us," which constitutes both salutation and a response to the greeting. As it is said in the *Ādipurāṇa*:
"Having seen the food, one should first bow down; then, with palms joined in reverence, one should say:
'May this be for us always. Thus praising with devotion, one should bow."
In every way, all food. 2.54.
For food that is always honored bestows strength and vigor;
but when eaten without honor, it destroys both of these. (2.55)

Regarding the phrase "honored": since honored food bestows capacity and vigor, whereas unhonored food destroys both of these, this statement of the result—"therefore one should always honor food"—forms a single syntactical unit with the preceding injunction. Just as the destruction of accumulated sins occurs through the *saṃdhyā* salutation and other rites, the scriptural mandate for what is obligatory (*nitya*) remains uncontradicted even when it is presented as an object of desire; for there is no conflict with the scriptural mandate of obligation. Medhātithi and Govindarāja, however, maintain that the mention of the result is for the purpose of praise (*stuti*). (2.55)
One should not give the remains of one's food to anyone, nor should one eat between the prescribed meals; one should not overeat, nor should one go anywhere while still impure from eating.

"Not the leavings": one should not give the remains of what has been eaten to anyone. When the fourth case-ending (*caturthī*) would have applied, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used because only the relationship [of "belonging to"] is intended to be expressed. Since the prohibition against giving leavings to a Śūdra is already established by this general prohibition, the specific prohibition regarding Śūdras in the verse "not the leavings, nor that which has been offered as an oblation" (4.80) is for the purpose of being a vow (*vrata*) for the Snātaka of the fourth stage. One should not eat between the two meals of morning and evening, nor should one overeat even during those two times. The instruction "one should not practice excessive satiety" is for the purpose of being a vow for the Snātaka of the fourth stage. Being in a state of impurity from eating, one should not go anywhere. (2.56)

He states the fault in overeating: "Overeating is detrimental to health, detrimental to longevity, and detrimental to rebirth in heaven; it is non-meritorious and loathed by the world; therefore, one should avoid it. (2.57)

"Unwholesome" (*anārogya*): health (*ārogya*) is the absence of disease; that which is beneficial for it is "wholesome. That which is beneficial for life is "life-sustaining" (*āyuṣya*). Since overeating results in both unwholesomeness and a lack of life-sustenance—because, by producing indigestion, it is a cause of disease and death—it is also "not conducive to heaven" (*asvargya*), because it is opposed to sacrifices and other rites that are the causes of heaven. It is "meritless" (*apuṇya*), because it is the opposite of other merits. It is "hated by the world," because it is censured by people due to excessive gluttony. Therefore, one should not do that. (2.57)
A Brahmin should always perform the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśet) using the Brāhma tīrtha; he may also use the Kāya or Traidaśika tīrthas, but never the Pitrya. 2.58.

Regarding the term *brāhmeṇa*: this designation "Brāhma" and so forth is used in the treatise for the sake of conventional usage and for the sake of praise; however, a primary state of having Brahman as its deity is not possible here, because [the act] does not have the nature of a sacrifice (*yāga*). The word *tīrtha* is also applied due to its connection with the quality of purifying (*pāvana*). A Brāhmaṇa or other [twice-born] person should always perform the sipping of water (*ācamana*) by means of the Brāhma *tīrtha*. [The suffix] *-ika* in *traidaśika* means "belonging to that," referring to Prajāpati; his body is [meant], and the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.3.120, with the vowel *i* as a substitute for the final syllable. Alternatively, *traidaśika* refers to the god [Indra] belonging to those two [Prajāpati and Agni]. One should never perform the sipping of water by means of the *pitrya* *tīrtha*, because it is not established [for such use]. (2.58)
He states the sacred sites beginning with that of Brahmā: "They declare the base of the thumb to be the Brāhma-tīrtha;
the Kāya-tīrtha is at the roots of the fingers, the Daiva-tīrtha at their tips, and the Pitrya-tīrtha below those two. (2.59)

Regarding the phrase "at the base of the thumb": Manu and others declare that the *brāhma* sacred site (*tīrtha*) is on the lower part of the base of the thumb; the *kāya* sacred site is at the base of the little finger; the *daiva* sacred site is at the tips of the fingers; and the *pitrya* sacred site is between the thumb and the forefinger. Although the *kāya* sacred site is said to be at the base of the fingers, and in the phrase "below those two" only the fingers in general are mentioned, nevertheless, a specific location is determined by another legal text (*smṛti*). Thus says Yājñavalkya (2.19):
"The bases of the little finger, the forefinger, and the thumb, and the tip of the hand—these are, in order, the sacred sites of Prajāpati, the Pitṛs, Brahmā, and the Devas."
He states the sequence for performing the sipping of water (ācamana) which was taught in general terms:
"One should first sip water three times, then wipe the mouth twice; one should touch the apertures with water, as well as the self and the head. (2.60)

"One should sip water three times": first, one should drink three mouthfuls of water by means of the *brāhma* and other *tīrthas*; immediately thereafter, having closed the lips, one should wipe them twice with the base of the thumb;
then, having closed [the lips], one should wipe the face twice with the base of the thumb.

Thus, because of this specific statement by Dakṣa, one should touch the *khāni*—the sense organs—with water. Due to the proximity of the word "mouth" (*mukhya*), these refer specifically to the apertures of the mouth. Gautama also says: "And one should touch the apertures of the head. Since the Upaniṣads state that the Self resides in the region of the heart—as in "The person is the inner light within the heart" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7)—one should touch the Self, the heart, and the head with water alone. (2.60)
One who knows the Dharma and desires purity should always sip water that is neither hot nor frothy, using the proper part of the hand, in a secluded place, facing either the east or the north. (2.61)

"By non-hot [waters]" means by those that have not been made warm and are free from foam. "Desiring purity through the *brāhma* and other *tīrthas*" means in a clean place, secluded and not crowded with people. One should always sip water (*ācamana*) facing either the east or the north. Since Āpastamba states, "And by hot [water] for a specific reason," one should not sip water except when there is a cause such as illness; however, in cases of illness and the like, there is no fault in sipping water with heated water. The *tīrtha* is mentioned again, despite having been stated previously, in order to show that there is no purity if one sips water without using the *tīrtha*. (2.61)

He states the quantity of water for sipping (ācamana): "A Brahmin is purified by water reaching the heart; a Kṣatriya, by water reaching the throat; a Vaiśya, by water that has been swallowed; and a Śūdra, by water merely touched at the extremity. (2.62)

Regarding the phrase "with [water] reaching the heart": a Brāhmaṇa becomes pure with water that reaches the heart; a Kṣatriya, with water reaching the throat; a Vaiśya, with water that has entered the interior of the mouth; and a Śūdra becomes pure with water touched even by the edge of the tongue and lips. In the word *antataḥ*, the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the third case (instrumental). 2.62.

In order to demonstrate that the sacred thread (*upavīta*) is an ancillary part of the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*), he first states its definition; then, by way of context, he provides the definitions for the *prācīnāvīta* and *nivīta* modes of wearing it:
"When the right arm is raised, the twice-born is said to be in the *upavīta* mode;
when the left is raised, he is in the *prācīnāvīta* mode; and when it hangs from the neck, he is in the *nivīta* mode. (2.63)

Regarding the term *uddhṛte*: when the right arm is raised and the sacred thread (*yajñasūtra*) or garment is placed upon the left shoulder with its end hanging down over the right shoulder, the twice-born is called *upavītī*. When the left arm is raised and it is placed upon the right shoulder with its end hanging down over the left shoulder, he is called *prācīnāvītī*. The word *savye* (on the left) in the phrase *prācīnāvītī* is stated for the sake of metrical convenience. Thus Gobhila says: "Having raised the right arm and placed it below the head, he settles it on the left shoulder; the end hangs down over the right shoulder, and in this way he becomes *upavītī*. Having raised the left arm and placed it below the head, he settles it on the right shoulder; the end hangs down under the left armpit, and in this way he becomes *prācīnāvītī*. *Nivītī* means [the thread] is suspended from the neck. That is to say, when the head is placed [below the raised arm] and even the right hand or other limb is not raised, but the sacred thread or garment is suspended directly from the neck and hangs straight down, one is *nivītī*. || 2.63 ||
Having thrown the girdle, the antelope skin, the staff, the sacrificial thread, and the water-pot into the water when they are worn out, he should take others with the appropriate mantras. (2.64)

Regarding the girdle (*mekhalā*): if the girdle and other such items are ruined, broken, or torn, one should cast them into water and take up others with the mantras prescribed in their respective *Gṛhya-sūtras*. || 2.64 ||
The tonsure ceremony (keśānta) is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa in the sixteenth year;
for a member of the royal caste (rājanya) in the twenty-second, and for a Vaiśya two years after that. (2.65)

Regarding the term *keśānta*: the sacrament known as *keśānta*, as prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras, should be performed for a Brāhmaṇa in the sixteenth year from conception, for a Kṣatriya in the twenty-second year from conception, and for a Vaiśya two years after that, in the twenty-fourth year from conception, according to the statement of Baudhāyana: "The number of years is counted from conception. (2.65)
This entire series of rites for women, however, should be performed without omission, for the sake of consecrating the body, at the proper time and in the proper order. (2.66)

"Without mantras": this sequence of rites, beginning with the birth-ceremony (*jātakarma*) and including the entire collection of rituals, must be performed for women without mantras for the purpose of purifying the body, according to the complete order of times previously stated. (2.66)
Since this [rule for initiation] would also apply to marriage, he states the distinction: "The Vedic rite of marriage is declared to be the sacrament (*saṃskāra*) for women;
service to the husband is their residence with the teacher, and household duties are their tending of the sacred fires. (2.67)

Regarding the term *vaivāhika*: the marriage rite itself is recorded by Manu and others as the Vedic sacrament (*saṃskāra*) for women, corresponding to the initiation (*upanayana*). Service to the husband corresponds to residence in the teacher’s house (*gurukula*) for the purpose of Vedic study. Household duties correspond to the service of the sacred fire (*agniparicaryā*), consisting of the offering of fuel at dawn and dusk. Therefore, because marriage and other such rites are prescribed in place of initiation, there is a cessation of initiation and the like. (2.67)
This has been declared as the sacred rite of initiation for the twice-born, which manifests their true birth; now learn the application of ritual action.

Regarding the word "eṣa" (this): the term *aupanāyanika* involves a vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) in both parts of the compound according to the rule for the *anuśatikādi* group. This collection of rites related to the initiation (*upanayana*) of the twice-born has been described as the indicator of the second birth, which follows from [the first] birth. (2.68)

Now, listen to the ritual by which the one who has been initiated is to be joined [to his duties]; thus he says: "Having initiated the pupil, the teacher should first instruct him in purity, as well as in proper conduct, the fire-ritual, and the twilight worship. (2.69)

"Having initiated [the pupil], the teacher... [means as follows: Having initiated the pupil, the teacher should first instruct him in the purification rites—beginning with "one [application of earth] on the penis and three on the anus" (5.136)—as well as the conduct of bathing, sipping water, and so forth; the performance of the fire-oblation (*samid-dhoma*) in the evening and morning; and the procedure for the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*) accompanied by mantras. (2.39)

But when about to be instructed, having sipped water according to the scriptures, facing north, with palms joined in the *brahmāñjali* gesture, wearing light clothing, and with senses subdued, he should be taught. (2.70)

Regarding the term *adhyeṣyamāṇa*: a student who is about to engage in study should be taught by the teacher after he has performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) according to the scriptures, facing north, with palms joined in reverence (*añjali*), wearing pure garments, and having restrained his senses. According to the statement of Gautama, "The teacher facing east and the student from the south, or [the teacher] facing north," study may also be conducted with the teacher facing east. The compound *brahmāñjalikṛta* follows the rule *vāhitāgnyādiṣu* (Pāṇini 2.2.37), which allows for the placement of the word *kṛta* at the end of the compound. 2.70.
At the beginning and at the end of Vedic recitation, one should always clasp the feet of the teacher;
having joined the palms together, one should study, for that is known as the *brahmāñjali*. (2.71)

"At the beginning and at the end of the Veda": when the commencement of Vedic study is to be made and when its completion has been performed, one must perform the clasping of the teacher's feet. Having joined and pressed the two hands together, one should study; for this is the explanation of the meaning of the term *brahmāñjali* mentioned in the preceding verse: "That indeed is known as the *brahmāñjali*. (2.71)
The salutation of the teacher must be performed with crossed hands:
the left [foot] is to be touched with the left [hand], and the right [foot] with the right [hand]. (2.72)

Regarding the phrase "with crossed hands": it was stated immediately prior that the clasping of the feet must be performed; this is now prescribed as being done with crossed hands. As to what kind of crossing should be performed, he says: the left foot of the teacher is to be touched with the left hand, and the right foot with the right hand. Furthermore, this touching of the feet must be done with both hands turned palms-upward. As Paiṭhīnasi says:

With palms turned upward, one should salute the right foot with the right hand and the left foot with the left hand; or, according to the practice of the learned, there may be a reversal by placing the right hand on top.
But when the pupil is about to begin his studies, the teacher, always alert and untiring, should say, "Recite, sir! and he should stop when [the pupil] says, "May there be a pause. (2.73)

Regarding the phrase "about to study": whenever a disciple is about to engage in study, the teacher, being always free from indolence, should first say, "Recite, sir! At the conclusion, having said, "May there be a pause," he should cease and desist. (2.73)
One should always place the *praṇava* at the beginning and at the end of the *brahman*.
That which is not preceded by the *oṃ* flows away, and that which is not followed by it falls apart at the outset. (2.74)

"The Praṇava of Brahman. At the beginning of the study of the Veda—that is, of the Brahman—one should utter the syllable Om at the commencement and at the conclusion of the recitation. For that which has not been preceded by the syllable Om flows away, perishing gradually; that which is not preceded by it falls apart and fails to attain stability. (2.74)
Seated upon grass-blades pointing eastward, purified by means of purifiers,
and cleansed by three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), he then becomes worthy of the syllable Om.

"Facing eastward" means: seated upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing eastward, purified by *pavitra* blades of *kuśa* held in both hands, and rendered pure by three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) of fifteen *mātrās* each—according to the traditional teaching of Gautama: "Three breath-restraints consist of fifteen *mātrās*" (1.49)—and where a *mātrā* is the duration of a short syllable such as the letter 'a'. Thereafter, he is entitled to the syllable *oṃ* for the purpose of study. (2.75)
Prajāpati milked forth from the three Vedas the syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m*, as well as the words *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*. (2.76)

"And the letter *a*": this is a supplement to what will be said in [2.44], "this syllable and this [Veda]. From the three Vedas—characterized as the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma—he milked out, that is, extracted, in due order, the letter *a*, the letter *u*, and the letter *m*, which constitute the parts of the *praṇava*, as well as the three *vyāhṛtis*: *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*. || 2.76 ||
From the three Vedas alone, Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati milked out foot by foot that [verse] beginning with "Tat" from this Sāvitrī. (2.77)

"From the three alone": likewise, from the three Vedas—the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman—the Brahman priest drew out the three feet of the Sāvitrī, which were recited by way of their opening phrases as "tad," "ṛc," and "iti. He who stands in the highest place is Parameṣṭhin. (2.77)
Therefore, for this reason:
"The Brahmin who knows the Veda, by muttering this syllable and these [Vyāhṛtis] preceded by the Vyāhṛtis at the two twilights, becomes endowed with the merit of the Veda. (2.78)

"This syllable" means this syllable in the form of Oṃ; and the injunction is to be inferred that one should recite this three-footed Sāvitrī preceded by the three Vyāhṛtis—at the time of the twilight prayers—the Sāvitrī accompanied by the Praṇava and the three Vyāhṛtis. (2.78)
But by practicing this triad externally a thousand times,
a twice-born man is freed from even great sin within a month, just as a snake is freed from its skin.

Regarding the phrase "a thousand times": at the twilight (saṃdhyā), or at another time, having recited this aforementioned triad—consisting of the Praṇava, the three Vyāhṛtis, and the Sāvitrī—a thousand times outside the village, such as on a riverbank or in the forest, one is released even from great sin, just as a snake sheds its skin. Therefore, although it is not part of the immediate context, it is stated here for the sake of brevity that this should be recited for the purpose of destroying sin; otherwise, the recitation of these three would have to be performed again elsewhere. || 2.79 ||
One who is deprived of this Ṛc, as well as of his own timely ritual action, though born of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya lineage, incurs censure among the virtuous. (2.80)

"By this verse... [The commentary explains: At the twilight (saṃdhyā), or at other times, one who is "separated from this verse"—that is, one who has abandoned the recitation of the Sāvitrī—whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or even a Vaiśya, incurs censure among virtuous people for having abandoned his own duties, such as the morning and evening fire-oblations (homa) and so forth, at their proper time. Therefore, one should not abandon the recitation of the Sāvitrī nor one's own duties at their proper time. || 2.80 ||
The three imperishable great utterances preceded by the syllable Oṃ, together with the three-footed Sāvitrī, should be known as the mouth of Brahman. (2.81)

"Preceded by the syllable *oṃ*": the three *vyāhṛtis*, namely *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*, preceded by the syllable *oṃ*, are imperishable because they have as their fruit the attainment of the Brahman consisting of the syllables (*akṣara-brahman*). And the three-footed *Sāvitrī* is the mouth—the beginning—of the Brahman, that is, the Veda, because the study of the Veda begins with it. Alternatively, this [set of mantras] is the door to the attainment of the Brahman, the Supreme Self; for one who has become free from sin through study, recitation, and so forth, liberation is attained through the excellence of the knowledge of Brahman. (2.81)
Therefore, he says:
"He who studies this day after day for three years without sloth, becoming like the wind and possessing a form of space, attains the supreme Brahman. (2.82)

Regarding the phrase "he who has studied": he who, being diligent, studies the Sāvitrī together with the Praṇava and the Vyāhṛtis for three years, goes toward the Supreme Brahman. He becomes like the wind; like the wind, he is born able to move at will. Since space is Brahman and that indeed is his form, he becomes one whose form is space (khamūrtimān); even upon the destruction of the body, he becomes Brahman itself. || 2.82 ||
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath control is the highest austerity;
there is nothing superior to the Sāvitrī; and truth excels silence. (2.83)

"Ekākṣaram" (the single syllable): the single syllable is the syllable *oṃ*, which is the Supreme Brahman, because it is the cause for attaining the Supreme Brahman. For by the recitation (*japa*) of the syllable *oṃ* and by the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of its meaning—the Supreme Brahman—one attains it. Prāṇāyāmas performed with three repetitions of the *Gāyatrī* mantra, together with the *praṇava*, the *savyāhṛtis*, and the *śiras*, constitute a supreme austerity even compared to the *Cāndrāyaṇa* and other penances. By the use of the plural number in the word "prāṇāyāmāḥ," it is stated that three [repetitions] must necessarily be performed. There is no other collection of mantras superior to the *Sāvitrī*. Truth excels speech even over silence. Through the praise of these four, an injunction is inferred that these four are to be practiced. However, Dharaṇīdhara reads: "The single syllable is the Supreme Brahman; prāṇāyāma is the supreme austerity," and explains it thus: "That whose supreme [object] is the single syllable is 'ekākṣaraparam'; likewise for 'prāṇāyāmaparam'."
Since it was not written down by the elders beginning with Medhātithi, Dharaṇīdhara, being independent, has recorded a different reading there. (2.83)
All Vedic rites of oblation and sacrifice flow away;
but the Imperishable is to be known as the Imperishable, as Brahman, and indeed as Prajāpati.

"They perish" means that all ritual actions prescribed by the Vedas, such as oblations (*homa*) and sacrifices (*yāga*), perish both in their own nature and in their results. The "Imperishable" (*akṣara*), however, is in the form of the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*); it is imperishable because it is the cause for attaining Brahman, being imperishable by way of its result, since the state of becoming one with Brahman is indestructible. To the question, "How is this the cause for attaining Brahman?", he says: "And indeed Brahman. The word "and" (*ca*) indicates a reason. Because that which is the Lord of creatures (*prajāpati*) is Brahman, that very thing is this *oṃkāra*. Its status as Brahman is due to its nature as the indicator of Brahman. Thus, it has been shown that whether by way of both [its nature and its indication] or simply as the indicator of Brahman, when worshipped during the time of recitation (*japa*), this is the cause of liberation. (2.84)
The sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) is ten times superior to the ritual sacrifice (vidhiyajña);
the whispered recitation (upāṃśu) is a hundredfold more effective, and the mental recitation (mānasa) is declared to be a thousandfold.

Regarding the phrase "than the ritual sacrifice" (*vidhiyajñāt*): a sacrifice that falls within the scope of prescribed injunctions is a "ritual sacrifice," such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and others. Compared to that, the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) of the aforementioned *praṇava* and other mantras is ten times superior. If that too is performed in a whisper (*upāṃśu*), then it is a hundred times superior. That which another person cannot hear even when standing nearby is whispered. However, mental recitation (*mānasa*) is a thousand times superior. That in which the tongue and lips do not move even slightly is mental. (2.75)

The four types of cooked sacrifices (pākayajña), together with the ritual sacrifices (vidhiyajña), all of them do not equal even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of silent recitation (japayajña). || 2.86 ||

"Those which are called *pākayajñas*": the other four *pākayajñas* included within the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*)—consisting of the *vaiśvadeva* oblation, the *balikarman*, the daily *śrāddha*, and the feeding of guests—are *vidhiyajñas* such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and others; together with them, they do not attain even a sixteenth part of the *japayajña*. The meaning is that they are not equal to even a sixteenth portion of the *japayajña*. (2.86)
A Brahmin shall attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt about this.
Whether he performs other rites or does not perform them, one who is friendly toward all is called a Brahmin. (2.87)

"By recitation alone": A Brāhmaṇa attains accomplishment free from doubt through recitation alone; he becomes fit for the attainment of liberation. Whether he performs other Vedic rites such as sacrifices or not is irrelevant. For it is stated in the Āgamas that "the Brāhmaṇa is *maitra* (friendly), belonging to Brahman, and merges into Brahman. *Maitra* means "one who is a friend" (*mitra*); the suffix *aṇ* is used here in its own sense. Since in sacrifices and the like there is no possibility of being dear to all living beings due to the killing of animals, seeds, and so forth, this is a praise of recitation—stating that even without sacrifice and the like, one crosses over by being devoted to the recitation of the *praṇava* and other mantras—but it is not a prohibition of sacrifices and the like, since they too are prescribed by the scriptures. (2.87)
Now he describes the restraint of the senses, which is to be practiced by all social classes and is conducive to the attainment of all human goals:
"A wise man should exert effort in restraining the senses as they wander among alluring objects, just as a charioteer restrains his horses. (2.88)

Regarding "of the senses": one should exert effort in restraint toward the senses—which by their very nature tend to carry one away toward sense objects—by knowing the defects of objects such as their perishability, just as a charioteer exerts effort over the horses yoked to his chariot. 2.88.
I shall correctly explain, in due order and as they truly are, those eleven faculties which the wise of old have taught. (2.89)

Regarding the "eleven": those eleven faculties which the former scholars have mentioned, I shall explain them all in order, both by name and by function, for the sake of the instruction of later generations. (2.89)
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth; the anus, the generative organ, the hands, the feet, and speech is recorded as the tenth. (2.90)

Regarding the term "ear": among those eleven [senses], these ten beginning with the ear are designated by name as the external sense organs (*bahirindriya*). As for "anus, genitals, hands, and feet," because they form a dual compound of animal parts according to Pāṇini 2.4.2—"And [a dual compound] of the limbs of living beings, musical instruments, and armies"—they are treated as a singular unit. (2.90)
Of these, the five sense organs are the ear and so forth in their respective order;
the five organs of action are said to be the anus and so forth. (2.91)

Regarding the phrase "the organs of cognition": among these ten, the five beginning with the ear are called the *buddhīndriyas* (organs of cognition) because they are instruments (*karaṇa*) of cognition, as stated in their respective order. Those who know [this] declare that the [five] beginning with the organ of speech are the *karmendriyas* (organs of action) because they are instruments for actions such as excretion and so forth.
The eleventh is to be known as the mind (manas), which by its own quality partakes of the nature of both;
when it is conquered, these two groups of five become conquered.

"Eleventh": the internal organ (*antarindriya*) in the form of the mind (*manas*), which completes the number eleven, is to be understood. By its own quality, namely the nature of volition (*saṃkalpa*), it is the driver of both groups of organs. For this very reason, when the mind is conquered, both pentads—the group of the sense organs (*buddhīndriya*) and the group of the organs of action (*karmendriya*)—are also conquered. Regarding the term "pentads" (*pañcaka*): following the rule *tad asya parimāṇam* (Pāṇini 5.1.57), the suffix *ka* is applied by *saṃkhyāyāḥ saṃjñāsaṅghasūtrādhyayaneṣu* (Pāṇini 5.1.58) in the sense of a collection measured by the number five. (2.92)
Since the activity of the senses generally has its root in the mental construction of objects, one might ask: for what purpose should the restraint of the senses be practiced? To this, he says:
"By attachment to the senses, one undoubtedly incurs fault; but by thoroughly restraining them, one attains perfection. (2.93)

Regarding the phrase "of the senses": because through attachment to the objects of the senses one undoubtedly incurs both seen and unseen faults, yet by properly restraining those very same senses one attains success in the form of fitness for the human goals such as liberation; therefore, the ellipsis is that one should practice restraint of the senses. (2.93)
Anticipating the objection that one might turn away from the enjoyment of sense objects through the restraint of the senses because one’s desire has not been fulfilled, he says:
Desire for sense objects is never quenched by the enjoyment of those objects;
rather, it increases all the more, like a fire fed with clarified butter. (2.94)

"Never" means: desire—that is, longing; for "desires" (*kāma*) are so called because they are desired, namely the sense-objects. Desire is never satisfied by the enjoyment of those objects; rather, like fire with clarified butter, it increases more and more. This is because even for one who has obtained enjoyment, a longing for even greater enjoyment is observed day after day. For this very reason, there is the statement of Yayāti in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"What rice, barley, gold, cattle, and women exist on earth—none of that is sufficient for even one person; therefore, one should abandon excessive thirst."
Likewise: "For a full thousand years my mind was attached to sense-objects; yet even so, thirst did not subside, for it arises toward those very same things. (2.94)
Between one who might attain all these things and one who might renounce them entirely, the renunciation of all desires is superior to their attainment. (2.95)

Regarding the phrase "and he who [attains these]": suppose one person were to obtain all these objects of the senses, while another were to remain indifferent toward these desires; of these two, the one who is indifferent to the objects is superior. Therefore, compared to the attainment of all desires, indifference toward them is more praiseworthy. For instance, for one who is greedy for sense-objects, there arises great hardship in procuring their means, and in the event of misfortune, there is an excess of suffering; this is not the case, however, for one who has become disenchanted with sense-objects. (2.95)

Now he states the means for the restraint of the senses: "These [senses], being intensely attached to their objects, cannot be restrained so effectively by non-indulgence as they can by constant knowledge. (2.96)

"Not so. These senses, being attached to their objects, cannot be restrained by such practice as avoiding the proximity of objects because they are difficult to ward off. This is unlike [restraining them] through constant knowledge of the defects of objects, such as their perishability, and through reflection on the defects of the body, which will be described later in the verse beginning with "a structure with pillars of bone" (6.76). Therefore, one should restrain the external senses and the mind by means of knowledge of the defects of objects and so forth. 2.96.
Since an uncontrolled mind would be the cause of corruption, he therefore says:
"Vedic study, renunciation, sacrifices, observances, and austerities—these never lead to perfection for one whose disposition is corrupted. (2.97)

Regarding the Vedas: for one whose character is intent upon the pursuit of objects such as enjoyments, the study of the Vedas, giving, sacrifices, observances, and austerities never lead to the attainment of their fruit. (2.97)
He describes the true nature of one who has conquered the senses:
"That man who, having heard, touched, seen, tasted, or smelled, neither rejoices nor desponds—he should be known as one who has conquered his senses. (2.98)

Having heard this—having heard both words of praise and words of censure; having touched what is pleasant to the touch, such as fine silk, and what is painful to the touch, such as a woolen blanket; having seen what is beautiful and what is ugly; having tasted what is sweet and what is not sweet; and having smelled what is fragrant and what is foul—he in whom there is neither joy nor dejection should be known as one who has conquered his senses. (2.98)
He says that even the lack of restraint regarding a single sense organ is to be avoided:
"But if among all the sense organs even one single organ leaks, by that his wisdom flows away, like water from the foot of a leather water-skin. (2.99)

"But among the senses... (II.99). Among all the senses, if even a single sense becomes inclined toward its object, then for one who is thus devoted to objects, the knowledge of reality flows away through the other senses as well and does not remain stable. Just as water contained in a leather vessel does not remain, even if there is only a single hole, because the water situated in every part [of the vessel] escapes; so it is here. II.99.
Showing that restraint of the senses is the cause of all human goals, [the author] says:
"Having brought the collection of the senses under control and likewise having restrained the mind, one should accomplish all goals through yoga without wasting the body. (2.100)

"Having brought under control" means: having made the group of external senses dependent [on the mind] and having restrained the mind, one should properly accomplish all human goals. By means of yoga—that is, by the proper method—one who is naturally happy, not afflicting even his own body, should gradually abandon refined food and the like as he partakes of it. || 2.100 ||
One should stand reciting the Sāvitrī during the morning twilight until the sun appears; but one should sit during the evening twilight until the stars are clearly visible. (2.101)

"During the morning twilight" (*pūrvāṃ saṃdhyām*) and "during the evening twilight" (*paścimām*): the accusative case is used here according to Pāṇini 2.3.5, *kālādhvanor atyantasaṃyoge* ("in the case of absolute connection with time or distance"). One should stand during the first twilight, reciting the *Sāvitrī*, until the sun appears; having risen from one's seat and ceased walking, one should remain in one place. But for the evening twilight, one should remain seated, reciting the *Sāvitrī*, until the stars are clearly visible. In this context, because it possesses a specific fruit, the recitation (*japa*) is the primary element, while standing and sitting are subordinate members (*aṅga*), according to the maxim: "In proximity to that which has a fruit, that which lacks a fruit is its member. The fruit of the recitation was previously stated [in verses] 2.78 and 2.79: "A Brahmin learned in the Veda who performs the two twilights is joined with the merit of the Veda," and "Having practiced it a thousand times. However, Medhātithi asserts that standing and sitting themselves are the primary elements. The duration of the twilight period is merely one *muhūrta*. Thus says Yogiyājñavalkya:
The decrease and increase of the days occur continuously in their respective order;
the twilight (saṃdhyā), however, is traditionally held to last for only one muhūrta during both the decrease and the increase.

Standing while reciting prayers during the morning twilight, one removes the sin committed at night; sitting during the evening twilight, however, one destroys the impurity created by the day. (2.102)

Regarding the phrase "the morning twilight": standing during the morning twilight and performing *japa* destroys the sin accumulated during the night; sitting during the evening twilight and performing *japa* strikes down the sin committed during the day. In that regard as well, the fruit resulting from *japa* has been stated. And this refers to sins committed through ignorance and the like. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:
"Whether by day or by night, whatever may have been done through ignorance—all that perishes by performing the three daily twilight devotions. (2.102)
But he who neither remains at the morning [libation] nor performs the evening one is to be excluded from all duties of the twice-born, like a Śūdra. (2.103)

"He does not abide" means: he who neither performs the morning twilight devotion (*pūrvasaṃdhyā*) nor attends to the evening one (*paścimā*), that is to say, he does not perform the recitations (*japa*) and other rites prescribed for those respective times—he is indeed a Śūdra, and must be excluded from all duties of the twice-born, including even the hospitable reception of guests. By this very transgression, the obligatory nature (*nityatva*) of the twilight devotion is declared; and although it is obligatory, there is no contradiction in its having as its fruit the destruction of sins that are always undesirable. (2.103)
Restrained and established in the daily rule, he should go to the forest and, with a concentrated mind, recite the Sāvitrī near water.

"Near water": even if one is unable to study many Vedic texts, this form of the *brahmayajña*—the study of the *Sāvitrī* alone—is prescribed. Having gone to a secluded place such as a forest or near a river and other bodies of water, with senses restrained, composed, and single-minded, one who wishes to perform the daily rite in the form of the *brahmayajña* should likewise recite the *Sāvitrī*, joined with the *praṇava* and the three *vyāhṛtis*, exactly as described. (2.104)

There is no restriction regarding days unsuitable for study (anadhyāya) with respect to the auxiliary sciences of the Veda, the daily private recitation (svādhyāya), and indeed the sacrificial formulas used in the fire-oblation (homa). (2.105)

Regarding the phrase "an auxiliary of the Veda": there is no concern regarding days unfit for study (*anadhyāya*) with respect to the auxiliaries of the Veda—that is, the *vedāṅgas* such as phonetics (*śikṣā*)—nor with respect to the daily recitation (*svādhyāya*) which is to be performed constantly in the form of the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), nor with respect to the mantras used in fire-offerings (*homa*). || 2.105 ||
In the daily recitation there is no suspension of study, for that is remembered as the "Brahma-sacrifice.
It is meritorious, offered with the oblation of the Veda, and consecrated by the *vaṣaṭ*-call even during times when study is otherwise suspended. (2.106)

Regarding the term *naityaka*: this is a restatement of the daily (*naityaka*) Vedic study mentioned previously. In the daily recitation sacrifice (*japayajña*), there is no suspension of study (*anadhyāya*), because it occurs constantly; for that has been remembered by Manu and others as the "Brahma-sacrifice" (*brahmasatra*). Brahman itself is the oblation (*āhuti*); the offering (*havis*) in that [sacrifice] is the study performed even during times when study is forbidden. Thus, even study during a period of suspension—being of the nature of study—is indeed meritorious, as it is consecrated by the *vaṣaṭ*-call of the suspension (*anadhyāyavaṣaṭkṛta*). (2.106)
For him who, being self-controlled and pure, studies his own Veda for a year according to the prescribed rule, this [fire] constantly yields milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey. (2.107)

Regarding the phrase "he who [studies] his own Veda": the accusative case in *abdam* ("for a year") expresses continuous duration. He who, for even a single year, recites his own Veda (*svādhyāya*) day after day—performing it with its prescribed ancillaries, with senses restrained and himself purified—for him alone the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) flows with milk and other offerings; he gratifies the gods and the ancestors with milk and the like. And they, being gratified, satisfy the performer of the sacrifice of recitation with all desired objects. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya (1.41) says: "With honey and with milk, that twice-born man shall satisfy the gods."
For he who studies the Rigvedic verses every day [satisfies] the ancestors with honey and clarified butter.
Having begun thus,
and having stated that the fruit of reciting the four Vedas, the Purāṇas,
and [other texts] is the satisfaction of the gods and ancestors, [he says] at the end:
For it has been said: "Being themselves satisfied, they satisfy him with the auspicious fruits of all desires" (1.47). || 2.107 ||

A twice-born man who has undergone initiation shall, until his formal return home, maintain the sacred fire, subsist on alms, sleep on the ground, and perform what is beneficial for his teacher. (2.108)

"Kindling the fire": the student who has undergone the initiation ceremony (*kṛtopanayana*) shall, until his formal return home (*samāvartana*), perform the evening and morning fire-oblation (*samiddhoma`), collect alms, sleep on the ground in the form of not using a bedstead (but not necessarily sleeping on the bare ground alone), and perform beneficial services for his teacher such as fetching water-jars and other tasks. 2.108.
Regarding what kind of disciple should be taught, he says:

The son of the teacher, one who is obedient, a giver of knowledge, righteous, pure, trustworthy, capable, a provider of wealth, virtuous, and one's own relative—these ten are to be taught according to the Dharma. (2.109)

Regarding the phrase "the teacher’s son": the teacher’s son, an attendant, one who bestows other branches of knowledge, one who knows the Dharma, one who is pure regarding soft materials such as seats and the like, a kinsman, one capable of grasping and retaining [the teachings], a giver of wealth, one who desires one's welfare, and a relative—these ten are to be taught the Dharma according to the rule.
One should not speak to anyone unless asked, nor to one who asks in an improper manner;
for even though he knows, the wise man should behave like a fool in the world. (2.110)

Regarding the phrase "not [to speak] when unasked": one should not explain the true nature of that which has been recited by another in few syllables or with incorrect accents. However, it must be told even to a disciple who does not ask; for it is improper to transgress the duty of answering questions out of devotion, faith, and so forth. Therefore, one should not fail to speak to one who asks. For even though he knows, a wise man should conduct himself in the world as if he were mute. (2.110)
He states the fault incurred by transgressing the two aforementioned prohibitions: "He who speaks unrighteously and he who asks unrighteously—one of these two perishes or incurs enmity. (2.111)

"By unrighteousness": even when questioned by one who acts unrighteously, he who speaks for such a person, and he who questions him unjustly—of these two, either the wrongdoer dies or he incurs enmity with him. (2.111)
Where neither virtue nor wealth is found, nor even a corresponding desire to serve, there knowledge should not be sown, just as good seed is not sown in barren soil. (2.112)

"Regarding the phrase 'dharma and artha': knowledge should not be imparted to a student in whom neither dharma nor artha are found, nor service corresponding to his studies; it would be like sowing excellent seeds of rice and the like in saline soil. Saline soil (*ūṣara*) is that wherein seed, once sown, does not sprout. Nor should one suspect that by accepting a fee he becomes a hired teacher (*bhṛtakādhyāpaka*), for there is no fixed rule such as, 'If this much is given to me, then I shall teach this much. (2.112)
A teacher of the Veda should die together with his knowledge at his own will;
even in the midst of terrible calamity, he must never sow it in barren soil.

Regarding the phrase "with knowledge": one should rather die along with the teacher of the Veda than, in the total absence of a disciple worthy of instruction, hand it over to an unworthy recipient. Thus says the Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa: "One should die together with one's knowledge; one should not sow knowledge in barren soil. (2.113)
He states its paraphrase:
"Knowledge, approaching a Brahmin, said: 'I am your treasure; protect me.
Do not give me to a scorner; thus may I be most powerful. (2.114)

“Knowledge [spoke] to the Brāhmaṇa. Knowledge, the presiding deity, approached a certain teacher who was a Brāhmaṇa and spoke thus: “I am your treasure. Protect me. Do not speak of me to one who possesses faults such as envy; for if you do so, I shall become exceedingly powerful. And likewise, the *Chāndogya-brāhmaṇa* states: “Knowledge indeed came to the Brāhmaṇa, saying: ‘I am yours; protect me. Do not give me to one who is unworthy or arrogant. Guard me, for then I shall be most beneficial. (2.114)
But speak to that brahmin whom you know to be pure, self-restrained, and a student of sacred knowledge—a guardian of the treasure who is never negligent. (2.115)

"Whomever," [he said], "you know to be a disciple who is pure, whose senses are restrained, and who lives a life of celibacy—to him, a protector of the treasure that is the form of knowledge and one free from negligence, speak of me. (2.115)
He who acquires the Veda from one who is reciting it without permission is guilty of stealing the Veda and falls into hell. (2.116)

"Brahman. Furthermore, he who, for the sake of practice, receives the Veda from one who is studying it or from anyone else teaching it without that person's permission, is guilty of stealing the Veda and goes to hell; therefore, this must not be done. (2.117)
Whether it be worldly, Vedic, or even spiritual knowledge, one should first pay homage to the person from whom that knowledge was received. 2.117

Regarding the term "worldly" (*laukika*): worldly knowledge refers to the science of polity (*arthaśāstra*) and so forth; Vedic knowledge refers to the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas; and spiritual knowledge (*ādhyātmika*) refers to the knowledge of Brahman. One should first salute that person from whom one receives [such knowledge], provided he stands among those worthy of great respect. Among these three types of teachers who bestow worldly and other forms of knowledge, their relative degree of respectability increases in the order mentioned. (2.117)

A Brahmin who is well-restrained is better even if his essence consists only of the Sāvitrī mantra, than one who is unrestrained, even if he knows the three Vedas, eats all things, and sells all things. (2.118)

Regarding the term *sāvitrī*: even one who knows only the *Sāvitrī* mantra is better—provided he is well-restrained and governed by the rules of the scriptures—and is thus to be honored as a Brahmin or the like; whereas one who knows all three Vedas but is unrestrained, habituated to forbidden food and the like, and a seller of prohibited goods, is not. This is merely an illustration, for by the word "well-restrained" (*suyantrita*), what is intended is devotion to both injunctions and prohibitions. (2.118)
One should not sit upon a bed or seat already occupied by a superior;
rather, while remaining on one's own bed or seat, one should rise and salute him. 2.119.

"Bed and seat" (*śayyāsana*) refers to both bed and seat; the singular form of the *dvandva* compound is according to Pāṇini 2.4.6, "the genus [is used] for things that are not living beings. When that has been used by a superior—a teacher who is preeminent in knowledge and so forth—and has been accepted as common property, one should not sit upon it even at that time. Furthermore, if the teacher arrives while one is oneself seated on a bed or seat, one should rise and perform a salutation. 2.119.
He states an explanatory passage (arthavāda) regarding this:
"For the vital breaths (prāṇa) of a youth depart when an elder approaches;
one recovers them again by rising to meet him and by saluting him. (2.120)

Regarding the word "upwards": because when a youth of little age approaches an elder who is advanced in years through [superiority in] age, learning, and so forth, the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) tend to move upwards, desiring to exit the body; by rising to meet him and saluting him, one makes those breaths stable once again. Therefore, one should rise to meet and salute an elder. 2.120.
Furthermore, he states the result:
"For one who is habitually respectful and constantly serves the elders, four things increase: longevity, knowledge, fame, and strength. (2.121)

Regarding the phrase "of one whose habit is to pay homage": for one who always rises to pay homage to elders and who serves the elderly, the four qualities of longevity, wisdom, fame, and strength increase correctly and preeminently. (2.121)
Now he states the rule for salutation: After having saluted an elder, a Brahmin, while performing the salutation, should announce his own name, saying, "I am so-and-so by name. (2.122)

Regarding the phrase "after the salutation" (*abhivādāt param*): when a Brahmin or other [high-caste person] salutes an elder, immediately after uttering the word "I salute" (*abhivādaye*) following the salutation, he should proclaim his own name, saying, "I am so-and-so by name. Therefore, because the word *nāma* here functions as a specific term, Medhātithi and Govindarāja’s assertion that the word *nāma* must also be employed within the formula of salutation after the utterance of one's specific name is without authority. For this very reason, Gautama (6.1) states: "Having pronounced his own name, he should say, 'I salute' (*aham abhivādaye*). Sāṅkhyāyana also said: "He should indicate his own name, saying, 'I am so-and-so, sir' (*asāv ahaṃ bho*). Furthermore, if the word *nāma* were to be used simply because of hearing the word *nāma*, then—given the rule "and the letter *a* at the end of this name" (2.125)—the word *nāma* would have to be uttered in the formula of the return-salutation (*pratyabhivādana*), yet that is not accepted by anyone.
To those who do not know how to respond to his name, a wise man should say "I am he," and he should do the same for all women. (2.123)

Regarding the phrase "of the name": when a name has been uttered, there may be certain persons who, due to ignorance of Sanskrit, do not understand the salutation or the purpose of the salutation; toward them, even in returning the salutation, because the meaning would not be the same, the wise person—the one who understands the capacity for salutation—should say "I salute" (*abhivādaye 'ham*). One should speak in exactly the same way to all women. (2.123)
In greeting, one should utter the word "bhoḥ" at the end of one's own name;
for the seers have declared that the nature of the word "bhoḥ" is the very essence of names.

Regarding the word *bhoḥ*: at the end of whatever name is employed in a salutation, one should utter the word *bhoḥ* for the purpose of addressing the person being saluted. For this very reason, he says: "of names. The sages have recorded that the essence (*bhāva*), the existence (*sattā*), of this word *bhoḥ* is the essential nature of the names of those being saluted. Therefore, the formula for salutation is as follows: "I salute; I am Śubhaśarman, O sir! (2.124).
When greeting a Brahmin, one should say, "May you be long-lived, O gentle one.
Furthermore, at the end of his name, the vowel 'a' should be pronounced with the preceding syllable as a protracted (pluta) vowel.

Regarding the term *āyuṣmān*: when a salutation has been performed, the one who returns the greeting must address the saluter—whether he be a Brahmin or another—by saying, "May you be long-lived, O gentle one (*āyuṣmān bhava saumya*). At the end of the name of this saluter, whatever vowel begins with *a*—since there is no rule that names must necessarily end in *a*—that vowel is to be protracted (*pluta*). This is because the status of ending in *a* depends on the vowel; thus, even if a name ends in a consonant, it is possible [for the vowel preceding it to be protracted]. That vowel beginning with *a* which is preceded by a syllable belonging to the name and joined to it—that is, not separated from the preceding syllable—is to be made protracted. And Pāṇini, while following the rule "The final syllable (*ṭi*) of a sentence is protracted and acute" (8.2.82), clearly stated in his rule "In a return greeting, except for a Śūdra" (8.2.83) that the protraction applies here. Vāmana, the author of the *Vṛtti*, explained this: "What is the purpose of [mentioning] *ṭi*? It is so that the protraction may apply only to the final syllable (*ṭi*) of a name ending in a consonant. Therefore, such a formula for a return greeting is: "May you be long-lived, O gentle Śubhaśramaṇa"; likewise for a Kṣatriya: "Balavarman"; and for a Vaiśya: "Vasubhūe. According to the statement of Kātyāyana, "The protraction is optional for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas" (Vārttika 4865), the protraction does not occur in the case of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas in one alternative. For a Śūdra, the protraction is not to be performed, according to Pāṇini’s rule "Except for a Śūdra" (8.2.83). Furthermore, according to Kātyāyana’s statement, "There is also a prohibition for women" (Vārttika 4864), there is no protraction in a return greeting to a woman either. Govindarāja, however, by first invariably adding the suffix *śarma* to a Brahmin’s name and then giving the example "May you be long-lived, O gentle Bhadra" in the return greeting—a form without a suffix—merely reveals his own ignorance regarding examples both with and without suffixes. Dharaṇīdhara also, despite seeing Manu’s verse "May you be long-lived, O gentle one" ending in the vocative case, provides the example "Amukaśarma," which ends in the nominative singular rather than the vocative; he is indeed to be disregarded even by the wise.
That Brahmin who does not know how to return a greeting is not to be saluted by a learned man; he is just like a Śūdra. (2.126)

"He who does not know" means: that Brahmin who does not know how to return a salutation in accordance with the original salutation is not to be saluted by one who knows the rules of salutation—even by one who follows the prescribed method of pronouncing his name—just like a Śūdra. However, the mere utterance of the words "I salute you," devoid of the grasping of the feet and other such formalities, is not forbidden, because it has been mentioned previously. (2.126)
Upon meeting a Brāhmaṇa, one should inquire about his welfare; a Kṣatriya, regarding his health; a Vaiśya, regarding his prosperity; and a Śūdra, regarding his well-being. 2.127.

Regarding the term *brāhmaṇam*: having come together—that is, when a meeting has occurred—one should greet a Brāhmaṇa who is younger than oneself or of equal age, even if he does not return the greeting, by asking after his "well-being" (*kuśalam*); a Kṣatriya, by asking after his "health" (*anāmayam*); a Vaiśya, by asking after his "welfare" (*kṣemam*); and a Śūdra, by asking after his "freedom from illness" (*ārogyam*). For this very reason, Āpastamba states: "One should ask a Brāhmaṇa who is younger or of equal age about his 'well-being' (*kuśalam*); a Kṣatriya about his 'health' (*anāmayam*); a Vaiśya about his 'welfare' (*kṣemam*); and a Śūdra about his 'freedom from illness' (*ārogyam*). [This applies to] one who is younger and who greets, as well as a peer who does not greet. Thus, Āpastamba clarifies the meaning of Manu’s verse. Govindarāja, however, maintains that based on the context, the inquiry regarding "well-being" and so forth applies only to one who returns the greeting. That is not correct, because it would follow that the act of coming together with the greeter is purposeless; furthermore, since the words *kuśala* and *kṣema* have the same meaning as the terms *anāmaya* and *ārogya*, the specific utterance of these particular words is what is intended. (2.127)

One who knows the Dharma should address an initiated person by name, even if he is younger than himself; however, he should address him using the honorifics "bhoḥ" or "bhavat" placed at the beginning.

"Regarding 'he should not be addressed by name': at the time of returning a greeting, as well as at other times from the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice until the final purificatory bath (*āvabhṛthasnāna*), even the younger person who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*) must not be addressed by name. Rather, a righteous person should address him using words such as *dīkṣita* and so forth, which express his superior status, preceded by the terms *bhoḥ* and *bhavat*: for example, 'O Initiate, do this,' or 'Let this be done by you, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). " (2.128)
But toward a woman who is another's wife and not related by birth, he should address her as "Madam," "O fortunate one," or "Sister. (2.129)

"Regarding the phrase 'another's wife' (parapatnī): when a woman is another's wife—that is, one who is not related by birth, such as a sister and so forth—one should address her at a time when conversation is not otherwise required with words such as 'Lady' or 'Fortunate Sister. Because of the mention of 'another's wife,' this rule does not apply to a maiden. However, for a sister, a maiden, or others, one should address them with terms such as 'Long-lived One' (*āyuṣmatī*). (2.129)
Upon rising to greet maternal uncles, paternal uncles, fathers-in-law, officiating priests, and teachers who are younger than himself, he should say, "I am so-and-so. (2.130)

"And maternal uncles": when younger maternal uncles and others have arrived, he should rise from his seat and say, "I am so-and-so," but he should not perform the formal salutation (*abhivādana*). The word "so-and-so" refers to the mention of one's own name. Since Hārīta, beginning with the statement "There are indeed many types of elders," proclaims the status of an elder for both those advanced in knowledge and those advanced in austerity—and since these two may also be younger than oneself—the term "elder" (*guru*) here refers to them. (2.130)
A maternal aunt, the wife of a maternal uncle, a mother-in-law, and a paternal aunt are to be honored like the wife of one's teacher; they are equal to the wife of a teacher. (2.131)

Regarding the term "mother’s sister": mother’s sisters and others are to be honored like the wives of one's gurus through rising to meet them, saluting them, offering them a seat, and so forth. Since this occurs in the section concerning salutation (*abhivādana*), it is understood that "honoring" here refers specifically to salutation; thus he said, "they are equal [to the guru's wife]. The meaning is that because they are equal to the wife of a guru, one must also perform acts such as rising to meet them. (2.131)
The wife of one's brother of the same caste may be clasped every day;
however, the wives of paternal kinsmen and maternal relatives must be clasped only after one has returned from a journey abroad. (2.132)

"Regarding 'the wife of the brother': the brother’s wife who is of the same caste (sajātīyā)—because this occurs in the section on honoring—is to be saluted by clasping her feet (*upasaṃgrāhyā*). This is to be done "day after day," that is, every single day. The word "api" has the sense of "eva" (only). As for "relatives" (*jñātayaḥ*), these are those on the father's side, such as paternal uncles and so forth; and "connections" (*saṃbandhinaḥ*) are those on the mother's side, such as fathers-in-law and so forth. Their wives, moreover, are to be saluted only upon returning from a journey (*viproṣya*), not with the rule of doing so every day. (2.132)
One should maintain the same conduct toward one's father’s sister, one’s mother’s sister, and one’s elder sister as toward one’s own mother; yet the mother is more venerable than they. (2.133)

Regarding the phrase "in the father's sister": one should behave toward the father's sister, the mother's sister, and one's own elder sister as toward one's mother. Furthermore, the mother is the most venerable of all these. Now, since the status of being worthy of honor like the wife of a guru was already stated by the verse "The mother’s sister, the maternal uncle’s wife... (2.131), what additional point is intended to be conveyed by this [present rule]?

It is said: this very point is expressed by the words, "The mother is more venerable than those two. Therefore, when permission has been granted by the father’s sister but there is a conflict with the mother, the mother’s command must be carried out. Alternatively, previously the status of the father’s sister and others as objects of honor was stated to be equal to that of the mother; however, by this [verse], their mode of conduct—such as affection—is also extended [to them]. Thus, there is no tautology. (2.133)
Friendship with fellow citizens is declared to last ten years; that with artists, five years;
that with Vedic scholars, three years; and with one's own kin, it lasts even for a very short time.

Regarding the phrase "known as ten years" (*daśābdākhya*): that which has ten years as its designation is "known as ten years," referring to friendship among city-dwellers. The meaning is this: for those residing in a single city who possess qualities such as learning to be described later, even if one is ten years older than another, their relationship is designated as friendship. The mention of "city" is for the sake of illustration; by it, [friendship] may also exist among those residing in a single village or similar locality. Through the mere practice of arts such as singing, friendship occurs in a short time. The particle *api* has the sense of *eva* (only/indeed). Everywhere, beyond the stated period of time, the conventional usage of "elder" (*jyeṣṭha*) applies. (2.134)
One should recognize a ten-year-old Brahmin and a hundred-year-old king as father and son; yet, of the two, the Brahmin is the father.

Regarding the term "Brāhmaṇa": one should understand that a ten-year-old Brāhmaṇa and a hundred-year-old Kṣatriya are father and son. Between these two, even the ten-year-old Brāhmaṇa is indeed the father of the hundred-year-old Kṣatriya; therefore, he is to be honored by him like a father. (2.135)
Wealth, kinship, age, ritual action, and learning as the fifth—these are the grounds for respect; each subsequent one is weightier than the preceding. (2.136)

Regarding "wealth" (*vitta*): wealth is property acquired through righteous means; *bandhu* refers to paternal uncles and other kinsmen; *vayas* is advanced age; *karma* consists of rites prescribed by the Vedas (*śrauta*) and the Smṛtis (*smārta*); and *vidyā* is the knowledge of the true meaning of the Vedas. These five are the grounds for respect. Among these, each subsequent one is superior to the preceding one; thus, the relative strength (*balābala*) within this collection of highly esteemed qualities has been stated. (2.136)
Among the three [higher] castes, he who possesses many qualities and is preeminent is worthy of honor here, even if he be a Śūdra who has reached the tenth stage. (2.137)

"Of the five": among the three castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, regarding wealth and the other qualities, that person in whom even one previously existed is more venerable than another who possesses only the subsequent ones. Thus, one endowed with wealth and kin is more venerable than one who is merely older in age. Likewise, one endowed with the triad of wealth and the rest is more venerable than one who possesses only ritual action. One endowed with the tetrad of wealth and the rest is more venerable than one who possesses only learning. "Virtuous" means possessing excellence; therefore, when both possess learning and the other qualities, it is excellence alone that is the cause of honor. Even a Śūdra, having reached the tenth stage—that is, being over ninety years old—is worthy of honor from the twice-born as well. When a hundred years are divided into ten parts, the tenth stage consists of those over ninety years of age. (2.137)
This manner of honoring is also mentioned here as a relevant point:
"Way must be yielded to one who holds a wheel, to one in his tenth decade, to the sick, to one carrying a burden, to a woman, to a Snātaka, to a king, and to a bridegroom. (2.138)

Regarding the word *cakriṇaḥ*: the path must be yielded to one mounted on a vehicle such as a chariot yoked with wheels, to one over ninety years of age, to one afflicted by disease, to one oppressed by a heavy burden, to a woman, to one who has recently completed his return from studentship (*samāvartana*), to a ruler of a country, and to one set out for a wedding. Because the root *dā* (to give) here signifies the act of yielding, the dative case is not employed. (2.138)
Among those gathered together, the *snātaka* and the king are to be honored;
and between the royal *snātaka* and the [ordinary] *snātaka*, the *snātaka* receives the honor due to a king.

Regarding the phrase "of them": among those gathered together in one place, the local ruler (*deśādhipa*) and the graduate (*snātaka*) are to be honored. Even between the king and the graduate, the graduate alone is to be honored in relation to the king. Therefore, the word "king" (*rājan*) in the preceding verse does not denote the mere caste; for, in view of the Kṣatriya caste, the mere Brāhmaṇa is declared to be honorable by the rule, "But a Brāhmaṇa of ten years... (2.135), and because [otherwise] the mention of the "graduate" would be redundant. (2.139)
He states the meaning of the term "teacher" (ācārya) and others:
"But that twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda along with the Kalpas and the secret portions (Upanishads), him they call a teacher. (2.140)

Regarding the term *upanīya*: because these words are commonly used in this treatise (*śāstra*), the ancient sages call that Brāhmaṇa an *ācārya* who, having initiated a pupil (*śiṣya*), teaches him the entire branch of the Veda (*vedaśākhā*) together with the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) and the secret doctrines (*rahasya*). The *kalpa* is the science of sacrifice; the *rahasya* is the Upaniṣad. Although the Upaniṣads are indeed part of the Veda, they are mentioned separately here with the intention of emphasizing their preeminence. (2.140)
But he who teaches a portion of the Veda, or even the Vedāṅgas, for the sake of his livelihood, is called an Upādhyāya. (2.141)

"Part of it" (ekadeśam): he who, for the sake of livelihood, teaches a part of the Veda—namely, the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas—as well as the auxiliary sciences such as grammar that are devoid of the Veda, is called an Upādhyāya. || 2.141 ||
That Brahmin who performs the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony according to the rules, and supports [the child] with food, is called a guru. (2.142)

Regarding the phrase "beginning with the *niṣeka*": *niṣeka* is the rite of impregnation (*garbhādhāna*). By this, the status of the father as a preceptor (*guru*) is taught. That Brahmin who performs the purificatory rites (*saṃskārakarma*), beginning with the impregnation, according to the scriptures for the father, and nourishes him with food, is called a preceptor (*guru*). (2.14)

He who, being chosen by someone, performs for him the establishment of the sacred fires, the cooked sacrifices (pākayajñas), and the soma-sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma and others, is called his officiating priest (ṛtvij) in this world.

Regarding the term *agnyādheya*: the *agnyādheya* is the rite that produces the Āhavanīya and other sacred fires. One who has performed the selection (*varaṇa*) and performs the *pākayajñas* such as the Aṣṭakās, or the [Soma] sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma, is designated here in this treatise as his *ṛtvij*. Although the definition of an *ṛtvij* is not required among the duties of a student (*brahmacārin*), it is mentioned incidentally to show that even one who is merely an *ṛtvij* deserves respect, just like a teacher (*ācārya*) and others. (2.143)
He who truly fills both ears with the Veda should be known as one's mother and father; one should never bear him malice.

"He who covers [them]" means he who fills both ears with the Veda—which is of the nature of truth and free from defects in phonemes and accents—without distortion; he should be known as both mother and father. Because of his quality of being a source of great benefit, this teacher is denoted by the words "mother" and "father"; one should never act against him once the Veda has been acquired. (2.144)
Ten sub-teachers equal one teacher; a hundred teachers equal one father; but a mother exceeds a thousand fathers in dignity. (2.145)

Regarding the phrase "towards the preceptors" (*upādhyāyān*): compared to ten preceptors, the *ācārya* is more venerable; compared to a hundred *ācāryas*, the father; and compared to a thousand fathers, the mother is superior in terms of reverence. Here, the *ācārya* intended is one who teaches only the *Sāvitrī* following the initiation (*upanayana*); compared to him, the father’s superiority is stated. There is no contradiction, for by the verse "Of the progenitor and the giver of the Veda" (2.146), the author will later declare the superiority of the primary *ācārya* over the father. || 2.145 ||
Between the progenitor and the giver of the Veda, the father who gives the Veda is the more venerable;
for the birth from the Veda is eternal for a Brahmin, both after death and in this world. (2.146)

Regarding the term "progenitor": both the biological father and the preceptor (*ācārya*) are fathers, because they grant birth. Of these two, the preceptor is the more venerable father. This is because for a Brahmin, the birth consisting of the initiatory rite (*upanayana*) for the purpose of receiving the Veda (*brahma-grahaṇa*) is eternal and constant, both in this world and in the next, since its fruit is the attainment of Brahman. (2.146)
One should know that the birth which occurs when his mother and father produce him together through desire is merely his physical origin within the womb. (2.147)

"Out of desire": when the mother and father procreate this child through mutual desire, that mere coming-into-being is common to him with animals and the like. That which is born in the womb, in the mother's belly, and acquires the major and minor limbs [is what is meant]. (2.147)
But that birth which the teacher, having mastered the Vedas, produces for him according to rule with the Sāvitrī—*that* is real; *that* is free from old age and death. (2.148)

Regarding the word "ācārya": Furthermore, the birth (*jāti*) which the teacher (*ācārya*), who knows the Veda, produces for this young student (*māṇavaka*) according to rule by means of the *Sāvitrī*—preceded by the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) together with its auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*) and accompanied by the recitation of the *Sāvitrī*—that birth is real, ageless, and immortal, because its fruit is the attainment of Brahman; for through the study of the Veda preceded by initiation, the knowledge of its meaning, and its performance, one who is free from desire attains liberation. (2.148)
One should know that person to be a teacher here in this world by virtue of that service of learning, whoever assists one with their study, whether it be little or much. (2.149)

"Or even a little" means by means of what has been heard (*śruta*). One should know that even a disciple whom a teacher assists—whether to a small or great extent—by means of what has been heard, is his *guru* in this treatise. For "what has been heard" itself is the assistance; it is by means of that assistance consisting of what has been heard. 2.149.
One who effects a Vedic birth and is a teacher of one's own duty becomes, according to dharma, the father of an elder even if he is a mere child. (2.150)

Regarding the phrase "of the Brahman": birth for the purpose of hearing the Veda is "Brahmic," which refers to the initiation (upanayana). Even such a child, as a teacher of his own duty—that is, an expounder of the meaning of the Vedas—becomes the father of an elder or an aged man. "According to dharma" means that the duties of a father must be performed toward him. (2.150)
He states an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda) consistent with the subject at hand: "The child Kavi, the son of Aṅgiras, taught his fathers;
having encompassed them with knowledge, he said, 'O my sons! (2.151).

"He taught" means that the son of Aṅgiras, though a youth, being a seer and a learned man, taught his elders—his paternal uncles, their sons, and others who were figuratively his fathers and were older in age. Having embraced them with knowledge and made them his disciples, he addressed them as "little sons" (*aputrakāḥ*). The indeclinable *iti ha* serves to indicate a past event. (2.151)
Filled with indignation, they questioned the gods regarding that matter;
and the gods, having assembled, said to them, "The child has spoken what is right for you."

“They asked about that matter. Being addressed as “little sons” (*putrakāḥ*) by him—those who were like fathers—they became angry and questioned the gods regarding the meaning of the word “little son. And the gods, having been questioned, gathered together and said to them: “It is appropriate that you were called ‘sons’ by that child with the word ‘son. (2.152)
Indeed, the ignorant one is a child, while the giver of the mantra is the father;
for they call the ignorant one a "child," but the giver of the mantra a "father. (2.153)

Regarding the word "ajña" (ignorant): the particle *vai* is used for emphasis. One becomes a child (*bāla*) precisely because of ignorance, not merely because of youth. The giver of the mantra (*mantrada*) is the father. The mention of the *mantra* is intended to indicate the Veda. He who teaches and explains the Veda is the father. He states the reason for this very point: "Because even the ancient sages called the ignorant one a 'child' (*bāla*), and they spoke of the giver of the mantra as indeed the 'father'" (2.153).
The seers did not establish dharma by means of years, nor by gray hair, nor by wealth, nor by kinsmen; he among us who is learned in the Vedas is great. 2.154.

"Not by years," etc.: greatness does not arise from many years, nor from white hair on the head, beard, and body, nor from great wealth, nor from kinship such as being a paternal uncle—even when all these are combined, there is no greatness; rather, it is the sages who established this law: "He who is a student of the Veda along with its auxiliary sciences (aṅgas), he is esteemed by us as great. (2.154)
Among Brahmins, seniority is determined by knowledge; among Kṣatriyas, however, by valor;
among Vaiśyas, by grain and wealth; and among Śūdras, solely by birth. (2.155)

Regarding the phrase "of the *vipras*": the superiority of Brahmins is by virtue of their learning (*vidyā*); that of Kṣatriyas, moreover, is by virtue of their valor (*vīrya*); that of Vaiśyas, by virtue of wealth such as grain and clothing; and that of Śūdras alone is by virtue of birth (*janman*). In all cases, the suffix *-tasi* is used in the sense of the instrumental case. (2.155)
One does not become old simply because one's head is gray; even if he is young, the gods know him as an elder who has studied the Vedas. 2.156
"Not by that," [it is said]: one does not become old merely because one's head has turned white; rather, even if he is young, the gods recognize him as an elder who is wise. 2.156.
As is an elephant made of wood, as is a deer made of leather, so is a Brahmin who has not studied; these three bear the name [only] in name. (2.157)

"Just as [the word] 'wooden'": just as an elephant fashioned from wood, a deer made of leather, and a Brahmin who does not study—these three bear only their names, yet they are incapable of performing the functions of an elephant and so forth, such as the slaying of enemies. (2.157)
As a eunuch is fruitless among women, as a cow is fruitless with another cow, and as a gift given to an ignorant man is fruitless, so is a Brahmin who knows not the Rigveda fruitless. || 2.158 ||
