Since these three opinions of the great sages can be systematically arranged, there is no inconsistency in their differing views regarding the grounds for falling. However, the view of Medhātithi and Govindarāja is that the statement "the *śūdrāvedī* falls" is a specific restriction on the previously mentioned prohibition against marrying a Śūdra woman. The statement "he falls by the birth of a son" is intended to provide a rule for cases where a marriage to a Śūdra woman occurs by divine fate: "one should not approach her during her season," because a son is born from approaching her during the fertile period (*ṛtu*). The phrase *tadapatyatayā* means: he whose offspring are those very children born of a Śūdra woman is *tadapatya*; the state of being such is *tadapatyatā*, and by that state he falls. By this it is meant: if he approaches her during her season, he may approach her after he has fathered offspring through other wives. (3.16)
By taking a Śūdra woman onto his bed, a Brāhmaṇa goes to a low state;
by procreating a son upon her, he is indeed fallen from his Brāhmaṇahood. (3.17)

Regarding the phrase "a Śūdra woman": this prohibition against a Brāhmaṇa who has married a Śūdra woman from sharing his bed—whether he did so by chance or out of affection—is based on the inference of a prohibitive Smṛti through censure; for it is said that "having approached a Śūdra woman, a Brāhmaṇa goes to hell. The statement "having begotten a son upon her" refers specifically to the prohibition against approaching her during her fertile period. The phrase "he falls from Brāhmaṇahood itself" is intended to indicate the gravity of the offense. (3.17)
But he whose rites for the gods, ancestors, and guests are centered primarily upon that [wealth], his ancestors and gods do not eat; he does not go to heaven. (3.18)

Regarding the verse beginning with *daiva*: if, by some chance, even a Śūdra woman is married—whether in the proper order of castes (*savarṇānukrama*) or not—then those rites performed by her which would otherwise be applicable as her duties are prohibited by this [verse]. "Divine" (*daiva*) refers to the *homa* and other such rites; "ancestral" (*pitrya*) refers to the *śrāddha* and so forth; "hospitality" (*ātitheya*) refers to the feeding of guests and the like. Whatever offerings to the gods (*havya*) or ancestors (*kavya*) are performed by means of a Śūdra woman, the Pitṛs and Devas do not partake of them. Nor does that householder attain heaven through such hospitality. This is not a redundant statement, for while the author will state in verse 9.87—"But he who, out of delusion, causes [the rites] to be performed by another woman when a wife of his own caste is present"—that prohibition applies when a wife of the same caste is available, this [present rule] applies even when she is not available. 3.18.
For one who has drunk the saliva of a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī), who has been defiled by her breath,
and who has procreated with her, no atonement is prescribed.

Regarding the term *vṛṣalī*: the saliva (*phena*) of a *vṛṣalī* is the moisture of her lips; he by whom that has been drunk is a *vṛṣalīphenapīta*. This compound is formed according to Pāṇini 2.2.37, *vāhitāgnyādiṣu*. By this, drinking the moisture from the lips of a Śūdra woman is prohibited. And regarding the phrase "of one defiled by her breath," there is a prohibition against sleeping in the same bed or similar circumstances with her. Since no purification is taught for a child born of her, this is a restatement of the prohibition against approaching her during her fertile period. (3.19)
Learn now, in brief, these eight forms of marriage for women among all four castes, which are beneficial or harmful both in this world and after death. (3.20)

"Of the four"—listen to these eight forms of marriage, which are briefly stated as the causes for obtaining a wife, some beneficial and some harmful, both in this world and in the next, for all four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas. (3.20)
The Brāhma, the Daiva, as well as the Ārṣa, the Prājāpatya, and the Āsura; the Gāndharva, the Rākṣasa, and the Paiśāca is the eighth and the lowest. (3.21)

"Brāhma," etc. These are specified by name. This designation, such as "Brāhmarākṣasa" and so forth, is for the purpose of technical usage within the treatise and for the purpose of demonstrating praise and blame. This [form] belongs to Brahmā, thus it is "Brāhma"; this belongs to a Rākṣasa, thus it is "Rākṣasa. However, the status of being deities such as Brahmā and others is not possible for these forms of marriage. The description of the Paiśāca as the lowest is for the sake of emphasizing its blameworthiness. (3.21)
I shall declare to you all that which is the duty for each caste, as well as the virtues and faults belonging to each; and I shall also explain the merits and demerits regarding procreation.

Regarding the word "ya" (which): that which does not deviate from dharma is *dharmya*. Whatever marriage is *dharmya*, whatever its virtues and faults may be—namely, its desirable and undesirable fruits—and whatever virtues and defects exist in the offspring born of that marriage, all of that I shall declare to you in detail. This is a summary of what is about to be said, intended for the easy comprehension of the disciples. (3.22)
One should know that for a Brahmin there are six marriages in order, for a Kshatriya four, and for a Vaishya and a Shudra those same [last] ones; these are lawful and not demonic. (3.23)

"Six": for a Brāhmaṇa, there are six in the order beginning with the Brahma [wedding]; for a Kṣatriya, there are four, excluding the lower ones such as the Āsura and so forth; but for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, one should know that those very same [forms]—excluding the Rākṣasa, namely the Āsura, Gāndharva, and Paiśāca—are lawful (dharmya), meaning not departing from dharma. (3.23)
Sages know that the first four [forms of marriage] are praiseworthy for a Brāhmaṇa;
the Rākṣasa alone is for a Kṣatriya, and the Āsura for Vaiśyas and Śūdras. (3.24)

"Four" refers to the four [forms] beginning with the Brāhma, which are prescribed first for the Brāhmaṇa; for the Kṣatriya, there is only the one, the Rākṣasa; and for the Vaiśya and Śūdra, the Āsura. Those who possess knowledge recognize these as the best. For this very reason, although the Āsura and others were previously ordained for the Brāhmaṇa and the rest, they are mentioned here again in order to indicate their inferiority. By this it is shown that when a praiseworthy form of marriage is not possible, even an inferior one may be accepted. In the same way, the avoidance of censurable forms should be understood in subsequent cases as well. (3.24)
Of these five, three are declared here to be lawful and two unlawful;
the Paiśāca and the Āsura forms should never be performed.

Regarding the phrase "of the five": here, because of the exclusion of the *paiśāca* [form of marriage], there is the inclusion of the five subsequent ones beginning with the *prājāpatya*. Among these, three—the *prājāpatya*, *gāndharva*, and *rākṣasa*—are not deviating from the Dharma (*dharmād anapetāḥ*). Among them, the *prājāpatya* is prescribed for those such as Kṣatriyas for whom it was not previously obtained; for a Brāhmaṇa, it is restated (anūdyate) because it has already been prescribed. And since the *gāndharva* is applicable to all four [castes], it is merely restated. The *rākṣasa* is also prescribed for Vaiśyas and Śūdras. Even for a Brāhmaṇa who has resorted to the occupation of a Kṣatriya, the *āsura* and *paiśāca* must not be performed. Because of the lack of qualification in the word "never" (*kadācana*), the prohibition applies to all four [castes]. In this matter, regarding whichever caste a particular marriage is either prescribed or prohibited, there is an option (*vikalpa*) for that caste with respect to that marriage; and that option is to be understood as applying when the prescribed [method] is unavailable.
Whether performed separately or combined, the two forms of marriage previously mentioned—the Gāndharva and the Rākṣasa—are recorded as lawful for the Kṣatriya. (3.26)

"Separately" (*pṛthak*): since it is already understood that they are "separately, separately," this is restated; "mixed" (*miśrau*) is what is being prescribed. Whether separate or mixed, the previously ordained Gāndharva and Rākṣasa forms are recorded by Manu and others as lawful for the Kṣatriya. When the bridegroom, through a mutual agreement preceded by mutual affection between the woman and the man, wins her by means of battle or the like and marries her, then the Gāndharva and Rākṣasa forms become mixed. (3.26)

Having clothed and honored her personally, and having invited a man who is learned in the Vedas and endowed with virtuous conduct, the giving away of the daughter is proclaimed as the Brāhma rite. (3.27)

"Let him clothe her. Since it is appropriate to provide merely clothing, the Brāhma marriage—described by Manu and others—is defined as the giving of a daughter to a suitor who possesses learning and good conduct, who has not requested her hand, after having clothed both the bride and groom with specially fine garments and honored them with ornaments and other gifts. (3.27)

When a sacrifice has been properly extended and the officiating priest performs the ritual, the giving away of a daughter after she has been adorned is declared to be the divine (daiva) dharma. (3.28)

Regarding the term "yajña" (sacrifice): when a sacrifice such as the Jyotiṣṭoma has been commenced according to the rules, the sages declare that giving a daughter in marriage to the officiating priest after having adorned him constitutes the Daiva form of marriage. (3.28)
Having taken one or two pairs of cattle from the bridegroom according to the law, the giving away of the daughter according to the prescribed rule is called the Ārṣa rite. (3.29)

"One pair" means a cow and a bull, which constitute a pair of cattle; that one or two [cattle] may be taken from the bridegroom for the sake of dharma—for the accomplishment of sacrifices and other rites according to the law—or to be given to the girl. But having accepted them with the intention of white [dharma], whatever gift of a maiden is performed according to the scripture, that is prescribed as the Ārṣa marriage. (3.29)
Having addressed the words, "May you both practice dharma together," and having honored the gift of the maiden, this is remembered as the Prājāpatya rite. (3.30)

"With you"—having first bound them by the words, "Perform the religious duty together," at the time of giving his daughter away, and having honored them, that gift of the maiden is known as the Prājāpatya marriage (3.30).
Having given wealth to the kinsmen and to the bride herself according to one's ability, the giving away of the bride at one's own will is called the Āsura dharma. (3.31)

Regarding the phrase "from the kinsmen": having given as much wealth as one can afford to the kinsmen of the maiden—such as her father and others—from whom she is received, the taking or acceptance of the maiden according to one's own will and desire, and not according to the scriptural regulations regarding the specific amount and kind of wealth as in the *ārṣa* rite, is called the *āsura* marriage (3.31).
The mutual union of the maiden and the bridegroom through desire is to be known as the Gāndharva rite; it is carnal and arises from passion. (3.32)

Regarding the term "by mutual desire" (*icchayā*): that mutual union consisting of embraces and so forth, which arises from the mutual affection between the bride and the groom, is to be known as the *gāndharva* [form of marriage]. It is called *saṃbhava* because it originates from this; for it comes into being from the longing of the bride and the groom. Precisely for this reason, it is "suitable for sexual union" (*maithunya*), meaning beneficial for sexual intercourse. Although all forms of marriage are suitable for sexual union, the specific designation of this one as "suitable for sexual union" is intended to demonstrate that there is no contradiction even when sexual union is actually taking place. (3.32)
The forcible abduction of a maiden from her home while she cries out and weeps, after having slain, wounded, or broken down [her guardians], is called the Rākṣasa rite. (3.33)

"Having slain" (*hatvā*)—the abduction of a maiden by force and compulsion is the very definition of the *rākṣasa* form of marriage. However, when the father and others, recognizing the superior power of the abductor, remain indifferent, then acts such as killing are not mandatory. If the maiden's party offers resistance, then even killing and the like must be performed; this is merely a restatement of what is already implied by the context. Having destroyed the maiden's party and mutilated their limbs, and having broken down walls and other fortifications, he carries the maiden away from her home while she weeps and cries out, "Alas, father! Alas, brother! I am being carried off, defenseless! By this, the lack of consent on the part of the maiden is stated, in order to distinguish this form from the *gāndharva* marriage. (3.33)
When one approaches a woman in secret while she is asleep, intoxicated, or mentally deranged,
that is the most sinful of marriages, known as the Paiśāca, the lowest of all.

"Sleeping" means one who is overcome by sleep, or rendered unconscious by intoxication from liquor, and thus devoid of the protection of her virtuous character. In a secluded place where one proceeds according to the practice of sexual union during a marriage, that is the sinful cause among marriages known as the *paiśāca*, the lowest of all. (3.34)
For the foremost of the twice-born, the giving away of a daughter with water alone is distinguished; but for the other castes, it occurs through mutual desire. (3.35)

"By means of water": the giving of a daughter to Brāhmaṇas is praised only when preceded by the offering of water; however, for Kṣatriyas and others, the giving of a daughter may take place even without water, through mere word alone by mutual consent. Thus, there is no fixed rule that it must be preceded by water. (3.35)
O Brahmins, listen fully as I correctly proclaim all those virtues of these forms of marriage which were celebrated by Manu.

Regarding the word "ya" (which): although the mention of virtues was already promised by the statement, "And whatever are the virtues and defects of each" (3.22), nevertheless, because many matters were promised to be discussed therein, this is restated again for the purpose of specifying the particular [virtues]. The genitive case in "of these marriages" (*eṣāṃ vivāhānām*) is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). Listen, O Brahmins, as I tell you all the virtues of whichever marriage among these has been described by Manu. (3.36)
The son of a Brāhmaṇa woman who has performed good deeds liberates ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself as the twenty-first from sin. (3.37)

"Ten" means ten ancestors, such as the father and so forth, and ten descendants, such as the son and so forth; and including himself as the twenty-first, if the son born of a Brāhmaṇa marriage performs meritorious deeds, he then liberates them from sin. The meaning of "liberation" is that he delivers the father and others from hell, and that his sons and others are born sinless in his lineage; for since they have not yet been born, it is impossible to destroy the sins [already committed by them]. (3.37)

A son born of a wife wedded according to the Daiva rite delivers seven generations before him and seven after; a son born of a wife wedded according to the Ārṣa rite delivers three before and three after; and a son born of a wife wedded according to the Kāya (Gāndharva) rite delivers six before and six after.

Regarding the phrase *daivoḍhā*: the son of one wedded by the *daiva* rite liberates seven ancestors, beginning with the father, and seven descendants, beginning with the son. The son of one wedded by the *ārṣa* rite liberates three ancestors, beginning with the father, and three descendants, beginning with the son. The son of one wedded by the *prājāpatya* rite liberates six ancestors, beginning with the father, six descendants, beginning with the son, and himself as well from sin; this [liberation] from the previous [verse] is to be supplied in all cases. In the term *kāyoḍhaja*, the shortening of the vowel occurs according to Pāṇini 6.3.63: *ṅyāpoḥ saṃjñāchandasor bahulam*. Here, the *ārṣa* rite, which yields a lesser result, is mentioned before the *prājāpatya*, which yields a greater result, in accordance with the order of the enumeration of the eight rites beginning with the *brāhma*. If it is asked why this order is followed in the verse enumerating the *brāhma* and other rites, it is for the purpose of including the *prājāpatya* in the statement, "Of the five, however, three are lawful" (3.25); otherwise, only the *ārṣa* would have been included.
Regarding what was said concerning the merits and defects in procreation, that is now explained:
"In the four forms of marriage, beginning with the Brāhma, sons who possess spiritual luster and are esteemed by the learned are born in due order. (3.39)

Regarding the word *brāhma*: among the four forms of marriage beginning with the *brāhma*, which are established in their respective order, sons endowed with the excellence of Vedic learning, study, and splendor are born who are dear to the learned. Because the word *saṃmata* has the sense of being "dear," there is no prohibition against a genitive compound by the rule *ktena ca pūjāyām* (Pāṇini 2.2.12); rather, this genitive, which refers to a general relationship, is compounded. (3.39)
Endowed with beauty, virtue, and excellence, wealthy and renowned, possessing abundant enjoyments and most righteous, they live for a hundred years. (3.40)

"Form" (*rūpa*) means a beautiful appearance; "being" (*sattva*) is that which will be described in the twelfth chapter; "qualities" (*guṇa*) refers to compassion and so forth. Endowed with these, sons are born who are wealthy, renowned, possessed of enjoyments such as desired garments, garlands, perfumes, and ointments, and righteous—this follows from what was stated previously. Furthermore, they live for a hundred years. (3.40)
But among the remaining [types of] improper marriages, cruel and untruthful sons are born who hate the Veda and the Dharma. (3.41)

"In the others": in the four [remaining] forms of marriage, beginning with the Āsura and following, other than the four beginning with the Brāhma, sons are born who perform cruel deeds, speak falsehoods, hate the Vedas, and hate religious duties such as sacrifice. (3.41)
Through blameless marriages with women, one's offspring become blameless; through censurable ones, they become censured among men. Therefore, one should avoid those who are censurable. (3.42)

"By blameless [marriages]"—this is a brief statement regarding the results of marriages. Through marriages that are not censured, which serve as the means for obtaining a wife, the progeny of men becomes blameless; but through censured ones, it becomes censured. Therefore, one should not perform censured marriages. (3.42)
The sacrament of taking the hand is prescribed for women of the same caste; this following rule is to be known for the marriage rite with women of different castes. (3.43)

Regarding the term "pāṇi" (hand): when women of the same caste are being taken [in marriage], the rite characterized by the grasping of the hand is prescribed by the Gṛhya and other scriptures. However, when women of a different caste are being wedded in the act of marriage, that rule which is to be stated in the immediately following verse should be understood as applying in place of the grasping of the hand. (3.43)
An arrow should be grasped by a Kṣatriya woman, a goad by a Vaiśya maiden, and the hem of the garment by a Śūdra woman when marrying a man of higher caste. (3.44)

Regarding the word "arrow" (*śara*): in the case of a Kṣatriya bride, at the place where the hand is taken during a Brāhmaṇa wedding, a portion of a shaft held in the hand of a Brāhmaṇa should be grasped. In the case of a Vaiśya bride during a wedding with either a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya, a portion of a goad held by a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya should be grasped. Furthermore, in the case of a Śūdra bride during a wedding with any of the three twice-born castes, the hem of her garment as she is being clothed should be grasped. (3.44)

He should approach his wife during her fertile period, always remaining devoted to his own wife; observing that vow, he may go to her out of a desire for pleasure, except on the forbidden lunar days. (3.45)

Regarding the word *ṛtu*: *ṛtu* is a specific state of women characterized by the appearance of menstrual blood and rendered fit for conception. The injunction that "he should approach her during that time" is a restrictive rule (*niyama-vidhi*), and not an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), because it would otherwise be vitiated by the three defects consisting of the abandonment of its own primary meaning, the assumption of a secondary meaning, and the sublation of what is already established. Even during the fertile period, since approaching her might occur in some cases due to passion, the injunction applies to those cases where it would otherwise not occur, just as in the rule "one should win on even ground. For this very reason, Parāśara speaks of the fault incurred by not approaching her during the fertile period: "He who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present near him..."
He falls into the terrible sin of killing an embryo; there is no doubt about this.

Furthermore, for one who has not yet produced a son, there is this restrictive rule: “A Brāhmaṇa, indeed, when being born, is born burdened with three debts: to the gods by means of sacrifice, to the ancestors by means of progeny, and to the seers by means of Vedic study. Since this [rule] can have its basis in such direct revelation (*śruti*), it is improper to postulate another source. Moreover, the author will state later: “Therefore, seeking a son, he should approach his wife during her season” (3.48). From this also, its basis in *śruti* is understood. Furthermore, since the scripture concerning the procreation of sons is fulfilled by the birth of even a single son—as seen in the observation, “They know the others to be born of desire” (9.107)—the restriction applies only to one who has not yet produced a son. As for the mantra, “Place ten sons in her,” that is intended as a praise of having many sons. Even for one who has already produced a son, the restriction regarding approaching the wife during her season does not cease at exactly ten; rather, because of the injunction, “Always devoted to his own wife” and “He should always be content with his own wife and should not approach the wife of another,” this is merely an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*). This is because the sentence would otherwise be redundant, because approaching one’s own wife is already commendable, and because a fault is heard of in not approaching her during her season: “He should go to her except on the forbidden days” (*parva*). The forbidden days, such as the new moon, will be mentioned later. One who is devoted to the vow of pleasing his wife may approach her even outside the season. For this very reason, it is done out of a desire for pleasure, and not with the thought that it is a scriptural mandate for procreating a son. Therefore, this consists of three rules: (1) he must certainly approach her during her season; (2) he must not approach the wife of another; and (3) he may approach her even outside the season for the sake of pleasing his wife. On this point, Gautama says: “He should approach her during her season, and also outside the season, except on the forbidden days” (GDh 5.1). Yājñavalkya also says (1.81): [“He should always be intent on pleasing his wife...”]
Or he may act according to his desire, mindful of the boon granted to women; the phrase "except on sacred days" applies to both cases—during the fertile period as well as outside of it. (3.45)
The natural menstrual period of women is said to consist of sixteen nights, together with four other days that are censured by the virtuous. (3.46)

Regarding the term "ṛtu" (the season): here, the words "night" and "day" refer to a full day-and-night (*ahorātra*). Beginning from the appearance of menses, the *ṛtu* of women lasts for sixteen day-and-nights in each month, including four other day-and-nights that are censured by the learned for engaging in sexual intercourse with a woman. That which exists by nature is "natural" (*svābhāvika*). However, due to illness and other causes, the duration may be shorter or longer. (3.46)
Of these, the first four nights, as well as the eleventh and the thirteenth, are censured; the remaining ten nights are praised. (3.47)

Regarding the phrase "of these": furthermore, among those sixteen nights beginning from the appearance of menses, the first four nights, as well as the eleventh and thirteenth nights, are censured for sexual intercourse; the remaining ten nights would be commendable. (3.47)
Sons are born on even nights, and daughters on uneven nights; therefore, one who desires a son should approach his wife during her season on an even night. (3.48)

Regarding the phrase "on even nights": even on those previously mentioned ten nights, such as the sixth, eighth, and so forth, sons are born if intercourse occurs; on odd nights, such as the fifth, seventh, and so forth, daughters are born. Therefore, one who desires a son should approach his wife during the fertile period (ṛtu) on even nights.
A male is born when the semen is in excess; a female when the female element is in excess.
When they are equal, a neuter is born, or a male and female twin; when they are diminished or scanty, the opposite occurs.

"A male" (pumān): when the male seed is in excess, even in uneven [conception] nights, a son is born; when the female seed is in excess, even in even nights, a daughter alone is born. Therefore, it is shown that one desiring a son should approach his wife even on even nights, having ascertained an abundance of his own seed through aphrodisiac food and the like, and a deficiency of the wife's seed through her light diet and so forth. However, when the seeds of the woman and man are equal, a "non-male" (apumān), i.e., a neuter, is born; and when they are both male and female, twins are born. When the seed of both is deficient or insubstantial, there is no conception of an embryo at all. (3.49)
Avoiding women on the eight censurable nights and the other [inauspicious] nights, he remains a celibate student (brahmacārī) regardless of which stage of life (āśrama) he inhabits. 3.50.

Regarding the word *nindyāsu*: during the six previously mentioned censurable nights, as well as on any other censurable nights, if one avoids women and approaches them only on the two remaining nights that are not *parvan* days, he remains one whose celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is unbroken. The phrase "dwelling in whichever stage of life (*āśrama*)" is said with reference to the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), for in his case, approaching his wife during her fertile period (*ṛtu*) is prescribed under certain circumstances. Nor should it be argued that there is no fertile period for a wife living in the forest; for this possibility exists when considering such scriptural injunctions as, "One should go to the forest at fifty," and "A man twice the age of his wife may marry her. Medhātithi, however, says: "The phrase 'dwelling in whichever stage of life' is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). Since the subduing of the senses is enjoined for the three stages of life other than the householder's, the permission to approach [the wife] on two nights is impossible [for them]. Govindarāja, however, says: "This is intended to demonstrate that there is no fault in approaching [the wife] on two nights even for one who has lost his sons or is in another stage of life, provided he does so out of desire for progeny. This is because of the statement 'dwelling in whichever stage of life,' and because the context begins with 'he who desires a son should approach [his wife],' and because a son is of great benefit."
Alas! By Govindarāja, who failed to explain the specific rule, it is clearly admitted that for an ascetic, sexual union with his own wife is permissible during her fertile period.
A wise father should not accept even the slightest bride-price for his daughter;
for by accepting a bride-price out of greed, a man becomes a seller of his offspring. (3.51)

"No. The father of a maiden, knowing the fault in accepting wealth, should not accept even a small amount of money on account of giving his daughter in marriage; for by accepting it out of greed, he becomes a seller of his offspring. (3.51)
But those kinsmen who, out of delusion, live off a woman's property—whether it be her vehicles or her clothing—are sinners who go to a downward state. (3.52)

Regarding "women's property": in connection with the prohibition against accepting a bride-price (*śulka*) at the time of giving a daughter in marriage, this [verse] establishes a prohibition against the seizure of women's property introduced in the ninth chapter. Those relatives—such as the husband, father, and others—who seize the wealth of a wife, daughter, and so forth; and the woman herself—the word "woman" (*nārī*) being used for illustrative purposes—[seize] vehicles such as horses and the like, as well as clothing: none of this wealth whatsoever should be taken. Those who seize it become doers of evil and go to hell. (3.52)
Regarding the rite of the seers (ārṣa), some say that a pair of cattle is the bride-price; but that is surely false.
Whether it be small or even great, it remains nothing other than a sale. (3.53)

Regarding the term "Ārṣa": some teachers say that in the Ārṣa form of marriage, a pair of cattle (*gomithuna*) should be received as a bride-price (*śulka*) from the groom; however, that is untrue. For whether it be small because it is accomplished by a low price, or great because it is accomplished by a high price, it remains a sale nonetheless. As for what was previously stated, "one pair of cattle" (3.29), Govindarāja claims that this is the opinion of others (*paramata*); but that is incorrect. According to Manu’s view, there would be no definition of the Ārṣa at all, because the very definition of the Ārṣa marriage is the giving of the girl preceded by the acceptance of a pair of cattle from the groom. If you argue that the definition of the Ārṣa intended by Manu is one thing, while the definition "one pair of cattle" is the opinion of others—[we reply: no.
If it is the opinion of others that there is one pair of cattle and two [others], then tell me: what is that characteristic of the Ṛṣis according to the view of Manu?
While enumerating the eight forms of marriage and praising the virtues of those wedded according to the Ārṣa rite,
was Manu unable to state the definition of the Ārṣa rite according to his own view?

Medhātithi, however, has not even attempted to resolve the contradiction between the preceding and following passages. Therefore, we explain it as follows: some teachers maintain that in the *ārṣa* form of marriage, a pair of cattle (*gomithuna*) is a bribe (*utkoca*). But this is not the opinion of Manu; for an acceptance of a fixed number of animals as prescribed by the scriptures is not of the nature of a bride-price (*śulka*). If it were a bride-price, then the smallness or greatness of its value would be irrelevant, and it would amount to a mere sale. Rather, for the sake of accomplishing the *ārṣa* marriage and for the successful performance of the necessary sacrifices and other rites, or to give to the girl herself, it is accepted strictly for the sake of dharma (*dharmārtha*) according to the scriptures. For this very reason, in the verse defining the *ārṣa* marriage, the phrase "having taken from the groom according to dharma" (3.29) means "according to dharma," i.e., for the sake of dharma. On the other hand, accepting wealth out of greed for enjoyment is of the nature of a bride-price and is unscriptural. It is for this reason that [Manu] uttered the censure: "For he who accepts a bride-price out of greed" (3.51). Therefore, upon a thorough consideration of the context from beginning to end, it is described as Manu’s own view that in the *ārṣa* marriage a pair of cattle is to be accepted for the sake of dharma and not for the sake of enjoyment. (3.53)
It was stated [in verse 3.53] that "in the Ārṣa rite, a pair of cattle is the bride-price (*śulka*). Now, he says that even the giving of wealth for the sake of the girl is not a bride-price:
"In those cases where the kinsmen do not take a bride-price, that is not a sale;
it is merely an honoring of the maidens and an act of pure benevolence. (3.54)

Regarding the phrase "of whom": when the father and others do not accept the wealth being given by the groom out of affection for those maidens, but instead present it to the maiden herself, that too is not a sale; because the honoring of young women is an act of compassion (*ānṛśaṃsya*), meaning non-violence, and is solely of the nature of mercy toward them. (3.54)
These women must be honored and adorned by their fathers, brothers, husbands, and brothers-in-law, who desire abundant prosperity for them. (3.55)

Regarding the phrase "by the fathers": not only is the wealth given by the groom at the time of marriage to be surrendered [to the husband], but even thereafter, these women must be honored with food and the like, and adorned with clothing, ornaments, and so forth, by the father and others who desire to attain great wealth and prosperity. (3.55)
Where women are honored, there the gods rejoice;
where they are not honored, all religious rites there become fruitless. (3.56)

Regarding the phrase "wherein": in whatever family women are honored by the father and others, there the deities are pleased. On the other hand, in a place where they are not honored, all ritual acts such as sacrifices become fruitless due to the absence of the deities' favor; this is a declamatory statement (arthavāda) intended as a censure.
That family where the female relatives grieve perishes quickly; but that family where they do not grieve indeed prospers forever. (3.57)

“They grieve”: according to lexicographers, *jāmi* refers to a sister or a woman of the same family (*Amara-kośa* 3.3.645). In whatever family the women—such as sisters, the wife, daughters, daughters-in-law, and other female relatives who are sapinda and raised within the household—are afflicted by grief and the like, that family quickly becomes destitute and is oppressed by fate, the king, or other such forces. Where these women do not grieve, that family always prospers through wealth and other means. However, Medhātithi and Govindarāja state that *jāmayaḥ* refers to newly married daughters, daughters-in-law, and so forth. (3.57)
Those houses which female relatives, when not properly honored, curse, perish on all sides as if struck by a magical spell (kṛtyā). || 3.58 ||

Regarding the word *jāmayaḥ*: those houses which the sisters, wives, daughters, daughters-in-law, and so forth, being unhonored, curse, saying, "May this misfortune befall these people," perish—struck down by that malevolent rite—along with their wealth, cattle, and other possessions. (3.58)
Therefore, those who desire prosperity should always honor these women with ornaments, clothing, and food, both at ceremonies and during festivals. (3.59)

"Therefore" means: for this reason, because it is so, these [women] should always be honored by men desiring prosperity during constant acts of hospitality such as the Kaumudī festival, and during festivals such as the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). || 3.59 ||
In that family where the husband is always content with his wife and the wife likewise with her husband, prosperity is indeed certain.

Regarding the word "satisfied" (*saṃtuṣṭa*): in the phrase "the husband by means of the wife," the instrumental case is used in the sense of cause. In whatever family the husband is pleased with his wife—meaning he does not harbor desires for other women—and the wife is likewise pleased with her husband, in that family prosperity endures for a long time. By the mention of "family" (*kula*), it is understood that it is not only the wife and husband who partake in this prosperity, but their lineage of sons, grandsons, and so forth as well.
For if a woman does not find pleasure, she will not delight the man; and from a lack of mutual delight, procreation does not proceed. (3.61)

Regarding the word *yadi*: here, *ruci* has the sense of "shining. If a woman were not radiant with beauty produced by garments, ornaments, and the like, then she would certainly not gladden her husband again. The word *hi* is used for emphasis. Because of the lack of such delight, procreation—that is, the husband’s conception of an embryo—does not come to pass. (3.61)
When a woman is pleasing, the entire family is pleased; but when she is displeasing, the whole family is indeed displeased. (3.62)

Regarding the word "in a woman": when a woman is radiant with beauty through ornaments and the like, and because she is the object of her husband's affection, she avoids contact with other men, and thus that family becomes illustrious. But when she is lacking in luster, because she is disliked by her husband, she associates with other men, and consequently the entire family becomes defiled. (3.62)
Through ill-arranged marriages, the omission of sacred rites, the failure to study the Vedas,
and by showing disrespect toward Brahmins, noble lineages fall into the state of being non-noble.

"By bad marriages" means that through marriages such as the Āsura and others which are forbidden for each respective caste, through the omission of rites such as the *jātakarman*, through the non-recitation of the Vedas, and through the failure to honor Brāhmaṇas, even renowned families fall into decline. (3.63)
By means of crafts, commerce, and solely through the offspring of Śūdra women;
by means of cattle, horses, vehicles, agriculture, and service to the king. (3.64)

Regarding the phrase "by craft": families perish through crafts such as painting and the like; through *kalā*, meaning the practice of money-lending and financial transactions; through having offspring who are merely Śūdras; and through the buying and selling of cattle, horses, and chariots, as well as through agriculture and service to kings—this is the connection with what follows.
Families that are deficient in sacred mantras quickly perish through officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, and through atheism regarding ritual actions. (3.65)

Regarding the phrase *ayājya* (one who should not be made to sacrifice): through officiating at sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice (*ayājya*), such as *vrātyas* and others, one causes the decline of rituals—both those prescribed by the *Śruti* and those by the *Smṛti*. *Nāstikya* (atheism) is defined here as "the conviction that there is no fruit in ritual acts that possess scripturally ordained results. Families devoid of Vedic study quickly fall into degradation. Furthermore, in this section on marriage, the omission of rites and other such faults have been censured in connection with the condemnation of marriage. By means of this censure, a prohibition is everywhere implied to the effect that "this must not be done. (3.65)
Now, following the incidental discussion regarding the censure of families resulting from the omission of ritual acts and so forth, he speaks of the excellence of a family:
"But families that are enriched by mantra, even if they possess little wealth, attain the status of being counted among noble families and draw great renown. (3.66)

He recites the mantra. Although it is well known in the world that "a family [is defined] by wealth," nevertheless, even families with little wealth—if they are devoted to the study of the Veda, the knowledge of its meaning, and its performance—are counted among the ranks of the most excellent families and acquire great renown. 3.66.

The section on marriage has been concluded. Now, he states the performance of the great sacrifices (mahāyajña) and so forth, which was promised as that which must be explained—both the rules for the great sacrifices and what is to be accomplished in the nuptial fire: "A householder should perform the domestic rites (gṛhyakarma) according to rule in the nuptial fire, as well as the procedure for the five sacrifices and the daily cooking. (3.67)

Regarding the term *vaivāhika*: that which pertains to marriage is *vaivāhika*. The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied here because it belongs to the *adhyātmādi* group. In that fire, the householder should perform the rites prescribed for the domestic fire (*gṛhya*), such as the morning and evening oblations (*sāyaṃprātar-homa*) and the *aṣṭakā* offerings, according to the scriptures; he should also perform the Vaiśvadeva and other rites included within the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) which are to be accomplished with fire, as well as the daily preparation of cooked food. 3.67.
A householder has five slaughterhouses: the hearth, the grinding stone, the broom, the mortar, and the water jar; by using these, he is bound. (3.68)

"Five" refers as follows: *sūnā* is a place for slaughtering animals. Just like a slaughterhouse (*sūnā*), the hearth and the other four are called *sūnās* because they possess the quality of being places of injury; these five are the seeds of injury and the sites of violence for the householder. The *cullī* is the cooking hearth. The *peṣaṇī* consists of the grinding stone and the muller. The *upaskara* refers to household utensils such as pots and brooms. The *kaṇḍanī* refers to the mortar and pestle. The *udakumbha* is the water-jar used for holding water. By employing these in their respective functions, one becomes bound by sin. (3.68)
For the sake of expiating all of these in due order, the great seers have prescribed five great sacrifices for householders to be performed every day. (3.69)

Regarding the phrase "of these": for the sake of expiation—that is, for the destruction of the sins incurred—of these [five] places such as the hearth and so forth, the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) have been prescribed by Manu and others as duties to be performed daily by householders. Thus, because they are designated as being "for the sake of expiation" and because they are proclaimed to be sites of violence, and because it will be stated later that "one is not tainted by the faults of the slaughter-places" (3.71), it is understood that the five slaughter-places (*pañcasūnā*) are causes of sin, and the five sacrifices are the destroyers of that sin. Furthermore, because of the mention of "daily," and since the destruction of that sin is expected every day, their obligatory nature (*nityatva*) is not contradicted, just as in the case of the twilight worship (*saṃdhyāvandana*) and other such rites. (3.69)

Teaching is the sacrifice to Brahman; the libation to the ancestors (tarpaṇa) is the sacrifice to the ancestors; the burnt offering (homa) is the sacrifice to the gods; the bali offering is the sacrifice to the spirits; and the honoring of guests is the sacrifice to men. (3.70)

Regarding the term "teaching" (*adhyāpana*): by the word "teaching," "studying" (*adhyayana*) is also included, because it will be stated later that "muttering [of mantras] is the *ahuta* sacrifice" (3.74). Therefore, both teaching and studying constitute the *brahmayajña*. "With food or with water" (3.82)—he will state this later—refers to the libation (*tarpaṇa*), which is the *pitṛyajña*. The oblation into the fire (*agnihotra*) to be described later is the *devayajña*. The offering to beings (*bhūtabali*) is the *bhūtayajña*. The honoring of guests is the *manuṣyayajña*. In the context of teaching and the others, the words "sacrifice" (*yajña*) and "great" (*mahat*) are used figuratively for the sake of praise. (3.70)
He who does not neglect these five great sacrifices according to his ability, even while living constantly in the household, is not defiled by the faults of the slaughterhouse. (3.71)

"Five": this is a restatement (anuvāda) for the purpose of prescribing [the number] according to one's capacity. These [rites] should be performed even by means of a secondary alternative (anukalpa), as far as possible. In the word "hāpayati," the causative suffix (ṇic) has the sense of the verbal root itself due to Vedic usage; its meaning is "he abandons" (jahāti). || 3.71 ||
He who does not offer sustenance to these five—the gods, guests, dependents, ancestors, and himself—does not truly live, even though he breathes. 3.72

Regarding the term "deities" (*devatā*): by the word "deity," even the elemental spirits (*bhūta*) are included, for they too possess the nature of deities when offerings (*bali*) are presented to them. Servants—such as elderly parents and others—must necessarily be nurtured. Furthermore, the nourishment of oneself must also be performed, as the Vedic scripture states: "One should protect oneself from all [sides]. The verse conveys the necessity of performing these duties through censure: he who does not give food to these five—the deities and so forth—even while breathing, does not truly live, because he fails to perform the functions of life. (3.72)
The unoffered sacrifice (ahuta), the offered sacrifice (huta), the likewise well-offered sacrifice (prahuta),
the sacrifice to Brahman (brāhmya-huta), and the consumed sacrifice (prāśita)— these they declare to be the five sacrifices.

"And [the term] 'ahuta'... In order to demonstrate that even when there is a difference in names, there is a difference in the sentences [they refer to], he himself explains those other designations—*ahuta* and so forth—which are the alternative names for the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) according to other sages. || 3.73 ||

Recitation is the *huta* offering; the fire sacrifice (*homa*) is the *prahuta*; the ritual offering to spirits (*bali*) is the *bhautika*; worship of the foremost of the twice-born is the *brāhmya-huta*; and the libation to the ancestors (*pitṛ-tarpaṇa*) is the *prāśita*. (3.74)

Regarding the term *japa*: by the word *ahuta* is meant the *japa* known as the *brahmayajña*; by the word *huta*, the oblation (*homa*) known as the *devayajña*; by the word *prahuta*, the offering to beings (*bhūtabali*) known as the *bhūtayajña*; by the word *brāhmyahuta*, the honoring of an excellent Brāhmaṇa known as the *manuṣyayajña*; and by the word *prāśita*, the daily *śrāddha* known as the *pitṛyajña*. (3.74)

One should be constantly engaged in the private recitation of the Vedas and in divine rites here; for it is by being devoted to divine rites that one sustains this world of the moving and the unmoving. (3.75)

Regarding "study" (svādhyāya): if, due to defects such as poverty, one is unable to perform the feeding of guests and other duties, then one should remain constantly engaged in the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña), as well as in rites for the gods and oblations into the fire. He speaks in praise of the oblation: "For he who is devoted to the rites for the gods sustains this world of moving and unmoving beings. (3.75)
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "The oblation duly cast into the fire reaches the sun; from the sun rain is born, from that comes food, and from that, living beings. (3.76)

"In the fire": the oblation, properly cast into the fire by the sacrificer, reaches the sun because it effects the drawing up of the essence. And that essence of the oblation arises from the sun in the form of rain; from that comes food; and through the consumption of that, living beings are born. (3.76)
Just as all living beings depend upon the wind for their life, so do all the other stages of life depend upon the householder. 3.77
"Yathā" means: just as all living beings live by depending on the vital air called *prāṇa*, so too do all those in the [other] stages of life subsist by depending on the householder. 3.77
It has been stated that the householder is equal to life itself for those in all stages of life; he now demonstrates this very point:
"Since even those in the other three stages of life are daily supported by the householder alone through both knowledge and food, therefore the householder is the highest stage. (3.78)

"Because"—that is to say: because even the three [other] orders of life, distinct from the householder, are constantly supported by the householders alone through the exposition of the meaning of the Vedas and the gift of food; therefore, the householder is the "eldest order. The term *jyeṣṭhāśrama* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose order (āśrama) is the eldest. (3.78)

This must be maintained with effort by one who desires imperishable heaven, and by one who constantly desires happiness here in this world—this which is difficult for those of weak faculties to maintain. (3.79)

"He" refers to this: since it is so, that stage of life, the householder's order (gṛhasthāśrama), should be diligently practiced by one who desires the bliss of heaven—as if it were infinite because of its long duration—and who desires in this world the continuous happiness of sexual union with women, the enjoyment of delicious food and the like; for it cannot be maintained by those whose senses are not restrained. (3.79)
Sages, ancestors, gods, living beings, and likewise guests, place their hopes upon householders; therefore, one who understands his duty must act for them. (3.80)
Regarding the word "sages" (ṛṣayaḥ): these [sages] request [gifts] from householders; therefore, one who knows the scriptures must give to them. 3.80.
What is that? He says:

"One should worship the sages with the private recitation of the Vedas, the gods with burnt offerings according to the rule, the ancestors with funeral rites (śrāddha), men with food, and the spirits with the bali offering. (3.81)

Regarding the phrase "by means of self-study" (*svādhyāyena*): since worship (*arcana*) takes many forms, it is appropriate that self-study and the like serve as modes of worship. One should worship the sages, gods, ancestors, guests, and living beings through the acts of self-study and so forth included within the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*), in accordance with the scriptures. (3.81)
Regarding that, he first speaks of the sacrifice to the ancestors:
"One should perform the *śrāddha* ceremony day after day with food and drink, or even with milk, roots, and fruits, bringing satisfaction to the ancestors. (3.82)

"One should perform" means that one should perform the *śrāddha* every day as far as possible. This word *śrāddha*, occurring in an injunction for a ritual act, serves—like the term *agnihotra* in the context of the *kauṇḍapāyinām ayana* sacrifice—to extend the application (*atideśa*) of the rules of the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* which will be described later. "With food and the like" includes sesame seeds, rice, barley, and so forth. "Milk" refers to cow's milk. (3.82)
For the sake of the ancestral rites among the five sacrifices, one should feed even a single Brahmin;
however, for the Vaiśvadeva rite, one should not feed any twice-born man at all.

"One" means that for the purpose of the ancestors, which is included within the five great sacrifices (pañcayajña), one should feed even a single Brāhmaṇa; by the use of the word "even," it is implied that if possible, many may be fed. And because the rules of the Pārvaṇa rite are adopted here, which would entail feeding Brāhmaṇas for the Vaiśvadeva, he says:
"One should not feed any Brāhmaṇa here for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva."
A Brahmin should daily perform an oblation in the domestic fire for these deities from the prepared Vaiśvadeva food, according to the prescribed rule. (3.84)

Regarding the term *vaiśvadeva*: that which is for the sake of the *viśvedevas*—that is, for the sake of all the deities—is the *vaiśvadeva*. Of that cooked food, a Brāhmaṇa should perform daily oblations (*homa*) into the domestic fire (*āvasathya-agni*), preceded by the ritual procedures such as sprinkling water (*paryukṣaṇa*) prescribed in his own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, for these deities who are about to be mentioned. The mention of "Brāhmaṇa" is intended to indicate the twice-born (*dvijāti*), since all three [castes] are under discussion here. (3.84)
First to Agni and to Soma, then to those two together, then to the Viśvedevas and to Dhanvantari. (3.85)

Regarding the word "of Agni": because of the traditional teaching of Kātyāyana that "the oblation is performed with the utterance of *svāhā*," one should first perform two independent offerings to the deities, namely "To Agni, *svāhā*" and "To Soma, *svāhā*," and then perform an offering to the combined deity, "To Agni and Soma, *svāhā*. After that, [offerings] to the Viśvedevas and to Dhanvantari. || 3.85 ||
To Kuhū and to Anumati, and to Prajāpati, and likewise to Dyāvāpṛthivī together, and finally to Sviṣṭakṛt. (3.86)

And [the offering] to Kuhū. One should perform the oblations ending with the utterance of *svāhā* as follows: to Anumati, to Prajāpati, to Heaven and Earth (*dvāpṛthivī*), and to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. Since in other Vedic texts *Sviṣṭakṛt* is prescribed as an epithet of Agni, even when only *Sviṣṭakṛt* is mentioned, it must be employed specifically as an epithet of Agni. Although the position at the end is already established by the very recitation of the text, the explicit statement "to Sviṣṭakṛt at the end" is intended to indicate that this position remains final even when the oblation is combined with those prescribed in other Smṛtis. (3.86)
Having thus offered the oblation correctly, he should present the bali-offering in a clockwise direction toward all the quarters to Indra, Antaka, Appati, and Indu, together with their followers.

"Thus. In this manner, as described, with a mind focused correctly on nothing else and intent solely upon meditation on the deity, one should perform the *homa* offerings and then present the *bali* offering to Indra and his attendants, moving clockwise through all the directions, beginning with the east. Thus: "Obeisance to Indra and obeisance to Indra’s attendants" in the east; "Obeisance to Yama and obeisance to Yama’s attendants" in the south; "Obeisance to Varuṇa and obeisance to Varuṇa’s attendants" in the west; "Obeisance to Soma and obeisance to Soma’s attendants" in the north. Although, since their status as deities is understood through verbal testimony (*śabda*), it would have been more appropriate to invoke them using the terms *Antaka*, *Āpyapati*, and *Indu*, nevertheless, because of the agreement with the practice of the Bahvṛcas and because the *Bahvṛca-gṛhya-sūtra* (1.2) reads, "To Yama and Yama’s attendants, to Varuṇa and Varuṇa’s attendants, to Soma and Soma’s attendants—thus for each direction," the ritual application is exactly as stated. 3.87.
One should cast [the food] at the door with the words, "To the Maruts," and likewise into the water with the words, "To the Waters";
one should offer it upon the pestle and mortar with the words, "To the Vanaspatis."

"Marudbhyaḥ" (to the Maruts). The word "iti" is intended to indicate the actual form [of the mantra]. One should offer the bali-oblation at the door with the words, "Marudbhyo namaḥ" (Salutation to the Maruts). At the water, [one offers] "adbhyaḥ" (to the waters). Because of the use of a copulative compound in "musalolūkhale" (mortar and pestle), one should offer the bali-oblation to the Vanaspatis (Trees) at either one of the two items joined together; for it is improper that the primary ritual act of offering the bali should be repeated merely in accordance with the subordinate factors. || 3.88 ||
One should offer to Śrī at the head of the bed and to Bhadrakālī at the feet;
one should present the bali offering to Brahmā and Vāstoṣpati in the middle of the dwelling.

Regarding the term *ucchīrṣake*: one should offer an oblation (*bali*) to Śrī in the north-eastern direction, which is the region of the head of the Vāstupuruṣa. To Bhadrakālī, one should offer it in the south-western direction, which is the region of his feet. Others, however, say that *ucchīrṣaka* refers to the head-end of the householder’s bed, and *pāda* refers to the foot-end of that same bed. The phrase “to Brahmā and Vāstoṣpati” is for the center of the house. Although they are mentioned as a copulative compound (*dvandva*), Brahmā and Vāstoṣpati are each distinct deities. Where a collective deity is intended in a copulative compound, the author uses a word such as *saha*; for example, “and [the offering] to Heaven and Earth together” (3.86). || 3.89 ||
And he should cast an offering into the air for all the gods,
as well as for the beings that roam by day and those that roam by night.

Regarding the phrase "to all" (*viśvebhyaḥ*): because of the words "and to all the gods" (*viśvebhyaś ca devebhyaḥ*), this is a single oblation. One should offer the *bali* in the open space of the house with the formula, "Homage to all the gods" (*viśvebhyo devebhyo namaḥ*). During the day, one offers with "to the beings that roam by day" (*divācarebhyo bhūtebhyaḥ*), and at night, with "to those that roam by night" (*naktaṃcaribhyaḥ*). This arrangement is established based on the observation of the *Bahvṛca-gṛhya-sūtra*, which states: "During the day, [offer] to those that roam by day" (*divācāribhyo divā*) and so forth (Baudhāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.2). || 3.90 ||
One should offer the bali-oblation on the ground behind [the house] for the sake of the welfare of all beings;
as for the remainder of the bali, one should carry it all to the south for the ancestors.

Regarding the word *pṛṣṭha*: that house which is above the [main] house is the *pṛṣṭhavāstu*. One should offer the oblation there with the words, “Salutation to the Soul of All,” either on the part of the ground behind the sacrificer or in the region behind him. Having offered all the remaining food from the aforementioned oblations, one should present the oblation in the southern direction, facing south, with the words, “Svadhā to the ancestors (*pitṛbhyaḥ*”). This oblation must be offered while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), because of the statement in the *Bahvṛca-gṛhya-sūtra*: “Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder, he should pour out the remainder facing south, saying ‘Svadhā to the ancestors’” (1.2). || 3.91 ||
One should slowly offer [the remnants] upon the ground for dogs, outcasts, dog-cookers, those afflicted with foul diseases, crows, and worms. (3.92)

"And for dogs": having set aside other food in a vessel, one should give it slowly to dogs, outcasts, and others on the ground, in such a way that it is not touched by dust. This refers to those afflicted with sinful diseases, such as leprosy or consumption. (3.92)
Thus, the Brahmin who constantly honors all beings goes by a straight path to the supreme abode, whose form is radiant light.

"Thus" means: he who constantly worships all beings by the aforementioned manner through the gift of food and so forth, reaches the supreme station—the radiant form consisting of Brahman—by the straight path, namely the path beginning with light (arcir-ādi-mārga). The meaning is that he merges into Brahman, because liberation is attained through both knowledge and action. Regarding the reading "tejomūrtiḥ" with a visarga, the explanation is: "having become one whose nature is the supreme realization of Brahman. 3.93
Having performed this rite of offerings in this manner, he should first feed his guest;
he should also give alms according to the rule to a mendicant and to a student of sacred knowledge.

"Having performed"—that is, having performed this *balikarman* in the manner described above—one should feed the guest before those who eat at home. To a mendicant (*bhikṣu*), a wandering ascetic (*parivrāja*), and a student (*brahmacārin*) of the first stage of life, one should give alms according to rule after pronouncing the blessing of well-being (*svastivācana*), following the procedure stated by Gautama and others: "Alms may also be given afterwards. Furthermore, the measure of alms is that of a mouthful (*grāsa*), because of the statement of Śātātapa: "Alms should consist of a single mouthful. However, if possible, even more than that should be given. (3.94)
Whatever merit one obtains by giving a cow to a guru according to the prescribed rule,
that same merit a twice-born householder obtains by giving alms.

Regarding the word "yat": whatever fruit one obtains by giving a cow to a preceptor according to the rule, including the prescribed procedure for [providing] golden horns and so forth, that same fruit a householder obtains by giving alms according to the rule. 3.95.
One should respectfully offer, according to the prescribed rule, even a portion of alms or a vessel of water to a Brāhmaṇa who knows the true meaning of the Vedas. (3.96)

Regarding the word "alms" (bhikṣām): in the absence of abundant food, one should give even a morsel-sized alms, honoring it with condiments and the like; and in the absence of that, even a vessel filled with water, honoring it with fruits, flowers, and so forth, one should give it to a Brāhmaṇa who truly knows the Vedas and their meaning, preceded by the ritual injunction beginning with "having caused [him] to pronounce 'svasti'. || 3.96 ||
The offerings to the gods and ancestors of ignorant men perish when given out of delusion by donors to Brahmins who have become like ashes. (3.97)

"They perish" means that, due to delusion, when food is given by donors to recipients who are unqualified—because those recipients lack the luster of Vedic study, knowledge of its meaning, and ritual performance, and are like mere ashes—the offerings made for the sake of the gods and ancestors become fruitless. (3.97)
An oblation offered into the fires of the mouths of Brahmins, who are enriched by knowledge and austerity, delivers one from misfortune and even from great sin. (3.98)

Regarding the phrase "among those enriched by knowledge and austerity": the mouths of Brahmins, who are endowed with the splendor of learning and asceticism, are described as being fire—the locus for the oblation (homa). What is cast into them, such as offerings to gods and ancestors (havya-kavya), protects one in this world from insurmountable fears such as disease, enemies, and oppression by kings, and from great sin; and in the next world, it protects one from hell. (3.98)
To a guest who has arrived, one should offer a seat and water, as well as food according to one's ability, having honored him with due ceremony in accordance with the prescribed rule. (3.99)

Regarding the phrase "to one who has arrived": for a guest who has come of his own accord, one should provide a seat, water for washing the feet and so forth, and food honored with side-dishes and the like as far as possible, according to the procedure to be described later in the verse beginning, "A seat and lodging" (3.107). || 3.99 ||
Even for one who constantly gathers grains by gleaning or offers oblations into the five fires, a Brahmin staying unhonored takes away all of his merit. (3.100)

Regarding the word *śilān*: *śilās* are the grains remaining in a harvested field; even for one who gathers these, provided he is endowed with restraint in his livelihood, there are five fires: the three sacred fires (*tretā*), the domestic fire (*āvasathya*), and the social fire (*sabhya*). The fire called *sabhya* is that which is brought forth there for the purpose of dispelling cold and so forth. Even for one performing oblations (*homa*) in these five fires, a guest staying in the house without being honored takes away all the merit acquired through those five fire-oblations by means of the restriction of his own livelihood. And by this censure, the obligatory nature (*nityatā*) of honoring guests is understood. (3.100)
Grass, ground, water, and fourthly, kind speech—these are never lacking in the homes of the virtuous. (3.101)

Regarding the phrase "grass": when food is unavailable, it is ordained that even grass, resting places, water for washing the feet, and kind words—which serve the purpose of hospitality—must never be withheld in the houses of the righteous; they are things that must necessarily be given. The mention of "grass" is intended to include bedding as well. (3.101)
Because [the term] is not well-known, he states the definition of a guest: "A Brāhmaṇa staying for only one night is traditionally called a guest (atithi);
because he stays impermanently, therefore he is called a guest. (3.102)

"One night": a Brāhmaṇa becomes a guest (*atithi*) by staying for only one night in another's house. He is called a guest because, due to his transient stay, no second day (*tithi*) belongs to him. || 3.102 ||

One should recognize as a guest a Brahmin who has come from another village, as well as one who has arrived as a companion, when he has presented himself at the house where the wife resides or even where the sacred fires are maintained. (3.103)

"Not one" (naika): One who dwells in the same village, with whom one has social contact through various jokes and stories in public, and who seeks a livelihood [from the host], even if he arrives at the time of the Vaiśvadeva offering in the house of one who possesses a wife and the sacred fires—that person one should not recognize as a guest (*atithi*). By this, it is indicated that for one who lacks a wife and the sacred fires, there is no status of being a guest when traveling abroad. 3.103.
Those foolish householders who subsist on the food provided by others go, after death, to the state of cattle for those who gave them that food and other gifts. (3.104)

Regarding the phrase "they wait upon": because of the context concerning guests, those householders who, out of greed for hospitality, travel to other villages and subsist on the food of others, are ignorant of the fault of consuming the food of another which has been forbidden. By that act of eating another's food, they go to the state of being cattle in a future birth for those who gave them food and other things. Therefore, the prohibition is inferred: "one should not do this. (3.104)

A guest brought by the setting sun in the evening must not be turned away by the householder; whether he arrives at the proper time or an improper time, he must not remain in the house without eating. (3.105)

Regarding the term *apraṇodya* ("not to be turned away"): when the sun has set, a guest must not be rejected by a householder. "Carried by the sun" (*sūryeṇoḍha*) means brought [to his home] at night because he is unable to go to his own house. This refers to one who arrives at the time of the second *vaiśvadeva* offering, or even at an improper time during the evening meal; this rule is established for the sake of the gravity of the penance [required if he is turned away]. For this very reason, the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* states: "O King, whatever sin is said to accrue when a daytime guest departs disappointed, that same sin is declared to be eightfold when a guest 'carried by the sun' departs disappointed."
Govindarāja, however, states that this [verse] is intended to provide a counter-exception to the prohibition regarding guests. 3.105.
One should certainly not eat that food oneself which one does not offer to a guest;
for the honoring of guests brings wealth, fame, long life, and leads to heaven. (3.106)

"Or not. That excellent food, such as clarified butter, curd, and so forth, a guest does not refuse; one must not eat that oneself without having given it to him. *Dhanya* means conducive to wealth or the cause of wealth. Words such as *yaśasya* (conducive to fame) and others are to be understood in the same way. This is a statement regarding the fruit of feeding a guest. Nor does this result in the food becoming unnecessary, for there is the scriptural warning of the fault: "He takes away all [the host's] merit" (3.100). 3.106.

One should provide a superior seat, lodging, bed, escorting, and attendance for those who are superior; for those who are inferior, one should provide an inferior degree; and for those who are equal, an equal degree. (3.107)

"Regarding 'seating' (āsena): a seat is a stool or a skin; a lodging is a place of rest; a bed is a couch and so forth; following is accompanying one who is departing; attendance is service. All of this—when many guests arrive simultaneously—one should arrange according to their relative superiority, inferiority, or mediocrity with respect to one another, and not treat all of them equally. (3.107)
But when the Vaiśvadeva offering has been completed, if another guest should arrive, one should give him food according to one's ability; however, one need not perform the Bali offering for him.

Regarding the term *vaiśvadeva*: because of the use of a distinct word [to denote it], once the *vaiśvadeva* has been performed up until the feeding of guests, if another guest should arrive, one should then cook again for that person and give him food. One should not, however, perform the carrying outside (*bahirharaṇa*) from that [original cooking]. Since there is a prohibition against the *bali* offerings, it is understood that the *vaiśvadeva* does not involve the consecration of the food. For if it were a matter of consecrating the food, how could he permit the eating of unconsecrated food? (3.108)
A Brahmin should not proclaim his own family and lineage for the sake of food;
for by praising them for the sake of a meal, he is called by the wise a "vomit-eater. (3.109)

"No," [he replied]. "For the sake of obtaining food, a Brahmin should not announce his own family or lineage. Because one who speaks for the sake of food is called by the wise 'one who has vomited forth his hope' (udgīrṇāśī). (3.109)
But a Kṣatriya is not called a guest in the house of a Brāhmaṇa; nor are a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, nor even a friend, a kinsman, or a teacher. (3.110)

"No," [says the opponent]. A Brāhmaṇa does not have Kṣatriyas and the like as guests, because the Brāhmaṇa is of a superior caste (*jāti*) compared to the Kṣatriyas and others; because friends and kinsmen are related to oneself; and because the Guru possesses authority. By this very logic, for a Kṣatriya, a Brāhmaṇa is a guest as one of a superior caste, and a Kṣatriya is a guest as one of the same caste (*sajātīya*), but not the inferior Vaiśya or Śūdra. Likewise, for a Vaiśya as well, the twice-born (*dvijāti*) are guests, but not the Śūdra. (3.110)
But if a Kṣatriya should come to the house in the manner of a guest, he may, if he so desires, feed him once the Brahmins have finished eating. (3.111)

Regarding the word "yadi" (if): if a Kṣatriya should come to the house of a Brāhmaṇa according to the duty toward a guest—because he has arrived from another village and has presented himself at the proper time for guests—then, when the Brāhmaṇas present in the Brāhmaṇa's house have finished their meal and are seated, one should feed him as well, according to one's desire.
If a Vaiśya or a Śūdra has arrived at his household as one who possesses the status of a guest, he should feed them together with his servants, practicing kindness toward them. (3.112)

Regarding the word "vaiśya": if even a Vaiśya or a Śūdra has arrived at the household or home of a Brāhmaṇa from another village and possesses the status of a guest, then he too should be fed with compassion at the time of feeding the servants, after the mealtime for the Kṣatriya and before the meal of the husband and wife. (3.112)
He should also, together with his wife, feed with affection his friends and others who have come to his house, providing them with food according to his means and their rank. (3.113)

"Others" refers to those other than Kṣatriyas and the like who have been mentioned as times for eating—namely, friends, fellow students, and so forth—who have come to the house out of affection, but not as guests (*atithi*), because that [category] is prohibited [for this occasion]. Having prepared excellent food according to one's ability, one should feed them at the time the wife eats. For the householder as well, that very same time is the time for eating, because it will be stated later: "But the remnants, however, [are for] the husband and wife" (3.116). Although one could simply say "together with himself," this variation in expression is the teacher's stylistic artifice. As for the teacher, his time for eating is not specified because, being the master, he may eat whenever he pleases. (3.113)
One should feed these—married women, young maidens, sick women, and pregnant women—before the guests, without hesitation. (3.114)

Regarding the term *suvāsinyaḥ*: these are newly married women, daughters-in-law, and daughters; as well as maidens and pregnant women, he should feed them first, even before the guests. This is said so that one does not entertain the thought, "How can they eat while the guests have not yet eaten? Medhātithi, however, reads the word as *anvagaiva* and explains it thus: "He should feed them following right after [the guests]," meaning at the same time as the guests; he further notes that others read the word as *agra*. (3.114)
But that unwise man who eats before giving to these [beings] does not realize, while eating, that he is being devoured by dogs and vultures. (3.115)

"Without having given"—meaning that one who eats first, without having given food to these [guests] starting from the guests and ending with the servants, and being unaware of the fault of eating in violation of the rule, does not realize after death that he will be devoured by dogs and vultures. This is stated through the rhetorical skill of the words: "This is the fruit of such transgression. (3.115)
Then, after the Brahmins and the servants have indeed finished eating,
the husband and wife may afterwards eat what remains.

"Once they have eaten" means: when the Brahmins, the guests, their own kinsmen, and the servants, slaves, and so forth, have finished their meal, then the husband and wife shall eat what remains of that food afterwards. (3.116)
Having honored the gods, the seers, human beings, the ancestors, and the household deities, the householder should thereafter eat what remains. (3.117)

Regarding the word "devān" (the gods): by the phrase "and the household deities," the *bhūtayajña* (sacrifice to beings) is indicated, since the performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) has been prescribed [previously], and the eating of the remains of the meal (*śeṣabhojana*) has been enjoined by the verse, "But the husband and wife [should eat] what remains" (3.116). This is a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the purpose of stating the faults that will be mentioned later. Alternatively, the *bhūtayajña* is also included by the very term "devān. The meaning of this [verse] is the injunction to worship images of Vāsudeva and others, [expressed as] "having worshipped the household deities (*gṛhyā devatāḥ*), those residing in the home. 3.117.
He who cooks for his own sake eats only sin; for it is ordained that the food of the virtuous consists of what remains from the sacrifice. 3.118.

"Sin" (agham): he who cooks food solely for his own sake and eats it, giving nothing to the gods and others, eats only sin and not food, because it is the cause of sin. Thus says the Śruti: "He who eats alone becomes a consumer of sin alone. Therefore, that very food which remains from the *pākayajña* sacrifice is taught as the food of the virtuous. (3.118)
In connection with the honoring of guests, he describes the special forms of worship due even to kings and others who have come to one's house:

"One should honor with the honey-mixture (madhuparka) a king, an officiating priest, a snātaka, a teacher, and one’s beloved father-in-law, father-in-law by marriage, and maternal uncle, provided it has been a year since they were last so honored. (3.119)

Regarding the term *rājā*: a Kṣatriya who has been consecrated to the kingdom is a *rājā*; an *ṛtvij* is one by whom the office of priest (*ārtvijya*) has been performed at a sacrifice; a *snātaka* is one who has completed his studies and vows; and a *priya* is a beloved son-in-law. One should honor these seven—beginning with the king—when they have arrived at the house, by means of the ritual known as *madhuparka*, as prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*. The phrase *parisaṃvatsarāt* means that after excluding the year—that is, after that time—one should again honor those who have arrived at the house with the *madhuparka*. This ablative case is used in the sense of exclusion according to the rule *pañcamy apāṅparibhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.10). For this very reason, Jayāditya stated in his commentary on this sūtra: "Because of its association with *apa*, the word *pari* is understood here in the sense of exclusion. Medhātithi, however, reads the text as *parisaṃvatsarān* and explains it as: "One should honor those for whom a year has passed [since their last visit]."
He states [the following] for the purpose of restricting the honor shown to a king and a *snātaka*:
"A king and a *śrotriya* who have arrived at a sacrificial rite are to be honored with the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), but not when there is no sacrifice; such is the settled rule. (3.120)

Regarding the term *rāja*: both the king and the *snātaka* are to be honored with the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) only at a sacrificial rite even after a year has passed, but not apart from a sacrifice. However, the son-in-law and others are worthy of the honey-mixture even without a sacrifice after a year. Within a year, however, for all of them, the honey-mixture is offered only at a sacrifice or a wedding. Thus says Gautama (5.25–27): "The honey-mixture is offered upon the arrival of the officiating priest, the teacher, the father-in-law, the paternal uncle, the maternal uncle, and so forth; again within a year, it is offered to a king and a learned *śrotriya* [only] at a sacrifice or a wedding. (3.120)
In the evening, when food has been prepared, the wife should offer an oblation without reciting mantras;
for this is called the Vaiśvadeva, which is prescribed for both morning and evening.

"At evening": at the end of the day, the wife should perform the offering of the prepared food without reciting the mantra—omitting the verbal recitation such as "Salutation to Indra" (*indrāya namaḥ*). However, the mental dedication to the deity is not prohibited. For this rite called *vaiśvadeva*, which consists of oblations, offerings, and feeding guests accomplished with food, is prescribed for the householder both morning and evening.

Having promised in the table of contents (*anukramaṇikā*) that he would explain "the eternal ritual for ancestral offerings" (*śrāddhakalpaṃ ca śāśvatam*, 1.112), he now begins that ritual for ancestral offerings:

"But having performed the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*), a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires should perform the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* ancestral offering at the waning of the moon, month after month. (3.122)

Regarding the phrase "the sacrifice to the ancestors" (pitṛyajña): one who maintains the sacred fires (sāgni) should perform the rite known as the Piṇḍapitṛyajña on the new moon day (amāvāsyā) and then perform the Śrāddha.
