It is called *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* because it is brought (āhriyate) after the rice-balls (piṇḍas) of the Pitṛyajña. It is performed month after month (*māsānumāsika*); that is, it occurs in each month (*māsa*) and every subsequent month (*anumāsa*). The meaning is that it must be performed every month. By this, its obligatory nature (*nityatva*) is stated. The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" (*vipra*) refers to the twice-born (*dvijāti*), since all three [classes] are the subject under discussion. (3.122)
Now, by means of an etymological explanation, he confirms that very sequence following the sacrifice to the ancestors:
"The wise know the monthly *śrāddha* for the ancestors as the *anvāhārya*;
and that should be performed with effort using excellent meat. (3.123)

Regarding the phrase "of the ancestors" (*pitṝṇām*): this monthly *śrāddha*, which occurs every month, is called *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* because it is performed after (*anu*) the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) of the ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*). Therefore, the learned know this to be the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka*. Consequently, its immediate succession to the ancestral sacrifice is appropriate. And that [śrāddha] should be performed with effort using meat—as will be described—[that is], with commendable, pleasing flesh, free from foul odors and the like. Alternatively, there is the reading: "the monthly *śrāddha* of the rice-balls. Here, "of the rice-balls" means of the rice-balls of the ancestral sacrifice. The rest is the same. (3.123)

In this regard, I shall explain in their entirety who among the best of the twice-born are to be fed, who are to be avoided, how many there are, and with what kinds of food they are to be served. (3.124)
Regarding that: in that *śrāddha*, I shall explain everything—those who are to be fed, those who are to be avoided, their number, and the foods with which [they are to be served]. (3.124)

In this context, although it would have been more appropriate to state who should be fed according to the order of enumeration, nevertheless, because there is little to be said, he states the number of Brāhmaṇas:
"Two for the rite for the gods, three for the rite for the ancestors, or one for each of the two;
even if very wealthy, one should feed [this many] and should not engage in excessive elaboration. (3.125)

"Two" means: at a *deva-śrāddha*, one should feed two Brahmins; for the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, three Brahmins; or alternatively, one may feed one Brahmin for the *deva* portion and one Brahmin for the triad beginning with the father. Even if one is capable of feeding more than the stated number, one should not engage in providing additional meals.

Medhātithi, however, says: "Three for the ancestral rite" means one should feed three Brahmins for the father, three Brahmins for the grandfather, and three Brahmins for the great-grandfather. Or, "one for each on both sides" means one for the divine rite (*daiva*) and one for each of the triad beginning with the father; it does not mean one for the triad beginning with the father, because that would contradict the *Āśvalāyana-gṛhya-sūtra* (16.7): "But by no means should there be only one for all; this is explained by the case of the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) even when there is no [regular] food. Just as a single rice-ball is not offered for the triad beginning with the father, so too a single Brahmin should not be fed. Therefore, there is no feeding of a single Brahmin for the triad beginning with the father.

That is incorrect. For the author of the *Gṛhyasūtra* himself, having stated, "But one [brāhmaṇa] for all [ancestors] is certainly not explained by means of the rice-balls" (*Āśv. Gṛ.* 4.7.16), subsequently declared, "At will, when there is no food" (*kāmam anādye*). The meaning of this is as follows: the first *śrāddha* among those dedicated to many deities, such as the fathers and so forth—namely, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*—is intended; in a *śrāddha* other than that, the sense is that "one brāhmaṇa may be employed at will for the fathers and so forth. Alternatively, "in the absence of food" (*anādye*) means that even if there is a lack of edible substances, even a single person should be fed. In both these interpretations, the feeding of a single brāhmaṇa for the triad of ancestors beginning with the father at the *pārvaṇa* and other rites has been stated by the author of the *Gṛhyasūtra* himself. Vasiṣṭha also says: (11.27) [text omitted].
If one should feed only a single person at a śrāddha, how can there be a ritual for the gods? [The procedure is as follows:
having set aside a portion of food from every prepared dish into a vessel...
Having performed this in a temple of the deities according to the prescribed rule,
one should cast the food into the fire or give it to a celibate student (brahmacārin).

Thus, he states that feeding a single Brāhmaṇa is for all [the ancestors]. Therefore, the rule is exactly as stated. Regarding the form *vistara*, although one might expect it from the rule "prathane vāvaśabde" (Pāṇini 3.3.33), which prescribes the suffix GHaÑ to mean 'extension', the form *vistara* is used here because the Smṛtis share the same status as Vedic *chandas*; according to the principle "all rules are optional in the case of *chandas*" (Kāśikā-Pariśiṣṭa 36). || 3.125 ||
Hospitality, proper time and place, purity, and the excellence of the Brahmins—these five are destroyed by prolixity; therefore, one should not seek prolixity.

"Sad" means: the hospitable treatment (*satkriyā*), which is the honoring of the Brahmins; the place, such as being sloped toward the south and so forth, which will be described later; the time, namely the afternoon; purity, pertaining to the performer of the *śrāddha*, the eating Brahmins, and the servants; and the acquisition of virtuous Brahmins—these things the excessive number of Brahmins (*brāhmaṇavistāra*) destroys. Therefore, one should not perform an excessive number of Brahmins. Because of this prohibition against an excessive number of Brahmins due to its conflict with hospitable treatment and the other requirements, when hospitable treatment and the rest are possible, even for each individual ancestor, three Brahmins are permitted. For this very reason, Gautama (15.2) says: "One should not feed fewer [than three], nor an odd number, but according to one's capacity. The author of the *Bahvṛca-gṛhya* also, having begun (16.7) with: "Now, therefore, at the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*, the optional (*kāmya*), the *ābhyudayika*, or the *ekoddiṣṭa*, [one should invite] Brahmins," concludes by saying: "One for each [ancestor], or two for each, or three for each; in the case of a prosperity rite (*vṛddhi*), there is greater fruit. The rule "two for each" refers specifically to the *ābhyudayika-śrāddha*, because it is ordained thus in other *smṛtis* and because here too the context begins with the *ābhyudayika*. (3.126)
This well-known performance for the deceased, called the ancestral rite (pitrya), occurs at the waning of the moon;
for one engaged in that, the worldly duty toward the dead is constantly fulfilled.

Regarding the word *prathitā*: this ancestral rite (*pitryaṃ karma*) in the form of a *śrāddha* is known as a "well-known funeral rite" (*pretakṛtyā*), a performance intended for the benefit of the ancestors. One who has departed (*preta*) in an eminent manner is said to be one residing in the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*). On the waning of the moon, that is, on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), for one engaged in this ancestral rite and intent upon it, this worldly and traditional funeral rite—performed for the sake of benefiting the ancestors—accrues to the performer in the form of a continuous stream of fruits such as virtuous sons, grandsons, wealth, and so forth; therefore, this must be performed. Govindarāja, however, reads "vidhiḥ kṣaya" and explains it thus: "This which is called the rule (*vidhi*) is the ancestral rite; 'on the waning' (*kṣaye*) means on the waning of the moon or in the house. But this is not according to tradition, because it was not accepted by Medhātithi and others—who are even more venerable than Govindarāja—and because the connection [of the words] would involve unnecessary difficulty. (3.127)
Sacrificial offerings to the gods and the ancestors must be given by donors only to one learned in the Vedas;
what is given to such a most worthy Brahmin yields great fruit.

Regarding the term *śrotriya*: one who has studied merely the Vedic meters is a *śrotriya*; for him, food intended for the gods and ancestors must be offered with great care. To one who is most worthy—most venerable by virtue of learning, conduct, lineage, and so forth—the gift given yields great fruit.
One should feed even a single learned man at a rite for the gods or the ancestors; one obtains abundant fruit, but not by feeding many who are ignorant of the mantras. (3.129)

"Each one": even for the rites for the gods (*daiva*) and the ancestors (*pitrya*), one should feed at least one Brāhmaṇa who knows the essence of the Vedas; even then, one obtains the distinguished fruit of the *śrāddha*, but not by feeding many who are ignorant. Thus Govindarāja says: "Because the fruit is heard [to result from it], the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas alone is the primary act (*pradhāna*), whereas the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and so forth are merely subsidiary acts (*aṅga*). We, however, maintain that the primary act denoted by the word *śrāddha* is the renunciation of property intended for the ancestors, extending until its acceptance by the Brāhmaṇas. That very act was prescribed by Manu (3.122): "One should perform the *śrāddha* known as the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka*. This is because Āpastamba has explained the meaning of Manu's statement. Thus says Āpastamba: "In this regard, Manu declared this rite to be designated by the word *śrāddha* for the sake of the ultimate welfare of progeny. In it, the ancestors are the deities (*devatā*), while the Brāhmaṇa serves the purpose of the *āhavanīya* fire, because he is the locus for the reception of the renounced substance. The afternoon of the waning fortnight (*aparapakṣa*) month after month is superior. The term *śrāddhaśabda* means that which has the word *śrāddha* as its designator. The Brāhmaṇa serves the purpose of the *āhavanīya* fire because, like the *āhavanīya*, he is the place for the reception of the renounced substance. Furthermore, the ancestors are the deities because the *śrāddha* has the ancestors as its fixed deities. The use of the word *śrāddha* in the context of the *devatā-śrāddha* and others is secondary (*gauṇa*), intended to extend those specific rules (*dharmaprāptyartha*), just as the word *agnihotra* is used for the *kauṇḍapāyinām ayana* sacrifice. As for the phrase "one obtains abundant fruit," this is an injunction of a subordinate fruit (*guṇaphalavidhi*) for one who desires a more nourishing reward. Even though the feeding is a subsidiary act, there is no contradiction in having that [feeding] as the basis for the fruit.
Āpastamba declared that this rite of śrāddha has the ancestors as its deity;
since it is performed for the sake of the Manu [tradition], it is not merely a feeding of Brāhmaṇas.
One should examine from afar a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas; he is the proper recipient for offerings to the gods and ancestors, and he is considered a guest. (3.130)

"From afar": from afar indeed, by ascertaining the purity of his lineage through his father, grandfather, and ancestors, one should examine a Brāhmaṇa who has studied an entire Vedic branch (*śākhā*). For such a Brāhmaṇa is the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) and the worthy recipient (*pātra*) for oblations and other offerings; in the act of giving, he is truly a guest, because he is the cause for attaining great fruit. (3.130)
For where thousands upon thousands of those ignorant of the Ṛgveda eat, a single person who knows the mantras, being pleased, rightfully outweighs them all. (3.131)

"Regarding the word 'thousand': where in a *śrāddha* ceremony ten million non-Vedic-knowing (*avidevid*) Brahmins eat, there a single Vedic-knower (*vedavid*), being satisfied by the meal, is worthy—by virtue of Dharma and through the production of merit—to encompass all of them; that is to say, he generates the fruit produced by their eating. The singular number is used because it follows Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). Alternatively, the intention of Manu is that the word 'thousand' stands in place of the plural. Govindarāja, however, says: 'In the Veda [it is said], "Let the beings go in thousands. 3.131"
Offerings for the ancestors and oblations for the gods should be given to one preeminent in knowledge;
for hands smeared with blood are not purified by blood alone. (3.132)

Regarding the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*): offerings to the gods (*havya*) and offerings to the ancestors (*kavya*) should be given to those distinguished by learning, not to fools. This is the poetic figure known as *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle). For hands stained with blood are not cleansed by blood itself, but rather by pure water; likewise, the fault produced by feeding a fool is not removed by feeding another fool, but only by a learned man. (3.132)

By censuring the ignorant, he praises the gift given to the learned through an indirect expression: "As many morsels as one who is ignorant of the mantras consumes at offerings to the gods and ancestors, so many glowing spikes, spears, and iron balls shall he consume after death. (3.133)

"As many as" means: however many mouthfuls of *havya* (offerings to gods) and *kavya* (offerings to ancestors) an ignorant person eats, the performer of the present *śrāddha* swallows that same number of glowing iron balls (*lohapiṇḍa*) known as spears and spikes. This description of the fruit of giving to the ignorant refers specifically to the performer of the *śrāddha*. As Vyāsa says: "Whatever number of sacrificial morsels an unlearned man consumes, he shall swallow that many spikes upon reaching the abode of Vaivasvata."
Some twice-born ones are devoted to knowledge, others likewise to austerity; some are devoted to austerity and self-study, and others likewise to ritual action. (3.134)

Regarding the word "jñāna" (knowledge): some Brāhmaṇas are devoted to the knowledge of the Self; others are primarily engaged in austerities such as those dedicated to Prajāpati; others are intent upon austerity and study; and still others are devoted to sacrifices and the like. || 3.134 ||

What follows from this? To this he says: "Offerings to the poets (kavya) should be diligently established among those who are devoted to knowledge; however, offerings to the gods (havya) should be given according to rule to all four [classes] alike. (3.135)

Regarding the word "jñāna": food intended for the ancestors (pitṛ) should be given with effort to those who prioritize knowledge; however, food for the gods (deva) should be given to all four [classes] in accordance with the treatises on wealth as determined by right principle. 3.135.
Having introduced the question of which of these two is superior, he states the distinction:
"If a man's father is unlearned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*) but his son has mastered the Vedas (*vedapāraga*), or if his son is unlearned in the Vedas but his father has mastered the Vedas... (3.136)
Regarding the term "aśrotriya": it refers to one whose father was not a *śrotriya* while he himself is a *śrotriya*, or one whose father was a *śrotriya* while he himself is not a *śrotriya*. (3.136)
One should know the elder of these two to be him whose father is a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya);
the other, however, deserves honor for the sake of honoring the sacred mantras. 3.137.

Regarding the phrase "the more venerable": between these two mentioned in the preceding verse, one should recognize the son of a *śrotriya* as the elder, even if he himself is not a *śrotriya*. This is based on respect for the father's learning. On the other hand, the son of a non-*śrotriya* who is himself a *śrotriya* deserves honor for the sake of honoring the Veda studied by him; since the Veda itself is honored through him, this is based on respect for the son's learning. Therefore, by way of this phrasing, it is stated that the son of a *śrotriya* who is himself a *śrotriya* should be fed at a *śrāddha*. It is not, however, an authorization for the son of a *śrotriya* who is himself a non-*śrotriya*, because that would contradict the rule: "Gifts should be given only to a *śrotriya*" (3.128). Thus, the injunction "one should examine [him] from afar" (3.130) remains applicable as a means of examining conduct and so forth, distinct from learning. (3.137)
One should not feed a friend at a *śrāddha*; rather, one should win him over with wealth.
One should feed that twice-born man at a *śrāddha* whom one knows to be neither an enemy nor a friend. (3.138)

"No," [it is said]. One should not feed a friend at a *śrāddha*. His friendship should be cultivated through other means of wealth. One should feed that Brāhmaṇa at the *śrāddha* whom one knows to be neither an enemy nor a friend. (3.138)
For him whose śrāddha rites and oblations are dominated by friends, there is no fruit after death from those śrāddhas or those oblations. (3.139)

Regarding the word *yasya*: this term *mitra* (friend) here emphasizes the state (*bhāva*). This statement is intended to express the absence of fruit—that for one whose offerings to gods and ancestors (*havyakavya*) are primarily characterized by friendliness (*maitrī*), there is no fruit in the next world. The word *pretya* is another indeclinable used in the sense of "in the next world" (*paraloka*), and not a form ending in the suffix *ktvā*; therefore, one should not raise the objection as to how the suffix *ktvā* could be used when the agents are not identical.
To demonstrate that heaven is the fruit of the *śrāddha*, he specifically describes the absence of the previously mentioned fruits:
"That man who, out of delusion, forms alliances through the *śrāddha*—he, a friend of the *śrāddha*, the lowest of the twice-born, falls from the heavenly world. (3.140)

"Who" refers to that man who, out of ignorance of the scriptures, forms friendships through *śrāddha*—for *śrāddha* itself is the "friend" because it is the cause of gaining friends—and such a base twice-born man (*dvijāpasada*) falls from the heavenly world; the meaning is that he does not attain it. Yājñavalkya also states that *śrāddha* has heaven as its fruit (1.270):
"Likewise, when they are pleased, the ancestors bestow upon men long life, progeny, wealth, knowledge, heaven, liberation, and happiness."
That which is called a communal feast is declared by the twice-born to be a *paiśācī* sacrificial gift;
it remains right here in this world like a blind cow in a single house.

Regarding the term *saṃbhojanī*: that sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*) is a *saṃbhojanī* because it is enjoyed together; it is a communal feast consisting of the feeding of many people. Because it possesses the nature of a *piśāca*, it is called *paiśācī* by Manu and others. And since its purpose is the cultivation of friendliness (*maitrī*), it does not have a fruit in the next world, but remains in this world alone—just as a blind cow stays in one house and lacks the capacity to go to another house. (3.141)
Just as one who sows seed in barren soil does not obtain fruit, so too the giver who offers an oblation to one ignorant of the Ṛgveda does not obtain the fruit. 3.142

Regarding the word "yathā" (as): a *īriṇa* is a saline wasteland where seed sown does not sprout; just as a farmer, having sown seed there, does not obtain fruit, so too a donor does not obtain the fruit of giving a *śrāddha* to one who lacks knowledge. 3.142.
By giving a sacrificial fee to a learned man according to the prescribed rule, one makes both the giver and the recipient partakers of the fruit, both in this world and after death. (3.143)

"Those who give": for one who knows the true essence of the Vedas, that which is given according to the scriptures makes the donors partakers of rewards both in this world and the next. Regarding the reward in this world, Medhātithi and Govindarāja maintain that it is the incidental attainment of fame resulting from the performance of the rites according to the scriptures. We, however, say that the reward in this world consists precisely of longevity and so forth; for Yājñavalkya and others have stated that the Śrāddha has results pertaining to this world, the next world, and so on, as in the verse: "They say [it grants] progeny, wealth, and knowledge" (YDh 1.270). Furthermore, he makes the recipients successful in the other world through the fruit of the sacrifices and other rites performed with the wealth obtained at the Śrāddha; for sacrifices and the like performed with wealth acquired by unjust means yield no fruit. In this world, he makes them successful because they obtain an abundance of fruits from agriculture and other activities undertaken with wealth acquired by righteous means. (3.143)
One may, if one wishes, form a friend at a funeral rite even if he is not handsome, but never an enemy;
for an oblation consumed by an adversary becomes fruitless after death. (3.144)

Regarding the word *kāmam*: it is better to feed a virtuous friend in the absence of learned Brahmins than even a learned enemy; for a *śrāddha* meal eaten by an enemy becomes fruitless in the next world. This [verse] is intended as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) for the sake of feeding a friend when the aforementioned worthy recipients (*pātra*) are unavailable. 3.144.

By the statement, “Gifts should be given only to a *śrotriya*” (3.128), it was declared that since the word *śrotriya* is applied to one who has studied merely the Vedic meters (*chandas*), reliance upon that [minimal qualification] is necessary; however, now, for the sake of greater merit, he states that the gift should be given to a *śrotriya* who has studied the entire branch (*śākhā*) consisting of both Mantra and Brāhmaṇa: “One should diligently feed at a *śrāddha* a Bahvṛca who has mastered the Veda, or an Adhvaryu who has reached the end of his recensional branch, or a Chandoga who has completed his study. (3.145)

Regarding the word "with effort" (*yatnena*): one should feed with care a student of the *Ṛgveda*, that is, one who studies a branch (*śākhā*) consisting of both mantra and brāhmaṇa. The same applies to such a student of the *Yajurveda*. One who goes to the further shore (*pāra*) of the Veda is a *vedapāraga*; one who goes to the end of a branch is a *śākhāntaga*; one who possesses completion (*samāpti*) is a *samāptika*. By all these terms, a student of the entire branch consisting of both mantra and brāhmaṇa is designated. (3.145)
Regarding the superior fruit of feeding them, he says:
"If any one of these, being honored, should eat at someone's ancestral offering (śrāddha), the satisfaction of that person’s ancestors shall be eternal, extending through seven generations. (3.146)

Regarding the word "eṣām" (of these): among these—such as the Bahvṛcas and others—who have studied their entire Vedic branches, whichever one eats at a Śrāddha ceremony having been properly honored, for that person there shall be eternal and uninterrupted satisfaction of the ancestors for seven generations, beginning with his own sons. In the term *sāptapauruṣī*, both members of the compound undergo vṛddhi by virtue of belonging to the *anuśatikādi* group, and this group is an open-ended category (*ākṛtigaṇa*). (3.146)
This indeed is the primary rule for the offering of oblations to the gods and the ancestors;
however, this secondary rule should be known as that which is always practiced by the virtuous.

Regarding the word "this": in the offering of both *havya* (oblations to the gods) and *kavya* (oblations to the ancestors), that which is given to unrelated *śrotriya*s and others is declared to be the primary rule (*mukhya-kalpa*). However, this [present case], which will be described, should be understood as the secondary rule (*anukalpa*) to be followed when the primary one is unavailable; it is always practiced by the virtuous. (3.137)

One should feed the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, the sister’s son, the father-in-law, the teacher, the daughter’s son, the husband of a sister, a relative, as well as the officiating priest and the one for whom he performs sacrifices. 3.148.

"Maternal grandfather" (mātāmaha) refers to the maternal uncle's son (svasrīya) and the nephew (bhāgineya); "teacher" (guru) refers to the preceptor of learning (vidyā-guru), the ācārya, and so forth; "husband of a courtesan" (viṭpati) refers to the daughter (viṭ-duhitṛ), her husband being the son-in-law (jāmātṛ); and "relative" (bandhu) refers to the sons of one's mother’s sister and father’s sister, and others. One should feed these ten—the maternal grandfather and the rest—in the event that a preeminent śrotriya and the like are unavailable. (3.148)
One who knows the Dharma should not examine a Brāhmaṇa for a rite dedicated to the gods; but when a rite dedicated to the ancestors has arrived, he should examine him with great care. (3.149)

"No," [says the author]. One who knows the Dharma need not scrutinize a Brāhmaṇa with great effort for the purpose of feeding him at a *daiva-śrāddha*. He may be fed as being virtuous based on mere worldly renown. However, when the rite for the ancestors (*paitrya-karman*) has arrived, an investigation into the lineage of the father, grandfather, and so forth must be performed; this is the meaning of the word "with effort" (*prayatnataḥ*). (3.149)

Those who are thieves, outcasts, or eunuchs, and those who follow the lifestyle of nihilists—Manu has declared such Brahmins to be unworthy of offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya). 3.150

"Yaḥ" (who): "stenaḥ" means a thief, and he is one other than a stealer of gold, since the latter is already included by the term "patita" (outcast). A "patita" is one who has committed a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*); a "klība" is a eunuch; a "nāstikavṛtti" is one whose conduct or inclination is such that they maintain "there is no next world. Manu declared that these individuals are unfit for both rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors. The mention of Manu is intended to show respect for the prohibition, as all dharmas have indeed been proclaimed by Manu. (3.150)

One should not feed at a śrāddha those who officiate as priests for a matted-hair ascetic who does not study, nor for one who is weak, nor for a gambler, nor for groups of men who perform sacrifices for such persons. (3.151)

Regarding the term *jaṭila*: a *jaṭila* is a religious student (*brahmacārī*). Since the state of having matted hair (*jaṭilatva*) serves as an indicative mark for the student mentioned in the rule, "He may be shaven-headed or have matted hair" (2.219), even the shaven-headed student is prohibited. This prohibition is intended to permit a student who has not yet undertaken the study of the Veda—that is, one for whom only the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) has been performed and no instruction in the Veda and so forth has occurred—even if he has not formally accepted the Veda, provided he is currently engaged in its study. Therefore, the rule "Gifts are to be given only to a *śrotriya*" (3.128) refers to those other than the religious student. *Durbala* means one with a skin disease. Medhātithi, however, reads *durvāla* and explains it as having three possible meanings: bald, red-haired, or suffering from a skin disease. *Kitava* means a gambler. *Pūgayājaka* means one who performs sacrifices for a multitude; lexicographers state that "a *pūga* is a group of people or a collection of ritual acts. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha says: "And he who performs sacrifices for many, and he who initiates many. The injunction "one should not feed them at a *śrāddha*" is a prohibition regarding the ancestral rite (*pitṛ*), not the divine rite (*daiva*). Where Manu intends a prohibition for both types of rites, he uses the expression "regarding both" (*ubhayatra*) or includes the terms *havya* and *kavya*.
Physicians, temple-priests, meat-sellers, and those who live by trade—these should be avoided at rites for the gods and the ancestors. (3.152)

"Physicians" (*cikitsakān*): a physician (*cikitsaka*) is a medical practitioner; a *devalaka* is one who attends to an image. This prohibition applies to those who perform this work for the sake of livelihood (*vartanārthatvena*), but not to those who do so for the sake of religious duty (*dharmārtha*). This is because of the statement of Devala: "One who consumes the treasury of a deity shall be known by the name *devalaka*. Regarding "meat-sellers": even if only once, as indicated by the scriptural mark (*liṅga*) stating, "One falls immediately through meat" (10.92). Regarding "by trade" (*vipaṇena*): trade (*vipaṇa*) means commerce; those living by that [are meant]. Since they are designated as such in relation to both "offerings to gods and ancestors" (*havyakavyayoḥ*), these persons are to be excluded from rites for the gods and the ancestors. (3.152)
A servant of a village or of a king, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one who opposes his teacher, one who has abandoned the sacred fires, and likewise a usurer; 3.153.

"An envoy" (preṣya): one who carries out the commands of villages and kings in exchange for receiving wages; one with deformed nails and black teeth; one whose habit is to act in opposition to his guru; one who has abandoned the sacred fires of the Śruti and Smṛti; and one who subsists by the arts—these are to be excluded from offerings to the gods and ancestors. The connection of the previous [verse] applies here as well as in the subsequent [verse]. 3.153.

One afflicted with consumption, a cattle-herder, one who marries before his elder brother, one who has been expelled from his caste, a hater of Brahmins, an elder brother whose younger brother has married before him, and one who belongs to a religious guild (gaṇa). || 3.154 ||

"Consumptive" (*yakṣmī*) means one suffering from consumption (*kṣaya*). A "herdsman" (*paśupāla*) is one who raises goats, sheep, and so forth for the sake of his livelihood. The "one who marries before his elder brother" (*parivettṛ*) and the "one superseded by a younger brother" (*parivitti*) have their characteristics described below. A "deprived one" (*nirākṛti*) is one who is devoid of the performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*). Accordingly, the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* states: "He who neglects the gods and others is to be known as a *nirākṛti*. An "enemy of Brahmins" (*brahmadviṭ*) is one who hates Brahmins and the like. One "belonging to a group" (*gaṇābhyantara*) is one who subsists on wealth and other resources belonging to a group with which he has entered into a connection. || 3.154 ||

One who is of bad character, one who has broken his vow of chastity, the husband of a low-caste woman, the son of a remarried woman, one who is one-eyed, and he in whose house lives a paramour; 3.155.

Regarding the term *kuśīlava*: a *kuśīlava* is one who makes a living as a dancer; an *avakīrṇin* is a student of the first stage of life (*brahmacārī*) or an ascetic (*yati*) whose celibacy has been violated through contact with women; a *vṛṣalīpati* is one who, without marrying a woman of his own caste, has married a Śūdra woman; a *paunarbhava* is the son of a remarried woman, as will be described later; and an *upapati* is one who has a paramour (*jāra*) in his house. (3.155)
One who teaches for a fee, one who has been taught for a fee, one whose pupil is a Śūdra, a teacher of a Śūdra, one of foul speech, and the Kuṇḍa and Golaka; 3.156.

Regarding the term *bhṛtaka*: one who receives wages (*bhṛti*) is a hired laborer (*vetana*); thus, a teacher who teaches for hire is so called, and likewise one taught by such a person. A *śūdra* disciple and his teacher in grammar and other sciences are also included. One with "defective speech" (*vāgduṣṭa*) is one who speaks harshly; others say it refers to one who is accused (*abhiśasta*). The *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* will be described later. (3.156)
One who has abandoned mother, father, or teacher without cause; and one who has entered into association with outcasts through Brahmanical or matrimonial alliances. (3.157)

"Without cause": one who has abandoned his mother, father, or teachers without a valid reason for such abandonment; one who fails to perform service and other duties; and one who has entered into association with outcasts through such relations as studying together or giving a daughter in marriage. If it is argued that this prohibition applies only because of his status as an outcaste, we say no; for this [prohibition] will apply even before a year has passed, since it will be stated later: "One becomes an outcaste after a year" (11.180). || 3.157 ||
One who sets fire to a house, a poisoner, one who eats food from a sacrificial vessel, a seller of Soma, one who travels by sea, a bard, an oil-presser, and a forger; 3.158.

"Agāre" means a house-burner, one who gives substances that cause death, or one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa*, who will be described later. Since this is for the sake of illustration, the term *kuṇḍa* includes the *golaka* as well. For this very reason, Devala says: "A son born of a paramour while the husband is alive is a *kuṇḍa*; when the husband is dead, he is a *golaka*. He who eats the food of these two is called a *kuṇḍāśin* (one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa*)."

A seller of soma-creepers; one who travels to another island by ship or other means across the ocean; a bard who recites praises; one who presses sesame seeds and other grains for the sake of oil; and a perpetrator of false testimony in a legal dispute. || 3.158 ||
One who quarrels with his father, a gambler, a drunkard, one afflicted by a foul disease, one accused of a crime, a hypocrite, and a seller of liquids (poisons). (3.159)

"By 'father' (pitṛ): he who disputes pointlessly with his father regarding the meaning of the scriptures or a worldly matter; a gambler (kitava), who, being himself unskilled at gambling, causes others to gamble for his own profit and is not a gambler himself—since such a person has already been mentioned [elsewhere]; nor is it the keeper of the gaming house (sabhika), because he will be designated by the term 'one whose livelihood is gambling. If the reading is 'kekaraḥ,' it means one with a squinting gaze, a drinker of intoxicants other than *surā*, a leper, one against whom a formal accusation has arisen even though a great sin (*mahāpātaka*) or the like has not yet been proven, one who practices dharma through deceit, and a seller of liquids. (3.159)

One who makes bows and arrows, one who is the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister remains unmarried, a betrayer of friends, one who lives by gambling, and likewise one who is a teacher of his own son.

Regarding the term *dhanuḥ*: he who prepares bows and arrows [is called a *dhanu*]. An *agredidhiṣū* is a younger sister who is given in marriage while her elder uterine sister remains unmarried; the husband of such a woman is likewise [designated]. Thus says Laugākṣi:
"If a younger daughter is married while the elder daughter remains unmarried, she is known as an *agredidhiṣū*, whereas the elder is remembered as a *didhiṣū*."

Govindarāja, however, states that by the verse "the wife of a deceased brother" (3.173), Manu will later refer to the husband of an *agredidhiṣū* as a *didhiṣūpati* through the omission of the word *agra* for metrical reasons; he asserts that this person is the one intended here. A betrayer of friends (*mitradhruk*) is one who acts to the detriment of a friend. A professional gambler (*dyūtavṛttiḥ*) is a keeper of a gambling house. A father taught by his son [is excluded] because a primary teacher-student relationship with a son is impossible. (3.160)
One suffering from epilepsy, one with scrofulous swellings, one with leucoderma, as well as a slanderer, a madman, a blind man, and likewise one who reviles the Vedas—these should be avoided. (3.161)

One suffering from epilepsy; one afflicted with the disease known as *gaṇḍamālā*; one possessed of white leprosy; a wicked person; one who is insane; one who is blind; and one who reviles the Vedas. || 3.161 ||
One who trains elephants, cattle, or camels; one who lives by means of the lunar mansions; one who raises birds; and likewise a teacher of warfare. (3.162)

"An elephant-keeper" refers to one who trains elephants, cattle, horses, and camels. By the word "nakṣatra," the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) is indicated; thus, it refers to one who practices that science. A "bird-keeper" is one who raises birds kept in cages for the sake of sport or for sale. An "instructor in the science of weapons" is one who teaches the art of weaponry for the purpose of war. (3.162)
One who diverts watercourses, one who delights in obstructing them, a builder of houses, a messenger, and likewise a planter of trees; 3.163.

Regarding the term *srotasām*: one who diverts streams of flowing water to another region by breaking dams and so forth; one who creates obstructions for those same waters, thereby hindering their natural course; one who subsists on the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*) as a designer of house layouts; a messenger, even if distinct from one sent by a king or a village; and one who plants trees for the sake of receiving wages rather than out of a desire for merit—since there is the injunction: "One who plants five mango trees does not go to hell. (3.163)

One who plays with dogs, one who lives by falcons, one who defiles a maiden, one who is cruel, one who subsists on the service of Śūdras, and one who performs sacrifices for groups (of people). (3.164)

"Śvakrīḍī" means one who raises dogs for the sake of sport; one who lives by means of hawks through buying, selling, and so forth; one who approaches virgins; one who delights in violence; and one whose livelihood is provided by Śūdras. There is an alternative reading, "vṛṣalaputraś ca," which means one whose sons are exclusively Śūdras. [He is also] one who performs sacrifices to the group of deities beginning with Vināyaka. 3.164.

One devoid of proper conduct, one who is impotent, a constant beggar, one who lives by agriculture, one with elephantiasis, and one who is censured by the virtuous—these are likewise excluded. (3.165)

Regarding "one who neglects proper conduct": he is one who has abandoned the conduct of rising for his guru, guests, and so forth; a "eunuch" (*klība*) is one who lacks enthusiasm for religious duties and the like, since the term has already been explained as referring to a neuter person; "one who constantly harasses others by begging"; one who lives by farming that he himself performs—or even by other means of livelihood, provided it is not self-performed; a "club-footed man" (*ślīpadī*) is one whose foot is swollen due to disease; and one who, for some reason, is an object of censure among the virtuous. (3.165)
A sheep-butcher, a buffalo-herder, the husband of a woman previously married to another, and likewise a funeral director—these must be avoided with great effort. (3.166)

“A sheep-butcher” (aurabhrika) is one who lives by means of sheep and buffaloes; a “remarried woman” (punarbhū) is one who has previously belonged to another, and her husband; and a “corpse-bearer” is one who carries out corpses for the sake of receiving wealth, and not for the sake of dharma, because this is enjoined by the Āvaśya-śruti: “This indeed is the supreme austerity—that they carry the deceased to the forest. (3.166)
A learned man who is the best among the twice-born should avoid both of these lowest of the twice-born, whose conduct is censurable and who are unworthy of a seat at the ritual feast.

"These" refers to these [persons]: thieves and others of censurable conduct, as well as those who are one-eyed and so forth—those who have attained the state of being one-eyed and so on through the remnants of censurable karma acquired in previous births—and who are unworthy of eating together with virtuous men; such outcasts among Brāhmaṇas, the best of Brāhmaṇas who knows the scriptures, should exclude from rites for the gods and the ancestors. 3.167.
But a Brahmin who has not studied the Vedas is extinguished like a fire of straw;
one should not offer sacrificial oblations to him, for an offering is not poured into ashes. (3.168)

Regarding the term "brāhmaṇa": Just as a fire of straw is incapable of burning the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) and is extinguished when the oblation is thrown into it—rendering the offering there fruitless—in the same way, a brāhmaṇa devoid of Vedic study is equal to a straw fire; the oblation intended for the Veda should not be given to him, because it would be as if offered into ashes. Since the prohibition of one who does not study is already established by the rule, "Gifts should be given only to a *śrotriya*" (3.128), this repetition is for the purpose of making known that such a person is a defiler of the row (*paṅktidūṣaka*), like a thief and others. Others, however, maintain that this repetition is for the purpose of indicating that in rites for the gods (*daiva*), only one who does not study is to be avoided, whereas one who studies—even if he has physical defects such as being one-eyed—is to be accepted despite his bodily flaws. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha says:
But if he is a knower of mantras and disciplined, even if he possesses bodily defects that would otherwise defile the row, Yama has declared him to be undefiled; indeed, he is a purifier of the row.
By means of bodily factors such as being the cause [of an action], and not by means of qualities to be produced in oneself such as theft and so forth. || 3.168 ||
I shall explain in its entirety that reward which arises for a donor after death from giving to one who is unworthy of the company at a rite for the gods or the ancestors. (3.169)

Regarding "giving to one unworthy of the company": I shall describe in its entirety the arising of the fruit for the giver after the gift has been bestowed upon a Brāhmaṇa unfit to eat in the company at an offering to the gods or an offering to the ancestors. (3.169)

Whatever is eaten by twice-born men who have not kept their vows, as well as by those who marry before their elder brothers and others excluded from the company at meals—that indeed the Rākṣasas consume. (3.170)

Regarding the phrase "by those who have not taken vows": the *rakṣasas* consume whatever sacrificial food (*havya*) is eaten by those devoid of vows for the purpose of Vedic study, as well as by others such as the *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder brother) and other persons unfit to sit in the row (*apāṅkteya*), including thieves and the like. The meaning is that such a *śrāddha* becomes fruitless. || 3.170 ||
Because they are not well known, he states the definitions of the *parivettṛ* and others:
"He who enters into the union of marriage and the *agnihotra* while his elder brother remains [unmarried] is to be known as a *parivettṛ*; the elder brother, however, is the *parivitti*. (3.171)

He explains: this term *agnihotra* refers to the establishment (*ādhāna*) of the *agnihotra* and other sacred fires. He who, while his elder uterine brother remains unmarried and without having established the sacred fires, takes a wife for himself and undertakes the maintenance of the Śrauta and Smārta fires, is a *parivettṛ*; and the elder brother becomes a *parivitti*. (3.171)
In this context, he states the undesirable fruit for all five parties connected with the remarriage of a younger brother:
"The one who is superseded, the one who supersedes, she by whom he is superseded—all these go to hell, with the giver and the officiating priest as the fifth. (3.172)

"Parīti": the elder brother who is superseded (parivitti), the younger brother who supersedes him (parīvettṛ), the girl by whom the supersession is performed, the giver of the girl, and the officiating priest who performs the marriage-homa—these five all go to hell. (3.172)
He who, out of lust, becomes attached to the wife of his deceased brother—even if she has been appointed according to the sacred law—is to be known as a *didhiṣūpati*. (3.173)

Regarding the word "brother": even when the wife of a deceased brother has been appointed according to the rules of *niyoga* to be described later—setting aside the injunctions such as "only once during each fertile period"—if he should, out of desire, cultivate passion for her by performing acts such as embracing and kissing, or engage with her repeatedly, he is to be known as a *didhiṣūpati*. Therefore, because he is listed among those whose vessels are forbidden at a *śrāddha*, it must be inferred that he is also excluded from being a recipient of offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*). (3.173)
Two types of sons, the Kuṇḍa and the Golaka, are born from another's wife:
the Kuṇḍa is one born while the husband is alive; the Golaka is one born when the husband is dead. (3.174)

Regarding adultery: two types of offspring, known as *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, are born from another's wife. Among them, one born to a woman whose husband is living is a *kuṇḍa*, and one born to a woman whose husband is dead is a *golaka*. (3.174)

But those two beings, born in the field of another, destroy both in this world and after death the offerings of sacrificial oblations (havya) and ancestral gifts (kavya) given by their donors. (3.175)

"Those two" refers to those born of another's wife, such as the *kuṇḍa* and others, who are designated as "living beings" (*prāṇin*) because they are seen to be useless. Although they are living beings and even Brāhmaṇas by caste, because they lack the performance of their duties, there is no fruit after death; and because there is no incidental fruit such as fame in the next world, and because there is no fame in this world, the offerings of *havya* and *kavya* given to them destroy—that is, cause the destruction of—the results. They render the *havya* and *kavya* given by the donors fruitless. (3.175)

As many as those worthy of the company (pāṅktya) whom an unworthy person (apāṅktya) looks upon while they are eating, so many [offerings] does that foolish donor fail to obtain the fruit of there. (3.176)

"Unfit for the row" (apāṅktya) means one who is unworthy of eating in the same row as the virtuous, such as a thief and so forth. Whatever number of those worthy of eating he sees, the donor does not obtain the fruit of feeding that many persons at that *śrāddha*. "Bāliśa" means ignorant. Therefore, one should act in such a way that the thief and others do not see [the guests]. 3.176.

Having looked at one who is blind, a giver becomes one-eyed; having looked at one with leprosy, he becomes leprous; but by looking at one with a hundred diseases, he becomes afflicted with a foul disease; thus he destroys the fruit of giving a thousand [cows]. (3.177)

Regarding the word "vīkṣya" (having seen): since it is impossible for a blind person to see, this [blind man], when situated in a place suitable for seeing within a row of ninety diners, destroys the fruit of that meal; likewise, a one-eyed man [destroys the fruit] of sixty, a leper with white spots [destroys the fruit] of a hundred, and one afflicted by a "king of diseases" (a severe illness) [destroys the fruit] of a thousand. The mention of "of a thousand" is intended to exclude the mere proximity of the blind and others. Furthermore, the establishment of these heavy and light numbers is to demonstrate that as the number increases, the gravity of the fault increases, and accordingly, the gravity of the penance increases. (3.177)
As many Brahmins as one who performs sacrifices for Śūdras may touch with his limbs, for that many [gifts] the donor shall not obtain the fruit of the meritorious gift. (3.177)

Regarding the phrase "as many as": when a Śūdra touches as many Brāhmaṇas as there are officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) at a sacrifice or similar rite—since a distinction of seats will be mentioned later in the verse beginning "when the seats have been prepared" (3.208)—if direct physical contact is impossible, then the fruit resulting from the *pūrta* (meritorious works) pertaining to as many persons as he sits in the row of those eating at the *śrāddha* does not accrue to the giver. Medhātithi and Govindarāja explain that this means the fruit of the *pūrta* belonging to that many people, as well as the fruit arising from giving outside the sacrificial altar (*bahirvedi*), do not belong to him. Therefore, by this very censure, the prohibition against feeding one who performs sacrifices for Śūdras is inferred, even though such a person is not explicitly listed among those whose company is forbidden. (3.178)
Even a Brahmin learned in the Vedas, having accepted a gift from him out of greed, quickly goes to destruction like an unbaked clay vessel in water. (3.179)

He experiences [the consequences]. Even a Brahmin who knows the Vedas, having accepted a gift out of greed from one who performs sacrifices for Śūdras, quickly undergoes destruction of his body and so forth; how much more so one who does not know the Vedas, like an unbaked earthen vessel in water. (3.179)
What is given to a seller of Soma becomes excrement; to a physician, pus and blood; what is given to a temple-attendant is lost; and what is given to a usurer finds no foundation. (3.180)

"From one who sells Soma": that which is given to a seller of Soma becomes excrement for the purpose of the giver's food; the meaning is that he is born into a species among those who eat excrement in another birth. The same should be explained regarding pus and blood. "Lost" (naṣṭa) is intended to mean fruitless by virtue of being subject to destruction; "without foundation" (apratiṣṭha) is likewise fruitless due to having no support. (3.180)

But that which is given to a merchant, or to a twice-born man who has returned to the household life, yields no fruit either in this world or the next; it is like an oblation poured into ashes. (3.181)

Regarding the phrase "but that which": that which is given at a *śrāddha* to a merchant’s son does not result in incidental rewards such as fame in this world, nor does it lead to rewards in the next world. That which is given to the son of a remarried woman (*punarbhū*) is equal to an oblation poured into ashes; the meaning is that it is fruitless. (3.181)
But regarding the others who are unworthy of the company, those unrighteous persons previously specified, the wise declare that their food is fat, blood, flesh, marrow, and bone. (3.182)

Regarding the phrase "to others": the wise declare that food given to those other than those for whom specific fruits have been mentioned—namely, to those unworthy of sitting in a row to eat, such as thieves and the rest as previously enumerated—becomes fat, blood, flesh, marrow, and bone for the giver at the time of his own meal. The meaning here is that in another birth, he is born among the species of beings who consume fat, blood, and so forth.
Learn now in their entirety those foremost of the twice-born who purify the row when it has been defiled by those unworthy of the row—those who are the sanctifiers of the assembly. (3.183)

Regarding the term *apāṅktya*: listen without exception to those purifying Brāhmaṇas by whom the row (*paṅkti*)—which has been defiled by a thief or others seated in the same row—is rendered pure. Even though it is impossible for thieves and others to eat in the same row due to prohibitions, this statement serves as proof because it refers to those whose offenses, such as theft, have been committed in secret and remain unknown. (3.183)

Those who are foremost in all the Vedas and in all the expositions [of the sacred texts], and who are born of a lineage of Vedic scholars (śrotriya), should be known as the purifiers of the assembly (paṅktipāvana). (3.184)

"Foremost" (*agryāḥ*): Among all the Vedas, even the four, those Brāhmaṇas who have correctly mastered the Vedas are the foremost and most excellent; they are the "purifiers of the assembly" (*paṅktipāvana*). For this very reason, Yama has included them in the enumeration of purifiers of the assembly by stating, "and one who knows the four Vedas. Likewise, because they speak the meaning of the Vedas preeminently, the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) are called "expositions"; among these too, those who know the six auxiliaries (*ṣaḍaṅgavid*) are foremost. And they, though knowing the four Vedas, are purifiers of the assembly, because Yama has listed them separately among the purifiers of the assembly with the words, "one who knows logic and one who knows the six auxiliaries. Similarly, from the statement of Uśanas, "one who has seen ten generations of the Vedic lineages," those born into a lineage where the tradition of the Vedas has remained unbroken for ten generations are purifiers of the assembly. (3.184)

One who has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, one who maintains the five sacred fires, one who knows the Trisuparṇa hymn, one who is learned in the six Vedāṅgas, one born from a lineage of Brahmin givers, and one who chants the Jyeṣṭhasāman. (3.185)

"Triṇāciketa": one who has performed the Triṇāciketa sacrifice; the Adhvaryu-veda and its associated vow are called *triṇāciketa*, and by connection with that, the person is also called *triṇāciketa*. "Pañcāgni" refers to an Agnihotrin. And so says Hārīta:
"He in whose house the five fires—the Pavamāna, the Pāvaka, the Tretā, and the two [fires] for evening and morning—are kindled, that Brahmin is a *paṅktipāvana* (a sanctifier of the assembly)."

The *pāvana* fire is the domestic fire (*āvasathyāgni*). The *sabhyo* fire is the fire for social gatherings; it is prescribed in many regions for the purpose of warding off cold and other such needs. The *trisuparṇa* is a portion of the Veda belonging to the Rigvedins (*bahvṛca*), as well as the vow associated with it; by virtue of that connection, a person who has undertaken it is also called *trisuparṇa*. One who expounds the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*) beginning with phonetics (*śikṣā*) is a *ṣaḍaṅgavid*; by the term "all-expounder" (*sarvapravacana*), one who has studied all six auxiliary sciences is meant. A *brahmadeyā* is a woman wedded according to the Brāhma form of marriage; her offspring, her son, is the *brahmadeyā-putra*. The *jyeṣṭhasāmans* are chanted in the *araṇyaka*; one who sings them is a *jyeṣṭhasāmagāyaka*. These six are connected with the subsequent verse [3.186] by the phrase, "these should be known as the sanctifiers of the company (*paṅktipāvanāḥ*). (3.185)

One who knows the meaning of the Vedas, a reciter, a celibate student, one who bestows a thousand [cows], and one who lives for a hundred years—these Brāhmaṇas should be known as purifiers of the assembly. (3.186)

He knows [the Vedas]. Even without having studied the auxiliary sciences of the Veda (*vedāṅga*), he has mastered the meaning of the Veda through the instruction of his teacher; he is a proclaimer of the very meaning of the Veda; he is a *brahmacārin*, one in the first stage of life; and he is a "giver of a thousand"—meaning either a giver of a thousand cows or a giver of much, since even when no specific gift is mentioned, we observe specific scriptural injunctions such as "Cows are indeed the mothers of sacrifice. He is "one with a hundred-year lifespan," meaning one whose age is a hundred years. Because of the restrictive rule, "Gifts are to be given only to a *śrotriya*," if he possesses the status of a *śrotriya*, he attains the quality of being a sanctifier of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*) due to the possession of the aforementioned qualities. (3.186)
On the day before or on the very day when the Śrāddha rite is at hand, he should properly invite at least three Brahmins who possess the qualities previously described. (3.187)

Regarding the phrase "on the previous day": when the time for the *śrāddha* rite has arrived, one should properly honor and invite Brahmins possessing the aforementioned characteristics on the day preceding the *śrāddha* day; however, if that is not possible, one may do so on the very day of the *śrāddha*. "Those of whom three are the minimum" (*tryavarāḥ*) means those who have at least three, but not exactly that many, because of the statement [in verse 3.129], "one for each [ancestor]. (3.187)
A twice-born man invited to a rite for the ancestors should always remain self-controlled;
he should not recite the Vedic hymns while that śrāddha is taking place. (3.188)

"Being invited": a Brāhmaṇa who has been invited to a *śrāddha* should, from the moment of invitation until the day and night of the *śrāddha*, observe the restraint of abstaining from sexual intercourse and maintain the rules of self-control. He should not engage in the study of the Veda, with the exception of the recitation (*japa*) and other such rites that must necessarily be performed. The performer of the *śrāddha* should likewise observe these same rules. (3.188)
For the ancestors attend upon those twice-born who have been invited;
they follow them like the wind and likewise wait upon them as they sit. (3.189)

Regarding the phrase "those who have been invited": this is a restatement of the previously established rule. Since the ancestors preside over those invited Brahmins in an invisible form—following them like the vital breath as they move, and likewise sitting near them when they are seated—therefore, they must remain fixed in their places. (3.189)

But the best of the twice-born who, having been invited, fails in some way to attend a sacrifice for the gods or the ancestors according to the rule, that sinner shall go to the state of a pig. (3.190)

Regarding the word "ketita": a Brāhmaṇa who has been invited according to the scriptures for offerings to the gods (havya) or the ancestors (kavya), having accepted, if he eats in some manner [unfittingly], shall become a pig in another birth because of that sin. || 3.190 ||
"‘He should always be self-restrained’ (3.188)—having thus prohibited sexual intercourse in general, the author speaks in order to make known the greater fault of approaching a *vṛṣalī*:
"But he who, having been invited to a *śrāddha*, rejoices with a *vṛṣalī*, incurs all whatever evil deed has been committed by the giver. (3.191)

Regarding the phrase "but having been invited": a *vṛṣalī* is a Śūdra woman; in that context, one who, out of delusion, while being invited to a *śrāddha*, indulges with a *vṛṣalī* according to the conduct of husband and wife through sexual intercourse and so forth, incurs the sin of the donor. What is intended here is merely the arising of sin. Otherwise, if the donor were sinless, no sin would arise [for the guest]. Nor is this prescribed as an expiation for the donor by which he might be released from sin. However, Medhātithi and Govindarāja state that since celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is prescribed in general, even a married Brāhmaṇa woman is intended here as a *vṛṣalī* by resorting to the etymological derivation: she "causes her husband to be like a bull" (*vṛṣasyantī*), because she makes him unsteady. (3.191)
Free from anger, devoted to purity, constantly practicing celibacy,
having laid down their weapons, the highly fortunate Pitṛs are the deities of the past.

"Free from anger" means devoid of wrath. "External purity" consists of cleansing with earth and water; "internal purity" is the abandonment of passion, hatred, and the like. Those endowed with these qualities, who are always free from sexual union and the like, who have renounced combat, and who possess the eightfold virtues such as compassion—this is "great fortune" (*mahābhāgatā*)—are the ancestors, whose nature is that of the primordial deity. Therefore, one must be both an enjoyer and an agent while remaining free from anger and other such defects.
Since the origin of all these [impurities] is entirely from these [sources], learn now those rules by which they are to be treated. 3.193.

Regarding the phrase "because": listen in its entirety to that from which the origin of all these ancestors arises, who those ancestors are, by whom—namely the Brāhmaṇas and others—and by what observances—that is, the ritual acts prescribed in the scriptures—they are to be venerated. 3.193.
The sons of all those sages— Marīci and the others, who are the offspring of Manu Hairaṇyagarbha— are recorded as the groups of ancestors (pitṛgaṇāḥ).

Regarding the word "Manoḥ": the sons of Manu, the offspring of Hiraṇyagarbha—namely Marīci and the others who were previously mentioned in the passage beginning with “Marīci, Atri, and Aṅgiras” (1.35)—are recorded by Manu and the other sages as having all the classes of ancestors (pitṛgaṇāḥ), such as the Somapās, as their sons. (3.194)
The sons of Virāṭ, known as the Somasads, are remembered as the ancestors of the Sādhyas;
and the Agniṣvāttas, renowned throughout the world, are the ancestors of the gods, being the offspring of Marīci.
"Virāj," [it is said]. Those known as the Somasads, sons of Virāj, are the Pitṛs of the Sādhyas; the Agniṣvāttas, sons of Marīci, are the world-renowned Pitṛs of the gods. (3.195)
The Barhiṣads, born of Atri, are remembered as the progenitors of the Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Uragas, Rākṣasas, Suparṇas, and Kinnaras.
Regarding the word "daitya": the ancestors of the Daityas and others—the various classes mentioned in the first chapter—are known as the Barhiṣads, the sons of Atri.
Among the Brahmins they are named Somapās; among the Kṣatriyas, Havirbhujs; among the Vaiśyas, Ājyapās; and among the Śūdras, Sukālins. (3.197)
"Somapās": the ancestors known as Somapās and others are traditionally held to belong to the four social classes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas. (3.197)
The Somapas were the sons of Kavi; the Haviṣmats were the sons of Aṅgiras;
the Ājyapas were the sons of Pulastya; and the Sukālins were the sons of Vasiṣṭha. (3.198)

Regarding "Somapās": the Somapās are the sons of Kavi Bhṛgu; the Haviṣmants, who are indeed the Havis-eaters, are the sons of Aṅgiras; the Ājyapas are the sons of Pulastya; and the Sukālins are the sons of Vasiṣṭha. (3.199)
One should designate the Agnidagdhas, the Anagnidagdhas, the Kavyas, the Barhishads, as well as the Agnishvattas and the Saumyas, as belonging exclusively to the Brahmins. (3.199)
Regarding the word "Agnis": one should know that the higher ancestors (pitṛs) of the Brahmins alone are designated as Agnidagdha, Anagnidagdha, Kāvya, Barhiṣat, Agniṣvātta, and Saumya. || 3.199 ||
Regarding these principal groups of ancestors that have been proclaimed,
it should be understood that their sons and grandsons here are infinite.

Regarding the word *ya* ("who"): those groups of ancestors (*pitṛgaṇa*) mentioned here as being primary—their own sons and grandsons, who are infinite in this world, are also to be understood as "fathers" (*pitaraḥ*). The compound *putrapautram* follows the rule *gavāśvaprabhṛtīni ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.11), which prescribes a singular form for such enumerations. Furthermore, other groups of ancestors indicated by this verse, such as *vara* and *vareṇya*, are heard of in the lineages of the sons of Mārkaṇḍeya and others. (3.200)
From the sages the ancestors were born; from the ancestors, gods and humans;
and from the gods, the entire world—both moving and stationary—arose in due succession. (3.201)

Regarding the phrase "to the sages": from the sages, such as Marīci and others, the ancestors were born in the manner previously described; from the ancestors, gods and humans were born; and from the gods, the world of moving and stationary beings was born in due order. Therefore, because they originate from Soma and the others, these [sages] are to be honored at the *śrāddha* for one’s own father, grandfather, and great-grandfather. Furthermore, when Soma and the others are themselves honored, they become capable of bestowing the fruits of the *śrāddha*. Moreover, this mention of the groups of ancestors headed by Soma is intended to praise the *śrāddha* for the father and others under discussion. Alternatively, at the time of invocation, one’s own father and the rest should be meditated upon by the Brahmins and others in the form of Soma and the others. In this way, there will be both knowledge of the established rule and devotion to its performance. (3.201)
Even water given with faith in silver vessels, or in those adorned with silver, conduces to inexhaustible results for them. (3.202)

Regarding the phrase "with silver [vessels]": even water given with faith using silver vessels for these ancestors, or copper and other vessels containing silver, becomes a cause for imperishable happiness; how much more so, then, excellent milk-rice and the like? || 3.202 ||
For the twice-born, the rite for the ancestors (pitṛkārya) is superior to the rite for the gods (devakārya);
indeed, the rite for the gods is traditionally held to be the preliminary nourishment for the rite for the ancestors. (3.203)

"Devakārya" refers to that which is performed for the sake of the gods; following that, the "pitṛkārya" (rite for the ancestors) is specifically enjoined as something to be performed by the twice-born. By this, he states that the *śrāddha* for the ancestors is primary, while the rite for the gods (*daiva*) is a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) therein. He clarifies this very point: "For the rite for the gods is always remembered as the nourishment and completion of the ancestral rite. (3.203)
One should first employ a deity as their protector;
for the Rākṣasas plunder a Śrāddha that is devoid of protection. (3.204)

Regarding the word "of them": *ārakṣa* means protection; one should first invite a Brahmin representing the Viśvedevas as a divine protector for those ancestors, because Rākṣasas seize a Śrāddha that is devoid of protection. (3.204)
One should seek that which has the gods as its beginning and end; it should not have the ancestors as its beginning and end.
For one who seeks that which has the ancestors as its beginning and end quickly perishes along with his lineage. (3.205)

Regarding the word "daiva": because it is so, that *śrāddha* has its beginning and end in the *daiva* [rite]; that is, in the *daiva* rite, it is that which has the beginning and end—the commencement and conclusion—at its start and finish. By this, the following is stated: everything starting from the invitation (*nimantraṇa*) is preceded by the *daiva* rite, but the dismissal (*visarjana*) of the gods occurs at the conclusion. For this very reason, Devala says: "Whatever rite is performed there toward the Brahmins in the *paitṛka* [ancestral] rite, all of that should be performed there preceded by the *vaiśvadevika* [rite]."
But he who performs that *śrāddha* which begins and ends with the ancestors—that is, which has the ancestors at both its commencement and conclusion—perishes quickly along with his progeny. (3.205)
One should smear a pure and secluded place with cow dung, and one should diligently ensure that it slopes toward the south. || 3.206 ||

"Pure" means that one should smear with cow dung a secluded place that is not defiled by bones, charcoal, or the like, and one should carefully ensure that it slopes toward the southern direction. (3.206)
In open spaces, in clean places, and indeed on the banks of rivers, as well as in secluded spots, the ancestors are always satisfied by what is offered. (3.207)

It is said: "Pure" means naturally clean; in such places as forests, on the banks of rivers and the like, and likewise in uninhabited regions, the ancestors are always satisfied by offerings such as *śrāddha* performed there. (3.207)
When separate seats covered with sacred grass have been prepared, he should cause those Brahmins, who have duly sipped water, to sit down upon them. (3.208)

Regarding the phrase "on the seats": in that place, when the seats have been arranged individually and provided with *kuśa* grass, one should cause the previously invited Brahmins—who have properly performed their ritual bathing and sipping of water (*ācamana*)—to sit down. Here, two *kuśa* blades should be placed on the seat for the Brahmins representing the gods (*deva-brāhmaṇa*), while on the seats for the ancestors (*pitṛ*), a single *kuśa* blade with its tip pointing south should be given to each. Thus says Devala: "And those Brahmins who have been previously invited here for the Viśvedevas—their seats should face east and be provided with two *darbha* [blades]."
The seats for the ancestors should be arranged facing south,
with single blades of darbha grass pointing toward the south, and they must be sprinkled with water mixed with sesame seeds.
Those joined with the southern face have their tips pointing south; "tip" (agra) is used here in relation to the root of the stalk (kāṇḍa). 3.208.
Having seated those blameless Brahmins upon their seats,
he should honor them with fragrant perfumes and garlands, beginning with the gods.

Having invited those brahmins and seated them upon their seats, he should worship them, beginning with the gods, with fragrant substances such as saffron, garlands, and incense—scents that are most desirable. 3.209.
Having brought water for them, as well as sesame seeds together with purifiers, the Brāhmaṇa, being authorized by the Brāhmaṇas, should perform the rite in the fire. (3.210)

"Of them" means: having mixed together the *arghya* water, the *pavitra* grass, and the sesame seeds for those Brahmins, he should—having been authorized by those Brahmins—perform the oblation (*homa*) in the fire as will be described hereafter. By the force of the requirement for authorization, the formal request must also be made beforehand. That request should be according to one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, such as "I shall do it," "I will do it," and so forth. The authorization, moreover, takes the form of "Om," or "Do so. (3.210)
Having first performed the satiation of Agni, Soma,
and Yama, he should afterwards satisfy the ancestors according to the rule by the offering of the oblation.

Regarding the word "of Agni": having first gratified Agni, as well as Soma and Yama, according to the rule by offering oblations preceded by the ritual sprinkling (*paryukṣaṇa*) and so forth, one should afterwards satisfy the ancestors with food and other offerings. Although Soma and Yama are mentioned here in a copulative compound (*dvandva*), they are each distinct deities, because no word such as *saha* (together) is employed. It was stated previously that where concomitance is intended, one uses a word such as *saha*. (3.211)
In the absence of fire, however, one should offer the oblation into the breaths of a Brahmin;
for that which is fire is called the twice-born Brahmin by the seers of the mantras. (3.212)

Regarding the phrase "in the absence of fire": in the absence of fire, however, one should offer the three prescribed oblations directly into the hand of a Brāhmaṇa. For it has been stated by Brāhmaṇas learned in the Vedas that "he who is the fire is indeed the Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, the absence of fire is possible for one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*); for one who has been initiated but has not yet returned home from his teacher's house (*samāvṛtta*), it occurs prior to taking a wife; or for one whose wife has died. (3.212)
The ancients speak of these best of the twice-born as gods of the śrāddha, free from anger, easily propitiated, and intent upon nourishing the world. (3.213)

Regarding the phrase "free from anger": Manu and others describe those who are devoid of anger, who are well-disposed, whose faces are serene, who are ancient due to their continuity of lineage, who—according to the principle that "the oblation cast into the fire [reaches the gods]" (3.76)—are intent on the prosperity of the world, and who have become worthy vessels for the *śrāddha* rite. Therefore, because they are equal to the deities, the *śrāddha* should be given into the hand of a Brāhmaṇa; this is a restatement of the previously established rule. || 3.213 ||
Having performed the circumambulation around the fire in the counter-clockwise direction and having completed the entire ritual sequence,
he should pour water upon the ground with his left hand.

[The rite] departs. Having performed the sequence for the execution of the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation—the subsidiary elements of which, such as the sprinkling around the fire (*paryukṣaṇa*), have been described—by moving counter-clockwise (*apasavya*) with the sacred thread over the right shoulder and ending toward the south, he should then, with his right hand while still in the *apasavya* position, pour water upon the ground that serves as the support for the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). (3.214)
Then, having formed three balls from the remainder of that sacrificial food, he, being composed,
should offer them facing south according to the very same rite prescribed for the water libation.

"Three": having formed three balls from the food remaining after what has been set aside from the oblation to Agni and the others, he—composed, with undistracted mind, and facing south—should offer them upon *darbha* grass, as will be stated [in verse 3.216] with the words "upon those *darbhas*," according to the very same procedure as that for the water libation (*audaka*), using his right hand. || 3.215 ||

Having offered those rice-balls (piṇḍas) according to the rule while remaining self-restrained, he should wipe that hand upon those darbha grasses for the sake of the "partakers of the smearings" (lepabhāgin).

Having gathered them according to the prescribed rule and having offered those staffs—or, as Dave notes, the *piṇḍas*—upon the *darbha* grasses according to the stated procedure, he should wipe his hands upon the root-end of those *darbhas*. This is because of the statement of Viṣṇu (ViDh 73.22): "The wiping of the hands is at the roots of the *darbhas*. He should thus make his hands free of residue upon those *darbhas* at their base for the satisfaction of the three ancestors who partake of the residue (*lepabhuj*), namely the great-grandfather, the grandfather, and the father. 3.216.
Having sipped water, turned toward the north, and slowly restrained his breath three times, he who knows the mantras should pay homage to the six seasons and to the ancestors. (3.217)

"Having sipped water," [it means]: immediately thereafter, having touched [water] and turned facing north, one should perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) according to one's ability and pay homage to the six seasons with the mantra beginning "Homage to you, O Spring," and so forth. One should also pay homage to the ancestors with the mantra beginning "Homage to you, O Fathers," etc., facing south, because of the observation in the *Gṛhyasūtra*: "having turned around" (GṛSū 4.8). || 3.217 ||
He should slowly pour out the remaining water near the *piṇḍas* again;
and with a concentrated mind, he should smell those *piṇḍas* in the same order in which they were placed.

(3.218) Regarding the word "water": before the offering of the *piṇḍas*, the remainder of the water that was poured at the place where the *piṇḍas* are to be placed—remaining in the water-vessel—he should release it again in sequence near each *piṇḍa*. And those *piṇḍas*, in the very order in which they were given, he should smell in that same sequence. "With a concentrated mind" means with a mind focused on nothing else. (3.218)
Having taken small portions from each of the lumps of food in successive order, he should first cause the seated Brahmins to eat according to the rule with that very [food]. (3.219)

Regarding the phrase "from the *piṇḍas*": *alpikā* refers to small portions or minute parts produced within the *piṇḍas*. Having taken these small portions in the very same order as the *piṇḍas*, he should feed them at the time of the meal, prior to the feeding itself, to the Brahmins representing the ancestors, such as the father and others, in accordance with the rule. Just as the *piṇḍas* were performed according to the injunctions, he should feed the Brahmin representing the father from that portion of the *piṇḍa* which was offered intended for the father. The same applies to the *piṇḍas* of the grandfather and the great-grandfather. (3.219)
While his father is still living, however, he should offer the oblation to the ancestors alone;
or else, as in the case of a Brahmin, he should cause his own father to partake in the śrāddha.

"But while [he] is living" means that while the father is alive, the *śrāddha* for the three ancestors beginning with the grandfather who have died must be performed. Alternatively, in the place of the [representative] Brahmin for the father, one should feed that very person as one's own father; and one should feed two Brahmins for the grandfather and great-grandfather and offer two *piṇḍas*. (3.220)
If one's father has passed away but the grandfather is still living, he should pronounce the name of his father and then proclaim the name of his great-grandfather. (3.221)

Regarding the word "father" (*pitā*): here, the mention of the name is intended as an indication for the *śrāddha* rite. Alternatively, this term may be used with reference to one whose father is still living. Furthermore, if one’s father should be deceased while the grandfather is still living, he should perform the *śrāddha* for his father and great-grandfather. Govindarāja, however, has explained: "In accordance with the statement of Viṣṇu—'He whose father and great-grandfather are deceased should, after placing the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) for his father, offer [the remaining two] beyond the grandfather'—he should offer to his great-grandfather and that [great-grandfather's] father. (3.221)
"Or the grandfather may eat that śrāddha," so Manu has declared;
"or, being duly permitted, he himself may perform it at his will. (3.222)

Regarding the term *pitāmaha*: just as one whose father is living is to be fed, so too is the grandfather; a Brahmin should be fed in the place of the grandfather, and one should perform the feeding of Brahmins and the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) for both the father and the great-grandfather. Alternatively, having been granted permission by the living grandfather with the words, "You yourself may do as you please," one may feed the grandfather according to one's own preference. Or, based on the statement of Viṣṇu that "one should perform two Śrāddhas for the father and the grandfather," one should perform three Śrāddhas for the father, the great-grandfather, and the great-great-grandfather. (3.222)
Having placed the *tilodaka* together with the *pavitra* grass into their hands, he should offer the first portion of that *piṇḍa*, saying, "May there be *svadhā* for them. (3.223)

Regarding the word "of them": this is the rule for the time and the rule for the portion to be given of that which was stated [in 3.219], "but a small measure from the balls. Having placed water with *darbha* grass and sesame seeds into the hands of those Brahmins, he should give it—referring to what was previously specified as "svadhā be to the father," and so forth—successively to the three Brahmins representing the ancestors, beginning with the father. (3.223)
Holding the vessel filled with food with both hands, he himself should slowly set it down near the Brahmins while meditating upon the ancestors. (3.224)
