"With both hands" means: the genitive case in "of food" (*annasya*) is used in the sense of the instrumental. Having himself taken with both hands a vessel such as a cooking pot that is filled or full, and while thinking of the ancestors, he should bring flavorful food from the house and place it near the Brahmins for the purpose of serving, without haste. (3.224)
When food is brought forth released from both hands, the evil-minded Asuras suddenly snatch it away. (3.225)

"Of both" means this is a locative case used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*). The food released from both hands—that which is brought into the presence of the Brāhmaṇas—the Asuras, being of wicked intellect, snatch away; therefore, one should not serve it by bringing it with only one hand. 3.225.
With self-restraint and composed mind, he should first place upon the ground the various condiments such as soups and vegetables, as well as milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey. (3.226)

"Seasonings" (guṇān) means condiments; or, because they are subordinate to the food, it refers to soups, vegetables, and so forth, which are endowed with such qualities. Being restrained, pure, and composed—with a one-pointed mind and no other thoughts—one should properly place them on the ground itself, in the location of one's own vessel, so that they do not spill, and not on a wooden board or similar surface. (3.226)
Various kinds of food to be chewed and swallowed, roots and fruits, as well as heart-pleasing meats and fragrant drinks. || 3.227 ||

Regarding the term "edible" (*bhakṣya*): edible food (*bhakṣya*) refers to solid, chewable items to be swallowed, such as sweetmeats (*modaka*) and the like; food to be eaten (*bhojya*) refers to items such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*), various kinds of fruits and roots, meats dear to the heart, and fragrant drinks—all of which, according to the preceding [verse], should be placed directly upon the ground. (3.227)
Having brought all that near, he should serve it slowly and with great composure, being self-restrained and extolling all its qualities.

He approaches. Having brought all this food and so forth near the Brahmin, he should serve it in due order—being restrained, pure, and single-minded—while describing its qualities such as sweetness, saying, "This is sweet," "This is sour," and so on. (3.228)
One should never shed tears, nor become angry, nor speak untruth;
one should not touch food with the foot, nor should one shake it. (3.229)

"Without tears": one should not weep, nor express anger, nor speak falsehoods. Nor should one touch the food with the foot, nor should one repeatedly pick up and drop the food back into the vessel. Although anger and falsehood are already prohibited as being contrary to human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), this prohibition is intended to make known that they are also forbidden specifically as auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) of the *śrāddha* rite. (3.229)
Tears cause the departed spirits (pretas) to depart; anger, enemies; falsehood, dogs; touching with the foot, the rākṣasas; and shaking [the feet], evildoers. (3.230)

Regarding the word "tears": tears shed cause the funeral offerings (*śrāddha-anna*) to reach the *pretas*, which are a specific class of spirits, but they do not provide benefit to the ancestors (*pitṛs*). Anger [reaches] enemies; false speech, dogs; touching food with the feet, *rākṣasas*; and shaking [the head], evildoers. Therefore, one should not perform weeping and the like. (3.230)
Whatever may please the learned Brahmins, that he should give without stinginess; and he should engage in discussions concerning the Veda, for this is what is desired by the ancestors. (3.231)

"Whatever...": Whatever food, condiments, and so forth are desired by the learned Brahmins, one should give that very thing without envy. One should also engage in discourses devoted to the exposition of the Supreme Self, for this is what is required of the ancestors. (3.231)
At a rite for the ancestors, one should indeed cause the recitation of the Veda, the treatises on Dharma, as well as narratives, histories, Purāṇas, and the supplementary texts (Khilas). (3.232)

Regarding the term *svādhyāya*: he should cause the Brahmins at the *śrāddha* to hear the *svādhyāya*, that is, the Veda; the Dharmaśāstras such as those of Manu; the *ākhyānas* such as the *Sauparṇa* and *Maitrāvaruṇa*; the *itihāsas* such as the *Mahābhārata*; the *purāṇas* such as the *Brahmapurāṇa*; and the *khilas* such as the *Śrīsūkta* and *Śivasaṃkalpa*. (3.232)
Being satisfied, he should gladden the Brahmins and feed them gradually; he should repeatedly encourage them with food and drink as well as with words of praise. (3.233)

"He should gladden" means that, having become joyful himself, he should satisfy the Brahmins with pleasant words and the like; he should feed them with food without delay. He should further urge the Brahmins on by describing the qualities of the sweet food, such as milk-rice and so forth, saying, "This milk-rice is delicious," "This sweetmeat is heart-pleasing, please take it," and so on. (3.233)
One should diligently feed even a daughter's son who is observing a vow at a śrāddha ceremony;
one should provide a kutapa blanket for his seat and scatter sesame seeds upon the ground.

Regarding the word "vratī" (one observing a vow): one should diligently feed even a *brahmacārin* grandson (*dauhitra*) at a *śrāddha* ceremony; by the use of the word "even" (*api*), it is implied that one may also feed a non-*brahmacārin*. Because of the specific injunction to make an effort regarding the *brahmacārin*—who is listed among the secondary options—it indicates his superiority even over other grandsons. One should provide a Nepalese woolen blanket for a seat and scatter sesame seeds upon the ground of the *śrāddha*. (3.234)
Three things are purifying at a funeral feast: a daughter's son, a kutapa blanket, and sesame seeds;
and three things they praise in this context: purity, freedom from anger, and lack of haste. (3.235)

"Three" refers to the fact that it is made known that the three previously mentioned [categories], beginning with the daughter's son (*dauhitra*), are purifiers at a *śrāddha* ceremony; and they praise the three [other categories] beginning with purity (*śauca*). (3.235)
All the food should be very hot, and they should eat while remaining silent;
nor should the twice-born speak of the qualities of the sacrificial offering when questioned by the giver.

Regarding the term *atyuṣṇam* ("very hot"): "very hot" means simply "hot. One should serve that which is hot and suitable for consumption, such as cooked food, but not even fruits and the like. For this very reason, Śaṅkha states (Śaṅkha Smṛti 14.12–13):
"The wise should devoutly present hot food to the twice-born, with the exception of fruits, roots, and beverages."

And the Brahmins, with their speech restrained, should eat. Even when asked by the giver about the qualities of the food and so forth—“Is this sweet or not sweet?”—they should not speak, even by means of gestures such as winking the eyes, because restraint of speech is specifically enjoined in this very context. (3.236)
As long as the food remains warm, as long as they eat in silence, and as long as the qualities of the sacrificial offering have not been mentioned, for so long do the ancestors eat. (3.237)

"As long as" means: as long as there is heat in the food, as long as the silent ones eat, and as long as the qualities of the sacrificial offering are not mentioned, so long do the ancestors eat; this is a praise of the very meaning previously stated. 3.237.
Whatever one eats with the head wrapped, whatever one eats facing south, and whatever one eats while wearing shoes—that indeed the Rākṣasas consume. (3.238)

Regarding the word "yad" (that which): if one eats food with one's head wrapped in a cloth or the like, or likewise while facing south, or while wearing sandals, the Rākṣasas consume that, not the ancestors. Therefore, one should not act in such a manner. (3.328)
A Cāṇḍāla, a boar, a cock, and likewise a dog, a woman in her courses, and a eunuch—these must not look at twice-born men while they are eating. (3.239)
Regarding the term "cāṇḍāla": arrangements should be made so that at the time of eating, the cāṇḍālas, village pigs, cocks, dogs, menstruating women, and eunuchs do not see the Brāhmaṇas. (3.239)
Whatever is looked upon by these [unworthy persons] at the giving of a house or at a meal—whether at an offering to the gods or to the ancestors—that goes awry. (3.240)

Regarding the term *homa*: because, in the case of *homa* such as the *agnihotra*, in giving such as cows or gold, in feeding Brāhmaṇas for one's own prosperity, in divine oblations such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, and in ancestral rites such as the *śrāddha*, whatever rite is performed while being looked upon by these [uninvited guests] does not accomplish the purpose for which it was performed. (3.240)
The pig destroys [the merit] by its smell, the cock by the wind of its wings, the dog by the casting of its gaze, and one born of the lowest caste by touch. (3.241)

"By smelling": having smelled the odor of that food and so forth, the pig renders the ritual act fruitless; therefore, it must be driven away from a place suitable for smelling the food. The cock, by the wind of its wings—such a bird also must be removed from a place suitable for the fanning of its wings. "By sight" refers to the dog; although the sight of a dog’s food and so forth is already prohibited, it is mentioned again to indicate the greater gravity of the fault. Alternatively, "by the casting of a glance" means by becoming the object of the glance of those performing or partaking in the *śrāddha*. An "inferior caste" (*avaravarṇa*) is a Śūdra; one born from such a person is "born of inferior caste" (*avaravarṇaja*), which is simply a Śūdra. He, through the touch of his food and so forth, renders the *śrāddha* of the twice-born fruitless. (3.241)
Whether he be lame or one-eyed, or even a servant of the donor, or one with deficient or redundant limbs—one should remove him as well. (3.242)

"Or a lame man": if he is one deficient in movement, or if he is blind, or a Śūdra who is the donor's slave—since it is prescribed that such a person must serve him alone; by the use of the word "api" (also), even another Śūdra or one with deficient or extra fingers and so forth should be removed from that place of the Śrāddha. || 3.242 ||
When a Brahmin or even a mendicant has arrived seeking food, he should, with the permission of the Brahmins, honor them according to his ability. (3.243)

"A Brāhmaṇa": one who has the nature of a Brāhmaṇa, whether in the form of a guest or another person accustomed to eating, who has arrived at that time for the purpose of a meal; him he should honor, with permission from the Brāhmaṇas who are the recipients of the Śrāddha, by providing food according to his ability and by giving alms. 3.243.
Having collected food of all kinds and sprinkled it with water,
he should cast it upon the ground before those who have eaten, scattering it about.

Regarding the word *sārva*: the term *varṇa* here denotes "kind. Having combined all kinds of food, such as rice and the like, with condiments and so forth, and having moistened them with water, one should place—or discard—them upon the ground before the Brāhmaṇas who have finished their meal, specifically upon *darbha* grass, because it will be stated later [in verse 3.245]: "and that which is the scattering upon the *darbhas*. || 3.244 ||

The food-remnants and whatever is scattered during the rites shall be the portion for those who have died without performing the sacraments, for those who have abandoned their families, and for virtuous women. (3.245)

Regarding the term *asaṃskṛta* (unconsecrated): because of the prohibition, "The fire-consecration (*agni-saṃskāra*) is not to be performed for him" (5.69), the portion [of the offering] shall belong to those children who are unfit for consecration, as well as to those women of good family who have been abandoned when they were free from visible defects. Others, however, explain that "those who abandon" refers to those who have forsaken their gurus and so forth, while "women of good family" refers to women of good family who have acted independently, namely unmarried maidens. Govindarāja, on the other hand, states: "Since the opening statement mentions 'those who abandon' and 'women of good family' in general, this is a specific designation, similar to the rule *saṃskṛtaṃ bhakṣāḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.16); therefore, it refers to women of good family who have left their own family. (3.245)
They declare that the food remaining on the ground after the meal belongs as its share to the group of servants who are straightforward and free from deceit during the ancestral rite.

Regarding the term *uccheṣaṇa*: Manu and others declare that what remains on the ground as leavings (*ucchiṣṭa*) is the share for the assembly of servants who are honest, diligent, and straightforward, in the ancestral *śrāddha* rite. (3.246)
For a twice-born man who has died, until the rite of sapindikarana is performed, one should offer a śrāddha meal without an invitation to the gods and present a single pinda. (3.247)

Regarding the phrase "up to the *sapiṇḍī*": the prefix *ā* here denotes a limit (*maryādā*) and not inclusion (*abhividhi*). For a twice-born person who has recently died, until the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* Śrāddha is performed, one should feed a Brāhmaṇa for the sake of the Śrāddha with food devoid of the *vaiśvadeva* offering and the feeding of Brāhmaṇas [for the Viśvedevas], and one should offer a single *piṇḍa*. And the performance of this Śrāddha is the *ekoddiṣṭa*: it is devoid of the *daiva* (Viśvedeva) portion, possesses a single *arghya* and a single *pavitraka*, and is indeed performed without the *āvāhana* and *agnaukaraṇa* rites, while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*). [YDh 1.251]
Thus it should be understood from the Smṛtis of Yājñavalkya and others. 3.247.
But when the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed for him according to the Dharma, the sons must perform the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) by this very same procedure. (3.248)

"Along with [the ancestors]" (*saha*). "Of this one" (*asya*) means: for that person for whom this *ekoddiṣṭa* rite has been prescribed, once the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* Śrāddha has been performed according to the law by means of the procedure of his own *Gṛhya-sūtra* and so forth, the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍanirvapaṇa*) and the Śrāddha according to the *pārvaṇa* rule must be performed by the sons on all occasions, such as the anniversary of death, using precisely this same procedure—the ritual application (*itikartavyatā*) prescribed for the New Moon Śrāddha. Now, an objection is raised: why is it not the case that by the phrase "by this very procedure," the *ekoddiṣṭa* under discussion itself is being referred to? It is replied: if that were so, there would be no distinction in the instruction—"the *ekoddiṣṭa* prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, and once the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed, again by this very procedure"—because the procedure would be identical. Therefore, it is understood that the ritual application of the New Moon Śrāddha alone is intended here. (3.248)
He who, having eaten at a śrāddha feast, gives the leavings to a śūdra, that fool goes headlong to the Kālasūtra hell. (3.249)

Regarding the word *śrāddham*: this is a prohibition against the practice of giving the remains of food (*ucchiṣṭa*) to a dependent Śūdra. That fool who gives the remains of a *śrāddha* meal to a Śūdra goes headfirst to the hell named Kālasūtra. (3.249)
If one who has partaken of a funeral feast approaches a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī) on that same day, his ancestors lie for that entire month in her excrement. (3.250)

Regarding the word *śrāddhā*: they say that here the term *vṛṣalī* refers to a woman. And the etymology is as follows: "She is called *vṛṣalī* because, being lustful (*vṛṣasyantī*), she causes her husband to waver; even a Brāhmaṇa woman who has been married by a Brāhmaṇa is a *vṛṣalī*. This is a censure intended for the purpose of deterrence: that for one who engages in sexual intercourse with a woman on the day or night following a *śrāddha*, his ancestors lie in her excrement for that entire month. (3.250)
Having asked, "Was it well-tasted? he should then cause those who are satisfied to rinse their mouths; once they have rinsed, he should dismiss them with the words, "May you be happy. (3.251)

Having asked thus, and having fed the Brāhmaṇas until they are satisfied, he should ask them, "Was it well-prepared? and cause them to perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana). Once they have performed the sipping, he should address them with "Bho! and say, "May you be pleased. If the reading is "abhitaḥ," the meaning is: "May you stay here, on both sides, or in your own homes. || 3.251 ||
Immediately after that, the Brahmins should say to him, "Svadhāstu.
For in the rites for the ancestors performed with ladles, the utterance of "svadhā" is indeed the supreme benediction.

"May it be *svadhā*!"—after granting permission, the Brāhmaṇas should say to the performer of the Śrāddha, "May there be *svadhā*. For in all rites for the ancestors, such as the Śrāddha and the libation (*tarpaṇa*), the utterance of the word *svadhā* constitutes the highest benediction. (3.252)
Then, once they have finished eating, he should present the remains of the food;
he should act according to what they say, having been authorized by the twice-born. (3.253)

Regarding the word "tataḥ" (then): after the utterance of the word *svadhā*, he should offer the remaining food, saying, "There is also some food left over from the Brahmins who have finished eating. Having been authorized by those Brahmins with the words, "Let this be done with this food," he should dispose of the remainder of the food exactly as they may direct. (3.253)

Now, as an incidental matter, he states the specific rules for other types of śrāddhas: "At a rite for the ancestors (pitrya), one should say 'It is well-eaten' (svaditam); at a rite in a cow-pen (goṣṭha), however, 'It is well-cooked' (suśṛtam); at an auspicious rite (abhyudaya), 'It is excellent' (saṃpannam); and at a rite for the gods (daiva), 'It is pleasing' (rucitam). (3.254)

Regarding the term *pitrye*: in the *pitrya*—that is, in the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha which has the individual ancestors and mother as its deities—the word *svaditam* (it is well-eaten) should be spoken for the purpose of inquiring about satisfaction (*tṛpti*). Accordingly, Gobhila and Sāṃkhyāyana state that the inquiry regarding satisfaction is “*svāditam*” (it is tasted). However, Medhātithi and Govindarāja explain that even by another person who has arrived at the time of the śrāddha, the word *svaditam* alone must be used. [The objection is: “In a śrāddha, this word *svaditam* must be spoken by someone other [than the performer]. This is not accepted by learned elders; we do not place faith in it. At a *goṣṭhīśrāddha* held in a cow-pen, one should say, "It is well-cooked" (*asuśṛtam*). Viśvāmitra has also listed the *goṣṭhīśrāddha* among the twelve types of *śrāddhas* in his enumeration, stating: "The eighth is for the sake of purification in a *goṣṭhī*. At an *abhyudaya-śrāddha* (a rite of prosperity), one should say, "It is excellent" (*saṃpannam*). In a *daiva-śrāddha* (a rite dedicated to the gods), the word "it is pleasing" (*rucitam*) should be spoken. As for the *daiva-śrāddha*, it is described in the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*: "That *śrāddha* which is performed with reference to the gods is called *daivika*;
it should be performed with effort on the seventh lunar day and other such occasions, using distinguished sacrificial food (*haviṣya*)."
The afternoon, as well as darbha grass, the preparation of the site, sesame seeds, abundance, refinement, and eminent brahmins are the perfections in rites for the ancestors. (3.255)

Regarding the term "afternoon" (*aparāhṇa*): since the *amāvāsyā-śrāddha* (the new-moon ancestral rite) is the subject under discussion, this afternoon time refers specifically to that. This is because other Smṛtis, such as Devala’s statement "The rite for an auspicious occasion (*vṛddhi-nimittaka*) is in the morning," prescribe morning and other times for the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* and similar rites. The phrase "perfection of the rite" (*saṃpatti*)—referring to the *darbha* grass for the seats and so forth, the purification of the ritual site with cow-dung and the like, the *tila* seeds for scattering, the *sṛṣṭi* (liberality) which is the distribution of food and other gifts without stinginess, the *mṛṣṭi* (excellence) which is a specific refinement of the food, and the Brahmins who are "purifiers of the row" (*paṅktipāvana*)—indicates that these possess a preeminence relative to other constituent parts of the rite, as they are designated as the perfections of the *śrāddha*. (3.255)

Darbha grass, the purifier, the forenoon, and all kinds of sacrificial foods (haviṣya), as well as whatever purifying substances were mentioned previously, should be understood as the perfections of the oblation. 3.256.

"Darbha grasses," "purifiers," "mantras," "the morning time," "sacrificial foods" such as the grains of sages and all other such things, as well as whatever purifier or means of purification was previously mentioned, such as the preparation of the site—these are the factors for the success of a rite intended for the gods. The word *havya* (oblation) is used here to indicate rites for the gods in general. (3.256)
The food of sages, milk, Soma, meat that is unseasoned, and salt that is not alkaline—these are by their very nature called sacrificial oblations (havis). (3.257)

Regarding the phrase "the foods of sages": the foods of the sage, namely the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), consist of wild grains such as *nīvāra* and the like; milk; the juice of the *soma* creeper; unadulterated—that is, unmodified—meat free from foul odors and the like; and salt that is not alkaline, meaning natural rock salt (*saindhava*) and so forth. These are declared by Manu and others to be, by their very nature, sacrificial oblations (*havis*). (3.257)

Having dismissed those brahmins, being self-restrained, silent, and pure, and gazing toward the southern direction, he should entreat these boons from the ancestors: 2.258. Having dismissed those brahmins, being self-restrained, silent, and pure, and gazing toward the southern direction, he should entreat these boons from the ancestors.

"Having dismissed," etc.: having dismissed those Brahmins, with undistracted mind, observing silence and remaining pure, looking toward the southern direction, he should pray to the ancestors for these desired *arghas* which are about to be described. || 3.258 ||
"May our donors increase, as well as our Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give. (3.259)

"May givers"—meaning, may the men who give in our family increase; and may the Vedas attain growth through study, teaching, the comprehension of their meaning, and the performance of sacrifices and other rites based on that meaning; and may sons, grandsons, and so forth increase; and may faith in the meaning of the Vedas never depart from our family; and may wealth and other things to be given become abundant. (3.259)
Having thus performed the offering of water, he should immediately thereafter cause those rice-balls to be consumed by a cow, a Brahmin, a goat, or the fire, or else cast them into the water. (3.260)

"Thus": having offered the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) in the manner described, immediately after requesting the boon as prescribed, one should feed those cakes to a cow, a Brāhmaṇa, or a goat, or else cast them into fire or water. || 3.260 ||
Some offer the funeral cakes even beforehand;
others feed them to birds, or cast them into fire or water. (3.261)

Regarding the term *piṇḍa*: some teachers perform the offering of the *piṇḍas* after the feeding of the Brahmins; others feed the *piṇḍas* to birds. This mention of both [methods], even though they have already been stated, is intended to show that this practice of feeding the birds is optional in relation to the throwing [of the *piṇḍas*] into fire or water. (3.261)
Then, the devoted and lawful wife, intent on the worship of the ancestors and desiring a son, should properly eat the middle *piṇḍa*. (3.262)

Regarding the term *pativratā*: she whose vow (*vrata*) is that "in matters of dharma, artha, and kāma, my husband alone is to be served by me through the actions of mind, speech, and body" is a *pativratā*. A lawful wife (*dharmapatnī*)—one of the same caste, married first, full of faith in the performance of *śrāddha* rites, and desiring a son—should eat the middle of those rice-balls (*piṇḍas*), namely the ball intended for the grandfather, while properly reciting the mantra prescribed in the Gṛhyasūtras beginning with: "O ancestors, bestow a fetus" (*ādhatta pitaro garbham*). (2.262)
She gives birth to a long-lived son, endowed with fame and intelligence, wealthy, possessed of progeny, virtuous, and likewise righteous. (3.263)

"O Long-lived One!"—by that consumption of the *piṇḍa*, he begets a son who is long-lived, endowed with an intellect characterized by the retention of fame, and possessed of qualities such as wealth, progeny, lineage, the practice of dharma, and courage. (3.263)
Having washed his hands and sipped water, he should provide food primarily for his kinsmen;
having given hospitality to his kinsmen, he should also feed his relatives. (3.264)

"Having washed," etc.: thereupon, having washed his hands, he should prepare food consisting primarily for his kinsmen (*jñātiprāyam*). It is called *jñātiprāyam* because it goes toward or reaches the kinsmen; that is, it is fit for the rite. The meaning is that he should feed his kinsmen. Having given food to them preceded by honor, he should also feed those on his mother's side with due respect. (3.264)
That remnant of the meal should remain until the Brahmins have been dismissed;
then one should perform the domestic bali offering—thus the law is established. (3.265)

Regarding the term *uccheṣaṇa*: this refers to the leavings of the Brāhmaṇas; it should remain for as long as it takes to dismiss the Brāhmaṇas, and once the Brāhmaṇas have departed, it should be wiped away—this is the meaning. Then, when the Śrāddha rite has been completed, the Vaiśvadeva, the Bali-homa, the daily Śrāddha (*nityaśrāddha*), and the feeding of guests must be performed, because the word "Bali" is used here illustratively. For this very reason, the *Matsyapurāṇa* states: "Having returned, the knower of mantras, having sprinkled water around the fire for the sake of ritual purification, should perform the Vaiśvadeva and the daily rite."

Although it was mentioned previously with the words "and by which foods," it may not have remained in the student's mind due to the intervening material; therefore, he promises to state it again for the sake of easy comprehension:
"I shall explain in its entirety that oblation which, when offered to the ancestors according to the rules, serves for a long time and even for eternity. (3.266)

Regarding the word *havir* (oblation): *cirarātrāya* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) word signifying a long duration of time. For this very reason, lexicographers state: “*cirāya*, *cirarātrāya*, *cirasya*, and so forth, have the sense of ‘long ago’ or ‘for a long time’. Whatever oblation is offered to the ancestors according to the prescribed rules, which results in satisfaction for a long duration and even infinite satisfaction—that I shall describe in its entirety. (3.266)
By the offering of sesame seeds, rice, barley, mung beans, water, or roots and fruits, the ancestors of men are satisfied for a month when given according to the prescribed rule. (3.267)

Regarding the word "sesame" (*tilaiḥ*): by giving any one of these—sesame, grain, barley, black gram (*māṣa*), water, roots, or fruits—with faith according to the scriptures, the ancestors of men remain satisfied for a month.
According to the statement in the *Vāyupurāṇa*, "Black beans, sesame, barley, and rice are the best," it should be understood that by "black gram" (*māṣaiḥ*) here, black beans are intended. (3.268)
For two months one may subsist on the flesh of fish, for three months on that of the deer,
for four on that of the sheep, and for five indeed on that of birds.

"Two": the connection with the preceding verse is that the ancestors are gratified for two months by the flesh of fish such as the *pāṭhīna*. For three months by the flesh of the *hāriṇa* deer; for four months by the flesh of the sheep; and for five months by the flesh of birds fit for consumption by the twice-born. (3.268)
For six months with the meat of a goat, and indeed for seven with that of the spotted deer (pārṣata);
for eight months with the meat of the black antelope (eṇa), and for nine with that of the ruru deer.

"Six months" means: they are gratified for six months by the flesh of a goat; for seven months by the flesh of the spotted deer (*pṛṣata*); for eight months by the flesh of the *eṇa* deer; and for nine months by the flesh of the *ruru* deer. The *eṇa* and *ruru* are specific varieties of the *hariṇa* (deer) species. (3.269)
They are satisfied for ten months by the flesh of boars and buffaloes;
however, by the flesh of hares and tortoises, they are satisfied for exactly eleven months.
"Ten" means: for ten months they are satisfied by the meat of wild boars and buffaloes; for eleven months by the meat of hares and tortoises. 3.270.
But with cow's milk and milk-rice (pāyasa) for one year,
and with the meat of the vārdhrīṇasa, there is satisfaction lasting for twelve years.

"Regarding 'for a year': they are satisfied for one year by means of cow's milk and the rice cooked with that milk, since it is in this very context that the term *pāyasa* (milk-rice) is well-established. Satisfaction of the ancestors (*pitṛs*) lasts for twelve years through the meat of the *vārdhrīṇasa*. And the *vārdhrīṇasa* is explained in the *Nigama*: 'The ritualists call that white, aged goat, which drinks with three [parts of its body], whose senses are decayed, and who is the lord of goats, a *vārdhrīṇasa* in the performance of ancestral rites.'"
For one who drinks water from a river or similar source, three things touch the water: the two ears and the tongue; because he drinks with these three, he is called a *tripiba*. (3.271)
Black potherbs, large-scaled fish, the flesh of the rhinoceros and red deer, honey, and all kinds of food fit for sages are prescribed for the sake of infinite results. (3.272)

*Kāla* refers to the vegetable known as *kālaśāka*. Regarding *mahāśalkāḥ*, Medhātithi says they are "those with scales," but it is more appropriate to take them as a specific kind of fish, based on the statement: "fish that have large scales. *Khaḍga* is the rhinoceros. *Loha* is simply a red-colored goat, according to the statement of Paiṭhīnasi: "By means of a goat entirely red, there is infinity [of merit]. A mixture of these two [the rhinoceros and the red goat] is intended. *Madhu* is honey. *Munyannāni* (sages' foods) include all wild grains such as *nīvāra* and others. These result in infinite satisfaction. (3.272)
Whatever one may offer mixed with honey on the thirteenth lunar day,
that too shall indeed be inexhaustible during the rainy season under the Maghā asterism.

Regarding the word *yat*: this is a collective reference to the seasons (*ṛtu*), lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), and lunar days (*tithi*). Whatever is not well-known, if it is mixed with honey and given during the rainy season on the thirteenth day of the month of Maghā, that too becomes indeed inexhaustible. Although the thirteenth day functions as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the accusative case is used either because there is an intention to express the object desired (*īpsitatva*) or by supplying the word *prāpya* ("having reached"). (3.273)
"May he be born in our family who would give us milk-rice with honey and clarified butter on the thirteenth lunar day, when the shadow of an elephant falls toward the east. (3.274)
Regarding the word "also" (*api*): the thirteenth day conjoined with the *Maghā* asterism during the rainy season is intended here, as previously mentioned. With respect to that as well, it is said:
"When the month of Prauṣṭhapada has passed, having reached the thirteenth day conjoined with *Maghā*, one should indeed perform the *śrāddha* with honey and milk-rice (*pāyasa*). (ŚaṃSm. 14.32)

According to this statement of Śaṅkha, the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada is understood here as well as in the preceding [text]. It is said that the ancestors make this aspiration: "Would that there might be someone of such a kind in our lineage who, on this very thirteenth day, or even on another lunar day, when the shadow has moved toward the eastern direction, would offer milk-rice mixed with honey and clarified butter. However, there is no requirement for the conjunction of both the thirteenth day and the "elephant-shadow" (hasticchāyā). Thus says Viṣṇu: "May there be born in our family some supreme man..."
In the rainy season, on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, being composed in mind.
"He who should perform a śrāddha with milk-rice soaked in honey throughout the entire month of Kārttika, or on the day when the shadow of an elephant falls toward the east," so it is said. (3.274)
Whatever one gives according to the rules, correctly and endowed with faith, that becomes infinite and inexhaustible for the ancestors in the hereafter. (3.275)

"Whatever, whatever"—this repetition (*vīpsā*) signifies "all. Whatever food that is not forbidden, offered according to the scriptures in its proper form and with faith to the ancestors, becomes infinite, inexhaustible at all times, and undiminished in the next world for the satisfaction of the ancestors. Therefore, it is enjoined that one who desires that fruit should give with faith. (3.275)
In the dark fortnight, from the tenth day onwards—excluding the fourteenth—the lunar days are commended for ancestral rites; others are not so. (3.276)

Regarding the word "kṛṣṇa": in the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), starting from the tenth day and excluding the fourteenth, the lunar days (tithis) used for the ancestral rite (śrāddha) are not as excellent or as highly fruitful as these [specific ones], such as the first day (pratipad) and others. || 3.276 ||
By performing [the rites] on odd lunar days and under odd asterisms, one attains all desires;
but by performing them on even days and under even asterisms, one obtains abundant progeny for the ancestors.

"Yukṣu" [means]: here the word *dina* refers to lunar days (*tithi*). Performing a *śrāddha* on even lunar days—the second, fourth, and so forth—and under even asterisms (*nakṣatra*)—Bharaṇī, Rohiṇī, and so forth—one obtains all desired objects. By worshipping the ancestors with a *śrāddha* on odd lunar days—the first, third, and so forth—and under odd asterisms—Aśvinī, Kṛttikā, and so forth—one obtains abundant progeny, such as sons, as well as wealth and learning. (3.277)
Just as the latter fortnight is superior to the former fortnight, so too the afternoon is superior to the forenoon for a śrāddha ceremony. || 3.278 ||

Regarding the word *yateti*: according to the rules of the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*), the months begin with the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) starting from Caitra; thus, the latter half of the month is like the latter half of the fortnight. Just as the latter half of the fortnight is superior in yielding specific results for the *śrāddha* compared to the bright fortnight, so too the latter half of the day is distinguished by its excellent results compared to the first half of the day. By this statement, [the text] teaches that the performance of the *śrāddha* is prescribed even during the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*). Now, one might ask: how can the latter half of the month serve as an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) for the latter half of the fortnight, since no such excellence has been mentioned for the former? For an illustration must be something well-known. It is replied: because excellence is expressly stated in a specific injunction elsewhere, namely in the verse: "In the dark fortnight, beginning from the tenth day" (3.276). Thus, [the example holds]. (3.278)
Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder, with the rite performed correctly from left to right, unwearied,
and holding *darbha* grass in his hand, he should perform the ancestral rite according to the rules until its conclusion.

"Facing the east": with the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) worn over the right shoulder, with a steady hand holding *darbha* grass, and with the sacrificial thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), all rites related to the ancestors must be performed according to the scriptures by means of the "ancestral path" (*pitṛtīrtha*) until the end—that is, until completion. Medhātithi and Govindarāja state that "until the end" means for as long as one lives. (3.279)
One should not perform a śrāddha at night, for that is proclaimed to be demonic;
nor during either of the two twilights, nor when the sun has only just risen.

"During the night": one should not perform a *śrāddha* at night, because this time has been described by Manu and others as "demonic" (*rākṣasī*) due to its association with qualities that destroy the *śrāddha*. Nor should one perform it during the two twilights (*saṃdhyā*). And regarding the sun having just risen: when there is a need for the time of the sun's rising, the morning period (*prātaḥkāla*) should be understood as consisting of three *muhūrtas*. As it is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "From the appearance of the first line [of the sun] until the sun has moved three *muhūrtas*, that is known as the morning; it is the fifth part of the day."

If it is asked, "Since the afternoon is prescribed as an integral part (*aṅga*) of the *śrāddha*, how can this be a prohibition of something that was not even a possibility?"—this is not a prohibition. For a prohibition would apply either to what is prompted by worldly desire (*rāga*) or to what is prompted by a scriptural injunction (*vidhi*). It cannot be the first, because here the daily *darśa-śrāddha* is not prompted by desire; thus, if there were a prohibition of what is prompted by an injunction, there would be an option (*vikalpa*), like the taking or not taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup. Therefore, this is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). One should perform the *śrāddha* at a time other than those excluded, such as the night, just as the mantra "ye yajāmahe" is used in sacrifices other than the *anuyāja*. Furthermore, the prescription for the afternoon is for the purpose of praising it. Hence it has been said: "Just as the afternoon is superior to the forenoon for the *śrāddha*" (3.278). || 3.380 ||
By this rule, one should perform the Śrāddha here three times a year—
during the winter, summer, and rainy seasons— and the Pāñcayajñika rites every day.

Regarding the phrase "by this": the monthly *śrāddha* was prescribed [in verse 3.122] with the words "one should perform it month after month. When that is impossible, the following rule is stated based on the view that four months constitute one season (*ṛtu*) and three seasons constitute a year: by this aforementioned method, the *śrāddha* should be performed three times within the year—during the winter, summer, and rainy seasons. Furthermore, according to established custom (*samayācāra*), when the sun is situated in Aquarius, Taurus, or Virgo, one should perform daily that which is included among the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), as prescribed by the rule "one should feed even a single Brahmin" (3.83); this is stated for the sake of reinforcing what was previously mentioned.
The oblation belonging to the ancestral sacrifice is not prescribed for the common fire;
nor is there a Śrāddha for a twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires without the New Moon sacrifice. (3.282)

"Not on the domestic fire. By the rule "for Agni, Soma, and Yama" (3.211), the oblation that constitutes a part of the Pitṛyajña is not prescribed by scripture to be performed in a worldly fire—that is, a fire other than those used for Śrauta and Smārta rites. Therefore, the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation must not be performed in a worldly fire. However, for one who maintains no sacred fires (*niragni*), it should be performed in the hand of a Brahmin or elsewhere, as stated in the rule: "In the absence of fire, however, [it is offered] in the hand of a Brahmin" (3.212). For a twice-born man who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), the *śrāddha* is prescribed during the dark fortnight on the tenth day and so forth, excluding the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). As for the *śrāddha* on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*), because it is obligatory, it is not prohibited even on other lunar days within the dark fortnight. (3.282)
When that best of the twice-born, having bathed, gratifies the ancestors with water, he thereby obtains the entire fruit of the performance of the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña). || 3.283 ||

Regarding the word "yad" (that which): this is the rule for when the *śrāddha* consisting of the five sacrifices (*pāñcayajñika*) is impossible. When a twice-born man performs the water libation (*udakatarpaṇa*) immediately after his bath, he obtains through that alone the entire fruit of the obligatory daily *śrāddha*. The term "dvijottama" (best of the twice-born) refers to the twice-born in general. (3.283)
They call the Vasus the fathers, the Rudras the grandfathers, and likewise the Ādityas the great-grandfathers; this is the eternal Vedic revelation.

Regarding the phrase "the Vasus": since there is a scriptural tradition (*śruti*) that the ancestors (*pitr*) and others are indeed the Vasus and so forth—being their primordial forms—it follows that Manu and others refer to the fathers as the gods called Vasus, the grandfathers as the Rudras, and the great-grandfathers as the Ādityas. Consequently, because an injunction to inform those who already know this would be redundant, a rule is inferred: "In the *śrāddha* ceremony, the ancestors are to be meditated upon in the form of the Vasus and the other deities. For this very reason, Paiṭhīnasi states: "He who, knowing this, worships the ancestors, finds the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas gratified by him. However, Medhātithi and Govindarāja have stated: "This is a statement of praise for the ancestors, superimposing the status of deities upon them, intended to urge toward the performance of ancestral rites those who do not engage in them due to hatred of the ancestors or out of atheism (*nāstikya*). (3.284)
One should always be an eater of vighasa, and always an eater of amṛta;
for vighasa is the remnant of what has been eaten, while amṛta is the remnant of a sacrifice.

"One who eats *vighasa*": he should always eat *vighasa*, and he should always be one who eats *amṛta*. Since the meanings of the terms *vighasa* and *amṛta* are not well-known, he explains them: what remains after a Brahmin or others have eaten is called *vighasa*; the sacrificial remnants such as the *puroḍāśa* cake from sacrifices like the *darśapūrṇamāsa* are *amṛta*. Although these are general designations, because of the context, this injunction refers specifically to eating the remnants of what has been eaten by Brahmins at a *śrāddha*. For this very reason [it is said]: "He should eat, together with his guests, everything that has been partaken of by the ancestors."

Thus says another Smṛti. As for the specific eating by the guests and others, that is already ordained by the verse itself: "But the remainder [is for] the husband and wife" (3.116). Govindarāja’s commentary—that this is a restatement for the purpose of praising that very act by establishing its equality with the remnants of a sacrifice—is unworthy of adoption as a specific rule of practice and is irrelevant to the context. 3.285.
All this rule concerning the five sacrifices has been declared to you;
now let the rule for the livelihoods of the foremost among the twice-born be heard. (3.286)

Thus ends the third chapter in the *Mānava Dharmaśāstra*, in the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu. Regarding the word "etad" (this): this entire performance arising from the five sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) has been declared to you; the concluding summary is provided even though the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* intervenes between them, for the purpose of making known their high importance. Medhātithi and Govindarāja, however, maintain that it is for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). Now, the twice-born are headed by the Brāhmaṇa; let the performance of his livelihoods, such as the *ṛta* and others, be heard—this is the introduction to a portion of the chapter about to be discussed. (3.286)
Thus ends the third chapter in the Manvarthamuktāvalī, a commentary on the Code of Manu, composed by the illustrious Kullūkabhaṭṭa.
The Fourth Chapter:

Following the section on the ritual for ancestral offerings (*śrāddhakalpa*), and because the means of livelihood (*vṛtti*) were promised explicitly in the statement, “And likewise, the protection of the means of livelihood” (1.113), and because the householder’s life depends upon those means of livelihood which must now be explained, [the author] speaks here of the time for studentship (*brahmacarya*) and the time for the householder’s life, in order to show that the householder’s life follows studentship and that the means of livelihood to be described here pertain to that very stage.
Having spent the first quarter of his life with the teacher, the twice-born...
Having taken a wife, he should dwell in the house during the second stage of life. || 4.1 ||

Regarding the phrase "the fourth": the statement that the first quarter of life [is for studentship] is intended as an indication of the period of *brahmacarya* (celibate studentship), because it is difficult to determine the fourth part of life due to the indefinite duration of human lifespan. Nor does the Vedic text, "Man has a lifespan of a hundred years," refer specifically to twenty-five years, as that would contradict such injunctions as, "The period of *brahmacarya* is thirty-six years. A Brāhmaṇa who adheres to the view of the sequential performance of all stages of life (*āśrama-samuccaya*) should, having remained in the teacher's house according to his ability during the aforementioned period of *brahmacarya*—which is reckoned from birth—practice the stage of the householder during the second quarter of his life. Since the rule, "But when the householder perceives [his strength waning]" (6.2), indicates no fixed time, the phrase "the second quarter of life" likewise refers specifically to the period of the householder's life. 4.1.
A Brahmin should live in times of no distress by adopting a livelihood that involves no injury to living beings, or at least very little injury. (4.2)

"Without injury" (*adroheṇa*): Non-injury is the absence of causing pain to another, such as through gleaning ears of grain, picking up single grains, or begging; slight injury, such as begging and the like, is "slight injury" (*alpadroha*). Injury (*droha*) does not mean mere violence, because that is already prohibited. When non-injury is impossible, one should live by resorting to that mode of livelihood which involves slight injury. A Brāhmaṇa—not a Kṣatriya or others—should live engaged in the maintenance of his wife and dependents and the performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), provided there is no distress. This rule will be prescribed for times of distress in the tenth chapter. Furthermore, this general instruction is intended to include officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving pure gifts, and so forth. If it were restricted solely to the specific [means] to be mentioned later, such as agriculture and the like, its natural scope would be diminished, it would lose its status as a general rule, and officiating at sacrifices and other such acts would not be included in the context of livelihoods; therefore, he may live even by those means. (4.2)
For the sake of accomplishing the mere requirements of life, one should accumulate wealth through one's own irreproachable occupations, without causing distress to the body. (4.3)

Regarding the term *yātrā*: *yātrā* means the maintenance of life (*prāṇasthiti*). It refers to the mere maintenance of life preceded by the performance of daily duties and the lawful nurturing of one's family, and not for the sake of enjoyment. One should effect the accumulation of wealth through actions consisting of acquisitions prescribed by the scriptures as being connected to oneself—such as those to be described later beginning with *ṛta*—without bodily hardship. (4.3)
Regarding the question "By what actions [should one live]?", he says here:
One may live by means of *ṛta* and *amṛta*, or by *mṛta* or *pramṛta*, or even by *satya* and *anṛta*; but never by the "dog's livelihood" (*śvavṛtti*). (4.4)

"By means of the *ṛta* and the *amṛta*"—the phrase "in times of non-distress" (*anāpadi*) is understood to carry over. One should live by means of the *ṛta* and so forth when not in distress; however, one should never subsist by service (*sevā*) when not in distress. (4.4)
Because these terms are not well known, he explains them: "Ṛta is to be understood as gleaning ears of grain; amṛta is that which is obtained unasked;
mṛta is alms obtained by begging; and pramṛta is traditionally held to be agriculture. (4.5)

*Ṛta* is *uñcha-śila*. According to the view of Baudhāyana: “In places not forbidden, on the road, or in fields where there is unobstructed space, wherever herbs are found, having gathered one grain at a time with the two fingers” (BDh 3.2.15), *uñcha* is the gathering of individual grains and the like. *Śila* is the gathering of various grains in the form of clusters (*mañjarī*). *Uñcha* and *śila* form a singular compound (*ekavadbhāva*). Because it yields a fruit equal to truth (*satya*), it is called *ṛta*. That which arrives unasked is *amṛta*, because it is a cause of happiness like nectar. On the other hand, when requested, alms (*bhaikṣa*)—consisting of a collection of begged food—is *mṛta*, because it produces suffering equal to death. Furthermore, for a householder who maintains the sacred fire (*sāgni*), this alms consists of raw rice and the like, but not cooked food, because there would be no offering (*homa*) into his own fire using what was cooked by another's fire. And agriculture (*karṣaṇa*) is *pramṛta*, as if exceedingly dead, because it results in much suffering due to being the cause of the death of many creatures dwelling in the earth. (4.5)
Trade consists of both truth and falsehood, and one may indeed live by it; service is declared to be the "dog's livelihood," therefore one should avoid it. (4.6)

"But commerce consists of truth and falsehood. Because it is generally accomplished through transactions involving both truth and falsehood, commerce is characterized as "truth-and-falsehood. However, this does not mean that commerce is permitted by the scripture through the use of both truth and falsehood. Furthermore, because of the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and by that also one lives," usury (*kusīda*) is also included, as it is taught alongside commerce. Agriculture mentioned in the preceding verse, as well as commerce and usury in this verse, should be understood—due to the continued application of the term "in times of distress"—as being performed by others and not by oneself. As Gautama (10.1) says: "Agriculture and commerce [are permissible] when not performed by oneself, as is usury. Service (*sevā*), however, is called the "dog's livelihood" (*śvavṛtti*) because it possesses characteristics such as looking upon the master with a humble gaze and performing menial tasks for him; therefore, the Brāhmaṇa under discussion should abandon it. 4.6.
He may possess grain sufficient for a granary, or enough for a single jar;
he may have enough for three days, or he may not even provide for tomorrow. || 4.7 ||

Regarding the term *kusūladhānyaka*: lexicographers state that “*kusūla* means a granary for rice. This refers to a store of grain kept in a house constructed of bricks and other materials. In this context, with regard to the specific time period required, [Manu Smṛti 11.7 states]:
“He who possesses enough food for three years to maintain his dependents, or even more than that, is worthy to drink the Soma.”

Thus, the time-period mentioned by Manu alone should be accepted. Therefore, a householder who, together with his family—consisting of those required for daily and occasional religious duties and those to be supported—is able to maintain himself for three years or more with a quantity of grain and other wealth, is called a *kusūladhānyaka* (one who possesses a granary of grain). One whose grain and other wealth are sufficient for a year's maintenance is a *kumbhīdhānyaka* (one who possesses a jar of grain). As it is said:
"One whose food supply lasts for a year should perform the rites pertaining to the Soma sacrifice."

Thus, because Yājñavalkya permits a householder to accumulate a year’s supply, Manu will likewise prescribe a year’s accumulation for the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) in the verse, “Or he may indeed have a year’s store” (6.18). In comparison to that, a year’s accumulation is appropriate for a householder who has a large family to support. Medhātithi, however, having stated that one is called a *kusūladhānya* even if he possesses gold and other wealth, provided he has enough grain and property to sustain his many dependents, such as servants and wife, for three years, explained that a *kumbhī* is a small leather bag or vessel, and a *kumbhīdhānyaka* is one who has a six-month supply of grain and so forth. Govindarāja, commenting on the term *kusūladhānyaka*, explains it as either a collection of grain measured by a granary (*koṣṭha*), or a *kumbhīdhānyaka* as one whose wealth suffices for only twelve days; or alternatively, a collection of grain and so forth measured by a small leather bag (*uṣṭrikā*), or one whose wealth suffices for only six days.
"Subsistence for twelve days by means of a granary and for six days by means of a jar"—
we do not follow this rootless statement of Govindarāja.

*Īhā* means effort; that which arises from it is *aihika*. One who possesses wealth sufficient for three days is called *tryahaika*; or it may be so. The meaning is: one whose wealth is suitable for subsistence for three days. Alternatively, it may be formed by adding the possessive suffix *ika* to *śvastana-bhakta*—meaning "one who has food for tomorrow"—and then forming a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*). Thus it should be understood. (4.7)
And among these four twice-born householders,
each subsequent one is to be known as superior according to dharma, and as the greatest conqueror of the worlds.

"Of all four as well": among these four types of householders beginning with those who possess grain in a granary, whichever one is mentioned later should be known as superior; for by means of the practice of restricting one's livelihood, he becomes the most excellent conqueror of the worlds such as heaven. 4.8.
Among these, one performs six duties; another proceeds with three;
one with two; but the fourth lives by means of the Brahmasattra.

Regarding the term *ṣaṭkarma* (one who performs six duties): among these householders, a certain householder who has a large circle of dependents becomes a *ṣaṭkarmā*—one who subsists by six duties—by means of the five [duties] previously mentioned, namely *ṛta*, *ayācita*, *bhaikṣa*, *kṛṣi*, and *vāṇijya*, together with "usury" (*kusīda*), which is conjoined by the word "and" (*ca*) in the verse "and by that very [means]" (4.6). Thus he lives by these six. It has been stated (GDh 10.1) that agriculture, trade, and usury are those permitted by Gautama when not performed by oneself. Another, however, having fewer dependents, proceeds by three: officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*), teaching (*adhyāpana*), and receiving gifts (*pratigraha*), as included in the verse beginning "without malice" (4.2). The prefix *pra-* here is meaningless; the sense is that he simply engages in them. Yet another, because of what will be said later—"receiving gifts is the lowest" (10.109)—proceeds by abandoning that and engaging in only two: officiating at sacrifices and teaching. Compared to the three mentioned above, the fourth, moreover, lives by the *brahmasattra*, i.e., by teaching. Medhātithi, however, says: among these [types of householders] starting from the one who possesses a granary full of grain (*kusūladhānyaka*), one—the *kusūladhānyaka*—becomes a *ṣaṭkarmā* by means of the aforementioned *uñcha*, *śila*, *ayācita*, *ayācitālābha*, *kṛṣi*, and *vāṇijya*; he lives by these six. Another, the second, the *kumbhīdhānyaka*, because agriculture and trade are censured, abandons them and may live according to his desire by three out of *uñcha*, *śila*, *ayācita*, and *ayācita*. One, the *tryahaihika*, excluding the acquisition of what is asked for, may live by two out of *uñcha*, *śila*, and *ayācita* according to his wish. The fourth, moreover, the *aśvastanika*, lives by the *brahmasattra*. He says that the *brahmasattra* is a livelihood consisting of either *śila* or *uñcha*, called a *sattra* because it belongs constantly to the *brahman*, i.e., the Brāhmaṇa. (4.9)
Subsisting by means of gleaning ears of corn and picking up single grains, and being devoted to the maintenance of the sacred fires,
he should always perform only the *iṣṭi* sacrifices prescribed for the new moon, the full moon, and the solstices.

"And while living by this means": subsisting by gleaning ears of grain and picking up single grains, because he lacks the capacity to perform other rites that require wealth, he should remain devoted solely to the *agnihotra*. He should perform only the *iṣṭis* associated with the *parvan* and the solstices (*ayana*). "Parvan" and "ayana" constitute *parvāyaṇe*; those pertaining to them are the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and *āgrayaṇa* sacrifices. (4.10)
One should never follow the ways of the world for the sake of a livelihood; one should live the pure, straightforward, and honest life of a Brahmin. 4.11

"Not the conduct of the world": he should not engage in worldly conduct for the sake of livelihood, such as speaking what is untrue and pleasant, or various kinds of humorous talk and the like. "Upright" means free from the sins of falsely proclaiming one's own virtues and so forth. "Honest" means devoid of deceit such as hypocrisy. He should practice the pure livelihood of a Brāhmaṇa, which is unmixed with the occupations of Vaiśyas and others. Since roots have multiple meanings, this root *jīv* here signifies "to practice"; thus, it takes an object. (4.11)
Relying upon supreme contentment, one who seeks happiness should become self-restrained;
for happiness has contentment as its root, while the opposite is the root of suffering. (4.12)

Regarding "contentment" (saṃtoṣam): contentment is the absence of desire for more wealth than what is required for maintaining servants as far as possible, sustaining one's own life, and performing the five daily sacrifices (pañcayajña) and other such duties. Relying on this excellence, one should exercise restraint in the acquisition of abundant wealth. For happiness is caused by contentment; and in the hereafter, through the performance of prescribed duties while free from anxiety, there is the happiness of heaven and so forth. Conversely, discontent is the root of suffering, because of the great pain resulting from the exertion of acquiring vast wealth, and because of the distress that arises when it is not attained or when it is lost. (4.12)
A twice-born Snātaka, however, living by any one of these modes of livelihood, should observe these following vows which lead to heaven, long life, and fame: 4.13.

"By any one of these": this is prescribed as "by any one" (*anyatamayā*) when it is possible for someone with few dependents to subsist through a single means of livelihood; however, for one with many dependents, since it is ordained that "one among these shall perform six duties" (4.9) when food is available, [the singular] would not apply. Alternatively, because the understanding of a single sentence and because it prescribes a vow (*vrata*), the term "by any one" is merely a restatement (*anuvādaka*), and thus the singular number is not intended to be restrictive. A *snātaka* Brāhmaṇa, living by any one of the aforementioned modes of livelihood, should perform these vows (*vrata*) to be described hereafter—which are conducive to heaven, long life, and fame—according to his capacity. A "vow" (*vrata*) consists of a specific resolve (*saṃkalpa*) such as: "This must be done by me; this must not be done. (4.13)
One should perform one's own duty as declared in the Veda constantly and without sloth;
for by performing that according to one's ability, one attains the supreme goal. (4.14)

"Revealed in the Veda": that which is taught in the Smṛtis is also "revealed in the Veda" because it is rooted in the Veda. One should perform one's own duty—that prescribed for one's particular stage of life—as long as one lives, being untiring and free from laziness. The particle *hi* indicates the reason: because by performing that [duty] according to one's capacity, one attains the supreme goal, characterized by liberation (*mokṣa*). This is because when evil is destroyed through the performance of obligatory duties (*nityakarman*), one attains liberation through the direct realization of Brahman by means of a purified internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). As it is said in the *Mokṣadharma*: "Knowledge arises in men from the destruction of sinful karma."
There, in that which resembles the surface of a mirror, one beholds the self within the self.
In the self, that is, in the internal organ. || 4.14 ||
One should not seek wealth through excessive attachment nor by contrary actions;
nor should one do so from hither and thither, whether wealth is already present or even in times of distress. (4.15)

"He shall not acquire wealth by such means" (4.15): that to which a person is attached is called *prasaṅga*, such as singing, instrumental music, and so forth; he shall not acquire wealth through these. Nor [shall he acquire it] by means of actions forbidden by the scriptures, such as officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice (*ayājya-yājana*), and so forth. Nor [should he acquire it] when wealth already exists. Nor even when wealth does not exist, provided there is another possible way [of obtaining it]; nor [should he acquire it] from anyone whatsoever, even from outcasts (*patita*) and the like.
One should not become attached to any objects of the senses out of desire;
one should also turn back from excessive attachment to them by means of the mind. (4.16)

Regarding the phrase "among the objects of the senses": the objects of the senses are form, taste, smell, touch, and so forth; even toward these—which are not prohibited, such as sexual union with one's own wife—one should not become attached, nor should one engage in excessive attachment, which consists of total indulgence for the sake of sensual enjoyment driven by desire. He states the means for the cessation of excessive attachment: "excessive attachment. One should properly turn away from it through the mind by cultivating the contemplation of the instability of sense-objects and their opposition to the highest good, which consists of heaven and liberation. 4.16.
One should abandon all pursuits that obstruct one's Vedic study; teaching them in whatever manner possible, for that indeed constitutes the fulfillment of one's duty. 4.17

"Regarding the word 'all': one should abandon all those matters that contradict the meaning of the Vedas, such as approaching the palace of an absolute monarch, agriculture, worldly affairs, and so forth. How, then, is the maintenance of dependents and oneself to be accomplished? Anticipating this doubt, he says: 'In whatever way possible, by any means whatsoever that does not conflict with one's Vedic study, one should sustain both dependents and oneself; for this is the state of having fulfilled one's duties and attained one's purpose for this *snātaka*: namely, constant devotion to Vedic study. (4.17)
One should conduct oneself here by practicing conformity in dress, speech, and intellect with one's age, occupation, wealth, learning, and lineage. (4.18)

Regarding the phrase "in accordance with one's age" (vayasā): one should conduct oneself in the world by adopting dress, speech, and intellect in conformity with one's age, occupation, wealth, learning, and lineage. Just as in youth one wears garlands, perfumes, ointments, and so forth, and employs speech and intellect in accordance with the three aims of life (trivarga), the same should be inferred for other stages such as action and the rest. 4.18.
One should constantly study the scriptures that increase the intellect, which are auspicious and beneficial, as well as the Vedic Nigamas. (4.19)

Regarding "intellect" (*buddhi*): he should constantly reflect upon those treatises that are not in conflict with the Vedas and which quickly produce the growth of intellect—namely grammar, Mīmāṃsā, the Smṛtis, the Purāṇas, Nyāya, and so forth; likewise, those that are "prosperous," meaning beneficial for wealth, such as the *Arthaśāstras* of Bṛhaspati, Uśanas, and others; likewise, those that are "beneficial," providing visible assistance, such as medicine, astrology, and so forth; and likewise, those known as the *Nigamas*, which explain the meaning of the Vedas through the exposition of synonyms. || 4.19 ||
For in whatever measure a person masters the scripture, in that same measure he understands it, and his discernment finds delight in it. 4.20

Regarding the phrase *yathā yathā*: because to the extent that a person correctly studies a treatise (*śāstra*), to that same extent he understands it more specifically; furthermore, his knowledge even concerning the subject matter of other treatises becomes pleasing and radiant to him. Since the root *ruc* has the sense of "shining" (*dīpti*) and not the sense of "desire" (*abhilāṣa*), the designation of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) does not apply under the rule *ruccarthānāṃ prīyamāṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.33).

One should never neglect the sacrifice to the sages, the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the spirits, the sacrifice to men, and the sacrifice to the ancestors, according to one's ability. (4.21)

"Regarding the sacrifice to the seers (ṛṣiyajña)": one should not abandon the five sacrifices, beginning with the private recitation of the Veda (svādhyāya), according to one's ability. Although these five sacrifices were already mentioned in the third chapter, they are restated here for the purpose of prescribing specific rules for them later on and to indicate that they constitute the observances (vratas) of a Snātaka.
Some people, who are learned in the treatises on sacrifice, constantly offer these great sacrifices into the senses themselves, remaining free from worldly desire. 4.22.

"Regarding 'some [perform] these as one': some householders, who are learned in the scriptures concerning the performance of external and internal sacrifices, accomplish these five great sacrifices by not performing them externally due to the excellence of their knowledge of Brahman, but rather by exercising restraint over the five objects of the sensory organs—namely, the perception of form and so forth—within the five sense organs themselves. Since it is impossible for these sacrifices to be actual oblations, the verb *juhoti* (he offers) is used here in the sense of accomplishment. (4.22)
Some offer the breath into speech and speech into breath at all times, perceiving within both speech and breath the imperishable accomplishment of sacrifice. (4.23)

Regarding the phrase "in speech": some householders who know Brahman, understanding that the performance of sacrifice within speech and breath yields inexhaustible fruit, constantly offer speech into breath and breath into speech. It is enjoined by this [text] that one should explain it thus: while speaking, one offers breath into speech; and while not speaking, through the act of breathing out, one offers speech into breath—as stated in the Kauṣītaki-rahasya-brāhmaṇa (2.4.1).

As long as a person speaks, he is not able to breathe; at that time, he offers the breath into speech. For as long as a person breathes, he is not able to speak; at that time, he offers speech into the breath. These two infinite, immortal oblations he constantly offers while waking and while sleeping. Now, other oblations placed in succession consist of action; for it was thus that the ancient knowers did not perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice for him. (4.23)
Other brahmins always perform these sacrifices with knowledge alone,
perceiving with the eye of knowledge that their ritual action has its root in knowledge.

"By knowledge alone": other Brahmins, established in Brahman, sacrifice with these very sacrifices by means of the knowledge of Brahman in every way, and they perform these sacrifices. To explain how this is so, he says: Knowledge is Brahman, as is well known from such scriptural passages as, "Truth, knowledge, infinite" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1). Knowing that the origin of these ritual actions is rooted in knowledge—that is, knowing that knowledge is like an eye, by which everything is perceived—they accomplish even the five sacrifices by means of the "eye of knowledge," namely the Upaniṣad beginning with, "All this is indeed Brahman, [from which it] is born, [into which it] dissolves, and [by which it is sustained]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3), while meditating upon them as being of the nature of Brahman at the time of their origin. The meaning is that they enjoy the fruit of the five sacrifices. These rules apply to householders who are renunciants of the Vedas and are established in Brahman; thus [it is said] in three verses.
One should always perform the Agnihotra sacrifice at the beginning and end of day and night,
and indeed with the Darśa sacrifice at the end of the half-month, as well as with the Paurṇamāsa sacrifice.

Regarding the *agnihotra*: in the case of the *uditahoma* (offering after sunrise), one should perform the *agnihotra* at the beginning of the day and the beginning of the night; in the case of the *anuditahoma* (offering before sunrise), at the end of the day and the end of the night. Alternatively, in the *uditahoma* system, one may perform it at the beginning and the end of the day; in the *anuditahoma* system, at the beginning and the end of the night. At the end of the half-month of the dark fortnight, one should sacrifice with the rite called *darśa*, and during the half of the bright fortnight, with the rite called *paurṇamāsa*. (4.25)

At the end of the grain harvest, a twice-born man should sacrifice with the New Grain offering; likewise, at the end of each season, he should perform the seasonal sacrifices; at the beginning of each solstice, he should offer an animal sacrifice; and at the end of the year, he should perform the Soma sacrifices.

Regarding the phrase "at the end of the grain" (*sasyānte*): when the previously harvested grain, such as rice, has been exhausted, one should perform the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice even if the previous crop has not yet fully run out, provided that new grain has appeared, according to the author of the Sūtras' statement, "In autumn, [one offers] new grain. This is because the depletion of grain is not fixed, and because the wealthy possess quantities of grain sufficient for several years' subsistence. Furthermore, by the inclusion of the term "end of the grain," the appearance of new grain alone is intended, since that occurs regularly and arises as a recurring occasion every year. According to the view that the year consists of six seasons (*ṛtu-saṃvatsara*), there are four months per season; at the end of these, one should sacrifice with the rituals known as the *Cāturmāsya*. At the beginning of both these solstices—the northern and the southern—one should sacrifice with an animal (*paśu*), meaning one should perform the sacrifice called the slaughter of an animal. Since the calculation of the year in the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥ-śāstra*) begins from the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, when the year has concluded with the winter (*śiśira*), one should sacrifice in the spring with the *Agniṣṭoma* and other sacrifices accomplished through the juice of the *Soma* plant. (4.26)

A twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires and desires to live a long life must not eat new grain or meat without first having performed the sacrifice for the new harvest and the animal sacrifice. (4.27)

"Not without having sacrificed": a twice-born man who has maintained the sacred fires and desires to live a long life shall not eat new grain without having performed the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice; nor shall he eat meat without having performed an animal sacrifice. (4.27)

Speaking of the fault, he states the impermanence of these two: "For his fires, not honored with new [offerings] and with the sacrificial victim, desire to consume his very life-breaths, being greedy for fresh grain and meat. (4.28)

Regarding the word *navena*: because the fires—unhonored by the new sacrificial offering, raw like the flesh of an animal, and having not yet performed the sacrifice—desire to devour the very life-breaths of this *āhitāgni* who maintains the *agnihotra*, being greedy for the meat of the new grain. *Gardhaḥ* means an excess of longing; it is a form derived from the root *gṛdh* with the suffix *añ*. One who possesses such greed is called *gardhī*; the suffix *ini* is used here according to Pāṇini 5.2.115. || 4.28 ||
No guest should dwell in his house without being honored to the best of his ability with a seat, food, a bed, water, or roots and fruits. (4.29)

Regarding the phrase "seating and food": a guest who has not been honored according to his ability with seating, food, and so forth, shall not dwell in the house of this householder. By this, the latter half of the verse reiterates what was already stated [in the preceding portion]: "one should honor a guest according to one's ability. (4.29)
One should not honor, even with a mere word, heretics, those who persist in improper actions, those who follow the "vow of the cat," rogues, rationalists, and those who act like herons. 4.30.

"Heretics (*pāṣaṇḍinaḥ*). Heretics are those who wear the marks and observe the vows outside the Veda, such as Buddhist monks (*śākya-bhikṣuka*), Jain mendicants (*kṣapaṇaka*), and others; those engaged in improper occupations (*vikarmasthāḥ*), who live by forbidden means of livelihood; those with the "vow of a cat" (*baiḍālavratika*) and the "vow of a heron" (*bakavṛtti*), whose characteristics will be described later; the "crafty" (*śaṭhāḥ*), who have no faith in the Vedas; and the "sophists" (*haitukāḥ*), who employ reasoning that contradicts the Vedas. One should not honor these people—even with mere words—when they arrive at the time of receiving guests. However, the mere gift of food to those unworthy of honor is indeed permitted by the rule: "to those who do not cook for themselves according to their ability" (4.32). || 4.30 ||

One should honor with offerings to the gods and ancestors those householders who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and have completed their Vedic studies and vows (*vedavidyāvratasnāta*), and one should avoid those who are the opposite. (4.31)

Regarding the phrase "vedavidyā" (those who have completed Vedic knowledge): by the expression "those who have bathed after completing Vedic knowledge, vows, or both," all three types are included—the *vidyā-snātaka*, the *vratasnātaka*, and the *ubhayasnātaka*. As Hārīta says: "He who returns home having completed the Vedas but not the vows is a *vidyā-snātaka*. He who returns home having completed the vows but not the Vedas is a *vratasnātaka*. He who returns home having completed both is a *vidyāvratasnātaka*."

Although the status of a *snātaka* alone would suffice for the inclusion of a *snātaka* by virtue of being a duty of the *snātaka*, nevertheless, the quality of being a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) is intended here. One should honor those *snātakas* who are learned scholars with offerings to the gods and ancestors (*havya-kavya*), but one should avoid those who are the opposite. (4.31)
A householder should give according to his ability to those who do not cook for themselves, and he should share with all living beings without causing hardship to his own dependents. (4.32)

"According to one's ability" means that those who do not cook—such as students (*brahmacārin*), wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*), heretics (*pāṣaṇḍin*), and so forth—are intended. Although the giving of food to students and wandering mendicants has already been mentioned, it is stated again here for the sake of emphasizing its superiority over the case of those who do cook, and because it constitutes a vow (*vrata*) of the *snātaka*. Medhātithi and Govindarāja, however, have stated that since students and wandering mendicants were already mentioned in the verse, "And he should give alms according to rule to a beggar and to a student" (3.94), this present statement refers specifically to heretics and the like. In accordance with the needs of one's own family, a distribution [of resources] must be made even to living beings down to trees and the like, by means of water and such. (4.32)

A Snātaka who is suffering from hunger may seek wealth from a king, or from a patron for whom he performs sacrifices, or from a pupil; it is the settled rule that he must not do so from anyone else. 4.33.

Regarding the phrase "from a king": because of the prohibition, "One should not accept gifts from a king who is not born of the Kṣatriya caste" (4.84), the word *rājan* here refers specifically to a Kṣatriya monarch. A Snātaka, even when suffering from hunger, should first seek wealth from a Kṣatriya king who acts according to the scriptures, or from his patron (*yājya*) or pupil (*śiṣya*), despite the possibility of accepting gifts from other twice-born men. This is because a king possesses great wealth and is thus free from distress, whereas a patron or pupil, having received assistance, is naturally inclined toward returning that favor. However, if these are unavailable, he may take wealth from another twice-born man as well. And if even that is absent, the author will later state the rule for times of distress (*āpaddharma*): "He may accept gifts from anyone" (10.102). Thus, this statement establishes a rule for non-distress situations, requiring that one first accept gifts from a Kṣatriya king, a patron, or a pupil. For this very reason, he says, "but not from others. "Stability" (*sthiti*) means the boundary of the scriptures. Nor should it be argued that this verse pertains only to the rules for times of distress because of the expression "suffering" (*saṃsīdan*); for that would be inconsistent, as the context concerns non-distress, and the term "suffering" here refers specifically to the lack of acquired wealth.
