Otherwise, even one who washes his feet immediately after eating would be considered to be living in a state of distress. Furthermore, if this verse were intended for times of distress, it would contradict the rule "but not from others" with the subsequent injunction "he may accept from anyone" (10.102). As for what was stated in the section on distress—"A lord of the earth should be entreated by those suffering and desiring base metals or wealth" (10.113)—that refers exclusively to a Śūdra king in the event that accepting gifts from kings of the higher castes is impossible. (4.33)
A learned Snātaka should never suffer from hunger if he is capable [of providing for himself], nor should he wear worn-out or dirty clothes if he possesses the means. 4.34.

"Lest he should perish": even though a bath-graduate (*snātaka*) Brāhmaṇa may be capable of receiving gifts due to his possession of knowledge and other virtues, when the aforementioned acceptance of gifts from kings and so forth becomes available, he should not be overcome by hunger. Furthermore, while wealth is available, he should not wear worn-out or dirty clothes. (4.34)

Having trimmed his hair, nails, and beard, self-controlled, wearing white garments, and pure, he should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Veda and to what is beneficial for the self. 4.35

Regarding the term "one whose hair is trimmed": "trimming" means cutting; thus, one should have one's hair, nails, and beard shorn, endure the hardships of austerity, be self-controlled, wear white garments, be endowed with both external and internal purity, be devoted to the study of the Vedas, and, through the use of medicinal herbs and other means, be intent on his own spiritual welfare.
He should carry a bamboo staff and a water-pot containing water;
he should wear the sacred thread, a Vedic girdle, and two auspicious golden earrings.
"Made of bamboo" means that he should carry a bamboo staff, a water-pot containing water, a sacred thread, a handful of *kuśa* grass, and two beautiful golden earrings. (4.36)

One should never look at the sun when it is rising, nor when it is setting; nor when it has just emerged from the water, nor when it is reflected in water, nor when it has reached the middle of the sky. (4.37)

"One should not look" means: one should not look at the solar disc when it is rising or setting, nor when it is full; nor when it is eclipsed by a planet, or afflicted by such portents as being curved; nor when it is reflected in water (*vāristha*); nor when it is situated in the middle of the sky at the time of midday. || 4.37 ||
One should not step over a calf’s tethering rope, nor run while it is raining;
one should not look at one's own reflection in water—this is the rule. (4.38)

"One should not leap" means one should not leap over the rope tethering a calf. Furthermore, one should run when the clouds are raining, and one should not look at the reflection of one's own body in water; such is the settled rule in the scriptures. 4.38.
One should circumambulate clockwise clay, a cow, a deity, a Brahmin, clarified butter, honey, a crossroads, and well-known trees. (4.39)

"Clay," he says. Having set out, he should pass with his right hand by way of the path those deities who reside in the clay that has not been excavated, in cow-dung, in stones, and so forth, as well as Brahmins, clarified butter, honey, crossroads, large well-known trees, and the like. Regarding the term *pradakṣiṇāni*, the neuter gender is used according to Pāṇini 1.2.69: "A neuter [noun] followed by a non-neuter [noun] may optionally become singular [in form]. || 4.39 ||
Even if he is intoxicated, he should not approach a woman when her menses are visible;
nor should he lie down with her on the same bed. 4.40.

"He shall not approach" means that even if he is negligent or afflicted by desire, he must not approach a woman during the three days when touching her is forbidden following the appearance of menses. Although the prohibition [of intercourse] is already established by the very prohibition of touch—by the rule "the first four [days] of theirs" (3.47)—this is stated again for the sake of the severity of the penance and because it constitutes a specific vow of a *snātaka*. Furthermore, even if he does not approach her, he must not sleep with her on the same bed. (4.40)
For when a man approaches a woman overwhelmed by her menses, his wisdom, vigor, strength, sight, and even his lifespan diminish. (4.41)
"Overwhelmed by *rajas*" means that because the wisdom, vigor, strength, sight, and lifespan of a man who approaches a woman during her menses perish, he should not approach her. (4.41)
For him who avoids that [woman] who is overwhelmed by passion, wisdom, splendor, strength, vision, and even life itself increase. (4.42)
Regarding the word "her": for one who approaches her while she is in her menses, his wisdom and other virtues increase; therefore, he should not approach her. 4.42.
He should not eat together with his wife, nor should he look at her while she is eating, or while she is sneezing or yawning, nor while she is sitting at her ease. 4.43.

"He shall not eat" means he shall not eat from the same vessel as his wife. Furthermore, while she is eating, he shall not look at her when she is sneezing or yawning, nor when she is situated in an unrestrained place according to her own pleasure. 4.43.
A twice-born man who desires luster should not look at a woman applying collyrium to her own eyes, nor one who is anointed with oil, nor one who is uncovered, nor one who is giving birth. (4.44)

“Nor one applying collyrium”: likewise, a Brahmin should not look at a woman applying collyrium to her own eyes, or one smeared with oil and the like, or one who is uncovered—that is, lacking a covering for her breasts—but not one who is naked, because it will be stated later: “He should not look at a naked woman” (4.53). Nor should he look at a woman giving birth to offspring. 4.44.
One should not eat food wearing only a single garment, nor should one perform a bath naked.
One should not void urine on a path, nor on ashes, nor in a cow-pen. (4.45)

"One should not eat food": one should not consume food while wearing only a single garment. One should not bathe while lacking clothing for the lower body or a covering for the upper body. The mention of "urine" is intended to include the discharge of bodily impurities from the lower part of the body; therefore, one should not void urine or feces on a path, in ashes, or in a cow-pen. (4.45)
Neither on ploughed ground, nor in water, nor on a funeral pyre, nor on a mountain; neither in a ruined temple nor ever on an anthill. (4.46)

"Not on ploughed land": likewise, one should never discharge feces or urine on ploughed fields and the like, in water, on a heap of bricks intended for fire-altars, on a mountain, in an ancient temple, or on a mound of earth formed by worms. 4.46.
Neither in pits inhabited by creatures, nor while walking, nor while standing; neither having reached a riverbank, nor on the summit of a mountain. (4.47)

"Not among living beings" means that one should not void urine or excrement while walking in holes containing creatures, nor while standing, nor by resorting to a riverbank, nor on a mountain peak. Since the prohibition of the mountain itself already establishes the prohibition of its peaks, the specific mention of "mountain peaks" is intended to allow for an option regarding other mountains. In this case, since an option based on personal preference would otherwise be possible even in the absence of a general prohibition, the option here is restricted: there is no fault in using a mountain when one is extremely distressed. (4.47)
While looking at the wind, fire, a Brahmin, the sun, water, or likewise cows, one should never discharge feces or urine. (4.48)

Regarding the phrase "wind, fire, a Brahmin": one should never perform the voiding of urine or feces while looking at wind, fire, a Brahmin, the sun, water, or a cow. Since it is impossible to see the wind because it lacks form, this prohibition refers to [looking at] grass, wood, and so forth driven by a whirlwind. (4.48)
Having covered [the body] with wood, clods of earth, leaves, grass, or the like, he should pass by, restraining his speech, being purified, with his limbs wrapped and his head veiled. (4.49)

"Having covered [the ground]," it is said: having concealed the earth with wood or other materials, one who is not impure from food remnants, whose limbs are covered and whose head is veiled, should perform the voiding of urine and feces.
"Having covered the earth with dry grass, or with wood, or with leaves, or with bamboo splinters, or even with earthen vessels."
According to this statement from the Vāyu Purāṇa, dry wood, leaves, and grass are to be understood [as the objects of the prohibition]. 4.49.
One should void urine and excrement facing north during the day;
at night, one should face south; and likewise during the two twilights, one should face north as during the day. (4.50)

Regarding the phrase "the voiding of urine and excrement": one should perform the voiding of urine and feces facing north during the day and at the two twilights, but facing south if it is at night. Dharaṇīdhara, however, having read the fourth quarter as *svastho 'nāśāya cetasaḥ*, explained it to mean "for the non-destruction of the mind," that is, the intellect (*buddhi*).
Having abandoned the traditional oral transmission (*āmnāya*) favored by the learned, Dharaṇīdhara here has fabricated an alternative reading for no purpose.
In shade or in darkness, by night or by day, a twice-born man may perform [the purification] facing whichever direction is comfortable, as also when there is fear of danger to life. (4.51)

Regarding the phrase "in the shade": at night, in the shade or in darkness; or during the day, in the shade or in darkness caused by mist and the like; and when the specific direction is unknown, or when there is fear of loss of life caused by thieves, tigers, and so forth—one may void urine and excrement with the face turned as one desires. (4.51)
The wisdom of one who urinates facing fire, the sun, the moon, water, a twice-born man, a cow, or the wind perishes. (4.52)

“Facing the fire”: By the rule “wind, fire, a Brahmin” (4.48), the seeing of fire and the others by one who is urinating is forbidden; by this [present verse], however, even for one who does not see them, facing toward them is prohibited. For one who performs urination or defecation while facing fire, the sun, the moon, water, a Brahmin, a cow, or the wind, wisdom perishes; therefore, this must not be done. In place of *prativātam* (“against the wind”), others read *apratisaṃdhyam* (“not facing the twilight”). 4.52.
One should not blow on a fire with one's mouth, nor look at a naked woman;
one should not throw impure things into the fire, nor warm one's feet over it. (4.53)

“Not fire”: fire must not be blown upon with the mouth; rather, it should be fanned with a fan or similar means. According to the Sāṃkhyāyana view, “one should not look at a naked woman except during sexual intercourse,” one should therefore not look at a naked woman except in the context of sexual union. One should not throw impure things, such as urine or feces, into the fire. Nor should one warm one’s feet [in the fire]. Because of the word *pra* (forth), one should not directly warm one’s feet by lifting them into the fire; there is no contradiction, however, in using it for the purpose of sweating clothes or similar items. (4.53)
One should not place it underneath, nor should one step over it;
one should not treat it with one's feet, nor should one cause any injury to living beings. (4.54)

"Below" means that one should not place charcoal-baskets or similar objects beneath beds and the like; nor should one walk by leaping over fire; nor should one place a fire at the foot of a sleeping person; nor should one perform any action that causes pain to living beings. (4.54)
One should not eat at the time of twilight, nor should one travel, nor should one lie down to sleep;
nor indeed should one scratch the ground, nor should one remove one's own garland.

"He shall not eat": at the time of the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), he shall not eat, nor travel to another village, nor sleep; nor shall he scratch the ground with a fingernail or the like; nor shall he himself remove a garland that has been worn; by implication, it is stated that he should have it removed by another. 4.55.
One should not discharge urine, feces, or spittle into water; nor anything else smeared with impurity, nor blood, nor poisons. (4.56)

"Not urine in water" (4.56): one should not discharge into water urine, feces, phlegm, clothing stained by such impurities as urine and the like, or other impure things such as food leavings, blood, or poisons—whether artificial or natural.
One should not sleep alone in an empty house, nor should one wake a superior person from sleep; one should not converse with a woman in her courses, nor go to a sacrifice unless invited. (4.57)

"Not alone": one should not sleep alone in a house where people normally reside. One should not wake someone who is sleeping and is superior in wealth, learning, or other qualities. One should not engage in conversation with a woman in her menses. And one who is not an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) should not go to a sacrifice unless he has been formally chosen; however, he may go if he desires to see it, according to the statement of Gautama: "But he may go at will to see [the sacrifice]" (GDh 9.55). 4.57.
In the fire-sanctuary, in a cow-pen, in the presence of Brahmins,
during Vedic study, and while eating, one should keep the right hand raised.

"In the fire-hall": in the house of the sacred fires, in the cow-pen, in the presence of Brahmins or cows, and during the times of Vedic study and eating, one should lift up the right hand together with the forearm from the garment—that is, one should draw it out. 4.58.
One should not stop a cow while it is suckling, nor should one tell anyone [of such an act].
A wise man, having seen a rainbow in the sky, should not point it out to anyone. 4.59

"One should not restrain" means that one should not turn back a cow while it is drinking water or milk; this prohibition applies to all cases except for the purpose of milking. Nor should one inform anyone else that she is drinking another's milk and so forth. Furthermore, having seen a rainbow in the sky, one who knows the fault of looking at forbidden things should not point it out to anyone. (4.59)
One should not dwell in an unrighteous village, nor in one where diseases are exceedingly prevalent;
one should not set out on a journey alone, nor should one reside for long on a mountain. (4.60)

"Not unrighteous" means that where unrighteous people dwell, residence there is not appropriate; nor is it highly appropriate to reside for a very long time where many people are afflicted by censurable and incurable diseases. One should never travel alone on a road, and one should not dwell for a long period on a mountain. (4.60)
One should not dwell in a kingdom ruled by a Śūdra, nor in one filled with unrighteous people; nor in one overrun by hosts of heretics, nor in one infested by men of the lowest castes. (4.61)

"Not in a kingdom of Śūdras": one should not dwell in a country where a Śūdra is the king. Nor should one dwell in villages and the like that are surrounded on all sides by unrighteous people; thus there is no tautology. Furthermore, one should not dwell in a place dominated by heretics (*pāṣaṇḍin*)—those who bear outward marks contrary to the Vedas—or one that is harassed by *caṇḍālas* and other outcastes. (4.61)
One should not eat food from which the oil has been extracted, nor should one practice excessive satiety;
one should not eat too early in the morning, nor too late in the evening, nor having already eaten in the evening, should one eat again in the morning. (4.62)

"One should not eat" means one should not consume oil-cakes and the like from which the oil has been extracted. Furthermore, one should not overeat even twice a day; for it is said: "One should fill half the stomach with food, one part with water, and one-fourth should be left remaining for the movement of the vital air."

According to such statements from the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, one should not eat at the time of sunrise or at the time of sunset. Having eaten a substantial breakfast, one should not eat again in the evening. (4.62)
One should not engage in futile exertion, nor drink water with cupped hands;
one should not eat food in one's lap, nor ever be a seeker of idle curiosity. (4.63)

"One should not do" means one should not engage in any activity devoid of purpose, whether for visible or invisible ends. One should not drink water with cupped hands. One should not eat sweets and the like by placing them upon one's thighs. One should never indulge in curiosity—the desire to know "what is this?"—unless there is a specific purpose. 4.63.
He should not dance, nor sing, nor play musical instruments; he should not clap his hands, nor shout, nor utter cries while impassioned. 4.64

"One should not dance" means that one should not perform dancing, singing, or instrumental music that is contrary to the scriptures. One should not make a sound by slapping the arm with the hand. One should not make a "kṣveḍana" sound consisting of indistinct dental noises. Nor should one, out of passion, make a sound like that of a donkey or similar animals.
One should never wash one's feet in a vessel made of bell-metal;
nor should one eat from a broken dish, nor from one that is defiled by its nature.

"Not on the feet": one should never wash one's feet in a bell-metal vessel (*kāṃsyapātra*). According to the statement of Paiṭhīnasi—"There is no fault [in using] vessels of copper, silver, or gold, whether they are broken or unbroken"—one should not eat from a broken vessel other than those made of these materials. One should not eat where the mind feels hesitation; that which is mentally repugnant is "corrupted by disposition" (*bhāvaduṣṭa*), and in such a case, one must not eat. (6.65)
One should not wear sandals, clothing, a sacred thread, ornaments, a garland, or even a water-pot that have been worn by others. (6.66)
"Regarding 'sandals': one should not wear sandals, clothing, the sacrificial thread, ornaments, flower garlands, or a water-pot that have been used by another. (6.66)
One should not travel with untrained draft animals, nor with those afflicted by hunger or disease;
nor with those whose horns, eyes, or hooves are broken, nor with those whose tails are mutilated. (6.67)

"Not with the undisciplined" means that one should not travel with mounts such as horses or elephants that have not been tamed, or that are afflicted by hunger or disease, or whose horns, eyes, or hooves are broken, or whose tails have been cut off. (6.67)
He should always travel with horses that are well-trained, swift, endowed with auspicious marks,
and perfect in color and form, without lashing them excessively with the goad.

"But with well-trained [horses]," it is said: he should proceed with those that are tamed, swift-moving, endowed with auspicious marks, of beautiful color, and pleasing in appearance, without excessively paining them with the goad. 6.68.
The morning sun, the smoke from a funeral pyre, and a broken seat are to be avoided;
one should not clip one's nails or body hair, nor should one tear at the nails with the teeth.

"Morning sunlight" (*bālātapa*) refers to the heat of the sun when it has first risen; Medhātithi states that this lasts for three *muhūrtas*, while others say it is the sunlight during the period of the sun in Virgo (*kanyā*). "Smoke from the dead" (*pretadhūma*) is the smoke from a burning corpse. A broken seat—these are things to be avoided. One should not cut nails or hair when they have grown long, nor should one tear at the nails with the teeth. (4.69)
One should not crush a clod of earth, nor should one tear grass with the fingernails;
one should not perform fruitless labor, nor anything that results in future suffering. (4.70)

"Not a clod of earth": according to the statement of Āpastamba—"One should not crush a clod of earth without cause, nor should one cut grass"—one should not crush a clod of earth or cut grass with the fingernails when there is no purpose for doing so.

[Objection: But surely, since the prohibition of this [action] is already established by the rule, "One should not engage in useless exertion" (4.63), this specific prohibition is intended to demonstrate the greater gravity of the fault and the severity of the expiation; for this very reason, he will later censure such a person as a "crusher of clods. Furthermore, one should not perform an action that is devoid of both visible and invisible results. [Reply: Is there not then a tautology with the rule, "One should not engage in useless exertion" (4.63)?

It is said: *Ceṣṭā* (activity) is the exertion of the body; that has been prohibited by the term "vain activity" (*vṛthāceṣṭā*). By this [verse], however, mental action (*mānasa-karma*)—consisting of intentions (*saṃkalpa*) such as those directed toward objects of the mind—is prohibited even if it is fruitless. Furthermore, one should not perform any action that brings unhappiness in the future, such as eating food when one has indigestion. (4.70)
The man who crushes clods of earth, cuts grass, or bites his nails, as well as the slanderer and the impure person, quickly goes to destruction. (4.71)

"Crusher of clods": that man who crushes clods, cuts grass, or bites his nails; likewise, the slanderer and the wicked person who proclaims the faults of others—whether real or unreal—and who is devoid of both external and internal purity—these quickly perish through their bodies, wealth, and so forth. 4.71.
One should not engage in censurable conversation, nor should one wear a garland on the outside;
riding on the backs of cattle is in every way condemned. (4.72)

"Not with reproachful speech" means that one should not engage in conversation—whether concerning technical (śāstrīya) matters or worldly ones—with dogmatic insistence. One should not wear a garland outside of the mass of hair. Regarding "riding on the back of cows": the word "in every way" implies that even using a saddle or similar covering brings about demerit. Since the term "on the back" is specified, there is no fault in using a cart or other vehicle drawn by oxen.
One should not enter an enclosed village or house except through the gate; and at night, one should avoid the roots of trees from afar. (4.73)

"And not by a non-door": one should not enter a house enclosed by a wall or similar structure after leaping over the wall or such in a place other than the door. Furthermore, one should avoid staying at the foot of a tree at night from afar. (4.73)
One should never play with dice, nor should one carry one's own sandals oneself;
one should not eat while reclining on a bed, nor with food held in the hand, nor while seated on a seat.

"Not with dice" means that one should never play with dice or similar objects, even in jest, except for the purpose of wagering. Because of the mention of "himself," he should not carry his own sandals to another place by means other than his feet, such as his hands. Furthermore, he should not eat while remaining on a bed or similar furniture. He should not eat by placing a large amount of food in his hand and consuming it all at once; nor should he eat while placing his eating vessel upon his seat. (4.74)
One should not eat anything mixed with sesame after the sun has set;
nor should one sleep here naked, nor go anywhere while still impure from food.

"Everything": whatever it may be, such as rice-pudding mixed with sesame or sweetmeats, he shall not eat after the sun has set. Deprived of a bed, a covering, and clothing, he shall not sleep in this world. Furthermore, being impure from food remnants, he shall not go elsewhere. (4.75)
One should eat with wet feet, but one should not go to bed with wet feet;
by eating with wet feet, one shall attain a long life. (4.76)
Regarding "with wet feet": one should take food with feet moistened by water; one should not sleep with wet feet. For by eating with wet feet, one becomes a hundred years old. 4.76.
One should never enter a difficult place that is beyond the range of sight;
one should not look at feces or urine, nor should one cross a river by means of one's arms.

"Out of the range of sight": one should not enter a difficult place such as a forest that is beyond the reach of the eye because it is dense with trees, shrubs, and creepers, for there may be hidden dangers such as snakes or thieves. One should not look at feces or urine. Nor should one cross a river by means of one's arms alone. 4.77.
One who desires to live a long life should not step upon hair, nor ashes, bones, or potsherds; nor should one step upon cotton seeds or husks. (4.78)
One should not step upon them. Desiring to live a long life, one should not tread upon hair and the like, nor upon potsherds—fragments of broken earthenware vessels. (4.78)

One should not dwell with those who have fallen from their caste, nor with Cāṇḍālas, nor with Pulkasas; nor with fools, nor with the arrogant, nor with outcasts, nor with those who live on the fringe of society. 4.79

"Let him not dwell together": he should not live in proximity even with those who have fallen from their caste (*patita*) and so forth, even if they reside in another village; that is, he should not stay near them under the shade of a single tree or in similar circumstances. This is distinct from the rule "let him not dwell in an unrighteous village" (4.60). A *pulkasa* is born from a *niṣāda* father and a *śūdra* mother; as the author will state: "Born from a *niṣāda* on a *śūdra* woman, one becomes a *pulkasa* by birth" (10.18). The *avaliptas* are those arrogant with pride due to wealth and other such things. The *antyās* are the outcastes (*antyajas*), such as washermen and others. The *antyāvasāyins* are those born from a *niṣāda* woman by a *caṇḍāla*; as the author will state: "A *niṣāda* woman [begets] from a *caṇḍāla* a son who is an *antyāvasāyin*" (10.39). || 4.79 ||
One should not give counsel to a Śūdra, nor his leavings, nor food prepared for a sacrifice;
one should not teach him the Dharma, nor prescribe a vow for him. (4.80)

"Not to a Śūdra": one should not give instruction on worldly matters (*mati*) to a Śūdra, because instruction on *dharma* is mentioned separately. One should not give the leavings of food (*ucchiṣṭa*) to a Śūdra who is not a slave; there is no fault in the case of a slave, since it will be stated later [in 10.125] that "food which is leavings should be given" with reference to slaves. And as for the rule for the eater, "one should feed him the leavings of the twice-born" (cf. 5.140), this applies to whatever may be obtained according to the circumstances, even though giving leavings to a giver is prohibited. Regarding "that which has been made into an oblation" (*haviṣkṛta*): that portion of an oblation of which a part has already been offered is a remnant of the oblation (*haviḥśeṣa*) and must not be given. Instruction on *dharma* should not be given to a Śūdra. Furthermore, one should not directly prescribe a vow (*vrata*) to him in the form of an expiation (*prāyaścitta*), but rather by interposing a Brāhmaṇa so that the instruction is mediated through him. As Aṅgiras says:
Likewise, having approached a Śūdra, one should always prescribe the penance while placing a Brāhmaṇa in between, with dharma as the primary guide.
The term "atonement" (prāyaścitta) is used as an illustration for the entire instruction on dharma. || 4.80 ||
For he who explains this dharma to him and he who likewise enjoins the vow—both sink together into that darkness called "the unrestrained" along with him. (4.81)

"Whoever [speaks to him]" means: because whoever explains the dharma to this Śūdra, and whoever instructs him in penance, enters along with that very Śūdra the dense darkness of hell known as *asaṃvṛta*. The mention of the fault regarding two out of the five previously mentioned cases is for the purpose of emphasizing the gravity of the penance. (4.81)
One should not scratch one's own head with both hands joined together;
nor should one touch it while impure from food, nor bathe without using water. 4.82.

"Not with both [hands] together": one should not scratch one's own head with two hands joined together. One who is impure (ucchiṣṭa) should not touch his own head. Regarding the head, one should not perform obligatory or occasional ritual bathing (*snāna*) except for immersion; however, there is no fault in washing the limbs other than the head when it serves a visible purpose. This prohibition applies to one who is capable of bathing; but for one who is incapable, Jābāli has indeed prescribed: "For those engaged in ritual acts, when bathing is impossible, the bath may be without the head. (4.82)
One should avoid seizing others by the hair and striking them on the head;
and having bathed one's head, one should not touch any part of the body with oil. (4.83)

"Regarding 'seizing by the hair': one should avoid seizing the hair or striking the head out of anger. Because these acts are caused by anger, they are forbidden for oneself as well as for others. For this very reason, there is no prohibition against a lover seizing the hair of his beloved during the time of sexual union. One should not touch even a single limb with oil after having bathed with the head still wet. Alternatively, the word "with oil" (*tailena*) is connected to both parts like the eye of a crow (i.e., it applies to both preceding and following clauses): one who has bathed the head with oil should not, moreover, touch even a single limb with oil. Therefore, it is not contradictory for cultured people (*śiṣṭas*) to practice anointing the feet with oil at night, provided they have not bathed their heads with oil. (4.83)
One should not accept gifts from a king who is not born of the Kṣatriya caste, nor from those who possess slaughterhouses, oil-presses, or taverns, nor from those who live by prostitution. (4.84)

"Not from a king": the word *rājanya* refers to a Kṣatriya. One should not accept wealth from a king who is not born of the Kṣatriya caste. Although it was stated, "One may seek wealth from a king" (4.33), this specific restriction is now declared. "From those with slaughterhouses, oil-presses, and taverns": from those possessing slaughterhouses (*sūnā*), oil-presses (*cakra*), and taverns (*dhvaja*). A slaughterhouse is a place for killing living beings; one who possesses such a place is a "slaughterhouse-owner," one who lives by selling meat after first slaughtering animals. An oil-press owner is an oil-miller who lives by crushing seeds. A tavern owner is a liquor-seller who lives by selling intoxicants. A "brothel" (*veśa*) is the wages of a prostitute; whoever lives by that—whether woman or man—is a "brothel-owner. From these as well, one should not accept gifts. (4.84)
A cart is equal to ten slaughterhouses; a banner is equal to ten carts;
a brothel is equal to ten banners; and a king is equal to ten brothels.

"Equal to ten slaughterhouses," etc. Govindarāja, however, reads "a king is equal to ten prostitutes. Medhātithi and other ancient authorities read "a king is equal to ten slaughterhouses. By words such as *sūnā* (slaughterhouse), that which possesses it is indicated. Whatever fault exists in those possessing ten slaughterhouses, that much fault exists in a single oil-presser (*tailika*) who is a sovereign; whatever fault exists in ten oil-pressers, that much fault exists in a single tavern-keeper (*śauṇḍika*) who has one flag (*dhvaja*); whatever fault exists in ten tavern-keepers, that much fault exists in a single brothel-keeper (*veśavat*); and whatever fault exists in ten brothel-keepers, that much fault exists in a single king. This series of progressively harsher censures is to be applied with due regard for the purpose of avoiding the latter when the former donor is available. (4.75)
A king is considered equal to a butcher who maintains ten thousand slaughterhouses; therefore, the acceptance of gifts from him is terrible. (4.86)

"Ten thousand slaughterhouses"—one who deals with a slaughterhouse is a *saunika* (butcher). Thus, by way of calculation, a king is declared by Manu and others to be equal to a butcher who slaughters ten thousand animals for his own sake. Therefore, accepting gifts from him is terrifying, because it is a cause for hell, even for a Kṣatriya. (4.86)
He who accepts gifts from a greedy king who acts contrary to the scriptures shall,
in due course, go to these twenty-one hells.

"Regarding 'he who [takes from] the king'": he who accepts gifts from a king who is wretched and acts in transgression of the scriptures goes, in due order, to these twenty-one hells that are about to be described. (4.87)
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Mahāraurava, Raurava, the hell Kālasūtra, and likewise Mahānaraka. 4.88
Saṃjīvana, Mahāvīci, Tapana, Saṃpratāpana,
Saṃhāta, Kākola, Kuḍmala, and Pratimūrtika.
The iron stake and the parched husks, the path and the Śālmalī river,
the forest of sword-leaves, and likewise the iron bristles.
The specific nature of these hells is described in detail in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa and other texts; it should be understood from those very sources. (4.88–90)
Knowing this, learned Brahmins who discourse on the Veda and desire the highest good after death do not accept gifts from a king. (4.91)

"Knowing this": knowing that the acceptance of gifts from a king is a cause for various hells, Brāhmaṇas—who are learned in the Dharmaśāstras, Purāṇas, and other texts, who are students of the Vedas, and who desire their own welfare in future births—should not accept gifts from a king. For there is no great fault in the acceptance of gifts by those who are [already] wise; as he will say later: "Therefore, the ignorant man should be afraid" (4.191). The mention of the "learned" and the mention of the "proponents of the Veda" (brahmavādin) are intended to show that even for them, the acceptance of gifts from a king is forbidden and results in abundant demerit. (4.91)
One should wake up during the *brāhma* hour and reflect upon dharma and artha, as well as the bodily afflictions rooted therein and the true meaning of the Vedas. (4.92)

Regarding the word *brāhma*: the *brāhma* moment (*muhūrta*) is the final watch of the night. The term *brāhmī* refers to the Goddess of Speech (*Bhāratī*), because she is the cause of awakening therein. Here, the word *muhūrta* denotes time in general; one should wake up during that period. Dakṣa also says: "One should spend the first and last watches of the night in the study of the Vedas; for by sleeping for only two watches, one becomes fit for union with Brahman."

By saying this, awakening at that time is permitted. Govindarāja, however, says: "One should awaken during the final watch of the night. One should determine how to practice virtue (*dharma*) and wealth (*artha*) so as not to let them conflict with one another. If there is great physical hardship for little virtue or wealth, then one should avoid that [effort]. At that time, through the illumination of the intellect, one should ascertain the true meaning of the Veda, which consists of the duties of Brahman. (4.92)
Having risen and performed the necessary duties, having purified himself and being composed,
he should stand for a long time reciting the prayers during the morning twilight, and likewise at its proper time during the evening twilight.

"Having risen": thus, having risen from bed at the time of dawn, and having discharged urine and feces when the urge arises, one who has performed the purification described hereafter should remain with undistracted mind, reciting the Gāyatrī for a long time during the morning twilight (pūrva-saṃdhyā) until the sun is seen. This rule has been stated regarding the morning twilight. This introductory statement is intended to prescribe that one should also recite [the mantra] after sunrise if one desires long life and other benefits. Likewise, having begun the evening twilight (aparā saṃdhyā) at its proper time, one should remain seated reciting it even after the appearance of the stars. 4.93.

Showing that this is the section concerning the desire for long life and so forth, he says: "Because of their long twilight [periods], the seers obtain long life, as well as wisdom, fame, renown, and spiritual luster. (4.94)

Regarding the word "sages" (*ṛṣayaḥ*): here the term *saṃdhyā* refers to the recitation (*japa*) and other rites to be performed at the junctions of time. Because sages, by performing the long-term *saṃdhyā*, live for a long life and attain wisdom, fame, and immortal glory—as well as renown endowed with learning and the like—therefore, one who desires long life and such benefits should worship the *saṃdhyā* for a long duration.

Having performed the ritual commencement according to the rules on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada, a Brahmin, being disciplined, should study the Vedas for four and a half months. (4.95)

"On the full moon of Śrāvaṇa": having performed the rite called *upākarma* on the full moon of either Śrāvaṇa or Bhādrapada according to his own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, a Brāhmaṇa should diligently study the Vedas for four and a half months. (4.95)
Under the Puṣya asterism, a twice-born man should perform the external ceremony of the suspension of Vedic study (utsarjana);
or he may do so on the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, during the forenoon.

Regarding the verse beginning with *puṣye tu*: Then, after four months and more than a fortnight have passed, on the day of the Puṣya asterism, he should go outside the village and perform the rite called *utsarga* according to his own *Gṛhya-sūtra*. Alternatively, he may perform it on the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha in the forenoon. And the rule for the bright fortnight of Māgha applies specifically to those who did not perform the *upākarma* on the full moon of Prauṣṭhapadī. 4.96.
Having thus performed the ritual dismissal of the Vedic meters outside according to the scriptures,
one should cease [recitation] for a "bird-night" (a night with its two flanking days), that is, for one full day and night.

"According to the scripture," however, means as follows: having performed the rite called *utsarga* (the ritual suspension of Vedic study) outside the village in accordance with the aforementioned scriptures, one should cease [studying] for a *pakṣiṇī* night—that is, one should not recite. A *pakṣiṇī* night is a middle night that has two days on either side like two wings (*pakṣau*). According to this view, one must not study on the day of the *utsarga* or on the second day, but one may study on the second night. Alternatively, one may observe that single *utsarga* day-and-night as a period of non-study. This rule regarding non-study for a day and night applies to one who desires excellence in learning. (4.97)
From this point forward, one who is self-restrained should recite the Vedic hymns during the bright fortnights, and one should study all the Vedāṅgas during the dark fortnights. (4.98)

"From this point forward": after the suspension of study, he should, being self-controlled, recite the Veda consisting of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas during the bright fortnights; however, he should recite all the Vedāṅgas, such as Phonetics (Śikṣā), Grammar (Vyākaraṇa), and so forth, during the dark fortnights. (4.98)
One should not study indistinctly, nor in the presence of Śūdras; having studied the Veda at the end of the night, one should not sleep again while still exhausted. (4.99)

"Not indistinctly" means that one should not study in the presence of a Śūdra, nor in a manner devoid of the clear manifestation of accents, phonemes, and so forth. Likewise, having risen from sleep during the final watch of the night and studied the Veda, one who is weary should not go back to sleep again. (4.99)
A twice-born man who is disciplined should always recite the Veda composed in meters according to the prescribed rule, except in times of distress. 4.100

Regarding the phrase "as stated": according to the prescribed rule, one should constantly recite only the *mantras* composed in meters—that is, those joined with meters such as *gāyatrī*—because *mantras* alone constitute the internal limb (*antaraṅga*) of ritual action. In the absence of an emergency, when the proper performance of rituals and so forth is possible, the twice-born (*dvija*), being disciplined, should recite the *brahman* (the *brāhmaṇa* texts) and the collection of *mantras* according to the stated rule. || 4.100 ||
One who is studying should always avoid these days of non-study, as should one who is teaching students according to the prescribed rule. (4.101)

"These" refers to these following occasions of non-study (*anadhyāya*); a teacher, while reciting in every way according to the prescribed rule and while engaged in teaching his pupils, should avoid them. (4.101)
When the wind is audible to the ear at night, and when there is a cloud of dust by day—
those who know the rules of study declare these two occasions during the rainy season to be times unfit for study.

Regarding the term *karṇaśrava*: when a wind blows at night that produces sounds audible to the ear, [it is an occasion for non-study]. Govindarāja, however, stated: "Since hearing occurs through the ears alone, the expression 'ear-hearing' (*karṇaśrava*) is used with the intention of emphasizing [this specific condition]; thus, it refers to when a wind blowing with excessive sound is present. And by day, when a wind capable of clearing away masses of dust is blowing, the sages who know the rules for the procedure of teaching declare these two times during the rainy season to be occasions for non-study (*anadhyāya*). || 4.102 ||
Manu has declared that when there is lightning, thunder, and rain, or when great meteors fall, there shall be a suspension of Vedic study for the remainder of the day. 4.103.

Regarding "lightning": when lightning, thunder, and rain occur simultaneously—as indicated by their mention as a pair—and when there is a falling of great meteors here and there, Manu has declared that for these occasions there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) for the duration of that time, beginning from the moment of the omen until the following day. (4.103)
One should know that when these [omens] appear while the sacred fires have been kindled, then one should recognize it as a time unfit for study; likewise, when clouds appear out of season.

"Regarding these": when one recognizes that these [phenomena], such as lightning and the rest, have arisen simultaneously during the twilight periods at the times when the fire has been made manifest for the purpose of the *homa* sacrifice, then one should observe a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) during the rainy season, but not at all times. Likewise, outside the rainy season, when the fire has been made manifest, there is a suspension of study upon the mere sight of clouds, but not during the rainy season. (4.105)
In the event of a thunderclap, an earthquake, or an eclipse of the heavenly bodies,
one should know these to be occasions for the suspension of study until the same time the following day, even during the proper season.

Regarding the term *nirghāta*: one should know that these following occasions for the suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) are "until the same time tomorrow" (*ākālika*) when there is the sound of portents occurring in the atmosphere, an earthquake, or an affliction of the sun, moon, and the host of stars. The meaning of the word *ākālika* has already been explained. The phrase "even during the [proper] season" is stated with the intention that, according to tradition, earthquakes and the like do not cause a defect during the rainy season; the word "even" (*api*) implies that this applies elsewhere as well. (4.105)

But when the fires have been kindled, if there is the sound of lightning and thunder, the suspension of study shall last as long as the light remains; for the remainder of the night, it is as [regulated] as during the day.

Regarding the phrase "when [the fires] have been made manifest": when the fires have been kindled for the purpose of the *homa* sacrifice, if at twilight there are only the sounds of lightning and thunder but no rain, then the suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) lasts as long as the light remains; it is not an untimely suspension. In that regard, if the sounds of lightning and thunder occur during the morning twilight, then the suspension lasts as long as the sun's light persists—that is, for the duration of the day alone. If those two should occur during the evening twilight, then the suspension lasts as long as the light of the stars persists—that is, for the duration of the night alone. As for the rule "during thunder, lightning, and rain at night," when the aforementioned triad—specifically the one called "rain"—has occurred, the suspension of study is the same at night as it is by day; the meaning is that it lasts for a full day and night. (4.106)
For those who desire proficiency in Dharma, there shall be a perpetual suspension of study in villages and cities, and in all cases where there is a foul odor. (4.107)

Regarding the phrase "constant suspension of study" (*nityānadhyāya*): for one who desires excellence in dharma, there should be a constant suspension of study in villages and towns, as these are spheres where proficiency [in worldly matters] prevails. Furthermore, when any foul odor is perceived, this instruction regarding the suspension of learning is intended for one who desires proficiency in dharma; it permits study at certain times for one who desires proficiency in knowledge (*vidyā*). Those disciples who, having already acquired the study of the Veda, desire the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) arising from that study are those who desire proficiency in dharma. Those who are first-time learners and seek merely the excellence of knowledge are those who desire proficiency in knowledge. (4.107)
There is no study when a corpse is inside a village, nor in the presence of a low-caste person (vṛṣala), nor while one is weeping, nor in a crowd of people. 4.108.

Regarding the word *antargata*: it refers to that village where a Śūdra person is known to reside. A *vṛṣala* is one who is unrighteous; the prohibition applies to his presence, not to a mere Śūdra, because of the prohibition [stated] at 4.99: "not in the presence of a Śūdra person. Regarding *rudyamāne*: this is a verbal form used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve lakāraḥ*). When there is a gathering of many people for the sake of some other business, there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*). 4.108.

While in water, at midnight, or when voiding excrement or urine, as well as when impure from food or having partaken in a *śrāddha* ceremony, one should not entertain even a thought [of reciting the Veda] in one's mind. (4.109)

Regarding the term "in water": this refers to being in the midst of water, at midnight, and during the four *muhūrta*s [of the night], based on the traditional teaching of Gautama: "And for four *muhūrta*s of the night" (GDh 16.44). Govindarāja, however, stated that it refers to the two middle watches of the night. Likewise, at the time of voiding urine or excrement, or when defiled by food and the like, one should not contemplate the Veda even mentally from the moment of the invitation until the end of the day and night of the *śrāddha* meal. (4.109)

Having accepted an invitation to an Ekoddiṣṭa rite, a learned twice-born man shall not recite the Veda for three days, nor during the impurity following the birth of a king or during an eclipse of Rāhu.

"Having accepted," etc.: that *śrāddha* at which only one person is designated is called an *ekoddiṣṭa*; having accepted the invitation (*ketana*) for such a new *śrāddha*, from the time of the invitation onward, one should not study the Veda for three nights during the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) of a Kṣatriya who is a ruler of a realm, nor during the "birth" of Rāhu, which is an eclipse of the moon or sun. 4.110.
As long as the fragrance and the smear of food offered to a single ancestor remain on the body of a learned Brahmin, so long should he not recite the Veda. 4.111

"Until"—that is to say, as long as the scent and the smear of even a single unconsecrated remnant of food, such as that containing saffron, remains on the body of a Brāhmaṇa who knows the scriptures, for so many days and nights thereafter he shall not study the Veda. (4.111)
One should not study while lying down, nor with one's feet raised, nor having crossed one's legs; nor after eating meat, nor food provided during a period of birth-impurity.

"Regarding the word 'lying down': one who has fallen limbs upon his bed, or whose feet have ascended to his seat, or who has assumed the cross-legged posture (paryaṅka), or who has eaten meat, or who has eaten the food of those impure due to birth or death—such a person shall not study. (4.112)
In mist, in the sound of arrows, and during both twilights;
on the new moon day, the fourteenth day, the full moon day, and the Aṣṭakā festivals. (4.113)

Regarding the word *nīhāra*: *nīhāra* refers to mist or dust; *vāṇa* refers to the sound of an arrow or an arrow-banner. Others say that *vāṇa* is a particular kind of lute. One should not study during the morning and evening twilights, nor on the new moon day, the fourteenth, the full moon, or the eighth lunar days. Since there is a prohibition regarding the *aṣṭakā* sacrifices later on, and because of its association with the full moon and other such dates, the word *aṣṭakā* here refers to the eighth lunar day (*tithi*). (4.113)
He states the specific fault:

"The new moon (amāvāsyā) kills the teacher; the fourteenth day (caturdaśī) kills the disciple; the Brahma-eighth (brahmāṣṭakā) and the full moon (paurṇamāsī) [do likewise]. Therefore, one should avoid them. (4.114)

Regarding the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*): since the new moon day destroys the teacher, the fourteenth day destroys the student, and both the eighth and full moon days cause one to forget the Veda, therefore one should avoid those [days] for study and teaching. (4.114)
A twice-born man should not recite while there is a rain of dust, when the quarters of the sky are ablaze, when jackals howl, or when dogs, donkeys, and camels are barking in a row.

Regarding the phrase "a rain of dust": when there is a rain of dust, when the quarters of the sky are ablaze, and when jackals, dogs, donkeys, and camels are howling, a Brahmin should not recite [the Veda] while sitting in a row—even though the subject under discussion refers specifically to jackals, dogs, donkeys, and so forth. (4.115)

One should not study at the edge of a cremation ground, at the edge of a village, or even in a cow-pen; nor after wearing a garment used for sexual intercourse, nor after accepting food offered at a śrāddha ceremony. (4.116)

"One should not study" means: one should not study near a cremation ground, near a village, or in a cow-pen; nor having put on a garment worn during sexual intercourse; nor having accepted food prepared for a *śrāddha* ceremony, such as cooked rice and other offerings. 4.116.

Whether it be animate or inanimate, whatever may be offered at a śrāddha ceremony, upon touching that, there is a suspension of study; for the twice-born is traditionally said to have his hand as his mouth. (4.117)

"Or [receiving] with the hand": it has been stated that there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) after eating food and the like at a *śrāddha* ceremony. Whether it be a living being, such as a cow or a horse, or a non-living thing, such as clothing or a garland, if one receives it by taking it with the hand at the time of acceptance, there is a suspension of study. For it is said in the *Smṛti*: "A Brāhmaṇa is indeed remembered as having his hand for a mouth (*pāṇyāsya*). (4.117)
When a village is harassed by thieves, during a disturbance caused by fire,
and in the case of all extraordinary portents, one should know that there is no study for the duration of the day.

"By thieves": one should know that when a village is harassed by thieves, when there is danger such as the burning of houses and so forth, or when extraordinary portents—celestial, atmospheric, or terrestrial—occur, there shall be a suspension of study for the remainder of the day. (4.118)
At the Upākarma and the Utsarga ceremonies, a suspension of study for three nights is prescribed;
at the Aṣṭakās, however, it is for one day and night, as well as on the nights marking the end of the seasons.

Regarding the *upākarma*: at both the *upākarma* and the *utsarga*, there is a suspension of study for three nights. At the *utsarga*, two *pakṣiṇī* days and nights have been declared as times of non-study; in that context, this instruction of three nights is intended for one who desires perfection in dharma. Likewise, after the *Agrahāyaṇī*, on the three or four eighth days (*aṣṭamī*) of the dark fortnight, there is non-study for a day and night. Even though the mere presence of the daytime period exists [on those other days], by the rule "and on the full moon and *aṣṭakā* days" (4.113), non-study lasts only until the eighth day itself; thus, on the other eighth days, it is not mentioned, and so there is no tautology. And there is non-study during the day and night at the end of the seasons. (4.119)

One should not study while mounted on a horse, nor on a tree, nor on an elephant; nor on a boat, nor on a donkey, nor on a camel; nor while standing on barren ground, nor while traveling in a vehicle. 4.120.

"One should not study": one mounted on a horse, a tree, an elephant, a boat, a donkey, or a camel; likewise, one standing in a saline or barren region (ūṣara), or traveling by means of a cart or other vehicle, should not study. 4.120.
Not during a dispute, nor in a quarrel, nor in an army, nor in battle;
not immediately after eating, nor while indigestion persists, nor after vomiting, nor when there is sour eructation. (4.121)

"Not during a dispute" means: during a verbal quarrel (*vāk-kahala*), during a physical fight involving punishment or non-punishment and the like, during an army where the elders have not yet assembled, during a battle (*saṃgara*), and after eating until the hands are still moist—according to the traditional teaching of Vasiṣṭha: "as long as the hands are moist" (VaDh 13.20). Likewise, one should not recite while food is undigested, nor after having vomited, nor when there is a sour belch. || 4.121 ||
Nor should one study after having failed to take leave of a guest, while a strong wind is blowing, when blood flows from the body, or when one is wounded by a weapon. (4.122)

Regarding the guest: as long as a guest has not been dismissed with the words "I am studying," one should not study; nor when the wind blows excessively, nor when blood flows from the body—even if there is no wound caused by a weapon, but merely a flow of blood—one should not study. (4.122)
One should never recite the *Ṛg* or *Yajur* Vedas while the sound of the *Sāman* is heard;
nor after having completed the study of the Veda, nor after having studied the *Āraṇyaka*. (4.123)

Regarding the phrase "in the sound of the Sāman": while the sound of the Sāman is being heard, one should not study the Ṛgveda or the Yajurveda at any time. Furthermore, having completed the Veda and studied the *Āraṇyaka*—which is a portion of the Veda—one should not study another Veda on that same day or night.
The Ṛgveda has the gods as its deities; the Yajurveda, however, belongs to humans;
the Sāmaveda is remembered as belonging to the ancestors; therefore, its sound is impure. (4.124)

Regarding the phrase "the Ṛgveda": when the chanting of the Sāmaveda is heard, a period of non-study (*anadhyāya*) for the Ṛgveda and Yajurveda has been prescribed; this [verse] is a restatement of that. The Ṛgveda is called *devadaivatya* because its deity is the gods themselves. The Yajurveda is called *mānuṣa* because it has humans as its deities, or because it generally teaches human rituals. The Sāmaveda is called *pitrya* because it has the ancestors as its deities; since they prescribe touching water after performing ancestral rites, its sound is as if impure, though not actually impure. Therefore, while it is being heard, one should not study the Ṛgveda or the Yajurveda. (4.124)
Knowing this, the wise daily practice the essence of the three Vedas in its proper sequence from the beginning, and only afterwards do they study the Veda itself. (4.125)

"Knowing this": knowing that these three Vedas have the gods, humans, and ancestors as their respective deities, those learned in the scriptures should first study, in due order, the *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *sāvitrī*—which constitute the extracted essence of the triple Veda—and only thereafter undertake the study of the Vedas themselves. Although this matter was already stated in the second chapter, it is mentioned again here in the section on forbidden days of study (*anadhyāya*) in order to show that there is no suspension of study when the *praṇava*, *vyāhṛtis*, and *sāvitrī* have not been recited, and to make known that teaching these to a pupil is itself a vow (*vrata*) of one who has completed his studies (*snātaka*). (4.125)
If cattle, frogs, cats, dogs, snakes, mongooses, or mice pass between [the teacher and the student], one should know that there is no study for a day and a night. (4.126)

Regarding the phrase "paśumaṇḍūka" (animals and frogs): "animals" refers to cows and the like; when a frog, a cat, a dog, a snake, a mongoose, or a rat passes between a teacher and his pupil, one should know that there is a suspension of study for a day and a night. (4.126)

Now, for the sake of one who desires proficiency in knowledge, he states the alternative rules regarding the aforementioned occasions when study is forbidden: "A twice-born man should always diligently avoid two things as unfit for study: a place of Vedic recitation that is impure, and himself when he is impure. (4.127)

"Only two": one should always avoid with great effort only these two occasions of non-study—the study-ground defiled by impurities such as food-remnants and the like, and oneself when devoid of the prescribed purification—but not the previously mentioned ones. One should also always avoid those [previously mentioned occasions] for which there is a mention of "always," a restatement, or an indicator of their obligatory nature; otherwise, there is an option. (4.127)
On the new moon day, the eighth, the full moon, and the fourteenth,
a twice-born Snātaka should always remain celibate, even during the fertile period.

"Regarding the phrase 'on the new moon' (amāvāsyām): on the new moon and other such days, even during the fertile season, a twice-born man who is a *snātaka* should not approach his wife. Although the prohibition is already established by the rule, ‘He may approach her except on the forbidden days’ (3.45), the repetition here serves the purpose of prescribing an expiation for the violation of the *snātaka*’s observances. (4.128)
One should not perform a bath after eating, nor when ill, nor at midnight; nor should one bathe constantly with clothes on, nor in a body of water that is unknown.

Regarding the phrase "not bathing": since obligatory daily bathing (*nityasnāna*) is not applicable immediately after eating, and since bathing necessitated by contact with *caṇḍālas* and the like cannot be prohibited—given the traditional teaching of Āpastamba, "One should not remain impure even for a moment when one has the capacity" (ĀpDh 1.15.8)—it is this voluntary bathing (*yadṛcchāsnāna*) that is forbidden here after a meal. Likewise, one who is ill should not perform even occasional bathing (*naimittikasnāna*), but rather according to his ability;
for those engaged in ritual acts, if bathing is impossible, the bath should be without the head, or they know that the purification of the body may be performed with a wet cloth.
Such passages from the Jābāla-Upaniṣad and other sources should be kept in mind. Likewise:
"The two middle watches of the night are to be known as Mahāniśā;
one should not perform a bath during that time, except for one that is optional (kāmya) or occasional (naimittika)."

According to this statement of Devala, one should not bathe there. Furthermore, one should never bathe while wearing many garments. However, when a specific occasion arises, such as contact with a *caṇḍāla* or others, bathing is not prohibited even for one wearing many garments; nor is it prohibited in the case of a body of water that is specifically unknown to be infested with crocodiles or the like, or where its depth cannot be discerned. (4.129)
One should not intentionally step upon the shadow of deities, a teacher, a king, a *snātaka*, an *ācārya*, a tawny man (*babhru*), or one who has been consecrated for a sacrifice. (4.130)

"Of deities" means of those made of stone and so forth; of the guru, such as one's father and others; of the king; and of the *snātaka* and the teacher (*ācārya*). Although the teacher is also a guru, he is mentioned separately with the intention of emphasizing his preeminence. "Of Babhru" means of the tawny-hued [Kapila]. At a sacrifice, one should not intentionally step on the shadow of one who has been initiated before the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha-snāna*). Because of the word "and" (*ca*), this also includes the shadows of *caṇḍālas* and others. Since it specifies "intentionally," there is no fault if it occurs unintentionally. (4.130)
At midday and at midnight, after eating a śrāddha meal containing meat,
and during both twilights, one should not frequent a crossroads.

"At midday": having eaten at a Śrāddha ceremony held at the exact midpoint of the day and night—that is, when two full watches have passed—one should not stand for long at a crossroads during the morning or evening twilights. (4.131)
One should not intentionally stand upon a used massage-powder, bath-water, feces, urine, blood, phlegm, spittle, or vomit. (4.132)

Regarding "udvartanam": *udvartana* refers to fragrant unguents, powders for removing dirt, pastes, and the like; *apasnāna* refers to bath-water, as well as urine, feces, blood, phlegm, spittle, and even substances in the form of excrement such as chewed and discarded betel-leaf; or vomit, and food that has been regurgitated after eating—one should not intentionally step upon these. "Adhiṣṭhāna" means standing upon them. (4.132)
One should not associate with an enemy, nor with the companion of an enemy, nor with one who is unrighteous, nor with a thief, nor with another's wife. (4.133)

"An enemy" means one should not serve an adversary, his minister, a person of unrighteous character, a thief, or another's wife. Although a thief is already included among the unrighteous, he is mentioned separately because he is extremely despicable. (4.133)
For there is nothing in this world so detrimental to long life as a man’s pursuit of another’s wife in this world. (4.134)
"Indeed, nothing is so [harmful]": because there is nothing in this world that is so detrimental to a man's longevity as approaching another's wife; therefore, this must not be done. (4.134)
One who desires prosperity should never, under any circumstances, despise a Kṣatriya, a serpent, or a learned Brāhmaṇa, even if they are weak. 4.135

Regarding the word *kṣatriya*: the root *bhū* is used here in the sense of "increasing. One who is *bhūṣṇu* or *vardhiṣṇu* is one whose nature is to increase through wealth, cattle, and so forth. One should not despise a *kṣatriya* serpent nor a highly learned (*bahuśruta*) Brahmin, even if they are emaciated and at that time incapable of retaliation. (4.135)
For these three, when treated with contempt, may utterly consume a man;
therefore, a wise person should never hold these three in contempt. (4.136)

"Regarding these three": when these three are treated with contempt, they bring destruction upon the one who treats them with contempt. The Kṣatriya and the serpent do so through their visible power, while the Brāhmaṇa does so through the unseen power of malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) and the like. Therefore, one of virtuous intent should never treat these three with contempt. (4.136)
One should not despise oneself on account of former failures; until death one should seek prosperity, nor should one consider it unattainable. (4.137)

"Nor [should one despise] oneself": when one has first made an effort for the sake of wealth, if that wealth is not attained, one should not despise oneself by thinking, "I am unfortunate. Rather, one should exert effort until death for the sake of attaining prosperity; one should not consider this [prosperity] to be impossible to obtain. (4.137)
One should speak the truth; one should speak what is pleasant; one should not speak a truth that is unpleasant; nor should one speak a pleasant falsehood—this is the eternal dharma. (4.138)

"One should speak the truth": one should speak the reality exactly as it has been seen and heard; likewise, one should speak what is pleasing, such as "a son has been born to you. One should not speak even what is true if it is unpleasant, such as "your son is dead," and so forth. Nor should one speak what is false even if it is pleasant. This is an eternal duty (dharma) because it is rooted in the Veda. 4.138
One should say "bhadraṃ bhadram" (well-being, well-being) or simply say "bhadram" (well-being); one should not engage in dry enmity or dispute with anyone. 4.139.

"May there be welfare" (*bhadram*). The first [instance of] *bhadra* refers to the word *pada*; the second refers to a synonym for the word *bhadra*. Whatever is "unfortunate" (*abhadra*), one should express that by means of a word synonymous with *bhadra*, such as "auspicious" (*praśasta*) and so forth. Thus says Āpastamba: "One should not call what is unfortunate 'unfortunate'; one should call it 'meritorious,' 'auspicious,' or simply 'welfare' (*bhadra*). Or rather, the word *bhadra* itself should be employed there. One should not engage in any dry, purposeless enmity or dispute with anyone. (4.139)
One should not travel too early, nor too late in the evening, nor when it is high noon;
one should not travel with an unknown person, nor alone, nor with outcasts.

"Not too early" means: one should not travel at dawn, at twilight, during the day, or during two full watches of the night, with a man whose family and character are unknown, nor with Śūdras. Although the prohibition "one should not set out on a journey alone" (4.30) has already been stated, this repeated prohibition against traveling alone is intended to emphasize the gravity of the penance required for violating the vows of a Snātaka. 4.141. One should not insult those who have missing limbs, those with redundant limbs, those deficient in learning, those advanced in age, those lacking beauty or wealth, or those of low birth.

"Those with deficient limbs": he does not revile those who have deficient or extra limbs, the ignorant, the elderly, the deformed, the indigent, or those of low birth by means of calling them "one-eyed," "deaf," and so forth. (4.141)
A Brahmin who is impure from eating should not touch with his hand a cow, a Brahmin, or fire;
nor, while remaining in a state of impurity, should he look at the hosts of luminaries in the sky when he is otherwise healthy.

"He should not touch" means that a Brāhmaṇa who has finished eating, or has voided urine or excrement and has not yet performed purification and ritual sipping (ācamana), should not touch cows, Brāhmaṇas, or fires with his hands or other limbs. Furthermore, being impure and not being ill, he should not look at the celestial luminaries such as the sun, moon, planets, and so forth. 4.142.
Having touched these while impure, one should always touch the vital breaths with water, as well as all the limbs and the navel with the palm of the hand. (4.143)

"Having touched these," etc.: having touched these [objects], such as cows and the like, while being impure, one who has performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) should touch with water held in his hand the vital breaths—the sense organs beginning with sight—the head, the shoulders, the knees, the feet, and the navel. This statement regarding the expiation (prāyaścitta) is made outside of the specific context for the sake of brevity; otherwise, within that context, it would have been necessary to include the mention of cows and the other objects as well.
Unless he is ill, he should not touch his own bodily apertures without a specific reason; he should avoid touching all the hairs of his private parts as well. (4.144)

"Without being ill": being free from illness, one should not, without cause, touch one's own cavities—the openings of the sense organs—nor the hairs of the private parts, the armpits, and other such areas that ought to be concealed. (4.144)
He should be devoted to auspicious conduct, self-restrained, and have his senses conquered;
he should constantly mutter prayers and offer oblations into the fire without weariness. (4.145)

"He should be endowed with auspicious conduct" (*maṅgalācārayuktaḥ*): *Maṅgala* (auspiciousness) is the accomplishment of one's desired goal; since it is the cause of that, wearing yellow orpiment (*gorocana*) and so forth is also *maṅgala*. *Ācāra* (conduct) refers to service to the guru and the like; he should be diligent in that. He should be possessed of external and internal purity and have his senses subdued. He should daily perform the recitation (*japa*) of the *Gāyatrī* and other mantras, as well as the prescribed fire-oblations (*homa*). "Unwearied" (*atandritaḥ*) means not lazy. Here, although conduct and the rest have already been mentioned, they are stated again for the purpose of preventing misfortune (*vinipāta*). (4.145)
Therefore he says:
"For those who are endowed with auspicious conduct, who are always self-restrained, and who recite prayers and offer oblations, no downfall exists. (4.146)

"For those endowed with auspicious conduct": for those who are constantly joined with auspicious practices, who are pure, and who delight in recitation and fire-offerings, no affliction from divine or human sources arises. (4.146)
One should constantly recite the Veda at the proper times without weariness; for they declare that to be his supreme duty, while any other is called a secondary duty. 4.147

"Only the Veda. At the time of performing obligatory duties, one should recite the Veda itself—the *praṇava*, *gāyatrī*, and so forth—without laziness, because Manu and others declare that to be the most excellent duty (*dharma*) of a Brāhmaṇa. Any other duty is said by the sages to be inferior to that. This repetition is intended to state that the aforementioned practice of Vedic study and the like is a cause for liberation by means of the recollection of previous births. (4.147)
By constant study of the Vedas, by purity, by austerity, and by non-injury toward living beings, one remembers one's former birth. (4.148)
"By the study of the Vedas": through constant study of the Vedas, purity, austerity, and non-violence, one remembers the birth of a previous existence. (4.148)
What follows from this? To this he says:
Recalling his former birth, he practices Brahman once again;
and through the constant practice of Brahman, he enjoys infinite bliss. (4.149)

"Former" means remembering his previous birth. The singular number in "birth" (*jāti*) is not intended to be significant because it is not required by the context; rather, remembering many births and, within those, even the sufferings of conception, birth, old age, and death, he becomes dispassionate toward *saṃsāra* and constantly practices Brahman alone through hearing, reflection, and meditation, thereby realizing it directly. Through that, he attains the bliss of liberation, characterized by the manifestation of infinite, indestructible supreme bliss. (4.149)
He should constantly perform the Sāvitra oblations and the propitiatory fire-sacrifices on the Parvan days;
and he should always worship the ancestors on the Aṣṭakā days and the Anvaṣṭakā days. (4.150)

Regarding the phrase "sāvitrān": one should always perform oblations dedicated to the deity Savitṛ and peace-offerings (*śānti-homa*) on the full moon and new moon days for the purpose of averting misfortune. Likewise, after the Āgrahāyaṇī festival, on the three eighth days of the dark fortnight, one should worship the ancestors who have gone to the other world with the rite known as Aṣṭakā and with a *śrāddha* feast; and on the ninth days of the dark fortnights intervening between those, one should worship them with the rite known as Anvaṣṭakā. (4.150)
One should discharge urine far from one's dwelling, far from the water used for washing the feet, and far indeed from where the remains of food have been poured out. (4.151)

"From afar from the dwelling"— meaning beyond the range of an arrow-shot (iṣuvikṣepa) in the southwest direction, and even further from the ground— according to such a statement from the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*, one should discharge urine, feces, the washing of feet, and all food remnants from a distance from the fire-chamber; and one should also emit semen [in that same manner].
One should perform the preparation of unguents, bathing, cleaning the teeth, applying collyrium, and the worship of the deities during the forenoon alone. (4.152)

Regarding the term *maitram*: because its presiding deity is Mitra (*mitradevatākatvāt*), it is called *maitra*; since the anus belongs to that [deity], the voiding of excrement is also *maitra*. Likewise, one should perform the adornment of the body—such as the morning bath, brushing the teeth, applying collyrium, and worshipping the deities—only during the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*). By the word "forenoon," both the remainder of the night and the first part of the day are intended here. Furthermore, since this [text] is intent upon enjoining the mere performance of the ritual acts, the order of the recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) need not be strictly observed; for indeed, the brushing of teeth does not necessarily follow immediately after the bath. (4.152)
On the sacred festival days (parvan), he should visit the deities, righteous and most excellent brahmins, the Lord for the sake of protection, and his gurus. 4.153.

Regarding the phrase "the deities": one should go out to face them on festival days such as the new moon (amāvāsyā) to behold the deities made of stone and other materials, Brahmins preeminent in dharma for the sake of protection, and elders such as one's father and others. 4.153.
He should salute his elders and offer them his own seat;
he should sit near them with palms joined in reverence and follow behind them as they depart. (4.154)

"One should salute": one should salute those who have come to the house as teachers. One should also offer them a seat to sit upon. One should remain near the teacher with palms joined in reverence (*añjali*). And when they depart, one should follow behind them. Although this conduct beginning with salutation has already been mentioned, it is stated again here for the purpose of declaring its rewards. (4.154)
One should, unwearied, always practice the conduct of the virtuous, which is the root of dharma, properly prescribed for one's own duties as declared in the Śruti and Smṛti. (4.155)

"Proclaimed by Śruti and Smṛti": this is a general instruction for the performance of conduct, intended to state its fruit—that one who is not indolent should thoroughly practice the conduct of the virtuous, which is the cause of Dharma, properly declared by the Vedas and Smṛtis, and connected as an auxiliary to one's own duties such as Vedic study. 4.155.
For through right conduct one obtains long life; through right conduct, desired offspring;
through right conduct, inexhaustible wealth; and right conduct destroys inauspicious marks. (4.156)

"From conduct": through conduct one obtains the lifespan declared in the Vedas, as well as desired offspring—consisting of sons, grandsons, and daughters—and prosperity in the form of wealth; furthermore, by means of the dharma known as conduct, one renders fruitless the bodily inauspicious marks that indicate evil results, because such conduct destroys the misfortunes (ariṣṭa) signaled by those inauspicious marks. (4.156)
For a man of evil conduct is censured in the world;
he constantly shares in suffering, being diseased and short-lived. (4.157)

"Because of bad conduct," it is said. Since a man of bad conduct would be censured in the world, and would always be beset by suffering, afflicted by disease, and short-lived, one should therefore be endowed with good conduct. (4.157)
Even if he lacks all auspicious marks, the man who possesses good conduct, who is full of faith and free from malice, lives for a hundred years. (4.158)

"Even one devoid of all auspicious marks": he who possesses good conduct, is endowed with faith, and does not speak of the faults of others, becomes a hundred years old even if he lacks the marks that indicate prosperity. || 4.158 ||
Whatever action is dependent on others, that one should avoid with effort;
but whatever is within one's own control, that one should practice diligently. (4.159)

"Whatever is directed outward": whatever action is dependent on others, to be accomplished through requesting others and so forth, that one should avoid with effort. Whatever is to be accomplished through the activity of one's own body, such as the grasping of the Supreme Self and so forth, that one should perform with effort. (4.159)
He states the reason for this:
"Everything dependent on another is suffering; everything dependent on oneself is happiness.
One should know this, in brief, to be the defining characteristic of happiness and suffering. (4.160)

"Everything is under the control of another": everything that is accomplished through the requests of others and so forth is a cause of suffering; everything dependent on oneself is a cause of happiness. One should understand this to be the cause of happiness and suffering. (4.160)
Whatever action brings satisfaction to one's inner self while performing it, that one should perform with diligence; but one should avoid the opposite. (4.161)

"Whatever action while performing... means that whatever action brings satisfaction to the inner self (*antarātman*) of this person who performs it—that should be diligently practiced; one should avoid that which causes dissatisfaction. And this refers to the domain of actions neither enjoined nor prohibited, as well as to matters of optional alternatives. (4.161)
One must not harm one's teacher, a lecturer, a father, a mother, a guru, Brāhmaṇas, cows, or any ascetics whatsoever. (4.162)

"And the teacher" (*ācāryam*): the *ācārya* is one who teaches the Veda preceded by the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*); the *pravaktṛ* is the expounder of the meaning of the Veda; and the *guru* is as described in [verse] 2.149: "He from whom [one has received] little or much... One must not harm the teacher and the others. Here, the word "harm" (*hiṃsā*) refers to acting in opposition to them.
