Govindarāja, however, has explained that because there is a general prohibition against harming, one should not harm even these persons if they are aggressors (*ātatāyin*). That is incorrect, because it contradicts [the rule]: "Whether it be a teacher, a child, or an elder" (8.350). 4.162.
One should avoid atheism, reviling the Vedas, and disparaging the deities; one should also avoid hatred, hypocrisy, pride, anger, and harshness. (4.163)

Regarding "atheism" (nāstikya): one should abandon the notion that there is no other world, the reviling of the Vedas and the deities, as well as envy, lack of enthusiasm for dharma, pride, anger, and cruelty. (4.163)
One should not raise a staff against another, nor should one strike down in anger; except for a pupil or a son, whom one may strike for the sake of discipline. (4.164)

"Regarding 'the rod for another': being angry for the sake of killing another, one should not lift up a stick or similar weapon, nor should one let it fall upon the body of another—except in the case of a son, a pupil, a wife, a slave, and so forth. For these who have committed an offense, one may strike them for the purpose of instruction in the manner to be described later, such as "with a rope or a split bamboo cane" (8.299). || 4.164 ||
A twice-born man who merely threatens a Brahmin with the intent to kill him shall wander for a hundred years in the Tāmisra hell. (4.165)

Regarding the phrase "for a Brāhmaṇa": even a twice-born man, by merely raising a staff or other weapon for the purpose of killing a Brāhmaṇa—but not actually striking him—wanders for a hundred years through the Tāmisra and other hells. (4.165)
Having intentionally struck [another] even with a blade of grass out of anger, one is born for twenty-one lifetimes in the wombs of the wicked. (4.166)

"Even by striking with a blade of grass": having intentionally struck a Brāhmaṇa out of anger even with a blade of grass, one is born for twenty-one lifetimes in evil wombs, such as the womb of a dog and so forth. (4.166)
By causing blood to flow from the body of a Brahmin who is not fighting, a man, through his lack of wisdom, incurs very great suffering after death. (4.167)

Regarding the phrase "of one not fighting": by causing blood to flow on the body of a Brāhmaṇa who is not fighting, due to ignorance of the scriptures, one incurs great suffering in the next world. (4.167)
For as many particles of dust as the blood gathers from the surface of the earth, for that many years shall the shedder of that blood be devoured by others in the next world. (4.168)

Regarding "blood": for as many particles of dust as the blood—issuing from the body of a Brahmin woman struck by a sword or similar weapon and fallen upon the ground—forms into aggregates, for that many years shall the assailant who produced that blood be devoured by other creatures such as dogs and jackals in the next world. (4.168)
Therefore, a learned man should never even threaten a twice-born person;
he should not strike him even with a blade of grass, nor should he cause blood to flow from his body. (4.169)

"Never at any time. Therefore, one who is aware of the faults such as threatening and so forth should not, even in times of distress, perform the raising of a staff or the like against a Brāhmaṇa, nor the striking down [of it], nor the shedding of blood; this is the summary of the three aforementioned actions. (4.170)
For that man who is unrighteous, whose wealth is based on falsehood, and who is constantly devoted to violence—such a person does not prosper in happiness in this world. (4.170)

"Unrighteous" (*adhārmika*) means one who acts contrary to *dharma*; that is, a human being who practices what is forbidden by the scriptures, such as approaching women who should not be approached, and for whom false testimony or deception is the very means of acquiring wealth—lying while taking bribes—and who is devoted to harming others. Such a person does not live endowed with happiness in this world. Therefore, through this censure, a prohibition is inferred: "This must not be done. (4.170)

Even when suffering on account of righteousness, one should not turn the mind toward unrighteousness, seeing quickly the reversal of fortune that befalls the wicked who act contrary to dharma. (4.171)

"Even when suffering" means: even if one should suffer due to the lack of wealth and other resources while practicing what is prescribed by the scriptures, one should never set one's mind upon unrighteousness (*adharma*). For although those who practice unrighteousness may at first sight appear to possess wealth and other forms of prosperity, nevertheless, for those unrighteous sinners who engage in practices such as theft and the like, and who are burdened by the evil resulting from those acts, a loss of wealth and so forth is soon observed. Seeing this, one should not apply the intellect to unrighteousness; thus, for the benefit of his disciples, he has shown this empirical fact. (4.171)
Unrighteousness practiced in this world does not bear fruit immediately like a cow;
but returning slowly, it cuts away the very roots of the doer. (4.172)

"Adharma does not [bear fruit immediately]. Because the time of maturation for auspicious and inauspicious actions is not fixed by the scriptures, adharma does not bear fruit at that very moment for one who practices it, like a cow. In this context, regarding the "earth" (bhūmi), there is an example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*): just as the earth, merely having seeds sown in it, does not become laden with clusters of abundant, ripe grain at that very moment, but rather awaits the specific time for the ripening of the fruit. Regarding the "cow" (go), there is an example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*): just as a cow or a beast yields fruit immediately through carrying or milking, so it is not with adharma; rather, proceeding gradually and becoming ready to yield its fruit, it cuts away the roots of the perpetrator of adharma. By the cutting of the root, total destruction is indicated: he perishes, deprived of his body, wealth, and so forth. (4.172)
If it does not bear fruit for oneself, nor for one's sons, nor even for one's grandsons, nevertheless, dharma performed never becomes fruitless for the doer. (4.173)

Regarding the word "yadi" (if): if [the act] does not produce a result consisting of the destruction of the body, wealth, and so forth for the agent himself, then it produces it for his sons; if not, it produces it for his grandsons; but it never becomes fruitless. Now, one might ask: how can an action performed by one person produce a result in another? It is said in reply: since the destruction of sons and others causes distress to the father, and because this matter is based on scripture (*śāstra*), there should be no lack of conviction. (4.173)
One prospers by unrighteousness for a time, and thereafter sees auspicious results;
then one conquers one's rivals, but finally perishes along with one's very roots. (4.174)

"By unrighteousness" means that through unrighteousness—such as malice toward others—one first prospers with villages, wealth, and so forth; then one acquires auspicious things such as many servants, cattle, and horses; thereafter, one conquers enemies who are inferior to oneself; and finally, after some time, by the power of the ripening of that unrighteousness, one perishes together with one's body, wealth, sons, and the like. (4.174)
One should always take delight in truth, righteousness, noble conduct, and purity; and one should instruct disciples in accordance with dharma, restraining speech, arms, and belly. (4.175)

"Regarding truth, dharma, and noble conduct": one should always take delight in truth, dharma, right behavior, and purity. Furthermore, one should instruct those under one's authority—wives, sons, slaves, and students—and discipline them in the manner prescribed [in verse 8.299]: "with a rope or with a split bamboo cane. Although these have already been mentioned, they are stated again for the sake of emphasis: one should be restrained in speech, arms, and stomach. Restraint of speech is speaking the truth. Restraint of the arms is not causing pain to anyone by the strength of one's arms. Restraint of the stomach is eating little, only as much as is obtained. (4.175)
One should abandon wealth and pleasure if they are devoid of righteousness, and one should also abandon righteousness if it results in future suffering and is censured by the world. (4.176)

"One should abandon" means that one should avoid those things which are wealth and pleasure when they conflict with Dharma. For example, the acquisition of wealth through theft and the like; or the approach of a sacrificer’s wife during the initiation ceremony and so forth. Regarding the "future consequence" (*udarka*), which refers to a subsequent time—one should abandon even that Dharma where there is unhappiness in that regard, such as the giving away of all one's possessions by one who has dependents to support, such as sons and others. Regarding "condemned by the world," this refers to where there is public outcry among people, such as the killing of cows and the like during the *madhyamāṣṭakā* and other rites in the Kali age. (4.176)
One should not be fickle with hands or feet, nor fickle with the eyes, nor crooked; one should likewise not be fickle with speech, nor have a mind intent on deeds that harm others. (4.177)

"Not fickle with hands or feet": one should abandon fickleness of the hands and so forth. Fickleness of the hands consists in grasping things that are not needed; fickleness of the feet consists in wandering about without purpose; fickleness of the eyes consists in gazing at the wives of others and the like; fickleness of speech consists in speaking many censurable things. One should not be "crooked," meaning devious. One should not form an intention or make an effort for the sake of harming others or doing them injury. (4.177)
By that path by which his fathers have gone, by which his grandfathers have gone—by that path of the virtuous he should go; going by that way, he does not come to harm. (4.178)

Regarding the word "by which": when multiple interpretations of the meaning of the scriptures are possible, one should practice only that scriptural meaning which was practiced by one's father, grandfather, and so forth. By proceeding in this way, one does not come to harm; that is, one is not injured by unrighteousness (adharma). (4.178)

With officiating priests, family priests, and teachers; with maternal uncles, guests, and dependents; with children, the elderly, and the sick; and with physicians, kinsmen, relatives, and friends. (4.179)
One should not engage in dispute with one's mother or father, sisters, brother, son, wife, daughter, or the group of servants. (4.180)

The term *ṛtvij* (sacrificial priest) refers to two [categories]. One should not engage in idle chatter with the *ṛtvij*s and others. A *purohita* is one who performs rites for peace (*śānti*) and so forth. *Saṃśritas* are dependents who live off others. *Jñātis* are those on the father’s side. *Saṃbandhins* are those such as sons-in-law and brothers-in-law. *Bāndhavas* are those on the mother’s side. *Jāmis* are sisters, daughters-in-law, and so forth. (4.179–180)
By abandoning disputes concerning these, one is liberated from all sins;
and by conquering these, a householder conquers all these worlds. (4.181)

"By these": by abandoning disputes with these [persons], such as officiating priests and others, one is liberated from unknown sins. Likewise, by disregarding these disputes, the householder conquers these worlds that are about to be described. 4.181.

The teacher is the lord of the world of Brahmā; the father is the master in the world of Prajāpati; the guest is the lord of Indra’s world; and the officiating priests are the lords of the world of the gods. (4.182)

Regarding the term "teacher" (*ācārya*): the teacher is the lord of the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*). By abandoning dispute with him and by pleasing him, one attains the world of Brahmā; thus, his status as the lord of the world of Brahmā is figurative (*gauṇa*). Likewise, the father is the lord of the world of Prajāpati (*prājāpatya-loka*), and the guest is the lord of Indra’s world (*indraloka*). The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are the lords of the world of the gods (*devaloka*). In this manner, the lordship over each respective world should be understood for those mentioned hereafter as well. (4.182)

Sisters-in-law are the kinsmen of the world of the Apsarases; maternal uncles and mothers are the kinsmen of the world of Vaiśvadeva; and relatives by marriage are the kinsmen of the world of the Waters on earth. (4.183)

Regarding "sisters-in-law": sisters-in-law prevail in the world of the Apsarases; kinsmen in the world of the Viśvedevas; relatives by marriage in the world of Varuṇa; and the mother and maternal uncle in the world of Bhūr. (4.183)
Children, the elderly, the emaciated, and the sick should be known as lords over space;
an elder brother is equal to a father, and one's wife and son are one's own body. (4.184)

"But those who are dependent on others," it is said: one who is emaciated, one whose wealth is meager, one who is dependent, and one who is desirous of speaking [are included]. Children, the elderly, dependents, and the sick prevail in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Furthermore, the elder brother is equal to a father; therefore, he too is a lord over the world of Prajāpati. Wife and son are indeed one's own body; how, then, can a dispute with oneself be possible? (4.184)
One's own shadow, one's circle of servants, and a daughter are the utmost objects of pity; therefore, one should always endure being reviled by them without any feverish resentment.

"Shadow": because his own group of servants follows him constantly, they are like his own shadow and are not fit for dispute. Furthermore, a daughter is the supreme object of compassion. Therefore, being reviled by these, he should endure it without resentment, but must not engage in a quarrel. 4.185.
Even if he is capable of receiving gifts, he should avoid attachment to them;
for by accepting gifts, his spiritual luster (brāhmaṃ tejaḥ) is quickly extinguished. (4.186)

"Even though he is capable of receiving gifts": although he is qualified for receiving gifts by virtue of being endowed with learning, austerity, and good conduct, he should nevertheless abandon repeated engagement in them; for through the acceptance of gifts, his spiritual power—derived from causes such as the study of the Vedas—is destroyed very quickly. Although it was stated [in verse 4.3] "for the sake of accomplishing mere subsistence," which generally restricts the means of acquisition, this statement is made specifically to declare that the result of accepting gifts is the neutralization of one's Brahmanic power. 4.186.
Without knowing the righteous rules for the acceptance of gifts, a wise man should not accept them, even if he is perishing from hunger. (4.187)

"Not [accepting] liquids" means that regarding the acceptance of substances, even if he is suffering from hunger, a wise man should not accept them without knowing the rules for what is beneficial for dharma—such as the mantras for accepting the deity of the gift—and how much less so when there is no distress.
But an ignorant man who accepts gold, land, a horse, a cow, food, clothing, sesame seeds, or clarified butter is reduced to ashes like a piece of wood. (4.188)

"Gold," etc.: one who, having fallen away from the study of the revealed scriptures (*śruta-svādhyāya*), accepts gold and other such things, becomes reduced to ashes like wood through contact with fire and does not obtain rebirth. (4.188)
Gold bestows longevity and food; land, cattle, and offspring;
a horse, sight; clothing, skin; clarified butter, splendor; and sesame seeds, progeny. (4.189)

"Gold"—this refers to the earth and the cow which burn (consume) the body of an ignorant recipient. The root *uṣ* meaning "to burn" belongs to the Bhūvādigaṇa; this is its form. The dual number is used for "earth and cow" because two items are intended to be expressed. In the same way, gold and food consume life-span (*āyus*). In the cases of "the horse [consumes] the eye," and so forth, by changing the case ending, the singular form "it consumes" (*oṣati*) is supplied as an ellipsis.
But that twice-born man who is without self-restraint, who does not study, and who delights in accepting gifts, sinks along with him—just as one would sink with a stone raft in the water. (4.190)

"But the one who is not ascetic" (atapāḥ): that Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of austerity and knowledge and is desirous of receiving gifts sinks into hell together with the giver himself—who is joined with the sin of accepting what is unworthy—by virtue of that very [desire for gifts] which is inseparable from receiving and which is present in his mind; just as one crossing water by means of a boat made of stone sinks into the water along with that very boat. 4.190.
Therefore, an ignorant man should fear whatever gift he may receive; for even by means of a very small thing, the ignorant man sinks like a cow in the mud. (4.191)

"Therefore, [one should consider oneself] 'unlearned'": because even by accepting a small amount of wealth, a fool becomes submerged in hell like a cow in the mud; therefore, one should shrink from accepting anything whatsoever, even base materials such as lead and the like, other than gold and so forth. 4.191.
Having explained the duty regarding the recipient, he now speaks concerning the giver:

"A knower of the Dharma should not give even water to a twice-born man who observes the 'vow of a cat,' nor to a Brahmin who observes the 'vow of a heron,' nor to one who is ignorant of the Veda. (4.192)

“Nor even water”: by the hyperbolic statement that one who knows the Dharma should not give even that which is given to crows and the like—referring to those who act like cats—one prohibits the giving of other substances, but not the giving of water itself. By the verse “Heretics and those engaged in improper acts” (4.30), the giving of wealth and so forth after honoring them as guests is prohibited for those who act like cats; here, however, the giving of wealth is prohibited. For this very reason, he will say later: “Even wealth acquired according to rule” (4.193). “One who does not know the Veda” means one who is ignorant of the meaning of the Vedas. And this prohibition against one who does not know the Veda applies when a learned person is available. (4.192)
For wealth, even if acquired according to the rules, when given to these three types of persons, leads to misfortune for both the giver and the recipient in the next world. (4.193)

"In all three" means that in these three cases—beginning with those who follow the "vow of the cat"—wealth, even if acquired through lawful means, becomes a source of harm to both the giver and the recipient because it causes rebirth in hell in the next world. (4.193)
Just as one who attempts to cross water with a boat made of stone sinks, so too do the ignorant donor and recipient sink to the depths. 4.194

"Like with a raft": just as one crossing on water by means of a boat made of stone or similar material sinks down along with it, so too do the giver and the recipient—who are ignorant of the scriptures concerning giving and receiving—go to hell. The censure stated in the verse "But one who does not practice austerity and does not study" (4.190) was expressed primarily with respect to the recipient; here, however, it is expressed primarily with respect to the giver, and thus there is no tautology. (4.194)
One who carries the banner of the Dharma while being always greedy, hypocritical, and a deceiver of the world;
one who follows the "cat-vow," is violent, and deceives everyone—such a person should be known as a *baiḍālavratika*. (4.195)

"Flag-bearer of Dharma" (*dharmadhvajī*): one who practices the Dharma in the presence of many people and proclaims it to himself and others in the world; his Dharma is like a flag or a banner, hence he is a "flag-bearer of Dharma. "Greedy" (*lubdha*) means desirous of another's wealth. "Deceitful" (*chādmika*) means one who acts through fraud or pretext. "A deceiver of the world" (*lokadambhaka*) is one who cheats people by misappropriating deposits and so forth. "Violent" (*hiṃsra*) means one whose nature is to harm others. "A detractor of all" (*sarvābhisandhaka*) means one who casts aspersions on everyone due to an inability to tolerate the virtues of others. "One who acts with the conduct of a cat" (*baiḍālavratika*): for a cat generally remains humble and fixed in meditation-like stillness out of a fondness for harming mice and other creatures; thus, the term "cat-conduct" is used figuratively. (4.195)
A twice-born man who looks downward, who is cruel, intent on achieving his own ends, deceitful, and falsely humble, is one who practices the "heron-vow. (4.196)

"Adhidṛṣṭi" means downward-looking; he constantly gazes down to proclaim his own humility. "Niṣkṛti" means cruelty; one who acts with that is "naiṣkṛtika. One intent on achieving his own ends by destroying the interests of others is "śaṭha," meaning crooked. "Mithyāvinīta" means possessing hypocritical humility. One who practices the "vow of the heron" (bakavrata) is a "bakavratacara. For a heron, generally having a delight in killing fish, becomes of such a character while appearing hypocritically humble; thus, the term "bakavrata" is used figuratively. 4.196.
Those Brahmins who practice the vow of the heron and those who bear the marks of a cat fall into the Andhatāmisra hell because of that sinful action.

"Those who practice the vow of the heron": those who observe the vow of the heron or the vow of the cat, those Brahmins fall by reason of that sinful cause, through that action, into the hell named Andhatāmisra. 4.197.
One should not perform a vow after committing a sin under the pretext of dharma;
by concealing a sin with a vow, one merely practices deception upon women and Śūdras. (4.198)

"Not for the sake of dharma": having committed a sin, one might perform a penance in the form of a vow such as the *prājāpatya* and so forth, thinking that it removes the sin; but this is not true penance. Rather, one should not perform it while deceiving women, Śūdras, fools, and others by saying, "I am performing this for the sake of dharma. (4.198)
Such Brahmins, both in this world and after death, are censured by those who discourse on the Veda; and any vow practiced through hypocrisy goes to the Rākṣasas. (4.199)
He who, being without the marks, subsists by the livelihood of one wearing the marks, takes upon himself the sin of those who wear the marks and is born among the animals. (4.200)

The two verses beginning with *pretya* and *iha* are easy to understand. First, regarding the first verse: a Brahmin who is not a student (*abrahmacārī*)—that is, one characterized by the outward signs of studentship such as the girdle, deerskin, staff, and so forth, yet lives by their mode of life, such as wandering for alms—takes upon himself whatever sin belongs to those who are true students and the like, and he is reborn among the animal species, such as dogs. Therefore, the prohibition is inferred that "this must not be done. (4.199–200)
One should never bathe in water reservoirs belonging to others; for by bathing there, one becomes tainted by a portion of the misdeeds of the person who constructed the reservoir. (4.201)

Regarding the term *parakīyā*: a *nipāna* is a reservoir of water. One should never bathe in lotus ponds (*puṣkariṇī*) and the like constructed by others. By bathing there, one becomes connected with a portion of the sin of the maker of that pond and so forth—a portion consisting of the fourth part which will be described below. In the absence of natural rivers and such, even in a pond made by another, one should bathe only after first removing five lumps of earth (*piṇḍa*). As Yājñavalkya says (1.159): "One should not bathe in the waters of another without having removed five lumps of earth;
having removed four lumps, one may perform the bath in what belongs to another."
And having bathed, he should offer libations especially to the gods and the ancestors.
One who makes use of another's vehicles, beds, seats, wells, gardens, or houses without them being given incurs a fourth part of the sin. (4.202)

Regarding the phrase "vehicle, bed, etc.": the word "this" (asya) refers back to the subject under discussion. One who makes use of another's vehicles and so forth without they being given becomes a partaker of a fourth part of that person's demerit. By the term "without being given," the absence of the other's consent is intended. Consequently, there is no contradiction in using things like monasteries or wells that have been relinquished for the sake of all, or in using them for one's own bathing and such purposes. (4.202)
One should always perform one's bath in rivers, in natural pools dug by the gods, in tanks, in lakes, and also in pits and springs. (4.203)

Regarding the phrase "in rivers": one should always perform bathing in rivers and similar bodies of water. The term "renowned as divine" (*devakhyāteṣu*) is an adjective qualifying ponds (*taḍāga*). It refers to lakes or pools well-known for their association with the gods, which are less than eight thousand *dhanus* in extent. As it is stated in the *Candogapariśiṣṭa*: "Those whose course does not extend for eight thousand *dhanus*, they do not bear the name 'river'; they are proclaimed to be mere pits (*gartas*)."

A bow measures four cubits. Since the prohibition against using another's water-troughs is already established by this very rule regarding springs and cascades, the separate mention of them is for the purpose of permitting bathing and other such acts in one's own abandoned ponds and the like; furthermore, that permission should be understood to apply only when rivers and other sources of water are unavailable. (4.203)
A wise person should constantly practice the restraints (yamas), but not exclusively the observances (niyamas);
for one who fails to perform the restraints while devoting oneself solely to the observances falls. (4.204)

Regarding the term *yamān*: this is intended to indicate the gravity of the practice of the *yamas* in comparison with the *niyamas*, and not for the purpose of prohibiting the *niyamas*, since both constitute the subject matter of the scripture. The distinction between *yama* and *niyama* was made by the sages themselves. Thus Yājñavalkya (3.312–13) says:
"Celibacy, compassion, patience, meditation, truthfulness, sincerity, non-violence, non-stealing, gentleness, and self-restraint—these are recorded as the *yamas*."
Bathing, silence, fasting, sacrifice, Vedic study, restraint of the generative organ,
service to the teacher, purity, freedom from anger, and vigilance constitute *niyama*.

One who knows the true nature of *yama* and *niyama* should practice *yama*—consisting of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and so forth—even by abandoning all *niyamas* such as ritual bathing. For even while practicing the *niyamas*, one falls [from grace] if devoid of the practice of *yama*; thus, this section begins for the purpose of praising *yama*. Medhātithi and Govindarāja, however, explain that the *yamās* are prohibitions against violence and the like, whereas the *niyamas* are forms of observances such as "one should constantly recite the Veda" (4.147). Non-violence, truthful speech, celibacy, freedom from guile, and non-stealing—these five are indeed proclaimed as the *yamās*.
Absence of anger, service to the teacher, purity, moderation in food,
and constant vigilance— these five are recorded as the observances (niyamas).
A Brāhmaṇa should never eat at a sacrifice performed by one who is not learned in the Vedas, nor at one performed by a priest for an entire village, nor at one offered by a woman or a eunuch. (4.205)

"Not from one who is not a Śrotriya": when a sacrifice has been commenced by one who has not studied the Vedas, a Brāhmaṇa shall not eat even at a time suitable for eating, after the offering to Agni and Soma; likewise, he shall not eat at a sacrifice where the oblation is offered by many priests, or by a female, or by a eunuch. (4.205)
This is offensive to the virtuous wherein these men offer oblations;
this is contrary to the will of the gods, therefore one should avoid it. (4.206)

"Ugliness" (aślīkam): that rite in which the aforementioned many sacrificers and others perform the oblation is "ugly" (aślīkam)—meaning unrefined (aśrīkam) or destructive of prosperity (śrīghnam). The letter *l* is substituted for the letter *r*. It is unfavorable to the gods; therefore, one should not cause this [rite] to be performed as a sacrifice. (4.206)
One should never eat the food of those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted; nor that which is infested with hair or insects, nor that which has been intentionally touched by a foot. (4.207)

"Of those intoxicated, angry, or afflicted": one should not eat the food of those who are drunk, angry, or diseased; nor food defiled by contact with hair or insects, nor food intentionally touched with the foot. (4.207)
Food looked upon by a killer of an embryo, touched by a woman in her courses, pecked by a bird, or even touched by a dog [is unfit to be eaten]. (4.208)

Regarding the term *bhrūṇaghna* (feticide): by way of this illustration, one should not eat food that has been looked upon by those who have fallen from their caste—such as a cow-killer (*goghna*) and others—or that which has been touched by a woman in her menses, or tasted by a bird such as a crow, or touched by a dog. (4.208)
Food smelled by a cow, and especially food proclaimed for all; the food of a multitude, the food of a courtesan, and that which is despised by the learned—[these should be avoided]. (4.209)

"Ann given by a cow" refers to food that has been smelled by a cow. "Ann proclaimed" is that which is given at the beginning of a sacrificial session (*satra*) after it has been publicly announced, "Who will eat this? "Especially" means that because of its many defects, the penance required is heavy. "Food of a group" (*gaṇānna*) is the food of a company of a hundred Brahmins. "Food of a courtesan" (*gaṇikānna*) is the food of a prostitute. And that which is "condemned by one who knows the scriptures"—that which is censured—one should not eat. (4.209)
The food of a thief and a singer, of a carpenter and a usurer, of one who has been consecrated for sacrifice, of a miser, and of one who is bound or fettered—[these are not to be eaten]. (4.210)

"From a thief": one should not eat the food of those who live by singing as thieves, nor of one who lives by the profession of a carpenter, nor of one who subsists on usury. Likewise, from one consecrated for a sacrifice before the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice; from a miserly person; and from "one with a shackle"—here the genitive is used in the sense of the instrumental—meaning one bound by a shackle. Govindarāja, however, has explained the word "bound" (*baddha*) to mean "one shackled even without fetters [but] by non-yoni-shackles," that is, one to whom non-yoni-shackles have been applied. (4.210)
The food of one accused of a crime, of a eunuch, of an unchaste woman, and of a hypocrite;
as well as food that is sour, stale, or the leavings of a Śūdra—[these must not be eaten]. (4.211)

"Of one who is accused" means of one whose reputation has been ruined by public outcry due to being charged with a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*). One should not eat the food of a *napuṃsaka* (impotent person), of a *puṃścalī* (an unchaste woman), of a *veśyā* (prostitute), nor of a hypocrite (*dāmbhika*)—one who practices dharma through deception, such as those who follow the "cat-vow" (*baiḍālavratika*). "Sour" (*śukta*) refers to that which is naturally sweet but has become sour or acidic through contact with curds and the like, or through water and so forth. "Stale" (*paryuṣita*) means that which has been kept overnight. The connection is that one should not eat the food of a Śūdra. Furthermore, one should not eat "leavings" (*ucchiṣṭa*), meaning food remaining after someone has eaten, unless specified otherwise. However, the leavings of a guru are to be eaten because it is prescribed. Govindarāja, however, says that one should not eat the leavings of a Śūdra—that is, what remains after he has eaten—even if it is still in the cooking pot. (4.211)
The food of a physician, a hunter, a cruel person, or one who eats leftovers;
the food of an Ugra, the food of a woman who has recently given birth, and that which has been tasted by another before being offered—these must not be eaten for ten days after the birth. (4.212)

Regarding the term "of the physician": one should not eat the food of a physician who lives by the practice of medicine; of a hunter (*mṛgayu*), who kills deer and other animals for the sake of selling their meat; of a cruel person (*krūra*) of dishonest character; and of one who eats forbidden leavings. "Of the fierce" (*ugra*) refers to the food of one who performs harsh deeds. Govindarāja, in his *Mañjarī*, stated that "fierce" (*ugra*) refers to a king.
And in his commentary on Manu, he identified it as one born of a Kṣatriya father and a Śūdra mother.
In the Yājñavalkīya [Smṛti], because of the statement regarding the distinction [of castes], he does not say "the fierce king";
this is a marvel, a true ornament within his own heart.

Food from a woman who has recently given birth (*sūtikānna*)—that food which is prepared for the sake of the woman giving birth—must not be eaten even by those born of her own family. That food in which someone performs the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) while others seated in the same row are eating, disregarding them, is called *paryācānta*. One should not eat food from a woman who has recently given birth during the ten-day period (*anirdaśa*), as this will be explained later [in verse 4.213]. || 4.212 ||

Meat not consecrated by sacrifice, meat obtained for no purpose, the food of a woman who has no hero (husband), the food of an enemy, the food of a city, the food of an outcast, and that which has been sneezed upon—[these one should avoid]. (4.213)

"Unhonored" means: one should not eat food that is given with contempt to one who is worthy of honor; meat offered in vain (vṛthāmāṃsa); food prepared without reference to the gods and others; food from a woman who lacks a hero (avīrā), meaning one deprived of husband and sons; food from those who have fallen into an enemy's city; and food upon which a sneeze has been made. || 4.213 ||

The food of the slanderer and the liar, as well as that of one who sells sacrifices, the food of a eunuch and a tailor, and likewise the food of an ungrateful person—[these should not be eaten]. (4.214)

Regarding the term *piśuna*: a *piśuna* is one who, in the absence of others, is intent on speaking ill of them; an excessive liar, such as one who gives false testimony and the like; a seller of sacrifices, who takes wealth after saying, "May the fruit of my sacrifice be yours"; a *śailūṣa*, which is an actor; a *tunnavāya*, which is a tailor; and an ungrateful person, who proceeds to harm one who has rendered him assistance—one should not eat the food of such a person. (4.214)
Of a blacksmith, a Niṣāda, a stage-player, a goldsmith, a bamboo-worker, and likewise a seller of weapons. (4.215)

"Of the smith" means of the blacksmith (*lohakāra*), of the *niṣāda* mentioned in the tenth chapter, of one who lives by entering the stage other than as an actor or singer, of the goldsmith, and of one who lives by splitting bamboos—Viśvarūpa says this refers to the "buruḍa. One should not eat the food of those who sell weapons or iron. (4.215)
[One should not eat the food] of dog-keepers, of liquor-sellers, of a washerman, of a dyer, of a cruel man, or of one in whose house a paramour resides. (4.216)

"Of those who keep dogs" means: one should not eat in the house of those who rear dogs for hunting and similar purposes; nor in the house of liquor-sellers, a washerman, one who dyes cloth with safflower and other dyes, a merciless person, or one in whose house a paramour or a lover stays even by mistake. (4.216)

Those who tolerate a paramour, those who are entirely conquered by their wives, and food from a deceased person within ten days of death, as well as food that is simply unpalatable—[these one should avoid]. (4.217)

"They tolerate" (*mṛṣyanti*). The word "in the house" (*gṛhe*) is supplied from the context. One should not eat the food of those who tolerate a wife's paramour known within the home. By this, there is no fault in tolerating a paramour for a woman who has been expelled from the house. Likewise, one should not eat the food of those who are dependent on women in all their affairs, nor food from a birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) where the period of impurity has not yet passed, nor that which is simply disagreeable. (4.217)
The food of a king takes away one's vital energy; the food of a Śūdra, spiritual luster;
the food of a goldsmith, longevity; and the food of a leather-cutter, fame. (4.218)

"Kings' food": the food of a king destroys one's *tejas* (vital luster). It is precisely from the observation of such a defect that the prohibition against eating that food is inferred. The same applies to the subsequent cases as well. Where a practice has not been previously forbidden, the prohibition is inferred solely from the observation of a defect. [The author] will later state the prohibition: "One should not eat the cooked food of a Śūdra" (4.223). This present verse describes the fruit of transgressing that rule. The cooked food of a Śūdra destroys the *tejas* resulting from study and other such pursuits. The food of a goldsmith destroys longevity. The food of a leather-worker destroys fame. (4.218)
The food of artisans destroys one's progeny, and that of a washerman destroys one's strength; the food of a multitude and the food of a courtesan cut one off from the higher worlds. (4.219)

Regarding the phrase "the food of an artisan" (*kārukānna*): the food of an artisan, such as a cook and the like, destroys one's progeny—that is, one's offspring. Although leather-workers and others are also artisans, they are mentioned separately according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull. The food of a washerman destroys one's strength. And the food of a member of a guild (*gaṇa*) and a courtesan (*gaṇikā*) snatches away from one the worlds of heaven and so forth, which are earned through other meritorious deeds. (4.219)
The food of a physician is pus; the food of an unchaste woman is semen;
the food of a usurer is excrement; the food of a seller of weapons is filth. (4.220)

"Putrid matter" (*pūya*): the food of a physician is "putrid matter," having a defect equal to that of eating pus. Likewise, the food of an unchaste woman is semen; the food of a usurer is excrement; the food of a seller of iron is phlegm and the like, other than feces. Govindarāja, however, says that by eating the food of a physician, one is born into such a caste where one becomes a consumer of pus. (4.220)
Regarding those others who have been described in succession as those whose food should not be eaten, the wise declare that their food consists of skin, bone, and hair. (4.221)

Regarding the phrase "those others": those who are different from those specifically mentioned [in the preceding rules], who are enumerated in this section as persons whose food should not be eaten in due order—the food of these is their skin, bone, and hair. One should understand that whatever defect exists in eating their skin, their bones, or their hair, that very same defect applies to eating their food as well. (4.221)
Having unintentionally eaten the food of any one of these, one should fast for three days;
but having eaten it intentionally, or having consumed semen, feces, or urine, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance. (4.222)

Regarding the word "having eaten" (*bhuktvā*): among these [forbidden foods], having unknowingly eaten food associated with any one of them, there is a fast for three days; but if done knowingly, it is a *kṛcchra* penance. The same applies to eating semen, feces, or urine. Furthermore, because of the use of the genitive case in the phrase "of any one of these" (*anyatamasya*), this expiation applies only to food that is defiled by its source of acquisition (*parigraha-duṣṭa*), such as that belonging to a drunkard and so forth, and not to food defiled by contact (*saṃsarga-duṣṭa*)—such as that infested with hair or insects—nor to food defiled by time (*kāla-duṣṭa*)—such as stale food—and nor to food defiled by its cause of preparation (*nimitta-duṣṭa*)—such as that announced for sale (*ghuṣṭa*). Moreover, the teaching of these together in a single section is intended to indicate their status as *snātaka* (initiated householders). And he will state the expiation for these in the eleventh chapter. If, however, the expiation were the same for all of them, he would have said, "having eaten the food of any one of these when it is defiled," rather than saying, "having eaten [the food] of any one of these."
Therefore, that expiation which Medhātithi asserted for cases such as eating what has turned sour (*śukta*) based on this single context is not appropriate.

Furthermore, the mention of the penance here outside of its specific context is for the sake of brevity; if it were placed there, the inclusion of terms such as "intoxicated" and so forth would also have had to be made. (4.222)

A learned twice-born man should not eat the cooked food of a Śūdra who does not perform ancestral rites (śrāddha); however, if he has no other means of subsistence, he may take from him raw grain sufficient for one night. 4.223.

"One should not eat" (verse 4.223): The food of a Śūdra has been prohibited without distinction; now its specific scope is being stated. A twice-born man who knows the scriptures should not eat cooked food from a Śūdra who does not perform the *śrāddha*—that is, one who is devoid of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*). However, in the absence of other food, he may take from him only raw grain sufficient for the maintenance of a single night, but never cooked food.
Having deliberated upon both the miserly Vedic scholar and the liberal usurer, the gods ordained that their food be equal. (4.224)

Regarding the phrase "of the *śrotriya*": one is a learned Vedic scholar who is miserly, while the other is a donor who lives on usury. Having deliberated upon the possession of virtues and defects by both of them, the gods determined that the food for these two is equal, because the virtues and defects of both are balanced. (4.224)
Prajāpati, having approached them, said: "Do not make the unequal equal!
That which is purified by faith belongs to the generous man; the other is destroyed by lack of faith. (4.225)

Regarding the word "tān" (them): Brahmā, having approached those gods, said, "Do not make the unequal food equal. It is improper to equalize what is unequal. When the question arose as to what the distinction between these two is, he himself spoke: "Even the food of a usurer who is by nature charitable becomes pure if given with faith. But the food of a miser, being devoid of faith, is struck down, defiled, and base. Although both types were previously prohibited, this verse is intended to demonstrate the purity of the food of a learned usurer when it is given with faith. (4.225)
Therefore he says:

"One should always perform sacrifices and works of public utility with diligence; for when performed with faith and with wealth acquired through righteous means, those two become inexhaustible. (4.226)

Regarding the word *śraddhayā*: *iṣṭa* refers to sacrificial rites such as the *yajña* performed within the sacrificial altar (*antarvedi*); *pūrta* refers to other works, such as the construction of lotus ponds, wells, water-stations, and groves. Thus, being free from laziness, one should constantly perform these with faith, devoid of desire for fruits such as heaven. For when those *iṣṭa* and *pūrta* acts are performed with wealth acquired through righteous means and with faith, they become inexhaustible and result in liberation. (4.226)

One should constantly practice the duty of giving—both that pertaining to sacrifices and that pertaining to public works—with a state of complete contentment, whenever one encounters a worthy recipient, according to one's ability. (4.227)

Regarding the "duty of giving" (dānadharmam): one should perform the duty known as giving—whether it be of the *iṣṭi* or *pūrta* type, whether within the sacrificial enclosure (*antarvedika*) or outside the sacrificial enclosure (*bahirvedika*)—at all times, provided that one has approached a Brāhmaṇa endowed with learning and austerity, with a heart full of complete satisfaction, according to one's ability.
Whatever may be asked for should be given by one who is free from malice;
for a worthy recipient will surely arise who delivers one from all [suffering]. (4.228)

"Whatever it may be": one who is requested should give even food according to one's ability, without envy toward the virtues of others. For at some time, a worthy recipient (pātra) will come to one who is always habituated to giving, and that recipient will liberate one from everything that causes rebirth in hell. 4.228.
The giver of water obtains satisfaction; the giver of food, imperishable happiness;
the giver of sesame seeds, desired offspring; and the giver of lamps, supreme vision. (4.229)

Regarding the phrase "vārida" (giver of water): the giver of water attains satisfaction through the removal of hunger and thirst; the giver of food attains extreme happiness; the giver of a balance scale obtains desired offspring and so forth; and the giver of a lamp obtains unimpaired vision in the dwellings of Brahmins and other such places. || 4.229 ||
The giver of land obtains land; the giver of gold, long life; the giver of a house, the finest dwellings; the giver of silver, supreme beauty. (4.230)

Regarding the phrase "giver of land": the giver of land obtains sovereignty over the earth; the giver of gold, long life; the giver of a house, excellent dwellings; and the giver of silver, a form that captivates the eyes and minds of all people. (4.230)
The giver of clothing attains the same world as Candra; the giver of horses, the same world as the Aśvins;
the giver of a bull, abundant prosperity; and the giver of a cow, the realm of the Sun.

Regarding the phrase "vāsoda" (giver of clothing): the giver of garments attains worlds equal to those of the Moon; he dwells in the world of the Moon with a splendor equal to that of the Moon. In the same way, the giver of a horse attains the world of Aśvin; the giver of a bull attains abundant prosperity; and the giver of a milch cow attains the world of the Sun. 4.231.

The giver of vehicles and beds obtains a wife; the giver of fearlessness obtains sovereignty; the giver of grain obtains eternal happiness; and the giver of the Veda obtains equality with Brahman. (4.232)

Regarding the phrase "vehicles and beds": one who gives vehicles such as chariots and beds obtains a wife; one who grants fearlessness—that is, one who is non-violent toward living beings—obtains lordship; one who gives grain—that is, a giver of crops such as rice, barley, mung beans, and lentils—obtains long-lasting happiness; and one who gives *brahman*—that is, a teacher or commentator of the Veda—attains *sārṣṭitā*, which is equality of state or identity with *brahman*. (4.232)
Of all gifts whatsoever—water, food, cattle, land, clothing, sesame seeds, gold, and clarified butter—the gift of the Veda is preeminent. (4.233)

"Of all"—that is, among all gifts such as water, food, cows, land, clothing, sesame seeds, gold, clarified butter, and so forth, the gift of the Veda is distinguished; it becomes the giver of the most excellent fruit. (4.233)
With whatever disposition one bestows whatever gift, one receives it back, duly honored, with that very same disposition. (4.234)

"By whatever [means]"—the word *tu* (but) is used here for emphasis. By whichever state of mind or intention he gives a gift—whether it be with the desire for fruit, thinking "May heaven be mine," or by one seeking liberation, with the intention of liberation and free from desire—he, characterized by that very state of mind, attains [his goal] in another birth, being honored, through the gateway of the respective fruits of those various gifts. (4.234)
He who accepts what has been honored and he who gives what has likewise been honored—both of them go to heaven; but in the opposite case, they go to hell. (4.235)

Regarding the phrase "one who honors": both he who gives only after first honoring [the recipient], and he who accepts what has been given only after first honoring [the giver], go to heaven; whereas for giving or accepting without honor, one goes to hell. However, in the case of accepting for the sake of human goals (*puruṣārtha*), there is no contradiction in obtaining the fruit, because of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) that "I must accept only without honor, and not otherwise. (4.235)

One should not take pride in one's asceticism, nor should one speak untruth after performing a sacrifice; even when distressed, one should not revile Brahmins, nor should one boast after giving a gift. 4.236

"He should not be filled with pride" means that he should not take pride, thinking, "How have I performed this difficult penance," such as the Cāndrāyaṇa and other austerities. Furthermore, having performed a sacrifice, he must not speak untruth; for although speaking untruth is already prohibited as a general rule for human conduct (*puruṣārtha*), this is a prohibition specifically for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*). Even when oppressed by Brahmins, he should not revile them. And having given cows or other gifts, he should not tell another, "This was given by me. (4.236)
Sacrifice perishes through falsehood; austerity perishes through pride; life-span perishes by reviling Brahmins; and a gift perishes by boasting of it. (4.237)

Regarding sacrifice: through the cause of falsehood, the sacrifice perishes; only by means of truth does it accomplish its fruit. The same applies to austerity and giving. Furthermore, one’s lifespan is diminished by reviling a Brahmin. (4.237)
One should gradually accumulate merit, like termites building an anthill, for the sake of a companion in the next world, without causing pain to any living beings. (4.238)

Regarding "dharma": avoiding injury to all living beings, one should practice dharma gradually and according to one's ability for the sake of having a companion in the next world. Just as small ants and various kinds of termites gradually build up a great mound of earth. 4.238.
For in the next world, neither father nor mother remains as a companion;
neither son, nor wife, nor kinsman remains—only Dharma alone stands by one. (4.239)

"Not here" means that in the next world, neither father, mother, wife, nor kinsmen remain to accomplish one's purpose as companions; rather, Dharma alone remains for the sake of assistance in its singular, peerless state. Therefore, one should practice Dharma, which is of greater benefit even than sons and other such relations. (4.239)
A living being is born alone, and alone indeed it perishes;
alone one experiences the fruit of good deeds, and alone likewise that of evil deeds. (4.240)

"Alone" means that a living being is born alone, not accompanied by kinsmen; and alone indeed one dies. One alone experiences the fruit of good deeds, such as heaven and the like, and the fruit of evil deeds, such as hell and the like, not together with one's mother or others. Therefore, one should not abandon dharma even for the sake of one's mother and so forth. (4.240)
Having cast off the dead body upon the earth like a piece of wood or a clod of earth, the relatives depart with averted faces; dharma alone follows him. (4.241)

"Regarding the dead": having cast the dead body—devoid of mind and breath, insentient like a clod of earth—upon the ground, the kinsmen turn their faces away and depart; they do not follow the dead person while he still lives, for it is dharma alone that follows him. (4.241)
Therefore, one should always gradually accumulate Dharma for the sake of a companion;
for with Dharma as a companion, one crosses over the darkness that is so difficult to traverse. 4.242

"Therefore" means: since one crosses over the darkness of the suffering of hell and other realms—which is difficult to cross—with dharma as a companion, therefore one should constantly and gradually practice dharma by way of making it one's companion. (4.242)
The radiant one, whose body is ethereal, swiftly leads to the next world that person for whom dharma is paramount and whose sins have been destroyed by austerity. (4.243)

Regarding the phrase "one for whom dharma is primary": when sin arises by chance in a person devoted to dharma, dharma itself—once that sin has been destroyed through expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) such as the *Prājāpatya* penance—quickly leads that radiant individual to the world beyond, namely Brahman in the form of heaven and so forth. In Upaniṣadic passages such as "Brahman is the void" (*khaṃ brahma*, ChUp 4.10.5), the word *kha* is used for Brahman; the meaning is that [the soul] has Brahman as its true nature while having the void as its body. Although it is the individual soul (*jīva*), delimited by the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*), that actually travels, nevertheless, because it is a portion of Brahman, it is logical to describe it as having the nature of Brahman. Therefore, if it is indeed dharma that leads one to the supreme world, one should practice dharma.
For neither the Vedas well-studied nor various treatises go to that place where his single virtue alone follows him.
One who desires to lead his family to excellence should always form connections with the most excellent; he should avoid those who are inferior. (4.244)

Regarding the phrase "with the best": one who desires to lead his lineage to excellence should always cultivate relationships—such as giving a daughter in marriage and so forth—with those who are superior in terms of learning, conduct, birth, and other such qualities. He should, however, avoid inferior connections. Since the avoidance of the base is already established by the injunction to follow the best, the fact that he states again, "he should abandon the base," is for the purpose of permitting [marriage] with those equal to himself and others in the event that the best are unavailable. (4.244)
By associating with the most excellent and avoiding those who are base, a Brāhmaṇa attains preeminence; through the opposite conduct, he falls to the state of a Śūdra. (4.245)

"Regarding the word *uttamān* (superior): by approaching the superior and forming a connection with them, a Brāhmaṇa attains excellence. Through transgression—that is, through contrary conduct consisting of association with the inferior—he undergoes a degradation of his caste and reaches a state equal to that of a Śūdra. (4.245)

Firm in action, gentle, self-controlled, and not associating with those of cruel conduct, one who is non-violent and observes such vows shall conquer heaven through self-restraint and generosity. (4.246)

"One who acts firmly" means one who brings to completion what has been begun; "firmly acting" implies being gentle and not harsh. Since self-restraint (*dama*) is mentioned separately, the term "self-controlled" (*dānta*) should be understood as one who endures the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat. Avoiding association with persons of cruel conduct and abstaining from harming others, one who is thus devoted to his vows attains heaven through the gift known as the restraint of the senses, which consists of discipline and self-control. (4.246)
One may accept from anyone fuel for the fire, water, roots, fruits, food that is offered, honey, and the gift of safety. (4.247)

Regarding "fuel and water": according to the statement of Yājñavalkya, "Fuel, water, fruits, roots, honey, and food that is offered and brought unasked—except from an unchaste woman, a eunuch, an outcast, and likewise an enemy" (YDh 1.215)—one may accept gifts from all sources, even from Śūdras and others, with the exception of those such as unchaste women. Since it is stated, "One should take only raw [food] from him" (4.223), only raw food is to be accepted from a Śūdra. Furthermore, one should accept from even Caṇḍālas and others the gift of fearlessness (*abhaya*), which consists of protection for oneself, because it causes joy and is equal to a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). (4.247)
Prajāpati has declared that alms brought forward and offered spontaneously, without having been previously solicited, may be accepted even from one of evil deeds. (4.248)

Regarding the phrase "brought and offered": "brought" means carried to the place of the gift; "offered" means placed directly before one. It refers to alms such as gold and the like that have not been previously solicited by the recipient—either by himself or through another—and which the donor has not previously announced with the words, "I give this to you. It does not refer to prepared food, because of the statement in verse 4.247, "and food that is offered. Viriñci considered that even from a wrongdoer, such things should be accepted, provided they are not from those who are outcastes or otherwise fallen. 4.248.
The ancestors do not eat for fifteen years, nor does the fire carry his oblations, of him who treats her with contempt. (4.249)

"They do not eat": for fifteen years, the ancestors do not consume the *kavya* (offerings to the manes) prepared by him at the *śrāddha* rites; nor does Agni carry to the gods the *havya* (offerings to the gods), such as the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and so forth, given by him in sacrifices, if he does not accept that alms. 4.249.
One should not refuse a bed, a house, kusha grass, perfumes, water, flowers, jewels, curd, parched grain, fish, milk, meat, or even vegetables. (4.250)

Regarding "a bed": perfumes are fragrant substances such as camphor and the like; *dhānāḥ* are parched barley and rice grains; *payaḥ* is milk. Previously, by means of the rule concerning the bringing of gifts, it was stated that one should not refuse cows and other such things; however, regarding beds and the like, even if they are brought unasked, if they are already situated in the giver's own house and provided unsolicited, one should not reject them. (4.250)
Desiring to support his teachers and dependents, and wishing to honor the deities and guests, he may accept gifts from all sources; however, he himself must not find satisfaction therein. 4.251.

Regarding the word "gurus": desiring to rescue from hunger his gurus, such as his mother and father, and his dependents, such as his wife and others—with the exception of those who have fallen from their caste (patita) and so forth—he may accept gifts from all sources, even from Śūdras and other unworthy persons; however, he must not live for himself upon that wealth. (4.251)
But when the teachers have passed away, or when living at home without them, one seeking one's own livelihood should always accept [gifts] from a virtuous person. (4.252)

Regarding the word "guruṣu" (towards elders): when one's mother, father, and others have died, or even while they are still living but remain in their own state of yoga, one who dwells within the house and seeks his own livelihood should always indeed receive [alms] from virtuous people. 4.252.
A partner in business, a family friend, a cowherd, a slave, and a barber—these among Śūdras are those whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [as a servant]. (4.253)

"Ārdhika" means a partner in plowing; these are relative terms. He who performs the cultivation for another is one whose food may be eaten by that person. Likewise, a friend of one's own family; he who is one's cowherd; he who is one's servant; he who is one's barber and performs work; and he who offers himself to someone, saying, "I am in a miserable state and shall perform service for you," and lives in one's presence—such a Śūdra is one whose food may be eaten. (4.253)
Regarding how a Śūdra should offer himself [to his master], he says:
"In whatever state his own self may be, whatever he intends to do, and in whatever manner he would serve him—in that same way he should offer himself. (4.254)

"Of what kind" (yādṛśa): he should describe himself in such a manner—according to the nature of this Śūdra’s own character, family, and so forth; according to whatever action is desired by the master; and according to the way in which service must be performed by him. (4.254)
He who represents himself as something other than what he truly is when among others is the greatest evildoer in the world; he is a thief who robs his own self. (4.255)

"He who [speaks] otherwise": because of the general designation "he who," this refers not only to the Śūdra under discussion, but to anyone else who, being otherwise [inferior] in terms of lineage and so forth, describes himself to virtuous people as something other than what he is; he is an exceedingly great evildoer and a thief in the world, because he is a stealer of the self. A common thief steals another's property, but this one steals the self, which is the most preeminent of all things.
All objects of speech are fixed; they have speech as their root and have issued forth from speech.
That man who steals this speech is a thief of everything. (4.256)

"Expressed meanings" means that all objects are fixed within words as their expressed content; and words have speech as their root, for in the comprehension of those [objects], they are understood from the words themselves. Since they are performed after one has understood—by way of comprehension—that they are rooted in speech, they are said to "have issued forth from speech. For this very reason, in the verse "In the beginning, [the world] from the Vedic words alone" (1.21), even the creation of Brahman is stated to be rooted in the Vedic words. Therefore, the man who would steal that speech—that is, who causes it to deviate from its own meaning—becomes a thief of all things. 4.256.
Having discharged his debts to the great seers, the ancestors, and the gods according to the prescribed rule,
and having entrusted everything to his son, he may dwell having taken recourse to the state of a madman.

Regarding the term "great sage" (*maharṣi*): this method of renunciation is prescribed specifically for the householder. Having attained freedom from debt toward the great sages through Vedic study, toward the ancestors by procreating sons, and toward the gods by performing sacrifices according to the scriptures; having entrusted the entire burden of family concerns to a worthy son and adopted a state of equanimity; having abandoned the sense of "mine-ness" regarding son, wife, wealth, and so forth; and perceiving everything with the intellect of Brahman as equal everywhere—one should dwell in the home itself. (4.257)
One should always reflect alone in solitude upon what is beneficial for oneself; for by reflecting alone, one attains the supreme good. 4.258

"Alone" (ekākī): Having renounced ritual acts performed for desire as well as the acquisition of wealth—as will be described in the sixth chapter—he should, while subsisting on the means of livelihood provided by his son, remain alone in a secluded place and constantly meditate upon the welfare of the self, which is the state of Brahman for the individual soul as taught in the Vedānta. For by meditating upon that, one attains the supreme good characterized by liberation through the direct realization of Brahman.
Thus has been declared the eternal mode of life for a Brahmin householder,
as well as the ritual rules for the Snātaka vows, which are auspicious and increase one's inner strength.

"This" refers to the summary of the chapter's subject matter. This mode of conduct beginning with the seasonal sacrifices (*ṛta*) has been declared for the householder Brāhmaṇa; it is eternal (*śāśvatī*), meaning constant. However, that which applies in times of distress will be described as non-eternal. Furthermore, the rule for the observances of one who has completed his Vedic studies (*snātaka*) has been declared as excellent for increasing the quality of goodness (*sattvaguṇa*). (4.259)
A Brahmin who lives according to this conduct, being learned in the Vedas and the Shastras,
is eternally freed from sin and is glorified in the world of Brahma.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu. || 4 ||

"By this" refers to the statement of the fruit of everything previously mentioned. By following the conduct prescribed in this scripture, a Brāhmaṇa who knows the Vedas, having his sins destroyed through the performance of obligatory rites, becomes absorbed in that very Brahman which is the world [itself] by means of the excellence of the knowledge of Brahman, and thus attains greatness, which is the state of being pre-eminent above all. 4.260.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Manu-bhāṣya, titled *Manvarthamuktāvalī*, composed by the illustrious Kullūka Bhaṭṭa.
The Fifth Chapter.
Having heard these duties of the *snātaka* as they have been declared, the sages spoke thus to the high-souled Bhṛgu, who was born from fire: 5.1.

"Having heard these... means that the sages, having heard these duties of the *snātaka* as they have been described, spoke these words to the high-souled Bhṛgu, who was intent upon the supreme goal. Although in the first chapter, among the ten Prajāpatis, the creation of Bhṛgu is also stated by Manu himself in the verse "Bhṛgu and Nārada" (1.35), nevertheless, due to the difference between *kalpas*, his origin from fire is here mentioned. And thus says the Śruti: "That which was the first radiance of his seed became this Sun; that which was the second was Bhṛgu. For this very reason, because he was produced from what had fallen (*bhraṣṭa*) from the seed, he is called Bhṛgu. (5.1)
O Lord, how does death prevail over those brahmins who, as previously described, perform their own duty and are learned in the Vedas and the scriptures? (5.2)

"Thus. In this way, for those Brahmins who perform their own duty as described, who know the Śruti and the Śāstras, and whose lifespan was previously ordained by the Vedas—how could death prevail against them? Because there is an absence of the practice of unrighteousness, which is the cause of a short life. The address "O Lord" is used because [the Lord] is capable of cutting through all doubts. (5.2)
That righteous-souled Bhṛgu, the son of Manu, said to those great seers:
"Listen to the fault by which Death seeks to slay the Brahmins. (5.3)

"Listen to that fault," he said to them—referring to Bhṛgu, the son of Manu, whose very nature was dharma, yet who desired to slay the brahmins in a short time due to a certain defect—and thus he spoke to those great seers. (5.3)
Through the lack of study of the Vedas, the abandonment of proper conduct, laziness, and defects in food, death seeks to strike down the Brahmins. (5.4)

Regarding the phrase "by lack of practice": through the non-study of the Vedas, the abandonment of one's own traditional conduct, laziness—characterized by a lack of enthusiasm for performing what must necessarily be done despite having the capacity—and the defects of improper food, death seeks to slay the Brahmins; for these, by way of generating unrighteousness, are the causes for the exhaustion of their lifespan. (5.4)
Since the [prohibition against] the study of the Vedas and so forth has already been stated, he now mentions the fault regarding food that was not previously mentioned:
"Garlic, leeks, onions, and mushrooms, as well as those things produced from impure matter, are unfit to be eaten by the twice-born. (5.5)

"Garlic" (*laśuna*) refers to three types of bulbous vegetables known as garlic, *gṛñjana*, and onion; mushrooms (*kavaka*); and those produced from impure matter, such as *tandulīya* and other plants growing from excrement and the like. According to the statement of Yājñavalkya, "of the twice-born," these are forbidden foods for the twice-born. The mention of "the twice-born" is intended to exclude the Śūdra. (5.5)
One should carefully avoid red exudations from trees, as well as those produced by incisions, and the *śelu* fruit, along with cow's colostrum (*peyūṣa*). (5.6)

"Red ones": those of red color; resinous exudations from trees—substances that have emerged from trees and attained a solid state—and those originating from cutting or felling, even if they are not red. Thus says the Taittirīya Śruti: "Furthermore, indeed, one may eat at will the [resin] of that which is red, or of that which flows from a cut, but not of anything else. *Śelu* is the fruit of the *bahuvāraka*. *Gobhava* is the milk of a cow that has recently calved (*peyūṣa*); this becomes solidified through contact with fire. One should carefully avoid these. Although the prohibition of *peyūṣa* is already established by the rule "the milk of a cow within ten days [of calving]" (5.8), it is mentioned separately because it involves a greater fault, in order to indicate the severity of the penance. For this very reason, the word "carefully" (*yatnataḥ*) is used. 5.6.
One should avoid kṛsara, saṃyāva, milk-rice, and cakes made in vain; likewise, meat that has not been consecrated, food intended for the gods, and sacrificial oblations.

Regarding the phrase "vṛthākṛsara": that which is cooked for one's own sake without being dedicated to a deity or other [recipient] is called *vṛthā*. *Kṛsara* is rice cooked together with sesame seeds. Thus it is stated in the *Chandoga-prātiśākhya*:
"That which is cooked from the mixture of sesame and rice is designated as *kṛsara*."

*Saṃyāva* is a preparation made from ghee, milk, molasses, and wheat flour; it is commonly known as *karika*. *Pāyasa* is rice mixed with milk. *Apūpa* is a cake made of ground flour. One should avoid these when they have been cooked for no sacred purpose (*vṛthā*). *Upākaraṇa* is the touching of the sacrificial animal (*paśu*) with many mantras at the beginning of an animal sacrifice; the meat of an animal that has not undergone this rite is "unconsecrated" (*anupākṛta*). One should avoid foods intended for the gods—food meant for offerings (*naivedya*) before it has been offered—and sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) such as the *puroḍāśa* cake before the fire-oblation (*homa*). Because of the observation of this specific prohibition regarding "meat of unconsecrated animals," the general prohibition—"unceremonial meat cooked for no purpose" (4.213)—is understood, according to the maxim of the cow and the bull, to apply specifically to the eating of meat intended for other occasions such as *śrāddha*, excluding the meat of unconsecrated animals. (5.7)

The milk of a cow within ten days [of calving], that of a camel, that of one-hoofed animals, as well as the milk of a sheep, the milk of a *saṃdhinī* cow, and the milk of a cow whose calf has been taken away—[these are forbidden]. 5.8.

"Of one that has not passed ten days": this refers to the milk of a cow that has recently calved and whose ten-day period has not yet elapsed. The mention of "cow" (*go*) is intended to indicate all animals whose milk is to be drunk; by this, the prohibition also applies to goats and buffaloes during the first ten days after calving. And so says Yama: "The milk of a cow, a goat, or a buffalo that has not passed its ten-day period..."

Likewise, [one should avoid] milk from a camel, from animals with solid hooves such as horses, and from a sheep. Furthermore, regarding the *saṃdhinī*—that is, a cow in heat who desires a bull—Hārīta says: “One should not drink the milk of a *saṃdhinī*, for that milk belongs to her while she is in her season. One should also avoid the milk of a cow whose calf has died (*vivatsā*), a cow whose calf is dead (*mṛtavatsā*), and a cow whose calf is absent (*asaṃnihitavatsā*). Although the word “calf” (*vatse*) alone would suffice to include the cow by the principle of the locus of the term *dhenu*, the explicit mention of the “cow” (*go*) again is intended to indicate that this prohibition applies specifically to the cow and not to goats or buffaloes. (5.8)
And among all wild animals, with the exception of the buffalo, the milk of females must be avoided; likewise, all substances that have turned sour are indeed to be shunned. 5.9.

Regarding the phrase "of wild animals" (*araṇyānām*): here, because the buffalo is specifically excluded by the word *mṛga*, it refers to all other animals. With the exception of buffalo milk, the milk of all wild animals—such as elephants and so forth—as well as the milk of females, and all fermented acids (*śukta*) must be avoided. Those substances which are sweet by nature but become sour through the influence of time, water, and so on, are denoted by the term *śukta*. Although the prohibition of *śukta* was already established in the fourth chapter with the words "fermented [food] and that which has stood overnight" (4.211), it is stated here again for the purpose of providing an exception (*pratiprasava*) for curd. 5.9.
Curd is edible among sour substances, as is everything produced from curd,
and those [liquors] which are distilled from auspicious flowers, roots, and fruits.

"And curd is edible. Among sour substances (*śukta*), curd is edible, as is everything produced from curd, such as buttermilk (*takra*) and the like. However, those which are fermented with flowers, roots, fruits, or water are to be eaten. By the inclusion of the qualification "pure" (*śubhaiḥ*), there is a prohibition against that which has been fermented by things causing morbid transformations, such as through delusion (*moha*). And so says Bṛhaspati: "One should not avoid sours made with bulbs, roots, fruits, or commendable flowers;
that which does not cause a morbid transformation is edible, while that which causes such a transformation is inedible."
One should avoid all carnivorous birds as well as those that dwell in villages, those with unclawed single hooves, and the ṭiṭṭibha bird. (5.11)

"Meat-eaters" (kravyāda): those who consume raw flesh are meat-eaters; one should avoid all such birds, including vultures and the like, as well as village-dwelling birds such as pigeons and others. Furthermore, certain single-hoofed animals are specified in the Śruti as fit for consumption, as in: "One should sacrifice a camel or a mule and eat its meat. One should avoid the meat of those that are not so specified, such as donkeys and the like. Even regarding those prescribed as parts of a sacrifice, the eating of their meat is permitted only during the sacrifice, not at all times. And one should avoid the bird known as the *ṭiṭṭibha*. (5.11)
The kalaviṅka, the plava, the haṃsa, the cakrāhva, the village cock, the sārasa, the rajjudāla, the dātyūha, the parrot, and the maina. 5.12.

"Kalaviṅka": the *kalaviṅka* is the sparrow; because it dwells both in villages and in the forest, its prohibition [is stated] by means of a generic term (*jātiśabda*) in order to establish that even the wild variety is not to be eaten. [He should avoid] the bird called *plava*. Likewise, he should avoid the birds known as the swan (*haṃsa*), the ruddy goose (*cakravāka*), the village cock (*grāmakukkuṭa*), the crane (*sārasa*), the *rajjudāla*, the water-hen (*dātyūha*), the parrot (*śuka*), and the maina (*sārikā*). Since the prohibition of the swan and the ruddy goose is already established by the forthcoming prohibition of "web-footed" (*jālapāda*) birds, their separate mention here is for the purpose of providing an option for other web-footed birds in times of distress (*āpad*). That [option] should be understood as restricted: they may be eaten in times of distress, but not when there is no distress, since the option based on personal desire is already established through natural inclination (*rāga*). As for the "village cock," the inclusion of the word "village" is intended to permit the wild cock and others, but not to provide an option for other village-dwelling birds distinct from these. This serves the purpose of addressing times of distress, for it is improper to assume that a specific restriction contained in one sentence applies to something else. (5.12)
Pecking birds, web-footed birds, the koyaṣṭi, birds that scratch with their claws, fish-eating aquatic birds, meat from a slaughterhouse, and dried meat. 5.13.

"Pecking birds" (*pratuda*) refers to those such as woodpeckers (*dārvāghāṭa*) that eat by pecking with their beaks; "web-footed birds" (*jālapāda*) refers to those such as cranes (*śara*) whose feet are webbed; the bird called the *koyaṣṭi*; and "claw-scatterers" (*nakha-viṣkira*) refers to those such as hawks (*śyena*) who scatter [food] with their claws and eat it—excluding permitted wild cocks and the like. Likewise, one should avoid those such as pike-eels (*madgu*) that eat fish by diving, as well as meat situated at a slaughterhouse (*sūnā*), which is a place of killing, even if it is fit to be eaten, and dried meat (*vallūra*). || 5.13 ||
The crane, the heron, the raven, the wagtail, fish-eaters, village pigs, and all kinds of fish; 5.14.

"And the crane," etc. One should avoid the crane, the balākā crane, the droṇa crow, the wagtail, as well as fish-eaters other than birds such as crocodiles and the like, and village pigs—the term "village" (*viḍ*) being used as a qualifier for the purpose of permitting wild boars. And one should avoid all fish. (5.14)
He speaks in condemnation of eating fish:
"Whoever eats the flesh of another is called an eater of that [creature's] flesh.
An eater of fish is an eater of all flesh; therefore, one should avoid fish. (5.15)

"Whose [meat] it is": whoever eats the meat belonging to another is designated specifically as an eater of that meat; for example, a cat is an "eater of mice. However, one who eats fish is fit to be designated as an eater of all meats; therefore, one should not eat fish. (5.15)
Now he speaks of the fish that may be eaten:
"The *pāṭhīna* and the *rohit* are prescribed at the beginning for offerings to the gods and the ancestors;
likewise, the *rājīva*, the *siṃhatuṇḍa*, and all those with scales. (5.16)

Regarding the phrase "the *pāṭhīna* and the *rohit*": the *pāṭhīna* and the *rohit* are two species of fish that may be eaten. The expression "appointed for offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*)" is intended as an illustration of all the eating restrictions that will be stated hereafter. By this, there is no fault in cases such as when one's life is at stake. Likewise, one may eat those called *rājīva*, *siṃhatuṇḍa*, and all *saśalka* [fish], provided they possess the characteristics to be described later. Medhātithi and Govindarāja, however, state: "The *pāṭhīna* and *rohit* are to be eaten only when appointed for rites dedicated to the gods and ancestors, but not at other times; whereas the *rājīva*, *siṃhatuṇḍa*, and *saśalka* fish may be eaten even outside of offerings to the gods and ancestors. This is not convincing.
