For the rule that the *pāṭhīna* and *rohit* are to be eaten only by the guests at a *śrāddha* when appointed for the *śrāddha*, and not even by the performer of the *śrāddha*, lacks authoritative support; furthermore, other sages have declared the *rohit*, *pāṭhīna*, *rājīva*, and others to be equal [in status]. Thus says Śaṅkha (17.25): [Śaṅkha 17.25] *Pāṭhīnarohitau matsyau bhakṣyau havyakavyayoḥ | rājīvān siṃhatuṇḍāṃś ca saśalkāṃś caiva sarvaśaḥ ||* "The *pāṭhīna* and *rohit* fish are to be eaten at offerings to the gods and ancestors; likewise, the *rājīva*, *siṃhatuṇḍa*, and *saśalka* fish may be eaten in every way."
The rājīva, the siṃhatuṇḍa, and likewise the saśalka,
as well as the pāṭhīna and the rohita— these are declared among fish to be fit for consumption.
Yājñavalkya (1.177): Among five-toed animals, the porcupine, the monitor lizard, the tortoise, the hedgehog, and the hare may be eaten;
and among fish, the siṃhatuṇḍaka and the rohita may be eaten.
Likewise, the pāṭhīna, rājīva, and saśalka fish may be eaten by the twice-born.
Hārīta says: "One may eat fish that have scales, provided they are obtained through lawful means. And thus:
"In a Śrāddha, the Pāṭhīna and Rohita fish are to be eaten by the eater alone, not even by the performer;
likewise, the Rājīva and others are not [to be eaten]. This interpretation is not approved by the sages.
One should not eat solitary animals or birds that are unknown, nor any five-toed creatures, even if they are specified among those permitted for consumption. (5.17)

"One should not eat" refers to those that generally move alone, such as snakes and the like—those "solitary wanderers"—as well as those wild animals and birds which, even by those who are experts, cannot be identified through distinctions of name or species nor distinguished by their specific divisions. Furthermore, regarding those "designated among the edible," since there is no prohibition of either the general or the particular, one should not eat those included within the category of the edible that are specifically designated as such; likewise, one should not eat any five-toed animals, such as monkeys and the like. (5.17)
Regarding this, he states an exception:

"The porcupine, the hedgehog, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, the tortoise, and likewise the hare—these they declare to be edible among five-toed animals, as well as those with a single row of teeth, excluding the camel. (5.18)

Regarding the term *śvāvidham*: Manu and others declare that among five-nailed animals, the *śvāvidh*—the animal known as the porcupine (*sedha*)—as well as the *śalyaka*, which is similar to it but has coarse hair, and likewise the monitor lizard (*godhā*), the iguana (*gaṇḍaka*), the tortoise (*kacchapa*), and the hare (*śaśa*), are edible. Likewise, those with a single row of teeth are edible, with the exception of the camel. (5.18)
Having intentionally eaten a mushroom, a village pig, garlic, a village cock, an onion, or a leek, a twice-born man shall fall [from his caste]. (5.19)

Regarding the term *chatrāka*: if a twice-born man intentionally and repeatedly eats any one of the following—mushrooms, *kavaka* mushrooms, village pigs, garlic, and so forth—he falls from his caste (*patati*) due to the instruction that this entails a heavy penance. Consequently, he must perform the penance for one who has fallen. As it is said: "Eating forbidden food or what should not be eaten, along with six other acts, are equal to drinking liquor" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.256). 5.19.
Having unknowingly eaten these six, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance or the Yati-Cāndrāyaṇa; for the remaining [forbidden foods], one should fast for a day.

Regarding the phrase "amatyet" (if one eats unintentionally): having intentionally eaten these six items beginning with mushrooms (*chatrāka*), one should perform either the *sāntapana* penance lasting seven days or the *yaticāndrāyaṇa*, because the eating of the named items serves as the occasion for the rite and their simultaneous occurrence is not intended to be significant. For the consumption of each of the other substances, such as the resin of red trees, one should fast for a day and night. The reduction in the penance for mushrooms and the rest is for the purpose of showing special regard for their avoidance; otherwise, the rule "one should fast for a day for the remainder" would have been stated for the sake of brevity. For if that were applied here, the mention of "red resin" (*lohitaniryāsa*) would also have had to be included. (5.20)

An excellent twice-born man should perform even a single *kṛcchra* penance for the sake of purifying food eaten unknowingly; however, it must be performed especially for food known [to have been forbidden]. (5.21)

Regarding the phrase "of the year": the term *dvijottama* refers to the twice-born (*dvijāti*), because the three [castes] are the subject under discussion and because of the concluding summary, "This has been stated for the twice-born" (5.26). A twice-born person should perform at least one *kṛcchra* penance—specifically that called *prājāpatya*, due to its mention first—within the course of a year to pacify the fault of eating what was unintentionally consumed. However, for the fault of intentionally consuming forbidden food, one should perform specifically that expiation which is prescribed for that particular case. As for the verse: "The gods ordained three purifiers for the Brahmins..."

"That which is unseen, that which is cleansed with water, and that which is praised by word" (MDh 5.127) refers specifically to particular methods of purifying objects, distinct from the expiations prescribed in the section on the purification of substances. 5.21.
Now, in connection with the topic of eating, he permits even violence for the sake of sacrifice and so forth:

"Commendable wild animals and birds are to be killed by Brahmins for the sake of sacrifice; likewise, for the sake of the livelihood of dependents, Agastya indeed practiced this in ancient times. (5.22)

"Regarding the phrase 'for the sake of sacrifice': deer and birds that are praised and prescribed by the scriptures for the purpose of sacrifice by Brāhmaṇas and others may be killed; as well as for the sake of nourishing dependents who must necessarily be supported, such as aged parents and so forth. For the sage Agastya did so in former times. This is a descriptive restatement (anuvāda) of what is natural. (5.22)
For in ancient times, during the sacrifices of the seers and the rites of the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, the sacrificial cakes were made from the flesh of wild animals and birds. (5.23)

"They became so," it is said. Since even in ancient times, during sacrifices performed by the ṛṣis, the sacrificial cakes were made with the meat of edible wild animals and birds, therefore, for the sake of sacrifice, wild animals and birds may also be killed by people of the present day.

Whatever food, whether hard or soft, is mixed with oil or fat and is not otherwise censured, that may be eaten even if it has stood overnight; such food becomes like the remains of a sacrificial oblation.

"Whatever [is available]" means: whatever hard or soft food is fit for consumption—such as sweetmeats (*modaka*) and the like, or boiled milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and the like—that is not censurable, meaning free from other forms of damage; even if it has become stale (*paryuṣita*), having been kept overnight, it may be eaten after being mixed with ghee, oil, curd, and so forth. However, it should not be explained that "whatever is already mixed with fat may be eaten even if it is stale," for if that were the case, since the remnants of sacrificial oblation (*haviḥśeṣa*) necessarily involve contact with fat, eating would already be established by the phrase "whatever is mixed with fat" alone, and the phrase "and whatever may be the remnant of a sacrificial oblation" would be redundant. Furthermore, in another *Smṛti* text, the sprinkling of fat is prescribed specifically at the time of eating. And thus says Yama:
That which is mixed with lentils or black gram, as well as that which has become stale,
one should eat after having washed it and sprinkled clarified butter over it.

The remnants of the oblation, such as the *caru* and *puroḍāśa*, even if they have stood overnight, are to be consumed at the time of eating only when they are devoid of contact with oily substances, because of the specific instruction to that effect. (5.24)

Even if it has been kept for a long time, all products derived from barley and wheat, as well as preparations of milk, are pure when not mixed with oil, provided they have been handled by the twice-born. (5.25)

Regarding the phrase "long-standing": even products derived from barley, wheat, and milk that have been stored for many nights may be consumed by the twice-born, provided they are not mixed with oily substances. 5.25.
Thus has been declared in its entirety what is fit and unfit to be eaten by the twice-born;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the rule regarding the eating and the avoidance of meat.

"This has been stated" means: this which pertains to what is edible and what is inedible for the twice-born has been stated; hereafter, I shall describe in its entirety the rules regarding the eating and the avoidance of meat. (5.26)
One may eat meat that has been consecrated by sprinkling, or at the desire of Brahmins, when one is enjoined by rule, or indeed when life is in danger. (5.27)

Regarding the term *prokṣitam* (“consecrated by sprinkling”): the statement “one should eat what is consecrated” may be either an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) or a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*). If it were an exclusion, the meaning of the sentence would be that one must not eat anything other than what is consecrated; however, since that prohibition is already established by the rule “meats not consecrated with [mantras]” (5.7), this cannot be an exclusion. Therefore, this eating of the meat of an animal sacrificed in a rite (*yajña*)—which is characterized by the refinement known as *prokṣaṇa* performed with mantras—is enjoined here as a constituent part of the sacrifice. For this very reason, he will later provide a restatement of the rule “animals not consecrated with mantras” (5.36). Furthermore, when Brāhmaṇas have a desire for it, meat must necessarily be eaten; even then, one should eat it only once, according to the rule of Yama: “once, out of the desire of a Brāhmaṇa. Likewise, at a *śrāddha* and during the *madhuparka*, meat must be eaten by one who is so appointed, because of the *Gṛhya* rule: “the *madhuparka* is not without meat” (1.24). For this same reason, he will later describe the fault of transgression in the verse: “but one who is appointed, according to the rule” (5.35). And in the event of a threat to life—whether caused by the absence of other food or by disease—one must eat meat as a matter of necessity.
He states a restatement regarding the eating of meat in times of life-threatening danger:
"Prajāpati ordained all this as food for the vital breath—both the stationary and the moving; everything is the sustenance of the vital breath. (5.28)

"Food for the vital breath. The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the living soul (*jīva*), the experiencer situated within the body; Brahmā fashioned all this as its food. What is that? He says: everything moving, such as animals, and everything stationary, such as rice and barley—all that is its nourishment. Therefore, for the sake of sustaining the vital breath, the living being may eat meat. 5.28.
“‘All this is food for the vital breath’—thus he elaborates:
the immobile are food for the mobile; those without fangs are food for those with fangs; the handless are food for those with hands; and the timid are food for the brave. (5.29)

Regarding the phrase "of the moving": for the moving, such as deer and the like, the non-moving, such as grass and the like, are the food; for the fanged, such as tigers and the like, the toothless, such as deer and the like, are the food; for the hand-possessing, such as humans and the like, the handless, such as fish and the like, are the food; and for the brave, such as lions and the like, the timid, such as elephants and the like, are the food. Such is the creation of the Creator himself. (5.29)
The eater is not defiled by eating the living beings that are his food, even day after day; for both the eaters and the beings to be eaten were created by the Creator himself. (5.30)

"Nor [is there a fault] for the eater": even if one eats every day those living beings who are fit to be eaten, one incurs no fault, because it was by the Creator himself that both those fit to be eaten and those who eat were ordained. With these three verses, this is a praise of eating meat in cases where life is at stake. (5.30)
Now he states an explanatory passage (arthavāda) regarding the rule for consuming consecrated meat:
"The eating of meat for the sake of sacrifice—this is remembered as the divine ordinance; but activity otherwise than this is called the demonic ordinance. (5.31)

"yajñāya" means for the sake of the success of a sacrifice; the eating—that is, the consumption—of meat that has become an ancillary part of that [sacrifice] is the divine practice. On the other hand, to kill an animal solely for one's own sake and engage in the consumption of its meat in a manner other than what was prescribed is a practice fit for Rākṣasas; thus, the second half of the verse is a restatement (anuvāda) intended to prohibit the consumption of meat for no purpose. (5.31)
Having purchased it, or having produced it oneself, or even having received it from another, one does not incur fault by eating meat after having worshipped the gods and the ancestors. (5.32)

Regarding the word "having purchased": having purchased it oneself, or produced it oneself, or having had it brought and given by someone else, one who gives that meat to the gods and ancestors and eats the remainder incurs no sin. Therefore, like the eating of the four types [of meat] beginning with *prokṣita*, this eating is not an obligatory practice, because of the statement "he is not defiled" (5.30). Furthermore, the rule for the avoidance of meat to be mentioned later—beginning with "year after year with the horse-sacrifice" (5.53)—also pertains specifically to this case, as there is no contradiction. 5.32.

A twice-born man who knows the law should not eat meat contrary to the rule when there is no distress; for by eating meat contrary to the rule, he becomes a ghost and is helplessly devoured by those very creatures. (5.33)

"One should not eat" means that a twice-born person who knows the fault in the practice of eating meat should not consume meat when not in a state of distress, except as prescribed for the worship of various deities and others. For he who eats meat without such prescription, having died, is eaten by those very creatures whose meat he consumed in the next world, being himself unable to protect himself; this is a summary of all the verses. (5.33)
The sin of a hunter seeking wealth who kills deer is not as great as the sin that befalls one who eats meat in vain after death. (5.34)

"It is not like that": the sin incurred by a hunter or similar person who lives by killing deer for the sake of wealth is not of such a kind as the sin that occurs in the next world for one who eats meat that has not been offered to the gods or the ancestors; this is merely a restatement of what was said previously. (5.34)
But that man who, when duly appointed according to the rule, does not eat meat,
goes after death to the state of a beast for twenty-one births.

"But when appointed" (5.35): A man who, having been duly appointed according to the scriptures for a *śrāddha* or a *madhuparka*, does not eat meat, becomes an animal for twenty-one births after he dies. This is the prescription of the fruit resulting from the transgression of the rule stated in the verse: "But when appointed according to the rule" (5.27).
A Brahmin should never eat animals that have not been consecrated with mantras;
however, abiding by the eternal rule, he may eat those consecrated with mantras. (5.36)

"Unrefined" (*asaṃskṛtān*) means that a Brahmin or others should never eat animals that are devoid of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as sprinkling water (*prokṣaṇa*), which are prescribed by the Vedas. One who is established in the eternal—meaning constant due to its beginninglessness in the stream of tradition—sacrificial system of animal sacrifice and the like, should eat only those [animals] consecrated by mantras. This is for the purpose of restating the rule: "One may eat meat that has been consecrated" (5.27). || 5.36 ||
In a time of distress, one may perform an animal sacrifice using clarified butter, or likewise use an animal made of flour;
however, one should never desire to kill an animal in vain.

"One should act" [means this]: out of attachment—that is, an addiction to eating animals—one should make an image of an animal out of ghee or flour and eat it; one should never, however, desire to kill animals even for the sake of a deity or any other purpose. 5.37.
As many hairs as there are on the animal, so many times does the one who slaughters an animal in vain undergo death after passing away, in birth after birth. (5.38)

"Yāvantīti" means: he who kills animals for his own sake, without dedicating them to a deity or other such purpose, is a "vṛthāpaśughna" (one who slaughters animals in vain). Upon dying, he undergoes death in birth after birth as many times as there are hairs on those animals. Therefore, one should not kill an animal in vain. The suffix *kṛtvasuc* is applied here after the word ending in *vat* (*tāvat*) to denote the counting of the repetition of an action. Here, the particle *ha* is used to indicate that this is well-known in traditional scripture (*āgama*). 5.38.
"Beasts were created by the Self-existent One himself for the sake of sacrifice; sacrifice is for the prosperity of this entire world. Therefore, killing in a sacrifice is not killing. (5.39)

"Animals are for the sake of sacrifice. For the purpose of accomplishing sacrifice, Prajāpati himself created animals with great care. And sacrifice, according to the principle of the oblation cast into the fire, is for the sake of the growth of this entire world. Therefore, killing in sacrifice is indeed not killing, because there is an absence of the fault arising from slaughter. (5.39)
Moreover:
"Herbs, cattle, trees, animals, and likewise birds—having met their death for the sake of sacrifice, they attain higher states once again. (5.40)

Regarding the phrase "the herbs": the herbs are rice, barley, and so forth; the animals are goats and so forth; the trees are those intended for sacrificial posts and the like; the reptiles are tortoises and so forth; and the birds are the kapiñjala partridges and so forth. Having met their destruction for the sake of sacrifice, they attain an elevation of birth once again. 5.40.
"Manu has declared that animals may be slain only at the honey-mixture offering, at a sacrifice, and at rites for the ancestors or the gods; not elsewhere. (5.41)

"And in the *madhuparka*. Because of the injunction, "The *madhuparka* contains no meat" (*Gṛhyasūtra* 1.24), Manu has declared that animals are to be slain in the *madhuparka*, in sacrifices such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, and in rites for the ancestors or the gods such as the *Śrāddha*; but not elsewhere. (5.41)
A twice-born man who knows the true meaning of the Veda, when killing animals for these purposes, leads both himself and the animal to the highest state. (5.42)

Regarding the phrase "in these matters": in these matters such as the *madhuparka* offering and so forth, one who harms animals causes both himself and the animal to attain the highest state—a connection with a condition of the body and so on that is distinct from [ordinary states] and suitable for the enjoyment of heaven and other realms. The expression "one who knows the true meaning of the Veda" is intended to indicate that this applies specifically to the learned (*vidvat*).
Now, if the ritual action pertains to another [qualified person], how can the attainment of the highest state as a result accrue to an animal or similar being who is not qualified for the rite?

It is said: because the scripture is the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Just as in the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice—which pertains to the father—the son obtains the fruit even though he lacks the right [to perform the rite], so too here, since the attainment of the fruit residing in the animal is possible, the sacrificer alone, out of compassion, will desire a fruit characterized precisely by the fruit residing in the animal. For this very reason, from the statement "both himself and the animal," it is declared that the accomplishment of the fruit residing in the animal results solely from the activity of the sacrificer. (5.42)
Whether living at home, with his teacher, or in the forest, a self-possessed twice-born man should never practice violence not ordained by the Veda, even in times of distress. (5.43)

"In the house, with the teacher, or in the forest": while dwelling in the householder stage, the student stage, or the forest-dweller stage, a twice-born man of refined soul should not, even in times of distress, practice violence that is contrary to the scriptures. (5.43)
How then is it that, although the nature of violence is the same, Vedic violence such as that involved in the *daikṣa* sacrifice does not lead to demerit? To this he says:
"Whatever violence is ordained by the Veda, restricted to this world of moving and unmoving beings—one should know that very thing to be non-violence; for from the Veda, dharma shone forth. (5.44)

"Whatever is ordained by the Veda": one should know that as non-violence alone which is prescribed by the Śruti, restricted by specific rites, places, times, and so forth, within this world consisting of the moving and the unmoving, because it is devoid of the demerit born of violence. The inference—"The slaughter of the sacrificial animal is unrighteous (adharma), because it is the killing of a living being, like the killing of a Brāhmaṇa"—does not proceed at all due to the sublation of scripture (*śāstra-bādha*). Scripture itself must be relied upon even regarding the unrighteousness of the Brāhmaṇa-slaughter used as the illustrative example. For "Dharma shone forth from the Veda," since Dharma has no other source of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and has been revealed in its entirety from the Veda alone. (5.44)
He who harms harmless beings out of a desire for his own pleasure finds no happiness anywhere, neither while living nor when dead. (5.45)

Regarding the phrase "those who do not harm": he who kills harmless creatures, such as deer and the like, out of a desire for his own pleasure, does not prosper with happiness either in this world or in the next. (5.45)
He who does not desire to inflict upon living beings the afflictions of bondage and death, seeking the welfare of all, attains ultimate happiness. (5.46)

"He who [does not bind]," etc.: he who does not wish to inflict upon living beings the bonds, killing, afflictions, and so forth, being one who desires the attainment of the welfare of all, attains infinite happiness. 5.46.
And furthermore:
Whatever one meditates upon, whatever one does, and toward whatever one fixes one's resolve—that one obtains without effort, provided that one harms nothing at all. (5.47)

Regarding the phrase "that which he meditates upon": whatever he thinks of, such as [the attainment of] dharmas and so forth, thinking "may this be mine," and whatever action conducive to the highest good he performs, and wherein he fixes his resolve—such as in the meditation on ultimate reality—he obtains all that without affliction; he does not even harm gadflies, mosquitoes, or the like, for the sake of causing injury. (5.47)
Having explained the merits and faults of violence in connection with the practice of eating meat, he speaks again regarding the original subject, the non-eating of meat:
"Meat is never produced without having committed violence against living beings; and the slaughter of living beings does not lead to heaven. Therefore, one should avoid meat. (5.48)

"Without having performed [an act]" means that meat is never produced except through the harming of living beings. And the killing of living beings is not a cause for heaven; rather, it is solely a cause for hell. Therefore, one should not eat meat in a manner contrary to the rule. 5.48.
Having carefully considered the origin of meat and the killing and binding of embodied beings, one should desist from the consumption of all meat. (5.49)

"And as for its origin": having understood that the origin [of beings] consists of the transformation of semen and blood—a process that inspires revulsion—and having observed that the killing and binding of living beings are of the nature of cruel acts, one should desist even from the consumption of meat that has been prescribed, let alone from the consumption of meat that is not prescribed; thus is reiterated the censure of consuming meat contrary to the rules. (5.49)
He who does not eat meat, even though following the [customary] rule, like a *piśāca*, becomes beloved in the world and is not afflicted by diseases. (5.50)

"He does not eat" means he who does not eat meat apart from the aforementioned rules. "Like a *piśāca*" is an example by way of contrast (*vyatireka*); it means that he does not eat in the manner that a *piśāca* eats. He becomes dear to the world and is not afflicted by diseases. Thus, it is shown that diseases arise from the non-scriptural eating of meat. 5.50
The consenter, the butcher, the slayer, the buyer and seller, the preparer, the server, and the eater—all these are killers. (5.51)

"Consent": he who is the consenter is one without whose consent killing cannot be performed; the butcher is he who separates the limbs with a knife or similar instrument; the buyer and seller of meat are the purchaser and the vendor of the flesh; the preparer is the cook; the server is the waiter; and the eater is the consumer. Govindarāja, however, says that "the buyer and seller" refers to a single person who, having bought, sells [meat]; that is incorrect, for the killer is such by virtue of the act of killing, while the buyer is such by virtue of the money.
The seller [is at fault] because of the non-payment of the price, while the preparer [is at fault] because of the promotion of that [act].

Because of this separate mention in the words of Yama, the statement regarding the "slayer" is intended to show that even consent and the like should not be given for the slaughter of animals not sanctioned by the scriptures, since the scripture is devoted to injunctions and prohibitions, and because penances are seen to be prescribed separately for the eaters and others. (5.51)
There is no doer of greater demerit than he who desires to increase his own flesh with the flesh of another, without having first honored the ancestors and the gods. (5.52)

"His own flesh": he who wishes to bring his own body's flesh to increase without honoring the gods, ancestors, and others with the flesh of another—there is no doer of unmeritorious acts other than him; this is a restatement of the censure of eating meat contrary to the rules. (5.52)
Now, in order to show that the cessation of the unrestricted and unprohibited eating of meat leads to spiritual merit (*dharma*), he says:
“He who might perform the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) every year for a hundred years, and he who does not eat meat—the merit and fruit of these two are equal. (5.53)

"Year by year": the fruit of the merit of one who might perform the horse sacrifice every year for a hundred years and that of one who does not eat meat for as long as he lives are equal, such as heaven and the like. (5.53)
One does not obtain that fruit by subsisting on pure fruits and roots, nor by eating the food of sages, which one obtains from the total avoidance of meat. (5.54)

Regarding the phrase "by eating fruits and roots": one does not obtain that fruit which one gains by abstaining from meat that is neither prescribed nor forbidden by the scriptures, even by subsisting on the pure fruits and roots of forest-dwellers or by eating the grains such as *nīvāra* that are the food of those in the forest-hermitage stage (*vānaprastha*). || 5.54 ||
"He who eats my flesh here shall eat me in the next world;
the wise declare this to be the 'meat-ness' of meat. (5.55)

"He shall devour me. "In this world, he whose flesh I eat shall devour me in the next world"—this is what the wise proclaim as the etymological derivation (*nirukta*) of the word *māṃsa* (flesh). This definition of the word *māṃsa* is intended to refute the sinful fruit resulting from the consumption of forbidden meat. 5.55.
There is no fault in eating meat, nor in liquor, nor in sexual intercourse; this is the natural inclination of living beings, but abstention from them yields great fruit. (5.56)

Regarding the phrase "not the eating of meat": for the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, there is no fault whatsoever in the eating of things that are neither prescribed nor forbidden according to their respective entitlements. This is because the inclination of living beings toward eating, drinking, sexual intercourse, and so forth, is a natural law (*svābhāviko dharma*). However, abstaining from them yields great fruit. This [verse] is a restatement of the previously mentioned teaching on the great fruit of abstaining from meat, intended to state that the desisting from wine and sexual intercourse—which are neither prescribed nor forbidden—is likewise of great fruit.
I shall now declare the purification of the deceased as well as the purification of objects, for all four castes, duly and in their proper order. (5.57)

"Regarding 'the purification after death' (pretaśuddhi): I shall describe the purification of the four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, for deceased ancestors and others according to their respective order; as well as the purification of substances such as those made of metal and so forth. (5.57)

In that regard, since purity is dependent upon impurity, he speaks in order to define it: "When one has died after the eruption of teeth, after the subsequent growth of teeth, or after the performance of the tonsure ceremony, all relatives are impure; the same is declared regarding birth (sūtaka). (5.58)

Regarding the term *dantajāta*: "one whose teeth have appeared" means one who has grown teeth. The word *jāta* is placed at the end of the compound by the rule *vāhitāgnyādiṣu* (Pāṇini 2.2.37). *Anujāta* refers to one immediately following the appearance of teeth. When one who has had the *cūḍākaraṇa* performed—and by the force of the word "and," one for whom the *upanayana* has been performed—has passed away (*saṃsthita*), the kinsmen, both *sapiṇḍas* and *samānodakas*, become impure (*aśuddha*). It is stated that they likewise become impure upon birth (*prasava*). This is merely a classification according to age, intended for the sake of easily understanding the distinctions in the periods of impurity (*āśauca*) that will be described hereafter. (5.58)
Impurity on account of a death is ordained for ten days among the sapindas;
it lasts for three days until the collection of the bones, or for one day. (5.59)

“Ten days”: he will later state that *sapiṇḍa* status extends up to the seventh generation. For *sapiṇḍas*, impurity (*āśauca*) caused by a corpse is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa as ten days and nights, because it will be stated later: “A Brāhmaṇa becomes pure in ten days” (5.83). The phrase “prior to the collection of the bones” is an elliptical expression for four days; for Viṣṇu states: “On the fourth day, one should perform the collection of the bones. Thus, [the period may be] three days or one day. The word *ahaḥ* refers to a full day and night (*ahorātra*). This is a regulated option depending on qualities such as [mastery of] the sacred fires and the Vedas, as Dakṣa says (6.6): [text follows].
A Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires and possesses the Vedas is purified in one day;
if he lacks these, the period shall be progressively longer—three days, and likewise four days for those even more deficient.

For one who maintains the *śrauta* fires and studies the entire branch (*śākhā*) consisting of both the *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa* portions, the impurity lasts for one day. Among these, one who lacks one of the two qualities—maintaining the *śrauta* fires or studying the Veda—is "inferior" (*hīna*), and his impurity lasts for three days; one who lacks both qualities is "more inferior" (*hīnatara*), as is one who possesses only the *smārta* fires, whose impurity lasts four days; and for one devoid of all these qualities, it lasts ten days. Thus says Parāśara (PārSm 3.5): "One devoid of qualities [is purified] in ten days. (5.59)
He states the definition of sapinda-relationship:
"The sapinda-status ceases with the seventh person; however, the status of being a samānodaka (distant kinsman) persists as long as there is knowledge of the birth and the name. (5.60)

Regarding the phrase "sapiṇḍatā tu" (but sapinda-relationship): taking a particular person as the counter-correlate, once one has passed beyond six generations beginning with his grandfather, sapinda-relationship ceases upon reaching the seventh generation. This should be understood in the same way for sons, grandsons, and so forth. This sapinda-relationship is based on the connection through the *piṇḍa* (funeral cake). For instance—there is the offering of *piṇḍas* to the three ancestors, namely the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather; the three descendants of the great-grandfather, namely his father and so on, are the partakers of the smearings (*lepa*) of the *piṇḍas*; but for the seventh ancestor prior to that, there is no connection to the *piṇḍas*, and thus there is no sapinda-relationship. These six persons are the sapindas of that [seventh] person, and he too is their sapinda, because of the connection to those *piṇḍas* by virtue of being the offerer of the *piṇḍas*. Therefore, sapinda-relationship extends to seven generations. Thus it is stated in the Matsya Purāṇa: [The text continues with the citation from the Matsya Purāṇa.]
The fourth and subsequent generations are partakers of the unguent; the father and subsequent ancestors are partakers of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa).
The giver of the cake is the seventh among them; thus, the sapinda relationship extends for seven generations.
And this sapinda relationship exists only when there is a common lineage (gotra). For this very reason, Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"The sapinda relationship for all [persons] extends to seven generations on the basis of lineage.

Consequently, although the maternal grandfather and others share a connection through the same funeral oblation (piṇḍa), they do not possess the status of sapinda. Furthermore, the status of being a *samānodaka* (one who shares the water libation) ceases when both the family name and the personal name—such as "there was one named so-and-so in our family"—are no longer known. (5.60)
Just as this impurity on account of death is prescribed for the sapindas, so too should it be in the case of birth for those who desire complete purity. (5.61)

"Just as this" means: just as this impurity (*āśauca*) caused by a corpse—characterized by unfitness for ritual acts (*karmānarhatva*)—is prescribed for *sapiṇḍas* for ten days and so forth by the rule "impurity on account of a corpse lasts ten days" (5.59), so too would such impurity apply to *sapiṇḍas* who desire complete purification even after a birth. 5.61.
When equality has been established through the fact that [impurity] cannot be specifically defined, he states the distinction:
"The impurity for all is *śāva* (due to death), but for the mother and father it is *sūtaka* (due to birth).
The *sūtaka* belongs to the mother alone; the father becomes pure by performing ritual ablution. (5.62)

Regarding the phrase "of all": the impurity characterized by untouchability caused by death is common to all *sapiṇḍas* alike. However, that caused by birth pertains only to the mother and the father. Even therein, the distinction is as follows: the untouchability caused by birth lasts for ten nights for the mother alone; the father, however, becomes touchable after bathing. This very relationship has been made explicit by Saṃvarta:
"When a son is born, a bath with one's clothes on is prescribed for the father;
the mother becomes pure after ten days, but the father may touch [her] after bathing."
But having emitted semen, a man becomes pure simply by sipping water;
however, due to the connection arising from seed, he should observe impurity for three days.

Regarding the phrase "having cast out" (*nirasya*): by stating, "Bathing is prescribed for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse" (5.144), he will enjoin bathing in the case of coitus; therefore, even without coitus, a man becomes pure after bathing when there is an intentional emission of semen. However, in the case of an unintentional emission during sleep or similar circumstances, purity is attained by the householder even without bathing, according to the statement of Āpastamba: "The discharge of semen is like that of urine. For a religious student (*brahmacārin*), however, even in the case of an unintentional emission, purification through bathing and other means is prescribed by the rule: "Having emitted [semen] in sleep, a religious student... (2.181). But in the case of a "seed-connection" (*baijika*)—that is, the procreation of offspring with a wife who previously belonged to another—the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts for three days. And so says Viṣṇu: "In the case of wives who previously belonged to another, [the impurity lasts] for three nights. Although the impurity of those who emit semen was not the primary subject under discussion, it has been mentioned here incidentally in the section on birth, as it is related to that topic. Where bathing is required merely for the emission of semen, it is appropriate that there be a three-night period of impurity upon the birth of an offspring. (5.63)
Those who touch a corpse are purified in one day and night, and those who carry water for three nights; those who offer water are purified after three days. (5.64)

"By one day" means by one day and one night—that is, by a full day and night. "By three nights" means by nine days and nights combined; thus, it is said with ingenuity that it is "by ten days. Now, one might ask: since it should simply have been said "by ten days," what is the purpose of this elaborate verbal expression?
It is replied: "The eloquent fashion their speech either most grandly or most briefly;
yet they are not bound by necessity to be restricted to brevity alone."

Those sapinda relatives who, by virtue of their conduct, Vedic study, or other merits, are entitled to only a short period of impurity, such as one day, if they touch a corpse out of affection or similar motives, they become pure only after ten days. As for those who offer water, namely the samānodakas, they are purified in three days. Govindarāja, however, states that this ten-day impurity refers specifically to Brahmin relatives who carry out the removal of a corpse in exchange for receiving wealth. (5.64)
But a disciple performing the funeral rites for his deceased guru becomes pure after ten nights, together with those who carry the corpse. || 5.65 ||

"Of the guru" (guror iti): Having performed the funeral rites for a deceased teacher, preceptor, or similar person who is not a sapinda relative, the disciple becomes pure after ten nights, being equal to those sapinda relatives of the guru who carry out the removal of the corpse. || 5.65 ||
In the case of a miscarriage, a woman is purified in as many nights as there were months of pregnancy;
once her menstrual flow has ceased, a virtuous woman who has become soiled by menses is purified by bathing. (5.66)

Regarding the phrase "by nights": here, because the plurality inherent in the predicate "by nights" is intended to be significant, and because a specific rule is stated for miscarriages from the third month onwards—namely, that women of the four castes are purified by a number of days and nights equal to the months of gestation—this applies up until the sixth month. As it is said in the *Ādi-purāṇa*:
"If a miscarriage should occur within six months, then their purification is held to be by days equal to the [number of] months."
But beyond this, the impurity prescribed for their respective castes applies to them.

Medhātithi, Govindarāja, and others, however, because they do not find a specific statement in the Ādipurāṇa, extend the rule by analogy: "In the case of a miscarriage occurring before seven months, the purification for women is by means of days and nights equal to the number of months. In the case of a miscarriage during the first or second month, the purification for women is three nights. As Hārīta says: "In the case of a miscarriage, the purification for women is three nights, because of the particular nature of the menstrual flow; but for the paternal *sapiṇḍas* and others, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) in this instance. As Sumantu says: "The days [of impurity] are equal to the months of pregnancy, or there may be immediate purification. This is a settled option: the rule regarding "days equal to the months of pregnancy" refers to the woman herself, while "or immediate purification" refers to the paternal *sapiṇḍas* and others. Furthermore, a menstruating woman becomes fit for rites intended for transcendental results (*adṛṣṭārtha*) on the fifth day after her flow has ceased, through bathing. She becomes fit for physical contact, however, on the fourth day after the three nights have passed, being purified simply by that bath. (5.66)
For men whose tonsure ceremony has not been performed, purification is declared to take one night;
but for those whose tonsure has been completed, purification is held to occur after three nights. (5.67)

Regarding the phrase "of men": upon the death of children who have not yet had the tonsure ceremony (cūḍā), the purification for the sapindas occurs after one day and night. However, upon the death of those who have had the tonsure ceremony but before their initiation (upanayana), purification occurs after three nights. (5.67)

Relatives should place a deceased child who has not yet reached two years of age outside [the village], having adorned it and buried it in clean ground, except for the rite of collecting the bones. 5.68.

"Less than two years old": when a child who has not yet completed two years of age dies before the *cūḍākaraṇa* (tonsure) ceremony, the relatives, having adorned him with garlands and other ornaments, should carry him outside the village and cast him upon pure ground; after some time, once the body has decayed, they may discard him there—excluding the collection of bones—as it is no longer possible [to perform the rites]. Viśvarūpa, however, explains: "They should place him on that ground where the collection of bones for another person has not been performed. (5.68)
No funeral rites with fire should be performed for him, nor should the water-libation ceremony be performed;
having abandoned him like a log in the forest, one should pass only three days in mourning. 5.69.

"Of this one"—for this child less than two years of age, neither cremation with fire nor the water-rite (*udakakriyā*) should be performed. This prohibition of the offering of water is intended to exclude all funeral rites for the deceased, such as the *śrāddha* and so forth. Rather, having abandoned the child like a log in the forest—"like a log" expresses the absence of grief. Just as there is no grief when a log is abandoned in the forest, so too, having thus abandoned him, one should pass three days, that is, observe the impurity (*āśauca*) for three days. And this rule of three days' impurity for one whose tonsure (*cūḍā*) has not been performed is an alternative to the previously mentioned one-day impurity. That [one-day period] is settled: it is one day for one endowed with good conduct, Vedic study, and so forth; for one lacking those, it is three days. Although Manu has prescribed merely abandonment, nevertheless, according to Yājñavalkya’s statement, "One less than two years old should be buried" (YDh 3.1), he should be abandoned only after being buried in pure ground. (5.69)
The ritual offering of water should not be performed by relatives for one who has not reached three years of age;
however, they may perform it once the child’s teeth have appeared, or when the naming ceremony has been completed.

"Nor for one under three years of age": although it was previously prohibited that water-rites (*udakakriyā*) should not be performed by the *sapiṇḍas*, such as the father, for one who has not reached his third year, this is restated here for the sake of what follows. Alternatively, the offering of water should be performed for one whose teeth have emerged, or once the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) has been performed; since these are mentioned in conjunction with the water-rite, the cremation (*agnisaṃskāra*) is also merely permitted. And although performing the funeral rice-ball (*pretapiṇḍa*), the *śrāddha*, and so forth might be troublesome when their omission is possible, nevertheless, because both performance and non-performance are prescribed for those whose teeth have emerged and who have been named, it is understood that by performing them there is benefit for the deceased, while by not performing them there is no transgression (*pratyavāya*).
If a fellow religious student has died, purification is prescribed after one day;
however, for those who offer water libations together at a single birth, purity is held to occur after three nights. (5.71)

Regarding the term *sabrahmacāriṇī*: when a fellow student (*sahādhyāyin*) has died, one must observe impurity for one night. Furthermore, when a son is born among those who share the same ancestral water (*samānodaka*), purification occurs after three nights. The rule "after three days [is the purification] for those who offer water" (5.64) was stated with reference to the subject of death. 5.71.
But for the kinsmen of women who have not been consecrated [by marriage], purification occurs after three days;
however, those of the same lineage (sanābhayaḥ) are purified according to the very rule already stated.

Regarding the phrase "of women": when unmarried women who have been betrothed (*vāgdattā*) die, their relatives on the husband’s side, such as the husband himself and others, become pure after three days (*tryaha*). Since there is no kinship on the husband’s side prior to the betrothal, it should be understood—even though not explicitly stated—that this rule applies up until the point of the betrothal. As for the "blood relations" (*sanābhayaḥ*) on the father’s side, when those betrothed women die before marriage, they become pure by the very same procedure mentioned [in the] first half of this verse, namely, by the three-night period. This has been stated in the *Ādi-purāṇa*: "If a girl dies anywhere from birth until the end of the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*)," [the rule follows].
In that case, immediate purification shall always apply to all castes.
Therefore, up until the giving of the bride in marriage, it lasts for only one day;
beyond that, for those who have reached adulthood, the settled rule is three nights.

But when the giving of the word has been performed there, it should be known that for three days both the father and the groom [are impure]; thereafter, however, for those who have been given away, it belongs only to the husband.
The impurity (aśauca) in both death and birth shall be as prescribed for one's own caste.

However, Medhātithi and Govindarāja explain that [the verse] "by the aforementioned rule" means they become pure according to the procedure stated in the rule beginning with "of men whose tonsure has not been performed. According to this interpretation, in the case of a daughter as well, there would be three days of impurity upon her death after the performance of the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*), just as in the case of a son; yet this contradicts numerous statements from the *Ādityapurāṇa* and other sources. (5.72)
They should eat food that is neither pungent nor salty, and they should immerse themselves in water for three days;
they should not eat meat, and they should sleep separately on the ground. (5.73)

Regarding the term *akṣāra*: they should eat food free from alkaline salt—that is, artificial salt—and for three nights they should perform ritual bathing in a river or similar body of water; they should not consume meat, and they should sleep alone on the ground. (5.73)
The rule for impurity due to death has indeed been proclaimed for when one is present;
this procedure for relatives and kinsmen is to be understood as applying when one is absent. (5.74)

Regarding the phrase "in the vicinity": this rule for impurity due to death (*śāvāśauca*) has been stated for when the day [of death] is known because the deceased was situated in one place in their vicinity. When there is no knowledge [of the day] because they were situated in another country, this rule which is about to be stated must be understood by the relatives and kinsmen. The *saṃbandhin* are the *sapiṇḍas*; the *bāndhavas* are the *samānodakas*. (5.74)
But he who hears that one who has gone abroad has died within the ten-day period shall remain impure for only as long as the remainder of those ten days may be. 5.75.

Regarding the term *vigatam* (departed): one who hears that a kinsman has departed—meaning deceased, residing in a foreign land, or situated in a distant region—and that the ten-day period of impurity (*āśauca*) has not yet elapsed, remains impure for as long as the remainder of those ten days or other such period may be. The term *vigatam* is illustrative; this should be understood to apply to birth as well. Thus says Bṛhaspati: "Upon hearing of a kinsman who has died in another country, or of the birth of a son, if the ten-day period has not passed, one becomes pure by means of the remaining days."
When ten days have passed, one shall remain impure for three nights;
but when a year has elapsed, one becomes pure simply by touching water.
Regarding the phrase "having passed":

according to the statement of Devala, "There is no impurity for childbirth even when the days have elapsed," this statement concerns the subject of death. When the ten-day period of impurity following the death of a *sapiṇḍa* has passed, one remains impure for three nights; however, if a full year has passed, one becomes pure simply by bathing. Since this is stated without qualification, it applies to all four social classes (*cāturvarṇya*). (5.76)
Upon hearing of the death of a relative after the ten-day period has passed, or of the birth of a son, a man becomes pure by immersing himself in water along with his clothes. || 5.77 ||

"Beyond ten days": since it has been stated that after the lapse of the ten-day period of impurity (*āśauca*), there remains a three-day impurity characterized by unfitness for ritual acts, this [rule] refers to the matter of not touching those who are part of that subsidiary [impurity]. Having heard of the death of a *sapiṇḍa* relative beyond ten days, and having heard of the birth of a son, one becomes touchable after bathing with one's clothes on. (5.77)
If a child, a person residing in another country, or one who has entered a separate lineage (pṛthakpiṇḍa) dies,
one becomes pure immediately after immersing oneself in water along with one's clothes.

Regarding the term "infant" (*bāla*): when an infant who has not yet cut its teeth dies, or when a person whose teeth have been cut but who has not yet had the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*) dies—according to [the rule] "for men who have not had the tonsure" (5.67)—which prescribes one day and night; and when a *sapiṇḍa* residing in another country dies, these are cases for which a single day’s impurity (*ekāha-āśauca*) applies. Since the previous verse prescribed a three-day period for those subject to ten days of impurity, a three-night period was stated for a *samānodaka* relative who offers a separate funeral ball (*pṛthak-piṇḍa*). Upon the lapse of those three nights, having bathed with one's clothes on (*sacaila*), one becomes immediately purified in all these cases. (5.78)
If death and birth should occur again within ten days, the Brahmin shall remain impure for as long as that [second] period has not yet reached its tenth day. (5.79)

Regarding the phrase "within ten days": if, during the midst of a ten-day period or similar duration, there should again occur a death or a birth—since the word "again" implies a recurrence of the same kind—then for that same length of time, a Brāhmaṇa or other [caste] shall remain impure. The meaning is that as long as the initial impurity of the ten days or other period has not yet passed, purification occurs only upon the cessation of the first impurity, even in the case of a second death or birth. (5.79)
They say that when an Ācārya has died, the period of impurity lasts for three nights;
likewise for his son and his wife, it is one day and night—this is the settled rule. (5.80)

"Three nights": when the teacher has died, they declare that the student's period of impurity lasts for three nights; and when his son or wife have died, it lasts for one day and night—this is the boundary of the sacred law. 5.80.
Upon the death of a learned Śrotriya who has arrived as a guest, one shall remain impure for three nights;
likewise for a maternal uncle, a pupil, an officiating priest, or a kinsman, for a night with its two flanking days (pakṣiṇī).

Regarding the term *śrotriya*: it refers to one who has studied the Vedic scriptures and is endowed with [virtue], such as friendliness, and resides in his proximity; the meaning is that she lives in his house. When he dies, one becomes pure after three nights. In the case of a maternal uncle, a sacrificial priest (*ṛtvij*), a pupil (*śiṣya*), and others, the impurity lasts for a "two-night" period (*pakṣiṇīrātri*). That which spans two days—the preceding and the following—constitutes a "two-night" period. (5.81)
When the king has died, one who resides within his realm remains impure for as long as the light [of the sun] lasts;
but if the king is not learned in the Vedas, the impurity lasts for a full day, as does that for a teacher who is well-versed in the scriptures.

Regarding the rule for a deceased king: when a consecrated Kṣatriya king, in whose realm a Brāhmaṇa or others reside, has died, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) shall last as long as the light (*sajyotis*). That which exists together with light is called *sajyotis*. If he dies by day, then the impurity lasts as long as the light of the sun; if he dies at night, then the impurity lasts as long as the light of the stars. For a *Śrotriya* (one learned in the Veda), a three-night period has been prescribed. However, if one who is not a *Śrotriya* dies in his house, the impurity lasts for the entire duration of the day only, and not even into the night. It should be understood that if he dies at night, it lasts only through that night. Even in the case of a teacher (*guru*) defined by the verse, "Whether little or much [of the Veda] he has studied" (2.149)—that is, one who has studied the Veda along with its auxiliary branches—the impurity lasts for only a single day. 5.82.
A Brahmin is purified in ten days, a Kṣatriya in twelve days, a Vaiśya in fifteen days, and a Śūdra is purified in a month. (5.83)

"One shall be purified": upon the death of a *sapiṇḍa* who has been initiated (*upanīta*), or upon a birth occurring within the full period [of impurity], a Brāhmaṇa who has completed his studies but lacks other [qualifications] becomes pure after ten days; a Kṣatriya after twelve days; a Vaiśya after fifteen days; and a Śūdra after a month. And for him, marriage takes the place of initiation (*upanayana*). (5.83)
One should not prolong the days of impurity, nor should one obstruct the rites performed with the sacred fires; and while performing that rite, even a kinsman does not become impure. (5.84)

"One should not extend [the period]" means that one who, due to considerations such as his conduct or Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), has previously been told of a contraction of the impurity period—such as in the rule "prior to the collection of the bones" (5.59)—should not, with the thought "I shall remain at ease while free from ritual duties," extend the days of impurity beyond the ten-day period or other such durations, even during those days when the period was contracted. Regarding the word "fires" (*agniṣu*) in the plural, one should not cause an interruption of the *agnihotra* oblations in the *śrauta* fires. One should perform them oneself, or, if unable, have them performed by a son or others. He states the reason for this very point: because a sapinda relative, such as a son, who performs that rite in the form of the *agnihotra*, does not become impure. As Pāraskara says: "The obligatory rites are suspended, with the exception of those pertaining to the *vaitāna* [sacrificial fires]. The *vaitāna* is the *śrauta* oblation; it is so called because it is performed by spreading out the fires situated in the *gārhapatya* hearth into the *āhavanīya* and other hearths. Likewise, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "For the sake of the *agnihotra*, one is pure through bathing and touching water. Jābāla also says:
In the event of the loss of a birth (or death), there is no lapse of ritual duty regarding the canopy;
however, the homa sacrifice must be performed exclusively in the domestic fire by those belonging to other gotras.
The *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* also states:
"During a period of impurity (*mṛtaka*), the abandonment of rituals such as the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) is prescribed;
however, the fire-oblation (*homa*) in the *śrauta* fires must still be performed, even with dry food or fruits."

Therefore, when there is a reduction of the period of impurity (*āśauca*) to one day, three days, or the like, only the *saṃdhyā* prayers and similar rites are to be abandoned, but not the *śrauta* fire-oblation (*homa*). However, upon the lapse of those one or three days, everything—including the *saṃdhyā*, the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), and so forth—must be performed. Consequently, that which was asserted otherwise by Medhātithi and Govindarāja—namely, "This reduction of impurity to one or three days applies only to the *homa* and Vedic study (*svādhyāya*); however, even for him, the *saṃdhyā* worship and other such rites must not be performed for ten days"—is without authority. As for the fact that Gautama (GDh 14.9) stated, "And for kings, because of the conflict with their duties, and for a Brāhmaṇa, so that his Vedic study may not cease," and Yājñavalkya (YDh 3.28) stated, "For officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and those who have been initiated (*dīkṣita*)," etc., and thus prescribed immediate purity (*sadyaḥśauca*), that refers to specific ritual contexts for all those who are subject to the ten-day period of impurity and the like. Furthermore, as for those statements found in both [texts] regarding the ten-day period—such as "one should not eat the food of the family" and others—which prohibit specific acts for ten days, they pertain to the context of the ten-day impurity; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. Therefore, the claim that "the lightening of impurity is for the sake of the *homa* and Vedic study alone, while [full] *saṃdhyā* worship is for [other] purposes" is without authority. || 5.84 ||
Having touched a professional bard, a woman in her courses, an outcast, a woman who has recently given birth, a corpse, or one who has touched a corpse, one becomes pure by bathing. 5.85.

Regarding the word "divā" (by day): having touched a *caṇḍāla*, a woman in her menses (*rajasvalā*), one who has killed a Brahmin (*brahmahā*) and the like, a woman within ten days of childbirth, a corpse, or one who has touched a corpse, one becomes pure by bathing. Some, however, connect the term "one who has touched them" (*tatspṛṣṭinam*) with all [the preceding categories], including the *caṇḍāla* and the woman in her menses. Govindarāja, however, on the basis of Yājñavalkya’s statement, says that "one who has touched them" refers only to one who has touched a corpse, and not to one who has touched a woman in her menses and so forth, because for the latter, the rule for sipping water (*ācamana*) is prescribed. Thus says Yājñavalkya (YDh 3.30): "One should bathe after being touched by those who are in their menses or impure; if touched by those [who have themselves been touched], one should merely sip water."

One touched by a woman in her courses or by those who are impure should bathe; however, one touched by those who have themselves been touched by such persons should merely sip water and perform the ritual rinsing (ācamana). 5.85.
Having sipped water and being purified, he should always mutter, upon seeing something impure, solar mantras according to his enthusiasm and the *pāvamānī* verses according to his ability. (5.86)

"Having sipped water": one who desires to perform the worship of the deities of the *śrāddha* and other rites, being purified by bathing, sipping water, and so forth, should—upon seeing an impurity such as a *caṇḍāla* mentioned in the present context—recite, according to his ability, mantras dedicated to the Sun such as "Upwards that Jātavedas" (*ud u tyaṃ jātavedasam*, RV 1.4.7), as well as the *pāvamānī* verses, to the best of his capacity. 5.86.
Having touched a human bone that is still moist with fat, a Brahmin becomes pure by bathing;
however, if it is free of fat, he is purified simply by sipping water (ācamana) and then touching a cow or looking at the sun. (5.87)

"Regarding 'not a man' (nāram): having touched human bone combined with fat, a Brāhmaṇa or others become pure by bathing; however, having touched it when devoid of fat, one becomes pure by sipping water (ācamana) and performing either the touching of a cow or the gazing at the sun. (5.87) "One who has been initiated [for a vow] shall not offer water libations until the completion of the vow."
But when [the period] is completed, having performed the water-libation, one becomes pure after exactly three nights. || 5.88 ||

"Ādiṣṭī" means one who has received instruction (*ādeśana*). A student (*brahmacārī*) is so called because he possesses that instruction; such a person should not perform the water-libation for the deceased until the completion of his vow. The term "water" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the entire range of funeral rites for the deceased, including the filling of the water-vessel, the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*), the sixteen *śrāddhas*, and so forth. Once his period of studentship is completed, however, having performed the water-libation for the deceased and observed impurity (*āśauca*) for three nights, he becomes pure. And this applies to cases other than those involving his mother, father, or teacher. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "For a student, there is a cessation from his vows due to the performance of funeral rites for the dead, except in the case of his mother, father, or guru. By "funeral rites for the dead," he means the rites occasioned by a corpse, beginning with the carrying out, cremation, and offering of water, followed by the offering of the rice-ball and the sixteen *śrāddhas*. And he will state later: "His own teacher, or his sub-teacher... (5.91).
The water-libation ceremony shall be withheld for those born of illicit unions, for those who persist in heretical ascetic orders, and for those who commit suicide. (5.89)

Regarding the word "vṛthā" (in vain): it is connected with each [term] individually. For those born in vain—meaning those who have for the most part abandoned their own dharma, those of mixed birth (*saṃkarajāta*), those born of low-caste men from superior women, and those who abide in heretical ascetic orders such as the red-robed Buddhists and others; and for those who intentionally commit suicide by means not sanctioned by the scriptures, such as through poison or hanging—the rites of water and so forth must not be performed. (5.89)
And for women who have resorted to heretical sects, those who act according to their lust, those who harm the fetus or their husband, and those who drink liquor; || 5.90 ||

Regarding the term *pāṣaṇḍa*: heresy (*pāṣaṇḍa*) refers to the practice of vows such as those of the red-robed outsiders to the Veda or those wearing girdles of muñja grass. For twice-born women who follow such heretical practices—who act according to their own will by having relations with one or many men, who cause abortions or commit the murder of their husbands, and who drink liquor—the water-libation rites and the funeral ceremonies shall be withheld; this is how it connects with the preceding [verse]. (5.90)
Having carried out the funeral rites for one's own teacher, sub-teacher, father, mother, or preceptor who has passed away, the one observing a vow is not deprived of his vow. 5.91

Regarding the term *ācārya*: an *ācārya* is one who, preceded by the initiation (*upanayana*), teaches the complete Vedic branch (*śākhā*); an *upādhyāya* is a teacher of a single portion of the Veda or of its auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*); and a *guru* is the expounder of the Veda or even a single portion of the Vedas. Since the funeral rites (*pretakṛtya*) are preceded by the carrying out of the corpse (*nirharaṇa*), the phrase "having carried out" (*nirhṛtya*) is intended to indicate the entirety of the funeral rites, such as cremation, the ten-day period, the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), and the sixteen *śrāddha* offerings. Thus, by carrying out the corpses of these five—the *ācārya* and the others—the student does not become one whose vow is broken (*luptavrata*). It is understood from this that by carrying out the corpses of others, a breach of the vow (*vratalopa*) occurs. Because of the expression "his own *ācārya*" (*svam ācāryam*), according to the principle that "when the teacher's teacher is present, one should behave toward him as toward the teacher" (2.205), one does not incur a breach by carrying out the corpse of one's own *ācārya*'s *ācārya*. The word "his own" (*svam*) is connected everywhere [to each category]. Therefore, even by carrying out the corpse of one's own *upādhyāya*'s *upādhyāya*, there is indeed a breach of the vow. (5.91)
One should carry out a dead Śūdra through the southern city gate; however, for the twice-born, one should do so through the western, northern, or eastern gates as appropriate. 5.92.

"By the southern [gate]" means that because it is inauspicious, it is designated according to the order of the most degraded Śūdra. One should carry out a deceased Śūdra by the southern city gate; however, for the twice-born, one should carry them out by the western, northern, and eastern gates respectively, according to their appropriate rank—that is, in the order of the lower Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, and Brāhmaṇa. (5.92)
There is no fault of sin for kings, nor for those observing vows, nor for ministers;
for they always occupy the station of Indra and have become one with Brahman.

"Not for kings": there is no fault of impurity (*aśauca*) for kings—namely, consecrated Kṣatriyas—even upon the death of a sapinda relative and so forth. This is because kings have attained the station of Indra, known as royal consecration (*rājyābhiṣeka*), which is the cause of sovereignty. "Vow-observers" (*vratinaḥ*) refers to celibate students (*brahmacārin*) and those performing vows such as the *Cāndrāyaṇa*. "Sacrificers" (*satriṇaḥ*) refers to those engaged in sacrifices such as the *Gavām ayana*. Since they have become Brahman, they are as sinless as Brahman itself. And this absence of impurity applies to specific ritual acts. Thus Viṣṇu says: "There is no impurity for kings in their royal duties, nor for vow-observers during their vow, nor for sacrificers during their sacrifice. "In royal duties" refers to activities such as presiding over legal proceedings, rites for peace, and fire-oblations. (5.93)
Immediate purification is prescribed for a king in his state of high office;
the reason for this is his seat [of authority], for the sake of protecting the subjects. (5.94)

Regarding the word "of the king": this exalted station called the royal office, characterized by supreme sovereignty, is attained only by a great-souled one through his prior merit (*puṇya*). For one who occupies that position, immediate purity (*sadyaḥśauca*) is prescribed; however, it is not for one who has fallen from the kingdom, even if he belongs to the Kṣatriya caste. By this verse, it is shown that caste (*jāti*) is not intended here as the defining factor. For, by means of administering justice, providing food during famine, and performing propitiatory oblations (*śāntihoma*) and so forth during calamities, the purpose of protecting the subjects while seated on the throne is the cause for the absence of impurity. And this applies equally to Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who perform those duties, even if they are not Kṣatriyas. For this very reason, the properties of *Soma* apply to the *phalacamasa* (a cup of fruit-juice) when it performs the function of the *Soma*. Likewise, although threshing and other rites are heard of in the scriptures as being associated with the properties of rice (*vrīhi*), because the performance of that specific function is what is intended, they are connected to barley in the archetype (*prakṛti*) and to wild rice (*nīvāra*) and the like in the ectype (*vikṛti*). This was determined in various sections (*adhikaraṇa*) of the *Karmamīmāṃsā*. (5.94)
And for those killed in childhood, by lightning, or by a king;
or for the sake of cows and Brahmins, or for whomever the king so desires.

Regarding the phrase "in a battle of children" (*ḍiṃbhāhave*): a "battle of children" is a war devoid of kings; for those killed therein, or for those killed by lightning or a thunderbolt, or for those killed by water, fire, tigers, and so forth—even without a battle—for the sake of protecting cows and Brāhmaṇas when an offense deserving of death has been committed against the king, or for a priest and others whose own duties the king desires to remain free from impurity, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*). || 5.95 ||
The king assumes the form of the eight guardians of the world: Soma, Agni, Arka, Anila, Indra, Vittapati, Appati, and Yama. (5.96)

"O Soma! [Thus it is said: A king bears the body belonging to these eight world-protectors (lokapāla): the Moon, Fire, Sun, Wind, Indra, Yama, and the two lords of wealth and waters, Kubera and Varuṇa. 5.96.
A king who is empowered by Lokeśa is not subject to ritual impurity;
for the purity and impurity of mortals originate from and dissolve back into Lokeśa.

Regarding the term *lokeśa*: since the king is occupied by a portion of Lokeśa (the Lord of the World), therefore no impurity (*aśauca*) is prescribed for him. For whatever purity or impurity belongs to human beings, that originates from and perishes with the Lords of the World (*lokeśa*). *Apaya* means destruction. By this, it is praised that there is an absence of the aforementioned impurity for the king, who is the embodiment of Lokeśvara and possesses the power to produce and destroy the purity and impurity of others; how then could he have his own personal impurity? (5.97)

For one slain in battle with uplifted weapons while following the duty of a Kshatriya, the sacrifice is immediately completed and so too is the period of impurity; such is the established rule. (5.98)

"By those who are prepared" means: for one who is killed in battle while facing the enemy and endowed with the duty of a Kṣatriya—such as by weapons like swords that are raised, but not by clubs, stones, and the like—the sacrifice of the Jyotiṣṭoma and others is completed and reaches its conclusion at that very moment. The meaning is that he becomes endowed with the merit thereof. Likewise, the period of impurity (āśauca) also reaches its conclusion at that very moment. This is the established rule in the scriptures. (5.98)
A Brahmin becomes pure by touching water; a Kṣatriya, by his mount or weapon;
a Vaiśya, by his goad or reins; and a Śūdra who has performed his duties, by his staff.

Regarding the term "vipra": at the end of the period of impurity, after having performed the funeral rites such as the *śrāddha*, a Brāhmaṇa becomes pure by merely touching water with his right hand—that is, by a simple touch of moving water—and not, as it is said elsewhere:
"But when a year has passed, he is purified by touched waters" (MDh 5.75).

As in the case of the expression "having bathed," because of the association with touching vehicles and so forth, it is improper for a single word such as *spṛṣṭvā* ("having touched") to have different meanings [in each instance]. Thus: a Kṣatriya [should touch] a vehicle such as an elephant and a weapon such as a sword; a Vaiśya, an ox-goad or a yoke with a metal-tipped point; and a Śūdra, a staff or a bamboo rod. (5.99)
This purity regarding sapinda relatives has been declared to you, O best of the twice-born;
now learn the purification for the dead among all those who are not sapindas. (5.100)

"Regarding this: O best of the twice-born, this purification in the case of sapinda relatives who have died has been declared to you. Now, listen to the purification for those who are not sapindas. (5.100)
Having carried out the corpse of a deceased twice-born man who is not a sapinda, a Brahmin becomes pure after three nights, as does one who carries out the kinsmen on his mother’s side. (5.101)

Regarding the term *asapiṇḍa*: the meaning is that when a Brāhmaṇa dies who is not a *sapiṇḍa*, a Brāhmaṇa should carry out the funeral out of affection for a kinsman (*bandhu*), and not merely with the thought of performing a religious duty (*adṛṣṭabuddhi*). Having carried out the relatives (*bāndhava*) of his mother who are "attained" (*āpta*), that is, closely related such as uterine brothers, sisters, and so forth, he becomes pure after three nights. (5.101)
If he eats their food, however, he becomes pure in ten days;
if he does not eat their food, he is purified in a single day, provided he does not dwell in that house.

"If [it is] food": if the carrier eats the food of those deceased sapinda relatives who are under impurity, then he becomes pure only after ten days, not after three nights. But if he does not eat their food, does not dwell in their house, and carries out the body, then he becomes pure in just one day and night. And thus, when there is residence in their house, for the carrier who does not eat their food, the previously mentioned period of three nights applies. (5.102)

If one follows out of desire a deceased person, whether they be a relative or even a stranger, one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter. (5.103)

Regarding the term "having followed": whether it be a relative or a non-relative who has died, if one follows them out of desire, one becomes purified from the impurity caused by following [the corpse] after having bathed with one's clothes on, touched fire, and subsequently consumed clarified butter. (5.103)
While his own kinsmen are present, he must not have a deceased Brahmin carried by a Śūdra; for that oblation, defiled by the touch of a Śūdra, would not lead to heaven. 5.104.

"Not a Brahmin" means that when a deceased person of the Brāhmaṇa or other higher classes is present among those of the same caste, a son or other relative should not have him carried out by a Śūdra. This is because that bodily oblation, being defiled by the touch of a Śūdra, would not be conducive to the deceased's attainment of heaven; the meaning is that it does not cause the deceased to reach heaven. By the expression "while his own [kinsmen] are present," it is implied that in the absence of Brāhmaṇas, he may be carried out by a Kṣatriya; in their absence, by a Vaiśya; and in their absence, even by a Śūdra. However, the defect of not reaching heaven due to the inferiority of the preceding [classes] must be understood to apply when a Śūdra carries out the body while Brāhmaṇas and others are available. Govindarāja, however, says that because of the mention of a specific fault, the phrase "while his own are present" is not intended to be restrictive (*avivakṣita*). That is incorrect, because it would result in the redundancy of uttering two words whose meanings are possible, and because the understanding derived from the introduction must be followed according to the logic of Vedic injunctions. Furthermore, if one were to disregard the primary factor (caste) for the sake of the subordinate factor (purity), it would contradict the maxim: "When there is a conflict between the primary and the subordinate, the primary prevails. Therefore, the two words "while his own are present" are not intended to be restrictive.
We do not respect this royal command of Govindarāja.
Knowledge, austerity, fire, food, earth, mind, water, smearing [with clay], wind, ritual action, the sun, and time are the agents of purification for embodied beings. (4.105)

Regarding the term *jñāna* (knowledge): knowledge and the other [factors] are the means for purification. Among these, the knowledge of Brahman is the means for the purification of the internal organ in the form of the intellect (*buddhi*), as he will state (5.109): "The intellect is purified by knowledge. Austerity (*tapas*) is as in (5.107): "Those most learned in the Vedas through austerity... Fire (*agni*) is as in (5.122): "...by re-firing the earthen [vessel]. Food (*āhāra*) is as in (11.106): "...with sacrificial food or barley-gruel. Earth and water (*mṛdvāri*) are as in (5.134): "Earth and water should be accepted when they serve a purpose. The mind (*manas*) is as in (3.146): "One should perform actions purified by the mind. The distinction between the mind and the intellect is that the mind consists of volition and doubt, whereas the intellect consists of determination. Smearing and plastering (*upāñjana*) are as in (5.122): "A house by sweeping and smearing. Ritual action (*karman*) is as in (11.174): "Or one should sacrifice with the horse-sacrifice," and so forth. The sun (*arka*) is as in (5.87): "Having touched a cow or having looked at the sun... Time (*kāla*) is as in (5.83): "A Brāhmaṇa is purified in ten days. As for wind (*vāyu*) being a cause of purification, although not mentioned by Manu, it should be accepted as stated in the Viṣṇu-smṛti and elsewhere: "And roads are purified by the rays of the moon and sun and by the wind. (5.105)
Of all forms of purity, purity in regard to wealth is declared to be the highest;
for he who is pure in regard to wealth is truly pure, not he who is purified by clay and water. (5.106)

"Of all these indeed.
