Among all [purifications]—such as purification by clay and water, purification of the body, and purification of the mind—it is purification regarding wealth (*artha-śauca*) that has been declared by Manu and others to be the supreme or most excellent, provided it is practiced by avoiding the unjust seizure of another's property; for that desire for wealth which is free from such means is what is intended. Because one who is pure regarding wealth becomes truly pure; whereas one who, though purified by clay and water, is impure regarding wealth, remains indeed impure. (5.106)
The wise are purified by patience; those who have committed forbidden acts, by charity;
those whose sins are concealed, by the recitation of prayers; and those most learned in the Vedas, by austerity. (5.107)

"By forbearance": when harm is inflicted by another, the wise are purified by the non-arising of the thought of retaliation. And as he will say (11.245): "Capable of performing the great sacrifices, they quickly destroy sins. [They are purified] by giving to one who commits what should not be done, as he will say (11.76): "One's entire property to a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas. Those whose sins are not publicly known are purified by muttering prayers (*japa*), as he will say (2.220): "But while muttering, one should fast for a day. Those most proficient in the Vedas—those who know the meaning of the Vedas and the penances such as the *cāndrāyaṇa*—are purified by austerity (*tapas*), according to what will be stated in the eleventh chapter (11.101). || 5.107 ||
That which is to be purified is cleansed by earth and water; a river is purified by its current;
a woman defiled in mind is purified by her menses; and the best of the twice-born are purified by renunciation.

Regarding the phrase "by earth and water": that which is defiled by impurities and the like is purified by cleansing with earth and water; the current of a river, though corrupted by phlegm and other impurities, becomes pure through its forceful flow; and a woman whose mind is defiled by thoughts of sexual union with another man becomes purified from that sin by her monthly menses. A Brāhmaṇa is purified from sin through renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), as described in the sixth chapter. 5.108.
The limbs are purified by water; the mind is purified by truth; the inner self is purified by knowledge and austerity; and the intellect is purified by wisdom. 5.109

"By waters": limbs afflicted by sweat and the like become pure when washed with water. And the mind, having been defiled by forbidden thoughts and the like, becomes pure through the speaking of truth. The *bhūtātman*—the individual soul (*jīvātman*) as delimited by the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) consisting of the subtle elements and so forth—becomes pure through the knowledge of Brahman, which is the cause for the destruction of sin, and through austerity. Being pure, it abides in the form of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). And the intellect (*buddhi*), having been afflicted by erroneous cognition, becomes pure through knowledge whose object is reality as it is. 5.109.
This decision concerning bodily purification has been declared to you;
now hear the decision regarding the purification of various kinds of objects.

"This," he says: this determination regarding the purification of those things connected to the body has been stated for you. Now, listen to the decision concerning which various kinds of substances are purified by what means. (5.110)
The purification of luminous gems, and of all that consists of stone,
has been declared by the wise to be by means of ashes, water, and earth.

Regarding the verse beginning with *taijasaiḥ*: Manu and others have declared that the purification of all metallic objects such as gold, of gems such as emeralds, and of everything made of stone is by means of ashes, water, and clay. Since it will be stated later that for an object free from stains, internal purification is achieved by water alone, this present rule concerns objects smeared with food-leavings, ghee, and the like. In that regard, there is an option between clay and ashes, as their sole purpose is the removal of odor; however, water is to be combined with both. (5.111)
A gold vessel that is free from stains is purified by water alone,
as are those made of lotus-fiber, stone, and silver, provided they are not ornamented.

"Untainted" (nirlepa) means that a golden vessel free from stains such as food remnants, as well as water-born objects like conch shells and pearls, and stone-made items such as silver that are unadorned—meaning they have not been subjected to the addition of other qualities such as engraving lines—are purified by water alone, provided it is free from ash and the like, because such stains cannot possibly exist upon them. (5.112)
Gold and silver emerged from the union of water and fire; therefore, their purification by means of their own source is more effective. (5.113)

Regarding the phrase "of water and fire": it is heard in the Veda, beginning with, "Agni indeed desired Varuṇānīs," and so forth. Likewise, in such scriptural passages as, "Gold is the power (*indriya*) of Agni; silver is that of the Varuṇānīs," gold and silver are produced from the union of fire and water. Therefore, because their own causes are respectively water and fire, the purification (*nirṇeka*) of these two by those very causes—namely, by water through excessive soaking and by fire—is the cause of purity that is more excellent and more praiseworthy. (5.113)
The purification of copper, iron, bronze, brass, tin, and lead should be performed as appropriate with alkaline substances, acids, and water.

Regarding "tāmrāya" (copper and iron): *ayas* is iron; *rīti* is brass (*pittala*), and a vessel made from that is called *raitya*; *trapu* is tin and *raṅga* is lead. Their purification must be performed with ashes and acidic liquids. "As appropriate" means whatever is suitable for each specific substance. Gold, silver, iron, and bell-metal are purified by water; copper and brass by ashes; and earthenware by repeated firing.
Thus, based on the words of Bṛhaspati and others, a specific distinction must be understood here. || 5.114 ||
For all liquids, purification is declared to be straining;
for solid objects, sprinkling; and for wooden items, scraping.

"And of liquids": regarding liquids such as clarified butter and oil that have been defiled by crows, insects, and the like, purification occurs through straining with two blades of *kuśa* grass one span (*prādeśa*) long, provided they do not exceed the measure of a handful (*prasṛti*), according to the statements of Baudhāyana and others. And for solid objects such as beds and the like, when defiled by food-remnants and so forth, purification is by sprinkling; and for wooden objects, when there is extreme defilement, it is by planing. 5.115.
In the performance of a sacrifice, the purification of the sacrificial vessels is by wiping with the hand;
however, the purification of the *camasa* cups and the *graha* ladles is by washing.

Regarding "cleansing" (mārjana): for the *camasa* cups, the *graha* vessels, and other sacrificial implements, cleansing should first be performed with the hand; subsequently, by means of washing, purity is achieved when the sacrifice is to be performed. 5.116.

The purification of the *caru* vessels, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, as well as the wooden sword (*sphya*), the winnowing basket, the cart, the pestle, and the mortar, is by means of hot water. (5.117)

Regarding "of the carus": the purification of ladles for caru and other such vessels smeared with oily substances is by means of hot water; however, for sacrificial purposes, those not joined with oil and the like are purified by water alone. 5.117.
For large quantities of grain and clothing, purification by sprinkling with water is prescribed;
however, for small quantities, purification by washing with water is ordained. (5.118)

Regarding the verse beginning with "adbhis tv" (by water, however): when many grains or clothes are defiled by Cāṇḍālas and the like, purification occurs through sprinkling with water. They explain that "many" means more than what can be carried by a person's load; however, for those that are few, purification through washing is taught by Manu and others. (5.118)
The purification of hides is like that of clothes, and the same applies to articles made of split cane; for vegetables, roots, and fruits, purification is held to be the same as for grain. 5.119.

"Like cloth": the purification of touchable but impure hides and of items made from split bamboo and the like is the same as that of cloth. And the purification of vegetables, roots, and fruits is the same as that of grain. (5.119)
Silk and woolen cloths [are purified] with alkaline salts; blankets of Kutapa wool with Ariṣṭaka fruits; fine cotton fabrics with Bilva fruits; and linen cloths with white mustard seeds. (5.120)

Regarding the verse beginning with "kauśeya": for cloth produced from the cocoons of silkworms (*kauśeya*); for blankets and the like produced from the wool of sheep and other animals; with alkaline earths (*ūṣaiḥ*, i.e., *kṣāramṛttikābhiḥ*); for *kutapa* blankets, namely Nepalese woolens (*nepālakambala*), with *ariṣṭaka* powders (*ariṣṭacūrṇaiḥ*); for fine silk cloths (*aṃśupaṭṭa*, i.e., *paṭṭaśāṭaka*) with *bilva* fruits; and for linen cloths (*kṣauma*, i.e., *dukūla*), which are garments made from the bark of the *kṣumā* plant—the purification [of these] is by washing with ground white mustard seeds. (5.120)
One who knows the rules should perform the purification of objects made of conch, horn, bone, or ivory, as well as those made of linen, using either cow's urine or water. (5.121)

"Like linen": for conch shells, animal horns, the bones of animals that are touchable, and the tusks of elephants and other such creatures, purification should be performed by one learned in the scriptures using a paste of white mustard seeds ground with either cow's urine or water, just as in the case of linen. 5.121.
Grass, wood, and straw are purified by sprinkling;
a house by sweeping and smearing with cow-dung; and an earthen vessel by being fired again. (5.122)

"By sprinkling, grass and wood [are purified]. Grass, wood, and straw defiled by the touch of *caṇḍālas* and others are purified by sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). Because of its association with grass and straw, this refers to firewood and similar types of wood. "And for wooden objects, scraping" (5.115) refers to constructed wooden houses and vessels. A house defiled by the residence of a woman in her courses (*udakyā*) and so forth is purified by sweeping and smearing with cow dung and the like. An earthen vessel defiled by contact with food-leavings and such is purified by re-firing. 5.122.
An earthen vessel that has been touched by intoxicating liquors, urine, feces, spittle, pus, or blood cannot be purified even by baking it again. (5.123)

Regarding the phrase "by intoxicants": an earthen vessel that has been touched by intoxicants and the like is not purified even by re-firing. Spittle is phlegm; pus is a corruption of the blood. (5.123)
The ground is purified by these five means: by sweeping, by smearing with cow-dung, by sprinkling, by scraping, and by the dwelling of cows. (5.124)

Regarding "by sweeping" (saṃmārjanā): by clearing away refuse, by smearing with cow-dung and the like, by sprinkling with cow-urine, water, and so forth, by digging and removing a certain amount of earth, and by the cows' dwelling there for a day and night—the ground is purified by these five methods, each one individually. Furthermore, depending on the gravity or lightness of the defilement caused by contact with food-leavings, urine, feces, outcastes (caṇḍāla), or their dwellings, one should understand that these methods may be combined or used alternatively. 5.124.
Food that has been pecked at by birds, smelled by a cow, blown upon, or sneezed over, and that which is defiled by hair or insects, becomes pure by the scattering of earth over it. (5.125)

Regarding the term "eaten by birds": if some portion of it has been eaten by edible birds—but not by crows, vultures, and the like—and if it has been sniffed by a cow, trampled with a foot, had a sneeze made over it, or was defiled by hair or insects, then that food, being small in quantity as indicated by the word *jagdha* ("eaten"), is purified by the scattering of earth. (5.125)
As long as the odor and the stain caused by contact with impurity do not depart from an object smeared with it, so long must earth and water be applied in all purifications of substances. 5.126

"Up to" means as follows: from a substance smeared with feces and so forth, one should remove that substance and apply earth and water for as long as its odor and stain persist. Furthermore, where purification by earth is required—as in the case of fat, marrow, and the like—one must employ water together with earth; however, it should be understood that where purification by water alone suffices—as in the case of earwax and the like—water by itself is sufficient. (5.126)
The gods ordained three purifiers for Brahmins:
that which is unseen, that which is washed with water, and that which is commended by word. (5.127)

"Three things, O King," [are pure]. In whatever way contact with a cause of invisible (adṛṣṭa) defilement has occurred, it is invisible; when there is a suspicion of defilement, it is cleansed with water. Regarding this, Hārīta says: "Whatever may be subject to investigation, that becomes pure by contact with water. Only when there is a suspicion of defilement are those three things declared pure by the speech of Brāhmaṇas saying, "May they be pure"; these, O King, the Brāhmaṇas have ordained as the three purifiers. 5.127.
Water on the ground is pure if it is sufficient to satisfy the thirst of a cow, provided it is not contaminated by impurities and possesses its natural fragrance, color, and taste. (5.128)

"Water is pure": when water is of such a quantity that it satisfies the thirst of a cow, and if it possesses fragrance, color, and taste, provided it is not smeared with impurities, then being situated on pure ground, it shall be pure. The phrase "situated on the ground" is intended to indicate a connection with pure ground, but not for the purpose of excluding water located in the atmosphere. (5.128)
The hand of an artisan is always pure, as is merchandise spread out for sale; almsfood received by a student of sacred knowledge is pure—this is the established rule. 5.129

"Always pure": even when a craftsman, such as a garland-maker and the like, weaves garlands and other items for the sake of gods or Brahmins, his hand is always pure by its very nature, even if he does not perform specific purificatory rites depending on the material or purpose. Likewise, he remains pure in his own work even during birth or death, according to the statement: "There is no impurity for craftsmen in their craft. Similarly, that which is to be sold and displayed in the marketplace is pure even when touched by the hands of many buyers, because of the injunction of Śaṅkha: "One should not eat food brought from a market. Furthermore, alms received by a student (brahmacārin) and others are always pure, even if given by a woman who has not rinsed her mouth or if they have been stepped over on a road; such is the established limit of the scriptures. 5.129.
The mouth of women is always pure; a bird is pure when it causes fruit to fall; a calf is pure while it is suckling; and a dog is pure when seizing game. (5.130)

"Always the mouth": the face of women is always pure; likewise, the fruit fallen from the beaks of crows and other birds is pure; the calf's mouth is pure at the time of milking when the milk flows; and a dog is pure in that specific activity when it seizes deer and other prey in order to kill them. (5.130)
Manu has declared that the flesh of an animal killed by dogs is pure, as is that killed by other carnivorous beasts, by Caṇḍālas and the like, or by robbers. (5.131)

"By dogs" means: Manu has declared that the flesh of deer and other animals killed by dogs is pure; this should be understood to apply specifically to occasions such as *śrāddha* ceremonies and the feeding of guests. This also applies to the flesh of those killed by others—such as tigers, hawks, and the like—or by hunters who live by killing deer, even if they kill with raw meat and so forth. (5.131)
Those apertures of the body which are above the navel are entirely pure; those which are below are impure, as are the excretions that fall from the body. (5.132)

"Above the navel" means that all those apertures of the sense organs which are above the navel are pure; therefore, there is no impurity from touching them. Those [apertures] below the navel are impure, as are the lower orifices. The plural number is used with reference to the multiplicity of individual instances. Furthermore, the bodily excretions such as fat and so forth, which are about to be mentioned, become impure when they have issued from the body. (5.132)
One should specify that flies, droplets, a shadow, a cow, a horse, the rays of the sun, dust, earth, wind, and fire are pure to the touch. (5.133)

Regarding the verse beginning with *makṣikā*: one should know that flies, even though they touch impure things; droplets (*vipruṣaḥ*), which are tiny drops of water issuing from the mouth; a shadow, even that of something fallen or otherwise of low touch; and [animals] beginning with cows and ending with fire—even when touched by outcastes (*caṇḍāla*) and the like—are pure upon contact.
For the purpose of purifying the discharge of feces and urine, earth and water should be taken as required; likewise for the purification of the twelve bodily impurities. (5.134)

Regarding the phrase "feces and urine": that by which feces and urine are discharged is the "discharge of feces and urine," namely the anus and so forth; for the sake of its purification, earth and water should be taken in a purposeful manner—that is, as much as is necessary until the odor and the stain are removed. Likewise, with respect to the twelve [parts] associated with bodily impurities such as fat and the like, earth and water should be taken for the sake of removing the odor and the stain. In this regard, according to another Smṛti, earth and water are to be used for the first six [parts], while for the latter six, water alone is to be used. Baudhāyana states: "One should take earth and water for purification during the first six [parts]."
And for the six subsequent [sins], one is purified by water alone.

Therefore, the statement of Manu—"in all twelve [cases]"—regarding the taking of earth and water is not contradicted, provided that the taking of earth and water is understood according to this settled rule (*vyavasthā*). Govindarāja, however, having observed the statements of Manu and Baudhāyana, asserts that there is an option even in the latter six cases; and he maintains that this option is restricted such that one may take earth even in the latter cases when engaged in rites for the gods, ancestors, and other unseen purposes (*adṛṣṭakarman*), but not otherwise. (5.134)
Fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, nasal mucus, earwax, snot, tears, rheum of the eyes, and sweat—these twelve are the impurities of human beings. (5.135)

"Fat" (*vasā*) is the oil of the body; "semen" (*śukra*) is the vital seed; "blood" (*asṛk*) is the blood; "marrow" (*majjā*) is the congealed oil within the head; "ocular discharge" (*dūṣikā*) is the film of the eyes; "sweat" (*sveda*) is the water exuded from the body due to exertion and so forth. These twelve, beginning with fat, are the bodily impurities of human beings. (5.135)
One application of earth on the penis, three on the anus, ten on one hand, and seven on both hands should be applied by one desiring purification. (5.136)

"One [application] on the penis": when there has been the voiding of urine or feces, by one desiring purification, "earth and water should be taken in sufficient quantity" (5.134) having been stated, one application of earth together with water should be made to the penis; three applications of earth to the anus; and likewise one to the left hand.
One who knows the rules of purification should not employ the right hand for cleansing below the waist. Likewise, one should not cleanse above the navel with the left hand.

According to this statement of Devala, since that [the penis] alone is the means for the removal of impurity, ten applications of clay should be made there. Therefore, seven should be applied to both hands. However, when the odor and the smear are not removed even by the prescribed amount of cleansing, then, according to the rule, "As long as the impurity remains on what has been smeared," a greater number of applications of clay must also be given. It is precisely with reference to such cases that the sages have stated higher numbers of clay applications. Regarding the quantity of clay, Dakṣa says (5.8): "The clay for the penis is said to be that which fills three finger-joints."
"The second and the third are proclaimed to be half and half again of that.

However, when the removal of odor and stain occurs even with fewer than the stated number, then the number must indeed be completed, by virtue of the force of the commencement of the statement regarding that number. (5.136)
This is the standard of purity for householders; it is double for students, triple for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics. (5.137)

"This is the rule for purification. The purification that has been described beginning with "one [application] on the penis" (5.136) applies specifically to householders; for students it is twofold, for forest-dwellers threefold, and for ascetics, moreover, fourfold.
Having voided urine or feces, one who has sipped water for purification should touch the cavities of the head;
likewise always when about to study the Veda or when eating food. (5.138)

"Having done so": having voided urine or excrement and performed the prescribed purification, he should sip water three times and touch the cavities of the senses and those on the head, if he intends to study the Veda or is about to eat food. As for the two statements made in the second chapter—“But one who is about to study, having sipped water” (2.70) and “having offered [the food] to his teacher, he should eat after sipping water” (2.51)—those were intended to establish the rules as auxiliary to the vow (*vrata*); this, however, is for the sake of personal purification (*puruṣārtha-śauca*), and thus there is no tautology. 5.138.
One who desires bodily purity should first sip water three times and then wipe the mouth twice; however, a woman or a Śūdra should do so once each. (5.139)

"One should sip water three times": desiring the purification of the body, one should first consume water three times; then, one should wipe the mouth twice. A woman and a Śūdra, however, should consume water for the purpose of sipping only once. (5.139)
For Śūdras who live according to the law, a monthly shaving of the head must be performed;
their rules for purification are like those of Vaiśyas, and they may eat the remnants of the food of the twice-born. (5.140)

"Of the Śūdras": regarding the phrase "the duty of the Śūdras," the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent according to Pāṇini 2.3.71, *kṛtyānāṃ kartari vā*. Śūdras who conduct themselves according to the scriptures and serve the twice-born must have their heads shaved every month, and they must observe the rules of purification during periods of birth or death just like Vaiśyas; furthermore, their food consists of the remnants of the twice-born. It is called "food" (*bhojana*) because it is eaten (*bhujyate*). || 5.140 ||

Regarding the rule, “Having spat and having spoken untruths” (5.145), since the injunction for sipping water (*ācamana*) is prescribed for those who spit, it might follow that even for the learned, anything issuing from the mouth constitutes spitting. To address this contingency, he states an exception for the sake of purification: “Drops [of saliva] falling on the body do not make one impure; nor do those [drops] which fall on the face. Beard-hair that has entered the mouth does not make one impure, nor what remains stuck between the teeth. (5.141)

"Not as impure" means that drops originating from the mouth which fall upon the body do not render one impure. Likewise, facial hair and body hair that have entered the mouth do not produce the state of being *ucchiṣṭa*. Furthermore, fragments of food and the like remaining in the gaps between the teeth do not make one impure. Regarding this, there is a specific rule in the Gautama Dharma Sūtra (1.5): "In the case of [particles] adhering to the teeth, they are treated like the teeth themselves, except when they have fallen off after being touched by the tongue. Some authorities hold: "One should know that what has fallen [from the teeth] is like food; one becomes pure only by swallowing it" (GDh 1.40). || 5.141 ||
Those drops which touch the feet of one who is rinsing the mouth for others should be known as equal to those on the ground; one does not become impure because of them.

"Regarding the phrase 'they touch': when others give water for the purpose of sipping (ācamana), those drops which touch the feet—and not the shins or other parts—are equal to water standing on pure ground; therefore, one does not become subject to the requirement of sipping [water again]. In that case, one who has not performed the sipping is purified by the water remaining there after it has fallen, and the object [the feet] is also purified. (5.142)
If one who holds a substance in his hand is somehow touched by something defiled by food remnants, he shall attain purity by sipping water (ācamana) without first setting that object down. 5.143.

Regarding the phrase "with what is left over" (*ucchiṣṭena*): by the expression "one who has an object in hand," the mere physical contact of the object with the body is intended. Since it is impossible for one who has an object in hand to perform ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), as stated in the rule "having washed the hand up to the wrist" (GDh 1.36), if one whose object rests on the shoulder or elsewhere becomes touched by something left over, then he becomes pure by performing the sipping of water without having set down the object; and the object also becomes pure. || 5.143 ||
One who has vomited or been purged should bathe and then consume clarified butter;
one who has eaten food should simply sip water, while bathing is prescribed for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse.

Regarding the term *vanta*: one who has vomited—that is, one who has undergone emesis—should bathe and consume clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*). Govindarāja states: "One who has been purged [of ten measures] undergoes ten purgings. If, however, one vomits immediately after eating, then one should perform only the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), not the bathing and the consumption of clarified butter. Furthermore, having engaged in sexual intercourse, one should bathe; however, this single rule applies specifically to the case of a woman during her menses. (5.144)

Having slept, having sneezed, having eaten, having spat, and having spoken untruths; and after drinking water or when about to recite the Veda, one should sip water even if one is already pure. 5.145.

Regarding the phrase "having slept": even one who is already pure should sip water (ācamana) when desiring to study after having performed such acts as sleeping, eating to relieve hunger, expelling phlegm, speaking falsehoods, or drinking water. As for what was stated in the second chapter—namely, "and having eaten, he should properly touch [water]" (2.53), and likewise "but one about to study, having sipped water" (2.70)—that is prescribed as an ancillary part of the vow (*vrata*). However, the rule for sipping water after eating mentioned here is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), whereas the rule for sipping water as an ancillary to study applies to householders and others as well. 5.145.
This entire rule for purification, as well as the purification of objects, has been declared to you for all social classes; now learn the duties of women. (5.146)

"This is the rule for purification. This entire rule for impurity (*aśauca*)—lasting ten nights and so forth—for the social classes (*varṇas*) at birth, death, and other occasions, as well as the rule for the purification of substances such as those made of metal and clothing with water and other means, has been declared to you. Now, listen to the duty (*dharma*) to be observed by women. (5.146)
Whether she be a child, a young woman, or even an old woman, a woman must not perform any action independently, even within her own home. (5.147)
"Or by one who is a child": whether she is in childhood, youth, or old age, she must not perform even the slightest action independently that is not authorized by her husband or others. (5.147)

In childhood, she should remain under the authority of her father; in youth, under that of her husband; and when her husband has died, under that of her sons. A woman should never enjoy independence. (5.148)

"In childhood [she is] under her father"—but rather, in childhood she should remain under the control of her father; in youth, under her husband; when the husband is dead, under her sons. In their absence, and if there are no sapinda relatives on the father's side, the paternal kin are the masters of the woman. But at the end of both these groups, the king is considered the husband of the woman.
According to these words of Nārada, she shall be dependent upon her kinsmen, the king, and others; she may never be independent. (5.148)
A woman should not desire separation from her father, her husband, or even her sons; for through separation from these, she brings reproach upon both families. (5.149)

"By her father, by her husband, or by her sons"—she should not bring about separation from these. For, through separation from them, a woman becomes an unchaste woman and brings reproach upon the families of both her husband and her father. (5.149)
She should always be cheerful, skillful in her household duties, keep the utensils well-maintained, and be not wasteful in her expenditures. (5.150)

"Always cheerful" means that even when her husband is at odds with her, a woman should always maintain a bright countenance; she should be skillful in domestic duties, keep household vessels such as bowls and cauldrons thoroughly cleaned, and be sparing in expenditure. (5.150)
To whomsoever her father or her brother— acting with the father’s consent— may give her,
she shall serve him while he lives, and once he has passed away, she must not transgress against him.

"To whomsoever he may give her": to whomsoever the father may give her, or his brother with the father's consent—to him she should serve while he lives and not neglect him when he is dead; for by infidelity, she would fail in her duties pertaining to the next world through the omission of *śrāddha* offerings, libations (*tarpaṇa*), and other such rites due to him. (5.151)
For the sake of auspiciousness, a rite for well-being, and sacrifice to Prajāpati are performed at weddings; the giving away [of the bride] is the cause of [the husband's] ownership. (5.152)

"Regarding the phrase 'for the sake of auspiciousness' (*maṅgalārtham*): that which consists of the recitation of benedictory, pacificatory, and consecratory mantras for them, as well as the sacrifice to Prajāpati—which in marriages takes the form of an oblation of clarified butter (*ājya*) offered with Prajāpati as the deity—is a rite performed for the sake of auspiciousness, meaning for the attainment of desired ends. However, the first gift, consisting of the verbal betrothal (*vāgdāna*), is precisely what generates the husband’s ownership [over her]. Consequently, from the moment of the betrothal onwards, the woman is dependent upon her husband; therefore, "she should rely on him" is the remainder of what was stated previously. As for what will be said in the eighth chapter—"But their completion (*niṣṭhā*) should be known by the wise to occur at the seventh step" (8.227)—that is for the purpose of the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) establishing her status as a wife; thus there is no contradiction. (5.152)

A husband who has performed the sacramental rite with sacred mantras is the constant bestower of happiness upon his wife, both in this world and in the next, whether she is outside her season or during her fertile period. (5.153)

Regarding the phrase "at the improper time": since marriage is a sacramental rite performed by means of mantras, the husband is its performer. According to the statement of Gautama—"He should approach her during her season, or at all times except when it is forbidden" (GDh 5.1)—he is the constant bestower of happiness in this world, both during the fertile period and otherwise; and because one attains heaven and other realms through his propitiation, he is also the bestower of happiness in the next world. || 5.153 ||
Therefore—
whether he be lacking in virtue, given over to sensual desires, or devoid of good qualities,
a husband must always be served by a virtuous wife like a god. (5.154)

"Virtuousless" means one who is devoid of good conduct, or one who is infatuated with another woman, or one who is lacking in qualities such as learning; nevertheless, a husband must be worshipped like a god by a virtuous wife. 5.154.
And because: "For women there is no separate sacrifice, nor a vow, nor even a fast; she is exalted in heaven by that through which she serves her husband. (5.155)

"There are no [independent rites] for women. Just as when a certain wife is absent due to menstruation or other reasons, the sacrifice is still accomplished by means of another wife, so too there is no accomplishment of the sacrifice for women without their husband. Nor are vows and fasts permitted without the husband's consent; rather, it is solely through service to her husband that a woman is honored in the heavenly world. (5.155)
A virtuous wife, desiring the world of her husband, whether he be living or dead, should never do anything displeasing to him. (5.156)

Regarding the phrase "of the one who took her hand": a virtuous woman, desiring that world of heaven and other realms acquired by performing dharma together with her husband, should not do anything displeasing to her husband, whether he be living or dead. For one who is dead, what is displeasing consists of unchastity and the neglect of the prescribed *śrāddha* rites. (5.156)
She may indeed emaciate her body with pure flowers, roots, and fruits;
but she must not even utter the name of another man once her husband has died. (5.157)

"But even if she has the means to subsist," [it is said], "she should emaciate her body with pure flowers, roots, and fruits, and by eating little, she should bring it to a state of wasting. And when her husband is dead, she must not utter even the name of another man out of a mind inclined toward infidelity.
And this being so:
"Until death she remained patient, steadfast, and chaste, longing for that supreme Dharma which belongs to women who have but one husband. (5.158)

"Let her remain," it is said. Endowed with forbearance and observant of religious restraints, desiring that most excellent dharma of women who have but one husband, she should remain until death, characterized by celibacy consisting of the avoidance of honey, meat, and sexual intercourse; even if childless, she should not serve another man for the sake of obtaining a son. (5.158)
For this reason:
"Many thousands of brahmins who practiced celibacy from their youth have gone to heaven without having produced offspring for the continuity of their lineage. (5.159)

"Many indeed": from their very childhood, many thousands of Brahmins such as Sanaka, the Vālakhilyas, and others, who remained celibate and did not take wives, have gone to heaven even without producing offspring for the sake of increasing their lineage. (5.159)
When her husband has died, a virtuous woman who remains established in celibacy goes to heaven even if she is childless, just like those who practice lifelong celibacy. (5.160)

"Regarding the phrase 'when the husband has died': a woman of virtuous conduct who, upon her husband's death, does not engage in sexual intercourse with another man, goes to heaven even if she is without a son—just as Sanaka, the Vālakhilyas, and others went to heaven despite being childless. (5.160)
But that woman who, out of greed for offspring, transgresses against her husband, incurs reproach in this world and is excluded from the next world. (5.161)

"Out of greed for offspring": this refers to a woman who, out of the greed thinking, "May a son be born to me; through him I shall attain heaven," transgresses her husband—that is, she commits adultery. Such a woman incurs reproach in this world, and she does not obtain heaven in the next world by means of that son. (5.161)
Right here he states the reason:
"In this world, no offspring is born from another man, nor is there offspring in the possession of another;
furthermore, a second husband is nowhere prescribed for virtuous women. (5.162)

"Nor one born of another": because a child begotten by a man other than the husband does not belong to him according to the sacred law (*śāstra*). Nor does a child produced in the wife of another become the offspring of the progenitor. And this refers to cases where the child was produced without formal authorization (*aniyoga*). Since she is commonly known in the world as "having many husbands," even the second man is indeed a husband; therefore, the claim that she was "begotten by another" is unproven. Anticipating this objection, he says: "No. Even though she is notorious in the world, for those of virtuous conduct, a second husband is nowhere taught in the sacred law. This being the case, her status as a remarried woman (*punarbhū*) is likewise forbidden. (5.162)
She who, having abandoned her own inferior husband, devotes herself to a superior one, shall be censured in the world and is called "one who has had a previous husband. (5.163)

Regarding the word *pati*: she who, having abandoned her own husband—who may be inferior, such as a Kṣatriya or the like—resorts to one who is superior, such as a Brāhmaṇa or the like, becomes indeed contemptible in the world. She is spoken of by people as "one whose former husband was another.
He states the result of infidelity: "But through infidelity toward her husband, a woman incurs censure in the world;
she enters the womb of a jackal and is tormented by foul diseases. (5.164)

"Because of infidelity": in this world, a woman who enjoys the company of another man incurs public reproach; after death, she becomes a female jackal and is tormented by diseases such as leprosy. (5.164)
She who does not deceive her husband, being restrained in mind, speech, and body, attains the world of her husband and is called a virtuous woman by the righteous. (5.165)

Regarding the word "husband": because of the inclusion of the qualification "restrained in mind, speech, and body," she who does not transgress against her husband by means of mind, speech, and body alone—since her mental, vocal, and physical activities are directed solely toward her husband—attains the worlds acquired together with her husband. Furthermore, in this world, she is called "virtuous" (sādhvī) by the learned. The injunction "she should not transgress against her husband even in speech or thought" is intended as a rule for the cessation of physical transgression; it is a restatement of what has already been mentioned [in verse 5.164]. (5.165)
By this conduct, a woman who is restrained in mind, speech, and body attains preeminent fame in this world and the world of her husband in the next. (5.166)

"By this": by means of this aforementioned mode of conduct pertaining to the duties of women—consisting of service to the husband, non-infringement upon the husband, and so forth—a woman who is restrained in mind, speech, and body attains preeminent fame in this world, and in the next world, she attains the heavenly realms and other worlds acquired together with her husband; such is the summary of the meaning of the section. (5.166)
A twice-born man who knows the Dharma should have his wife—who is of the same caste, of such conduct, and who dies before him—cremated with the Agnihotra fire and the sacrificial implements. (5.167)

"Conducting herself in this manner": a twice-born man who knows the law of cremation should burn his wife of equal caste—who has acted according to the prescribed conduct and has died previously—using the fires of the Śrauta and Smārta rites along with the sacrificial vessels. 5.167.
Having given the sacred fires to his wife, who has died before him, for her funeral rites, he should perform the rite of taking a wife again and likewise re-establish the sacred fires. (5.168)

Regarding the wife: having offered the sacred fires for the cremation as part of the funeral rites for a wife who has died previously, a householder who desires to continue his domestic life—whether he has already fathered sons or not—may marry again; he may then establish either the Smārta fires or the Śrauta fires. (5.168)
By this rule, he should never neglect the five great sacrifices;
having taken a wife, he should dwell in his house during the second stage of life. (5.169)
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.

"By this": by means of this method prescribed at the beginning of the third chapter, one should not abandon the five sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) every day. Having taken a wife, during the second portion of one's life, one should perform the duties ordained for the householder by this very same method as described. Although the five sacrifices are indeed among the duties of a householder, they are mentioned separately in order to indicate that they are preeminent duties. (5.169)
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the Manu-bhāṣya, titled *Manvarthamuktāvalī*, composed by the illustrious Kullūkabhaṭṭa.

The Sixth Chapter. Having thus remained in the householder stage of life according to the rules, the twice-born who has completed his Vedic studies shall dwell in the forest, self-restrained, duly controlling his senses. (6.1)

"Thus": A twice-born man who has adopted the view of the combination of all stages of life (*āśrama-samuccaya*), having performed the *samāvartana* ceremony and practiced the householder stage (*gṛhāśrama*) according to the scriptures in the manner described, being self-restrained and firm in his resolve, and having duly—according to the rules and the specific dharma to be described hereafter—conquered his senses (which means he has matured his inner impurities), should enter upon the forest-dweller stage (*vānaprasthāśrama*). 6.1.
But when a householder perceives his own wrinkles and grey hair, and sees the offspring of his offspring, then he should take refuge in the forest. (6.2)

"But as for the householder": when a householder perceives the loosening of the skin of his own body, the whiteness of his hair, and even the son of his son, he should, in such a state of age and with his passion for sense-objects departed, take refuge in the forest. 6.2.
Having completely abandoned village food and all his belongings, and having entrusted his wife to his sons, he should go to the forest, either alone or together with her. (6.3)

"Having renounced," and so forth: having abandoned all domestic food such as rice and barley, as well as all household requisites such as cattle, horses, and beds, he should go to dwell in the forest—either entrusting his wife to his sons if she is unwilling, or going to the forest together with her if she is willing. (6.3)
Having taken up the Agnihotra sacrifice and the household implements for the sacred fires, he should depart from the village to the forest and dwell there with his senses restrained. (6.4)

Regarding the *agnihotra*: having taken the *śrauta* fire, the *āvasathya* fire, and the implements for the fire such as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, he should depart from the village for the forest and dwell there with his senses restrained. 6.4.
With various kinds of pure food fit for sages, or with vegetables, roots, and fruits, he should perform these very great sacrifices according to the prescribed rule. (6.5)

Regarding the phrase "with the food of sages": with various kinds of pure food of sages such as wild rice (*nīvāra*) and so forth, or with forest-grown vegetables, roots, and fruits; he should perform these very same great sacrifices previously mentioned for the householder according to the sacred injunctions. 6.5.
He should wear either a deerskin or a garment of bark; he should bathe in the evening as well as in the morning;
and he should always maintain his matted locks, beard, body hair, and nails.

“Vasīta” means he should clothe himself in the skin of a deer or the like, or in tree bark. However, Hārīta, by prescribing “clothing made of bark, hemp, skin, rags, kuśa grass, muñja grass, or wooden planks,” has also permitted bark and similar materials. He should bathe every morning and evening. He should constantly maintain his matted hair, beard, body hair, and nails. (6.6)
From whatever food he may have, he should offer the ritual oblation (bali) and alms according to his ability;
he should honor those who have come to his hermitage with offerings of water, roots, fruits, and alms. (6.7)

"Whatever is to be eaten": from whatever he may eat, he should offer a portion as a *bali* and as alms (*bhikṣā*) according to his ability. The term "*bali*" here is an elliptical designation for both the *vaiśvadeva* offering and the daily ancestral rite (*nityaśrāddha*), because these have been prescribed [by Manu] in the rule, "Some [perform] these great sacrifices" (4.22). He should honor those who have come to his hermitage by giving them water, fruits, roots, and alms. 6.7.
He should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas, self-controlled, friendly, and composed;
he should be a giver, never a taker, and compassionate toward all living beings. 6.8

Regarding the phrase "in self-study": he should be constantly engaged in the study of the Vedas. He should be patient toward the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat, helpful to all, restrained in mind, a constant giver, abstaining from accepting gifts, and full of compassion for all living beings. (6.8)
He should offer the Vaitānika Agnihotra according to the rule,
not omitting the New Moon sacrifice and performing the Full Moon sacrifice with proper application.

Regarding the term *vaitānika*: one should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice according to the scriptures, which pertains to the *vitāna*—the ritual arrangement or spreading out of the fires situated in the *gārhapatya* hearth and those transferred to the *āhavanīya* and *dakṣiṇāgni* hearths. Furthermore, regarding the *darśapaurṇamāsa*, one should not omit or neglect these *śrauta* and *smārta* sacrifices at their proper times through negligence. Moreover, in the case where the wife has been entrusted [to others], it is appropriate to perform these rites even when the wife is in her menses, as no specific prohibition is heard. 6.9.
He should perform the Ṛkṣeṣṭi, the Āgrayaṇa, and the Cāturmāsyas;
he should also perform the Turāyaṇa and the Dākṣāyaṇa in their proper sequence.

Regarding the word *ṛkṣā*: *ṛkṣeṣṭi* is the sacrifice to the stars (*nakṣatreṣṭi*), and *āgrayaṇa* is the sacrifice of the first-fruits (*navasasyeṣṭi*); thus, *ṛkṣeṣṭyāgrayaṇam* is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandva*). Likewise, he should perform in due order the Śrauta rites of the Cāturmāsya, Turāyaṇa, and Dākṣāyaṇa sacrifices. On this point, some say: "All these Śrauta rites, such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa and others, are mentioned for the sake of praising the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), but they are not to be performed by him, because these rites are accomplished through cultivated grains (*vrīhi*) and the like, which are not available to him. Furthermore, a Smṛti text has no power to subvert a Śrauta injunction. This is incorrect; for in the subsequent verse, "with [grains] grown in spring and autumn" (6.11), there is an injunction regarding the sacrificial pap (*caru*) and cake (*puroḍāśa*) intended for the forest-dweller using wild grains such as *nīvāra*, and it would be improper to subvert that clear injunction. Govindarāja, however, says that these rites may somehow be accomplished even with cultivated grains (*vrīhi*) etc., provided they are produced in the forest. 6.10.
With pure forest foods fit for sages, gathered by himself during the spring and autumn seasons,
he should separately prepare the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) and the cooked rice offerings (caru) according to the prescribed rules.

"Vāsantaiḥ," and so forth. For the sake of accomplishing various sacrifices and other rites according to the scriptures, he should himself procure and prepare sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) and oblations (*caru*) from pure forest foods (*munyanna*)—such as wild rice (*nīvāra*) and the like—which arise in spring or autumn and serve as components of the sacrifice.
Having offered that most pure forest-grown oblation to the deities, he should consume the remainder himself, along with salt prepared by his own hand. (6.12)

"From the deities," and so forth. Having prepared for the deities an oblation (*havis*)—consisting of wild rice (*nīvāra*) and other such grains grown in the forest—which is exceptionally worthy of sacrifice, he should consume the remaining food. And he himself may consume salt produced from saline soil (*ūṣara-lavaṇa*) and the like. 6.12.
One should eat vegetables grown on land or in water, as well as flowers, roots, and fruits produced from pure trees, along with oils derived from fruits.

Regarding the phrase "land-grown": one should eat vegetables grown on land and in water, flowers, roots, and fruits produced from trees suitable for forest sacrifices, as well as oils derived from fruits such as the *iṅgudī*. (6.13)
One should avoid honey, meat, mushrooms growing from the ground,
bhūstṛṇa grass, śigruka, and the fruits of the śleṣmātaka tree.

"One should avoid," and so forth. *Mākṣika* (honey), *māṃsa* (meat), and "earth-born" (*bhaumāni*)—the latter term is used for the sake of showing common usage; thus, one should avoid earth-born fungi (*kavakāni*), mushrooms (*chatrākān*), *bhūstṛṇa* (a vegetable well-known in the Mālava country), *śigruka* (a vegetable well-known among the Vāhīkas), and the fruits of the *śleṣmātaka* tree. Govindarāja, however, desiring that "earth-born" be a restrictive qualifier for "fungi," asserts a prohibition of earth-born fungi but allows the eating of those growing on trees. That is incorrect, because Manu himself, in the fifth chapter, prohibits fungi in general for the twice-born alone, and such a strict rule is appropriate as it pertains specifically to forest-dwellers. Yama, however, says:
Those who eat mushrooms, whether they grow from the earth or from trees,
one should know them as slayers of Brahmins, despised among those who discourse on the Veda.

Thus, he states an explicit prohibition even regarding mushrooms growing on trees. Medhātithi, however, treating *bhaumāni* as an independent term, asserts that it refers to a certain substance known among forest-dwellers by the name *gojihvikā*; yet we cannot accept this, as it is not well-known in many lexicons and other sources. Although there is already a prohibition for specific twice-born classes regarding mushrooms (*kavaka*), their mention again—and likewise the mention of *bhūstṛṇa* and so forth—is for the purpose of prescribing the same expiation for all of them. (6.14)
In the month of Āśvayuja, he should discard the food of sages previously stored, as well as worn-out garments, vegetables, roots, and fruits. (6.15)

"Should abandon" means that, according to the view of accumulating for a year, one should abandon in the month of Āśvina the previously gathered food such as nīvāra grain, as well as worn-out clothes, vegetables, roots, and fruits. (6.15)
One should not eat what has been ploughed by a ploughshare, even if it has been abandoned by someone; nor, even when distressed, should one eat roots and fruits grown within a village.

He shall not plow. Even in the forest, he shall not eat rice or other grains grown on land tilled by the plow, even if they have been abandoned by their owner. Likewise, even when oppressed by hunger, he shall not consume the roots of creepers and trees or fruits growing in a village, even on ground not tilled by the plow. (6.16)
He may eat food cooked by fire, or indeed eat only what is ripened by time;
he may be one who grinds with a stone, or even one who uses his teeth as a mortar.

"He eats" refers to forest-grown food cooked by fire, or fruits and the like ripened by time; or rather, he should eat what is uncooked, having ground it with a stone instead of using a mortar and pestle; or he may be one for whom the teeth themselves serve as the place of the mortar. (6.17)
He may be one who washes [his bowl] immediately after eating, or one who stores for a month;
he may be one who stores for six months, or even one who stores for a year. (6.18)

"Immediately," and so forth. He should gather wild rice (*nīvāra*) and the like, sufficient for a single day’s subsistence, or accumulated for a month’s livelihood, or enough to sustain him for six months or a year. As before, there is an intensification of his observances. A "monthly store" (*māsasaṃcaya*) is a collection suitable for a month's livelihood; one who possesses such a store is called *māsasaṃcayika*, formed with the suffix *-ika* according to Pāṇini 5.2.115 (*ata ini-ṭhanau*). || 6.18 ||
One should eat food at night, or having brought it during the day according to one's ability; or one may take food only every fourth mealtime, or even every eighth mealtime. (6.19)

"By night," and so forth: having brought food according to his capacity, he should eat at the onset of evening; or he may eat only during the day; or he may observe the "fourth-meal" rule (*caturthakālāśana*). Regarding the injunction, "Eating in the evening and morning is the meal ordained for humans by the gods" (MBh 12.186.10), he should fast on one day and eat in the evening on the following day. Or he may be one who eats at the eighth meal-time (*aṣṭamakālika*). Having fasted for three nights, he should eat on the night of the fourth day. || 6.19 ||
Or he may pass the bright and dark fortnights according to the rules of the Cāndrāyaṇa;
or else, at the end of each fortnight, he may eat a single meal of boiled barley-gruel.

Regarding the term *cāndrāyaṇa*: he may subsist according to the *cāndrāyaṇa* fasts to be described in the eleventh chapter, beginning with the rule, "In the bright fortnight one should decrease the morsels by one each day, and in the dark fortnight one should increase them" (11.216). Alternatively, at the ends of the two fortnights—the full moon and the new moon—he may eat barley gruel boiled [in milk], either once in the evening or once in the morning. 6.20.
Or, remaining steadfast in the doctrine of the Vaikhānasas, he should always subsist solely on flowers, roots, and fruits that have ripened in due time and fallen of their own accord.

"By flowers, roots," and so forth: he should subsist on flowers, roots, and fruits that have ripened in their own time, not those cooked by fire, and which have fallen of their own accord. A *vaikhānasa* is a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) who stands firm according to the teachings found in the scriptures that set forth his specific duties. By this it is meant that he should also practice other duties prescribed in the *Vaikhānasa-śāstra*. (6.21)

He should roll about on the ground or stand on his tiptoes for the day; he should pass his time by alternating between standing and sitting, approaching water at the prescribed times for ritual libations.

“On the ground,” and so forth. One should roll about on the bare ground, performing movements back and forth; one should sit in standing or sitting postures, and rise or wander—this is the meaning. This rule applies except for times when one must attend to necessary activities such as bathing and eating; the same applies in subsequent cases. Alternatively, one may stand on the tips of one’s toes for a day, remaining standing for some time and sitting for some time, but not wandering in between. One should bathe at the three *savanas*: evening, morning, and midday. As for what was stated [in verse 6.6], “One should bathe in the evening and likewise in the morning,” that presents an option based on the requirement for an even stricter observance. 6.22.

In summer he should practice the penance of the five fires; during the rains, he should live under the open sky; and in winter, he should wear wet clothes, thus gradually increasing his austerity. (6.23)

"In summer," and so forth. For the sake of increasing his self-discipline through austerity, he should heat himself in summer by means of fires placed in the four directions and the heat of the sun above. In the rainy season, he should take shelter under the open sky; the meaning is that he should remain in whatever place it rains, without coverings such as an umbrella. In the winter, he should wear wet clothes. This is a rule for a full year, based on the adoption of three seasons as a year. (6.23)
Performing ablutions at the three sessions of the day, he should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
practicing even more rigorous austerity, he should wither his own body.

He undertakes it. Even the prescribed bathing at the three sessions of the day is restated here for the purpose of performing the libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors. Performing the libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors during all three sessions—morning, midday, and evening—he practices other forms of intense vows and austerity, such as fasting for a fortnight or a month. As Yama has said: "Some fast for a fortnight; some fast for a month.
Thus he should wither his own body. (6.24)

Having formally consigned the sacrificial fires into himself according to the prescribed rule, he should be without fire and without a fixed dwelling, a silent sage subsisting on roots and fruits. (6.25)

“Having [consigning] the fires,” and so forth: having consigned the Śrauta fires into his own self by means of the ritual prescribed in the Vaikhānasa scriptures—such as by consuming ashes and so on—he is one whose worldly fire and house are empty. As he will say: “having his dwelling at the foot of a tree” (6.26). A *muni* is one who observes the vow of silence; he should subsist solely on fruits and roots. He should not even eat wild rice (*nīvāra*) and the like. And this [practice] is for a period exceeding six months, because of the statement of Vasiṣṭha: “without fire, without a dwelling” (9.11); thus, after six months, there is the state of being without fire and without a dwelling. 6.25.
Exerting no effort for the sake of pleasures, he was a celibate student who slept on the ground;
he had no sense of ownership over shelters and made his dwelling at the foot of trees.

"Without effort" means that regarding objects for the sake of pleasure—such as eating sweet fruits, avoiding cold and heat, and so forth—he should be free from exertion; he should not engage in sexual intercourse with women, sleep on the ground, and, being devoid of the sense of "mine" toward dwellings, he should live at the foot of trees. (6.26)
He should obtain alms for his sustenance only from brahmins who are ascetics, or from other twice-born householders living in the forest. (6.27)

Regarding the phrase "among ascetics": in the event that fruits and roots are unavailable, he should obtain alms sufficient merely to sustain life from brahmin forest-dwellers (vānaprasthas). In their absence, he should seek it from other twice-born householders (gṛhasthas) living in the forest. (6.27)
Or, dwelling in the forest, he may eat eight mouthfuls after bringing them from a village, having received them either in a leaf-cup, in his hand, or in a potsherd. (6.28)

Regarding the word "village": even if that is unavailable, the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) should bring food from a village and eat eight mouthfuls of the village's food, either with a fragment of a leaf-cup or with his hand alone. 6.28.
Living in the forest, a Brahmin who has been initiated should practice these and other observances, as well as various Upaniṣadic scriptures for the sake of self-perfection. (6.29)

"And these": the forest-dweller (vanaprastha) should practice these initiations (dīkṣās), these observances (niyamās), and other [rules] prescribed in the scriptures for forest-dwellers; and he should practice the Upaniṣadic scriptures—the various passages recited in the Upaniṣads that establish Brahman—both in their wording and in their meaning, for the sake of attaining Brahman for this very self. 6.29.
These have been practiced by sages and brahmins, as well as by householders, for the sake of increasing knowledge and austerity, and for the purification of the body. (6.30)

"By the sages": because these Upaniṣadic scriptures have been cultivated by the sages—both wandering mendicants and householders who perceive Brahman, as well as forest-dwellers—for the sake of increasing the knowledge of non-dual Brahman and its corresponding dharma; therefore, "one should cultivate them"—this is a restatement of what was previously enjoined.
Or, having taken his stand in the unconquered [northeastern] direction, he should proceed straight on until the fall of his body, disciplined, subsisting on water and air. (6.31)

"Others," [the commentator] says: when incurable diseases and the like arise, one who is disciplined, established in yoga, and subsisting on water and air should set out toward the unconquered northeastern direction (*aiśānī*) with a straight course until the fall of the body. This death is prescribed in the scriptures as the "Great Departure" (*mahāprasthāna*); therefore, there is no contradiction even with the Vedic injunction: "One who desires heaven should not depart before the end of his lifespan.
"Having abandoned the body by means of any one of these practices of the great seers, a Brahmin, freed from sorrow and fear, is glorified in the world of Brahman. (6.32)

"Of these," and so forth. By means of any one of these aforementioned practices, having abandoned the body and being freed from suffering and fear, he attains worship in Brahman itself, which is the world; the meaning is that he attains liberation (*mokṣa*). If it is asked how there can be liberation for a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) who performs only ritual action (*karman*), the answer is no, because self-knowledge is possible even for him, as stated in verse 6.29: "And various Upaniṣadic scriptures [he studies] for the purification of the self. 6.32.
But for one who is subject to death, he says:
"Having thus spent the third part of his life in the forests, he should renounce all attachments and wander as a mendicant during the fourth part of his life. (6.33)

"In the forests," and so forth. Because the duration of life is indefinite, the third part of that life is difficult to determine; therefore, the phrase "the third part of life" is intended as an indication for the period of the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) up until the exhaustion of passion. For this very reason, Śaṅkha and Likhita stated: "After the forest-dwelling, for one who is tranquil and whose age is fully reached, there is the state of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrajya*). Having thus spent time in the forests and having practiced the forest-dweller stage of life for some time according to the prescribed method of performing difficult austerities in order to pacify attachment to sense objects, one should—during the remainder of one's life, as indicated by the phrase "the fourth part of life"—completely abandon all attachments to sense objects and enter upon the stage of the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*). (6.33)
Having gone from stage to stage of life, having offered oblations and conquered his senses,
one who has grown weary of seeking alms and making offerings prospers after death by embracing the life of a wandering mendicant.

"From the stage of life" (āśramāt) means: having gone from each preceding stage of life to each succeeding stage—having practiced the student life (brahmacarya), then the householder stage (gṛhasthāśrama), and then the forest-dweller stage (vānaprasthāśrama)—one who has performed the oblations according to one's capacity, who has conquered the senses, and who is weary from long service consisting of alms-gathering and offerings, while practicing the wandering mendicant stage (parivrajyāśrama), attains through the acquisition of liberation in the next world a supreme excellence of becoming one with Brahman (brahmabhūta). || 6.34 ||
Having discharged the three debts, one should fix the mind on liberation;
but he who pursues liberation without having discharged them goes downward. (6.35)

"Debts," and so forth. A Brāhmaṇa who has adopted the view of the cumulative succession of the stages of life (*āśrama-samuccaya*) should, after having discharged the three debts to be described in the following verse, apply his mind toward liberation—that is, toward the stage of the wandering mendicant (*parivrājyāśrama*), which is the innermost limb of liberation. However, by practicing for liberation—the fourth stage of life—without having discharged those debts, he goes to hell. (6.35)

He shows those very stages: "Having studied the Vedas according to the rules, having procreated sons in accordance with dharma, and having sacrificed with sacrifices to the best of one's ability, one should direct the mind toward liberation. (6.36)

Regarding the word "having studied": it is heard in the Śruti, "A Brāhmaṇa, being born, is indeed born with three debts: to the gods by sacrifice, to the ancestors by progeny, and to the sages by the study of the Veda. Therefore, having studied the Vedas according to one's own branch (śākhā), having produced sons through the performance of duties such as avoiding sexual intercourse on sacred days (parva), and having performed sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma according to one's capacity, one should apply the mind to the fourth stage of life (āśrama), which is an internal limb of liberation. 6.36.
A twice-born man who, without having studied the Vedas, without having procreated sons, and without having performed sacrifices, desires liberation, goes downward. (6.37)

"Without having studied," etc.: without having performed the study of the Vedas, without having procreated a son, and without having performed sacrifices, one who desires liberation goes to hell. (6.37)
Having performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice, in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee,
and having internalized the sacred fires within himself, a Brāhmaṇa may go forth from his home as a wandering ascetic.

Regarding the phrase "prājāpatyām": having performed the sacrifice dedicated to Prajāpati, which involves giving away all one's possessions as the sacrificial fee (*sarvasva-dakṣiṇā*) as described in the narrative texts (*upākhyāna-grantha*) of the Yajurveda, and having entered the forest-dwelling stage (*vānaprastha-āśrama*) precisely according to the prescribed rule—since it is stated [in the scriptures] that "having consigned the sacred fires into oneself, one should depart from the home"—one should then practice the fourth stage of life (*caturtha-āśrama*). By this, Manu has also shown the possibility of the combined observance (*samuccaya*) of the four stages of life. Furthermore, the combinations of one, two, three, or four stages established by the Śruti are presented as optional alternatives (*vikalpita*). Thus says the Jābāla Śruti (4): "Having completed the student stage (*brahmacarya*), one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller; having been a forest-dweller, one should renounce. Otherwise, one may renounce directly from the student stage, or from the home, or from the forest. (6.38)
For him who, having granted fearlessness to all beings, goes forth from his home,
there are worlds consisting of splendor, O teacher of Brahman.

"Who," and so forth. He who, having granted fearlessness to all beings—both stationary and moving, which are composed of the elements—renounces the life of a householder, becomes established in the Upaniṣads that reveal Brahman; for him, the worlds of Hiraṇyagarbha and others, which are devoid of the light of the sun and other luminaries, become illuminated by his own splendor. The meaning is that he attains them. (6.39)
Since not even the slightest fear arises for the twice-born from living beings, there is no fear from any quarter for him who is liberated from the body. (6.40)

"Because," and so forth. Since no living being experiences even the slightest fear from a twice-born person, that person, once liberated from the body, has no fear from anything whatsoever upon the destruction of his current body. 6.40.
Having gone forth from the home, the sage, purified by his observances, should wander as a mendicant, indifferent even when sensual pleasures are presented to him. 6.41

"From the home": having gone forth from the house, equipped with pure items such as the staff and water-pot, the sage—remaining silent—should wander as a mendicant, free from longing even when various desirable things, such as sweet food and the like, have been properly brought near to him by someone. Medhātithi, however, explains: "Equipped with purifying means, that is, either by the recitation of mantras or by purifying penances (*kṛcchra*). (6.41)
One should always wander alone, without companions, for the sake of accomplishment; seeing that accomplishment belongs to the solitary one, he neither abandons nor is abandoned. (6.42)

"Alone," and so forth. Knowing that the attainment of liberation belongs to one who is free from all attachments, one should always practice for the sake of liberation alone. By the phrase "alone indeed," the abandonment of sons and others previously known is expressed. By the term "without companion," it is meant that if one wanders solitary, one abandons nothing; one does not experience suffering through the loss of anyone, nor is one abandoned by anyone, nor is anyone made to experience the pain of abandonment by oneself. Consequently, being free from the sense of "mine" (nirmamatva) in all things, one easily attains liberation. (6.42)
He should be without fire and without a fixed dwelling, resorting to a village only for the sake of food;
indifferent, free from agitation, a sage whose mind is absorbed in being. 6.43

“Without fire,” and so forth. “Without fire” means devoid of contact with ordinary (laukika) fire, because it was previously stated, “having superimposed the scriptural (śāstrīya) fire. “Without a dwelling” means one who is free from a house. “Indifferent” means one who, when illness or other afflictions arise in the body, remains without seeking their remedy. “Unwavering” means one of steady mind. Others read “without accumulation” (*asaṃcayika*). A “sage” (*muni*) is so called because of his contemplation of Brahman, since *mauna* (the state of a sage) has been explained previously. With his being absorbed in Brahman—that is, with his mind fixed on that alone—dwelling in the forest both by day and night, he should enter a village solely for the purpose of alms. 6.43.
A skull, the roots of trees, ragged clothing, solitude,
and equanimity toward all things— these are the characteristics of one who is liberated.

"Skull," and so forth: an alms-bowl made of clay or similar materials; tree roots for the purpose of dwelling; coarse, worn-out clothing; a loincloth and a patched garment; and, in all circumstances, the absence of enmity or friendship through the perception of Brahman everywhere—because these are the means to liberation, they are the signs of one who is liberated. 6.44
One should not rejoice in death, nor should one rejoice in life; one should simply await one’s time, just as a hired servant awaits his wages. 6.45

"Not so," and so forth. One should desire neither death nor life; rather, one should simply await the time of death determined by one's own karma. It is "indicated" (nirdeśa), meaning wages; just as a laborer awaits the time for the settlement of his wages. 6.45.
One should place one's foot down purified by sight; one should drink water purified by a cloth;
one should speak words purified by truth; and one should act with a mind that is pure. (6.46)

"Pure by sight," and so forth: one should place one's feet on ground purified by sight in order to avoid hair, bones, and the like; one should drink water filtered through a cloth in order to avoid small creatures and such in the water; one should speak words purified by truth. Thus, there is an option between silence and truth. One whose mind is free from the intention to do what is forbidden should always be pure in soul. (6.46)
One should endure harsh words and should not despise anyone;
nor, depending upon this body, should one harbor enmity toward anyone. (4.47)

"Excessive words," and so forth: one should endure excessive speech uttered by others and should not despise anyone. One should not, for the sake of this unstable body—which is the locus of disease—engage in enmity with anyone. (4.47)
One should not respond with anger to one who is angry; when reviled, one should speak kindly;
and one should not utter false speech scattered through the seven gates. 4.48

"Towards one who is angry," and so forth: one should not return anger to anyone who has become angry. Even when reviled by another, one should speak auspicious words and not revile in return. Regarding the phrase "scattered across the seven gates": in the Vedānta philosophy, these refer to the five external sensory organs beginning with the eyes, plus the mind (*manas*) and the intellect (*buddhi*), which constitute the two internal organs. Since speech functions through what is grasped by these, they are called the "seven gates. One should not utter speech that is scattered across or cast into these—that is, speech whose objects are the things grasped by them—but rather speech whose object is Brahman alone.

Now, it might be argued that Brahman is meditated upon by the mind alone, and even the utterance of speech concerning Brahman is an activity of the mind; therefore, even though both are equally scattered through the seven gates, how can it be established that one should speak regarding Brahman and not speak regarding other objects?

It is said: for this very reason, he specified the term "unreal" (*anṛtām*). "Unreal" means false, that is to say, perishable; speech concerning such [objects] is also called unreal. Therefore, one should not utter speech whose object is a perishable effect. Rather, one should speak that which has the imperishable Brahman as its object, in the form of the *praṇava*, the *Upaniṣads*, and so forth. Govindarāja, however, explains that dharma, wealth, pleasure, dharma and wealth, wealth and pleasure, and dharma, wealth, and pleasure—these seven are the gateways for the engagement of speech by virtue of being objects of speech. One should not speak speech that is scattered among or distracted by these, which is of an unreal nature because all differentiation is non-existent.

Others, however, maintain that the seven worlds themselves are the "seven doors" because they are objects of speech; since these are subject to differentiation and destruction, they are unreal. Therefore, one should not utter speech concerning them, which is itself unreal, but should speak only of that which has Brahman as its object. 6.48.
Delighting in the inner self, seated, indifferent, and free from worldly desires, one who seeks happiness should wander here with the self alone as his companion. (6.49)

"Adhyātma" means one whose delight is directed toward the Self, which is Brahman; such a person is "delighting in the inner self" (adhyātmarati), being constantly intent on meditation upon Brahman. "Seated" (āsīna) means established in a yogic posture such as the Svastika. "Independent" (nirapekṣaḥ) means devoid of any special longing even for items like the staff or water-pot. "Free from worldly objects" (nirāmiṣaḥ) means devoid of desire for sense-objects, which are called "flesh" (āmiṣa). Seeking the bliss of liberation with the body alone as his companion, he should wander here in this world of saṃsāra. 6.49
He should never seek alms by means of portents or omens, nor by the science of astrology and bodily marks, nor by instructions or discourses. (6.50)

"Not so," and so forth. He should never desire to obtain alms by means of prophesying the results of omens such as earthquakes or the twitching of the eyes; nor by the "science of the body" (*aṅgavidyā*), such as saying, "Today is Aśvinī; the result of the lines on the hand is such-and-such"; nor by giving instruction through the exposition of scriptural meaning, such as saying, "This is the path of policy; one should conduct oneself in this manner. (6.50)
One should not approach a house crowded with ascetics, Brahmins, birds, dogs, or other mendicants. (6.51)

"Not by ascetics," and so forth: one should not enter for the sake of alms a house that is occupied by forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*), other Brahmins who are accustomed to eating, birds, or dogs. (6.51)
With his hair, nails, and beard trimmed, carrying a bowl, a staff, and a water-pot,
he should wander constantly, self-restrained, without causing pain to any living beings.

"Having trimmed," and so forth. Having his hair, nails, and beard trimmed, carrying a mendicant's bowl and a staff, and equipped with a *kusumbha* water-pot, he should wander at all times without causing pain to any living beings. (6.52)
His vessels should be non-metallic and free from blemishes;
their purification with water is prescribed, just as that of the *camasa* cups in a sacrifice.
"Non-metallic" means that a mendicant's alms-bowls should be made of materials other than gold and so forth, and they should be without holes. Likewise, Yama says:
"There is no dharma for one who accepts alms in vessels of gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, or iron; having accepted them, he shall go to hell."
And the purification of those ascetic bowls is by water alone, just like that of the *camasa* cups at a sacrifice. || 6.53 ||
He shows those very [vessels]:
"A gourd, a wooden bowl, one made of clay, and likewise one made of split bamboo—these, Svāyambhuva Manu declared, are the vessels for ascetics. (6.54)

"Alābu," and so forth. Svāyambhuva Manu declared that the begging bowls of ascetics (yatins) are made from pieces of gourd, wood, clay, bamboo, and the like. Govindarāja explains that "vaidala" means made from the bark of trees. 6.54.
One should go for alms only once a day and should not be attached to an abundance;
for a mendicant who is overly intent on alms becomes attached even to sense-objects. (6.55)

"At one time" means he should go for alms once a day for the sake of sustaining life; even then, he should not indulge in obtaining an abundance of alms.
