For a mendicant who is addicted to eating excessive alms becomes prone to an increase in the primary humors (*dhātu*), and thereby falls even into the objects of sense-pleasure, such as women. (6.55)

When the smoke has ceased, when the pestle lies still, when the embers are extinguished, when the people have finished their meal, and when the removal of the dishes has been completed, the ascetic should always go for alms. (6.56)

"Free from smoke," and so forth. When the smoke of cooking has vanished, when the pestle for threshing has been set aside, when the embers for cooking have been extinguished, when the people of the household have finished their meal, and when the bowls containing the remnants have been discarded—at these times the ascetic should always go for alms. This is an indication of the evening period consisting of the three *muhūrta*s remaining at the end of the day. Thus Yājñavalkya (3.59) says:
"He should wander for alms with vigilance during the evening, not with fixed intent [for specific food].

One should not be despondent in the absence of gain, nor should one rejoice in its presence. One should possess only what is necessary for the maintenance of life, having emerged from attachment to material requisites. (6.57)

"Non-acquisition," and so forth: one should not despond when there is no acquisition of alms and the like, nor should one feel joy upon obtaining them. One should be intent on consuming only such food as is sufficient for the maintenance of life. Even regarding merely a staff and a water-pot, one should not indulge in thoughts such as, "I discard this because it is unattractive" or "I accept this because it is pleasing. (6.57)
One should utterly despise gains obtained through being honored;
for even a mendicant who is already liberated becomes bound by gains obtained through being honored. (6.58)

"Abhi," and so forth. One should censure at all times the obtaining of alms preceded by worship; the meaning is that one should not accept them. For, by accepting gains preceded by worship, even an ascetic who is close to liberation incurs the bonds of birth through affection, possessiveness, and the like directed toward the donor. (6.58)
By consuming little food and by staying and sitting in solitude, one should withdraw the senses when they are being carried away by the objects of the senses. 6.59

"By means of light food," and so forth. By means of the lightness of one's diet and by staying in uninhabited places and the like, one should withdraw the senses that are being drawn away by objects such as forms and other sense-objects. 6.59.
Through the restraint of the senses, through the destruction of passion and hatred, and through non-violence toward living beings, one becomes fit for immortality. 6.60
"Of the senses," and so forth. Because through the restraint of the senses, the absence of passion and hatred, and abstention from harming living beings, one becomes fit for liberation. 6.60
Now, for the sake of detachment from the objects of the senses through the discipline of the faculties, he teaches reflection on the reality of saṃsāra:
"One should contemplate the destinies of men arising from the defects of their karma, as well as their falling into hell and the torments in the abode of Yama. (6.61)

"One should contemplate," and so forth. One should reflect upon the attainment by humans of bodies such as those of animals and the like, caused by the defects of karma consisting in the non-performance of prescribed duties and the performance of censured acts; one should contemplate their falling into hells, and the intense agonies—such as being cut with sharpened swords while residing in hell in the world of Yama—as described in the Śrutis, Purāṇas, and other texts. (6.61)
Separation from the beloved and union with the unloved, as well as being overcome by old age and tormented by diseases. (6.62)

"Separation," and so forth: one should reflect upon separation from beloved sons and others, union with undesirable things such as harm-doers, being overcome by old age, and the affliction caused by diseases and the like—all of which arise from the defects of karma. (6.62)
The departure from this body, the subsequent rebirth in a womb, and the wanderings of this inner self through thousands of millions of wombs—[all these he perceives]. (6.63)

"From the body," and so forth. One should reflect upon how this individual soul (jīvātman) departs from the body; likewise, one should contemplate the great agony of one afflicted by a fatal disease that pierces the vital organs (marman), whose throat is constricted by the humors such as phlegm, the intense suffering of birth within the womb, and the passage through thousands of millions of inferior species of birth, such as dogs and jackals, which are the bonds of one's own karma. 6.63.
The connection with suffering for embodied beings arises from unrighteousness, while the inexhaustible union with happiness arises from righteousness and purpose. 6.64

"Adharma," and so forth. One should contemplate the connection with suffering caused by unrighteousness (*adharma*) for embodied living beings (*jīvātman*); the goal born from righteousness (*dharma*), which is the direct realization of Brahman; and the imperishable union with the bliss of Brahman characterized as liberation (*mokṣa*), which arises from that [realization]. (6.64)
And by means of yoga, one should discern the subtlety of the Supreme Self,
as well as its manifestation within bodies, both high and low.

"Subtlety," and so forth. Through yoga—that is, by the cessation of mental fluctuations directed toward other objects—one should contemplate the subtlety and partlessness of the Supreme Self, which, as the inner controller of all things relative to the gross body and so on, exists as the most subtle; and one should contemplate the birth and presiding presence of individual souls within superior and inferior bodies, such as those of gods or animals, for the sake of experiencing the fruits of their auspicious and inauspicious karma. (6.65)
Even if he is corrupted, one should practice dharma, devoted to whichever stage of life (āśrama) he may be in;
equal toward all beings, the external mark is not the cause of dharma.

"Corrupted": even one who, while residing in any particular stage of life (*āśrama*), is corrupted by conduct contrary to that stage, or even one who is devoid of the external marks (*liṅga*) of that stage, should practice righteousness (*dharma*) while maintaining an equal vision toward all beings through the realization of Brahman in them all. For the mere wearing of marks such as the staff is not the cause of righteousness; rather, it is the performance of what is prescribed. And this has been stated for the purpose of making known the primacy of righteousness, not for the sake of abandoning the marks. (6.66)
Regarding this, he provides an illustration:
"Though the fruit of the *kataka* tree clarifies water, the water does not become clear merely by uttering its name. (6.67)

Regarding the word "fruit": although the fruit of the *kataka* tree produces clarity in turbid water, it does not become clear merely by the utterance of its name; rather, it becomes clear by the casting in of the fruit. Likewise, the mere wearing of the insignia (*liṅga*) is not the cause of dharma, but rather the performance of what is prescribed. 6.67
For the sake of protecting living beings, whether by night or by day, he should always walk upon the earth with careful observation, even at the cost of his own life. (6.68)

"For the sake of protection," and so forth. Even when there is pain to his own body, he should always walk after inspecting the ground, whether by night or by day, for the sake of protecting living beings such as tiny ants. Previously, it was stated—"he should place his foot purified by sight" (6.46)—for the purpose of avoiding hair and the like; this, however, is for the purpose of avoiding injury [to living beings], and thus there is no tautology. 6.68.

Regarding this, he states the penance: "Whatever living beings a mendicant kills unintentionally during the day or the night, for the sake of purifying himself from those [karmas], he should perform six breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) after bathing. (6.69)

"By day or by night": whatever living beings an ascetic (*yati*) kills unintentionally during the day or at night, for the sake of destroying the sin produced by that killing, he should bathe and perform six breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*). And as for the breath-restraint:
"One who has restrained his breath should recite the *Gāyatrī* together with the *Vyāhṛtis*, the *Praṇava*, and the *Śiras* three times; that is called a breath-restraint" (VaDh 25.13).
Thus it should be understood here according to the statement of Vasiṣṭha. 6.69.
Even three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) performed according to rule by a Brāhmaṇa,
joined with the Vyāhṛtis and the Praṇava, should be known as the supreme austerity.

Regarding the phrase "breath-restraints" (*prāṇāyāma*): because of the specification "of a Brāhmaṇa," this instruction applies to the Brāhmaṇa caste and not exclusively to the ascetic (*yati*). All three types of breath-restraints—when joined with the seven *vyāhṛtis* and ten *praṇavas*, and by the rule of "according to the ordinance" (*vidhivat*) joined with the *sāvitrī* and the *śiras*—and when performed according to the method of inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*), should be known as the highest austerity (*tapas*) for a Brāhmaṇa. The nature of inhalation and the others is to be understood from other *smṛtis*. Thus says Yājñavalkya the Yogin:
"An exhalation drawn out through the nostrils while [the air] is being blown in is called *pūraka*."
Kumbhaka is motionless breath; that which is being released is recaka.

Regarding the phrase "the three also," by the word "also" it is meant that these three must certainly be performed; however, by performing more than this, there is an even greater destruction of evil. (6.70)
Just as the impurities of metallic ores are burned away when they are being smelted, so too are the defects of the senses burned away through the restraint of the vital breath. 6.71

"They are burned" means that just as the impurities of metals such as gold and silver are burned when they are being smelted with fire in a crucible, so too are the defects of the mind, such as passion and the like, and those of the eyes and other senses, such as their tendency toward sense-objects, burned by breath control (prāṇāyāma) through the non-contemplation of objects. 6.71.

One should burn away defects by means of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), and evil by means of concentrations (dhāraṇā); one should burn away attachments by means of withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), and non-divine qualities by means of meditation (dhyāna). 6.72.

"By means of breath-restraints," and so forth. This being so, by means of breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) in the manner just described, one should burn away defects such as passion (*rāga*). *Dhāraṇā* is the fixing of the mind upon the desired object, such as the Supreme Brahman; by that, one should destroy evil. By *pratyāhāra*, through the withdrawal of the senses from their objects, one should ward off contact with sense-objects. Regarding "by meditation on Brahman": in the form of a continuous flow of similar cognitions, such as "I am He," one should ward off non-divine qualities—those qualities which do not belong to the Lord, the Supreme Self, such as anger, greed, envy, and the like. (6.72)
One should perceive, through the yoga of meditation, the course of this inner self among beings of high and low station—a course difficult to be known by those of unrefined soul. (6.73)

"Among high and low," and so forth. One should understand through the practice of meditation that the attainment of birth for this individual soul among various superior and inferior states—such as among gods or animals—is difficult to discern by those whose inner organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) have not been refined by the scriptures. Furthermore, having realized that this destiny is fashioned by ignorance, desire, and prohibited actions, one should become established in the knowledge of Brahman; such is the intended meaning. (6.73)
One endowed with right vision is not bound by actions;
but one devoid of vision enters into the cycle of transmigration. (6.74)

Regarding the term *samyagdarśana* (right vision): consequently, one who possesses the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman in its true nature is not bound by actions; for his actions no longer have the power to cause rebirth, since previously accumulated merit and demerit are destroyed by the knowledge of Brahman. Thus says the Śruti (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.24.3): "Just as the tuft of a reed-stalk thrown into a fire is consumed, even so are all his evils consumed; he becomes Brahman alone. Furthermore, by the general Śruti (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8), "And his actions are exhausted when He, the High and the Low, is seen," it is understood that there is a cessation of connection with merit as well. Moreover, even if a sinful action should occur by chance at a later time, there is no clinging of sin [to him]. Thus says the Śruti: "Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows thus. Only the connection with merit and demerit that initiated the present body perishes. This very point was determined by Bādarāyaṇa in the Brahmamīmāṃsā-sūtra (4.1.13): "Upon the attainment of That, there is the non-clinging and destruction of subsequent and prior sins, because of the scriptural declaration thereof. However, one devoid of the direct realization of Brahman undergoes the continuous cycle of birth and death. || 6.74 ||
By means of non-violence, detachment from the senses, Vedic rituals,
and the practice of severe austerities, they attain that state here in this world.

"By non-violence": by avoiding prohibited violence and by the senses' avoidance of attachment to sense-objects through the performance of obligatory Vedic rites—since optional rites are a cause of bondage—as it has been said (2.2): "To be possessed by desire is not praised. And by the practice of austerity (*tapas*) as far as possible, such as fasting, the *kṛcchra*, and the *cāndrāyaṇa* penances, they attain in this world that state, characterized by the ultimate dissolution [into Brahman]. By the preceding verse, the realization of Brahman was stated to be the cause of liberation; by this [verse], action is declared to be its auxiliary. 6.75.
Now, with two verses, he describes the nature of the body for the sake of cultivating detachment from saṃsāra, which is the internal means to liberation:
"Having bones for its pillars, joined by tendons, plastered with flesh and blood, covered with skin, foul-smelling, and filled with urine and excrement. (6.76)
One should abandon this abode of the elements, which is possessed by old age and sorrow, a dwelling place for disease, afflicted, full of passion, and impermanent. (6.77)

"Consisting of bones," and so forth; "assailed by old age," and so forth. That which has bones as its pillars is *asthisthūṇa*; it is bound together by the ropes of sinews, smeared with flesh, blood, and the like, covered with skin, filled with urine and excrement, and for that very reason foul-smelling. It is assailed by old age and affliction, the locus of various diseases, afflicted (*ātura*) by hunger, thirst, cold, heat, and the like, generally possessed of the quality of passion (*rajas*), and perishable by nature. One should abandon this body—the dwelling place, the house, the abode of the elements such as earth—which is described as the very home of the living soul (*jīva*). One should act in such a way that there is no further connection with the body. The similarity to a house is precisely what was stated by the words beginning with "bones. (6.76–77)
Just as a tree leaves the riverbank, or as a bird leaves a tree, so too, casting off this body, one is liberated from the crocodile of suffering. 6.78

"Like the riverbank": for one who worships Brahman, liberation occurs at the time of casting off the body, since the *prārabdha* (commenced) body is destroyed only through the experiencing of its fruits. Regarding this, he describes the two-fold nature of one who casts off the body: He who perceives the falling of the body as dependent on past karma is like a tree on a riverbank; without knowing its own fall, it is cast down by the force of the river. Likewise, he who—through the excellence of knowledge and action—possesses mastery over death like Bhīṣma and others, is like a bird that abandons a tree by its own will. Thus, casting off this body, he is liberated from the misery of saṃsāra, as if from a crocodile, which is a specific kind of aquatic creature. (6.78)
Having cast off both good deeds toward those dear to him and evil deeds toward those who are not dear, through the yoga of meditation, he attains the eternal Brahman. (6.79)

“Regarding beloved ones,” and so forth. The knower of Brahman, having deposited his good deeds upon those dear to him who act for his benefit, and his evil deeds upon those unpleasant to him who act against his interest, constantly approaches Brahman through the yoga of meditation; that is, he merges into Brahman. And thus says the Śruti: “His sons inherit his property; his friends [inherit] his good deeds, and his enemies [his] evil deeds. Having cited such passages, Bādarāyaṇa established in the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*—in the sūtras beginning with “But in the case of abandonment, there is the taking over [of deeds], because of the supplementary nature of the word ‘taking over,’ as in the case of the *kuśā* grass, the meters, the hymns, and the chanting” (BS 3.3.26)—that even though the texts merely mention the abandonment of good and evil deeds, their being taken over must be understood.
But how can the good and evil deeds (*sukṛta-duṣkṛta*) belonging to one person be transferred to another?

It is said: regarding the determination of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), scripture alone is the authority; the transfer of these two is also established solely by the authority of scripture. Therefore, on the basis of scripture, it is proven that these two are capable of being transferred. Consequently, because it is sublated by scripture, there is no emergence of a counter-inference (*pratipakṣānumāna*), such as: "A human skull is pure because it is a part of a living being, like a conch shell."

Medhātithi and Govindarāja, however, explain that when something pleasant is done to one's own dear ones by someone else, one attributes one's own past merit as the cause for it through the practice of meditation; likewise, when something unpleasant is done even to those who are not dear, one designates one's own previously acquired demerit as the cause. Having thus set aside the two persons who actually accomplished those acts—namely, those called passion and hatred—one eternally approaches Brahman, that is, one attains the nature of Brahman.

That is not so; for in the act of "relinquishing" (*visṛjet*), one would have to supply unmentioned objects by interpreting "good deed" and "evil deed" as the two things to be relinquished, and one would have to supply unmentioned actions by imagining that the two mentioned actions function as causes while abandoning their literal verbal status. Furthermore, I believe that this *Manusmṛti* was not thus interpreted out of pride by later scholars, but rather according to the meaning of the Veda as explained by Vyāsa.
When one becomes free from longing for all things through one's inner disposition, then one attains eternal happiness both in this world and after death. (6.80)

Regarding the phrase "when": when, through the cultivation of the defects of sense-objects from the perspective of ultimate reality, one becomes free from desire for all objects, then one attains here in this world the indestructible happiness born of contentment, and in the next world, the happiness of liberation. || 6.80 ||
By this method, having gradually abandoned all attachments, one who is completely freed from all dualities abides in Brahman alone. (6.81)

"By this": having gradually abandoned all attachments in the form of possessiveness toward children, wife, fields, and so forth, and being liberated from dualities such as honor and dishonor, one attains absolute dissolution into Brahman itself by means of this aforementioned practice of knowledge and action. (6.81)
All this that has been described here is indeed meditative;
for no one who is not a knower of the inner self ever enjoys the fruit of ritual action.

Regarding the term *dhyānika* (arising from meditation): by the phrase "this which," that which was stated in the preceding verse is referred to due to its extreme proximity. This which has been described—the renunciation of attachment to sons and so forth, the abandonment of honor and dishonor, and abiding in Brahman alone—all this arises from meditation (*dhyāna*), provided that there is meditation upon the Self as the Supreme Self. When one knows the Self to be the Supreme Self, then one does not distinguish oneself from all beings; for such a person, there is no sense of "mine-ness" nor any honor or dishonor whatsoever. And from such knowledge, the state of being Brahman arises. Because the specific object of meditation is attained through a specific mode of meditation, he speaks regarding the meditation on the Supreme Self: "For one who is not a knower of the inner self (*anadhyātmavit*). Since that which has been taught concerning the individual soul (*jīva*)—namely, its identity with the Supreme Self—he who does not know it or meditate upon it does not attain the fruit of the present meditative practice: the renunciation of possessiveness, the abandonment of honor and dishonor, and liberation. (6.82)
One should constantly recite the Brahman pertaining to sacrifice, as well as that pertaining to the deities, that pertaining to the self, and whatever is declared in the Vedāntas. (6.83)

Regarding the phrase "pertaining to sacrifice" (*adhiyajñam*): Previously, the nature of meditation on Brahman as an object of worship was described; now, as a subordinate limb (*aṅga*) of that, he enjoins the recitation of the Veda. Thus the Śruti (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22), "The Brāhmaṇas seek to know Him through the recitation of the Vedas," teaches the recitation of the Veda as a limb of knowledge—namely, "pertaining to sacrifice. One should always recite the Brahman—the Veda—which is set forth with reference to sacrifice, as well as that which is set forth with reference to the deity, and likewise that which is set forth with reference to the individual soul (*jīva*), as well as that which establishes Brahman in the Vedāntas, such as (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1): "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite. 6.83.
This is the refuge for the ignorant; this very thing is for those who possess knowledge.
This is for those seeking heaven; this is for those seeking the infinite.

"This" refers to this Brahman known as the Veda; it is the refuge and resort even for those ignorant of its meaning, because even mere recitation is a cause for the destruction of evil. It is all the more so the refuge for those who know it, who understand its meaning, and who desire heaven and liberation, because, by teaching the means thereto, it is the cause for attaining them. (6.84)
The twice-born who wanders forth as a mendicant by means of this sequential yoga,
having shaken off all evil in this world, attains the supreme Brahman.

"By this": by means of this practice performed in the order prescribed, he who takes recourse in the stage of renunciation (pravrajyā-āśrama) casts off evil in this world and attains the Supreme Brahman; through the direct realization of Brahman, upon the destruction of the body as a limiting adjunct (upādhi), he goes to oneness with Brahman. 6.85.
This dharma has been taught to you for ascetics of restrained self who have renounced the Vedas; now learn the yoga of action [for those who remain]. 6.86

"This is the Dharma. This common Dharma for you—the four types of ascetics (*yati*) who have restrained their selves, namely the *kuṭīcara*, *bahūdaka*, *haṃsa*, and *paramahaṃsa*—has been declared. Now, listen to the specific connection with ritual action (*karma*) that will be described for those particular ascetics known as *kuṭīcaras*, who are practitioners of the rites prescribed by the Vedas, beginning with the words: "One should dwell happily under the sovereignty of one's sons" (6.95). In the *Mahābhārata*, mendicants (*bhikṣu*) are said to be of four kinds: "There are four types of mendicants: the *kuṭīcara* and the *bahūdaka*... [and so forth].
"The Haṃsa and the Paramahaṃsa—whoever comes later is the superior.
This is the instruction regarding the specific duties of the Kuṭīcara, consisting of the practice of begging for food from his own sons.

Govindarāja, however, says that the Vedasaṃnyāsika is a particular kind of householder who has abandoned Vedic duties such as the Agnihotra and whose Vedic rites are accomplished through knowledge alone.

That is not so; for the scripture prescribes the employment of the fires in the funeral rites (*antyeṣṭi*) of a householder who maintains the sacred fires, and their internal re-deposit (*samāropa*) upon entering the fourth stage of life (*caturthāśrama*). Only in the absence of both these [options] would there be such an abandonment of the fires. Govindarāja, by describing the householder as one who renounces the Vedas (*vedasaṃnyāsika*), has effectively arrived at the same conclusion regarding the abandonment of the fires maintained by those who have consecrated them.
Medhātithi, however, declared the *vedasaṃnyāsika* to be one who is without any support (*nirāśraya*).
And according to that view, how could Manu’s statement regarding the rule for the four stages of life (cāturāśramya) be explained?

Now, although it would have been appropriate to speak immediately after the *karmayoga* promised for the renouncer of the Vedas (*vedasaṃnyāsika*), [the author] restates the previously mentioned stages of life (*āśrama*) in order to show that—whether one is a renouncer of the Vedas belonging to the fifth stage or one who belongs to no stage at all (*nirāśramī*)—only four stages of life are fixed:

"The student (*brahmacārī*), the householder (*gṛhastha*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and likewise the ascetic (*yati*)—these four distinct stages of life originate from the householder. (6.87)

Regarding the term *brahmacārī*: these various stages of life (*āśrama*) that have been mentioned, beginning with the student (*brahmacarya*), are all four produced from the householder (*gṛhastha*). 6.87.
All these, when practiced in due order according to the scriptures, lead a Brahmin who acts as prescribed to the supreme goal. (6.88)

"All these," and so forth. All these four stages of life (*āśrama*), when practiced without transgressing the scriptures—even by three, two, or even one—lead a Brahmin who practices as prescribed to the state characterized by liberation. (6.88)
He will describe the dwelling of one who has renounced the Vedas in the house, under the sovereignty of his sons or in happiness; for that purpose, he states the excellence of the householder:
"And among all these [orders], according to the injunctions of the Veda and Smṛti, the householder is said to be the best, for he supports these three. (6.89)

Regarding the word "of all": among all these classes beginning with the student (*brahmacārin*), the householder is declared by Manu and others to be the best because he is frequently heard of in the injunctions for the *agnihotra* and other rites. Furthermore, he is superior because he supports the students, forest-dwellers, and ascetics by providing them with alms. As it has been said (3.78): "Since even those belonging to the three [other] stages of life [are supported] daily by him through knowledge and food... (6.89).
Just as all rivers and streams find their resting place in the ocean, even so do all those in the various stages of life find their support in the householder. 6.90

"Yathā" and so forth: Just as all rivers and streams, such as the Gaṅgā, Śoṇa, and others, find their resting place in the ocean, even so all other stages of life (āśramins) besides the householder find their station in the proximity of the householder, because their livelihood is dependent upon him. 6.90.
Moreover, this tenfold dharma must always be practiced with diligent effort by the twice-born belonging to all four stages of life.

"By the four," and so forth. This tenfold dharma, whose nature will be described hereafter, must be constantly practiced with great effort by these four classes of twice-born men belonging to the stages of life (āśrama), beginning with the religious student (brahmacārin). (6.91)
He shows that very [dharma] by way of its essential nature and its enumeration:
Fortitude, forbearance, self-restraint, non-stealing, purity, control of the senses, wisdom, knowledge, truthfulness, and freedom from anger—this tenfold set is the characteristic of dharma. (6.92)

"Fortitude," and so forth. Fortitude (*dhṛti*) is contentment. Forbearance (*kṣamā*) is the refraining from retaliation when harm is inflicted by another. Self-restraint (*dama*) is the state of the mind remaining unagitated even when objects that cause transformation are present; for Sanandana says, "Self-restraint is the taming of the mind. Govindarāja states that self-restraint is the endurance of dualities such as cold and heat. Non-stealing (*asteya*) is the opposite of theft, which is the taking of another's property and so forth by unjust means. Purity (*śauca*) is the cleansing of the body with earth and water according to the scriptures. Control of the senses (*indriyanigraha*) is the withdrawal of the eyes and other organs from their objects. Intelligence (*dhī*) is the knowledge of the reality of the scriptures and so forth. Knowledge (*vidyā*) is the knowledge of the Self. Truthfulness (*satya*) is speech that accords with reality. Non-anger (*akrodha*) is the non-arising of anger even when there is a cause for anger. This is the tenfold nature of Dharma. (6.92)
Those brahmins who thoroughly study the ten characteristics of dharma, and having studied them, live in accordance with them, attain the supreme goal. (6.93)

Regarding the "ten characteristics": those Brahmins who recite these tenfold forms of dharma and, having recited them, practice them in conjunction with self-knowledge, attain the supreme goal characterized by liberation through the excellence of the knowledge of Brahman. (6.93)
Practicing the Dharma characterized by the ten marks and remaining composed, the twice-born man, having heard the Vedānta according to the prescribed rule, should renounce, free from debt. (6.94)

"Regarding the phrase 'consisting of ten characteristics': having practiced the Dharma consisting of ten characteristics with a restrained mind, and having understood from the mouth of a guru the duties of study as prescribed for the stage of a householder—such as the meaning of the *Upaniṣads* and so forth—one who has purified the three debts to the gods and others should practice renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). (6.94)
Having renounced all actions and cast off the defects of action, he should live happily under the sovereignty of his sons, self-restrained and devoted to the study of the Veda. (6.95)

"Having renounced" (*saṃnyasya*): having abandoned all duties such as the *agnihotra* to be performed by a householder, and having destroyed the sins produced by the unintentional killing of living beings and other acts through breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and similar means, with his senses restrained, he should dwell happily, having practiced the *Upaniṣads* both in letter and in meaning, free from anxiety regarding his livelihood because of the sovereignty of his sons—that is, by means of food and clothing provided by his son in his son's house. This alone is declared to be the specific duty of the *kuṭīcara*. It was stated previously [in verse 6.86], "But for those who have renounced the Veda," precisely in order to express this very point. 6.95.
Having thus renounced all actions, intent upon his own duty and free from longing, he destroys sin through renunciation and attains the supreme goal. (6.96)

"Thus. In this manner, acting as described, one who has abandoned the duties of a householder such as the *agnihotra* and made the realization of the Self his primary task—being free from desire even for heaven and the like because they are causes of bondage—destroys sins through renunciation (*pravrajyā*) and attains the supreme goal characterized by liberation through the direct realization of Brahman. 6.96.
This fourfold dharma of the Brahmin, which is meritorious and yields imperishable fruit after death, has been declared to you; now learn the dharma of kings.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.

"This" refers to what is said after addressing the sages: "This ritual complex belonging to you Brāhmaṇas is Dharma; it has been declared to have fourfold results in the hereafter according to the distinctions of student, householder, forest-dweller, and so forth. Now hear the Dharma pertaining to the King. And since this verse teaches the four stages of life (cāturāśramya) for the Brāhmaṇa, and because it was previously stated that "a Brāhmaṇa may renounce," the qualification for renunciation belongs to the Brāhmaṇa alone. (6.97)
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Manvarthamuktāvalī, a commentary on the Code of Manu, composed by the illustrious Kullūkabhaṭṭa.
The seventh chapter begins.
I shall proclaim the duties of kings, how a monarch should conduct himself, how his origin comes about, and how his supreme success is achieved. (7.1)

Regarding the phrase "the duties of kings" (*rājadharmān*): here, the word *dharma* refers to those practices to be performed for the sake of both visible and invisible results, since the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*) and other such matters will also be discussed later. Furthermore, the word *rājan* here does not denote the Kṣatriya caste, but rather a person who has been consecrated as the protector of a people and a city. For this very reason, he says: "In what manner a king should conduct himself. I shall describe the duties to be performed by him so that the king may become one whose conduct is proper. I shall also explain how his origin occurred—beginning with the verse, "The Lord created the King" (7.3)—and in what manner the attainment of visible and invisible fruits comes about. (7.1)
By a Kṣatriya who has duly received the Brāhmaṇical consecration, the protection of all this [world] must be performed according to the law. (7.2)

"Brāhma," and so forth. *Brahman* refers to the Veda; the sacrament of initiation (*upanayana*) is for the purpose of attaining that. A Kṣatriya who has received that according to the scriptures must, as a rule, provide protection for all this [world] situated within his own domain in accordance with the treatises. By this, it is shown that only a Kṣatriya—and no other—is entitled to sovereignty. For this very reason, he will state that the true essence of the meaning of the scriptures is for the livelihood of a Kṣatriya, and likewise that protection is the most excellent among the duties of a Kṣatriya. Indeed, regarding a Brāhmaṇa in times of distress, he will declare: "He may live by the duty of a Kṣatriya" (10.81). Nārada also stated that in times of distress, a Vaiśya may follow the duty of a Kṣatriya, and a Śūdra may follow the duties of both a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya for the sake of livelihood.
A Brāhmaṇa should never perform the work of a Śūdra, nor should a Śūdra perform the work of a Brāhmaṇa; for those two [tasks] lead to their downfall.
Neither superior nor inferior karma exists for those two;
for, having abandoned middling karma, they are indeed common to all.

"The protection of the Vedas and the Dharma is the austerity of the Kṣatriya, whose duty is protection. And because it will be stated later, "A sixth part of the merit from all [virtuous acts] accrues to the king who protects" (8.304), the taking of a sixth part of the tribute by the protector serves a visible purpose; yet, as for one who "takes tribute without protecting," the author will declare his fall into hell (8.307).
For when this world was without a king and everyone fled in every direction out of fear, the Lord created a king for the protection of all this. (7.3)

Regarding the phrase "without a king": because when the world is without a king, it is shaken on all sides by fear of the powerful, [Brahmā] created a king for the protection of all this world of moving and non-moving beings; therefore, protection must be performed by him. 7.3.
He explains how he created [the world]: "Having extracted the eternal constituent parts (mātrā) of Indra, Anila, Yama, and Arka, as well as of Agni, Varuṇa, and of Candra and Vitteśa. (7.4)
Regarding the word "Indra": having drawn forth the portions—the essential parts—of Indra, Vāyu, Yama, Sūrya, Agni, Varuṇa, Candra, and Kubera, he created the king. || 7.4 ||
Since this king was fashioned from portions of these lords of the gods, he therefore surpasses all beings in his splendor. (7.5)
"Because of which" means: because the king was created from the portions of Indra and the other foremost gods, therefore he surpasses all living beings in prowess. (7.5)
Like the sun, he scorches both eyes and minds;
no one on earth is able even to look upon him. (7.6)
"He scorches," and so forth. This king, like the sun by his own splendor, torments the eyes and minds of those who behold him; yet no one on earth is able to look directly at this king. (7.6)
By his power, he becomes fire and wind; he is the sun, the moon, and the King of Dharma; he is Kubera, Varuṇa, and Mahendra. || 7.7 ||

“*Sa*,” and so forth. Thus, because fire and the other elements arise from the aforementioned portions and because they perform their respective functions, their *pratāpa* (majestic power) is described; for this will be explained in the ninth chapter with the words “*tejasvī*” (9.310) and so on. That king, through his excellence of power, becomes the very form of fire and the other elements. 7.7.
A ruler of the earth must not be despised even if he is a child, thinking "he is but a man";
for he is a great divinity dwelling in human form. (7.8)

"Though a child," and so forth. Therefore, even a child should not be despised with the thought that he is merely a human being; for this is some great deity abiding in human form. By this, the unseen faults such as demerit (adharma) resulting from the contempt of a deity have been stated.
Now he speaks of the visible fault:
"Ordinary fire burns only the man who approaches it carelessly;
but the king's fire burns the entire family, along with its livestock and accumulated wealth. (7.9)

"Only one," and so forth. The fire burns only that single person who approaches it too closely without caution; it does not burn his sons and the rest. When enraged, the king-fire destroys the entire family—including sons, wife, brothers, and so on—along with their collection of wealth such as cattle, horses, livestock, and gold, provided they are guilty of the offense. (7.9)
Having truly considered the task at hand, as well as his own power, place, and time,
he repeatedly assumes various forms for the sake of accomplishing dharma.

"Action," and so forth. That king, having regard for his purpose and considering his own power as well as the place and time, assumes in reality many forms—the universal form (*viśvarūpa*)—for the sake of accomplishing his objectives. The singular number is used for the plural by virtue of the intention to express the genus. In a state of weakness he endures; having attained power, he uproots [the enemy]. Thus, even in a single place and at a single time, he may become an enemy, a friend, or neutral according to the requirements of the situation. Therefore, one should not despise him with the thought, "I am a favorite of the king. (7.10)
In whose favor dwells the lotus-seated Śrī, in whose prowess lies victory,
and in whose wrath abides death— for he is composed of all splendor.

"Of whom," and so forth. Although the word *padmā* is a synonym for *śrī* (fortune), it is used here with the intention of emphasizing its greatness. Since great fortune arises through his grace, he is to be served by one who desires fortune. He destroys even those enemies who exist against him once they have been propitiated; therefore, he is also to be worshipped by one who desires the destruction of enemies. He brings about the death of whomever he becomes angry with; therefore, one who desires to live must not provoke his anger. This is because he bears the splendor of all things, such as the sun, fire, and the moon. (7.11)
But whoever hates him out of delusion will undoubtedly perish;
for the king sets his mind upon his swift destruction. (7.12)

"Tam" and so forth. He who, out of ignorance, hates that king causes him displeasure; he will certainly perish through the king's wrath, because the king quickly directs his mind toward his destruction. (7.12)
Therefore, that lord of men should apply whatever dharma is intended for those who are dear, and he should not deviate from that dharma even regarding those who are not dear. (7.13)

"Therefore," and so forth. Since the king consists of all splendor (*tejas*), therefore, regarding matters that require consideration, he determines and establishes what is desired—that which is to be practiced according to the scriptures and not contrary to the scriptures; and regarding matters that do not require consideration, he does not transgress the restrictive rule of what is undesired. (7.13)
For its sake, the Lord formerly created Dharma, his own son, the protector of all beings, the staff consisting of the splendor of Brahman.

"His purpose" means: for the sake of accomplishing that king's objective, Brahmā first created a son who was a protector of all living beings and the very embodiment of Dharma; he was fashioned from Brahmā’s own exclusive splendor (*tejas*), not from a body composed of the five elements. 7.14.
Out of fear of him, all beings, both stationary and moving, provide for his enjoyment and do not deviate from their own duties.

"Of that," and so forth. Through fear of that rod (*daṇḍa*), all living beings, both moving and unmoving, become capable of experiencing their enjoyments. Otherwise, if a strong person were to seize the wealth, wife, and so forth of a weak person, then even for that [strong person], enjoyment would not be established because he too would be subject to the stronger; thus, the enjoyment of trees and other stationary things would not be possible. Likewise, even for the virtuous, the performance of obligatory and occasional duties as well as their own specific duties occurs only out of fear of the torments of Yama should they fail to perform them. (7.15)
Having truly considered the place, the time, the power, and the learning [of those involved],
he should appropriately apply [punishment] toward men who act unjustly.

"Regarding that," and so forth: having accurately determined—according to the scriptures—the specific punishment, the time and place, and the capacity of the offender, such as his learning and other qualities, as well as the particular offense for which a certain punishment is appropriate, he should apply it toward those who have committed the offense. (7.16)
That king is the man, he is the rod, he is the leader and the ruler;
he is remembered as the guarantor of the dharma of the four stages of life.

"He," and so forth. He alone is the staff (*daṇḍa*), for in reality he is the king, since the power of kingship resides in him; he alone is the man (*puruṣa*), because all others are subject to him like women; he alone is the leader (*netā*), for by him all affairs are led—that is, brought to completion; he alone is the ruler (*śāsitā*), because he is the giver of *śāsana*, which means command; and he alone is recorded by the sages as being like a guarantor (*pratibhū*) for the fulfillment of the dharma common to all four stages of life (*āśrama*). (7.17)
The rod governs all subjects; the rod alone protects them.
The rod remains awake while others sleep; the wise know the rod to be Dharma. (7.18)

"The rod punishes" (daṇḍaḥ śāsti): because the rod issues commands to all subjects, it should be understood that it is rightly said to "govern" (śāsiteti). Because it alone protects the subjects, it is appropriately called "king" (rājā). Even when the protectors are asleep, the rod alone remains awake; for it is out of fear of it alone that thieves and others do not act. They know the rod itself to be "dharma," because it is the cause of dharma. This is a metaphorical attribution of the effect to the cause. It is precisely through the fear of punishment in this world and the next that the practice of dharma occurs. (7.18)
When properly supported through careful deliberation, he delights all his subjects;
but when applied without deliberation, he brings about destruction on every side. (7.19)

"Having examined," and so forth. That punishment, having been properly determined according to the scriptures and applied to the body, wealth, and so on in accordance with the offense, makes all subjects full of affection. However, when employed without deliberation due to greed and the like, it destroys all external objects, sons, and so forth. In the word "sarvataḥ," the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the accusative case. (7.19)
If the king were not vigilant in inflicting punishment upon those deserving of it, the stronger would roast the weaker like fish on a spit. (7.20)

"Yadi" and so forth. If the king, becoming indolent, were not to administer punishment, then the strong would devour the weak like fish on a spit; this is the form of the root *pac* ending in the conditional (*ḷṅ*). The meaning is that the powerful would have committed violence against those of little strength. "They would devour [them] like fish on a spit"—this is the reading recorded by Medhātithi and Govindarāja. There is also an alternative reading: "They would harm [them] like fish in water. In this context, it is stated that if the strong were to harm the weak, it would result in nothing but the "law of the fish" (*matsyanyāya*). (7.20)
A crow might eat the sacrificial cake, and a dog might lick the oblation; there would be no ownership of anything, and the lower would prevail over the higher. (7.21)

"Let him eat": if the king had not administered punishment, then in sacrifices the crow, being entirely unworthy of the oblation, would have eaten the *puroḍāśa* cake; likewise, the dog would have licked the milk-rice and other offerings. There would have been no ownership for anyone anywhere. Consequently, because the strong would seize [everything], among the castes such as the Brāhmaṇas, that which was inferior—such as the Śūdras and so forth—would have become superior and predominant. (7.21)
The entire world is subdued by punishment, for a pure man is hard to find;
indeed, out of fear of punishment, the whole world is fit for enjoyment.

"Everyone": this entire world remains on the path only when restrained by punishment. For a person naturally pure is found with great difficulty; likewise, this whole world is capable of even necessary enjoyments such as food only through the fear of punishment. (7.22)
Although it has already been stated that punishment brings about prosperity, it is stated once more for the sake of reinforcement:
"Even gods, dānavas, gandharvas, rākṣasas, birds, and serpents—they too are made fit for enjoyment only when restrained by punishment. (7.23)

"O gods!"—the gods such as Indra, Agni, Sūrya, Vāyu, and others, as well as the Dānavas, Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, birds, and serpents, are all indeed afflicted by the fear of the supreme reality of the Lord of the World, and it is for the sake of providing benefits such as rain that they engage in their activities. Thus says the Śruti (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.6.3):
"Out of fear of Him the fire burns; out of fear the sun shines;
out of fear Indra, Vāyu, and Death as the fifth run about."
All social classes would become corrupted and all boundaries would be shattered; moreover, there would be universal upheaval resulting from the misapplication of punishment. (7.24)

"Lest they should become corrupted": because punishment is not administered or is applied improperly, all the social orders (varṇas), beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, would become intermixed through sexual intercourse with one another's women; all scriptural injunctions, which yield the fruits of the four aims of human life, would perish; and through injury to others by means of theft, violence, and so forth, a universal upheaval of the world would arise. (7.24)
Where the dark-complexioned, red-eyed Punisher stalks about, destroying evil, there the subjects do not go astray, provided that the leader perceives rightly. (7.25)

"Wherever... [means]: in whatever region the staff—whose dark complexion, red eyes, and presiding deity have been understood through the authority of the scriptures—is seen wandering, there the subjects do not become agitated, provided that the wielder of the staff understands [his duty] correctly in accordance with the specific circumstances. (7.25)
They say that the one who should guide it is a king who speaks the truth,
who acts with circumspection, who is wise, and who is skilled in the matters of dharma, pleasure, and wealth.

"Of him," and so forth. Manu and others have also declared that the one who sets this rod of punishment into motion is the king, endowed with qualities such as consecration (*abhiṣeka*), who speaks truthfully, acts with circumspection, is fit for discerning reality from unreality, possesses wisdom, and knows the principles of dharma, artha, and kāma. (7.26)
A king who administers that [punishment] properly prospers through the three aims of life;
but one who is self-indulgent, unjust, and base is destroyed by that very punishment.

"Regarding that": by properly administering that rod of punishment, a king attains growth in virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), and pleasure (*kāma*). However, a king who is lustful for sense-objects, unjust, wrathful, mean, and a seeker of pretexts is destroyed by his very own subjects—the ministers and others—either through anger or through unrighteousness. (7.27)
For punishment is a very great power, difficult to be wielded by those of undisciplined soul;
it destroys the king himself, along with his kinsmen, if he deviates from righteousness.

Regarding the word "punishment" (*daṇḍa*): since punishment is of the nature of supreme splendor and is maintained with difficulty by those whose selves have not been refined by their own scriptures, it destroys the king himself—devoid of the duties of royalty—along with his sons and kinsmen. (7.28)
Then he would afflict the fortress, the kingdom, and the world with all its moving and unmoving beings,
as well as the sages and gods dwelling in the intermediate space.

Regarding the word "tataḥ": the punishment that is inflicted without regard for faults and the like will, immediately after the destruction of kinsmen and the king, afflict the region consisting of the kingdom with its forts such as deserts and the like, along with the world of the earth including all moving and stationary beings; for according to the Vedic text, "The gods live by the offering of oblations," in the absence of such offerings, it would distress the ṛṣis and gods residing in the intermediate space. (7.29)
Thus, he cannot be led by the right path by one who is without a companion, who is deluded, greedy, of unrefined intellect, and attached to the objects of the senses. (7.30)

"Sa" and so forth. That rod [of punishment] cannot be administered according to the scriptures by a king who is foolish, greedy, whose intellect is not refined by the treatises, and who is devoid of assistants such as ministers, generals, and chaplains. (7.30)
Punishment can be effectively administered by one who is pure, true to his word, follows the scriptures, possesses good assistants, and is wise. (7.31)

Regarding the word "pure" (*śuci*): it can be accomplished by one who is endowed with purity of purpose and so forth, who is true to his promise, who conducts himself according to the scriptures, who possesses excellent companions, and who knows reality. Thus, by this verse, the virtues that serve as the antidotes to the previously mentioned defects are stated. (7.31)
He should conduct himself with justice within his own kingdom, be severe in punishment toward enemies, straightforward toward friends, and full of devotion toward the Brahmins. (7.32)

"In one's own kingdom" means that he should conduct himself according to the scriptures within his own territory. Toward the territories of enemies, he should be severe in punishment. Toward friends who possess natural affection, he should be straightforward, but not toward those who are friends merely for the sake of business. And toward Brahmins, as well as those who have committed only minor offenses, he should be patient. (7.32)
For a king who conducts himself in this manner, even if he lives by gleaning ears of grain, his fame spreads throughout the world like a drop of oil upon the water. (7.33)

"Thus," and so forth. By "gleaning from ears of grain" (*śiloñcha*), the state of having one's treasury exhausted is intended. Even for a king whose treasury is depleted, if he follows the aforementioned conduct, his fame spreads throughout the world like a drop of oil upon water. (7.34)
But for a king who is the opposite of this—whose self is unsubdued—his fame in the world diminishes like a drop of clarified butter upon water. (7.34)
"Therefore" means: for a king who possesses conduct contrary to that which has been described, whose senses are unsubdued, his fame contracts in the world like a drop of ghee upon water. 7.34.
The king was created as the protector of all the social classes and stages of life, who are each established in their respective duties in due order. (7.35)

"Each in his own [duty]," and so forth. The Creator brought forth the King as the protector of the castes, such as the Brāhmaṇas, and the stages of life, such as the religious student (brahmacārin), who perform their respective duties in due order. Therefore, there is sin for a king who fails to protect them. However, the intended meaning is that there is no sin for him even if he does not protect those who have fallen away from their own duties. (7.35)
Therefore, whatever must be done by one who protects his subjects along with his retinue,
all that I shall declare to you correctly and in due order.

"By him," and so forth. This verse serves as an introduction to what is about to be said. Whatever must be done by that king, together with his ministers, while protecting his subjects, all of that I shall declare to you in its entirety. (7.36)
Having risen in the morning, the king should attend upon the Brahmins;
he should stand by those who are learned and advanced in the three Vedas, and abide by their instruction. (7.37)

"Brāhmaṇas" means that, having risen every morning, one should serve learned Brāhmaṇas—who are experts in the meaning of the texts of the three branches of knowledge known as Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma—and who are conversant with the science of ethics (nītiśāstra), and carry out their instructions. (7.37)
One should always serve elderly Brahmins who are pure and learned in the Vedas;
for one who constantly serves the elderly is honored even by the Rākṣasas. (7.38)

"Vṛddhān," and so forth. He should constantly serve those Brāhmaṇas who are advanced in age, austerity, and other such qualities; who know the Veda both in its meaning and its text; and who are pure outwardly and inwardly through the giving of wealth and other means. For one who serves the elderly is honored even by violent Rākṣasas, and they even act for his benefit; how much more so, then, by human beings? (7.38)
From them he should constantly learn discipline, even though his own self is already disciplined;
for a king whose self is disciplined never perishes. (7.39)

"From them," and so forth. Even though he is disciplined by means of innate wisdom and knowledge of the treatises on statecraft (*arthaśāstra*) and the like, he should practice discipline toward them even more intensely for the sake of excellence; for a king whose self is disciplined never perishes. (7.39)
"Many kings, together with their retinues, have perished through lack of discipline;
yet even those living in the forest have obtained kingdoms through discipline. (7.40)

"Many," and so forth. Even kings, though possessed of retinues such as elephants, horses, and treasuries, have perished if they lack discipline (*vinaya*). And many forest-dwellers, though without any retinue, have obtained sovereignty through discipline. (7.40)
In both cases, he provides an illustration with two verses: "Vena was ruined through lack of discipline, as were King Nahuṣa, Sudās Paijavana, Sumukha, and Nimi. (7.41)
Vena, and so forth: King Vena, Nahuṣa, Pijavana’s son named Sudās, Sumukha, and Nimi all perished through their lack of discipline. (7.41)
Pṛthu indeed obtained the kingdom through discipline, as did Manu;
Kubera obtained mastery over wealth, and the son of Gādhi obtained the status of a Brāhmaṇa.

"Pṛthu": Both Pṛthu and Manu obtained their kingdoms through discipline (*vinaya*). Kubera attained the lordship of wealth through discipline. And Viśvāmitra, the son of Gādhi, though born a Kṣatriya, attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa in that very body. Although the attainment of Brāhmaṇahood was not the immediate subject at the time of his acquisition of a kingdom, it is mentioned here for the sake of illustrating the excellence of discipline; such is this discipline—consisting of the performance of scriptural injunctions and the avoidance of what is forbidden—that even a Kṣatriya attained the Brāhmaṇahood so difficult to obtain.
From those learned in the three Vedas, he [learned] the triple knowledge, the eternal science of government,
the science of inquiry, the knowledge of the self, and the practical applications of the arts from the world.

"From those learned in the three Vedas": from those who know the science consisting of the three Vedas, he should study the three Vedas both in their meaning and their textual form; for the acquisition of the Vedas occurs during the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*), and it is only after returning home (*samāvṛtta*) that one has the authority to rule. This instruction is for the purpose of practice. Furthermore, he should learn the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*)—which consists of the treatises on material prosperity (*arthaśāstra*) and teaches the acquisition and preservation of wealth—from those who know it, as it is eternal by virtue of its traditional transmission. Likewise, he should train in *ānvīkṣikī*, the science of logic (*tarka-vidyā*), which is useful for understanding the activity of beings, and in the science of Brahman (*brahma-vidyā*), which is the cause for pacifying joy and sorrow in times of prosperity and adversity. He should learn the arts (*vārtā*)—such as agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing—which concern the means of acquiring wealth and the undertakings thereof—from farmers and others who are experts in them.
One should apply oneself day and night to the conquest of the senses;
for only one who has conquered his senses is able to keep his subjects under control. (7.44)

"Of the senses," and so forth. One should always exert effort to prevent the attachment of the senses—the eye and the others—to their objects; for one who has conquered his senses is able to govern his subjects, but not one who is distracted by the enjoyment of sense-objects. Although the conquest of the senses has already been mentioned among the duties of a religious student (*brahmacārin*) because it is to be adopted by all men, it is repeated here to make known its preeminence among the duties of a king and because it is the cause for the cessation of the vices that will be described immediately below. (7.44)
One should strive to avoid with great effort the ten vices arising from desire and the eight born of anger, which have miserable ends. (7.45)

“Ten,” and so forth. One should diligently abandon the ten vices born of desire and the eight born of anger that will be described hereafter. These are “ending badly” (durantāni), meaning they conclude in suffering; they provide pleasure at first but are painful in the end. For it is impossible to turn back those who are addicted to such vices. (7.45)

He states the purpose for avoiding them: "For a lord of the earth who is addicted to vices born of desire is deprived of both wealth and dharma; but one addicted to those born of anger is deprived even of himself. (7.46)

"Regarding those born of desire": because a king addicted to calamities born of desire is deprived of both dharma and artha; one addicted to those born of anger meets his own destruction through the provocation of his subjects. (7.46)
He shows those vices by name:
hunting, gambling, sleeping by day, slander, women, intoxication, the triple symphony [of song, dance, and music], and idle wandering—this is the tenfold group born of desire. (7.47)

"Regarding 'hunting' and so forth: hunting (*mṛgayā*) is the killing of wild animals known as *ākheṭa*; gambling with dice (*akṣa*); daytime sleep, which obstructs all undertakings; speaking of the faults of others; sexual union with women; intoxication produced by the drinking of liquor; the triple symphony (*tauryatrika*), consisting of dance, song, and instrumental music; and aimless wandering—this group of ten qualities arises from the desire for pleasure. (7.47)
Slander, violence, malice, envy, finding fault, and the corruption of wealth, as well as harshness of speech and severity of punishment—this is the eightfold group born of anger. (7.48)

Regarding "slander" (*paiśunya*): slander is the disclosure of faults that have not been ascertained; violence (*sāhasa*) is the restraint of a virtuous person through imprisonment and the like; malice (*droha*) is killing by means of a stratagem; envy (*īrṣyā*) is intolerance of another's virtues; jealousy (*asūyā*) is the disclosure of faults in others' virtues; the corruption of wealth (*arthadūṣaṇa*) is the seizure of property and the non-payment of what is due; verbal cruelty (*vākpāruṣya*) is abuse and the like; physical cruelty (*daṇḍapāruṣya*) is beating and the like. This group of eight vices arises from anger. (7.48)
One should strive to conquer that greed which all poets know to be the root of both these; for from it both these groups arise.

Regarding the phrase "of the two": the authors of the Smṛtis know that the cause of both these collections of calamities—desire and anger—is greed; therefore, one should abandon greed with effort. For this pair of categories arises from greed, since they proceed sometimes from greed for wealth and sometimes from greed for other things. (7.49)
Drinking, dice, women, and hunting—in this sequence, one should know this tetrad to be the most grievous among the group born of desire. (7.50)

"Drinking" refers to the drinking of intoxicants, gambling with dice, sexual indulgence with women, and hunting; one should know that this tetrad, listed in this order among the vices arising from desire (*kāmajavyasana*), is an especially potent cause of suffering because it possesses many faults. (7.50)
One should always recognize this triad as grievous, even within the group born of anger: the infliction of punishment, verbal abuse, and the violation of property. (7.51)

"Of punishment," and so forth. One should consider that even within the group of vices born of anger—namely, the infliction of physical punishment, verbal abuse, and the destruction of property—it is a means of producing excessive suffering due to the abundance of its faults. (7.51)
A self-possessed person should know that among this group of seven vices, which are everywhere interconnected, each preceding one is more grievous than the next. (7.52)

Regarding the phrase "of the sevenfold": a king of refined soul should recognize that among this entire class of vices—consisting of drinking and so forth, arising from desire and anger, numbering seven, and generally present throughout the whole circle of kings—the preceding vice is more grievous than the succeeding one. To illustrate: gambling is more grievous than drinking. For while one intoxicated by drink loses consciousness and thus engages in arbitrary conduct leading to the ruin of body, wealth, and so on, in gambling there is even the possibility of gaining wealth; yet gambling is worse than addiction to women, for in gambling there are the faults taught in the treatises on statecraft (*nītiśāstra*), such as the provocation of enmity. Furthermore, the suppression of the urges of urine and feces leads to the outbreak of disease. In the case of addiction to women, however, there is even the presence of virtues, such as the procreation of offspring. Between hunting and addiction to women, addiction to women is the more grievous. In that case, through the delay of necessary affairs, there are faults such as the neglect of *dharma*; whereas in hunting, there is even the presence of virtues such as health due to physical exercise. Thus, among the four vices born of desire, each preceding one has a more serious fault. Among the three vices born of anger as well, physical assault is more grievous than verbal abuse. Because cutting off limbs and the like cannot be easily remedied, whereas the fire of anger in verbal abuse can be extinguished by the water-sprinkling of gifts and honors. Verbal abuse is more harmful than the embezzlement of wealth because it causes pain to the vital points (*marman*) and is difficult to cure. As it is said: "What is done by words does not heal. Embezzlement of wealth, however, can be remedied by the giving of even greater wealth. Thus, among the triad born of anger, each preceding one is more grievous; he should therefore abandon them with great effort. (7.52)
Between calamity and death, calamity is said to be the more grievous;
the man of calamity sinks lower and lower, while the man free from calamity goes to heaven when he dies. (7.53)

Regarding the phrase "of calamity" (*vyasanasya*): although both death and calamity are equal in this world as causes of suffering such as the loss of consciousness, and as being contrary to the practice of the scriptures, nevertheless, calamity is more grievous because it is a cause for falling into hell in the next world as well. Thus it is said: "The man of calamity goes lower and lower," meaning he goes to many hells. But one who is free from calamity, having died, goes to heaven because he lacks the calamities that oppose the practice of the scriptures. By this, excessive attachment to calamities is forbidden, but not their mere occurrence. (7.53)
He should appoint seven or eight ministers who are hereditary, learned in the scriptures, brave, skilled in hitting the mark, of noble birth, and thoroughly tested. (7.54)

"Hereditary" (*maulān*) means hereditary servants who have served through the lineage of father and grandfather; even among them, because of the possibility of deviation through treachery and the like, he should appoint those who know the scriptures regarding visible and invisible matters, who are valiant, and who are "marked" (*labdhalakṣān*), meaning those whose bodies and weapons have not missed their mark—i.e., experts in weaponry. He should appoint seven or eight such ministers, born of pure families and restrained by contact with deities and other observances, for counsel and other duties.
For this reason:
"Even an action that is easy to perform is difficult for one person alone;
how much more so a kingdom of great consequence when undertaken without assistance? (7.55)

"Even," and so forth. Even that action which is performed with ease becomes difficult for one person alone; how much more so that which yields great fruit—how could that be accomplished by one who is without assistance? (7.55)

Together with them, he should constantly deliberate upon matters common [to all kings]: peace and war, the strategic position, revenue, protection, and the consolidation of what has been acquired. (7.56)

"By them," and so forth. Together with his ministers, he should deliberate upon matters that must not be kept secret, such as peace and war. Likewise, he should consider the *sthāna*—so called because one stands firm by means of it—which consists of four parts: the army (*daṇḍa*), the treasury (*kośa*), the city (*pura*), and the kingdom (*rāṣṭra*). That which is used for punishing is the *daṇḍa*, consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry; their maintenance, protection, and so forth must be considered. The *kośa* is the accumulation of wealth; its income, expenditure, and so forth must be considered. The protection of the city and the nature of the kingdom—the land and its capacity to support the inhabitants, such as men and cattle—must be considered. Likewise, he should examine the *samudaya*, so called because from it wealth "arises" (*samudayanti*) or is produced; this refers to the sources of production such as grain and gold. Furthermore, he should attend to *gupti*, or protection, both personal and pertaining to the kingdom. He will describe personal protection in the passage beginning, "And these women should be examined" (7.219), and the protection of the kingdom in the passage beginning, "Constantly in the administration of the kingdom" (7.113). Finally, he should consider the "pacifying" of acquired wealth, such as bestowing it upon worthy recipients; as he will say: "Having conquered, he should worship the gods" (7.201), and so forth. (7.56)
Having ascertained each of their individual intentions,
he should act for his own benefit in matters concerning all of them collectively.

"Of them" means: since it is possible to know the thoughts dwelling in the hearts of those ministers in private due to the absence of opposition, one should understand the intention of each individually as well as the intention of all together simultaneously, and then act in the matter that is beneficial for oneself. (7.57)
But the king should deliberate on the supreme counsel concerning the sixfold policy with a distinguished, wise Brahmin among all his advisors. (7.58)

"Of all these": from among all these very ministers, he should invite for consultation a distinguished and learned Brāhmaṇa, endowed with righteousness and other qualities, regarding the excellent counsel characterized by the six attributes of policy (saṃdhi, vigraha, etc. to be described hereafter. 7.58.
Always placing his full trust in him, he should entrust all affairs to him;
having deliberated with him, he should then undertake his work. (7.59)

"Always": having become one who has gained constant confidence in that Brahmin, he should entrust all his affairs to him; having reached a decision together with him, he should undertake every action. (7.59)
He should also appoint other ministers who are pure, wise, steadfast, thoroughly tested, and capable of properly collecting revenue.

"Others," and so forth: he should also appoint as ministers others who are pure through the giving of wealth and other such acts, who possess wisdom, who are habituated to acquiring wealth rightly, and who have been examined by means of their dharma and other qualities. (7.60)
He should appoint as many men—vigilant, skillful, and discerning—as are required to carry out his duties. (7.61)

"Nirvarteta" means: he should appoint that same number of men—free from laziness, energetic in their tasks, and knowledgeable in those specific duties—as are required by this king to accomplish the multitude of works. (7.61)
For their sake, he should employ those who are brave, capable, and of noble birth at the mines and in industrial works;
and those who are pure and timid within the inner apartments.

Regarding the phrase "of them": among those ministers, he should appoint those who are valiant, clever, restrained by the goad of their noble lineage (*kulāṅkuśa*), pure, and free from desire for wealth to positions at the source of revenue. An illustration of this is the phrase "mines and workshops" (*ākarakarmānta*): in mines, which are places where gold and other minerals are produced, and in workshops, which are places for the collection of sugarcane, grain, and so forth, he should appoint those who are timid. For brave men might, on occasion, kill the king there—since he is usually alone or surrounded by women—having been corrupted by enemies through instigation. (7.62)
And he should appoint as his envoy one who is learned in all the scriptures, who understands gestures, facial expressions, and conduct, and who is pure, capable, and of noble birth. (7.63)

Regarding the messenger (*dūta*): one should appoint as a messenger someone who knows the treatises concerning both visible and invisible matters, who understands gestures and can discern intentions through speech, tone of voice, and so forth; whose *ākāra*—the physical state such as the complexion of the face and body—is indicative of affection or displeasure; who knows the truth of his [the king's] *ceṣṭā*—actions such as clapping the hands that indicate anger and the like; and who is endowed with purity, consisting of the absence of addiction to wealth, women, and so on, and who is clever and of noble birth. (7.63)
For it is said: "A messenger who is loyal, pure, skillful, mindful, knowledgeable of place and time, handsome, fearless, and eloquent is praised by a king. (7.64)

"Devoted" means possessing affection for the people; by this, he is not an object of hatred even for rival kings and others. "Endowed with wealth, women, and purity" means that he cannot be subverted by the giving of riches, women, and so forth. "Dexterous" means clever; by this, he does not let the time for action pass. "Possessing a retentive memory" means that he does not forget the message. "Knowing place and time" means that, having understood the place and time, he may even communicate other instructed matters in a way suited to the specific place and time. "Handsome" means his words are acceptable. "Free from fear" means he is a speaker even of unpleasant messages. "Eloquent" means he is capable of employing refined language and logical arguments. An envoy of such a kind is praiseworthy for a king. (7.64)
The army depends upon the minister; the administration of justice depends upon the army; the treasury and the kingdom depend upon the king; and peace and its opposite depend upon the envoy. (7.65)

Regarding the minister (*amātya*): the army (*daṇḍa*), consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, and so forth, is dependent upon the minister, for its engagement in affairs proceeds according to his will. That which is discipline (*vinaya*) is dependent upon the minister; whatever discipline there is, that is under his control. Regarding the king: the place where the accumulation of wealth is kept and the regions [of the realm] must not be made dependent on others by the monarch; he himself must personally consider the money and the villages. Regarding the envoy (*dūta*): peace and war are dependent upon him, for they proceed according to his will. (7.65)
For it is the messenger alone who unites those who are divided and indeed breaks apart those who are united;
the messenger performs that action by which men are alienated from one another. (7.66)

"Only the envoy," etc. Because it is the envoy alone who is capable of effecting peace among those who are divided and causing dissension among those who are united; and because the envoy performs such work in a foreign land by which those who are united are split apart—therefore, this [verse] is an elaboration of that which was stated in verse 7.65: "Peace and its opposite depend upon the envoy," namely, peace and war. || 7.66 ||

He states another duty for the messenger: "In his affairs, he should discern [the king's] disposition, gesture, and conduct through secret hints and movements, as well as what he intends to do toward his servants. (7.67)

"He should know" means that the envoy should understand the outward appearance, gestures, and movements intended for action by this rival king. He should also discern through the gestures and movements of the hidden agents—who are actually the attendants of the enemy king and are stationed near him—even when they are in his presence. Furthermore, he should know what the rival king desires to do among the servants who are agitated, greedy, or disgraced. || 7.67 ||
Having understood in truth everything intended by the enemy king, one should apply such effort as will not cause oneself suffering. (7.68)

"And having understood" means: having ascertained in reality everything that the opposing king intends to do by means of an envoy possessing the characteristics previously described, one should exert effort in such a way that no affliction befalls oneself. (7.68)

One should dwell in a region that is arid yet rich in crops, predominantly inhabited by noble people, free from turmoil, delightful, with submissive vassals, and providing a means of livelihood. (7.69)
Regarding "jāṅgala":
that region which has little water and grass, is windy, and has abundant sunshine,
yet is endowed with much grain and other resources, should be known as a jāṅgala country.

One should establish a residence by relying on a place that has an abundance of righteous people, is undisturbed by diseases, calamities, and the like, is enchanting with fruits, flowers, trees, creepers, and so forth, where the forest-dwellers and other inhabitants nearby are submissive, and where livelihoods such as agriculture and trade are easily obtained.
Having taken refuge in a fortification of bows, an earth-fort, a water-fort, or even a forest-fort, or a human-fort, or a mountain-fort, one should dwell in a city. (7.70)

"Regarding *dhanvadurga* (the desert fort): it is surrounded on all four sides by a desert for five *yojanas*, devoid of water. *Mahīdurga* (the earthen fort) is surrounded by a rampart made of stone or brick, twice as high as its width, rising twelve cubits, suitable for maneuvering atop during battle, and provided with coverings, lattices, and so forth. *Jaladurga* (the water fort) is encircled on all sides by unfathomable water. *Vārkṣadurga* (the forest fort) is covered everywhere outside for a distance of one *yojana* with large trees, thorny shrubs, creepers, and the like. *Nṛdurga* (the human fort) is protected by numerous infantrymen accompanied by elephants, horses, and chariots stationed on all four sides. *Giridurga* (the mountain fort) consists of a mountain ridge that is extremely difficult to ascend, possessing only a single narrow path, containing internal rivers, springs, and other water sources, and endowed with fields and trees producing abundant crops. Having taken refuge in any one of these forts, he should construct his city. (7.70)
One should, however, with every effort take refuge in a mountain fortress;
