for, by virtue of its many advantages, the mountain fortress is distinguished above all others.

"By all means": because among these types of forts, the mountain fort (*giridurga*) excels due to its abundance of defensive qualities, therefore one should take refuge in it with every effort. In a mountain fort, there are many advantages, such as being difficult for the enemy to ascend and the destruction of a large army of opponents by means of stones and other projectiles hurled with little effort from a vast expanse. (7.71)
Of these, the first three are inhabited by wild beasts, those dwelling in pits, and the Apsarases; the latter three are inhabited respectively by monkeys, humans, and gods. (7.72)

"Three": among these fortresses, the first three mentioned are inhabited by animals and the like. Here, the bow-fortress (dhanurdurga) is inhabited by deer; the earth-fortress (mahīdurga) by moles and others who dwell in holes; the water-fortress (abdurga) by aquatic creatures such as crocodiles and the like. As for the other three, beginning with the tree-fortress (vṛkṣadurga), they are inhabited by monkeys and others; therein, the tree-fortress is inhabited by monkeys, the man-fortress (nṛdurga) by humans, and the mountain-fortress (giridurga) by the gods. || 7.72 ||
Just as enemies do not harm those who have taken refuge in a fortress, so too do foes not harm a king who has taken refuge in a fortress. (7.73)
"Yathā" and so forth: Just as hunters and other enemies do not harm these deer and other creatures dwelling in a fortress, so too enemies do not harm a king who has taken refuge in a fortress. 7.73.
A single archer standing upon a rampart can fight a hundred; a hundred can fight ten thousand. Therefore, a fortress is established. (7.74)

Regarding the word "one": because a single archer standing on a rampart can fight a hundred enemies, and a hundred archers standing on a rampart can fight ten thousand enemies, therefore it is taught that one should construct a fortress. (7.74)
That city shall be well-provided with weapons, wealth, grain, and vehicles; it shall be rich in brahmins, artisans, machines, fodder, and water. (7.75)

"Regarding that," and so forth: one should make that fort abundant with weapons such as swords, wealth such as gold, grain, vehicles such as elephants and horses, provisions for Brāhmaṇas, craftsmen, machines, fodder, and water. (7.75)
In the center of that [site], he should have his own house constructed—spacious, secure against all seasons, bright, and provided with water and trees. (7.76)

"Of that," and so forth. In the center of that fortress, he should have his own residence constructed—sufficiently spacious, with separate quarters for women's quarters, temples, armories, fire-halls, and so on; protected by moats, ramparts, and other defenses; providing for all seasons through the presence of fruits, flowers, and the like; plastered with white lime; provided with ponds and water sources; and surrounded by trees. (7.76)
Having occupied that [seat], he should marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious marks, born of a noble family, pleasing, and endowed with beauty and virtue. (7.77)

"Taking refuge in that [house]," and so forth: having taken up residence in that house, he should marry a wife of the same caste, endowed with auspicious marks, born of a noble family, captivating, beautiful, and virtuous. (7.77)
He should appoint a domestic priest and choose officiating priests; they shall perform for him the domestic rites as well as those pertaining to the sacrificial fires. (7.78)

Regarding the domestic priest: he should appoint a domestic priest according to the Atharvavedic rites, and he should select officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) to perform the rituals. They, in turn, shall perform for him the domestic rites prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras* as well as those to be accomplished with the three sacred fires (*tretā*). (7.78)
The king should sacrifice with various rites accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees;
and for the sake of dharma, he should bestow enjoyments and wealth upon the Brahmins. (7.79)

"He should sacrifice": the king should perform various kinds of sacrifices, such as the Aśvamedha and others, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). And he should give to the Brāhmaṇas enjoyments such as women, houses, and beds, as well as wealth such as gold and clothing. (7.79)
He should cause the annual tribute to be collected from the kingdom by trustworthy men;
he should be devoted to the sacred tradition in this world and behave toward his subjects like a father.

"Annual": the ministers, being attentive to the king, should cause the annual share of grain and other produce to be collected; furthermore, he should be firmly grounded in the scriptures regarding the collection of taxes and so forth in the world, and he should behave toward the people living in his own country with affection and the like, as if they were his own father. (7.80)
He should appoint various learned supervisors here and there;
they shall oversee all the affairs of the men as they carry out their work.

Regarding the term "superintendents" (*adhyakṣān*): in various locations such as those for elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, and other matters, he should appoint diverse superintendents—individual overseers who are wise and skilled in their respective tasks. They shall oversee all the affairs of the people engaged in those positions of elephants, horses, and so forth, for the sake of properly accomplishing the king's business. (7.81)
He should be a worshiper of those Brahmins who have returned from the teacher’s house;
for this is declared to be the imperishable Brahman-treasure of kings. (7.82)

"Of those who have returned" means that one should invariably honor with wealth and grain those Brāhmaṇas who have completed their studies in the teacher's house and desire the life of a householder. For this inexhaustible treasure—consisting of wealth, grain, and so forth—which is established among the Brāhmaṇas as a "Brāhma-treasure," is taught by the scripture to kings; it is imperishable because its fruit is the Brahman. (7.82)
Therefore:
"Neither thieves nor enemies can carry it off, nor does it perish;
therefore, the king should deposit this imperishable treasure with the Brāhmaṇas. (7.83)

"Nor that" means: neither thieves nor enemies carry off that treasure deposited by a brahmin; unlike other treasures deposited in the earth or elsewhere, it does not perish through the power of time. Or rather, it may come to light through a confusion regarding its location. Therefore, this inexhaustible mass of wealth—which, like a treasure, yields infinite fruit—should be deposited by the king with the brahmins; the meaning is that it should be given to them. (7.83)
It overflows not, it does not fail, and it never perishes;
that which is offered into the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa is superior to the Agnihotra sacrifices. (7.84)

"Not so," and so forth. When an oblation is poured into the fire, it sometimes overflows or trickles down; sometimes it falters or dries up; and sometimes it is destroyed by burning and the like. But that which is offered into the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa—meaning that which is given from the hand of a Brāhmaṇa, according to the rule, "For the twice-born is said to have his hand as his mouth" (4.117)—for that, no such defects are mentioned. Therefore, the meaning is that giving to a Brāhmaṇa is superior to the Agnihotra and other such rites. || 7.84 ||

A gift given to one who is not a Brahmin yields equal merit; to one who merely calls himself a Brahmin, it yields double; to one who has studied the Vedas, it yields a hundred-thousandfold; and to one who has mastered the Vedas, it yields infinite merit.

"Equal," and so forth: A gift given to one who is not a Brāhmaṇa—such as a Kṣatriya or others—yields an equal fruit; that is, it is neither more nor less than the fruit which is traditionally heard to belong to the substance being given. One who, though devoid of Vedic rites, calls himself a Brāhmaṇa is a "Brāhmaṇa-in-name" (*brāhmaṇabruva*); a gift given to such a person yields double the fruit compared to the previous case. Likewise, when a Brāhmaṇa has begun his studies (*prādhīta*), the fruit is a hundred-thousandfold. For one who has studied all the branches (*samastaśākhādhyāyin*), the fruit is infinite. Alternatively, the third quarter of the verse reads: "A thousandfold for a teacher" (*sahasraguṇam ācārye*). (7.85)
Indeed, depending specifically on the recipient and through the very nature of one's faith, one enjoys the fruit of giving—whether it be small or great—after death. (7.86)

Regarding the phrase "of the recipient": depending on the gradation of the recipient—who is a worthy vessel by virtue of being endowed with knowledge, austerity, and right conduct—the giver attains in the next world a fruit, whether small or great, corresponding to the degree of faith (śraddhā) characterized by conviction in the scriptures as it is. || 7.86 ||
When challenged by those who are equal, superior, or inferior, a king protecting his subjects must not retreat from battle, mindful of the duty of a Kshatriya. (7.87)

"By those who are equal, superior, or inferior": A king, when challenged for battle by a king of equal strength, greater strength, or lesser strength, should not turn back from the fight while protecting his subjects; remembering the duty of a Kṣatriya that one challenged to battle must certainly fight. (7.87)
For this reason:
"Not retreating in battles, the protection of subjects, and service to the Brahmins—this is the supreme means for the welfare of kings. (7.88)

"In battles" means not turning one's back in wars and the protection of subjects; along with service to Brahmins, this is the preeminent ground for kings to attain the excellence of heaven and other higher realms. (7.88)
Therefore it is said:
"In battles, kings who desire to slay one another, fighting with their utmost strength and not turning their backs, go to heaven. (7.89)

Regarding the phrase "in battles": kings competing with one another, desiring to slay each other in combat, and fighting face-to-face with superior strength, go to heaven. Although the visible fruit of battle consists merely of the acquisition of wealth from enemy people and the like, rather than heaven, there is no fault here; for heaven is the fruit of the rule of not turning one's back, which is dependent upon battle. (7.89)
While fighting his enemies in battle, he should not strike them with deceptive weapons, nor with barbed ones, nor with poisoned ones, nor with those whose points are ablaze with fire. (7.90)

"Not so," and so forth. One fighting in battle with these [weapons]—namely, *kūṭas*, which are weapons made of wood and other materials on the outside but containing sharp blades hidden within—would not slay enemies. Nor would one slay them with arrows having blade-shaped heads (*karṇyākāraphalaka*), nor with those smeared with poison, nor even with those having heads set ablaze with fire. (7.90)
One should not strike one who has ascended to dry land, nor a eunuch, nor one with palms joined in reverence;
nor one with disheveled hair, nor one who is seated, nor one who says, "I am yours. (7.91)

And not [as follows]: one who is himself in a chariot should not strike one who has abandoned the chariot and is standing on the ground; likewise, one should not strike a eunuch, one with joined palms, one with disheveled hair, one who is seated, or one who says, "I am yours. (7.91)

Not one who is asleep, nor one who has not donned his armor, nor one who is naked, nor one who is unarmed, nor one who is not fighting, nor one who is merely looking on, nor one who is engaged with another [opponent]. (7.92)

"Not while asleep": one should not strike one who is asleep, one who has cast off his armor, one who is unclothed, one who is unarmed, one who is not fighting, one who is a spectator, or one who is fighting with another. 7.92.

Recalling the dharma of the virtuous, he did not strike one who was suffering from a weapon-wound, nor one who was distressed, nor one who was severely mangled, nor one who was terrified, nor one who had turned away. (7.93)

"Not so," and so forth. One should not strike one whose weapons such as swords are broken, one who is afflicted by grief for a son or other causes, one who is overwhelmed by many wounds, one who is terrified, or one who has turned away from the battle; rather, one should remember the duty of the noble Kṣatriyas. || 7.93 ||
But he who, out of fear, turns his back in battle and is slain by enemies, takes upon himself whatever evil deeds his master has committed. (7.94)

"But he who... (7.94). However, that warrior who, being afraid, turns his back and is slain by enemies in battle, incurs all the evil deeds (*duṣkṛta*) of the master who supported him. Since merit and demerit are established by the authority of the scriptures, they can only be transferred in accordance with what is prescribed in those scriptures. For this very reason, because it is sublated by the foundational scripture, there is no possibility of a counter-inference arising. This has been explained by us under the verse "In [the case of] his own dear ones, [his] good deed" (6.79). Govindarāja maintains: "It is intended here that this sin belongs to one who is killed while turning his back; however, the master's sin would not [be transferred] in this case. Medhātithi, however, characterizes this as a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). I consider neither of these two views to be correct, as they clearly abandon the literal meaning of the words. Since the author of the Vedānta Sūtras, Bādarāyaṇa, has determined this matter through the authority of the scriptures—that "the merit and demerit belonging to one person may be transferred to another"—the explanation exactly as stated [by me] is the most appropriate. 7.94.
Moreover, whatever merit he has acquired for the sake of the hereafter, the husband takes all of that from one who is slain while retreating. (7.95)
"And that which," etc. Whatever merit for the sake of the next world has been acquired by this man while he was facing away and struck down, the master obtains all of that. (7.95)
Since it might follow that the king as master should take all the property, he states this exception:
"Chariots, horses, elephants, parasols, wealth, grain, livestock, women, all other goods, and base metals—whatever anyone wins belongs to him. (7.96)

"Chariots, horses," and so forth. Chariots, horses, elephants, umbrellas, garments, and the like; wealth and grain, cattle, and so on; female slaves and other women; all types of goods such as molasses, salt, and the like; and base metals (*kupya*)—that is, wealth consisting of copper and other materials distinct from gold and silver—he who, having conquered separately, constantly brings these to his own home, they belong to him alone. However, gold, silver, land, jewels, and other non-extractable wealth must be surrendered to the king; it is for this very purpose that these items are enumerated here [in verse 7.96].
Therefore he says:
"And they shall give a share to the king; such is the Vedic revelation.
And the king must give what was not won individually to all the warriors. (7.97)

"Of the king," and so forth. The warriors shall give a *uddhāra* (extra share) to the king. That which is extracted (*uddhriyate*) is called *uddhāra*. From the wealth won in battle, superior property—such as gold, silver, and base metals—is to be surrendered to the king. Even vehicles such as elephants and horses must be given to the king, according to the statement of Gautama: "The vehicle and the *uddhāra* belong to the king. Regarding the giving of the *uddhāra*, there is a Vedic passage: beginning with "Indra, having slain Vṛtra... and continuing, "Having become great, he said to the gods: 'Extract for yourselves an *uddhāra*. And the king shall distribute among all the warriors the spoils not already separately taken—that is, the collective booty—according to their respective prowess. (7.97)
This eternal warrior code has been declared as unadorned;
a Kṣatriya, slaying his enemies in battle, should not deviate from this dharma.

"This," and so forth. This warrior-duty (*yodhadharma*) that has been described is irreproachable; because it arises from the beginningless flow of creation, it is eternal. A Kṣatriya, while slaying enemies in battle, must not abandon this duty. The mention of the "Kṣatriya" is because he is the one entitled to engage in battle; however, even another person who occupies that position should not abandon it. (7.98)
One should seek to obtain what has not yet been obtained, guard with effort what has been obtained, increase what has been guarded, and bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients. (7.99)

"Regarding 'what has not been obtained': one should desire to conquer what has not been conquered, such as land, gold, and so forth; one should protect with effort what has been conquered; one should increase through trade and other means what has been protected; and one should give what has been increased to worthy recipients. (7.99)
One should know that this fourfold [duty] is the means for achieving the goals of human life;
one should perform its practice constantly and correctly, without sloth. (7.100)

"Regarding this": one should understand that these fourfold types have as their purpose that human goal which consists of heaven and so forth; since they are of such a nature, one should therefore always perform their practice without indolence. (7.100)

One should seek what is not yet obtained by means of force; protect what has been obtained with vigilance; increase what has been protected by means of growth; and bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients. (7.101)

"Unobtained" means that which one would wish to conquer by means of an army consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. What has been conquered should be protected through supervision. What has been protected should be increased by means of methods for growth, such as trade by land and water routes. What has been increased should be given to worthy recipients according to the divisions prescribed in the scriptures. (7.101)
He should always have his rod of punishment raised, always display his manly prowess, always keep his secrets concealed, and always watch for the vulnerabilities of his enemy. (7.102)

"Constantly" means: he should be one for whom the constant practice of training in combat with elephants, horses, and so forth constitutes his discipline (*daṇḍa*). And he should be one whose manliness is constantly made manifest through the science of weapons and other skills. And he should be intent upon constantly investigating the vulnerabilities of his enemy in the form of calamities, weaknesses, and the like. (7.102)
The entire world trembles before one who constantly holds up the rod of punishment;
therefore, he should subdue all beings by means of that very rod alone. (7.103)

"Constantly": because the world would tremble before one who is constantly ready with the rod of punishment, therefore he should bring all living beings under his own control by means of the rod alone. (7.103)
One should conduct oneself with absolute sincerity and never with deceit;
remaining ever self-guarded, one should also recognize the deception employed by the enemy.

"Without deceit" means that he should not behave with guile or hypocrisy toward his ministers and others; for if he were so, he would become untrustworthy to everyone. For the sake of protecting the Dharma, he should conduct himself according to reality alone. Having made diligent effort to protect his own side, he should discover through spies the deceit of his enemies in the form of sowing dissension among his subjects. (7.104)
An enemy should not know one's own vulnerability, but one should know the vulnerability of the enemy;
like a tortoise, one should withdraw one's limbs and guard one's own weak points. (7.105)

"Not so," and so forth. He should exert such effort that the enemy does not discover his vulnerabilities, such as dissension among his subjects; however, he should learn of the enemy's dissension among subjects and other weaknesses through spies. Just as a tortoise withdraws its limbs—the mouth, feet, and so on—into its own body for protection, so too should a king bring his own constituents, such as ministers and others, under his control by means of gifts, honors, and the like. Furthermore, if a vulnerability in the form of dissension among subjects or similar faults should arise by chance, he must diligently apply a remedy. (7.105)
One should contemplate one's goals like a crane, exert prowess like a lion, snatch away like a wolf, and flee like a hare. (7.106)

"Like a heron": just as a heron, for the sake of catching fish, concentrates its inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa) even upon a fish that is by nature extremely restless in the water, so too should one contemplate matters such as seizing the territory of an enemy, even when that enemy is well-guarded in secret. And just as a lion attacks and slays even a powerful, massive elephant, so too one who is weak and attacked by a stronger foe—when other means such as seeking refuge are unavailable—should attack and slay the enemy with all his might. And just as a wolf slays an animal even though it is protected by a keeper, having encountered the keeper's negligence through fate, so too should one slay an enemy, even one stationed in a fortress or similar stronghold, having somehow encountered his negligence. And just as a hare, even when caught in the midst of various hunters intent on killing him, escapes by leaping away with a zigzag course, so too one who is himself weak and surrounded by a powerful enemy should, having somehow caused confusion among the enemies, approach another virtuous king to seek refuge. 7.106.
Thus, while he is victorious, whatever adversaries he may have,
he should bring them all under his control by means of the expedients beginning with conciliation.

"Thus," and so forth. In this manner, by the method already described, a king engaged in conquest should bring under his control all those who may be hostile to his victory by means of the strategic expedients of conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and force. (7.107)
If, however, they do not abide by these through the first three expedients, one should gradually bring them under control by force alone, using punishment. 7.108.

Regarding the passage beginning with "yadi" and so forth: if those who oppose his victory do not desist by means of the first three expedients, then he should gradually bring them under control through force—by means of war involving the destruction of their territory and so on, and by means of punishment according to the sequence of light and heavy penalties. || 7.108 ||
Regarding the four expedients beginning with conciliation, the wise always praise both conciliation and force for the constant prosperity of the kingdom. (7.109)

Regarding the phrase "of conciliation and the others": among the four means (*upāya*) beginning with conciliation, the wise praise only conciliation (*sāma*) and force (*daṇḍa*) for the sake of increasing the kingdom. This is because in the case of conciliation, there is an absence of faults such as exertion, expenditure of wealth, and the depletion of troops; whereas in the case of force, although these faults do exist, the accomplishment of the task is superior. (7.109)
Just as a reaper pulls out the weeds while protecting the grain, so should the king protect his kingdom and slay those who stand as obstacles. 7.110

"Yathā" and so forth. Just as in a field, when grain and weeds have grown together, the reaper preserves the grain and removes the weeds; likewise, a king should slay the wicked in his realm but not the innocent, even if they are his own natural-born brothers—this is understood from the illustration of the reaper. Furthermore, he should protect the kingdom together with the virtuous. (7.110)
That king who, out of delusion and through lack of foresight, oppresses his own kingdom, shall before long fall from both his realm and his life, along with his kinsmen. (7.111)

"Out of delusion," and so forth. That king who, through lack of discernment and ignorance of the distinction between the wicked and the virtuous, oppresses all the people of his own realm with the hardship of seizing wealth according to the scriptures, or by execution and other such cruelties, is swiftly deprived—along with his sons and others—both of his kingdom and of his life due to the unrighteousness arising from the provocation of his subjects known as "hostility toward the country. (7.111)
Just as the vital breaths of living beings waste away from the emaciation of the body, so too do the vital breaths of kings waste away from the emaciation of the kingdom. 7.112

Regarding the phrase "by emaciating the body": just as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of living beings are diminished through the drying up of the body by means of fasting and the like, so too the vital breaths of kings perish through the oppression of the realm and the resulting provocation of the subjects. Therefore, it has been stated that a king must protect his kingdom just as he protects his own body. (7.112)
One should always carry out this regulation for the consolidation of the kingdom;
for a king whose kingdom is well-consolidated prospers in happiness. (7.113)

"Of the kingdom," and so forth. For the protection of the kingdom, he should employ this method which is about to be described; for a king whose kingdom is well protected prospers without effort. (7.113)
He should establish a *gulma* (military outpost) among two, three, or five [villages], and likewise he should organize the collection of taxes for hundreds of villages throughout the kingdom. (7.114)

"Between two"—that is, between two villages, or three villages, or five hundred villages—one should establish a *gulma*, a troop consisting of a body of men for protection, presided over by men whose primary quality is truthfulness, as a center for the administration and defense of the realm. This aforementioned alternative is intended to take into account the relative lightness or gravity of the situation. (7.114)
He should appoint a lord of a village, as well as a lord of ten villages,
a lord of twenty, a lord of a hundred, and likewise a lord of a thousand.
"Of the village": he should appoint lords of one village, ten villages, and so forth. || 7.115 ||
The village headman himself should gradually report any faults arising in the village to the lord of ten villages;
the lord of ten should report them to the lord of twenty.
The lord of twenty should report all of that to the lord of a hundred;
the lord of a hundred villages, however, should himself announce it to the lord of a thousand.

Regarding the term "village": the *viṃśatīśa* (leader of twenty) and the village head (*grāmādhipati*), being unable to personally remedy the evils such as theft that have arisen in the village due to their own inferiority, shall report them to the leader of ten villages (*daśagrāmādhipati*). In this manner, the leaders of ten villages shall report to the lords of twenty villages and so forth. When this is done, there occurs the proper eradication of thorns such as thieves.
He states the livelihood of the village headman (ekagrāmādhikṛta):
"Whatever food, drink, fuel, and other such things are to be paid daily by the villagers to the king, the village headman shall receive those. (7.118)

Regarding the word "yāni" ("which"): those items such as food, drink, and fuel which are to be given daily by the village dwellers to the king—but not the annual tax (*abdakara*) consisting of "the eighth part of grain," and so forth—the lord of the village may take them for the sake of his own maintenance.

The collector of ten should enjoy the produce of one family, the collector of twenty that of five families; the overseer of a hundred villages should enjoy a village, and the lord of a thousand should enjoy a city.
Regarding the number of oxen for the plough:
"The plough of Dharma has eight oxen; six oxen for those seeking a livelihood;
four oxen for householders; and three oxen for those who have killed a Brahmin."

Thus, according to the traditional teaching (smṛti) of Hārīta: "A middle-sized plough consists of six oxen. He states that a *kula* is as much land as can be cultivated by two such ploughs. The lord of ten villages may enjoy that for his livelihood; likewise, the lord of twenty [villages] enjoys five *kulas*, the lord of a hundred [villages] enjoys a middle-sized village, and the lord of a thousand [villages] enjoys a middle-sized city. (7.119)
Indeed, another minister of the king, one who is affectionate and vigilant, should oversee their village affairs as well as their private matters. (7.120)

"Of them," and so forth. When there is a mutual dispute among those people, such as village-dwellers and others, whatever matters arise in the village—whether they concern what has been done or not done, or various individual affairs—another person who acts for the king's benefit, appointed by him, and is diligent, shall attend to them.
In every city, he should appoint one overseer of all affairs,
stationed in a high place and possessing a formidable appearance, like a planet among the stars.

Regarding the term "city": in every city, one should appoint a single person as the city governor (*nagarādhipati*), who stands preeminent, who is great by virtue of his lineage and other qualities, who is of principal status, of formidable appearance, and who—by means of a full array of elephants, horses, and so forth—is as radiant among the stars and other celestial bodies that cause fear as the planet Venus (*bhārgava*) is; he shall be the overseer of affairs. 7.121.
He himself should always personally inspect them all;
he should thoroughly ascertain their conduct in the realms through spies.

"Sa" and so forth. That official in charge of the city should always personally accompany all those officials, such as the village headmen and others, whenever there is no other business, accompanied by his own force. Furthermore, he should cause all these officials, down to the city magistrate, to correctly ascertain—through spies appointed to their respective jurisdictions—the conduct of the subjects within the kingdom. (7.122)
For the king's protectors are generally servants who seize the property of others and are deceitful; he should guard these subjects from them. (7.123)

"Of the king," and so forth. Since those appointed by the king to protect him are for the most part habituated to seizing the property of others and are deceitful, the king must therefore protect these subjects of his own from them. (7.123)
Those of evil intent who seize wealth solely from litigants, the king shall confiscate all their property and carry out their banishment. (7.124)

"Those who," and so forth. Those officials in charge of protection who, out of greed and with sinful intent, bring forward such things as pretexts regarding speech against those seeking justice and thereby seize wealth not sanctioned by the scriptures—the king, having confiscated their entire property, shall banish them from the country. (7.124)
The king should provide daily maintenance for women and servants engaged in his works, according to their rank and the nature of their tasks. (7.125)

"Of the king," and so forth. The king shall provide daily maintenance for women employed in his service—such as female slaves—and for the laboring class, in accordance with their respective status as superior, middling, or inferior, and in proportion to their specific duties.
He shows that very point:
"A paṇa shall be given as wages for the lowest laborer, and six for the highest;
likewise, clothing every six months, and one droṇa of grain every month. (7.126)

Regarding the term *paṇa*: for a lowly laborer, such as a house-sweeper or water-carrier, a daily wage (*paṇa*) of the kind to be described below must be given; and every six months, a garment—specifically a pair of clothes—must be provided.
Eight handfuls (*muṣṭi*) make one *kuñci*; eight *kuñcis* make one *puṣkala*;
and four *puṣkalas* are proclaimed to be one *āḍhaka*.

Four *āḍhakas* make one *droṇa*; by this calculation, a *droṇa* of grain is to be given every month. For the highest [grade of servant], however, six *paṇas* are to be given as wages. According to this same arrangement, six pairs of garments are to be given every six months. Every six months, three *droṇas* of grain are to be given each month. By this same extension of the rule, for the middle [grade], three *paṇas* should be given as wages; and every six months, three pairs of garments and, monthly, three *droṇas* of grain are to be given. (7.126)

Having carefully considered the buying and selling, the distance traveled, the food along with its incidental expenses, and the security of property and person, the king should cause taxes to be paid by the merchants.

"Buying and selling," and so forth: having examined how much was paid for this cloth as its price, how much is obtained here for the salt and other goods being sold, from what distance it was brought, how much has been spent by this merchant on food expenses such as vegetables and soup, how much has gone toward securing safety through protection against thieves and the like in forests and other places, and what his current profit margin is—having considered all this, he should cause taxes to be paid by the merchants. (7.127)
Just as the king and the doer of deeds are joined with their fruit,
so should the king, having duly considered this, always determine the taxes within his realm.

Regarding the word "yathā" (as): Just as [people] are connected with the fruit of actions such as serving a king, and just as seasonal merchants and others are connected with the fruit of actions such as agriculture and trade, so too, having determined this, the king should always collect taxes from the subjects.
Regarding this, he provides an illustration:
"Just as the calf, the parrot, and the bee consume their food little by little, so should the annual tax be collected by the king from the realm in small increments. (7.129)

"Yathā" and so forth. Just as leeches, calves, and bees consume blood, milk, and honey only in small amounts, so too should the king, without cutting off the principal capital, collect from the realm a very small annual tax. (7.129)
He said this to him:
"The king shall take a fiftieth part of cattle and gold;
an eighth part of grain, or a sixth, or even a twelfth. (7.130)

"An fiftieth part," and so forth. Of cattle and gold that exceed the original value, a fiftieth part is to be taken by the king. Likewise, of grains, a sixth, eighth, or twelfth part is to be taken by the king. This option regarding the taking of a large or small portion depends on the increase or decrease in the value of the land, as well as the relative lightness or heaviness of the hardship involved in cultivation and other such efforts. (7.130)
Furthermore, he may take a sixth part of trees, meat, honey, and clarified butter;
and of perfumes, medicinal herbs, juices, flowers, roots, and fruits.
Of leaf-vegetables, grasses, skins, and split-bamboo vessels; of earthenware pots and of everything made of stone. || 7.132 ||

"He may take," and so forth; "leaf-vegetables," and so forth. Here the word *dru* denotes a tree. One-sixth part of the produce of the seventeen types of things, beginning with trees and ending with those made of stone, should be taken from their profit. (7.131–132)
Even when dying, a king shall not take a tax from a Śrotriya;
nor shall a Śrotriya dwelling in his realm perish from hunger. (7.133)

Regarding the phrase "one who is dying": even if his wealth is exhausted, a king shall not collect taxes from a learned Brāhmaṇa; nor shall a learned Brāhmaṇa living in his territory fall into ruin through hunger. (7.133)
In whose kingdom a learned Vedic scholar perishes from hunger, his entire realm likewise perishes from hunger before long. (7.134)

"Of whom," and so forth: in the territory of whichever king a *śrotriya* (one learned in the Vedas) becomes distressed by hunger, that king's kingdom also quickly falls into distress through hunger, famine, and the like. (7.134)
Since this is so, therefore:
"Having ascertained his learning and conduct, one should prescribe for him a righteous livelihood;
and one should protect him in every way, like a father protects his own biological son. (7.135)

"Having heard"—that is, having understood the application of the knowledge of the scriptures—he should provide him with a livelihood consistent with that [knowledge], one that does not deviate from dharma. Furthermore, he should protect him from thieves and others, just as a father protects his own biological son. (7.135)
For: Whatever dharma he performs day by day while being protected by the king, through that the king’s lifespan, wealth, and kingdom increase. (7.136)

"Being well protected," and so forth. And when that Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) is properly protected by the king, the longevity, wealth, and kingdom of that king increase through the merit he performs every day. (7.136)
Whatever little [tax] one may cause to be paid annually, designated as "tribute," the king should collect from the common people in his realm who live by trade. (7.137)

Regarding the word "yat" (which): the king should cause even a lowly person living in his own country by means of buying and selling small-value goods such as leafy vegetables to pay, even if it be a small amount, a tax known as *kara* for each year. 7.137.
The lord of the earth should cause artisans, craftsmen, and Śūdras who subsist by their own labor to perform work for one day each month. (7.138)

"Artisans" (kārukān): he should cause artisans—such as cooks and others who are slightly superior to craftsmen—as well as craftsmen—such as blacksmiths and others—and Śūdras who subsist by manual labor, such as porters and the like, to perform work for one day every month. 7.138.
One should not cut off one's own root nor that of others through excessive greed;
for by cutting off one's own root, one afflicts both oneself and them. (7.139)

"One should not cut off" means: out of affection for one's subjects, the failure to collect taxes, tolls, and so forth, constitutes cutting off one's own root; collecting excessive taxes and the like out of greed constitutes cutting off the roots of others. One should not do either of these two. For, by cutting off one's own root, one would afflict oneself through the depletion of the treasury. This connects with the first half [of the verse], and "of others" is understood from the second half: by cutting off the roots of others, one would afflict them. (7.139)
The lord of the earth should be both stern and mild, having regard for what must be done;
a king who is both stern and mild becomes esteemed.

Regarding the term "sharp": having understood the specific nature of a task, he should be sharp toward some tasks and mild toward others, rather than adopting a single uniform manner. For a king of the aforementioned character becomes beloved by all. (7.140)
When weary from overseeing the affairs of men, he should appoint to that seat a chief minister who knows the Dharma, is wise, self-controlled, and of noble birth. (7.141)

"Regarding the minister": being exhausted by personally overseeing affairs, he should appoint a preeminent minister—one who knows the law, is wise, has conquered his senses, and is of noble birth—to that position of overseeing affairs. (7.141)
Having thus performed all these duties for himself, he should protect these subjects with diligence and vigilance. (7.142)
"Thus," and so forth. Having thus accomplished his entire range of duties in the manner described, he should protect his own subjects, being disciplined and free from negligence. || 7.142 ||
He from whose kingdom the subjects are carried off by bandits while they cry out for help—even though he looks on with his servants—he is dead and does not truly live. (7.143)

Regarding the phrase "crying out": when a king, along with his ministers and others, looks on while his subjects are being carried off by thieves and the like even as they cry out from the kingdom, he is truly dead and does not live. Because he lacks the functions of life, his very life is nothing but death; such is the meaning. (7.143)
Therefore, he confirms that very point which was previously stated as a supplement to the rule "he should protect his subjects vigilantly" (7.142):
"The supreme duty of a Kṣatriya is the protection of his subjects alone;
for the king who enjoys the prescribed rewards is joined with righteousness. (7.144)

Regarding the phrase "of the Kṣatriya": among other duties, the protection of the subjects is the preeminent and most excellent duty of the Kṣatriya. For it is through this that the king—who enjoys the fruits and other rewards characterized as previously described—becomes connected with righteousness (*dharma*). (7.144)
Having risen in the final watch of the night, purified and composed,
having offered oblations to the fire and honored the Brahmins, he should enter the auspicious assembly hall.

"Having risen": that king, having risen during the last watch of the night, having performed the purification consisting of the voiding of urine and excrement and so forth, with undistracted mind, and having performed the *agnihotra* and *āvasathya* oblations, should enter the assembly hall—which possesses the characteristics of a royal residence—and the hall for seeing his ministers and others, after having honored the Brahmins. (7.145)
Remaining there, he should bid farewell to all his subjects after greeting them;
and having dismissed all his subjects, he should deliberate together with his ministers.

Regarding the word "therein": having stood in that assembly hall, he should bid farewell to all the subjects who have come for an audience by means of conversation, a glance, and so forth, and then dismiss them. Having dismissed them, he should deliberate upon peace, war, and other matters together with his ministers.
Having ascended to a mountain ridge or a palace, or having gone to a secluded place, or in a forest free from undergrowth, he should deliberate unobserved. (7.147)

"Upon the mountain ridge": having ascended a mountain peak and staying in a deserted forest dwelling or in a secluded wilderness region, unobserved by those who would divulge his counsel, he should deliberate upon the fivefold counsel consisting of: the means for initiating undertakings, the excellence of personnel and resources, the distinction between place and time, the remedy for setbacks, and the successful accomplishment of the task.
That king whose counsel ordinary people do not discover even when they have gathered together, enjoys the entire earth, even if he is destitute of treasure. (7.148)
"Of whom" means: that king whose secret counsel other people, apart from his ministers, do not know even when gathered together—he, though his treasury be depleted, enjoys the entire earth. (7.148)
At the time of reciting the mantra, one should remove those who are dull-witted, mute, blind, deaf, animals, the very aged, women, barbarians, the diseased, and the deformed. (7.149)

"Those who are dull-witted, mute, blind, or deaf" refers to those deficient in intellect, speech, sight, or hearing; one should also remove from the time of the mantra-rite those born as animals such as parrots and mainas, as well as very old women, barbarians, the sick, and those with missing limbs. (7.149)
Because those who are despised, as well as animals and especially women, betray a secret counsel; therefore, one should be cautious in that regard. 7.150

"Those who break [the secret]" and so forth: even these people, such as the dull-witted and others, having attained their state of dullness and so on through the power of past misdeeds, break the secret counsel precisely because they are treated with contempt due to their unrighteousness. Likewise, parrots and the like, as well as very elderly persons and women, break the secret counsel especially because of their unstable intellects. Therefore, one should be diligent in removing them [from the council]. 7.150.
At midday or at midnight, being rested and free from fatigue, he should contemplate the goals of Dharma, Kāma, and Artha, either alone or together with them. (7.151)

"At midday": whether in the middle of the day or the middle of the night, free from mental fatigue and devoid of physical distress, he should contemplate with his ministers or alone how to practice virtue, wealth, and pleasure. 7.151.
The acquisition of those things which are mutually contradictory, the giving away of daughters in marriage, and the protection of sons. (7.152)

Regarding the phrase "mutually": he should consider the means for acquiring those [three goals]—dharma, artha, and kāma—which are generally characterized by mutual conflict, by way of resolving their contradictions. He should determine the giving away of his daughters for the sake of accomplishing his own purpose. And he should consider the protection of his sons, the young princes, for the sake of instilling discipline and training them in statecraft. || 7.152 ||
The dispatching of envoys, as well as the remaining tasks,
the movements within the inner apartments, and the activities of the secret agents.

Regarding "the envoy": one should consider the dispatching of envoys to foreign kingdoms by means of carrying secret messages and the like; likewise, one should consider completing the remainder of an enterprise already begun. This is because the conduct of women is exceedingly treacherous. For instance: the queen slew Vidūratha with a sword concealed within her braid of hair.
And it is said that the queen, having become disaffected, [killed] the King of Kāśi with an anklet smeared with poison.

Having understood these and other matters, he should ascertain the conduct of the women in the inner apartments through female companions, maidservants, and the like, for the sake of his own protection; and he should determine the activities of the spies appointed among rival kings and others by means of other spies. (7.153)
He [should know] in truth the entire eightfold work and the five groups,
as well as affection and enmity, and the conduct of the circle of states.
"Entirely" means one should contemplate the eightfold duty in its completeness. And that has been stated by Uśanas:
"In taking and in giving, likewise in commanding and in forbidding, in the fifth, in the speaking of meaningful words, and in the supervision of legal proceedings."
Constantly engaged in both punishment and purification, the king who possesses these eightfold paths and performs the eight duties goes to heaven, honored by Śakra.

In this context, "taking" (ādāna) refers to the collection of taxes and so forth; "giving" (visarga) is the distribution of wealth to servants and others; "commanding" (praiṣa) is the directing of ministers and others toward actions contrary to visible or invisible [dharma]; "speaking for a purpose" (arthavacana) is the issuing of royal decrees when there is doubt regarding a matter, since the king's authority is the sole regulator therein; "supervision of legal proceedings" (vyavahārekṣaṇa) is the oversight of subjects in cases of disputes over debts and the like; "punishment" (daṇḍa) is the seizure of wealth from those defeated as prescribed by the scriptures; and "purification" (śuddhi) is the performance of expiation (prāyaścitta) when a sinful act has been committed. However, Medhātithi [states]:

Undertaking what has not been done, performing what has been undertaken, excellence in execution, and the collection of the fruits of action; likewise, conciliation, bribery, force, and sowing dissension—this is the eightfold action. Alternatively, it consists of: trade routes, the construction of waterworks and embankments, the building of fortresses, the determination of improvements for those already built, the capture of elephants, mining, the settlement of uninhabited lands, and the felling of timber forests.

Thus he said: In this manner, one should truly contemplate the fivefold group of spies (*cāravarga*), designated by the term "the five-fold group" (*pañcavarga*), consisting of the hypocrite (*kāpaṭika*), the renegade ascetic (*udāsthita*), the householder (*gṛhapati*), the merchant (*vaidehika*), and the ascetic (*tāpasa*). Among these, a *kāpaṭika* is one who knows the secrets of others and is a bold student; because of his deceptive conduct, the king should win him over with wealth and honor when he seeks a livelihood, and say to him in secret: "Whatever you see that is wicked must be reported to me immediately. An *udāsthita* is one who has fallen from the state of an ascetic. Having made him known for his faults in the world, yet endowed with wisdom and purity, and having provided him with a livelihood when he seeks one, the king should speak to him as before in secret. He should establish him in a monastery with many resources and provide him with another piece of land yielding abundant crops for his subsistence. Furthermore, the king should provide food, clothing, and other necessities to other ascetics who perform the work of spies. A *gṛhapativyañjana* is a farmer whose livelihood is failing but who is endowed with wisdom and purity. Having spoken to him as before, the king should have him perform agricultural work on his own land. A *vaidehikavyañjana* is a merchant whose livelihood is failing. Having spoken to him as before and won him over with wealth and honor, the king should have him carry out trade. A *tāpasavyañjana* is one who desires a livelihood and appears as an ascetic, either shaven-headed or with matted hair. Dwelling in some hermitage among many other shaven-headed or matted-haired ascetics, surrounded by a circle of fraudulent disciples, and receiving a secret livelihood provided by the king, he should practice asceticism. Every month or every two months, he should publicly eat a handful of jujube fruits and the like, but in secret, he should consume food provided by the king. His disciples should proclaim his knowledge of the past and future and so forth. Having gained a large following of people, they ask everyone about all matters—both what should be done and what should not—because he is trusted by all, and they report the misconduct of others. One should properly contemplate such a five-fold group. Having thus organized the five-fold group, one should use that very five-fold group as a means to ascertain the loyalty or disloyalty of rival kings and one's own ministers and others, and then deliberate accordingly. One should consider the movements of the royal circle to be described later, such as: "Who seeks peace? Who seeks war? and so forth. Having understood that, one should deliberate in accordance with it.
He should diligently investigate the conduct of the middle king, the activities of the one seeking conquest, the movements of the neutral king, and those of the enemy. (7.155)

"Of the middle king": one should consider the conduct of the middle king, who is the neighbor of the enemy and the conqueror (*vijigīṣu*), capable of favoring them when they are united and capable of suppressing them when they are not. Likewise, one should consider the activity of the conqueror, who is naturally endowed with the qualities of wisdom and energy. Likewise, one should consider the conduct of the neutral king (*udāsīna*), who is capable of favoring the conqueror and the middle king when they are united and capable of suppressing them when they are not. And one should diligently consider the conduct of the three kinds of enemies—the natural, the artificial, and the immediate neighbor—relative to the former [categories]. (7.155)
In brief, these constituent elements are the root of the circle;
eight others are also enumerated, and thus they are traditionally remembered as twelve. (7.156)

"Etāḥ" and so forth. These four constituent elements (*prakṛti*), beginning with the middle king (*madhyama*), are said to be, in brief, the root of the mandala—the root of the other constituent elements, such as the ministers and others, which are about to be described. Furthermore, eight others are enumerated. Namely: in front [of the conqueror], there are four constituent elements—namely, the ally (*mitra*) of the enemy's territory, the enemy's ally (*arimitra*), the ally of the ally (*mitramitra*), and the ally of the enemy's ally (*arimitramitra*). Behind [the conqueror], there are likewise four: the rear-attacker (*pārṣṇigrāha*), the ally of the rear-attacker (*ākranda*), the supporter of the rear-attacker (*pārṣṇigrāhāsāra*), and the supporter of the ally of the rear-attacker (*ākrandāsāra*). Thus, there are eight constituent elements. Together with the previously mentioned four root constituent elements consisting of the middle king, the enemy, the conqueror (*vijigīṣu*), and the neutral king (*udāsīna*), these twelve constituent elements are traditionally taught. (7.156)
The five others are known as minister, realm, fortress, wealth, and army;
each of these has been described in brief, totaling seventy-two.

Regarding the term "minister" (*amātya*): for each one of these aforementioned four root constituents (*mūlaprakṛti*) and eight branch constituents (*śākhāprakṛti*), there are five material constituents (*dravyaprakṛti*) known as minister, territory, fortress, treasury, and army. Since these five exist for each of the twelve [constituents], they constitute sixty material constituents produced by the twelvefold multiplication. Thus, together with the four root constituents and the eight branch constituents, seventy-two constituents in total have been described by the sages in brief. (7.157)
Immediately after [the enemy], one should know the ally of the enemy; immediately after the enemy, the friend; and beyond those two, the neutral party. (7.158)

"Immediately following" means that the king seeking victory should recognize the enemy nature (*ari-prakṛti*) extending in all four directions immediately adjacent to him; likewise, he should know even one who serves that [enemy] to be an enemy. He should know the friend nature (*mitra-prakṛti*) to be situated one step beyond the enemy, immediately following the king seeking victory. Beyond those two—the enemy and the friend—he should know the neutral nature (*udāsīna-prakṛti*) of the king seeking victory. There is a difference in designation for these very natures based on the distinction between being in front or behind. In that regard, those situated in front have the designation of "enemy" alone. However, those situated behind, although they are enemies, have the designation of "rear-attacker" (*pārṣṇigrāha*). (7.158)
He should win over all of them by means of conciliation and other such measures,
whether employed individually or collectively, through personal effort and statesmanship.

"Those"—that is, all those kings—he should bring under his control by means of the expedients of conciliation (*sāma*), bribery (*dāna*), dissension (*bheda*), and force (*daṇḍa*), either individually or collectively as the situation requires. Alternatively, he may bring them under his own power through manly force alone, or through strategic policy (*naya*), or even through conciliation (*sāman*) exclusively. As it has been said: "They always praise conciliation and force for the prosperity of the kingdom" (7.109). 7.159.
He should always contemplate the six measures of policy: peace, war, marching, halting, dividing the army, and seeking refuge. (7.160)

Regarding "alliance" (*saṃdhi*): therein, for the sake of mutual benefit, an alliance (*saṃdhi*) is a formal agreement that "we two must assist one another by means of elephants, horses, chariots, gold, and so forth. Hostility (*vaira*) consists in the excessive practice of war and the like. Marching (*yāna*) is the movement toward an enemy. Waiting (*āsana*) is indifference. Double-dealing (*dvaidhībhāva*) is the splitting of one's forces for the sake of achieving one's own purpose. Seeking refuge (*saṃśraya*) is the taking of shelter with another more powerful king when oppressed by an enemy. One should always contemplate these strategic qualities (*guṇa*) and benefits; whichever quality, upon being adopted, results in one's own advancement and the decline of the enemy—that quality one should adopt.
Having carefully considered the task at hand, he should employ sitting encampment, marching, alliance, and war, as well as the double policy and seeking protection. (7.161)

Regarding "the seat" (āsana): the performance of the qualities such as peace (*saṃdhi*) and so forth, independently [of other means], was mentioned immediately prior; this present undertaking is for the purpose of performing what is appropriate for that. Having observed the task at hand—such as one's own prosperity or the enemy's decline—one should practice making peace, waging war, marching, or dividing the forces, or seeking refuge, such as by making peace with one and waging war with another, and so forth. (7.161)
A king should know that alliance and war are each of two kinds; likewise, marching and sitting encamped are both twofold, and seeking refuge is recorded as being of two types. (7.162)

"But as for 'alliance' (saṃdhi)": this is intended to show that one should understand that there are exactly six types of policy (guṇa), including alliance and the rest, each of which is of two kinds; thus, the specific mention [of "alliance"] is not meant to be exhaustive. (7.162)
When the action of the journey is common, and likewise when it is contrary, then that peace (saṃdhi) should be known as having two characteristics, being connected with the future. 7.163.

"Equalizing" (samāna): This refers to a treaty (*saṃdhi*) involving joint action, such as marching in an expedition, undertaken with another king against a third party, either for the sake of obtaining immediate results or for the sake of obtaining results at a later time. Furthermore, that which is undertaken on the basis of a desire for both present and future results—expressed as, "You go there, and I shall go there"—is known as "non-equalizing joint action. Thus, this treaty should be understood as being of two kinds. (7.163)

War is declared to be of two kinds: that waged by oneself for the sake of one's own purpose, either out of season or at the proper time, and that waged against a friend who has committed an offense. || 7.164 ||

"By oneself," and so forth. One type of war (*vigraha*) is that which is undertaken by oneself for the purpose of achieving a goal such as the conquest of *Śatruñjaya*, having assessed the enemy's calamities and the like, either at a time other than the upcoming months of Mārgaśīrṣa and so on, or precisely at the aforementioned time. Another type of war is that undertaken when harm has been done—that is, an injury inflicted upon a friend by another king; this is for the sake of protecting the friend. Thus, war is of two kinds. Govindarāja, however, reads and explains the text as "and also when harm is done by a friend": "When the enemy of another is a friend of the one seeking victory (*vijigīṣu*), and harm is being done to him while that [other] enemy is in calamity."
Therefore, the meanings of the written text as explained by Govindarāja and others such as Medhātithi have been recorded by the elders and accepted by me.
When an urgent matter arises by chance, marching alone or in alliance with a friend—these two types of marching are prescribed. (7.165)

"Alone," and so forth. When an urgent matter—such as an enemy's calamity or misfortune—arises unexpectedly, marching alone is prescribed for one who is capable, whereas for one who is incapable, marching accompanied by allies is prescribed; thus, marching is said to be of two kinds. (7.165)
When one's power has gradually diminished due to fate or past actions, or out of consideration for a friend, neutrality is declared to be of two kinds. (7.166)

Regarding the term "of one who is diminished": the sages have recorded two kinds of *āsana* (waiting/patience): that of one whose elephants, horses, treasury, and so forth have been gradually depleted by evil deeds committed in a previous birth or in this life; and that of one who, despite being prosperous, remains out of deference to a friend for the sake of protecting his interests. Thus, these two types of *āsana* are remembered by the sages. (7.166)

The maintenance of both the army and the master for the sake of accomplishing the objective is proclaimed as being of two kinds—namely, the state of neutrality (*dvaidha*)—by those who know the qualities of the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*). (7.167)

Regarding the phrase "of the army": for the sake of accomplishing one's own objectives to be achieved, the stationing of the army—consisting of elephants, horses, and so forth, under the command of a general—in one place to ward off the incursions of an enemy king, while the king himself, accompanied by a small portion of his forces, remains elsewhere in a secure location; thus, those who understand the benefits of the six measures of policy, such as peace and the rest, describe this twofold division (*dvaidha*) in two ways. (7.167)
Seeking refuge is recorded as being of two kinds: for the sake of accomplishing one's objectives when oppressed by enemies, and for the sake of gaining a reputation among the virtuous. (7.168)

"Artheti" [means]: Seeking the shelter of a powerful one is recorded in the Smṛti as being of two kinds: for the sake of achieving a purpose known as the cessation of oppression by enemies for one who is being harassed by them; or, even if there is no actual oppression at that time, for the sake of generating a reputation everywhere—by claiming, "This person has taken refuge with such-and-such a very powerful king"—out of fear of future harassment by enemies. Thus, shelter is said to be twofold. (7.168)
When one perceives that one's own future will certainly be superior, while the present suffering is slight, then one should resort to peace. (7.169)

"Yadā" and so forth: when, after the conclusion of war, one knows for certain that one's own superiority has been established, at that time—even if it involves the loss of some wealth and other resources—one should resort to peace, even by accepting minor concessions. (7.169)
When he considers all his subjects to be exceedingly well-pleased, and likewise himself to be highly exalted, then he should wage war. (7.170)

Regarding the phrase "when": when he considers all his subjects, such as the ministers and others, to be exceedingly gratified by gifts, honors, and the like, and when he considers himself augmented by the three powers consisting of elephants, horses, and the treasury, then he should resort to war. (7.170)
When he perceives that his own army is joyful and well-nourished in spirit, while that of the enemy is the opposite, then he should march against the foe. (7.171)

"Yadā" and so forth: when one truly knows that one's own army, consisting of ministers and others, is filled with joy and strengthened by wealth and other resources, whereas the enemy's force of ministers and so on is the opposite, then one should set out for battle, making him the target. || 7.171 ||
But when he is depleted of both mounts and forces, then he should sit with diligence, gradually conciliating his enemies. (7.172)

"Yadā" and so forth: when, moreover, one has become utterly depleted through the loss of mounts such as elephants and horses, or through the failure of ministers and other [resources], then, by pacifying enemies through conciliation, gifts, and the like, one should diligently resort to a position of neutrality. 7.172.
When the king considers his enemy to be stronger in every respect, then,
having divided his army into two parts, he should accomplish his own purpose.

"Should he think thus": when the king perceives that his enemy is stronger in every respect and incapable of making a treaty, then he himself, accompanied by a small portion of his forces, should take refuge in a fort. With one part of his army, he should engage the enemy in conflict. Having thus divided his forces into two parts, he should accomplish his own objectives, such as securing allies and so forth. (7.173)
But when he becomes most vulnerable to the forces of the enemy, then he should quickly seek refuge with a righteous and powerful king. (7.174)

Regarding the phrase "when": when, however, due to an excess of defects in his ministers and other constituents, he becomes vulnerable to attack by the enemy's forces—such that even by dividing his army and taking refuge in a fort, he is unable to protect himself—then he should immediately seek refuge with a righteous and powerful king. (7.174)
To explain what kind of person that powerful one is, he says:
One should always serve with every effort, like a teacher, him who would exercise restraint over both his subjects and the enemy's forces. (7.175)

Regarding "subjugation": that king who is capable of subduing both those subjects by whose fault he has become most vulnerable and that enemy force from which his fear has arisen—one should serve such a king with all one's effort, constantly, as if he were a guru. (7.175)
If he should perceive even there a fault arising from seeking refuge, he should nevertheless engage in fair combat there without hesitation. (7.176)

Regarding the word "yadi" (if): for resorting [to battle] is indeed a course of action for one who has no other alternative. Even in that case, if he perceives a fault arising from such a resort, then, having become free from doubt, he should engage in a fair fight at that time; for even a weak man may see victory over the strong, and because one who is slain attains heaven. (7.176)
A king who understands policy should employ every means such that his friends, neutrals, and enemies do not become superior to him. (7.177)

"By all means" means that a king who understands statecraft should strive by all means—conciliation and the rest—so that his friends, neutrals, and enemies do not become superior to him. For if they become superior, he becomes vulnerable; for through greed for wealth, even a friend may fall into enmity. (7.177)
One should examine the future of all undertakings as well as their present state, and one should also truly discern the merits and faults of all past actions. (7.178)

"Regarding the future": one should examine the future—the subsequent time—of all undertakings, whether small or great, to discern their merits and defects. One should also examine the present for the sake of swift accomplishment and so forth. Furthermore, regarding all past undertakings, one should properly examine their merits and defects, considering: "What was done by these? What has been resolved? Or what remains? || 7.178 ||
For this reason:
"One who knows the virtues and faults regarding the future, who makes swift decisions in the present, and who understands the consequences of past actions, is not overcome by enemies. (7.179)

Regarding the phrase "in the future": he who knows the future merits and defects of undertakings begins an undertaking that possesses merit and abandons one that possesses defect. He who, in the present time, performs his duty after having quickly determined it, and he who, regarding past actions, knows the remainder of those tasks—he obtains the fruit of that task upon its completion. Because he is thus attentive toward these three times, he is never overcome by his enemies. (7.179)
What need is there for much?
He should arrange everything in such a way that friends, neutrals, and enemies do not gain the upper hand over him; this is the summary of political strategy.

"Yathā" and so forth: he should arrange all the necessary provisions in such a way that the aforementioned friends and others do not cause harm to this king. This is the summary of the method, the policy. (7.180)
But when the lord intends to set out toward the enemy's kingdom, he should then proceed slowly toward the enemy's city according to this following rule. (7.181)

Regarding the word "yadā" (when): when, moreover, being capable, he should begin an expedition against the enemy's kingdom, then he should proceed toward the enemy's territory without haste, in the manner that will be described hereafter. || 7.181 ||
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, or in Phālguna or Caitra, the lord of the earth should set out on his expedition according to his strength.

Regarding the month of Mārgaśīrṣa: A king who is equipped with a fourfold army and whose march is slowed by the slow movement of elephants and chariots, desiring to go to an enemy kingdom rich in winter crops, should set out on his expedition in the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa. On the other hand, a monarch who relies primarily on cavalry, moves swiftly, and wishes to invade an enemy kingdom abundant in all types of crops, should march in the months of Phālguna or Caitra, without missing the time suitable for his own forces. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya’s statement—intended as a concise summary of the application of Manu’s meaning—states: "When the enemy kingdom is endowed with excellent crops, then he should march" (YDh 1.348). || 7.182 ||
Moreover, at other times as well, when he perceives certain victory, he should march forth after declaring war, or when a calamity has arisen for the enemy. (7.183)

Regarding the phrase "in other [times]": when one perceives that victory for oneself is certain at a time distinct from those previously mentioned, then—even during the summer and other such seasons that are otherwise unsuitable for one's own forces—one should generally undertake a march after mobilizing the army of elephants, cavalry, and so forth. Furthermore, when a calamity has arisen within the enemy’s constituent elements (*prakṛti*), such as the ministers and others, involving the severity of punishment or other misfortunes, one may march against that hostile faction even outside of the aforementioned times. || 7.183 ||
Having performed the ritual arrangements at the base according to the rules, as well as those for the journey, and having secured his station and properly stationed his spies; (7.184)
Having cleared the three types of roads and his own sixfold forces according to the rules for a campaign against an enemy,
he should advance slowly toward the enemy's city.

"Having done," and so forth. "Having purified": having made arrangements for the rear-guard (*pārṣṇigrāha*) in his own base, namely his fortress and kingdom—this being the provision consisting of stationing a portion of the army under the supervision of principal officers for the sake of protection—and having made the preparations for the expedition according to the scriptures, such as the equipment of vehicles, weapons, and armor suitable for the journey; and having won over the enemy's circle—that is, having secured those who serve him and have joined his side—and having dispatched spies such as fraudulent agents (*kāpaṭika*) to gather intelligence on the enemy's territory; and having thoroughly purified the three types of roads—distinguished by whether they are arid, marshy, or forested—by clearing trees and thickets and leveling depressions and elevations; and likewise having purified the sixfold force consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, laborers, and attendants, according to their needs through the provision of food, medicine, and honors—he should proceed without haste toward the enemy's territory according to the rules for a state of war (*sāṃparāyika*), for "war" (*saṃparāya*) is combat. (7.184–185)
One should be especially vigilant toward a hidden enemy who serves as a friend, and likewise toward one who has gone away and returned; for such a person is indeed the most dangerous foe.

Regarding "one who serves the enemy": one should be on guard against both a friend who, having remained hidden, serves the enemy, and a servant or similar person who, having previously departed due to alienation, has returned later; for these two are enemies exceedingly difficult to restrain. (7.186)
He should march along that path in either the staff array or the wagon array, or else in the boar, the crocodile, the needle, or the garuḍa array. (7.187)

Regarding "daṇḍa" (staff): the *daṇḍavyūha* is an array formed in the shape of a staff (*daṇḍākṛti*). The same applies to the *śakaṭa* (cart) and other arrays. In that [staff array], the commander of the forces is at the front, the king is in the middle, the general is in the rear, elephants are on the flanks, horses are near them, and foot soldiers are beyond those; thus arranged, it is long and evenly distributed on all sides. One should march along a path where there is danger from all directions using this staff array. The *śakaṭavyūha* has a needle-like point at the front and is broad in the rear; one should go with this when there is danger from behind. The *varāhavyūha* has a narrow front and rear and is broad in the middle. This same array, with an even broader middle, is the *garuḍavyūha*; one should advance with these two when there is danger on the flanks. The *makaravyūha* is the reverse of the *varāhavyūha*; one should go with this when there is danger both in front and in the rear. Where the troops are stationed in a compact formation, like a line of ants, with front and rear, having swift and heroic men at the head, that is the *sūcīvyūha*; one should march with this when there is danger in front. (7.187)
From whichever direction he suspects danger, there he should extend his forces;
and he himself should always take up his position in the lotus array.

"From which," and so forth. From whichever direction one might suspect danger from an enemy, in that very direction one should extend the army. Having emerged from the city in the *padma* (lotus) array—with the circumference evenly spread and the seeker of victory stationed in the center—one should always maintain a feigned encampment. (7.188)
The commander-in-chief and the army supervisor should station themselves in all directions;
and from whichever direction danger is anticipated, that quarter they should designate as the east.

Regarding the *senāpati*: a single commander should be appointed for each of the ten constituent parts consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry; he is called a *pattika*. A single commander for ten *pattikas* is called a *senāpati*. A single commander for ten of those is a *senānāyaka*, who is also the *balādhyakṣa*. The *senāpati* and the *balādhyakṣa* should be deployed for combat against rival forces in all directions. Furthermore, whichever direction from which danger is anticipated, that should be made the front line. (7.189)
And he should station trusted troops as outposts on all sides—men skilled in both their positions and in combat, who are fearless and steadfast. (7.190)

"Divisions," and so forth. One should station divisions (*gulma*)—which are units of the army commanded by trusted men, equipped with signals such as kettledrums, drums, and conchs for the purpose of staying put, withdrawing, or fighting, and consisting of those skilled in both stationary defense and combat, fearless, and reliable—as commanders of the army and troop leaders, positioned at a distance in all directions to prevent the enemy's entry and to ascertain the enemy's movements. (7.190)
One should make a few soldiers fight in a compact formation, but one may at will spread out many;
having arrayed them in the needle or the thunderbolt formation, one should cause them to fight.

"Having made them compact" means that having gathered a small number of warriors into a compact formation, one should then expand them as desired. Having arranged the warriors by means of the previously mentioned needle-like array (*sūcīvyūha*) or the so-called thunderbolt array (*vajravyūha*), with the forces stationed in three divisions, one should cause them to fight.
One should fight with chariots and horses on level ground; likewise, with boats and elephants in marshy terrain;
with bows in places covered by trees and shrubs; and with swords, shields, and other handheld weapons on firm ground.

"By means of chariots and horses," and so forth. One should fight with chariots and cavalry on level ground, because of the effectiveness of those [vehicles] for fighting there. With elephants that can traverse water, one should fight in water that follows such terrain. In places covered by trees and shrubs, one should fight with bowmen; and on ground free from pits, thorns, stones, and the like, one should fight with weapons such as swords, shields, and spears. (7.192)
He should station the men of Kurukṣetra, Matsya, Pañcāla, and Śūrasena, as well as those who are tall and those who are short, at the vanguard of the army. (7.193)

"From Kurukṣetra," etc. One should station at the front of the army those born in Kurukṣetra, the Matsyas who dwell in the Virāṭa country, the Pañcālas originating from Kānyakubja and Ahicchatra, and the Śūrasenas born in Mathurā—mostly because they possess large bodies and an egoistic pride in their valor. Likewise, one should station even those men born in other countries at the very front of the army, provided they have long or short bodies and are full of martial pride. || 7.193 ||
Having arrayed his forces, he should gladden them and examine them thoroughly;
he should also discern their movements even as they are fighting the enemies. (7.194)

"Should gladden them," and so forth. Having marshaled his forces, he should encourage those intent on battle through explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as: "In victory there is the gain of merit; for one slain facing the enemy, there is the attainment of heaven; but by fleeing, one incurs great sin and goes to hell. He should also examine those warriors with the intention of discerning why they are elated or provoked. Likewise, he should observe the conduct of the warriors while fighting with the enemies, whether their actions are deceitful or honest. (7.194)
Having besieged the enemy, he should remain there and harass his kingdom;
he should also constantly spoil his supplies of fodder, food, water, and fuel. (7.195)

"Having approached," and so forth. One should besiege and sit encircling an enemy—whether he has taken refuge in a fortress or not—even if he is not fighting, and one should devastate his territory. Likewise, one should always spoil his fodder, food, water, and fuel by mixing them with harmful substances and other such means. (7.195)
He should break down the tanks as well as the walls and moats; he should launch a full-scale assault upon him at night and likewise cause terror. 7.196.

"He should destroy," and so forth. He should destroy the enemy's sources of livelihood, such as tanks and the like; likewise, he should breach the fortifications, walls, and so on, and render the enemy's moats waterless by breaking them or filling them. In this manner, he should launch a full-scale assault upon the enemies while they are completely unawares, and thus seize their power. Furthermore, at night, he should terrify them with the sound of drums, trumpets, and similar instruments. (7.196)
And at that time—
