one desiring victory and free from fear— should instigate those who can be instigated, remain aware of their actions, and fight when fate is favorable. (7.197)

"Having approached," and so forth: one should cause dissension among those of the enemy's lineage who are susceptible to intrigue, those seeking the kingdom, and agitated ministers and others. Through such instigation, one should ascertain their activities and those performed by one's own agents. When it is understood that fate—such as the period (*daśā*) of auspicious planets—is endowed with favorable results, one should fight, free from fear and desiring victory. (7.197)
One should strive to conquer enemies through conciliation, bribery, or sowing dissension—either all together or individually—and never by means of war. (7.198)

"By conciliation," and so forth. One should make an effort to conquer enemies by means of conciliation—which consists of affection, showing respect, speaking for their welfare, and the like—by means of gifts such as elephants, horses, chariots, and gold, and by means of sowing dissension among their subjects and followers who desire the kingdom. One should employ these means either collectively or individually according to one's capacity, but never by means of war. (7.198)
Since victory is seen to be uncertain for two who fight, and defeat likewise occurs in battle, one should therefore avoid war. (7.199)

"Unstable": because it is observed that for two combatants, victory and defeat occur unpredictably, regardless of whether one has a large army and the other a small army; therefore, when another means is available, one should avoid war. (7.199)
When even the three previously mentioned expedients are not possible, one should fight in such a manner that, being well-equipped, one may conquer the enemies. (7.200)

"Of the three," and so forth. When even the three previously mentioned means—conciliation and the rest—are ineffective, and when there is doubt as to victory or defeat, one should nevertheless fight properly with such effort that one may conquer the enemies; for in victory there is the acquisition of wealth, and in dying while facing the foe, there is the attainment of heaven. However, when defeat is certain, it is better to withdraw from battle, as [the author] will say: "One should always protect oneself" (7.213). Thus say Medhātithi and Govindarāja. 7.200.
Having conquered, he should worship the gods and righteous Brahmins;
he should grant exemptions and proclaim amnesties of safety. (7.201)

"Having conquered," etc. Having conquered a foreign kingdom, he should honor the gods therein as well as those Brāhmaṇas who are preeminent in righteousness (*dharma*) by means of gifts of land, gold, and the like, and by acts of respect. This honoring is accomplished precisely through the giving of a portion of the conquered wealth and so forth. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya (1.323) says: "There is no higher duty for kings than this: that the wealth acquired in battle is given to Brāhmaṇas, and that security is always granted to the subjects."

Likewise, he should grant exemptions to the inhabitants of that region, saying, "This has been given by me for the sake of the gods and the Brahmins. Similarly, he should proclaim assurances of safety (*abhaya*), saying, "Whatever wrong has been done to us by those out of devotion to their masters, that has been forgiven by me; now, being free from fear, carry out your own affairs in happiness. (7.201)
But having understood the intended purpose of all these people in brief, he should install a member of their own lineage there and establish a covenant. (7.202)

"Of all of them": having briefly ascertained the intention of all these—the enemies' kings and ministers—he should have one whose royal lineage has been destroyed by force consecrated in the kingdom over that realm. He should then establish a regulation for him and his ministers, specifying: "This task must be done by you; this must not. (7.202)
And one should establish for them the righteous laws as they have been declared;
and one should honor him with jewels, together with his principal officers. (7.203)

Regarding the phrase "authoritative means" (*pramāṇāni*): one should accept as authoritative the practices of others that do not deviate from the Dharma, which are established as local customs (*deśadharma*) and accepted by the treatises (*śāstra*). Furthermore, one should honor this consecrated king along with his ministers and others by bestowing gifts such as jewels. (7.203)
For this reason:
"Taking away is unpleasant, while giving is a source of pleasure;
at the proper time, the practice of bestowing desired objects is praised. (7.204)

Regarding "taking": although the general rule is that seizing desired objects causes displeasure while giving them causes pleasure, nevertheless, in certain specific circumstances, both giving and taking are praised. Therefore, at that very time, one should honor [the guest] in this manner. 7.204.
All this action depends upon the two-fold ordinance, that of the gods and that of men;
of these two, the divine is indeed inconceivable, whereas in the human there exists the possibility of action.

"All this," and so forth. Whatever is to be accomplished depends upon two things: on the *daiva* (destiny), which is the action consisting of merit and demerit acquired in previous births and designated by the term "fate"; and likewise on the activity designated by the term "human" (*mānuṣa*), which is acquired in this world. Between these two, fate cannot be deliberated upon; however, regarding the human element, there is room for reflection. Therefore, one should strive for the accomplishment of one's purpose solely through the human means. || 7.205 ||
Or, being disciplined, he may even march together after having carefully made a treaty, perceiving the threefold fruit consisting of allies, gold, or land. (7.206)

"Along with him," and so forth. Thus, one should not wage war against an enemy who is susceptible to being approached. Alternatively, if that very enemy becomes an ally and offers gold or a portion of land—these three being the fruits of an expedition—one should proceed with diligence after making a peace treaty with him. (7.206)
Having carefully considered the rear-attacker and likewise the ally within the circle of states, one should obtain the fruit of an expedition from either a friend or even an enemy. (7.207)

"Regarding the rear-attacker," and so forth. When one desiring victory has marched out against an enemy, that king who stands behind him and practices such acts as invading his territory is the *pārṣṇigrāha* (rear-attacker). The king immediately adjacent to one who acts thus as a restrainer is the *ākranda* (ally). One should march after taking both of them into account. One should secure the fruit of the expedition from either a friend or an enemy who has become an ally. By seizing [the fruit] without regard for those two, one may sometimes be seized by the fault committed by them. (7.207)

A king does not prosper so much by the acquisition of gold and land as he does by gaining a firm friend, even if that friend is currently weak, provided he is capable of enduring for the future. (7.208)

Regarding the phrase "gold and land": a king does not attain such growth by the acquisition of gold and land as he does now by obtaining even a weak, but stable, friend who will be possessed of growth in the future. (7.208)
A friend who knows the dharma, is grateful, and is naturally contented; who is devoted, steadfast in his undertakings, and light—such a friend is highly praised. (7.209)

"Knowing the Dharma": one who knows the Dharma, who remembers a favor received, who is affectionate and devoted, who is firm in the undertaking of tasks, and whose nature is full of kindness—that friend is praised beyond measure. 7.209.
The wise say it is a hardship to have an enemy who is intelligent, of noble birth, brave, skillful, generous, grateful, and resolute. (7.210)

"Wise," and so forth: the learned say that an enemy who is wise, of noble lineage, courageous, clever, generous, mindful of favors received, and remains the same in both happiness and suffering is difficult to eliminate. One should therefore form an alliance with such an enemy. (7.210)
Nobility, knowledge of men, heroism, and compassion; constant magnanimity and the arising of the qualities of one who remains impartial. (7.211)

"Being noble," and so forth. [These qualities are: goodness, knowledge of the specific character of men, valor, compassion, and always being *sthaulalakṣya*, that is, a liberal giver. For this very reason, lexicographers state: "The words *vadānya*, *sthūlalakṣya*, *dānaśauṇḍa*, and *bahuprada* all denote a liberal giver. As for Medhātithi and Govindarāja’s explanation of the term *sthūlalakṣya* as "insight into subtle matters" regarding wealth, that is without scriptural authority (*anāgama*). This is the complete set of qualities of a neutral king; therefore, having relied upon such a neutral king, one should wage war even against an enemy possessing the aforementioned characteristics. (7.211)
A king should, without hesitation, abandon even land that is secure, always productive of crops, and conducive to the increase of cattle, for his own sake. (7.212)

Regarding the term "secure" (*kṣemya*): even if the land is capable of providing health and other forms of well-being, and always yields all kinds of crops due to being watered by rivers, and promotes the increase of livestock because of its abundance of grass and fodder, a king—provided he does not delay—should abandon it for the sake of protecting himself, as there is no other means of self-protection available. (7.212)
For this rule is remembered as having universal application:
"One should protect wealth for the sake of emergencies; one should protect one's wife even at the cost of wealth;
but one should always protect oneself, even at the cost of both wife and wealth. (7.213)

"Against misfortune," and so forth. Wealth should be preserved for the purpose of averting calamity; one should protect one's wife even by the relinquishment of wealth. Furthermore, one should always protect oneself even by the relinquishment of both wife and wealth, because of the scriptural injunction—"One should guard oneself from everything"—which teaches that self-preservation must be maintained except in cases of death prescribed by the sacred texts. (7.213)
Having closely observed all calamities that have arisen together, the wise man should employ every means, both those that are combined and those that are separate. (7.214)

"Simultaneously," and so forth: having recognized that all calamities—such as the depletion of the treasury, natural upheavals, and the misfortune of friends—have arisen together and in excess, one should not fall into delusion. Rather, one who knows the treatises should employ the means, such as conciliation (*sāma*) and the rest, whether individually or collectively.
Relying upon these three—the practitioner, the goal to be attained, and all the means in their entirety—one should strive for the accomplishment of the purpose. (7.215)

Regarding the term "the one who has approached" (*upetāram*): it refers to the self as the one who has approached; the "goal to be approached" (*upeyam*) is that which is to be attained; and the "means" (*upāyāḥ*) are all [the methods] such as conciliation (*sāma*) and so forth. Relying upon these three in their entirety, one should exert effort for the accomplishment of the purpose according to one's capacity. || 7.215 ||
Having thus deliberated on all this with his ministers, the king, after exercising himself and bathing at midday, shall enter the inner apartments to eat. (7.216)

"Thus": having deliberated on the conduct of all kings in this manner, as described, together with his ministers, and immediately thereafter having performed physical exercise such as the practice of arms, he should enter the inner apartments at midday to eat, after having completed the midday rites such as bathing. 7.216.

There, one should eat food that has been thoroughly examined by attendants who are like his own self, who know the proper time, who cannot be led astray, and who have neutralized poison with mantras. (7.217)

Regarding that: there, in the inner apartments, food prepared by cooks and others who are like himself, who know the proper time for meals, and who are unassailable, has been thoroughly tested by means of observing *cakora* birds and the like. Upon seeing poisoned food, the eyes of the *cakora* turn red. One should eat food over which mantras that remove poison have been recited. (7.217)
He should apply all medicinal substances that destroy poison to him, and, being self-controlled, he should always wear gems that counteract poison. (7.218)
"By means of poison-destroyers": he should mix all edible substances with medicinal herbs that neutralize poison. And being diligent, he should always wear gems that ward off poison. (7.218)
And women who have been thoroughly examined, purified by their dress and ornaments, and being well-composed, should touch him with fans, water, and incense. (7.219)

Regarding the phrase "having been tested": women who have been examined through the agency of secret agents—having altered their dress and ornaments out of fear that they might be carrying concealed weapons or wearing poison-smeared jewelry—and who are single-mindedly devoted, should attend upon this king with fans, bathing water, drinking water, and perfumed vapors. (7.219)
In this manner, one should exert effort regarding vehicles, beds, seats, and food; likewise in bathing, grooming, and all forms of personal adornment. (7.220)

"Thus": one should apply such efforts of examination and so forth in all matters concerning vehicles, beds, seats, food, bathing, and unguents, as well as in all things intended for adornment. (7.220)
Having eaten, he should indeed enjoy himself with the women in the inner apartments;
but having enjoyed himself at the proper time, he should again attend to his duties. (7.221)

"Having eaten": having finished his meal, he should sport there in the inner apartments with his wives. Without letting time pass, after sporting there during the seventh part of the day, he should again attend to his duties during the eighth part. (7.221)
And having adorned himself, he should again inspect the martial folk, as well as all the mounts, weapons, and ornaments. (7.222)

"Adorned" means that, having put on his ornaments, he should look upon those who live by weapons, vehicles such as elephants and horses, all weapons such as swords and the like, and the arrangement of ornaments and so forth. 7.222.
Having performed the twilight devotions, he should, bearing his weapon, listen within the inner apartments to the reports of those who reveal secrets and to the activities of his spies.
Having gone to another chamber and dismissed those people, he should enter the inner apartments again for the purpose of eating, surrounded by women. (7.224)

"Regarding the twilight prayer": "Having gone"—that is, having performed the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and departed from that place, he should go to another chamber, a secluded inner apartment within the house, and there, bearing his weapon, listen to the reports on his own activities from the spies (*cara*) who communicate secrets. Then, having dismissed that spy and surrounded by female attendants, he should enter the inner apartments (*antaḥpura*) again to eat. 7.223–224.
Having eaten there again a little, gladdened by the sounds of musical instruments, he should go to rest at the proper time and rise with his fatigue dispelled. (7.225)

Regarding the passage beginning with "tatra" and so forth: there, in the inner apartments, gladdened by the sounds of musical instruments pleasing to the ear, having eaten a little more and not yet being fully satiated, he should sleep during the latter watch of the night when the business of the day has passed. Then, having rested during the final watch of the night, he should rise. (7.225)
A healthy lord of the earth should observe this rule;
however, if he is unwell, he should entrust all of this to his servants. (7.226)
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Mānava Dharmaśāstra*, in the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu.

Regarding this [verse]: the king himself, being free from illness, should personally carry out all this—namely, the protection of the subjects and so forth, in the manner described. However, if he is unwell, he should entrust all of this to his most capable and excellent ministers. (7.226)
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Manvarthamuktāvalī, a commentary on the Code of Manu composed by the illustrious Kullūkabhaṭṭa.
The Eighth Chapter. But a king, desiring to examine legal cases, should enter the court modestly, together with Brāhmaṇas and with ministers who are experts in counsel. 8.1.

Regarding the term *vyavahārān*: from such hostile kings, having obtained his livelihood by protecting the subjects, he—acting for the sake of removing the mutual disputes and afflictions of those very subjects—engages in judicial inquiry (*vicāra*) to dispel the doubts arising from the statements of the plaintiff and defendant in the eighteen titles of law, beginning with non-payment of debt; that inquiry itself is *vyavahāra*. As Kātyāyana says:
"The prefix *vi-* signifies 'diversity' (*nānārtha*), and *hāra* is said to mean 'removal' (*haraṇa*) in the sense of doubt (*saṃdeha*);
because it removes diverse doubts, it is traditionally known as *vyavahāra*."

Desiring to examine those legal proceedings, the lord of the earth—modest, being free from the restlessness of speech, hands, and feet, and thus not arrogant; for if the king were undisciplined, the determination of truth would not occur due to the failure of the plaintiff and defendant to state their cases correctly because of a loss of presence of mind—should enter the court to be described below, together with Brahmins and ministers characterized by the definitions to be stated, and accompanied by the five-limbed counsel mentioned in the seventh chapter. And this examination of legal proceedings is fruitful only through the result of accomplishing the visible purpose to be described: the protection of subjects by determining the truth when they suffer mutual injury. (8.1)
Seated there or even standing, having raised his right hand and wearing modest dress and ornaments, he should examine the legal cases of the litigants.

Regarding the passage beginning with "tatra" and so forth: in that assembly, he should deliberate on matters of business—whether seated due to the gravity of the matter, or standing even when the matter is minor. The word *pāṇi* refers here to the arm; raising his right arm, yet without ostentatious dress or ornaments—just as non-ostentation of the senses was mentioned in the preceding verse—he should thus examine the cases. (8.2)
Day by day, through reasons observed in the world and observed in the scriptures, [these matters] were recorded separately within each of the eighteen branches of learning. (8.3)

"Every day," and so forth. And those matters, beginning with the non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*), which are enumerated among the eighteen paths of legal procedure (*vyavahāramārga*), he should investigate daily, one by one, through means such as witnesses and ordeals—both those understood from local, tribal, and family customs, and those understood from the scriptures. (8.3)
He enumerates those very eighteen [titles of law]:
"Of these, the first is the non-payment of debt; then deposit, sale without ownership, joint enterprise, and the non-delivery of what has been given. (8.4)
The non-payment of wages, the breach of an agreement, rescission of purchase and sale, and disputes between an owner and a keeper; 8.5.
The law concerning boundary disputes, verbal and physical assault, theft, violence, and the abduction of women; 8.6.
The duties of husband and wife, partition [of inheritance], gambling, and betting—these eighteen are the titles of law established here in this world. (8.7)

Regarding the phrase "of those": [the list includes] "wages," "boundary," and "man and woman. Among these eighteen titles, *ṛṇādāna* (recovery of debts) is investigated here first. Its essential nature was stated by Nārada: "That which is a debt to be paid and that which is not to be paid, by whom, where, and in what manner, as well as the rules for giving and receiving—it is called *ṛṇādāna*."

And from that [arise]: *nikṣepa* (deposit), which consists of the entrusting of one’s own property to another; *vikraya* (sale) performed by one who is not the owner; the collective performance of business by merchants and others; the taking back of wealth already given due to the realization that the recipient was unworthy, or out of anger and so forth; the non-payment of wages to a laborer; the violation of an established agreement; the reversal of a transaction after it has been completed due to regret; disputes between an owner and a herdsman; disputes regarding the boundaries of villages and the like; verbal abuse such as reviling; physical assault such as beating; theft, which is the taking of wealth through concealment; violence (*sāhasa*), which is the forcible seizure of wealth and the like; the illicit connection of a woman with another man; the legal determination of the duties of a man accompanied by his wife; and the partition of paternal and other types of property. Gambling with dice and the like, preceded by the establishment of stakes; and the fighting of animals such as birds and rams—these are the eighteen titles (*padāni*). These are the bases for the commencement of legal proceedings. Since *samāhvaya* (challenging to a fight) is a specific sub-type of gambling because it takes the form of animal gambling, the number eighteen is justified. (8.4–7)
In these matters, for men who are mostly engaged in disputes, one should determine the legal case by resorting to the eternal Dharma. || 8.8 ||

"In these," and so forth. In these judicial forums, such as the non-payment of debts and the rest, the king should determine the case by relying on eternal *dharma*, which has been handed down through beginningless tradition, for those people who engage in disputes there in great numbers. By the word "most" (*bhūyiṣṭha*), it is indicated that there are other grounds for dispute as well. For this very reason, Nārada says:
"And whatever has not been seen among the former [grounds], all that shall be classified as miscellaneous (*prakīrṇaka*).
But when the king himself does not personally attend to the inspection of legal cases, then he should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa to inspect those cases. (8.9)

"Yadā" and so forth: when, due to being preoccupied with other affairs or because of illness and the like, the king himself does not conduct the inspection of legal cases, then he should appoint a Brāhmaṇa who is experienced in the inspection of legal cases for the purpose of conducting that inspection. (8.9)
Surrounded by three members of the court, he should examine his legal cases,
having entered the foremost assembly hall, either seated or standing.

"Regarding 'so ‘sya' (he for him): that Brahmin, having been appointed by the king to oversee the legal cases to be seen, together with three other Brahmins who are virtuous, righteous, and skilled in the administration of justice, shall enter that very assembly hall; having sat down or stood there, and not while walking about—since walking might cause distraction of mind—he shall examine such matters as the recovery of debts and the like. (8.10)
In whatever place three Brahmins learned in the Vedas sit together, along with a learned official of the king, they know that assembly to be a court of Brahmā. (8.11)

"In which" means: in whatever place three Brāhmaṇas learned in the Ṛg-, Yajur-, and Sāma-vedas reside, and a learned Brāhmaṇa appointed by the king also resides—since he is the subject under discussion—they consider that assembly to be like the assembly of the Four-faced One (Brahmā). (8.11)
When dharma, pierced by adharma, enters an assembly and the members of that assembly do not extract the dart, they themselves are pierced. (8.12)

Regarding the word *dharma*: it means light (*bhās*), and that which exists together with it is the assembly of the learned (*vidvatsaṃhati*); this alone is intended here by the term *sabhā*. In whatever place such an assembly, consisting of a gathering of the learned, is present, if *dharma*—produced by the declaration of truth—is oppressed by *adharma* produced by the declaration of falsehood, occurring between a plaintiff and a defendant due to the truth-telling of one and the lying of the other, and if those members of the assembly do not extract that *adharma* as if it were a thorn because it causes pain to this *dharma*, then they themselves become pierced by that thorn of *adharma*. (8.12)
Since this is so, therefore:
One should either not enter an assembly, or one should speak what is right;
for by not speaking or by speaking falsely, a man becomes a sinner. (8.13)

"Regarding the phrase 'the assembly': having understood that it is an assembly, one must not enter it for the purpose of legal proceedings. If questioned, one must speak only the truth; otherwise, by remaining silent or by speaking falsely, one becomes a sinner immediately in either case. Medhātithi, however, has read it more straightforwardly as: 'Or the assembly must not be entered. (8.13)
For where dharma is slain by adharma, and truth by falsehood, while those present look on, there the members of the assembly are themselves slain. (8.14)

Regarding the passage beginning with "yatra" and so forth: in whatever assembly (*sabhā*) dharma is not seen through unrighteousness by the plaintiff and defendant, and where truth is destroyed by falsehood by the witnesses—despite the members of the assembly looking on and disregarding them—the meaning is that they are incapable of providing a remedy. The genitive case is used here according to Pāṇini 2.3.38, *ṣaṣṭhī cānādare* ("the genitive is also used in the sense of disregard"). In that case, those very members of the assembly are struck down by that sin. (8.14)
Dharma, when violated, destroys; Dharma, when preserved, protects.
Therefore, one must not violate Dharma, lest Dharma, being violated, slay us. (8.15)

"Law," and so forth. Because it is *dharma* alone that, when transgressed, destroys [the parties] along with their desired and undesired ends—unlike the plaintiff, the defendant, and others—and because it is *dharma* alone that, when not transgressed, protects them along with those ends; therefore, *dharma* must not be transgressed. "Lest *dharma*, having been transgressed by us together with you, destroy us"—this is an address to the judge who has set out upon a wrong path. Alternatively, *naḥ* is an indeclinable used in the sense of prohibition (*niṣedhe*). The intention is: "Let not *dharma*, being struck down, kill us; it does not indeed kill. (8.15)
For the Blessed One, Dharma, is indeed the Bull; those who treat him with contempt, the gods know as *vṛṣalas*. Therefore, one should not violate the Dharma. (8.16)

"Vṛṣa," and so forth. He who showers down desires (*kāma*) is a *vṛṣa*; by the word *vṛṣa*, dharma itself is designated. The word *alam* has the sense of prohibition. Therefore, the gods know him as a *vṛṣala* who prohibits dharma, not one who is a *vṛṣala* by birth. Thus, the etymological definition of the word *vṛṣala* is intended to refute the violation of dharma, [with the injunction]: "Therefore, one should not cut off dharma. (8.16)
Dharma alone is the true friend who follows one even unto death;
for everything else indeed goes to destruction along with the body. (8.17)

"Only one," and so forth. Dharma alone is the true friend, for it follows one even at the time of death in order to bestow its desired fruit; whereas everything else—wife, sons, and the like—vanishes along with the body itself. Therefore, one must not abandon dharma even out of regard for affection toward sons and others. (8.17)
One quarter of the unrighteousness falls upon the perpetrator, one quarter reaches the witness, one quarter reaches all the members of the court, and one quarter reaches the king. (8.18)

"Foot," and so forth. Because of witnessing an unjust proceeding, a fourth part of the unrighteousness attaches to the litigant—whether he be the plaintiff or the defendant—who committed the injustice; another fourth part attaches to the witness who speaks falsely; another quarter reaches all the members of the court who failed to prevent the occurrence of unrighteousness; and a quarter goes to the king. The intended meaning here is that all of them incur a connection with sin. (8.18)
The king becomes free from sin, and the members of the assembly are released;
the guilt goes to the perpetrator where one deserving of censure is censured. (8.19)

"O King," and so forth. Furthermore, in that assembly where a lying litigant—whether plaintiff or defendant—is properly censured for his falsehood through the administration of justice, there the king becomes free from sin, and the members of the court are not tainted by the evil; rather, the evil falls upon the perpetrator alone. (8.19)
One who lives merely by his birth may indeed be called a "pseudo-Brahmin" (brāhmaṇabruva), but a Śūdra can never be a teacher of dharma to the king. (8.20)

"Merely by birth": he who possesses merely the Brāhmaṇa birth, but not the performance of Brāhmaṇa duties—like a merchant or others—and who is capable of discerning clear justice and injustice through means such as testimony; or even one whose Brāhmaṇa birth is doubtful, yet who declares himself to be a Brāhmaṇa—he is preferable. And in the absence of a Brāhmaṇa endowed with the aforementioned qualifications, when a legal matter arises, he may be the king's expounder of dharma; however, a Śūdra, even if righteous and even if knowledgeable in legal procedure, shall not be so. Since the rule "a Brāhmaṇa is the expounder of dharma" already establishes the exclusion of the Śūdra, the specific prohibition "but not a Śūdra" is intended to grant permission for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas in the absence of a qualified Brāhmaṇa. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says:
Where there is no learned Brahmin, one should employ a Kṣatriya;
or a Vaiśya who knows the treatises on Dharma; but one should carefully avoid a Śūdra.
For it is said:
"The kingdom of that king for whom a Śūdra performs the discernment of dharma perishes, like a cow in the mud, while he looks on. (8.21)
"Of whom," and so forth. When a Śūdra performs the judicial discernment of dharma for a king, that kingdom perishes even as he looks on, like a cow sinking in the mud. (8.21)
That kingdom which is dominated by Śūdras, overrun by nihilists, and devoid of the twice-born, quickly perishes in its entirety, afflicted by famine and disease. (8.22)

"Whatever," and so forth. Whatever kingdom is full of Śūdras, overrun by many proponents of the non-existence of the next world, and devoid of the twice-born—that entire realm is afflicted by famine and disease and perishes quickly. This is because, due to the absence of the principle expressed in the verse, "An oblation properly cast into the fire... (3.76), there is a lack of rain; and because there is an absence of ritual acts intended to pacify the calamities such as famine and disease that have arisen. (8.22)
Having occupied the Dharma-seat, with his limbs properly covered and his mind composed,
he should begin the examination of legal cases after bowing to the guardians of the world.

Regarding the phrase "the seat of dharma": having sat upon the seat for the purpose of seeing [legal] matters, with his body covered and his mind undistracted, he should perform the examination of the case after having paid homage to the guardians of the world. 8.23.
Having discerned both profit and loss, as well as merit and demerit in their entirety, he should examine all the legal cases of the litigants according to the order of their castes. (8.24)

"Regarding the word *artha*: having understood that worldly gain (*artha*) and loss (*anartha*) consist of protecting the subjects or destroying them, one who seeks his own welfare should look after the affairs of those seeking their own ends in such a way that they do not conflict with the pursuit of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)—the sole goals for the sake of the next world. However, when there is a gathering of many castes, he should look after them according to the order beginning with the Brāhmaṇas. (8.24)
One should discern the internal state of men by external signs:
through their voice, complexion, gestures, facial expressions, gaze, and movements. (8.25)

"By external [signs]" means: by means of external indicators such as voice and so forth—whose functions are determined precisely by that designation—one should discern the internal intention of the plaintiff and the defendant. Voice refers to a faltering tone and the like; complexion refers to a change from one's natural color, such as a darkening of the face and so forth; gesture refers to looking downward and the like; appearance refers to perspiration, horripilation, and so forth arising in the body; and movement refers to the clapping of hands and the like. (8.25)
For this reason:
"By outward forms, by gestures, by gait, by activity, and by speech;
and by changes in the eyes and face, the internal mind is perceived. (8.26)

"By means of the modes" (ākāraiḥ) means: by the aforementioned modes such as [facial] expression, and by the gait characterized by faltering steps and so forth, that which has been transformed into the form of the internal mind and intellect is discerned. || 8.26 ||
The king shall protect the empty estate of a minor heir until he has returned from his studies or until he has passed his childhood. (8.27)

Regarding the term *bāladāya* (the property of a minor): the king shall protect the wealth belonging to a minor who is without a guardian, which is being seized unjustly by paternal uncles or others, until that minor has returned from the teacher’s house (*gurukula*) in the manner prescribed [in Manu Smṛti 3.1], such as “celibacy for thirty-six years,” etc., because for such a person, childhood necessarily comes to an end. However, if one returns from the teacher’s house while still a minor due to incapacity or other reasons, the king shall protect his wealth until he passes out of childhood. And childhood lasts until the sixteenth year, according to the statement of Nārada: “A child is [so] until the sixteenth year. (8.27)

The same protection should be afforded to women who have sons from barren wives, to those whose families have perished, to women devoted to their husbands, and to widows who are afflicted by illness. (8.28)

"Vaśāsu," and so forth. Regarding barren women (*vaśā*), the husband—who has taken other wives—becomes indifferent toward those for whom the means of subsistence have been provided; likewise, regarding childless women, those whose husbands are away on a journey, those who are without kin (*niṣkulā*) meaning devoid of *sapiṇḍas*, virtuous women, widows, and sick women—their wealth must be protected by the king just like the property of a minor. Here, the employment of multiple terms avoids redundancy according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalivardanyāya*). (8.28)
But those kinsmen who should seize the property of these women while they are still alive, a righteous lord of the earth should punish them with the punishment prescribed for thieves. 8.29.

"Of those who are living": by such pretexts as "We are the immediate heirs here and shall protect this wealth," those kinsmen who take that wealth while [the women] are still alive—the righteous king should punish them with the punishment prescribed for thieves, as will be described below. (8.29)
The king shall cause a vacant treasure whose owner has disappeared to be kept for three years;
within three years the owner may take it, but after that time the king shall take it. 8.30.

"Regarding 'pranaṣṭa' (lost property): the king, having proclaimed by means of a drum or other such instruments that "whose lost property is this? and having guarded it at the palace gate or similar location, shall keep it for three years. If the owner of the wealth arrives within those three years, he alone shall take it; but after that, the king may put it to use. (8.30)
He who says "this is mine" shall be questioned according to the rule;
having verified the form, number, and other details, the owner deserves that property. (8.31)

"‘This is mine,’ and so forth: one who says, ‘This wealth is mine,’ must be questioned according to the procedure: ‘What is the form of that wealth? What is its quantity? Where was it lost? If he then states the form, the number, and other details truthfully, then he is the owner of that wealth and is entitled to take it. (8.31)
One who fails to report the location and time of the lost item accurately, as well as its color, form, and size, deserves a fine equal to that [stolen property]. (8.32)

"Without declaring," and so forth: one who, not knowing the place and time of the lost property—thinking "it was lost in this place at this time"—nor its color such as white and so on, nor its shape such as a bracelet or a crown, nor its dimensions exactly as they were, deserves a fine equal to the value of the lost property. 8.32.
Furthermore, when there is agreement regarding the place, time, and other details, the king,
remembering the duty of the virtuous, shall take a sixth, a tenth, or even a twelfth part of what has been recovered from lost property. (8.33)

"He should take"—meaning that from whatever lost property has been recovered by the king, he should take a sixth, tenth, or twelfth part as a reward for protection, knowing that this is the duty of former virtuous kings. This option regarding the taking of a sixth part and so forth depends on whether the owner of the wealth is devoid of merit or possesses merit. He should hand over the remainder to the owner.
Property that has been lost and subsequently found shall remain under the supervision of appointed officials;
any thieves the king may catch therein, he shall cause to be executed by an elephant.

Regarding the phrase "lost" (*pranaṣṭa*): when any property belonging to someone has been lost and recovered by royal officers, it should be kept after being placed under the protection of guards. And as for those thieves who might seize that property, the king should have them executed by an elephant. Govindarāja, however, citing the rule "execution [is the penalty] for more than a hundred [gold pieces]" (8.231), asserts that here too execution applies to the theft of property exceeding a value of one hundred gold pieces. That is not correct; because in that context, following the specific injunction regarding the breaking of a breach (*saṃdhiṃ chittvā*)—namely, "that which is theft" (9.276)—execution is specifically prescribed for the very act of stealing property that has been lost and protected by the king, even though the owner still exists. This is because the rule "execution for more than a hundred" (8.231) refers to cases other than those where a specific punishment has been taught. 8.34.
If a man should truthfully declare, "This treasure is mine," the king should take a sixth part, or indeed a twelfth part, from him. (8.35)

"‘This is mine’: if a man, having himself found a treasure, or when a treasure has been discovered by another, says ‘this treasure is mine’ and establishes his connection to it through truthful testimony and evidence, the king shall take from that treasure either a sixth part or a twelfth part, depending on whether that person is devoid of merit or possesses merit; he shall hand over the remainder to him. (8.35)
But one who speaks falsely shall be fined an eighth part of his own wealth, or a smaller fraction calculated according to the value of that very deposit. (8.36)

Regarding the term "untruth": one who declares what is not his own to be his own shall be fined an eighth part of his own wealth; or rather, having calculated an extremely small portion of that very treasure such that he neither suffers ruin nor gains the territory [of the king], by that much he shall be fined. Because of the use of the suffix *-īyas* in the word *alpīyasīm*, this is a different penalty from the previous one. And the option between the two depends on whether the person is devoid of merit or possesses merit. (8.36)
But a learned Brāhmaṇa, having discovered a treasure previously deposited, may take it entirely, for he is the master of all. (8.37)

“Learned,” and so forth. Furthermore, a learned Brāhmaṇa, having seen a treasure previously deposited, may take it all; he shall not pay a sixth part. Because he is the master of the entire collection of wealth, it has therefore been said: “This [treasure] belongs entirely to the Brāhmaṇa” (1.100). Consequently, this statement refers to the case of a treasure deposited by another. And thus says Nārada:
“Having found a treasure deposited by another, the king indeed should take away the treasure;
for all treasure goes to the king, with the exception of the Brāhmaṇa” (7.6).
Yājñavalkya also says: "A king, having found a treasure-trove, shall give half to the twice-born; a learned twice-born man, however, may take it all, since he is the master of everything. (2.34)

Therefore, that which was stated by Medhātithi and Govindarāja regarding the verse "He who says, 'This is mine'" (8.35)—namely, that they explained this statement as referring only to property deposited by a father or others, in order to exclude objects belonging to the king—is not the word of the Sage. One should not respect the interpretation of Medhātithi and Govindarāja, which is self-invented and contrary to the explanations of sages such as Nārada.
But whatever ancient treasure a king may discover buried in the earth, he should give half of it to the twice-born and deposit the other half in his treasury. (8.38)

"But that which... (verse 8.38). Furthermore, whatever ancient treasure (*nidhi*) without an owner the king finds buried within the earth, from that he shall give half to the Brāhmaṇas and deposit the other half in his own treasury.
For the king is the lord of the earth; since he protects the ancient treasures and the mineral ores within the ground, he receives half the share as his reward. (8.39)

"Of treasures" means: the king is the taker of half of ancient treasures that do not belong to him, which have been found by someone other than a learned Brāhmaṇa, as well as of places where gold and other minerals are produced; for he protects them and is the lord of the earth. (8.39)
The king must restore to all castes the wealth stolen by thieves;
by using that for himself, the king incurs the guilt of the thief. (8.40)

"It must be given": whatever wealth has been stolen from people by thieves, that the king, having recovered from the thieves, should give back to the owners of the wealth. If the king himself uses that wealth, he incurs the sin of the thief.
One who knows the law, having carefully examined the laws of castes and regions, the laws of guilds, and the laws of families, should establish the individual's own duty. (8.41)

"Jāti" refers to those duties fixed by birth for Brahmins and others, such as officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*), and those local customs (*jānapada*) established in specific regions that do not contradict the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*). Regarding the laws of regions, castes, and families, there is the traditional teaching of Gautama: "Those [customs] which are not prohibited by the sacred scriptures are authoritative" (GDh 11.7). Having understood the guild laws (*śreṇīdharma*)—the regulations of merchants and others—established within their respective families, the king should, in legal proceedings, establish those various laws even if they appear to conflict with one another. (8.41)
For this reason:
"Even when they are far away, men who perform their own duties and remain steadfast in their respective tasks become dear to the world. (8.42)

"Regarding their own": those who perform their own duties—such as the laws of their caste, region, and family—and remain steadfast in their respective obligatory and occasional rites, become dear to the world even when they are far away, despite the absence of affection based on physical proximity. (8.42)
Having stated this as a digression, he speaks again of the subject at hand:
The king himself should not initiate a legal case, nor should his official;
nor should he ever swallow up a matter brought forward by another. (8.43)

"One should not initiate" means that a king, or one appointed by the king, should not, out of greed for wealth or similar motives, initiate a legal proceeding such as a dispute over debts. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
"But a king, whether through his own authority or out of greed for wealth, should not himself initiate legal actions against men who are not disputing."
Nor should he overlook a lawsuit brought by a plaintiff or a defendant out of greed for wealth or other interests. (8.43)
Just as a hunter traces the track of a deer by drops of blood, so should a king trace the path of dharma through inference. 8.44

"Yathā" means: just as a hunter reaches the track or location of a deer killed by a weapon by following the drops of blood, so too should one determine the true nature of Dharma through inference or through direct perception. 8.44

Established in the procedure of legal proceedings, he should carefully examine the truth and the matter at hand, as well as himself, the witnesses, the place, the nature of the case, and the time. (8.45)

"Truth," and so forth. A king engaged in the administration of justice should, setting aside deceit, perceive the truth and likewise the matter (*artha*). [The suffix] *ac* is used here in the sense of possession, as in the case of words beginning with *arśas*. He should perceive the matter—that is, the legal dispute (*vyavahāra*) concerning wealth such as cattle, gold, and the like—but not himself, thinking, "I have been mocked by this person with a wink of the eye," regarding even a minor offense. Furthermore, he should perceive the determination of the facts as one who partakes in the fruit of heaven and other rewards; the witnesses as speakers of truth; and the place and time—the nature appropriate to the place and time, the nature of the legal dispute itself, its gravity or lightness, and so forth. (8.45)
Whatever has been practiced by the virtuous and by righteous twice-born men, that one should establish for countries, families, and castes, provided it is not in conflict with the sacred law. 8.46

Having adopted that scriptural tradition which is observed and practiced by virtuous, learned twice-born men who prioritize dharma, and which is not in conflict with the customs of the region, family, or caste, he shall determine the legal decision. 8.46.
This general rule, consisting of technical definitions applicable to all legal proceedings, has been stated; now, with reference to the non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*), he says:
"Urged by the creditor for the sake of recovering his wealth, the king shall cause the debtor to pay the amount proved to belong to the creditor. (8.47)

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the debtor's wealth": when the king has been petitioned by the owner of the wealth for the purpose of recovering the capital lent, he should cause the debtor to pay the wealth—established by the evidence to be described hereafter, such as written documents—to the creditor. The meaning is that he should cause the debtor to give [the debt] to the creditor. (8.47)
How he should cause [the debt] to be paid is stated:
"By whatever means a creditor may recover his own wealth, by those very same means he should win over the debtor and cause him to pay. (8.48)

"By whatever means": by whichever methods about to be described the creditor obtains his wealth, he should, having brought [the debtor] under control through those very means, cause him to pay that wealth. (8.48)
He states those means:
"One should accomplish one's purpose by employing legal action, litigation, artifice, and conduct, as well as by force as the fifth. (8.49)
"By means of *dharma*, etc. means that one should accomplish the purpose by employing *dharma* and so forth. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states concerning *dharma*:
"A debtor should generally be made to pay through the mediation of friends and relatives, by conciliation, and by following [the creditor]—this is declared to be *dharma*."

When the debt is payable and the debtor does not default, [the creditor may recover it] through legal proceedings (*vyavahāra*). As he will state: "But one who denies the debt... (8.51). Medhātithi, however, says: "One who is destitute should be made to pay through legal proceedings; having provided him with other tools for work, he should be made to engage in business such as agriculture or trade. From that, the creditor should take the wealth produced. Bṛhaspati mentions three methods, beginning with fraud (*chala*): "Having brought back the wealth requested by fraud, the stronger [creditor] [should recover it] from the debtor."
When one is made to pay after having taken what was brought from another, that is a fraudulent transaction.

Having killed his wife, sons, and cattle, and having performed the ritual of seating his wife [on the funeral pyre], he is made to pay his own wealth for the sake of the journey; that is called "customary practice" (ācarita).
Where a debtor is brought to his own home by force and compelled to pay through methods such as beating and the like, that is proclaimed as "coercion" (balātkāra).
A creditor who recovers his own wealth from a debtor by his own means must not be prosecuted by the king for recovering what is his own. (8.50)

Regarding the passage beginning with "ya" and so forth: if a creditor (*uttamarṇa*) recovers from a debtor (*adhamarṇa*) a debt that has been admitted by himself through force or other means, he should not be prohibited by the king on the grounds that, while properly recovering his own wealth, he failed to inform us and instead resorted to force and the like. (8.50)
But if the debtor denies the debt when it has been made clear by means of evidence, the judge shall compel him to pay the creditor's claim and a small fine according to his ability. (8.51)

Regarding the word "artha" (the object): when a debtor—who denies the matter concerning wealth by saying, "I do not owe this to him"—is established through legal means such as documents, witnesses, or ordeals, the king shall cause that object to be paid to the creditor. Furthermore, he shall cause a small fine to be paid according to the man's capacity, even less than the tenth-part fine mentioned later in the verse, "In case of denial, it is double that" (8.139). || 8.51 ||
When a debtor, upon being told "Pay! in an assembly, denies the debt, the plaintiff must point out the place [where it was contracted] or specify another means of proof. (8.52)

[The defendant] departs. When the debtor, having been told by the judge in court, "Give the creditor his wealth," denies it by saying, "I do not owe him anything," the plaintiff (the accuser) shall point out a witness residing in the place where the loan was made. Since a decision regarding women, fools, and others is generally reached primarily through witnesses, the production of witnesses is mentioned first. Alternatively, he may state another means of proof, such as a document and so forth. (8.52)

He who points out what should not be pointed out, he who denies after having pointed it out, and he who does not understand the contradictory meanings of what precedes and follows—[these are the three types of witnesses]. (8.53)
Furthermore, he who, having stated and restated his case, then evades it;
or who, when questioned, does not accept a matter that has been correctly established. (8.54)
He who converses secretly with witnesses in a place where conversation is forbidden, he who does not wish to answer when being questioned, or he who runs away; 8.55.
If, when told "Speak!", he does not speak, or if he fails to clarify what has been said, or if he cannot discern the sequence of what precedes and follows, he is defeated on that point. (8.56)

"Indescribable" (*adeśya*), "unassignable" (*apadiśya*), "incommunicable" (*asaṃbhāṣya*), and so forth. "Indescribable" refers to a case where, having pointed out a location where the debtor could not possibly have resided at all since the time of contracting the debt, he then withdraws from that assignment and so on, saying, "This was not designated by me. Furthermore, one who understands previously stated matters to be contrary to his own interests or his own statements; or one who, having pointed out, "A *pala* of gold was taken by him from my hand," then retreats by saying, "It was taken from the hand of my son," and so forth. Furthermore, one who, when questioned by the judge (*prāḍvivāka*) as to why he gave a properly pledged object at night without witnesses, does not provide an answer. One who converses with witnesses in a secluded place or similar location where conversation is improper. One who, when the judge repeatedly urges him to clarify the meaning of his statement, refuses to accept the question. One who would flee—having described the legal proceedings already stated—as if moving from one place to another. And one who, when told "Speak," says nothing at all. One who does not establish the point to be proven (*sādhya*) through evidence. One who does not know what comes first—the proof (*sādhana*)—and what comes after—the point to be proven (*sādhya*). One who points out what is not a proof as being a proof. One who points out what is not a provable matter as being provable through evidence, such as saying, "The bow made of a hundred peaks is to be known [as such]," and so forth—he is defeated regarding that point to be proven. (8.53–56)
If one says, "I have witnesses," and when told "Produce them," fails to produce them,
the judge shall declare him to be defeated on these grounds.

Regarding the term "sākṣiṇaḥ" (witnesses): having said, "I have witnesses," when one who is told to point them out fails to do so, the judge (*dharmastha*) or presiding officer (*prāḍvivāka*) shall declare him defeated on account of these previously mentioned reasons. Alternatively, there is the reading, "jñātāraḥ santi me ity uktvā" (having said, "There are knowers [of my case] for me"). Here, the change of the vowel *i* to its preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) is an archaic Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). (8.57)
If the plaintiff does not speak, he shall be punished with a fine according to the law; if he does not speak within three fortnights regarding the matter of justice, he is defeated. (8.58)

Regarding the term "plaintiff" (*abhiyoktṛ*): if one who is a claimant, having presented his case in the royal court, fails to state it in the formal plea (*bhāṣā*), then—depending on the gravity of the matter—he shall be imprisoned and, according to the law, fined for a minor offense. However, if the defendant (*pratyarthin*) fails to respond within three fortnights, he shall be defeated by the law itself, and not merely through technicality (*chala*). (8.58)
Whatever amount one may conceal, or whatever amount one may falsely state, both of those who are ignorant of the law shall be made by the king to pay a fine double that amount. (8.59)

"Whoever"—meaning, whichever defendant misappropriates wealth of a certain amount, or whichever plaintiff speaks falsely regarding wealth of a certain amount—both of those unrighteous persons shall be compelled to pay double the value of the wealth they have denied or falsely stated as a fine. Because of the expression "ignorant of dharma," this refers to cases of denial and false testimony committed intentionally. For denial and false claims resulting from negligence or the like, he will state that the fine is one-tenth of a hundred [verses 8.16–17]. (8.59)

But one who, having been questioned, denies [the debt] while being established in his position by a creditor seeking wealth, must be judged by at least three witnesses in the presence of the king and Brāhmaṇas. 8.60.

"Being questioned": when one who has been summoned by a creditor seeking his wealth is questioned by the presiding judge after having brought about the attendance of royal officers, and he then denies it, saying "I do not owe [the debt]," then he must be made to prove his case before the king’s appointed Brahmin official by means of at least three witnesses—those of whom three are the minimum. (8.60)
I shall now fully describe the kind of witnesses who should be employed by wealthy men in legal proceedings, and how the truth must be spoken by them. (8.61)

Regarding the phrase "of such a kind": I shall describe the types of witnesses who should be appointed by creditors and others in legal proceedings such as the non-payment of debts; likewise, I shall explain the manner in which even they must speak the truth. (8.61)

Householders who have sons, who are native-born, and who belong to the kṣatriya, vaiśya, or śūdra castes, are worthy of being called as witnesses when summoned for a legal matter, provided they are not in a state of distress; but no others whatsoever are so worthy.

Thus: those who have taken wives, who have sons, who are born in that same country, and who belong to the Kṣatriya, Śūdra, or Vaiśya castes, become fit to be witnesses when designated by the litigant. For they do not speak otherwise out of fear for their prepared defenses or their sons, nor due to hostility toward a resident of that country; however, anyone at all should not be a witness in legal proceedings such as the non-payment of debts. But in times of emergency, those other than the aforementioned may be witnesses in cases of verbal assault, physical assault, adultery with women, and the like. (8.62)
Trustworthy persons from all castes should be made witnesses in legal matters;
those who know all the laws and are free from greed should be appointed, while those of the opposite character must be avoided. (8.63)

"Trustworthy persons," and so forth. Since it was stated [in verse 8.62] that "[those born from the wombs of] Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras," the expression "among all castes" is used here in order to include Brāhmaṇas as well. Among all castes, those who speak according to the facts as they have understood them, who know all duties (*dharma*), and who are free from greed—these should be appointed as witnesses. One should avoid those who are the opposite of what has been described. (8.63)

One should not employ those who have a financial interest, nor those who are trustworthy, nor companions, nor enemies; nor those whose faults are known, nor those afflicted by disease, nor those who are corrupt. (8.64)

"Nor those connected with a financial interest," and so forth. Those connected with a financial interest such as debts include debtors and the like; "trustworthy persons" (*āpta*) refers to friends; "associates" refers to their attendants; as well as enemies, those known to have given false testimony in other cases, those afflicted by disease, and those defiled by mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*) and the like—these must not be made witnesses, because there is the possibility of motives for perjury, such as greed, passion, hatred, or loss of memory. (8.64)
The king must not be made a witness, nor artisans or actors;
nor a Vedic scholar, nor one dwelling in a religious order, nor one who has renounced all worldly attachments. (8.65)

"Not a witness": because of his sovereign authority, the king is unfit to be questioned according to the rules governing witnesses; therefore, the king must not be made a witness. An artisan (*kāru*) refers to a cook and the like; a performer (*kuśīlava*) refers to an actor and the like; both are disqualified from being witnesses because they are generally preoccupied with their own work and possess a tendency toward greed for wealth. A *śrotriya* (one learned in the Vedas) is also not a witness due to his preoccupation with study, the *agnihotra* sacrifice, and other such duties. A "resident of a religious order" (*liṅgastha*) is a student (*brahmacārī*), and one who has "withdrawn from society" (*saṅgavinirgata*) is a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*); these two are also disqualified from being witnesses because they are preoccupied with their respective duties and are fixed in the Brahman. By the mention of the *śrotriya*, there is no prohibition against a Brāhmaṇa other than those preoccupied with study, the *agnihotra*, and so forth. (8.65)
Neither one who is dependent on another, nor one who is censurable, nor a thief, nor one who performs forbidden acts;
neither an old man, nor a child, nor one alone, nor an outcaste, nor one with impaired faculties. (8.66)

"Not one who is dependent" (*nādhyadhīna*): one who is "dependent" (*adhyadhīna*)—meaning utterly subservient, such as a slave born in the house (*garbhadāsa*)—should not be made a witness, because he would abandon his prescribed duties and is thus censured by the world. A "bandit" (*dasyu*) is one of cruel deeds; for it will be stated later [in verse 8.67]: "Neither when angry nor when a thief. One who performs forbidden acts (*vikarmakṛt*) is one who does what is prohibited, because in these cases passion, hatred, and so forth may arise. Not an "old man," because there is generally a possibility of loss of memory. Not a "child," because he has not attained legal capacity (*vyavahāra*). Not "one alone," because of the fear of his destruction or flight, since the rule [in verse 8.60] prescribes "at least three. This prohibition is stated even though the prohibition of a single person is already established by implication, in order to permit two persons in certain circumstances. An "outcaste" (*antya*), such as a *caṇḍāla* and the like, should not be made a witness because he is ignorant of the Dharma. One with impaired faculties (*vikalendriya*) should not be made a witness because of the deficiency in his perception. || 8.66 ||
Neither one who is distressed, nor intoxicated, nor insane; neither one afflicted by hunger or thirst, nor oppressed by fatigue, nor tormented by desire, nor angry, nor even a thief. (8.67)

"Not one who is distressed" (*nārtaḥ*): "distressed" means by the loss of a relative or similar cause; "intoxicated" by liquor and the like; "insane" by possession by spirits or epilepsy and so forth; "afflicted by hunger or thirst"; "oppressed by fatigue," exhausted by traveling on a road and the like; "oppressed by lust"; and "one whose anger has arisen," as well as a "thief"—in every case, the phrase "should not be made a witness" is to be connected. Among these, the distressed and others [are excluded] due to a deficiency of intellect, while the thief because of his unrighteousness. (8.67)
Women shall give testimony for women; twice-born men of similar status for twice-born men; virtuous Śūdras for Śūdras; and those of low birth for those of the lowest castes. (8.68)

"Of women," and so forth. In legal disputes between women, such as those concerning the non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*) and the like, women shall serve as witnesses. For the twice-born—namely Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas—similar persons of the same caste (*sajātīya*) shall be witnesses. Likewise, virtuous Śūdras for Śūdras, and Cāṇḍālas and others for Cāṇḍālas and others, shall be witnesses. This, however, is a prescription regarding witnesses of the same caste. In the absence of witnesses of the same caste who possess the aforementioned characteristics, even those of a different caste may serve as witnesses. Therefore, Yājñavalkya says: "According to caste and according to class, all are declared [to be witnesses] for all. (YDh 2.69)
But whoever, being an eyewitness, should give testimony for litigants within a house, in a forest, or even in the event of a threat to life; 8.69.

Regarding the term *anubhāvī*: when some person is found within a house, in a forest, or elsewhere, in the midst of an affliction caused by thieves and the like, or an injury to the body caused by assassins and the like, that person becomes a witness for the two litigants themselves; he does not need to possess the characteristics previously described, as is required in cases such as the non-payment of debts. (8.69)
He clarifies that very point through an illustration:
"In the absence of even a woman, the task may be performed by a child, an elderly person, a disciple, a kinsman, a slave, or even a hired servant. (8.70)

"By a woman as well": when the aforementioned witnesses are unavailable within the interior of a house or similar locations, women, children, the elderly, pupils, kinsmen, slaves, and laborers may also serve as witnesses. (8.70)
Now, one might ask: "How can women, children, and others, due to their unstable intellects and so forth, serve as witnesses even in this case? To this he says:
"One should recognize that the speech of children, the elderly, and the sick, when they testify, is false; likewise, the speech of those with overexcited minds is unstable. (8.71)

Regarding the phrase "children and the elderly": the speech of children, the elderly, the sick, those with disturbed minds, and the intoxicated or insane becomes unstable when they speak falsely in testimony. Therefore, one should recognize that instability through inference, as it has been said: "One should discern [it] by external signs" (8.25). || 8.71 ||
In all cases of violence, theft, and adultery, as well as in verbal and physical assault, one should not examine the witnesses too closely. (8.72)

Regarding the phrase "in cases of violence": in cases of violence such as arson and the like, or in the seduction of a teacher’s wife, or in verbal and physical assault, the examination of witnesses as prescribed for householders in verse 8.62 need not be performed. This is an elaboration by way of example of the rule in verse 8.70: "The testimony may even be given by a woman when there is no other possibility. || 8.72 ||

In the event of a conflict between witnesses, O King, the ruler should accept the majority; but if they are equal in number, he should accept those distinguished by their virtues; and if there is a conflict even among those distinguished by virtue, he should accept the best of the twice-born.

"Plurality," and so forth: when witnesses are mutually contradictory, the king should accept that which has been stated by the majority for the purpose of reaching a decision. But when there is an equal number of witnesses stating contradictory matters, he should rely on those who possess [excellent] qualities (*guṇavat*). Regarding the contradiction among those very persons possessing qualities, [the text mentions] "the best of the twice-born" (*dvijottama*); among the twice-born, these are the most excellent. The meaning is "those possessed of ritual action" (*kriyāvant*). For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says: "In a conflict between those possessing qualities, one joined with ritual action [prevails]. Govindarāja, however, states that in the case of a contradiction among those possessing qualities, one should rely on the "best of the twice-born," namely, Brāhmaṇas. (8.73)
Testimony is established through seeing in person and likewise through hearing;
by speaking the truth therein, a witness does not fall away from dharma or worldly prosperity. (8.74)

Regarding the term "in person" (*samakṣa*): testimony is established through direct perception when the object is perceivable by the eye, and through hearing when it is perceivable by the ear. In that regard, a witness who speaks the truth is not deprived of either merit (*dharma*) or wealth (*artha*); for by speaking the truth, merit is attained, and in the absence of punishment, there is no loss of wealth. (8.74)
A witness who gives testimony in an assembly of noble men concerning anything other than what was seen or heard goes headlong to hell after death and is excluded from heaven. (8.75)

"An eyewitness," and so forth. An eyewitness who speaks in an assembly of the virtuous something other than what was seen or heard goes to hell with his face cast downward. And in the next world, he is deprived by that sin of the fruit consisting of heaven, which would have been produced by other [wholesome] actions. || 8.75 ||
Even where one might see or hear something unintentionally, there too one should speak of it exactly as seen and exactly as heard. (8.76)

Regarding the phrase "where" and so forth: even if one has not been formally appointed as a witness in this matter, if he sees any transaction such as the non-payment of a debt (*ṛṇādāna*) or hears of verbal abuse (*vākpāruṣya*) and the like, he too is a witness; being questioned, he should state what he has perceived. This [category of] unappointed witness was stated by Manu in general terms. Its sixfold classification was stated by Nārada and others in the passage beginning with, "The village headman, the judge, and the king... (NSm 1.131). || 8.76 ||
A single witness who is free from greed may be accepted, but even many women, though pure, are not; because the intellect of women is unstable, as are others who are possessed by defects. (8.77)

"Only one," and so forth. In the phrase "only one who is not greedy," the elision of the vowel *a* (i.e., *alubdhaḥ*) should be understood. Even a single witness may be free from greed and other such vices. For this very reason, Vyāsa says:
"One whose actions are pure, who knows the Dharma, and whose speech is based on personal experience—even he alone may be authoritative as a witness, especially in cases of violence."

Medhātithi and Govindarāja read and explain the verse as: "But one who is greedy shall not be a witness. This means that a single witness whose nature is characterized by greed is not admissible. Thus, a person who is free from greed and possesses good qualities may, under certain circumstances, serve as a witness even if he is alone. Women, however, even if they possess personal purity and other virtues, are not to be witnesses in legal proceedings involving debt and the like, because of their unstable intellects. But in cases that do not require deliberation, such as theft, verbal abuse, or physical assault, it is stated that "in the absence of others, the case may be done even by a woman" (8.70), and thus her status as a witness is permitted. Others as well, who are tainted by defects such as theft and so forth, would likewise not be witnesses in a proceeding that requires deliberation. (8.77)
Whatever they may say by their very nature should be accepted as conventional;
therefore, whatever else they might speak for the sake of dharma is useless. (8.78)

"By their own nature" means that whatever they may say by way of their own nature, free from fear and other such influences, that should be accepted for the purpose of deciding the legal proceeding. However, whatever they say that is other than natural, due to some external cause, is useless regarding matters of dharma and should not be accepted. || 8.78 ||

When the witnesses have arrived within the assembly hall in the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant, the judge shall interrogate them, consoling them with this following procedure: sabhāntaḥ sākṣiṇaḥ prāptān arthipratyarthisaṃnidhau | prāḍvivāko ‘nuyuñjīta vidhinānena sāntvayan || 8.79 || "O witnesses, you who have come here in the midst of the court in the presence of both the claimant and the respondent, the presiding judge shall question you according to this rule, speaking to you with gentleness."

"Within the assembly," and so forth. Having summoned the witnesses into the midst of the assembly in the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant, the king’s appointed Brāhmaṇa, composing pleasant speech, shall question them in the manner to be described hereafter. (8.79)
"Whatever you know of the mutual conduct of these two regarding this matter, tell it all in truth; for you possess the status of witnesses here. (8.80)

"Regarding that which is between the two": whatever you know to have been done between these two, the plaintiff and the defendant, concerning this matter, tell all of that truthfully; for you possess the status of witnesses in this case. (8.80)
A witness who speaks the truth in testimony attains abundant worlds;
and in this world, he gains unsurpassed fame—this speech is honored by Brahmā.

"Truth indeed. A witness, speaking the truth regarding the matter at hand, attains abundant and superior realms such as the world of Brahmā, and gains supreme renown here in these worlds; for this speech, whose essence is truth, is honored by the Four-Faced One. (8.81)
Speaking falsely when giving testimony, one is bound tightly with the nooses of Varuṇa for a hundred lifetimes, rendered helpless; therefore, one should speak the truth in testimony. (8.82)

"Regarding the witness," and so forth: because a witness who speaks a false word is made dependent by the nooses belonging to Varuṇa—namely, serpent-ropes and dropsy—and is excessively tormented for as long as a hundred births; therefore, one should speak the truth in testimony. 8.82.
A witness is purified by truth; righteousness increases through truth.
Therefore, truth must indeed be spoken by witnesses among all social classes.

"By truth," and so forth. Since a witness is liberated from even previously accumulated sin by means of truth, and since his merit increases through the speaking of truth, therefore truth must be spoken by witnesses in matters concerning all social classes (varṇas). || 8.83 ||
For the self alone is capable of being the self's refuge; the self is likewise the self's own resort.
Do not despise your own self, the supreme witness of men. (8.84)

"Self alone. Since the self alone is the foundation for one's good and evil deeds and the self alone is one's own refuge, you should not, by means of false speech, treat your own self with contempt—this self which is the witness among men, superior even to the mediocre. (8.84)
"Evil-doers indeed think, 'No one sees us';
but the gods see them, as does the inner person within themselves. (8.85)

"They think" means that evildoers think thus: "No one sees us who have set out upon unrighteousness. Yet those very gods, who are about to be mentioned, see them; and their own inner self (antarapuruṣa) sees them. 8.85.
Heaven, earth, the waters, the heart, the moon, sun, fire, Yama, and wind, as well as night, the two twilights, and Dharma—these are the witnesses of the conduct of all embodied beings. (8.86)

"Day," and so forth. The deities presiding over the heavens, the earth, the waters, the heart, the individual soul, the moon, the sun, fire, Yama, Vāyu, night, and the two twilights know the auspicious and inauspicious actions of all embodied beings. Furthermore, there exists a presiding deity for these [elements] such as day, and she, being embodied and stationed in one place, knows all that; this has been stated by accepting the Vedānta philosophy, which is authoritative according to the scriptures (āgama).

In the presence of the gods and Brahmins, the judge, being himself pure, should question the pure twice-born men regarding the truth in the forenoon, while they face either northward or eastward. (8.87)

"Before the gods and the Brahmins": the image is the deity; in the presence of Brahmins, the judge himself, being pure, should at the time of forenoon ask the twice-born and others—who are themselves pure and facing either east or north—to give testimony exactly as it is.
One should ask a Brāhmaṇa, "Speak"; a king, "Speak the truth";
a Vaiśya, with [threats of] cattle, grain, and gold; and a Śūdra, with all [the aforementioned] sins.

"Speak," and so forth. Having uttered the word "speak" (*brūhi*), one should question a Brāhmaṇa. One should question a Kṣatriya, a member of the royal caste, saying, "Speak the truth. One should question a Vaiśya saying, "Whatever sin there is in the theft of cattle, grain, or gold, that shall be yours if you speak falsely. Furthermore, one should question a Śūdra saying, "If you speak falsely, you will be joined with all the sins about to be described. (8.88)
Whatever worlds are ordained for the slayer of a Brahmin, for those who kill women or children,
for the betrayer of friends, and for the ungrateful— those same worlds shall befall him who speaks falsely.

"O slayer of a Brāhmaṇa!"—those worlds such as hell that have been described by the seers for the killer of a Brāhmaṇa, the killer of a woman, and the killer of a child; and those for the betrayer of friends and the like, and those for the one who does harm to a benefactor—all those would be false for you, who speak falsely. (8.89)
"O Bhadra, whatever merit you have accumulated since birth—all of that would go to a dog if you were to speak otherwise. (8.90)
"From birth onwards," and so forth: O man of virtuous conduct, whatever merit you have performed since your birth—all of that transfers to your dog and other [animals] if you speak an untruth. (8.90)
"O virtuous one, as for this self that you consider to be 'I am alone,' this sage who observes merit and demerit is eternally situated within your heart. (8.91)

"‘I am alone,’ and so forth: O noble one, do not think thus of yourself—that you alone exist as the individual soul (jīvātman). For the Supreme Self, the witness of both sins and merits, the sage who perceives through reflection and is all-knowing, is eternally established within your heart. And so says the Śruti:
‘Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree.’"
Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit of the *pippala* tree, while the other looks on without eating. (RV 2.3.17) 8.91.
The god Yama Vaivasvata who dwells here within your heart—
if you have no dispute with him, then go neither to the Gaṅgā nor to the Kuru land.

Regarding the term *yama*: He is *Yama* because he restrains all; he is *Vaivasvata* because he wields the rod of punishment; he is *deva* because he shines (*divanāt*). If you have no dispute with that which dwells within your heart regarding the truthful declaration of what is there, then there would be no contradiction with the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) when He knows what is in your mind while you speak otherwise. Thus, by speaking the truth here, you are freed from sin and have fulfilled your purpose. Do not go to the Gaṅgā nor to Kurukṣetra for the sake of removing sin. The equality between the Gaṅgā and Kurukṣetra mentioned by Manu has been clarified here by Vyāsa in the *Matsya Purāṇa*.

"The Gaṅgā is equal to Kurukṣetra wherever one bathes in her. Regarding this, Medhātithi and Govindarāja, however, explain it thus: "If there is no dispute with Yama—the son of Vivasvat, the lord of the southern quarter—who is well known in the world and now flashes within your heart, because he is the cause of your unrighteousness, then do not go to the Gaṅgā, nor to Kurukṣetra. (8.92)
Naked, shaven-headed, carrying a skull-bowl, hungry and thirsty, blind—he who gives false testimony shall go to the house of his enemies begging for alms. (8.93)

"Regarding 'naked': he who should speak false testimony shall go naked—subjected to the humiliation of having his head shaved, blind, marked by a skull-bowl, and seeking alms—at the house of his enemy. (8.93)
