Headlong into blind darkness shall the sinner go to hell, he who, when questioned regarding the determination of dharma, speaks falsely. (8.94)
"Downward" means this: he who, when questioned for the sake of determining the Dharma, speaks untruthfully—he, being sinful, goes downward into that great darkness which is hell. (8.94)
That man who, having entered the assembly, speaks what is inconsistent with the facts and not based on direct perception, eats fish along with their bones like a blind man. (8.95)

"Blind" refers to one who, having entered an assembly, describes a deficiency in the facts of a matter, a misrepresentation of the true intent, or something not witnessed or perceived, for the sake of a mere fragment of pleasure such as a bribe; that man, like a blind person eating fish with thorns, engages with the perception of pleasure and obtains only great suffering. (8.96)
For the gods know no other man in this world more excellent than that learned one whose inner self, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), has no suspicion regarding his speech. 8.96

"Of whom": of that speaker, no one would suspect—whether he be the Omniscient One or the Inner Controller—that "does he speak the truth or the falsehood? rather, one becomes free from doubt, thinking, "He speaks only the truth. Therefore, the gods know no other person more praiseworthy than him. 8.96.
Listen, O gentle one, to the number of kinsmen he slays by speaking falsely in testimony, in that case, in due order: 8.97.

"As many as" means: O virtuous one, listen in due order to the enumeration I shall now declare of as many paternal and other relatives as one brings into hell by speaking falsehood when giving testimony regarding a cause such as cattle; or alternatively, listen to how many relatives one destroys—that is, how many relatives one incurs the fruit of killing—regarding whichever [cause]. In both cases, this is for the purpose of censuring falsehood. (8.97)
One kills five by lying about cattle, ten by lying about cows;
one kills a hundred by lying about horses, and a thousand by lying about men. (8.98)

"Five": regarding a falsehood concerning cattle, one casts five kinsmen into hell; one incurs the same fruit as killing five kinsmen. Likewise, ten in the case of cows, a hundred in the case of horses, and a thousand in the case of men. This increase in number is intended to indicate a corresponding increase in the severity of the penance. (8.98)
One who speaks falsehood for the sake of gold destroys both those born and those unborn;
one destroys everything by speaking falsehood regarding land. Do not, therefore, speak a falsehood concerning land. (8.99)

"He kills" means that by speaking a falsehood for the sake of gold, one consigns one's sons and others—both those already born and those yet unborn—to hell; one thus incurs the fruit of killing them. And by speaking a falsehood regarding land, one incurs the fruit of killing all living beings. Therefore, the specific mention is made: "Do not speak a falsehood regarding land. (8.99)
Regarding one who speaks falsely about lapis lazuli and other such things, he states the fault is like that regarding land:
"They say it is as with water, and with the enjoyment of women and sexual intercourse, and with all gems produced from water and all those made of stone. (8.100)

Regarding water—specifically that found in ponds, wells, and reservoirs—as well as falsehood concerning women in matters of sexual enjoyment, and regarding aquatic gems such as pearls and other stone-based jewels like lapis lazuli, they say the fault is the same as in the case of land. (8.100)
Having considered all these faults in speaking untruth,
speak everything exactly as it was heard and as it was seen, straightforwardly.
"Regarding these": having understood these faults of speaking untruth, speak everything directly and according to reality, without deviating from what has been seen or heard. 8.101.
One should treat cowherds, merchants, artisans, actors, servants, and usurers as Śūdras, even if they are Brāhmaṇas. (8.102)

"Those who tend cattle," and so forth: those who live by tending cattle, those who live by trade, those who live by the work of artisans such as cooks, those who live by the labor of servants, those who live by the profession of actors, dancing, singing, and the like, and Brahmins who live by forbidden means—one should question these when they appear as witnesses in the case at hand, just as one would a Śūdra. (8.102)
When a man speaks thus regarding matters of dharma, even though he knows otherwise, he does not fall from the heavenly world; they call that the speech of the gods.

"Similarly": even though a person knows this testimony to be otherwise, if he speaks differently in legal proceedings out of a sense of duty, compassion, and so forth, he does not fall from the heavenly worlds; for Manu and others declare that this speaking of untruth on account of a specific reason is speech connected with the gods. (8.103)
But where, then, should that untruth be spoken? To this he says:
"In a case where the telling of the truth would result in the death of a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya, or a Brāhmaṇa, there one should speak an untruth; for that is superior to the truth. (8.104)

Regarding the word "śūdra": in a legal proceeding where, if the truth is told, the death of a Śūdra, Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, or Brāhmaṇa would result, one must speak untruth. This is because, in such a case, that which is untruth is superior to truth by virtue of saving a life. And this applies to instances of error or inadvertence, but not to cases involving those who are utterly wicked, such as those engaged in secret conspiracies or theft. Thus says Gautama: "There is no fault in speaking untruth if life depends upon it, but not for the sake of the life of a more sinful person. Nor should it be argued that there is no possibility of the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, since Manu himself will state later: "One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is guilty of every possible crime" (8.380); for since the aforementioned punishment has been prescribed, the possibility of [the king] killing him might somehow arise. In this statement, the mention of the Śūdra and others in their respective order is due to the inauspicious nature of death. (8.104)
And they should worship Sarasvatī with sacrificial offerings of cooked rice (caru) dedicated to the goddess of speech, thereby effecting the supreme expiation for that sin of falsehood. (8.105)

"Those whose deity is Speech": those witnesses who speak falsely shall worship Sarasvatī with *caru* offerings dedicated to the goddess of speech (*vāgdevatā*). By doing so, they effect the complete purification of the sin produced by that false testimony. This rule applies to multiple witnesses; it does not mean that a single witness should offer three *carus* according to the *kapiñjala-nyāya* (the maxim of the partridge). Although in a *caru* dedicated to the goddess of speech, the divinity is established by the word "Speech" itself rather than by the word "Sarasvatī"—in accordance with the principle that "the form of the injunction must exist in the mantra"—nevertheless, because of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) stating "Speech is indeed Sarasvatī," the two terms "Speech" and "Sarasvatī" have the same referent; thus, the concluding reference is made to "Sarasvatī. Furthermore, this statement of expiation within this context is for the sake of brevity; otherwise, if it were stated here, one would also have to mention those who speak falsely regarding the killing of Śūdras, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, and Brāhmaṇas. (8.105)
Or he should offer clarified butter into the fire according to the prescribed rule with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras,
or with the verse beginning "ud," which is addressed to Varuṇa, or with the three verses whose deity is the Waters.

Regarding the phrase "with the Kūṣmāṇḍa [mantras]": the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras belonging to the Yajurveda are those beginning with "yad devā devaheḍanam" (YV 20.14). With these, one should offer clarified butter into the fire for the deity of the mantra, according to the prescribed rule, including the ritual strewing of grass and so forth, by means of its own specific duty as taught in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra. One should offer clarified butter into the fire with the verse addressed to Varuṇa, "ud uttamaṃ varuṇa pāśam" (RV 1.2.15), or with the triplet beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhāḥ" (RV 7.6.5), which has Vāc as its deity; the phrase "one should offer clarified butter into the fire" is to be supplied in all cases. 8.106.
If a man, being healthy, does not give testimony regarding a debt or other matters within three fortnights,
he shall be liable for that entire debt and a fine of one-tenth of the total amount.

"Within three fortnights": if a witness who is not ill does not give testimony within the limit of three fortnights in a legal proceeding such as the non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*), then he shall pay the entire debt in dispute to the creditor (*uttamarṇa*), and he shall pay a tenth part of this entire debt as a fine to the king. (8.107)
If, within seven days of the testimony having been given, a witness suffers from disease, fire, or the death of a relative, he shall be compelled to pay the debt and a fine. (8.108)

Regarding the phrase "of whom": if, within seven days of the testimony having been given by a witness, any one of these occurs—namely, disease, being burnt by fire, or the death of a son or other close relative—it is because of the fault of falsehood indicated by fate that the creditor shall be made to pay the debt and the king shall impose the fine. (8.108)
But in matters concerning which there are no witnesses, when two parties are disputing with one another,
if he cannot ascertain the truth in reality, he should cause it to be established even by means of an oath.

"In cases without witnesses": in legal proceedings where no witnesses are present, the judge, failing to ascertain the truth from two parties disputing with one another—avoiding both deception and the like—should elicit the truth by means of the oath to be described hereafter. (8.109)
Great seers and gods have taken oaths for the sake of their purposes;
even Vasiṣṭha swore an oath before the king, the son of Pijavana.

And by the great seers (*maharṣi*). Oaths were taken by the seven seers and by the gods, Indra and the others, for the sake of deciding upon matters in doubt. Vasiṣṭha also, having been reviled by Viśvāmitra with the words "He has devoured a hundred sons," took an oath before King Sudās—the son of Pijavana—in order to prove his own innocence. Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *śap* (to swear) also carries the sense of "to do.
A wise man should not take a false oath even for a trivial matter;
for by taking a false oath, one perishes both in this world and after death. (8.111)

"Not in vain": a wise man should not take an oath even for a very small matter. By taking an oath in vain, one meets with ruin in both the next world and this world through the attainment of hell and the acquisition of ill repute. (8.111)
He states [the following] for the purpose of providing an exception to the rule regarding false oaths:
"In matters concerning women, at weddings, regarding fodder for cows, as well as for fuel, and in assisting a Brāhmaṇa—there is no sin in taking an oath. (8.112)

Regarding the phrase "among women": for one who has many wives, when making a specific declaration toward a woman for the sake of obtaining sexual union—such as, "I desire no other; you alone are my beloved"—or regarding marriage, such as, "I shall not marry another," or when offering fodder and the like for the sake of cattle, or offering fuel and the like into the fire for the purpose of a *homa* sacrifice, or when accepting wealth and so forth for the protection of Brahmins—in these cases, there is no sin in taking a false oath. (8.112)
One should cause a Brahmin to swear by the truth; a Kṣatriya, by his vehicle and weapons; a Vaiśya, by his cattle, seed, and gold; and a Śūdra, by all the mortal sins.

"By truth," [it is said]. One should cause a Brāhmaṇa to swear by pronouncing the word "truth. A Kṣatriya, with the words, "May my vehicles and weapons become useless to me. A Vaiśya, with the words, "May my cattle, seeds, and gold become useless to me. And a Śūdra, one should cause to swear with the words, "May all my sins be upon me. (8.113)
Depending on the gravity or lightness of the matter:
"One should cause him to carry fire, or make him dive into water;
or one should make him touch the heads of his son and wife individually. (8.114)

Regarding the fire ordeal: one should cause a person of the Śūdra class or others to carry for seven steps, according to the procedure prescribed by the Grandfather (Brahmā) and others, an iron ball weighing fifty palas, resembling fire, measuring eight finger-breadths, with seven leaves of the *aśvattha* tree placed upon it in both hands; and one should cause him to immerse it in water free from leeches and other such creatures. The entire ritual procedure is to be learned from another Smṛti. One should touch this [iron ball] separately on the heads of sons and wives. (8.114)
He whom the kindled fire does not burn, whom the waters do not cause to float up, and who does not quickly meet with misfortune—he should be known as pure in his oath. 8.115.
Regarding the word "yam": he whom a blazing fire does not burn, whom the waters do not carry upward, and who does not suffer great distress—he should be known as purified by the oath. (8.115)
In this regard, he states a corroborative explanatory passage (arthavāda) relevant to the subject at hand:
"For in the past, when Vatsa was falsely accused by his younger brother, the fire—the spy of the world—did not burn even a single hair of him because of his truthfulness. (8.116)

Regarding the word "Vatsasya": because in former times, when he was reviled by his younger half-brother, who said, "You are no Brāhmaṇa; you are the offspring of a Śūdra woman," and he entered the fire [to prove his status], the Fire—being the witness to all the world in matters of good and evil—did not burn even a single hair of his by virtue of his truthfulness. 8.116.
In whatever lawsuit false testimony has been given, that very case shall be reversed; what has been done shall be as if undone. (8.117)

"In which [case]" means: in whatever legal proceeding it is determined that false testimony has been given by the witnesses, the judge shall set aside that case even if it is not yet concluded; and even that which has been brought to the point of final sentencing, he shall re-examine. (8.117)
In order to explain the specific meanings that will be discussed, he enumerates greed and the others separately:
"From greed, from delusion, from fear, from friendship, from lust, and likewise from anger, as well as from ignorance and childishness, testimony is declared to be false. (8.118)
"Out of greed," etc.: false testimony is given out of greed, out of perverted knowledge, out of fear, out of affection, out of lust, out of anger, out of ignorance, or out of inattention. (8.118)
I shall now declare, in due order, the specific punishments for one who gives false testimony in any of these cases. (8.119)

"Of these": from among these—greed and the rest—if one should give false testimony when any one of these motives is present, I shall state the specific punishments for him in their respective order. (8.119)

For taking [property] out of greed, one should be fined a thousand; for out of delusion, the first *sāhasa* fine; for out of fear, two middle *sāhasa* fines; and for out of friendship, four times the first *sāhasa*. (8.120)

"Out of greed": when there is a false statement through greed, he shall be fined one thousand of the *paṇas* to be mentioned; through delusion, the first *sāhasa* to be mentioned; through fear, the two middle *sāhasas* to be mentioned; and through friendship, four times the first *sāhasa*. (8.120)
Ten times more than that [result] comes from desire; three times more from anger;
two full hundreds from ignorance; and exactly one hundred from childishness.

"Out of lust": speaking falsely out of compliance with a desire for sexual union with a woman, he shall be fined ten times the first *sāhasa* fine. Out of anger, however, the highest *sāhasa* fine—threefold as will be described—shall be imposed. Out of ignorance, two hundred; out of childishness, that is, lack of attention, he shall be fined exactly one hundred *paṇas*. This applies everywhere as a recurring rule. (8.121)
The wise have declared these punishments for false testimony, intended to ensure that justice does not fail and to restrain unrighteousness. (8.122)

Regarding the phrase "these": Manu and others have declared these punishments, which were spoken by ancient sages concerning the subject of false testimony, for the purpose of not abolishing the dharma that has the nature of truth and for the purpose of warding off the adharma that has the nature of falsehood; and this applies to a single instance of false testimony.
But in cases of repeated giving of false testimony: "A righteous king, having punished the three castes who give false testimony, shall banish them; however, he shall only exile a Brāhmaṇa. (8.123)

Regarding "false testimony": having punished the three castes beginning with the Kṣatriya for false testimony according to the previously stated penalty, a righteous king should banish them from his kingdom. But a Brāhmaṇa, other than by means of a monetary fine, the king should expel from his kingdom;
he must never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is guilty of every possible crime. He should send him out of the country with all his wealth intact and unharmed. (8.380)

This is because banishment along with the forfeiture of wealth is what will be described [in the following verse]. Govindarāja, however, explains: "Having punished the Brāhmaṇa again with the previous fine, one should make him naked. Medhātithi, on the other hand, explains that for a Brāhmaṇa, "banishment" means the removal of his clothes or the destruction of his house. (8.123)
Manu, the son of the Self-Existent, has declared ten places for punishment; in these three castes [the offender] may be punished, but a Brāhmaṇa should depart unhurt. (8.124)

"Ten," it is said: Manu, the son of Hiranyagarbha, has enumerated ten grounds for punishment which apply to the three social orders beginning with the Kṣatriya; however, a Brāhmaṇa, even upon a grave offense, is banished from the country provided his body remains unhurt. (8.124)
The generative organ, the belly, the tongue, the two hands, and the feet as the fifth;
the eyes, the nose, the ears, wealth, and likewise the body. (8.125)

"Upastha" refers to these ten locations for punishment, beginning with the penis; therefore, when an offense has been committed, one should inflict flogging, pain, or other penalties on the respective limb, depending on the gravity or lightness of the offense. In the case of a minor offense, a monetary fine is prescribed according to the text; corporal punishment or execution applies in cases such as the great sins (*mahāpātaka*). 8.125.

Having fully understood the consequences, as well as the place and time in their true nature, and having considered both the capacity [of the offender] and the gravity of the offense, he should inflict punishment upon those deserving of it. (8.126)

Regarding the term *anubandha*: having considered the repeated commission of an offense out of desire, the location of the offense such as a village or forest, or the time of the offense such as night; having considered the strength of the offender, whether in terms of wealth, body, or other capacities; and having observed the gravity or lightness of the offense, one should inflict punishment upon those deserving of it. This [term] is supplementary to the punishments already mentioned and those yet to be described. (8.126)
Unjust punishment in this world destroys one's reputation and ruins one's fame; it also prevents access to heaven in the next life. Therefore, one should avoid it entirely. (8.127)

Regarding the term *adharma*: fame (*khyāti*) belongs to one who is living, while renown (*kīrti*) belongs to one who is dead. Since punishment inflicted here in this world without regard for consequences and so forth destroys the fame of the living and the renown of the deceased, and furthermore acts as an obstacle to the attainment of heaven earned through other meritorious deeds in the next world, one should therefore avoid it. (8.127)
A king who punishes those who do not deserve punishment, and fails to punish those who do deserve it, incurs great infamy and goes to hell. (8.128)

"Those who should not be punished": by punishing those unworthy of punishment out of greed for wealth and the like, or by releasing those worthy of punishment out of favoritism and the like, the king incurs great infamy and goes to hell. (8.128)
One should first impose the punishment of verbal censure, followed by the punishment of "fie" (reproach).
Third is the punishment of fines, and after that, the punishment of corporal death. (8.129)

Regarding "verbal punishment": for a virtuous person who has committed a first offense, one should administer verbal censure, saying, “You have not acted rightly; do not do so again. Even if he does not desist, then one should address him with such words as, “Shame on you, fool! May there be no loss of life for you, O sinner! If he still does not remain steadfast, then beyond this, one may inflict corporal punishment consisting of beating or the amputation of limbs, but never execution. (8.129)
For it will be said:
"But when one is unable to restrain these [enemies] even by execution, then one should employ all four of these methods against them. (8.130)

"But when, even by execution... (8.130): if he should be unable to bring them under control even by means of the mutilation of limbs performed in various ways, then he should employ against them all four types of punishment, beginning with verbal censure.
I shall explain in their entirety those designations for copper, silver, and gold that are well-known on earth for the purpose of worldly transaction.

Regarding the term *loka*: those designations such as *paṇa* and so forth for copper, silver, and gold, which are well-known on earth for the purpose of worldly transactions like buying and selling—I shall explain them in their entirety for the purpose of applying them to punishments and other legal matters. (8.131)
When the sun shines through a lattice, that subtle particle which is seen is called the *trasareṇu*, the first among all measures of magnitude. (8.132)

Regarding the phrase "within a lattice": that subtle dust which is seen in the rays of the sun entering through the openings of a window is called a *trasareṇu*, the first among those things whose dimensions are perceptible. (8.132)
Eight *trasareṇus* should be known as one *likṣā* by measure;
three of those [likṣās] are a royal mustard seed (*rājasarṣapa*), and three of those are a white mustard seed (*gaurasarṣapa*). (8.133)

Regarding "trasareṇus": eight *trasareṇus* should be known as one *likṣā* in terms of measurement; three of those *likṣās* should be known as a *rājasarṣapa*; and three of those *rājasarṣapas* should be known as a *gaurasarṣapa*. (8.133)
Six mustard seeds make one medium barley grain; three barley grains make one *kṛṣṇala*; five *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*; and sixteen of those make one *suvarṇa*. (8.134)

Regarding "mustard seeds": six white mustard seeds (*gaurasarṣapa*) constitute one middle-sized barley grain, which is neither thick nor thin. Three barley grains make one *kṛṣṇala*, commonly known as a *raktikā*. Five *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*. Sixteen *māṣas* constitute one *suvarṇa*; this term, being masculine, denotes a measure of weight. (8.134)
Four *suvarṇas* make one *pala*; ten *palas* make one *dharaṇa*.
Two *kṛṣṇalas* weighed together should be known as one silver *māṣaka*. (8.135)

"A *pala*": four *suvarṇas* shall be one *pala*. Ten *palas* are a *dharaṇa*. Having made two *kṛṣṇalas* equal and weighed them on a scale, it should be understood that this is a silver *māṣaka*. (8.135)
Sixteen of those silver *dharaṇas* constitute one *purāṇa*; furthermore, a copper coin weighing one *karṣa* is to be known as a *kārṣāpaṇa*, also called a *paṇa*. (8.136)

"Those sixteen": those sixteen silver *māṣakas* constitute a *raupyadharaṇa* and a *purāṇa*, which is related to silver (*rājata*). A *kārṣika* copper coin is to be understood as a *kārṣāpaṇa* or a *paṇa*. Furthermore, a *kārṣika* should be known as one-fourth of a standard *pala*. For this very reason, lexicographers state: "A *pala* consists of four *karṣas*. (8.136)
Ten *dharaṇas* are to be known as one silver *śatamāna*;
a *niṣka* is to be understood by its measure as consisting of four *sauvarṇikas*.
Regarding "daraṇas": ten silver *dharaṇas* should be known as one silver *śatamāna*. A *niṣka* should be understood by measure as being equal to four *suvarṇas*. || 8.137 ||
Two hundred and fifty paṇas are declared to be the first amercement; five hundred should be known as the middle, and one thousand as the highest. (8.138)

Regarding "of paṇas": two hundred and fifty paṇas is recorded by Manu and others as the first amercement (prathamasāhasa). Five hundred paṇas is to be known as the middle amercement (madhyamasāhasa). One thousand paṇas, however, is to be known as the highest amercement (uttamasāhasa). || 8.138 ||
When a debt that is due has been admitted, one deserves a fine of five percent; if it is denied, the fine is double that—such is the ordinance of Manu. (8.139)

Regarding the term "debt": when a debtor has stated in court, "I must pay the creditor's wealth," he deserves a fine of five *paṇas* for every hundred *paṇas*. But when he denies even in court, saying, "I owe him nothing at all," then he deserves a fine of ten *paṇas* for every hundred *paṇas*. Such is the method of punishment in the *Manusmṛti*, verse 8.139.
A moneylender may stipulate an interest that increases his wealth as ordained by Vasiṣṭha;
he may take one-eightieth part of a hundred per month. (8.140)

Regarding the term *vasiṣṭha*: one who lives by lending money may take the interest declared by Vasiṣṭha, which, because it is righteous, increases wealth. He shows that very rate: "When a hundred is lent, he may take an eightieth part as interest every month" (8.140).
Or he may take two per cent, keeping in mind the duty of the virtuous;
for by taking two per cent, one does not become a sinner regarding wealth. (8.141)

"Two per cent": thinking "this is the duty of the virtuous," he may take two *paṇas* per month when a hundred *paṇas* have been lent. For by taking two per cent, he does not incur sin in the receipt of interest on the capital. (8.141)
One may take interest at the rate of two, three, four, five, or ten percent per month, according to the respective order of the social classes. (8.142)

"Two per cent": for the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, one should take interest relating to the month in the order of two, three, four, five, and ten percent respectively; there is nothing more than this, nor less. Now, one might object: "The eightieth part [of the principal] is light, while taking two percent is heavy; how can these two, being light and heavy options, be alternatives for the Brāhmaṇa? On this point, Medhātithi and Govindarāja explain that the acceptance of two percent applies when it is impossible to manage with the previously mentioned rate of interest. However, we say this: the taking of the eightieth part applies to loans with collateral (*sabandhaka*); whereas in the absence of collateral, the acceptance of two percent interest applies. Thus says Yājñavalkya: [Text of Yājñavalkya: *aśītibhāgo vṛddhiḥ syān māsi māsi sabandhake | varṇakramāt dvikaṃ trikaṃ catuṣkaṃ pañcakaṃ ca tat ||* "In the case of a loan with collateral, the monthly interest shall be the eightieth part [of the principal]. According to the order of the castes, that [interest] shall be two, three, four, and five percent. Thus, the former rule applies to secured debts, while the latter applies to unsecured ones. This is the distinction between the two options.
The interest shall be one-eightieth part each month when there is security;
otherwise, according to the order of the castes, it shall be one-hundredth, one-fiftieth, one-thirtieth, one-twentieth, or one-tenth.
I honor the commentary of the Sage whose splendor is proclaimed by the Vedānta.
And that which is contrary to it has been composed by moderns according to their own intellect.
But one shall not receive interest on a secured loan if it is used for the benefit of the debtor;
nor, due to the lapse of time, can there be a transfer or sale of the pledge. (8.143)

"No. When land, cattle, or other property is given as collateral for the purpose of enjoyment, the creditor does not receive the interest mentioned immediately above arising from the loan of wealth. Due to "long-term retention"—that is, because it has remained so for a long time—even when the principal has doubled, there is no *nisarga*, meaning neither its transfer to another nor its sale to anyone else. Medhātithi and Govindarāja, however, explain that even if the pledge remains for a long time, there is no *nisarga*—meaning it is not to be delivered elsewhere as a further pledge. But in this case, such an interpretation contradicts the practice of the learned in all lands, since it is customary to use land and other property already pledged as collateral for yet another loan. (8.143)
A pledge must not be used by force; one who uses it shall forfeit the interest.
He should satisfy the owner with its value; otherwise, he becomes a thief of the pledge. (8.144)

"He must not enjoy it. This statement refers to a pledge given for the purpose of concealment (*gopyādhi*). A pledge consisting of clothing or ornaments must not be enjoyed by force. One who enjoys it shall forfeit the interest; he should satisfy the owner here with the price of five times [the value]. Alternatively, if the pledge has been rendered worthless through use, he should satisfy the owner by paying the value of the pledge in its state of excellence; otherwise, he would be a thief of the deposit. (8.144)
Both a pledge and a deposit do not deserve to suffer the lapse of time;
if they remain for a long duration, both may be forfeited. 8.145.

"And [the terms] *ādhi* and *upanidhi*: *ādhi* means a pledge; *upanidhi* is that which is deposited, meaning property handed over for the purpose of enjoyment out of friendship. Furthermore, it is the *nikṣepa* (deposit) and *upanidhi* defined in the *Nāradasmṛti* that are understood here by the term *upanidhi*. These two, the *ādhi* and the *upanidhi*, even when remaining for a long time, do not suffer loss due to the lapse of time. The meaning is that as soon as they are requested by the owner, they must be surrendered and returned at that very moment. (8.145)
Things enjoyed with mutual affection never perish:
a cow, a camel, a draft horse, and whatever animal is employed for training. (8.146)

Regarding the phrase "by means of affection" (*saṃprītyā*): immediately after [the verse], he will state that ownership is lost through enjoyment for ten years (8.147). This [present verse] is intended as an exception (*apavāda*) to that. A cow, a camel, or a horse currently being seen, or a bull and so forth employed for the purpose of carrying or taming—these, when enjoyed by another through affection, never perish for the owner. This is stated for the sake of illustration; the intended meaning is that what is enjoyed through affection does not perish. Furthermore, since this specific statement begins with a general one, the neuter gender is used. (8.146)
Whatever property an owner observes being enjoyed by others for ten years while he stands by silently, he is not entitled to recover it. (8.147)

"Whatever it may be": whatever kind of wealth, while being enjoyed by others for ten years in his very presence, the owner looks upon with indifference—neither out of affection nor otherwise—and does not utter a word of prohibition such as "Do not enjoy it," he is no longer entitled to recover it. The meaning is that his ownership over it ceases. || 8.147 ||
If the owner is not an idiot and has not been a minor, and his property is enjoyed by another, that [possession] is defeated by legal action; the enjoyer deserves that wealth. (8.148)
"Non-jaḍa" means not dull-witted; "jaḍa" refers to one who is deficient in intellect. A "pogaṇḍa" is one less than sixteen years of age. Thus says Nārada:
"A child is [defined] up to sixteen years, and is also termed a *pogaṇḍa*.

If that owner of wealth is both dull-witted and a *pogaṇḍa*, and his property is enjoyed while he is out of sight, then that property is lost through the legal action of the owner, and it belongs solely to the enjoyer. (8.148)
A mortgage, a boundary, the property of a minor, a deposit, an open deposit, women, royal property, and the property of a Vedic scholar do not perish through adverse possession. (8.149)

"Adhi" means a pledge (*bandha*), the boundary of a village and so forth, the property of a minor, and a deposit (*nikṣepa*)—defined by Nārada as "that which is placed in a container without being disclosed, like a treasure"—as well as the characteristics of an open deposit (*upanidhi*), female slaves and other women, and the property of kings and *śrotriyas*; these do not perish for the owner through the aforementioned ten-year enjoyment, nor does ownership accrue to the possessor. (8.149)
The unwise man who enjoys a pledge without the permission of the owner must relinquish half of the interest as compensation for that enjoyment. (8.150)

Regarding the phrase "he who [says] 'to the owner'": if a fool, by means of denial, enjoys a pledge that was given on interest without the permission of the owner, he must relinquish half the interest for the sake of purifying that enjoyment. However, regarding enjoyment through force, when one enjoys the pledge by force, it is stated that there is a total forfeiture of all interest. (8.150)
Interest on a loan, when collected at one time, shall not exceed double the principal;
in the case of grain, fruit, wool, or beasts of burden, it shall not exceed five times the original amount. (8.151)

Regarding "on usury" (*kusīde*): lending money for interest is *kusīda*; the interest therein, once received, does not exceed doubling [the principal]. That is, the interest together with the principal becomes exactly double. The intended meaning is that this applies to interest to be collected daily, monthly, and so forth. Furthermore, regarding grain lent for interest and the like, as well as tree-fruits, wool (from what is shorn), and draft animals such as oxen—when lent out—even over a long period of time, they shall not exceed five times the original amount of grain and so on.
An interest exceeding the legal rate is not valid;
they call that the path of usury, for it is only right to charge five percent per month. (8.152)

Regarding the phrase *kṛtānusārāt*: "made" (*kṛtā*) refers to interest prescribed by the legal treatises (*śāstra*) according to the order of castes, such as two percent or three percent. Interest that is "excessive" (*adhikā*) means interest exceeding that which is made according to the treatises; thus, the meaning is that any other interest is "unmade" (*akṛtā*). However, even interest that is "made" must be taken month by month according to the order of castes in the form of two, three, or more percent. And so Viṣṇu says: "They shall pay interest, even if unmade, upon the lapse of a year, as prescribed according to the order of castes," meaning in the form of two, three percent, and so forth. But he states another distinction regarding even unmade interest: this path spreads from what is contemptible, hence it is called *kusīdapatha* (the path of usury). This debtor—who takes five percent from a twice-born person, even though it is stated [in the texts] that this applies to the Śūdra—is one who follows a contemptible path. Manu and others have said that this is inferior to the previously mentioned lawful interest-bearing [rate]. Thus, unmade interest should be understood to apply to the case of a loan (*uddhāra*) after the time of request. Kātyāyana says the same.
A gift given out of affection increases as long as it is not asked for;
if it is asked for and not given, it increases by five percent per month.

One should not take back interest that exceeds the annual rate, nor that which is not sanctioned; likewise, there is compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*), periodical interest (*kālavṛddhi*), stipulated interest (*kāritā*), and corporeal interest (*kāyikā*). (8.153)

"Not exceeding" means that the creditor (*uttamarṇa*) may take interest according to an agreement such as, "When one month, two months, or three months have passed for me, you must pay after calculating its increase," provided this is done for a period not exceeding one year. He should not take interest beyond the limit of the stipulated agreement once the year has elapsed. Nor should he take an interest rate not seen in the scriptures—namely, more than the two or three percent per month which is declared to be lawful. This prohibition is intended to demonstrate that [excessive rates] are unlawful. Furthermore, he should not take the four types of interest, such as *cakravṛddhi* (compound interest) and the rest, which are not sanctioned by the scriptures. Bṛhaspati describes their nature as follows:
Interest is of four kinds: bodily, connected with the body, monthly, and periodic;
then there is compound interest, wheel-interest, and that which is stipulated by the debtor himself.

Among these, *cakravṛddhi* (compound interest) is reprehensible by its very nature. *Kālavṛddhi* (periodic interest), however, is that which is incurred by taking more than double the principal, or by bodily labor such as excessive carriage or milking, or which is imposed by the creditor upon the debtor at a time of distress. One should not accept any of these four types of interest that are contrary to the scriptures. Thus says Bṛhaspati:
"That share which is taken beyond double [the principal], and *cakravṛddhi*, and when the principal with interest has been fully realized, and thereafter—such usury is censured."
Kātyāyana says: Interest that has been stipulated by the debtor, whether it be excessive,
contracted during a time of distress, or otherwise agreed upon, must always be paid.
Interest stipulated otherwise must never be paid under any circumstances.
He who is unable to pay the debt and wishes to enter into a new transaction shall, after paying the interest that has accrued, renew the bond. 8.154.

"Regarding the repayment of debt": if a debtor, due to an inability to pay the principal, wishes to perform a fresh transaction such as the execution of a new document, he shall, after paying the interest that has been won over and brought under his own control by the creditor, execute a new instrument (lekhya). (8.154)
Without having shown the gold back there, one may exchange it;
one ought to give back as much interest as has accrued. (8.155)

"Without having shown," etc.: if, by the turn of fate, he is unable to pay even the interest and principal at the appointed time, then, having taken that very [debt], when a new document or the like is executed there again, he should include the remainder of the interest and principal therein; he ought to pay whatever amount of *cakravṛddhi* (compound interest) wealth is possible at that time. || 8.155 ||
One who has ascended to the increase of the wheel, being established in the proper place and time, will not obtain that fruit if he transgresses the requirements of place and time. (8.156)

Regarding the term *cakravṛddhi*: here, by the word *cakravṛddhi*, an increase in the form of a load—such as that of a cart—is intended. A creditor who has resorted to *cakravṛddhi* establishes a rule regarding place and time, such as: "If I transport salt and other goods by cart as far as Vārāṇasī, then this wealth of mine must be paid," which is the establishment of a rule regarding place in the form of wages; or, "If I transport them for one month, then the wealth [due] for one month must be paid," which is the establishment of a rule regarding time. Thus, when both the place and time agreed upon have not been fulfilled due to fate while transporting by cart and so forth, he does not obtain the entire fruit in the form of profit. (8.156)
Moreover—those skilled in sea voyages, who perceive the proper place, time, and purpose, establish whatever profit there may be; that [profit] constitutes the attainment in that case. (8.157)

Regarding the word "samudra" (the ocean): merchants and others who know the distances and profits of land and sea travel—knowing that when a journey is undertaken for such a distance or for such a period of time, this much profit is appropriate to take—establish a certain rate of interest in such matters. That very established rate is the authority regarding the acquisition of wealth in that case. 8.157.
If a man stands as a surety for another's appearance here, failing to produce him, he shall pay the debt from his own property. (8.158)

"Who for whom": if a man stands as a surety for the appearance of another, thinking at the time of paying the debt, "I must produce this debtor for my creditor," he should strive to pay that debt if he fails to produce him for the creditor at that time.
A son is not liable to pay for a guarantee, a frivolous loan, what is due from gambling or liquor, nor the remainder of a fine or a tax. (8.159)

Regarding the term *prātibhāvya*: that debt which is to be paid by virtue of being a surety (*pratibhū*) is called *prātibhāvya*. A "vain gift" (*vṛthādāna*) is that which was promised by a father to be given out of jest, or as a fine and so forth; likewise, that which was promised on account of gambling or for the sake of liquor, and the fine itself (*daṇḍa*), and the toll (*śulka*)—that which is to be paid at ferry-crossings and the like, along with its remainder—the son is not liable to pay these obligations pertaining to his father once the father has died. (8.159)
But regarding a surety for appearance, the previously mentioned rule shall apply;
however, if a surety for payment dies, one should compel even his heirs to pay. (8.160)

Regarding the term "darśana": as for the previous instruction that a son is not required to pay a fine or a surety-bond (*prātibhāvya*) incurred for the sake of a liquor-drinker, this should be understood as applicable when the father was a surety for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*). However, if the father was a surety for payment (*dāna-pratibhū*), one should cause the son to pay the debt upon the father's death. (8.160)
But when the debtor has not paid, and the guarantor—who was known for his character—is subsequently dead, by what means may the creditor seek to recover the debt? (8.161)

Regarding the term *adātari*: when the non-giver—other than the surety for payment (*dāna-pratibhū*), namely one who is a surety for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*) or a surety for confidence (*pratyaya-pratibhū*)—has died, and that person had received wealth appropriate for the clearing of the root-cause of the debt for which the suretyship was known, why does the creditor (*uttamarṇa*) subsequently desire to obtain the wealth? (8.161)

Anticipating the objection that because the surety is dead and his son was not a surety for non-payment, he is therefore not liable, [the author] says: "But if the surety has been assigned property and possesses sufficient wealth, he shall pay that from his own property; such is the rule regarding one 'assigned' (nirādiṣṭa). (8.162)

Regarding the term "nirdiṣṭa" (designated): if this surety—whether a surety for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*) or a surety for payment (*pratyaya-pratibhū*)—is one whose wealth has been designated (*nirādiṣṭa-dhana*), meaning his wealth has been assigned by the debtor, such that he possesses sufficient wealth to discharge that debt for which he stood as surety; then, if that wealth is from his own property, he must pay that money from his own assets. Here, the term *nirādiṣṭa-dhana* refers metaphorically to one who has designated his son [as the source of payment]. It is the established tradition of the legal treatises (*śāstra-sampradāya*) that the debt must be paid to the creditor. (8.162)

A legal transaction entered into by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted by pain, or dependent; or one performed by a child, an elderly person, or one who is incoherent, is not valid according to the law. (8.163)

1. "Intoxicated or insane" (mattonmatta): A legal transaction involving the taking or giving of debt (*ṛṇādāna*) that is performed by one who is intoxicated by liquor or the like, or one who is insane, or one who is afflicted by disease and the like, or one who is deprived of his senses, or one who is not independent—such as a child, an old man, or one who is under another's control—is not valid, except when it has been carried out by a father, a brother, or someone authorized by them. (8.163)
A speech does not become true even if it is firmly established, if it speaks of dharmas that are external to the fixed conventional [truth]. (8.164)

Regarding the word "truth" (*satya*): even if something has been made firm by means of speech, writing, or the like—such as "This is to be performed by me"—if it is stated outside of scriptural dharma, traditional lineage, and righteous conduct, that is not truth; therefore, its meaning must be put into practice. (8.164)
Whatever is mortgaged or sold through fraud, or received as a gift or in exchange through fraud, or wherein one perceives deceit—that entire transaction he shall annul. (8.165)

Regarding the phrase "fraudulent mortgage" (*yogādhamana*): the word *yoga* here signifies fraud (*chala*). Whatever acts of pledging, selling, giving, or receiving are performed through fraud—and not according to reality—whether in the case of a deposit (*nikṣepa*) or elsewhere, where one recognizes such deception, all that is nullified; for in reality, no deposit or similar transaction was ever made. (8.165)
If the borrower should perish after having spent the money for the sake of the family, it must be paid by his kinsmen, even if they are divided, from their own property. 8.166

"By the borrower": if the debtor should die, and if he incurred that debt for the purpose of maintaining the family of all his brothers—whether already divided or undivided—by means of the previously partitioned property, then that debt must be paid by those brothers, both divided and undivided, from their own wealth. (8.166)
Whatever legal transaction a person dependent on others may carry out for the sake of the family, whether in his own country or abroad, the head of the household shall not annul it. (8.167)

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the family": even if a slave should incur debts or perform other such acts for the purpose of the expenses of the master's family—whether the master is residing in that same place or in another country—the master should nevertheless give his consent to it. (8.167)
"Whatever is given by force, enjoyed by force, or even recorded by force—Manu has declared all transactions effected by force to be null and void. (8.168)

"Given by force," and so forth: that which was given by force, such as to one who should not accept a gift; that which was enjoyed by force, such as land and the like; that which was caused to be written by force, such as a document for compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*). This is merely an illustration. Manu has declared that all legal transactions (*vyavahāra*) performed by force must be annulled. (8.168)
Three suffer for the sake of others: witnesses, a guarantor, and a family;
whereas four prosper: a brahmin, a wealthy man, a merchant, and a king. (8.169)

"Three act for the sake of others": witnesses, sureties, and family members—these three undergo suffering for the sake of others when acting as observers of legal proceedings concerning dharma and wealth; therefore, they should not be compelled by force to give testimony, stand as surety, or oversee legal cases. On the other hand, four—the Brāhmaṇa, the highest caste, the merchant, and the king—when performing acts for the sake of others in the form of receiving the fruit of giving, delivering money and goods on loan, buying and selling, and overseeing legal proceedings, obtain an accumulation of wealth. Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should be made to give as a donor, a wealthy man made to pay as a debtor, a merchant made to buy, and a king made to adjudicate legal cases by means of compulsion. This is an elaboration of the prohibition against compulsion mentioned in the preceding verse. (8.189)
Even when impoverished, a king should not take what ought not to be taken;
nor, even when prosperous, should he relinquish what ought to be taken, however small the matter may be. (8.170)

"Regarding 'what is not to be taken': even a king whose wealth is exhausted should not seize property that ought not to be seized; likewise, even when prosperous, he should not relinquish any wealth that is rightfully due to him, however small. (8.170)
For:
"By seizing what should not be seized and by neglecting what should be seized, the king's weakness is proclaimed; he perishes both in this world and after death. (8.171)

Regarding the phrase "of that which is not to be taken": by taking what is not to be taken and by abandoning what is to be taken according to the scriptures, the king's incapacity is made known to the citizens. Consequently, after death, he perishes through unrighteousness by experiencing hell and other such states, and in this world, he is ruined by infamy. (8.171)
Through the enjoyment [of taxes], through the blending of castes, and through the protection of women, the strength of the king is born; he prospers both in this world and after death. (8.172)

"From enjoyment" (*svādānāt*) means from the lawful acquisition of wealth by the social classes (*varṇas*), and from their connection with those of the same class through scripturally ordained marriages and so forth. Alternatively, even in the context of "from the mixing of classes" (*varṇasaṃsargāt*), which refers to the intermixture of classes (*varṇasaṃkara*), the term "from protection" (*rakṣaṇāt*) should be supplied. For the king’s power arises from protecting his subjects—even the weak—from those who are stronger; and because of that, he prospers both in this world and in the next. (8.172)

Since this is so— therefore, like Yama himself, a lord should personally abandon both the pleasant and the unpleasant, and conduct himself according to the manner of Yama, having conquered anger and subdued the senses. (8.173)

Therefore, [he is called] Yama. Consequently, like King Yama, having brought anger under control and conquered the senses, one should act everywhere with equanimity through the conduct of Yama, having renounced even one's own likes and dislikes. 8.173.
But that evil-minded king who, out of delusion, conducts affairs according to unrighteousness, his enemies soon bring under their control. (8.174)

"Whoever acts unrighteously": moreover, whatever king, out of greed and the like, performs his duties—such as presiding over legal proceedings—unrighteously through his judicial administration, his enemies will swiftly seize that evil-minded one due to the alienation of his subjects and citizens. 8.174.
But he who, having restrained desire and anger, perceives matters according to dharma—toward him the subjects turn, as rivers flow toward the ocean. (8.175)

Regarding "lust and anger": the subjects resort to that king who, having abandoned passion and hatred, examines affairs according to dharma, just as rivers resort to the ocean. Just as rivers do not turn back from the ocean but attain oneness with it, so too the subjects do not turn away from that king but become one with him; such is the analogy. 8.175.
If one should report to the king that a creditor is recovering his debt by his own will, he shall be made by the king to pay one-fourth of that amount as a fine to the creditor. (8.176)

"He who [accuses] one who is recovering [the debt]" (verse 8.176): if a debtor, out of pride thinking "I am a favorite of the king," should report to the king a creditor who is recovering his money according to his own will, he shall be fined by the king one-fourth of the debt and compelled to pay that money to him.
A debtor should repay the creditor in equal measure even with labor;
one of lower caste who is equal [in status] should pay, but one of superior caste should pay that gradually. (8.177)

"By work as well": when the debtor is of the same caste or of a lower caste and lacks wealth, he should discharge the debt even by performing work appropriate to his own caste. By ceasing the designations of "creditor" and "debtor," he should make himself equal to the moneylender. Here, "one of the same caste" refers to anyone other than a Brāhmaṇa, because Kātyāyana has specified that one should make those of "lower castes"—namely Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—perform work for those of the same caste. However, one of superior caste (śreyān), being of a higher birth, must not be made to perform work; rather, he should pay that debt gradually, according to his ability. (8.177)
By this procedure, the king shall bring to a state of impartiality the legal cases of men disputing with one another, which have been established through the testimony of witnesses.

"By this" means: by this aforementioned method, the king should settle the cases of plaintiffs and defendants who are disputing with one another, having determined the facts through evidence such as witnesses, by refuting their conflicting claims. (8.178)
A wise man should deposit a trust with one who is of noble birth, endowed with good conduct, knowledgeable in dharma, truthful, possessed of a large following, wealthy, and honorable. (8.179)

"Born of a noble family" means: one should entrust a deposit to a person who is born of a good lineage, possesses virtuous conduct, knows the Dharma, speaks the truth, has many children and attendants, and is upright by nature; for such a person, there is no possibility of deviation. (8.179)
Whatever object a man deposits in another's hand in whatever manner, that must be received back in exactly that same way; as was the delivery, so shall be the receipt. (8.180)

"Whatever [was deposited] in whatever manner": whatever person deposits in the hand of another a certain object, such as gold, whether it be sealed or unsealed, or whether it be with witnesses or without witnesses—in whatever manner that object was handed over, in that very same manner it must be received by the depositor. This is because it is only right that the receipt should correspond to the manner of the delivery. When a depositor of gold or other items placed in a sealed deposit (*samudra*) himself breaks the seal and says, "Weigh this and return it to me," such a statement is made for the purpose of punishment and the like. (8.180)
He who, when asked for a deposit, does not return it to the depositor, shall be questioned by the judge in the absence of that depositor. (8.181)

Regarding the phrase "he who [denies] a deposit": when a man, being thus entreated by the depositor with the words, "Give me back the gold or other property deposited," does not restore it, he should then be summoned by the judge upon the depositor's complaint, even in the absence of that depositor. (8.181)
Having done what, and what should be requested? To this he says:
"In the absence of witnesses, having deposited gold with those endowed with vows, age, and beauty, and by means of pretexts, according to the truth. (8.182)

Regarding the term "sākṣye" (in the presence of witnesses): In the case of the first type of deposit (*nikṣepa*), if there are no witnesses, the judge should have that depositor summoned by those same secret agents (*cārapuruṣa*)—who are members of his own court, who have passed their childhood, who are gentle, and who report under the pretext of having suffered royal harassment—and who have actually deposited gold there; by those very secret agents, the holder of the deposit is to be asked for the gold deposited by the secret agents. (8.182)
If he should act according to what was deposited and according to what was done, there would be nothing therein by which he could be accused by others. (8.183)

"Regarding the phrase *sa yadi*: if that holder of the deposit should return the deposit exactly as it was placed—whether it be a sealed chest (*samudra*) or something fashioned in a specific form such as a bracelet or a crown—and should say, 'It is truly here; take it,' when he is charged by the original depositor (who is known through the testimony of the presiding judge) with the claim, 'This is what was deposited,' then it should be understood that nothing at all exists [as claimed]. (8.183)
If, however, he does not give that gold to them according to the prescribed rule, he shall be seized by both [parties] and compelled to pay; such is the settled law. (8.184)

"Of them" means: if those secret agents (*cārapuruṣa*) do not return the gold that was deposited with them exactly as it was placed, then he should be compelled to pay both deposits—the one belonging to the depositor and the one related to the secret agent—by squeezing him; such is the established legal principle (*dharmasya dhāraṇā*), the settled rule. This very sequence of the four verses beginning with "He who [takes back] a deposit" (8.181) has been determined by Medhātithi, Bhojadeva, and others. However, Govindarāja has placed the verse beginning with "In the absence of witnesses, by secret agents" (8.182) at the very end; therein, there is neither logical consistency nor respect for the traditional authority of the elders. (8.184)
A sealed deposit and an open deposit must never be given to a next-of-kin;
they are lost in his misfortune, but they are not lost if he does not suffer misfortune. (8.185)

Regarding "deposit" (*nikṣepa*): it is called a deposit because it is deposited. An *upanidhi* is that which is placed down, either marked with a seal or uncounted. There is a distinction in the teaching here, similar to the case of the "Brahmin and the Wanderer. These two—deposit and *upanidhi*—should never be returned by the holder to the depositor or the *upanidhi*-giver while they are alive, nor to their immediate successors such as their sons, nor to their subsequent heirs who hold authority over that wealth. This is because, if the father fails to hand them over and they perish, both the deposit and the *upanidhi* are lost even to his sons and others. However, if there is no destruction on the part of the father and his heirs, and they are handed over, they might perhaps not be lost. Therefore, due to the risk of loss, they should not be returned.
But he who should himself give [the property] to the next-of-kin of the deceased must not be compelled by the king, nor by the kinsmen of the depositor. (8.186)

"Of his own accord" means: when the depositor has died, he who restores the deposit to the depositor's heir—such as a son or other successor—in charge of that wealth, without being requested by them, does so of his own volition; such a person shall not be interrogated by the king or by the depositor’s heirs with the words, "There is something else deposited with you. (8.186)
If, somehow, there should be delusion, then one should seek that matter with guilelessness and preceded by affection;
or, having investigated his conduct, one should settle it through conciliation alone. (8.187)

"By means of guile alone": in that situation, one should determine [the truth] with affection, avoiding verbal quibbles and the like that characterize the existence of other assets; however, one should not do so abruptly by administering ordeals and such. Having observed the character of that depositary and knowing him to be righteous, one should resolve the matter through the employment of conciliation. || 8.187 ||
In all these cases of deposits, the rule for their recovery shall be as follows:
if the depositary does not produce the deposit from the ocean, he shall not receive anything [from the claimant]. (8.188)

Regarding the phrase "in deposits": in all cases of deposits being misappropriated, the previously mentioned rule beginning with "in the absence of witnesses" (8.182) shall serve to establish the decision. However, in the case of a sealed deposit and so forth, if the holder of that deposit does not take anything away by means of a counter-seal or similar method, then what fault would he incur for that? || 8.188 ||
If it has been stolen by thieves, carried away by water, or consumed by fire, he need not pay for it, provided that he did not take anything from it himself. (8.189)

"By thieves," etc.: if the depositary does not take anything for himself from it, he need not restore a deposit that has been stolen by thieves, carried away to another country by water, or consumed by fire. (8.189)
One should investigate the thief of a deposit, as well as the one who never deposited it, by all possible means and even by Vedic oaths. (8.190)

Regarding the phrase "of the deposit": the king shall investigate the one who denies a deposit by employing all means—conciliation and the rest—as well as Vedic oaths such as carrying fire and so forth, [to determine] whether he has failed to return what was deposited upon being asked for it. (8.190)
He who does not return a deposit, and he who demands it without having made a deposit—both of them should be punished like thieves, or compelled to pay a fine equal to its value. (8.191)

"Regarding 'who [claims] a deposit'": he who does not restore deposited wealth, and he who demands what was not deposited—these two should be punished like thieves in cases involving gold, pearls, and the like, or where the matter is of great value; in cases of small value, such as copper and so forth, they should be punished with a fine equal to the value of the object. (8.191)
The king shall cause the one who misappropriates a deposit to pay a fine equal to its value; likewise, he shall do so for the one who misappropriates a sealed deposit, without distinction.

"Of the deposit": the king shall punish one who misappropriates a deposit by making him pay an amount equal to the deposited wealth. Because the instruction is the same, this applies even to one who, without having received a deposit, demands it from the depositor. Nor is there a redundancy; for while corporal punishment might have been applicable to a non-Brāhmaṇa in the case of a grave offense according to the preceding verse, this [present rule] is intended to preclude that. The phrase "he shall cause [him] to pay" establishes a rule regarding monetary fines. Furthermore, the preceding verse is not rendered useless, because this [present rule] pertains to a first offense, whereas the previously mentioned [punishment] applies to repeated offenses and is restricted by the monetary fines for great violence (*mahāsāhasa*) and so forth prescribed for thieves. "A deposit" (*upanidhi*) is wealth placed in storage marked with a seal or other signs; the king shall punish the misappropriator of such a thing, provided he possesses the aforementioned qualifications. (8.192)
Any man who, by means of fraudulent tests, should seize the property of another, shall be put to death publicly with various modes of execution along with his accomplices. (8.193)

"By means of stratagems" (*upadhābhiḥ*): having uttered a falsehood through the instruments of greed for wealth, grain, and so forth—such as "The king is angry with you; therefore I protect you, give me your wealth"—he who takes another's property by such deceits, accompanied by those accomplices with whom he shared the fraudulent wealth, shall be executed by the king in the presence of many people through various methods of killing, such as the amputation of hands, feet, and head. (8.193)
Whatever deposit was made by someone, and however much it was, in the presence of witnesses—that very same amount must be recognized as such; one who speaks falsely deserves punishment. (8.194)

Regarding "deposits": when gold or other property has been deposited by someone in the presence of witnesses for a specific quantity, if there is a dispute concerning that quantity or other details, it must be understood to be exactly as stated in the testimony of the witnesses. Even if one party attempts to contest this, they should be made to pay a fine in accordance with what has been stated. (8.194)
If a gift was made by someone privately, or received privately, it must be returned privately; as the giving was, so must be the taking. (8.195)

"Secret delivery": when a deposit has been handed over in secret by one person and accepted in secret by the holder of the deposit, that deposit must be returned in secret. There is no requirement for witnesses in such a return. This is because of the scriptural injunction: "In whatever manner the gift was made, in that very same manner the return must be given. Thus, this is a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*) concerning the holder of the deposit. However, the verse "In whatever manner one may place [it] in another's hand" (8.180) is intended as a restrictive rule for the depositor, because of the hearing of the word "to be received" (8.180). Therefore, there is no tautology. || 8.195 ||
In such cases, the king should reach a decision regarding deposited wealth as well as that which was entrusted out of friendship, without causing hardship to the holder of the deposit. (8.196)

Regarding the phrase "of that which has been deposited": whether it be wealth deposited by a king—either unsealed or accompanied by a seal—in the form of a *upanidhi* (a sealed deposit), or likewise property handed over out of affection for the purpose of enjoyment for a certain period, the judge should reach a decision in the manner described, without causing distress to the holder of the deposited wealth. 8.196.
One who sells another’s property as his own, being neither the owner nor authorized by the owner, should not be admitted as a witness; he is a thief who considers himself no thief. (8.197)

"Regarding 'let him sell': one who is not the owner and has not been authorized by the owner to sell another's property—though he is in fact a thief—he considers himself a non-thief; such a person one should not cause to act as a witness. The meaning is that one should not accept him as authoritative in any matter whatsoever. (8.197)
He shall be liable to forfeit his property along with his family and pay a fine of six hundred panas;
if he has no family property and offers no excuse, he shall incur the guilt of a thief. 8.198.

Regarding the term *avahārya*: this seller of another's property, if he is a kinsman related to the owner—such as a brother or the like—is to be fined six hundred *paṇas* and thus *avahārya*, meaning liable to punishment. However, if he is not a relative of the owner and is *anapasaras*—where *apasara* refers to a means of justification such as a gift or a purchase by which one might withdraw from the charge against him—if he lacks such a justification from someone related to the owner, such as a son, then he incurs the guilt associated with a thief; that is to say, he is to be punished accordingly. (8.198)
But whatever gift or sale is made by one who is not the owner is to be known as invalid; such is the established rule in legal proceedings. (8.199)

"By one who is not the owner": whatever has been done, given, or sold by one who is not the owner must be understood as being as if it were not done at all. The meaning is that, in legal proceedings, it does not count as having been done according to the established rule. (8.199)
Where enjoyment is perceived but no scripture is seen anywhere, there the scripture is the cause and not the enjoyment; such is the established rule. (8.200)

Regarding "possession" (*saṃbhoga*): when possession exists with respect to a certain object, yet there is no title of acquisition (*āgama*) in the form of purchase or the like, the rule of the treatises is that in such a case, title alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) within the scope of the first person, and not possession. 8.200
If one should receive any wealth from a sale in the presence of the family, he indeed acquires that wealth lawfully through purchase; thus it is purified. 8.201.

Regarding the phrase "from sale": a "sale" (*vikraya*) is a place of sale (*vikrayadeśa*), so called because goods are sold therein; from that [place], whatever purchase-money (*krayadhana*) is paid for an item before a multitude of traders—that by which it is bought—is the price (*kraya*). Because he may receive [the property] by means of that, he thus obtains the property as cleared [of defects] precisely through the legal process of purchase from the seller who is not the owner. (8.201)

Now, if the root [of the sale] cannot be produced, but he has cleared himself by proving a public purchase, he is not to be punished by the king and is released; the original owner does not recover the property.

Regarding the word "atha" (now): if the seller is not the owner and can no longer be found because of death or departure to another country, and if the purchase was made openly (*prakāśakrayaṇa*), then the buyer is indeed exempt from punishment by the king. Furthermore, the owner who has lost his property shall recover from the buyer's hand whatever goods were sold by one who was not the owner. In this matter, the rule is that the owner may take back his own property after paying half the price to the buyer. As Bṛhaspati says: "Goods situated in a merchant’s row and recognized by the king’s officers..."
Where an article has been purchased from one whose identity is unknown, or where the seller is deceased;
The owner, having paid half the value, may recover his own property;
in that case, according to legal procedure, half of the stolen amount shall be forfeited by both parties.
An object whose form is mixed with another does not deserve to be sold;
nor one that is worthless, nor one that is deficient, nor one that is hidden at a distance. (8.203)

"Not otherwise" means that a substance such as saffron must not be sold after being mixed with substances like safflower; nor should one sell what is of poor quality by declaring it to be of high quality; nor should one sell less than the full measure using scales or other means; nor should one sell what is kept out of sight; nor should one sell what has its true form concealed by dyes and the like. In this case, because it resembles the sale of property by one who is not the owner, the same punishment for "sale by one who is not the owner" (asvāmivikraya) shall apply. (8.203)
If, after showing one girl, another is given to the bridegroom,
Manu has declared that he may marry both for the price of a single dowry.

Regarding the phrase "another": Manu has stated that if, after showing a girl who is faultless at the time of establishing the bride-price (*śulka*), one gives a faulty girl to the groom, then the groom shall marry both girls for that same single bride-price. Since the giving of a girl preceded by the receipt of a bride-price takes the form of a sale, this is mentioned here because of its similarity to a commercial purchase and sale. (8.204)

A giver deserves punishment if he gives away a girl who is not intoxicated, not afflicted with leprosy, and not one who has already experienced sexual intercourse, without first disclosing her prior defects. (8.205)

"Of one who is not insane": likewise, in the case of one who is insane, or afflicted with leprosy, or one who has already experienced sexual intercourse, if the suitor has disclosed such defects as insanity and so forth to her before a Brāhma or other form of marriage, he does not deserve punishment. By this, it is understood that he is liable to punishment for failing to disclose them; as the author will state later: "But he who [marries] a girl who has defects... (8.224). || 8.205 ||

Now he speaks of undertaking an act by mutual agreement: "If a priest chosen for a sacrifice should abandon his own duty, a share corresponding to that work must be given to him by the co-performers. (8.206)

Regarding the term "officiant" (*ṛtvij*): an officiant is one who has been formally chosen for a sacrifice. If, after performing some part of the ritual, he abandons the work due to illness or other causes, then his share of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) must be given by the other officiants after deliberation, in accordance with the portion already performed by him. (8.206)
If, after the sacrificial fees have been given, one causes his own work to be neglected, he shall receive his entire share even if he has it performed by another. (8.207)

Regarding the phrase "in the case of sacrificial fees" (dakṣiṇāsu): at the time of the sacrificial fees, at the beginning of the midday pressing (mādhyandina-savana) or other such occasions, if one abandons the ritual due to illness or similar reasons—and not out of malice—he shall receive the entire share of the sacrificial fees. He should have another perform the remainder of the ritual that was originally undertaken. (8.207)
In whatever rite specific fees for individual components have been prescribed, he alone shall receive them; or alternatively, all [the officiants] may receive them together. (8.208)

Regarding the phrase "in which": there arises a doubt as to whether, in a ritual such as the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) and others, the specific fee (*dakṣiṇā*) that is heard in scripture in connection with each individual part should be taken by that very person alone, or whether all should divide and take it together. (8.208)
On this point, he states the established conclusion:
"The Adhvaryu priest shall take the chariot, and the Brahman priest the horse at the fire-consecration;
the Hotṛ priest may also take the horse, and the Udgātṛ priest the cart at the purchase [of the Soma]. (8.209)

Regarding the chariot: in the *Ādhāna* (fire-consecration) ritual, according to certain Vedic schools (*śākhins*), a chariot is prescribed as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the *adhvaryu*, a swift horse for the *brahman*, a horse for the *hotṛ*, and a cart used for carrying the *soma* for purchase for the *udgātṛ*. Therefore, by the force of this specific prescription, whoever is heard in connection with a particular fee should be the one to receive it. (8.209)
Regarding the distribution of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in the performance of the ritual, he says:
"Of all [the priests], the principal ones are entitled to half; others are entitled to half of that;
those entitled to a third receive a third part, and those entitled to a fourth receive a fourth part. (8.210)

Regarding the phrase "of all": it is heard in the scripture, "He initiates him with a hundred [cows]. In that context, among all sixteen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), those who are the principal priests—the Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, Brahman, and Udgātṛ—receive the full sacrificial fee; they are the "half-takers" (*ardhahara*) and thus receive forty-eight cows. For this very reason, Kātyāyana prescribed the gift of twelve cows for each of them in the rule: "That which [is given] to the first twelve. Although half of a hundred is fifty, nevertheless, here these are called "half-takers" even by taking a lesser half, due to their proximity [to the full amount]. Others—the Maitrāvaruṇa, Pratiprasthātṛ, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, and Prastotṛ—are called "half-takers" because they receive the half of the fee taken by the principal priests. The "third-partakers" (*tṛtīyinaḥ*)—the Acchāvāka, Neṣṭṛ, Agnīdhra, and Pratihartṛ—obtain a third share of what is taken by the principal priests. The "quarter-partakers" (*pādinaḥ*)—the Grāvastut, Unnetṛ, and Subrahmaṇya—obtain a fourth share of what is taken by the principal priests. This has been made clear by Kātyāyana in his Sūtra: "Six each for the second [group], four each for the third, and three each for the fourth. (8.210)
When men here perform their respective duties in association with one another, the apportionment of their shares must be determined by this application of the rule. (8.211)

Regarding the word *saṃbhūya*: having come together, while men such as architects (*sthapati*) and carpenters (*sūtradhārin*) perform their respective tasks like the construction of a house, a distribution of shares must be made by this person based on the rules for sacrificial fees (*yajñadakṣiṇā-vidhi*), taking into account the application of their specialized knowledge and so forth. (8.211)
Now he speaks regarding the revocation of what has been given:

"If wealth should have been given by someone to another who asks for it for the sake of dharma, and if that [wealth] subsequently does not turn out to be so, it should not have been given; thus, it shall be [considered as] not given. (8.212)

"Regarding the phrase 'for the sake of dharma': if wealth has been given or promised to someone who requests it for the purpose of performing sacrifices and other such rites, but that person subsequently does not employ the wealth for the sake of sacrifice, then even that wealth which was already given may be taken back, and what was promised need not be paid. As Gautama says: 'Even after having promised, one should not give to one who is engaged in unrighteousness. (8.212)
If, however, he should recover it out of pride or greed, he shall be made to pay one suvarṇa by the king as atonement for that theft. (8.213)

Regarding the word "yadi" (if): if, having received that gift, he does not relinquish it out of greed or egoism, or if he takes by force the wealth that was promised, then, for the sake of purifying the sin of theft, he must be made to pay a fine of gold by the king. (8.213)
Thus has been declared the lawful non-repudiation of what has been given;
hereafter, I shall explain the non-repudiation of wages. (8.214)

Regarding the phrase "of what has been given": this non-returning of what was given is said to be not inconsistent with dharma; therefore, immediately following this, I shall speak of the non-payment of wages and so forth. (8.214)
If a hired servant, being neither ill nor distressed, fails through arrogance to perform the work as it was prescribed, he shall be fined eight *kṛṣṇalas* and his wages shall not be paid. (8.215)

Regarding the term "hired": if one who has been engaged for wages, being afflicted by disease, should fail to perform the work as stipulated due to egoism, he shall be fined eight *kṛṣṇalas* of gold or other currency according to the nature of the work, and his wages shall not be paid to him. (8.215)
But one who was distressed and, having recovered his health, performs the work as originally instructed from the beginning, shall indeed receive that wage even after a long period of time. (8.216)

"Afflicted," and so forth. When one does not perform work due to suffering from illness or other causes, once he has recovered his health, he should perform the work exactly as it was described; and he shall certainly receive his wages, even after a long period of time. (8.216)
