As it has been said: "Whether he be distressed or healthy, if one does not cause that work to be performed, his wages must not be given, even for work that is only slightly incomplete. (8.217)

As it has been stated: "Whatever work has been described as to be performed by someone who, when oppressed by another, would not do it, or who, being in good health, would neither do it nor cause it to be done—for that work, even if only a small portion remains uncompleted, no wages shall be paid. (8.217)
This law regarding the non-payment of wages has been declared in its entirety;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the law concerning those who violate an agreement.

"This is the law": this rule regarding the act known as the taking of wages has been stated in its entirety. Immediately following this, I shall declare the rules concerning punishment and other matters for those who violate an agreement. 8.218.
A man who, having made a formal agreement with a village, a district, or a community by means of truth,
should break that agreement out of greed— he the king shall banish from the realm.

Regarding the word "ya" (who): by the words "village" and "region," those who dwell therein are indicated. A "guild" (*saṅgha*) is a collection such as that of merchants and so forth. Having made a formal agreement (*saṃketa*) of the form "this must be done by us" or "this must be avoided," by means of an oath of truth and the like—any man among them who should depart because of greed or other motives, the king shall banish from the realm. (8.219)
Having restrained him, the king shall cause that violator of the compact to pay four suvarṇas, six niṣkas, and one silver śatamāna. (8.220)

"Having restrained," [means]: then, having informed this offender of the breach of agreement, the king shall cause him to pay a fine consisting of four *suvarṇas*—each weighing four *suvarṇas*—and six *niṣkas*, as well as one hundred silver *mānas* (weighing three hundred and twenty *raktikas*). Depending on the relative gravity or lightness of the matter, he may impose these either collectively or individually. (8.220)
A righteous lord of the earth should apply this rule of punishment to those who violate their agreements within villages, castes, and assemblies. 8.221

"Regarding this": in villages—that is, among communities of the Brāhmaṇa caste—the king, whose primary concern is dharma, shall apply this rule of punishment to those who violate an agreement. (8.221)
If, after having bought or sold anything, one should have cause for regret in this matter, he may return that object or take it back within ten days. 8.222.

"Having purchased," etc. Having purchased or having sold some perishable commodity, if for a stable object such as land or a copper plate a regret arises in the world [of the buyer or seller] that "I have not acted wisely in purchasing this," he should return what was purchased within ten days; or, conversely, he may take back what was sold. (8.222)
But after ten days have passed, one should neither give nor cause to be given;
both he who takes it and he who gives it shall be fined six hundred by the king. (8.223)

"By another" means that what has been purchased after ten days shall not be returned; nor shall a seller be forced by force to accept what has been sold. One who forcibly takes back or forcibly abandons what has been sold shall be fined six hundred *paṇas* by the king. (8.223)
But for one who gives away a daughter who has defects without disclosing them, the king himself shall impose a fine of ninety-six paṇas. (8.224)

Regarding the phrase "yas tu": although it was stated generally that [the bridegroom may take back the girl] "if she is not insane" (8.205), this [verse] is intended to specify the particular punishment. If a man gives a defective maiden to a suitor without disclosing her defects such as insanity and the like, the king himself shall personally and with due care impose a fine of ninety-six *paṇas* upon him. This matter concerning the maiden is mentioned here in connection with the topic of rescission (*anuśaya*).
But if a man, out of malice, should declare a maiden to be "not a virgin" without demonstrating any fault in her, he shall incur a fine of one hundred [paṇas]. (8.225)

"Regarding 'not a maiden': if a man should say out of malice, 'This is not a maiden; her virginity has been violated,' the king shall impose a fine of one hundred paṇas upon him, provided that he does not prove the aforementioned defect. (8.225)
And a punishment is indeed appropriate for one who claims she is not a maiden, because:
"The mantras recited at the taking of the hand are established only for maidens;
they are never for non-maidens among men, for such women have lost their eligibility for religious rites. (8.226)

Regarding the term *pāṇi*: "The maidens have worshipped the god Agni and Aryaman," and so forth—these are the marriage mantras for human beings. Because of the hearing of the word "maiden" (*kanyā*), they are established as applying only to maidens and not to those who are no longer maidens. In some scriptures, they are established for the sake of accomplishing a *dharma*-marriage; however, because their literal meaning is not applicable [in other cases], he says this: "Even though those whose virginity has been violated (*kṣatayoni*) are consecrated with the marriage mantras, they remain devoid of the *dharma*-marriage and the like. The meaning is that such a marriage is not a righteous (*dharmya*) one. But this does not prohibit the use of marriage mantras, oblations, and so forth for one whose virginity has been violated, since Manu himself will state the marriage-consecration even for such a person in the passages: "She who is consecrated while pregnant" (p. 173), and likewise, "The son born of a maiden belongs to the husband" (9.172). However, by Devala:
In the case of Gāndharva marriages,
the formal marriage rite must again be performed by the three castes at the proper time, with fire as witness.

Thus, the rule for the *homamant* and other rites has been stated regarding *gāndharva* marriages. Since the *gāndharva* marriage may also be preceded by sexual union, its complete lawfulness in the case of Kṣatriyas has been declared by Manu. Therefore, according to the maxim of the general and the particular, this instruction concerning the unrighteousness of the *kṣatayoni* marriage refers to cases other than that of the Kṣatriyas. (8.226)
The mantras of the taking of the hand are the certain mark of a wife;
their completion, however, should be understood by the wise to occur at the seventh step. (8.227)

Regarding the phrase "those pertaining to the taking of the hand": the marriage mantras are the fixed and certain cause for the status of wife, because the status of wife is accomplished through the mantras when they are employed according to the scriptures. However, the accomplishment of those mantras should be understood by those learned in the scriptures to occur at the giving of the seventh step, based on the application of the mantra "Be my companion at the seventh step" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.7.7). Thus, since the status of wife is not accomplished prior to the giving of the seventh step, one may abandon her if there is a valid ground for repudiation; but not after that point. (8.227)
Whosoever should feel remorse regarding any action performed here, him one should establish on the path of righteousness by means of this procedure. || 8.228 ||

Regarding the phrase "in which": it is not only in the case of a purchase; in whatever other matter, whether as a relative or otherwise, for which remorse arises later, the king should establish that person on the path not deviating from dharma by means of this ten-day rule. (8.228)
I shall now fully explain, according to the true nature of dharma, the legal dispute arising from the transgressions of both owners and herdsmen regarding livestock.

"Regarding livestock": I shall explain how a dispute arising from a transgression by owners or herdsmen concerning livestock such as cattle should be properly settled in accordance with dharma. (8.229)

If the loss occurs during the day, the blame falls on the keeper; if at night, it falls on the owner, provided the animal was in that house. Otherwise, if the security of the property was otherwise maintained, the keeper shall incur the blame. (8.230)

"By day," [it is said]. By day, regarding the acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*) of animals placed in the hands of a herdsman, the blame lies with the herdsman. At night, however, for those returned to the herdsman and staying at the owner's house, the fault lies with the owner. Otherwise, if they remain in the hands of the herdsman even at night, then when a loss occurs therein, the herdsman alone incurs the blame. (8.230)
A cowherd who is maintained with milk may, with the consent of the owner of the cattle, milk the best cow out of ten; that shall be his wages if he is not otherwise paid. (8.231)

Regarding the term "gopa": if a servant known as a cowherd (*gopāla*), having been authorized by his master, should—by force (*dharṣita*)—milk one excellent cow from among the herd for his own benefit rather than with milk or other provisions, that [milk] shall constitute his wages when he is otherwise deprived of food and such. And thus it is said that by the gift of the milk of a single cow, he should tend ten cows. (8.231)
If an animal is lost, destroyed by worms, killed by dogs, or dies in a dangerous place, or if it is deficient in human effort, the keeper alone shall be made to pay. (8.232)

"Lost" means gone beyond the range of sight; destroyed by worms; eaten by dogs; killed; or dead from falling into a pit or similar place. This is merely an illustration. An animal that has died while being devoid of the activity of the person known as the "guardian" belonging to the owner, or a cow or other animal that has run away, the herdsman himself must give back to the owner. (8.232)
If cattle have been stolen by thieves after being publicly proclaimed, the herdsman is not liable to pay, provided he reports it to his own master at the proper place and time. (8.233)

Regarding the term *vighuṣya*: if the herd has been carried off by thieves after they have sounded the drum and other instruments, the herdsman is not liable to pay restitution. The phrase "having sounded [the drum]" is intended to indicate that there were many thieves and that they were powerful. If the herd is in a nearby location, he informs his own master immediately after the time of the theft. (8.233)
When animals have died, one should give the ears, hide, tail-hairs, bladder, sinew, and bile to the owners, and show them the identifying marks. (8.234)

Regarding the ears: when animals have died of their own accord, one should give the owners the skin of the ears, the tail, the dewlap, the lower part from the navel, the sinews, and the gallstones; furthermore, one should show other identifying marks such as the horns and hooves. (8.234)
But when goats and sheep are hemmed in by wolves and the herdsman does not come to their aid, whatever wolf may forcibly kill shall be the fault of the herdsman. (8.235)

Regarding the term *ajāvika*: it refers to goats (*ajā*) and sheep (*avikā*), which form a collective singular compound according to Pāṇini 2.4.11, "gavāśvaprabhṛtīni ca. When those goats and sheep are surrounded by wolves and the herdsman does not return, whatever goat or ewe a wolf may kill in the forest, that shall be the fault of the herdsman. (8.235)
If, among those cows kept within the herd while grazing together in the forest, a wolf should spring upon and kill one, the herdsman is not at fault in that matter. (8.236)

Regarding the word "tāsām" (of them): if, while those goats and sheep are being tended by a herdsman, have been penned together, and are roaming in the forest as a herd, some [predator] should happen to leap upon any one of them from somewhere unnoticed, and the herdsman does not kill it—then the herdsman incurs no fault in that matter. (8.236)
The common land around a village shall be one hundred bow-lengths on all sides, or else three throws of a wooden pin; for a city, however, it shall be three times that amount. 8.237.

"Regarding 'a hundred bows': a bow is four cubits (*hasta*) long. A *śamyā* is a wooden staff; its 'fall' is its throwing. Near a village, in all directions, one must maintain a space of four hundred cubits—or as far as three throws of the staff—to prevent the obstruction of sowing crops and the like for the sake of cattle grazing. However, near a city, this distance must be made threefold.
If cattle should damage grain that is not enclosed there, the king shall not inflict punishment upon the keepers of the animals. (8.238)

Regarding the phrase "unenclosed" therein: if, on such a site for cultivation, someone sows grain that has not been fenced off and cattle should eat it, the king shall not inflict punishment upon the herdsmen. (8.238)
One should construct a fence there such that a camel cannot look over it, and one should block every opening through which the snout of a dog or a pig might pass. 8.239.

Regarding the phrase "a fence": in that case, on the field where the defense is situated, one should construct such a fence made of thorns and other materials that it is raised so high that a camel cannot look over its opposite side; and whatever opening there may be in it that is capable of admitting the head of a dog or a pig, all of that one should close up. (8.239)

On a path, in a field that is enclosed, or at the edge of a village, the keeper is liable to a fine of one hundred [paṇas] for animals; however, he should drive away the cattle if they are unattended. (8.240)

"Path" (pathi): When an animal, such as a cow, enters—having been unobstructed by the keeper through a gate or other means—into a field that is situated near a road or near a village, which is set aside for avoidance and has been granted [as pasture], and it consumes [the crops] when it has somehow entered, then it should be fined one hundred paṇas. Since punishment is impossible for the animal itself, the keeper alone is to be punished. Furthermore, the guardian of the field should ward off those animals that are without a keeper and have set about consuming [the crops].
But in other fields, the animal deserves a fine of one paṇa and a quarter;
however, in all cases, a sixth part must be given to the owner of the field—this is the settled rule. (8.241)

Regarding the phrase "in fields": in fields other than those along roads or within villages, an animal that grazes there deserves a fine of one *paṇa* and a quarter. In this case as well, the keeper alone is to be punished. It is the settled rule that in every instance, the value of the crop eaten by the animal in the field must be paid to the owner—either by the keeper or by the owner himself—according to the extent of the damage. (8.241)

Manu has declared that one should not punish a cow that has recently calved, nor bulls, nor animals dedicated to the gods—whether they have a keeper or are without a keeper—within ten days of birth. (8.242)

Regarding the phrase "not ten days old": Manu has declared that a cow that has calved within ten days, as well as bulls marked with the discus and trident and abandoned [for breeding], and animals belonging to the images of Hari, Hara, and others—whether accompanied by their keepers or not—if they are engaged in eating crops, are exempt from punishment. Since even bulls set free for breeding are kept by keepers in the cow-pen for the sake of impregnating the cows, it is possible for them to be accompanied by keepers.

In case of a transgression by the landowner, the fine shall be ten times his share; for the servants, however, the fine shall be half of that, provided it was due to the landowner’s own ignorance. (8.243)

Regarding the phrase "of the landowner": when the field-tiller, by eating his own cattle or the crops, or through negligence such as sowing at the wrong time, causes a loss to the king's share, he shall be fined ten times that amount. If the aforementioned offense was committed by servants without the knowledge of the landowner, the landowner himself shall be fined half of ten times the amount. This has been stated here in connection with the topic of fields and crops.
A righteous lord of the earth should observe this rule in cases of transgression involving owners of cattle, the animals themselves, and their keepers. (8.244)

"Regarding this": when there is a fault on the part of owners or herdsmen for failing to provide protection, or a transgression by the cattle in the form of eating the crops, the king, whose primary concern is dharma, should carry out what has been previously stated. (8.244)
When a dispute has arisen concerning a boundary between two villages,
one should determine the boundary during the month of Jyeṣṭha when the landmarks are clearly visible.

Regarding the boundary: when a dispute has arisen concerning the boundary line between two villages, the king shall determine the boundary in the month of Jyeṣṭha, because the boundary markers have become manifest due to the drying up of the grass by the heat of the summer sun. (8.245)
And he should establish boundary trees—*nyagrodha*, *aśvattha*, and *kiṃśuka* trees, as well as *śālmalī*, *sāla*, *tāla*, and milky-sap trees. (8.246)

"Boundary trees" means that one should establish boundary markers consisting of trees such as the *nyagrodha* and others, or milky-sap trees such as the *udumbara* and others, because of their long-lasting nature. (8.246)
By means of thickets, various bamboos, *chamī* creepers, and grassy plots, as well as reeds and *kubjaka* shrubs, the boundary is not lost. (8.247)

"Shrubs" (*gulmān*): one should establish boundary markers consisting of shrubs—bamboos devoid of trunks—and various kinds of boundary trees distinguished by having many thorns or few thorns; as well as creepers (*vallī*), climbing plants (*latā*), mounds (*sthāna*) which are artificially raised portions of ground, reeds (*śara*), and *kubjaka* shrubs. These are mentioned separately for the sake of emphasis due to their varying degrees of abundance or scarcity, serving as the signs of the boundary. When this is done, the boundary does not perish. (8.247)
Ponds, wells, large tanks, and springs, as well as temples, should be constructed at the junctions of the boundaries. (8.248)

"Regarding 'tadāgāni' (those [marks] consisting of tanks): reservoirs, wells, long water-channels, and temples should be constructed at the junctions between two villages, which serve as the boundaries. When these have been made known for the purpose of determining the boundary, even those who come for water and other purposes become witnesses through the tradition of oral report, even after a long period of time. (8.248)
And he should cause other boundary markers to be made concealed, having observed that in the world there is constant confusion among men regarding the knowledge of boundaries. (8.249)

"Concealed," and so forth: having observed the constant confusion and ignorance of men in this world regarding the determination of boundaries, he should cause other hidden boundary marks—distinct from those already mentioned—to be established, as will be described hereafter. (8.249)
Stones, bones, cow-hair, husks, ashes, potsherds, dried cow-dung, bricks, charcoal, gravel, and likewise sand. (8.250)
And whatever objects of this kind the earth would not consume due to their age, those he should cause to be placed inconspicuously at junctions and boundaries. 8.251.

"Stones," "those which," etc. [Bṛhaspati says]: "One should place in jars—stones, bones, cow-hair, husks, ashes, rags, dried cow-dung, baked bricks, charcoal, stones, potsherds, sand, and other such things like black antimony, cotton-seeds, bones, and so forth—which the earth does not assimilate even over a long period—and having deposited them at the junctions of two villages on the boundary, one should have these placed in jars at the ends of the boundary.
According to this statement of Bṛhaspati, one should place items other than large stones in jars, bury them secretly in the ground, and maintain them. (8.250–251)
By these signs, as well as by long-standing possession and the constant flow of water, the king should determine the boundary between two disputing parties. (8.252)

"By these": when two villages are in dispute, the king shall determine the boundary by means of these aforementioned signs already described. Furthermore, the determination of the boundary is based on uninterrupted possession (*bhukti*) while residing there, and not merely on the fact that it has been held for three generations or more; for such [long-term possession] is excluded by the rule, "A boundary is [exempted from] being a pledge" (YDh 2.24.149). And he shall determine the boundary between the two villages situated on opposite banks by the flow of rivers and other such features located at the junction of the two villages. (8.252)
If there were doubt even when the boundary marks are visible, the determination of the boundary dispute would depend solely upon the testimony of witnesses. (8.253)

Regarding the word "yadi" (if): if, even when concealed or visible marks are observed, there should be a total doubt—such as whether these jars containing hidden charcoal, husks, and so forth have been carried to another place and buried, or whether this banyan tree at the boundary is not that one, but that [original] one has perished—and so on, then the determination of the boundary dispute would depend solely upon the evidence of witnesses. || 8.253 ||
In the presence of the local families and the two litigants themselves, witnesses shall be questioned regarding the boundary marks along the border. (8.254)

Regarding the term *grāmīyaka*: in the presence of the assemblies of villagers and of the plaintiff and defendant appointed from two villages, when there is a doubt concerning boundary marks regarding a boundary, the witnesses must be questioned about those marks. (8.254)
When they have been questioned, he should establish the boundary exactly as they all unanimously declare it, recording them all by name. (8.255)

Regarding the word "they": when those witnesses have been questioned as a group and, being free from discord, declare their decision concerning the boundary in a particular manner, the judge shall write down that boundary in a document in that same manner, for the purpose of preventing forgetfulness; and he shall record all those witnesses by their names and respective divisions. (8.255)
Bowing their heads to the earth, wearing garlands and red garments,
and bound by oaths upon their own good deeds, they shall lead him with justice.

Regarding the phrase "with their heads": although there is a general mention of them as witnesses, according to the statement of Yājñavalkya—"Wearing red garlands and garments, they shall lead [the boundary]" (YDh 2.152)—those wearing red flower garlands and red clothing, having taken clods of earth upon their heads and being sworn by their own merits with the words, "May whatever merit we have become fruitless," shall determine that boundary to the best of their ability. || 8.256 ||
Those who lead [the case] according to what has been stated are purified as truthful witnesses;
but those who lead it contrarily shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred. 8.257.

"According to what has been stated": those witnesses who prioritize the truth, having reached a decision according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, become free from sin. But those who determine the case through falsehood shall each be made to pay a fine of two hundred *paṇas*. (8.258)
But in the absence of witnesses, four neighboring villagers shall, being purified, determine the boundary in the presence of the king. (8.258)

Regarding the absence of witnesses: in the case of a boundary dispute between two villages where no witnesses exist, the neighbors situated on all four sides—four village-dwellers living in the vicinity—shall determine the boundary in the presence of the king according to the rules for witnesses. (8.258)
But in the absence of neighboring witnesses on the boundary of the original owners, he should also interrogate these men who frequent the forests: || 8.259 ||

Regarding the term "of the neighbors": when the village-dwellers—who have been hereditary residents since the time of the village's foundation—fail to provide a determination based on direct experience before the king according to the rules for witnesses, he shall question these following persons who dwell nearby in the forest, as they serve as boundary-witnesses through the succession of men residing in that village. (8.259)
He [instructed] hunters, fowlers, cowherds, fishermen, root-diggers, snake-catchers, gleaners, and other forest-dwellers. (8.260)

"Regarding hunters": he should question hunters (*lubdhaka*), those who live by killing birds, cowherds, those who live by catching fish, those who live by uprooting plants, snake-catchers, those who subsist on *śila* and *uñcha*, and others who frequent the forest for the sake of fruits, flowers, firewood, and so forth. For these people, in order to serve their own purposes, would constantly go to the forest from that village; thus, they are likely to be familiar with the boundaries of that village. (8.260)
Whatever marks they may describe when questioned regarding the boundaries and junctions, the king shall establish those exactly so for the two villages in accordance with the law. (8.261)

"They are questioned" means that the hunters and others, having been questioned regarding the boundary marks at the junctions of the villages, shall establish the boundary between the two villages in exactly the manner in which they describe the signs.
The determination of boundaries and embankments for fields, wells, tanks, groves, and houses is to be known as dependent upon the testimony of the neighbors. (8.262)

Regarding the term "field": even within a single village, when there is a dispute over the boundaries or markers of fields, wells, tanks, gardens, or houses, the determination of the boundary signs must be understood as being based solely on the evidence of witnesses who are residents of the entire district, and not on the evidence of hunters and the like. (8.262)
If the neighbors should speak falsely when men are disputing over a boundary, they shall all be punished individually by the king with the middle amercement. (8.263)

Regarding the term "neighbors" (sāmantāḥ): if neighbors residing in the vicinity should give false testimony when men are disputing over boundary marks and signs, then all of them are to be punished individually by the king with the middle amercement (madhyama-sāhasa). Likewise, it should be understood that for those who are not neighbors, the previously mentioned fine of two hundred [paṇas] applies. (8.263)
One who seizes a house, a pond, a garden, or a field by means of intimidation shall be fined five hundred [paṇas]; if it was done through ignorance, the fine shall be two hundred. (8.264)

Regarding "house": having first instilled fear through threats of execution, imprisonment, or other such penalties, one who seizes any one of the following—a house, a pond, a garden, or a field—shall be fined five hundred *paṇas*. For one who seizes them under the mistaken belief that they belong to him, the fine shall be two hundred *paṇas*.
If the boundary cannot be determined, the king himself, knowing the law, shall assign land to them for their benefit; such is the settled rule. (8.265)

Regarding the phrase "in the case of a boundary": when a boundary cannot be determined due to the absence of marks, witnesses, and so forth, the king himself—being a knower of dharma and free from partiality—should grant the disputed land situated between two villages to those village-dwellers who derive the greatest benefit from it and whose livelihood would otherwise suffer great hardship; such is the legal settlement prescribed by the scriptures.
This law concerning the determination of boundaries has been declared in its entirety.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the determination of verbal abuse. (8.266)

"This" refers to the following: this law concerning the determination of boundaries has been declared in its entirety. Hereafter, I shall speak of verbal assault (*vākpāruṣya*). Although verbal assault follows physical assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*) in its occurrence, it is mentioned first here; however, in the sequential enumeration [of the legal topics], it is stated, "In the two types of assault, the physical and the verbal" (8.6), where the word for physical assault (*daṇḍa*) is placed first because its vowel sound is shorter. 8.266.
A Kṣatriya who reviles a Brāhmaṇa deserves a fine of one hundred; a Vaiśya deserves either fifty or two hundred; but a Śūdra deserves corporal punishment. (8.267)

"Regarding 'one hundred': having spoken harsh words in the form of an insult such as 'thief' to a twice-born man, a Kṣatriya deserves a fine of one hundred paṇas. Likewise, a Vaiśya deserves one hundred and fifty or two hundred, depending on the relative gravity or lightness of the offense. A Śūdra, too, for insulting a Brāhmaṇa in this manner, deserves corporal punishment such as beating. (8.267)
A Brāhmaṇa should be fined fifty [paṇas] for defaming a Kṣatriya;
for a Vaiśya, the fine shall be twenty-five; and for a Śūdra, the punishment is twelve. (8.268)

"Fifty" means: if a Brāhmaṇa has uttered an insult of the aforementioned kind against a Kṣatriya, he shall be fined fifty paṇas. If such an insult as described is made against a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, the fine for the Brāhmaṇa shall be twenty-five and twelve paṇas respectively.
For offenses among the twice-born of equal caste, the fine shall be exactly twelve [paṇas];
in cases where speech is not permitted, that same fine shall be doubled. (8.269)

It is settled: when a member of the twice-born classes utters the aforementioned abusive speech toward another of the same caste, the fine is twelve paṇas. However, in the case of unutterable abuses—such as those consisting of vulgar terms directed at one’s mother, sister, and so forth—the same applies; because of the neuter reference [in the verse], that which was stated in "Having abused a Brāhmaṇa with [unutterable words], one shall pay a hundred" (8.267) and so forth, shall constitute a double fine. 8.269.
But one of low birth who insults those of twice-born status with harsh speech shall suffer the cutting off of his tongue, for he is of inferior origin. (8.270)

"Regarding 'one of them': a Śūdra, having insulted twice-born men with speech involving an accusation of a sin, shall suffer the cutting off of his tongue; for he was born from a lowly limb called the foot. (8.270)
But for one who maliciously utters their names or castes, a glowing iron spike ten fingers long shall be thrust into his mouth. (8.271)

"Name" refers to verbal abuse or insult. For one who addresses Brahmins and others with insults such as "Hey you, Yajñadatta, you outcaste Brahmin! while seizing upon their name, caste, and so forth, a red-hot iron nail ten fingers long, set ablaze by fire, shall be thrust into his mouth.
If he should out of pride give instruction in the Dharma to Brahmins, the king shall cause heated oil to be poured into his mouth and his ears. (8.272)

Regarding the word "dharma": if a Brahmin, having somehow grasped a mere fragment of dharma, should instruct a Śūdra out of pride, saying, "This dharma must be practiced by you," the king should pour boiling oil into that Śūdra's mouth and both ears. (8.272)
If one speaks falsely out of arrogance regarding another's learning, country, caste, or even their physical body, he shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred panas. (8.273)

Regarding the word *śrutam* ("heard"): this refers to a matter concerning persons of the same caste, as the punishment is light; it does not refer to a Śūdra’s accusation against a twice-born man. One who, out of arrogance, speaks falsely, saying, "This was not heard by you," "You were not born in that country," "This is not your caste," or "The bodily sacraments such as the initiation (*upanayana*) were not performed for you," shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas]. The instrumental case in *vitathena* ("by means of falsehood") is according to the rule: "In the prescription of the instrumental case, there is an addition [of the suffix] after *prakṛti* and so forth" (Kātyāyana on Pāṇini 2.3.18). 8.273.
Whether one says of another that they are one-eyed, lame, or otherwise similarly afflicted—even if it be the truth—one shall be made to pay a fine of at least one kārṣāpaṇa. (8.274)

"Regarding the term 'one-eyed' (kāṇaḥ)": if one speaks—even truthfully—using words such as "one-eyed" and so forth regarding someone who is deficient in one eye, deficient in a foot, or otherwise deficient in a limb such as a hand, he shall be made to pay a very small fine of one kārṣāpaṇa. (8.274)
One who defames his mother, father, wife, brother, son, or teacher shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred panas; likewise, one who does not yield the path to his teacher.

Regarding the word "mother": the commentators state that *ākṣārita*, *kṣārita*, and *abhiśasta* are synonymous. One who falsely accuses his mother and others of a mortal sin (*pātaka*) and the like, or one who abandons the path of his teacher, is liable to punishment. The equality of the penalty for falsely accusing one's wife and others of either a grave or a minor sin must be reconciled accordingly. Medhātithi, however, having stated that *ākṣāraṇa* means "causing division," explained this rule as applying to one who causes dissension among mother, son, father, and so forth. (8.275)
A wise king should inflict punishment upon both Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas:
for a Brāhmaṇa, the first amercement; but for a Kṣatriya, the middle amercement. (8.276)

Regarding the term "Brāhmaṇa": when a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya mutually utter insults that cause loss of caste (*patanīya*), the king who knows the science of punishment must impose a penalty. He states the specific penalty as follows: "A Brāhmaṇa"—if a Brāhmaṇa utters an insult against a Kṣatriya, the first amercement (*prathamasāhasa*) shall be imposed; however, if a Kṣatriya utters an insult against a Brāhmaṇa, the middle amercement (*madhyamasāhasa*) shall be imposed. (8.276)

In the case of a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, it is likewise determined that, with respect to their own respective castes, the application of punishment shall be exactly as prescribed, with the exception of corporal mutilation. 8.277.

Regarding the word *viḍ*: when a Vaiśya or a Śūdra utters an insulting word that causes loss of caste (*patanīya*) against one of the other [castes], the punishment for a Vaiśya who insults a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya is the first amercement, and for a Śūdra who insults a Vaiśya, the middle amercement; such is the application of the punishment, which must be carried out exactly as prescribed without the excision of the tongue—this is the settled conclusion of the scriptures. Thus, the excision of the tongue previously mentioned in the verse "But a once-born man [against] the twice-born" (8.270) is precluded in the case of a Vaiśya, and remains applicable only in the context of insulting a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya. (8.277)
This rule for punishment regarding verbal abuse has been declared according to the truth;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the determination of punishment for physical assault. 8.278

"This" refers to this aforementioned rule for punishment regarding verbal abuse as it truly is; immediately thereafter, I shall declare the determination of the punishment for physical assault and the like. (8.278)
If an outcaste should injure a superior by any limb whatsoever, that very limb of his shall be cut off; such is the ordinance of Manu. 8.279.

Regarding the phrase "by which": if an outcaste—a Śūdra—should strike a twice-born person directly with any limb whatsoever, such as a hand or a foot, or with an unmediated object such as a staff, that very limb of his must be cut off; this is the instruction of Manu. The mention of Manu is for the sake of showing reverence. (8.279)
This very point will be elaborated upon later: "Lifting up his hand or his staff, he deserves the cutting off of that hand;
striking with his foot out of anger, he deserves the cutting off of that foot. (8.280)
"Regarding 'the hand': having raised his hand or a staff to strike, he incurs the amputation of the hand. If he strikes with his foot out of anger, he suffers the amputation of the foot. (8.280)
One born of a lower caste who seeks to sit upon the same seat as one of superior caste shall be branded on the hip with a mark and banished; furthermore, his buttock shall be cut off. (8.281)

"Along with": a Śūdra who sits upon the same seat as a Brāhmaṇa shall be branded on the hip with the mark of a red-hot iron and banished; or his buttock shall be cut off in such a manner that he does not die. 8.281.
If one spits out of arrogance, the king shall cause both his lips to be cut off;
if he urinates [upon him], his penis; and if he passes wind [against him], his anus. (8.282)

It is said: A king shall cause the two lips of a Śūdra who, out of pride, insults Brāhmaṇas with phlegm to be cut off; if he insults them by urinating [upon them], his penis; if he insults them through flatulence—that is, an offensive sound from the anus—the king shall, out of pride and not through negligence, have his anus cut off. (8.282)
If one seizes him by the hair, the king shall cut off both hands without hesitation; the same applies for seizing him by the feet, the beard, the neck, or the testicles. (8.283)

"Regarding the hair": the word "out of pride" (darpāt) carries over from the previous rule. If a Śūdra, out of arrogance, seizes a Brāhmaṇa by the hair, the king shall have his two hands cut off without considering whether or not pain was actually caused to the Brāhmaṇa. If he seizes him by the feet, the beard, the neck, or the testicles for the purpose of injury, he shall likewise have both hands cut off. (8.283)
One who breaks the skin shall be fined one hundred [paṇas], as shall one who causes blood to flow;
but one who cuts the flesh shall pay six niṣkas, while one who breaks a bone shall be banished. 8.284.

Regarding the phrase "one who pierces the skin": one who merely pierces the hide, being of the same caste as the victim, and not a Śūdra, shall be fined one hundred *paṇas* for inflicting a lighter punishment upon a Brāhmaṇa. Likewise, even one who causes blood to flow shall be fined exactly one hundred *paṇas*. One who pierces the flesh shall be made to pay six *niṣkas*. But one who pierces a bone shall be banished from the country. (8.284)
It is the settled rule that the punishment for injuring any of the forest trees should be proportional to the degree of their utility. 8.285.

Regarding the phrase "of the lords of the forest" (*vanaspatīnām*): it is the settled rule that for all plants and trees, according to the manner in which their utility—whether through fruit, flower, leaf, or otherwise—is of superior, middling, or inferior quality, a corresponding punishment, such as the highest fine (*uttama-sāhasa*) and so forth, must be prescribed for their destruction. And thus says Viṣṇu: "One who cuts down a tree used for its fruit incurs the highest fine; one who cuts down a tree used for its flowers incurs the middle fine; one who cuts down a creeper, shrub, or climbing vine pays one hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*; and one who cuts down grass pays one [fine]. [ViDh 5.55–58]
And it should be understood that a *kārsāpaṇa* is also called a *paṇa* by Manu. (8.285)
When a blow is struck against humans or animals for the sake of causing pain, one should inflict a punishment that corresponds exactly to the magnitude of that suffering. (8.286)

Regarding the phrase "of human beings": when a blow is struck for the purpose of causing pain to humans or animals, the punishment shall be increased in proportion to the intensity of the suffering. Thus, in cases such as piercing the skin at vital points and so forth, a punishment greater than that prescribed by the rule, "one who pierces the skin shall be fined one hundred" (8.284), must be imposed according to the specific degree of the pain caused. (8.286)
In cases of crushing a limb, as well as in the case of wounds and bloodshed, the offender shall be made to pay the expenses of recovery or even the full fine. (8.287)

"Limbs" (aṅga) refers to the hands, feet, and so forth, as well as wounds and blood. When there is injury to these, the person who caused the pain must be made to pay the expenses of recovery; that is, for as long as it takes to restore the original condition—during which period the connection to recovery exists—the person must be made to pay whatever expense occurs through diet, medicine, and so on. If the one who caused the pain does not wish to pay those expenses, then the king shall make him pay both the expenses of recovery and the fine as a penalty. (8.287)
If one should damage the property of another, whether intentionally or even unintentionally, he should provide satisfaction to that person and pay an equivalent amount to the king. (8.288)

Regarding the term "substances" (*dravya*): substances are items such as bracelets, copper pots, and so forth, for which no specific fine has been prescribed. Whoever destroys another's property—whether through knowledge or ignorance—must satisfy the owner by providing another article of equal value, and must also pay the king a fine equal to the value of the destroyed property. (8.288)
For leather goods, articles made of leather, and those made of wood or clay, as well as for flowers, roots, and fruits, the fine shall be five times their value. (8.289)

"Regarding leather": when another's leather—such as straps made of leather—or vessels fashioned from leather, wood, or clay, or flowers, roots, and fruits are destroyed, a fine five times their value must be paid to the king; furthermore, the satisfaction of the owner must certainly be secured. (8.289)
They say there are ten exceptions concerning the vehicle, the driver, and the owner of the vehicle; in all other cases, a punishment is ordained. (8.290)

Regarding the phrase "of the vehicle" (*yānasya*): for a vehicle such as a chariot, for its driver such as a charioteer, and for the owner of the vehicle—whichever vehicle belongs to whichever of these—there are ten causes, beginning with the broken nose [of the animal], which exist beyond the scope of punishment. Manu and others have declared that when these causes are present, even if there is the killing of a living being or the destruction of property, no punishment shall be imposed upon the owners of the vehicles. However, in the case of causes other than these, punishment is indeed carried out. (8.290)

When the nose-rope is severed, when the yoke is broken, when the vehicle turns sideways or faces the opposite direction, and likewise when there is a breakage of the axle or the wheel of the vehicle. || 8.291 ||
In the case of the breaking of a vehicle’s yoke, its thongs, or its reins, and likewise when one cries out "Get away!", Manu has declared that there shall be no punishment. (8.292)

"Chinna" means "cutting. That which pertains to the nose is *nāsyam*; because it is a part of the body, the suffix *yat* is applied. Here, this refers to the rope connected to the nose of a draft ox. Manu states that there is no punishment for the charioteer or others when injury to living beings or destruction of property occurs through a vehicle under the following circumstances: when the nose-rope of the ox or other animal is severed; when the wooden yoke is broken; when the chariot or similar vehicle moves sideways due to uneven ground or other causes; when the axle-wood inside the wheel breaks; when the leather bindings of the machinery are cut; when the *yoktra*—the rope around the neck of the animal—is severed; when the *raśmi* (rein) or the weapon is cut; and when the driver or others loudly cries out, "Move aside! Move aside! [Manu 8.291–292].
If a vehicle turns off course due to the driver's negligence,
the owner shall be liable for the damage and must pay a fine of two hundred panas.

Regarding the phrase "wherein": where the vehicle proceeds otherwise due to the driver's lack of skill, the owner who appointed an untrained driver shall, in that case of injury, be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas]. (8.293)
If the driver is trustworthy, the driver alone deserves the punishment;
if the driver is untrustworthy, all those seated in the vehicle shall each be fined one hundred. (8.294)

Regarding the term *prājaka*: if the charioteer (*sārathi*) is skilled, then the charioteer alone deserves the aforementioned fine of two hundred and the punishment to be described later, beginning with "in the case of killing a human" (8.296), and not the owner. However, if he is unskilled, then others besides the charioteer and the owner—namely, all those mounted on the vehicle—are each to be fined one hundred for having ascended a vehicle driven by an unskilled charioteer. (8.294)
But if, being obstructed on the road by cattle or by a chariot, he should cause the death of a living being, the punishment in that case is not to be deliberated upon. (8.295)

"If he... means: if the driver, being obstructed by cattle or other animals in great numbers coming face-to-face, or by another chariot, is unable to maneuver his own chariot due to a lack of attention while driving it, and even in such a narrow space continues to urge on the horses of his own chariot, and thereby causes the death of living beings by means of those horses, the chariot, or parts of the chariot, then a punishment must indeed be inflicted upon him without hesitation. (8.295)
Regarding what the offense is like for a single transgression, he says:
"In the case of killing a human being, the guilt shall be immediate, as in that of a thief;
for large living beings such as cows, elephants, camels, horses, and so forth, it is half [of that]. (8.296)

Regarding the term "human": in that case, if a human is killed by a vehicle due to the driver's lack of attention, the punishment for the perpetrator shall be the highest amercement (uttama-sāhasa) immediately, but not the death penalty itself, because of the scriptural injunction: "In the case of large living beings, half [of the fine]. When large living beings such as cows, elephants, and so forth are killed, the punishment shall be half of the highest amercement, namely a fine of five hundred paṇas. || 8.296 ||
For the killing of small animals, the fine shall be two hundred;
but for auspicious beasts and birds, the punishment shall be fifty.

Regarding "small": for the killing of small animals—other than those specifically designated by species such as forest-dwellers and the like—and by age, such as foals and so forth, the fine shall be two hundred [paṇas]. For auspicious deer, such as the ruru and the pṛṣata, and for birds, such as parrots, swans, and cranes, when they are killed, the fine shall be fifty [paṇas]. (8.297)
For donkeys, goats, and sheep, the fine shall be five māṣas;
for the killing of a dog or a pig, the fine shall be one māṣa.

Regarding the term "donkey": for the killing of donkeys, goats, rams, and the like, the fine shall be five silver *māṣakas*. And here, the reference is not to gold *māṣakas*, because lighter fines are prescribed for each subsequent case. For the killing of dogs and pigs, however, the fine shall be one silver *māṣaka*. (8.298)
A wife, a son, a slave, a servant, and a uterine brother—when they have committed an offense, these may be beaten with a rope or a split bamboo cane. (8.299)

Regarding the word "wife": wives, sons, and others who have committed an offense may be struck with a rope or a very light bamboo splinter. Since striking is prescribed here for the purpose of discipline, this constitutes an exception to the prohibition against corporal punishment. (8.299)
But one must never strike on the back of the body, nor on the head;
for striking otherwise than this, one incurs the guilt of a thief. (8.300)

"From behind" means that even with ropes and the like, the body should be struck on the back region and not on the head. If one strikes otherwise than what has been prescribed, he shall incur the punishment for a thief, consisting of verbal censure, fines, and corporal punishment. (8.300)
Thus has the determination of punishment for assault been declared in its entirety;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the rule for the determination of punishment for a thief.
"Regarding this": this determination of the punishment for assault has been stated in its entirety. Hereafter, I shall declare the rule for the determination of the punishment for thieves. (8.301)
A king should exert the utmost effort in the suppression of thieves;
through the suppression of thieves, his fame and his kingdom increase. (8.302)

"Supreme" means that the king should exert the highest and most excellent effort in the restraint of thieves; for from the suppression of thieves comes the king's renown, and the kingdom prospers through the absence of affliction. (8.302)
For that king who is a giver of fearlessness is always worthy of worship;
indeed, his sacrificial session (sattra) is ever-prosperous, having the gift of fearlessness as its fee.

Regarding the word *abhayasya*: the particle *hi* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). That king alone who, by restraining thieves, grants fearlessness to the virtuous, is worthy of worship and becomes praiseworthy among his predecessors. A *satra* is a specific type of sacrifice, such as the *gavāmayana*. Because it is like a *satra*, that [kingdom]—having the gift of fearlessness consisting of the suppression of thieves as its sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)—always attains prosperity. For while other [sacrifices] are restricted to a fixed time and have fixed fees, this [kingdom] is for all times and has the gift of fearlessness as its fee; such is the statement. This is the figure of speech known as *vyatireka* (contrast). 8.303.
A sixth part of all merit belongs to the king who protects;
indeed, a sixth part of even demerit falls to him who does not protect. (8.304)

"From all sides" means that from a king who protects his subjects, from every employer such as a merchant and the like, and from every giver of wages such as a Vedic scholar and the like, a sixth part of their merit (*dharma*) accrues to him. And from one who does not protect them, a sixth part of the demerit (*adharma*) committed by the people would likewise accrue. Therefore, the king should diligently provide protection by suppressing thieves. Nor should it be argued that a sixth part of the merit is not appropriate for the king because he is hired for wages; for it is established by the scriptures that he is hired by the merit of a sixth part of the merit itself. (8.304)
Whatever one studies, whatever one sacrifices, whatever one gives, and whatever one worships—the king becomes a sharer of a sixth part of that through his proper protection. (8.305)
Regarding the word "yad" (that which): whatever recitation, sacrifice, gift-giving, worship of deities, and so forth anyone performs, the king obtains a sixth part of that by means of his protection.
By protecting all beings in accordance with dharma and executing those deserving of death, the king performs sacrifices every day with offerings of hundreds and thousands of sacrificial fees. (8.306)

"Protecting," it means protecting all beings—both stationary and moving, such as plants and animals—through the dharma consisting of the administration of punishment according to the scriptures; and by striking those who deserve execution, such as thieves and the like, he performs sacrifices every day with the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of a hundred thousand cows. The sense is that he thereby attains the merit arising from those acts. (8.306)
That king who, failing to provide protection, takes tribute, taxes, tolls, shares of produce, and fines, shall immediately go to hell. (8.307)

"He who does not protect" means that king who, failing to provide protection, collects from the village-dwellers the sixth part of their grain and other produce; or the *śulka* (tax) which must be collected monthly according to the rule of Bhādrapada or Pauṣa; or the *dāna* (gift/tribute), well known as being levied according to the value of goods at fixed locations for those engaged in trade by land or water routes; or the *pratibhāga*, consisting of fruits, flowers, vegetables, grass, and other offerings; or the *daṇḍa* (fine), which is to be collected daily from judicial proceedings and the like—he, upon dying, goes immediately to hell. (8.307)
They say that a king who fails to protect his subjects while taking a sixth part as tax is the one who carries away the entire impurity of all the world. (8.308)

Regarding the phrase "one who does not protect": Manu and others have declared that even a king who does not provide protection, yet nevertheless takes a sixth part of the grain and other produce as a tax, is the remover of all sins for all people. (8.308)
One should know that a king who disregards the bounds of propriety, who is an atheist, a plunderer, who fails to protect his subjects, and who devours them instead, is destined for a downward path.

"Without regard" means: one should know that a king who transgresses the boundaries of the scriptures, who denies the existence of the next world, who seizes wealth through improper punishments and the like, who fails to provide protection, and who devours his own subjects—such as camels and other beasts—is destined for hell. (8.309)
One should diligently restrain the unrighteous by three means:
by confinement, by imprisonment, and by various forms of corporal punishment. (8.310)

"Unrighteous" means that one should diligently restrain unrighteous persons, such as thieves and the like, according to their offenses by means of three methods. He states these: by means of confinement in prison, by binding with fetters and the like, and by various forms of corporal punishment such as the amputation of hands and feet. (8.310)
For by the suppression of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous, kings are constantly purified, just as the twice-born are by sacrifices. (8.311)

Regarding the phrase "by means of suppression": by suppressing those who are full of evil and by gathering in the virtuous, kings become purified at all times, just as the twice-born are purified by the great sacrifices and other rites. Therefore, one should suppress the unrighteous and favor the virtuous.
A lord who seeks his own welfare should always forgive those men who bring lawsuits against him, as well as children, the elderly, and the sick. (8.312)

"It must be forgiven": the master should forgive those who, being occupied with business, compose their petitions with difficulty, as well as children, the elderly, and the sick who submit them; he should do so desiring the benefit for himself that will be described below. (8.312)
He who endures when reviled by those in distress is exalted in heaven because of that;
he who, out of pride in his power, does not endure, goes to hell because of that. (8.313)

"He who is reviled" means he who endures being insulted by those in pain; by that, he receives honor in the heavenly world. He who does not endure it out of pride in his power goes to hell because of that. (8.1313)
A thief must go before the king with disheveled hair, running and confessing that theft, saying: "I am a man of such deeds; punish me. (8.314)
Taking up a club or a staff made of khadira wood, or a spear sharp at both ends, or even an iron rod. (8.315)

Regarding the word "rājā" (the king): regarding the word "skandena" (with the shoulder): although he will state in the section on penances (*prāyaścitta*) beginning with "A Brahmin who commits the theft of gold" (11.99), nevertheless, this passage is placed here in the section on punishments (*daṇḍaprakaraṇa*) to demonstrate that, with respect to the theft of gold, this [act] takes the form of a royal penalty. When a thief of a Brahmin’s gold has his hair disheveled and is running with speed, proclaiming, "I have stolen a Brahmin’s gold," he should go before the king carrying upon his shoulder either a club (*musala*) made of *khadira* wood, or a staff, or an iron spear (*śakti*) sharp at both ends. Then he should say to the king: "I am a stealer of a Brahmin’s gold; therefore, put me to death with this club or other weapon."

|| 8.314–315 || The wise man, having understood the nature of the world as it truly is, does not grieve; for he knows that all conditioned things are impermanent and subject to destruction. Just as a clay pot, once fashioned, inevitably breaks, so too do all formations perish; seeing this, the sage remains unperturbed. || 8.314–315 ||
Whether through punishment or through release, the thief is freed from his theft;
but by failing to punish him, the king incurs the guilt of the thief. (8.316)

"By the command" means that by depriving him of life with a single blow from a club or similar weapon, or by releasing him even while he is still alive but rendered as good as dead, the thief is liberated from that sin. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya [YDh 3.248] states:

"One who is afflicted by a blow and is as good as dead is purified, even if he remains alive. Furthermore, if the king does not strike that thief out of compassion or other such motives, the king incurs the same sin as the thief. (8.316)
The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to the one who eats his food; an unfaithful wife to her husband; a pupil and a sacrificer to their teacher; and a thief to the king. (8.317)

"An eater of food": the killer of a Brahmin transfers his own sin to one who eats food belonging to him; it is this that is intended here—that the sin of the killer of an embryo (bhrūṇahā) falls upon the eater of his food—but it does not mean that the sin of the slayer of a Brahmin is destroyed. Likewise, a wife who commits adultery transfers her sin to her husband when he condones the paramour. And a pupil casts upon his teacher the sin arising from the failure to perform the twilight devotions, fire-sacrifices, and so forth, if the teacher tolerates it. And a sacrificer deposits his sin in the officiating priest when the latter condones his transgression of the rules. And a thief delivers his sin to the king when the king overlooks it. Therefore, the king must punish the thief. (8.317)
But men who have committed sins and have been punished by kings go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed good deeds. (8.318)

Regarding the word "rājā" (king): having committed sins such as the theft of gold and so forth, men who are subsequently punished by kings go to heaven like virtuous doers of good deeds, due to the absence of obstructing demerit and by the power of previously acquired merit. Thus, it is stated that punishment, like expiation (*prāyaścitta*), is a cause for the destruction of sin. 8.318.
He who takes a rope or a water-jar from a well, or who destroys a water-station, shall receive a fine of one māṣa and shall restore that [item] to its place. (8.319)

Regarding the phrase "yas tu" (but he who): if one should take away the rope or the jar held near a well for the purpose of drawing water, or if one should break down a water-distribution house (*pānīyadānagṛha*), he shall incur a fine of one *māṣa* of gold; and as for that which is specified as a *māṣa* of gold, one should apply it accordingly.
This is because of the statement of Kātyāyana. And that rope and so forth, he shall restore to that very well. (8.319)
For one who steals more than ten jars of grain, the punishment is death;
for stealing less than that, he should be made to pay eleven times the value, and that property shall belong to the owner. (8.320)

Regarding grain: one hundred *palas* make a *droṇa*, and twenty *droṇas* make a *kumbha*. For one who steals more than ten *kumbhas* of grain, the punishment is death. This should be understood as consisting of flogging, amputation of a limb, or execution, depending on the qualities of the thief and the owner. Furthermore, for stealing less than that—from one *kumbha* up to ten *kumbhas*—if it was done secretly, he shall be made to pay a fine eleven times the value; and the owner shall be made to pay restitution for what was stolen. (8.320)
Likewise, for goods measured by weight, such as gold, silver, and the like, or for the finest garments, there shall be execution if the amount exceeds one hundred. (8.321)

"So be it. Just as death has been prescribed for stealing grain, so too, when more than one hundred *palas* of superior items—such as gold, silver, and the like, which are weighed by scales, or fine garments such as silk (*paṭṭa*) and so forth—are stolen, the death penalty must indeed be carried out. Furthermore, the equalization of the offense here must be avoided by taking into account the place, time, the thief, the substance, the owner, and the caste and qualities [of the victim]. This should be understood in the same way for what follows as well. (8.321)
But for a value exceeding fifty [paṇas], the cutting off of the hand is prescribed;
for the remainder, however, one should impose a fine eleven times the value. (8.322)

"Regarding 'fifty': for stealing more than fifty up to one hundred of the items previously mentioned, the cutting off of the hand has been prescribed by Manu and others. For the remaining cases—starting from the theft of one *pala* up to the theft of fifty *palas*—the thief shall be made to pay a fine eleven times the value of the stolen property. (8.322)
One deserves death for the theft of men of noble birth, and especially women, as well as for the theft of the most precious gems. (8.323)

"Of men" means: for the theft of persons born of noble families—especially women born of noble families—and of the finest jewels such as diamonds, lapis lazuli, and so forth, one deserves the death penalty. 8.323.
In cases of the theft of large animals, weapons, or medicine, the king shall determine the punishment after considering the time and the circumstances of the act. (8.324)

Regarding "of large animals": having examined the time—such as a period of famine—and the purpose or necessity, whether good or bad, consisting of the proper or improper application of large animals such as elephants, horses, cattle, and buffaloes, as well as weapons such as swords and medicinal substances such as auspicious clarified butter, the king shall prescribe punishment in the form of beating, mutilation of limbs, or execution.
In the case of cows belonging to Brahmins, for piercing them with a sharp instrument,
and likewise for the theft of livestock, one must immediately undergo the penance of half a foot.

Regarding the verse beginning with "In the case of cows": in the event of the theft of cows belonging to a Brāhmaṇa, or of cutting the nose of a barren cow for the purpose of riding it, or of stealing goats and sheep intended for sacrifices and other such rites—because the punishment for these is more severe—one must immediately have the offender's half-foot cut off. (8.325)
Of thread, cotton, and fermenting agents; of cow dung and molasses; of curd, milk, buttermilk, water, and grass. || 8.326 ||
For the theft of vessels made of bamboo or split cane, as well as salts, and likewise for the theft of earthenware, earth, or ashes; || 8.327 ||
Of fish, of birds, of oil, of clarified butter, of meat, of honey, and whatever else originates from animals. (8.328)
For other such items as these, for raw grain, for cooked rice, and for all kinds of cooked food, the fine shall be double their value. (8.329)

Regarding the phrase "sūtra" and so forth: for stealing woolen thread and cotton thread; yeast (the substance used for fermenting liquor); water-carrying vessels and the like made from pieces of fine bamboo; whatever else originates from animals, such as deer skins, rhinoceros horns, and the like; other similar items that are mostly of little value, such as red arsenic (manaḥśilā) and so on; the twelve kinds of intoxicating liquors; cooked foods other than boiled rice, such as cakes, sweetmeats, and the like; and for the theft of well-known items such as cotton and so forth—the punishment to be imposed shall be double the value [of the stolen goods]. (8.326–329)
For taking flowers, green grain, shrubs, creepers, trees,
or other things that have not been threshed, the fine shall be five kṛṣṇalas.

"Regarding flowers," etc.: for flowers; for green standing crops in a field; for shrubs, creepers, and trees that are unenclosed—that is, those whose trunks are not fenced off—and for grains, since they are mentioned among "grains and so forth" in the verse to be cited later and because it is possible to steal them by sowing around them; and for other things that can be carried by a strong man's load—if these are stolen, the fine shall be five *māṣas* of *kṛṣṇala* gold or silver, depending on the place, time, and other circumstances. (8.330)

When grain, vegetables, roots, and fruits have been cleaned, the fine shall be one hundred panas for those who act without prior connection, and fifty panas for those who act with prior connection. (8.331)

"Parīti" means: when trees, grain, vegetables, and so forth have been cleared of chaff and stolen, "anvaya" refers to a connection with the owners of the goods; if there is no connection whatsoever, such as living in the same village, one shall be fined one hundred [paṇas]. But if there is a connection, fifty paṇas shall be paid. And this fine applies to grain situated in threshing floors, for it is there that [theft] is completed. Regarding grain in houses, an elevenfold fine has been stated previously. (8.331)

An act committed by force, provided it is accompanied by a claim of ownership, constitutes *sāhasa* (violence); whereas taking property without such a claim and then denying it constitutes *steya* (theft). 8.332.

It may be so: that act such as the theft of grain which is taken by force in the presence of the owner of the property shall be *sāhasa* (violence); for *saha* means force, and that which arises from it is *sāhasa*. Therefore, in this case, the punishment for theft (*steya*) should not be applied. It is for this purpose that this [verse] is read in the section on theft. On the other hand, that which is taken away in the absence of the owner would be theft (*steya*); and that which one takes and then denies having done so is likewise indeed theft. (8.332)
But the king shall punish first that man who steals these prepared articles, as well as he who would steal the fire from the house. (8.333)

"But he who [steals] these..."—furthermore, if a man should steal these items such as thread and so forth after they have been processed for the purpose of use, or if he should steal the three sacred fires (tretāgni) or the domestic fire (gṛhyāgni) from the fire-chamber, the king shall punish him with the first *sāhasa* fine. And the loss incurred by the owner of the fire due to the failure to maintain it must be paid. Govindarāja, however, says that there is a punishment even for one who steals a common (laukika) fire; that is incorrect, because a heavy punishment is unjust for a minor offense. (8.333)
With whichever limb a thief commits an offense against a man or a sage, the king shall take away that very limb as a deterrent. (8.334)

"With which" means: with whichever limb—such as a hand or a foot—and in whatever manner—such as by cutting a joint or the like—a thief commits an act hostile to men, such as the theft of wealth, the king shall have that very limb amputated in order to prevent a recurrence. In this regard, the amputation of the limb is determined with respect to the excellence of the owner of the property. (8.334)
Neither father, teacher, friend, mother, wife, son, nor domestic priest—there is no one who, failing to abide by his own duty, is exempt from punishment by the king. (8.335)

Regarding the word "father": among father, teacher, friend, brother, mother, wife, son, and domestic priest, he who does not abide by his own duty is not one whom the king should fail to punish; rather, he must certainly be punished. (8.335)
Where an ordinary person would be fined one kārṣāpaṇa, there the king should be fined one thousand; such is the established rule. (8.336)

Regarding the term *kārṣāpaṇa*: the settled rule is that for whatever offense an ordinary person would be fined one *kārṣāpaṇa*, for that same offense the king should be fined one thousand *paṇas*. However, he should cast his own fine into the water or give it to Brāhmaṇas, because it will be stated later [in verse 9.245]: "Varuṇa is the lord of punishment. || 8.236 ||
But for a Śūdra, the guilt in the case of theft becomes eightfold;
for a Vaiśya, it is sixteenfold, and for a Kṣatriya, thirty-twofold. (8.337)
For a Brahmin, it may be sixty-four, or even a full hundred, or twice sixty-four; for he indeed knows the faults and virtues of those [offenses]. (8.338)

"Eightfold," "of a Brāhmaṇa"—the phrase "for he knows both the faults and the virtues thereof" is to be connected with every case. Whatever punishment has been declared for a particular theft, that [punishment] is multiplied eight times for a Śūdra who knows the merits and defects of the theft; it becomes sixteenfold for a Vaiśya who knows the merits and defects; thirty-twofold for a Kṣatriya of the same description; sixty-fourfold for a Brāhmaṇa who knows the merits and defects; or, depending on the excellence of his qualities, one hundredfold or one hundred and twenty-eightfold for a Brāhmaṇa alone. (8.337–338)
Manu has declared that taking roots and fruits from trees, wood for the purpose of fire, and grass for the fodder of cows, does not constitute theft. (8.339)

Regarding the phrase "products of trees": based on the statement of Gautama, "One may take flowers from creepers and trees as if they were one's own, and fruits from those that are unenclosed," Manu declares that the roots and fruits of unenclosed trees and the like, wood for the purpose of fire-offerings, and grass for the purpose of feeding cows, when belonging to another, do not constitute theft. Therefore, there is neither punishment nor unrighteousness [in taking them].
A Brahmin who seeks wealth from the hand of one who takes what is not given—even by officiating at sacrifices or by teaching—is just like a thief. (8.340)

Regarding the word "he" (yaḥ): a Brāhmaṇa who, knowing it to be the property of another, desires to obtain wealth from the hand of a thief who has taken it without permission—even by means of officiating at sacrifices, teaching, or receiving gifts—should be known as equal to that thief; therefore, he is to be punished like him.
A twice-born man traveling on a road whose provisions are exhausted, taking two stalks of sugarcane or two roots from another's field, does not deserve to pay a fine. (8.341)
Regarding the term "twice-born": a twice-born traveler whose provisions are exhausted does not deserve a fine for taking two stalks of sugarcane or two roots from another's field. (8.341)
One who binds those who are unbound and releases those who are bound, and one who seizes slaves, horses, and chariots, shall incur the guilt of a thief. (8.342)

Regarding the phrase "of those not tied up": he who, out of arrogance, binds horses and other animals belonging to others that were unbound; or he who releases those already bound in stables and the like; or he who steals slaves, horses, or chariots—he shall incur the punishment for a thief. This punishment should be understood as consisting of execution, mutilation of limbs, or confiscation of property, according to whether the offense is grave or minor. (8.342)
By suppressing thieves according to this rule, a king shall obtain fame in this world and unsurpassed happiness after death. (8.343)
"By this": by means of this aforementioned method, a king who exercises restraint over thieves shall obtain renown in this world and supreme happiness in the next world. || 8.343 ||
Now he speaks of rashness: "A king who desires to attain the station of Indra and imperishable, undecaying fame should not overlook a man of rashness even for a moment. (8.344)

Regarding the word "Aindra": desiring to pre-eminently attain the station characterized by universal sovereignty, as well as imperishable and inexhaustible fame, a king must not, even for a moment, overlook a man who commits arson or theft from his own house by force.
A man who commits violence through harsh speech, theft, or indeed by means of physical punishment, should be known as the worst among evildoers. (8.345)

Regarding the word "speech": it should be understood that among those who commit verbal abuse, thieves, and those who inflict physical violence, the person who commits an act of *sāhasa* (heinous violence) is the most preeminent evildoer. (8.345)
But that king who tolerates one who persists in violence quickly meets with destruction and incurs hatred. (8.346)

Regarding "violence": that king who tolerates one engaged in violence perishes through his neglect of evildoers and his inclination toward unrighteousness; furthermore, because his kingdom is being oppressed, he incurs the hatred of the people. (8.346)
A king should not, for the sake of friendship or from the acquisition of vast wealth, release those who act with violence and bring fear to all living beings. (8.347)

"Not out of friendship": even because of a friend's word or through the acquisition of great wealth, the king must not abandon those who commit acts of violence that cause fear to all living beings. (8.347)
The twice-born may take up arms when their duty is obstructed, or during a upheaval of the twice-born and the social orders caused by the exigencies of time. (8.348)
In defending oneself, in a conflict over sacrificial fees, and in coming to the aid of women and Brahmins, one who kills according to dharma does not incur sin. (8.349)

Regarding the term "the treatise" (*śāstra*) and "and for oneself": the three castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, may take up weapons such as swords. At a time when it is not possible for the castes and those in the stages of life (*āśrama*) to practice their duty (*dharma*) due to acts of violence and the like; likewise, when the three castes find themselves in kingdoms without a king, encountering the arrival of a foreign army and the like, or when they face situations such as sexual assault against women; and furthermore, for the sake of self-protection, for the purpose of repelling an attack on their sacrificial fees, wealth, cattle, and so forth, or in battle for the protection of women and Brāhmaṇas—by slaying enemies through righteous war (*dharmayuddha*) out of necessity and having no other recourse—one does not incur sin. Even in this case of killing another, the punishment for violence (*sāhasadaṇḍa*) shall not be imposed. (8.348–349)
Whether it be a teacher, a child, an elder, or a learned Brāhmaṇa—one should indeed slay an approaching assassin without hesitation. (8.350)

"Or a teacher" (*guruṃ vā*): One may, without hesitation, kill anyone among teachers, children, the elderly, or learned Brahmins who approaches intent on killing, provided that person is superior in learning, conduct, and so forth; this applies even if one is unable to escape by fleeing and other means. For this very reason, Uśanas says: "There is no fault in killing an armed assailant (*ātatāyin*). And Kātyāyana, by mentioning the word *bhṛgu*, has clearly explained the verse of Manu itself: "In the case of an assailant who is superior in asceticism, Vedic study, or birth, there shall be no sin in killing him; however, O Bhṛgu, if he is inferior, there is death [as a penalty]."

Medhātithi and Govindarāja, however, explain that this is a restatement of the preceding [verse], based on the rule: "And by killing for the sake of protecting a woman or a Brahmin, one does not incur sin according to dharma. They argue that it implies one may even kill a teacher or similar person, let alone anyone else. (8.350)
No fault whatsoever attaches to the slayer for killing an assassin, whether done openly or in secret; it is simply fury recoiling upon fury. (8.351)

"No," [it is said]. Whether in public or in private, for one who kills another intent on murder, there is no punishment for unrighteousness (*adharma*) known as expiation (*prāyaścitta*), nor any fault incurred. This is because the wrath residing in the slayer—a deity presiding over anger—intensifies the anger residing in the victim. Furthermore, in cases of violent assault (*sāhasa*), punishments such as the amputation of limbs corresponding to the parts used, or the confiscation of wealth, should be imposed according to the gravity of the offense. (8.351)
Now he describes the offense of adultery: "The king, having branded with terrifying punishments those men who have set out to violate another's wife, shall banish them. (8.352)

Regarding adultery: he should brand with marks such as the removal of the nose or lips those groups of men who have engaged in sexual intercourse with the wives of others, using punishments that cause them agitation, and then banish them from the country. (8.352)
For from that arises the intermingling of castes among the world, by which unrighteousness, which destroys the very root, leads to total ruin. (8.353)

Regarding the word "that": because from approaching another's wife, the intermingling of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*) comes about; and through that intermingling of castes, since there is an absence of sacrificers with pure wives, the rule—"An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun" (3.76)—no longer holds. In the absence of this, the destruction of the root of the world known as rain occurs; thus, unrighteousness (*adharma*) results in the destruction of the world. (8.353)
A man who engages in private conversation with another's wife, having been previously accused of such offenses, shall incur the first amercement. (8.354)

Regarding the phrase "of another": due to such faults as soliciting that man's wife, a person who—without any legitimate cause—engages in conversation with the wife of another, having been previously subject to accusations, solicitations, or curses, shall incur the first amercement as a fine. (8.354)
But he who, having previously been unaccused, speaks out for a valid reason, shall incur no fault whatsoever, for there is no transgression on his part. (8.355)

"But as for him... (8.355): furthermore, he who, previously free from the curse of soliciting that woman, should engage in conversation with her in the presence of people for some reason, shall not incur the fault of being subject to punishment or other such penalties; therefore, there is no offense on his part.
He who addresses another's wife at a sacred bathing place, in a wilderness, or even in a forest, or at the confluence of rivers, shall be guilty of adultery. (8.356)

[The word] *pari* [in the verse] is merely an illustration for desolate places such as riverbanks, forests, groves, and the like.
