That man who converses with another’s wife on a path leading down to water, in a forest outside a village thick with shrubs and creepers, in a secluded place, in a wood dense with many trees, or at the confluence of rivers—even if previously unaccused—shall incur the punishment of one thousand *paṇas* which will be described; this is called *saṃgrahaṇa*. It is so called because by it the desire for sexual union with another’s wife is properly grasped (*samyaṅ gṛhyate*) and known. (8.356)
Attending upon her, playful dalliance, touching her ornaments and garments, and even sitting together on the same bed—all this is recorded as *saṃgrahaṇa* (adultery). 8.357.

Regarding "courtship" (*upacāra*): the performance of courtship such as sending garlands, perfumes, ointments, and so forth; "play" (*keli*), which consists of joking, embracing, and the like; the touching of ornaments and garments; and sitting on the same bed—all this is recorded by Manu and others as "sexual intercourse" (*saṃgrahaṇa*). 8.357.

If a man touches a woman in an improper place, or if he allows himself to be touched by her when it is mutually agreed upon, all such acts are recorded in the legal tradition as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse).

Regarding the phrase "a woman": if one touches a woman on a part of her body such as the breasts or the hips—which is improper to touch—or if he is touched by her on a part such as the testicles and consents to it, then that mutual acceptance of contact is recorded by Manu and others as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse). 8.358.
A non-Brahmin who commits adultery deserves a punishment ending in death;
for the wives of all four castes must always be protected most carefully. (8.359)

Regarding the term "non-Brāhmaṇa": here, the non-Brāhmaṇa is the Śūdra, because of the severity of the punishment. For violating a Brāhmaṇa woman who does not consent when it is a case of adultery with a superior woman, one incurs the death penalty. Among all four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, wives—along with wealth, sons, and so forth—are to be protected at all times above all else. (8.359)
Beggars, prisoners, those initiated for sacrifice, and artisans may converse with women without being forbidden. (8.360)

"Beggars" refers to those who live on alms, reciters of praises, those initiated for the sake of a sacrifice, cooks, and so forth; they may engage in conversation with housewives for the purpose of their own tasks, such as begging, without restriction. Thus, there is no prohibition against their sexual intercourse. (8.360)
One who has been forbidden should not engage in conversation with the wives of others; but one who, having been forbidden, nevertheless converses, deserves a fine of one suvarṇa. (8.361)

"Regarding 'no conversation': if forbidden by his master, he shall not engage in conversation with women. One who, having been prohibited, nevertheless practices such conversation, becomes liable to pay a fine of sixteen māṣas of gold to the king. (8.361)
This rule does not apply to the wives of wandering performers nor to those who live off their own wives;
for they entice women and keep them hidden away. (8.362)

"Not this one": the injunction prohibiting conversation, beginning with "he who addresses another's wife" (8.356), does not apply to the wives of actors, singers, and the like. Likewise, because it has been stated that "the wife and the son are one's own body" (4.18), there is no such prohibitory rule even regarding those other than actors and the like who treat their wives as themselves for the sake of gaining wealth and tolerate their paramours. This is because performers and those who live off their own wives bring in other men and cause them to unite with their wives; and when other men come of their own accord, they conduct affairs while remaining concealed, feigning ignorance of the situation. (8.362)
But he who engages in conversation with such women shall be made to pay a small fine;
the same applies to female slaves who eat only once a day and those who have entered a religious life in secret. (8.363)

"Something" [is meant]: if a man converses with women who subsist by wandering as bards in a deserted place, the king shall cause him to pay a small portion of a fine, for they too are the wives of others. Likewise, if he converses with female slaves, women kept [as concubines], Buddhist nuns, or female students (*brahmacāriṇī*), he shall be made to pay merely a small fine. (8.363)
He who violates an unwilling maiden deserves immediate execution;
but a man who violates one who is willing, being equal to her in status, shall not suffer death. (8.364)

"Regarding 'one who [approaches] unwillingly': he of equal caste who approaches a maiden against her will deserves, at that very moment, death consisting of the cutting off of his organ and so forth, provided he is other than a Brāhmaṇa; however, one who approaches a willing woman does not deserve death as a human being. (8.364)
One should not cause a maiden who is associating with a superior man to pay anything at all;
however, one who is serving an inferior man should be kept confined in the house. (8.365)

"Regarding the maiden": he shall not cause even a small fine to be imposed on a maiden who, for the sake of sexual enjoyment, serves a man of superior caste; however, he should take great care to ensure that she does not serve a man of inferior caste, or else bring about such measures as will cause her desire to cease. (8.365)
But a man of lower caste who has intercourse with a woman of the highest caste deserves death;
if he has intercourse with a woman of equal caste, he should pay a fine, provided her father desires it. 8.366.

"An excellent woman" (uttamām): if a man of lower caste approaches a woman of superior caste who desires him or does not desire him, he deserves a punishment consisting of the amputation of his limbs or death. However, if he approaches a woman of equal caste who desires him, and if the father consents, then he shall either pay a sum of money corresponding to the bride-price (*śulka*) or nothing at all, and he is not to be punished; moreover, that maiden must be married by him alone.
But that man who, out of arrogance, violates a maiden by force, his two fingers shall be immediately cut off, and he deserves a fine of six hundred [paṇas]. (8.367)

"By force": if a man, by means of force—that is, through compulsion—excluding sexual intercourse with a woman of his own caste, should destroy her honor merely by the thrusting of a finger out of arrogance, his two fingers must be cut off immediately, and he shall be fined six hundred paṇas. (8.367)
One who defiles a willing woman shall not suffer the same punishment as one who cuts off her finger;
however, he shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred panas to prevent a recurrence. 8.368.

"Regarding 'one who desires it': if a man of the same caste destroys an unmarried girl who consents by the mere act of inserting a finger, he does not incur the cutting off of his fingers; however, to prevent excessive abuse, he shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas]. (8.368)
If a girl herself should defile another girl, she shall be fined two hundred panas;
she must also pay double the nuptial fee (śulka) and receive ten lashes with a rod. (8.369)

"Even a maiden" means: she who, while still a maiden, should destroy another [maiden] by casting her finger [into the fire], shall receive a fine of two hundred [paṇas]. She shall also pay double the maiden-price (*kanyāśulka*) to the father of the maiden and receive ten lashes with a whip. (8.369)
But a woman who violates a maiden deserves immediate shaving of the head, or else the cutting off of two fingers, as well as being led away on a donkey. (8.370)

"But as for her... (verse 8.370): Furthermore, that woman who destroys a maiden by means of inserting a finger shall, at that very moment, deserve the shaving of her head; depending on the circumstances, the cutting off of those very fingers, and being paraded on a donkey along the royal highway. 8.370.
But that woman who, arrogant because of her kinsmen or her own virtues, should transgress against her husband,
the king shall have her devoured by dogs in a public place crowded with people.

Regarding the word "husband": if a woman, out of pride in her powerful father, kinsmen, or wealth, and out of pride in her own beauty and other virtues, should transgress against her husband by approaching another man, the king shall have her devoured by dogs in a place crowded with many people. (8.371)
They should cause the sinful man to be burned on a heated iron bed;
they should pile wood upon it, and there the evildoer shall be consumed by fire. (8.372)

"Regarding the man": the king shall cause the man just mentioned—the paramour who has committed a wicked deed—to be burned on a blazing iron bed. On that bed, the executioners shall place logs until the evildoer is consumed by fire.
For a wicked man who has been accused for a year, the fine shall be double;
likewise for cohabiting with a *vrātyā* woman or a *caṇḍālī* woman, it shall be exactly that much.

Regarding the verse beginning with *saṃvatsare*: for a man who has committed adultery with another’s wife and remains unpunished, if he is accused again after a year has passed, a fine double the previous one must be imposed. Likewise, there is a specific punishment prescribed for approaching the daughter of a *vrātya*—which, by its mention alongside the *caṇḍālī*, takes the form of approaching a *caṇḍālī* woman—and the punishment for approaching a *caṇḍālī* woman is stated as: "But [a fine of] one thousand [paṇas] for an outcaste woman" (8.385). If, after a year has elapsed, he approaches that same daughter of a *vrātya* or that same *caṇḍālī* woman again, then a double fine must be applied. These two examples are provided to illustrate the application of the *caṇḍālī*-penalty even in the case of approaching a *vrātya*-daughter; however, it should be understood that for anyone previously accused or punished, if they approach that same woman again after a year has passed, a fine double the previous amount is to be understood. (8.373)
A Śūdra who cohabits with a woman of the twice-born castes, whether she be guarded or unguarded, is deprived of his limb if she was unguarded, and of his entire property if she was guarded. (8.374)

Regarding the verse beginning with *śūdra*: if a Śūdra should have intercourse with a woman of the twice-born castes—whether she is protected by her husband or otherwise—he, if he approaches one who is unprotected (meaning devoid of guardianship), shall be deprived of his penis and all his property. Although no specific limb is mentioned here, the cutting off of the penis (*liṅgoddhāra*) applies to approaching an Ārya woman, based on Gautama’s statement: “For violating a guarded woman, there is the seizure of all property; for [an unprotected] one, death is the additional penalty” (GDh 12.2–3). However, if he approaches a protected woman, he should be deprived of both body and wealth. (8.374)
A Vaiśya shall be punished with the forfeiture of all his property after being imprisoned for one year;
a Kṣatriya shall be fined one thousand [paṇas] and deserves to have his head shaved with urine.

Regarding the Vaiśya: if a Vaiśya has sexual intercourse with a guarded Brāhmaṇa woman, after a year’s imprisonment, a punishment consisting of the confiscation of all his property must be imposed. However, regarding intercourse with a Kṣatriya woman, the author will state later: "If a Vaiśya [approaches] a Kṣatriya... (8.382). A Kṣatriya, upon having sexual intercourse with a guarded Brāhmaṇa woman, is to be fined one thousand [paṇas], and his head must be shaved with donkey urine.
If a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya should have intercourse with an unguarded Brāhmaṇa woman,
the king should fine the Vaiśya five hundred [paṇas] and the Kṣatriya one thousand.

Regarding the term "Brahmin woman": if a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya has intercourse with an unprotected Brahmin woman, then he should impose a fine of five hundred on the Vaiśya, and a fine of one thousand on the Kṣatriya. This fine of five hundred for a Vaiśya applies specifically to the case of having intercourse with a Brahmin woman who is of low character, belonging to a mere caste by birth, and subsisting only on that status—such as a Śūdra woman or one who is deluded. In the case of intercourse with a Brahmin woman other than that, even for a Vaiśya, the fine is indeed one thousand. (8.376)
But both of them, having violated a protected Brahmin woman, shall be punished like Śūdras or burned in a fire of straw. (8.377)

"Both": both of those two, the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, having committed sexual intercourse with a protected Brāhmaṇa woman, are to be punished like a Śūdra—that is, they are to be deprived of everything—or else they are to be wrapped in straw and burned. In this regard, the specific rule stated by Vasiṣṭha—"having wrapped the Vaiśya in red *darbha* grass and the Kṣatriya in reed-leaves" (VaDh 21.2)—is to be adopted. Since it was previously stated that "the Kṣatriya is to be fined one thousand [paṇas]" (8.375) and "the Vaiśya his entire property" (8.375), this penalty involving the loss of life should be understood as applying to cases of approaching a Brāhmaṇa woman who possesses virtuous qualities. || 8.377 ||
A Brahmin who approaches a guarded Brahmin woman by force shall be fined one thousand; he who has sexual intercourse with a willing woman shall be fined five hundred. (8.378)

"Regarding the word 'thousand': a Brāhmaṇa who approaches by force a protected Brāhmaṇa woman shall be fined one thousand [paṇas]. But if she consents, he shall be fined five hundred for a single act of sexual intercourse. (8.378)
Shaving the head is prescribed as the punishment for a Brāhmaṇa whose life is at stake;
however, for the other castes, the punishment shall be one that ends in death. (8.379)

"Shaving the head": for a Brāhmaṇa, shaving the head is prescribed by the scripture as the punishment in place of the penalty of death; however, for Kṣatriyas and others, the punishment consists of the aforementioned execution. (8.379)
One must never kill a Brahmin, even if he is established in every kind of evil; one should banish him from the kingdom, leaving him with all his wealth and unharmed. (8.380)

"Never," and so forth: one must never kill a Brāhmaṇa even if he is a perpetrator of every possible crime; rather, one should banish him from the kingdom, stripped of all his possessions but with his body unharmed. (8.380)
No greater unrighteousness exists on earth than the killing of a brahmin;
therefore, a king should not even contemplate his execution in his mind. (8.381)

"No," [he replied]. "There is no greater unrighteousness on earth than the killing of a Brahmin. Therefore, a king should not even conceive in his mind the thought of killing a Brahmin who has committed every possible sin. (8.381)
If a Vaiśya should approach a protected Kṣatriya woman, or a Kṣatriya a protected Vaiśya woman, they both deserve the same punishment as one who approaches an unprotected Brāhmaṇa woman. (8.382)

Regarding the phrase "if a Vaiśya": if a Vaiśya should approach a protected Kṣatriya woman, or if a Kṣatriya should approach a protected Vaiśya woman, then for those two, the same two punishments that were prescribed for approaching an unprotected Brāhmaṇa woman—namely, "one should fine the Vaiśya five hundred and the Kṣatriya one thousand" (8.376)—apply to the Vaiśya and the Kṣatriya respectively. This fine of five hundred for a Vaiśya who approaches a protected Kṣatriya woman, being lighter, should be understood to apply to a Vaiśya of good qualities who approaches a Kṣatriya woman of low merit who subsists by her caste alone, under the delusion that she is a Śūdra or similar circumstances. For a Kṣatriya who knowingly approaches a protected Vaiśya woman, a fine of one thousand is appropriate. (8.382)
A Brahmin, however, moving with those two while they are guarded, shall be made to pay a fine of one thousand;
for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya having intercourse with a Śūdra woman, the punishment shall indeed be one thousand.

"Thousand," and so forth. When a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya has been protected [by the king], a Brāhmaṇa who approaches her should be made to pay a fine of one thousand [paṇas]. When a Śūdra woman has been protected, the fine for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who has sexual intercourse with her shall likewise be one thousand. (8.383)
If he discharges urine upon a protected Kṣatriya woman, the fine for a Vaiśya is five hundred;
but a Kṣatriya shall undergo tonsure with urine, or else pay a fine. (8.384)

Regarding the phrase "in the case of a Kṣatriya woman": for a Vaiśya who has sexual intercourse with an unprotected Kṣatriya woman, the fine shall be five hundred [paṇas]. But for a Kṣatriya who has sexual intercourse with an unprotected [Kṣatriya] woman, he shall undergo shaving with donkey's urine or incur a fine of five hundred [paṇas]. (8.384)

A Brāhmaṇa who approaches an unprotected Kṣatriya woman, a Vaiśya woman, or a Śūdra woman shall be fined five hundred; but if he approaches a woman of the lowest castes (antyaja), he shall be fined one thousand.

Regarding the phrase "unprotected": if a Brāhmaṇa approaches an unprotected woman of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra caste, he shall be fined five hundred [paṇas]. An *antyaja* is one who exists at the end; since there is no one lower than the Caṇḍāla and others, if he approaches the wife of such a person, he shall be fined one thousand [paṇas]. (8.385)
That king in whose city there is no thief, no adulterer, no speaker of evil words,
and no perpetrator of violence or one who strikes with punishment, partakes in the world of Śakra.

"Of whom": that king who has no thief, no adulterer, no speaker of harsh words, no perpetrator of violent acts such as arson, and no one who inflicts physical violence—he, that king, goes to the city of Śakra. (8.386)
The suppression of these five within his own realm by a king brings him imperial power over his kinsmen and confers glory upon him in the world. (8.387)

"Of these": of these five, beginning with the thief, the king who exercises restraint within his own kingdom among kings of the same caste becomes a sovereign ruler and attains glory in this world. (8.387)

If a sacrificer should abandon an officiating priest, or if an officiating priest should abandon a sacrificer—provided that he is capable of the task and free from fault—the punishment for both of them shall be one hundred [paṇas] each. (8.388)

Regarding the term "officiating priest" (*ṛtvij*): if a person for whom one acts as a sacrificer (*yājya*) abandons an officiating priest who is capable of performing the rites and free from such faults as mortal sins (*atipātaka*), or if the officiating priest abandons a sacrificer who is faultless, a fine of one hundred [paṇas] each shall be imposed upon them. This was stated here in connection with the subject of punishments.
Neither mother, nor father, nor wife, nor son deserves to be abandoned. He who abandons these when they have not fallen from their status shall be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king. (8.389)

"Not [abandoning] one's mother": parents, wife, and sons do not deserve abandonment, which consists of failing to provide for them, failing to nourish them, or failing to serve them. Therefore, if one abandons these persons who are free from such sins as *pātaka*, the king shall fine him six hundred [paṇas] for each individual abandonment. (8.389)
When twice-born men in their hermitages dispute with one another regarding their duties, a king who desires his own welfare should not pronounce a legal decision himself. 8.390.

Regarding the phrase "in the stages of life" (āśrameṣu): when twice-born men have arisen into mutual dispute concerning matters pertaining to the stages of life, such as the householder's stage, as to whether "this is the meaning of the scripture" or "this is not the meaning of the scripture," the king, desiring his own welfare, should not specifically declare "this is the meaning of the scripture" to those who are partial.
Having honored these men as was fitting along with the brahmins, the king, having first pacified them with gentle words, should establish them in their own duty. (8.391)

"According to what is fitting" means: having honored each person with such worship as they deserve, and having first made them free from anger through affection together with other Brahmins, one should then instruct them in their own specific duty. 8.391.
If a Brahmin fails to feed his immediate neighbor and next-door neighbor—who are worthy and among the twenty invited twice-born at an auspicious rite—he deserves a fine of one māṣaka. (8.392)

Regarding the term *prātiveśya*: a *prātiveśya* is one who dwells in an adjacent house; one who dwells in a house immediately beyond that is an *anuveśya*. At a festival where twenty other Brahmins are fed, if one fails to feed the *prātiveśya* and *anuveśya*—who, according to the statement of Viṣṇu, "and he who bypasses an adjacent Brahmin," are both worthy of being fed as Brahmins—the Brahmin incurs a fine of one silver *māṣa* here, since gold and other materials are prescribed for him later on. (8.392)
If a learned man does not feed another learned and virtuous man during auspicious ceremonies, he shall be made to pay double the value of that food, as well as one *māṣaka* of gold. (8.393)

Regarding the term "learned in the Vedas" (*śrotriya*): one who possesses knowledge and proper conduct—such a virtuous person, when invited to a social function such as a marriage or other similar occasion, must be fed; if the neighbor or the next-door neighbor fails to feed him, they shall be compelled by the king to pay twice the amount of food that was eaten, as well as a *māṣaka* of gold. (8.393)

One who is blind, mentally infirm, a cripple who moves about on a board, one who is seventy years old or older, and one who renders service to those learned in the Vedas—none of these shall be made to pay tax by anyone. (8.394)

"Blind" means blind or deaf; "lame" means seventy years of age. Regarding the word "seventy," the instrumental case is used according to the Vārttika: *prakṛtyādibhya upasaṃkhyānam* (Vārt. 2.3.18). Those who provide assistance to learned Brahmins (*śrotriyas*) through wealth, grain, service, and so forth, should be favored by the king—even if his treasury is depleted—and should not be made to pay taxes. (8.394)
The king should always honor one learned in the Vedas, those afflicted by illness or pain, children, the elderly, the destitute, those of noble lineage, and the virtuous. 8.395

Regarding the term "learned in the Vedas" (*śrotriya*): the king should always honor with gifts, respect, and acts of benefit a Brāhmaṇa who possesses learning and good conduct, one who is afflicted by illness, one distressed by the loss of a son or other misfortunes, as well as those who are young, old, poor, born of noble lineage, or of generous character.
On a smooth board made of *śālmalī* wood, a washerman should wash clothes slowly;
he should not rub one garment against another, nor should he let them dry together.

Regarding the word *śālmalī*: on a board made from the wood of the *śālmalī* or similar trees, which is rough, the washerman should wash the garments very slowly; he should not transfer clothes belonging to one person onto the garments of another, nor should he give the clothes of one person for the purpose of wearing by another. If he should act in this manner, he would be subject to punishment. (8.396)
A weaver shall give ten palas [of yarn] and receive one pala more;
if he acts otherwise than this, he shall be made to pay a fine of twelve [paṇas]. (8.397)

Regarding the weaver: for the purpose of making cloth, the weaver, having taken ten *palas* of thread, should give back eleven *palas* of cloth after the addition of flour, food, and other materials. If he should give less than that, he must be made to pay twelve *paṇas* to the king, and the satisfaction of the owner must certainly be secured. (8.397)
Those skilled at customs houses and expert in all types of merchandise shall determine the value according to the commodity; the king shall take one-twentieth as tax.

Regarding "śulka": *śulka* is the portion to be taken by the king from transactions involving land and water routes. From the profit derived from merchandise—after deducting what those skilled in its valuation and knowledgeable of the quality and worth of all goods determine to be the appropriate price for those commodities—the king shall take a twentieth part. (8.398)
If one, out of greed, exports those goods of the king that are well-known or prohibited, the king shall confiscate his entire property. (8.399)

"Of the king": whatever commodities are known to belong to the king, such as elephants, horses, and so forth, which are useful to the king, as well as those produced in that country which are prohibited—such as "during a famine, grain must not be taken to another region"—if a merchant, out of greed, takes these to another region, the king shall confiscate all his property. (8.399)
One who evades a customs station, one who buys or sells at an improper time,
or one who gives a false account in the reckoning of goods, shall be made to pay a fine eight times the amount of the duty.

"Regarding the customs station": he who goes by a wrong path in order to evade customs duties; or who conducts buying and selling at an improper time, such as at night and so forth; or who states a low value for the merchandise to be sold for the purpose of defrauding the customs office—he shall be made to pay eight times the amount of what was denied to the king as a fine. (8.400)
Having investigated the importation, exportation, and storage, as well as both the increase and decrease of all commodities, he should regulate their purchase and sale. (8.401)

Regarding "import" (*āgama*): he should cause the import and export of all commodities to be conducted in such a way that no hardship arises for either merchants or buyers. He must investigate: from what distance has the foreign commodity been imported; to what distance is the domestic product being exported; for how long has it been stored, and what price does it fetch; likewise, what is the rate of profit, and what is the depletion incurred by laborers due to food, clothing, and other expenses? Having considered these factors, he should regulate the buying and selling of all goods. (8.401)
Every five nights, or else every fortnight when it has passed,
the king should personally settle their legal matters.

Regarding the term *pañcarātra*: because commodities such as those subject to fluctuation in arrival and departure, or in demand and supply, have unstable prices, the king—through trustworthy agents—should personally establish regulations for merchants who know the market rates every five nights when prices have become relatively stable, or every fortnight [in other cases]. (8.402)
All scales and measures should be well-marked;
every six months, one should inspect them once again. (8.403)

He should weigh [the goods]. Whatever standard measure—such as a *prastha* or a *droṇa*—is used for the purpose of determining weights such as gold and so forth, all of that must be duly regulated; every six months having passed, the king should have it all re-examined by court officials. (8.403)
A vehicle shall be made to pay one paṇa at a ferry; for a man’s load, half a paṇa;
an animal and a woman, a quarter; and an empty-handed man, half of a quarter. (8.404)

Regarding the word *paṇa*: as he will state [in verse 8.405], "Vehicles laden with goods," by this it is meant that an empty cart or similar vehicle must pay one *paṇa* for crossing. Likewise, a person carrying a load must pay half a *paṇa* as the toll for crossing; and an animal such as a cow must pay a fourth part of a *paṇa*; a man without a load is to be made to pay an eighth part of a *paṇa*. || 8.404 ||
O Bhārata, vehicles filled with goods shall be made to pay the ferry toll;
those with empty vessels, as well as men without belongings, shall pay whatever little they can. (8.405)

Regarding the term *bhāṇḍa*: carts and other vehicles filled with merchandise are to be made to pay a ferry-toll (*tara*) in proportion to the excellence of the goods they carry. Blankets, woolen cloths, and so forth, which contain goods, are to be made to pay whatever small amount is appropriate as a toll. Those without possessions—the poor—are to be made to pay whatever little is possible, relative to the payment required for the aforementioned items. (8.405)
On a long journey, one should know how to cross according to the location and the time; this applies to riverbanks, but there is no such fixed sign for the ocean.

Regarding the word "long" (*dīrgha*): previously, it was mentioned in the context of crossing from one shore to the other (*pārāvāra*). Now, when traveling along a river route over a long distance, the ferry fare (*taramūlya*) must be determined in consideration of the place—such as a river with strong currents or obstructed waters—and the time—such as summer or the rainy season. This is to be understood as applying to rivers. However, on the ocean, because the movement of the ship depends upon the wind and thus lacks independence, there is no fixed measure such as two *yojanas* or more to indicate specific ferry fares as there is for rivers. Therefore, in that case, whatever fare is appropriate should be taken. (8.406)
A pregnant woman in her second month or beyond, as well as a wandering ascetic,
a sage, Brāhmaṇas, and those bearing religious marks, shall not be made to pay a ferry-toll when crossing a river.

"A pregnant woman" refers to a woman who has conceived and is more than two months advanced in pregnancy; likewise, a renunciant monk, a sage (muni) who is a forest-dweller (vānaprastha), Brāhmaṇas, and those bearing the marks of religious students (brahmacārin)—these shall not be made to pay the ferry fare. 8.407.
Whatever on a ship may be damaged through the fault of the boatmen, that must be paid by the boatmen themselves, having assembled together, each from his own share. (8.408)

Regarding the term *nāvīti*: whatever property has been lost by those aboard a ship due to the fault of the boatmen must be restored by the boatmen themselves, having pooled their resources, according to their respective shares. (8.408)
This has been declared as the legal decision regarding those traveling by boat:
in the case of water damage caused by the fault of the boatmen, there is no dispute; however, in the case of an act of God, there is no liability. (8.409)

Regarding the phrase "this [is the case]": whatever is lost in the water due to the fault of the boatmen must be paid back by the boatmen themselves. The previously mentioned statement, "there is no dispute regarding what is caused by fate," was restated in order to establish the legal decision specifically for those traveling by boat. When there is a loss of wealth or other property due to the breaking of a boat caused by wind and so forth arising from fate, there is no punishment for the boatmen. (8.409)
One should cause the Vaiśya to practice trade, money-lending, and agriculture, as well as the tending of cattle; and the Śūdra [should perform] service for the twice-born. (8.410)

"Trade" refers to this: the king should cause the Vaiśya to engage in trade, money-lending, agriculture, and the tending of cattle; and he should cause the Śūdra to perform service for the twice-born. This instruction here is for the purpose of ensuring that the Vaiśya and the Śūdra, if they fail to do so, shall be punished by the king.
A Brāhmaṇa should support with compassion a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who are distressed for a livelihood, making them perform their own respective duties.

Regarding the term "kṣatriya": if a Brāhmaṇa, out of compassion, causes a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya—who have been reduced to the status of servants—to perform his own tasks such as protection or agriculture, he should support them with food, clothing, and so forth. Thus, it is understood from the force of the context that a wealthy Brāhmaṇa who does not maintain those two when they have approached him for support is to be punished by the king. (8.411)
But a Brāhmaṇa who, out of greed, compels initiated twice-born men to perform servitude against their will through the exercise of his power, shall be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king. (8.412)

Regarding the term "servitude": *prābhavyam* is the state of being a master (*prabhavataḥ*). A Brāhmaṇa who, out of greed for his power over twice-born men who have undergone the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) and who do not consent, compels them to perform servile tasks such as washing his feet, shall be fined six hundred [paṇas].
But one may cause a Śūdra to perform service, whether he was purchased or not;
for he was created by the Self-existent One solely for the service of the Brāhmaṇa. (8.413)

"But a Śūdra," however: one may cause even a Śūdra—whether supported by food and other provisions or not—to perform service; therefore, he was created by Prajāpati solely for the service of the Brāhmaṇa. (8.413)
Even if released by his master, a Śūdra is not freed from servitude;
for that is innate to him, so who can remove it from him? (8.414)

"Not by the master," [it is said]. Because he has entered into servitude through being seized under a banner (*dhvajāhṛta*) and so forth, even if his own state of slavery is relinquished by that [master], a Śūdra is not released from service to a Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, servitude is innate to the Śūdra; who can remove this servitude, which is like the caste of Śūdra itself? This [verse] is intended to show that even for the sake of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*), a Śūdra must necessarily perform service to the twice-born, such as Brāhmaṇas and others. Otherwise, the enumeration of the performance of servitude to be mentioned later would be purposeless. (8.414)

One captured under a banner, one who is a slave by being given as food, one born in the house, one purchased, one given, one inherited from an ancestor, and one enslaved as a punishment—these seven are the origins of slavery. (8.415)

Regarding the term *dhvaja*: one who is conquered in battle from the presence of his master; a *bhaktadāsa* (slave for food), who has accepted servitude out of greed for sustenance; likewise, the son of a female slave; one purchased for a price; one given by another; one descended through the lineage of a father or other ancestors; and one who has entered into a state of slavery to clear a debt such as a fine—these seven, beginning with "captured under a banner" (*dhvajāhṛta*), are the causes for the condition of slavery. (8.415)
A wife, a son, and a slave—these three alone are declared to be without property;
whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they themselves belong. 8.416

Regarding the term "wife": these three—the son, the wife, and the slave—are traditionally declared by Manu and others to be without property. This is because whatever wealth they acquire belongs to him to whom they belong as a wife and so forth. Furthermore, this is intended primarily to demonstrate the dependent status of the wife and the others; for the six kinds of women’s property, beginning with that acquired at the nuptial fire, will be described later. Moreover, it is for the purpose of instructing on rites for visible ends that require wealth, and because—even though the wife's entitlement to perform sacrifices has been stated in the section on the wife—it is established that when husband and wife possess a single estate, the woman also possesses agency by way of consent.
A Brahmin may confidently take property from a Śūdra;
for he has nothing of his own, as his wealth is to be taken by his master. 8.417

"Confidently" means that a Brāhmaṇa may indeed take wealth from the aforementioned slave or Śūdra without any hesitation, because he possesses no property of his own whatsoever; for such a person's wealth is to be taken by his master. Thus, this is stated for the purpose of ensuring that a Brāhmaṇa, even if taking wealth from a slave by force during a time of distress, shall not be punished by the king. (8.417)
One should cause the Vaiśya and the Śūdra to perform their own duties with diligence; for if they fall away from their respective duties, they would throw this world into turmoil. (8.418)

Regarding the word "vaiśya": the king should diligently cause the Vaiśya to perform his duties such as agriculture and the like, and the Śūdra to perform his duties such as service to the twice-born. For if these two deviate from their own duties, they would throw the world into disorder by seizing wealth acquired through unscriptural means and by giving [it away] improperly.
Day by day he should inspect his undertakings and his vehicles, as well as his fixed income and expenditure, his mines, and his treasury. (8.419)

"Day after day": every day, through the officials in charge thereof, the king should supervise the completion of undertakings for visible and invisible purposes. Likewise, he should inspect the elephants, horses, and so forth—asking what has entered today and what has departed—as well as the sources of gold and gems, and the treasury. Although it was already stated that even when occupied with the administration of justice, the king must not neglect his duties, this is mentioned again to emphasize that point. (8.419)
Thus, by settling all these legal cases, the king, having cast off all sin, attains the supreme goal. || 8.420 ||
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Mānava Dharmaśāstra*, in the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu.

"In this manner" means: by thus bringing these entire legal proceedings, beginning with the non-payment of debts (*ṛṇādāna*), to their conclusion through a factual determination, one casts off all sin and attains the supreme goal consisting of the attainment of heaven and other such states. (8.420)
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Manvarthamuktāvalī, a commentary on the Laws of Manu composed by the illustrious Kullūkabhaṭṭa.
The Ninth Chapter.
I shall declare the eternal laws for a man and a woman who abide in the path of righteousness, both in their union and in their separation. 9.1

Regarding the phrase "of the man": for the sake of the dharma of both the man and his wife—who abide on the path characterized by mutual non-deviation and who are joined together and separated—I shall declare their eternal duties as they have been handed down through tradition. This instruction is given within the context of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) so that, when there is a transgression of each other’s duties between husband and wife, the king must establish them in their own respective duties even by means of punishment, should one or the other be found lacking. (9.1)
Women must be kept under control by their own men day and night; even when they are becoming attached to sensual objects, they must be established in one's own power. 9.2

"Dependent" means that women must always be kept under the control of their own [relatives], such as husbands and others. Even when attached to objects such as forms and tastes that are not forbidden, they must be kept under their own [family's] authority. || 9.2 ||
The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth; in old age, the sons protect her. A woman does not deserve independence. 9.3

Regarding the word "father": before marriage, the father shall protect the woman; afterwards, the husband; and in his absence, the sons. Therefore, a woman should never, under any circumstances, assume independence. The statement that "the husband protects her in youth" and so forth is merely general, for even when she has no husband or sons and is present [at home], she must be protected by her father and others. (9.3)

A father who does not give [a daughter] in marriage at the proper time is censurable; a husband who does not approach his wife is censurable; and when the husband has died, a son who does not protect his mother is censurable. (9.4)

Regarding the "proper time": if the father does not give her away at the proper time for giving, he becomes blameworthy. According to the statement of Gautama, "The giving [of the girl] is before puberty" (GDh 18.3), the period prior to puberty is the time for giving. Furthermore, if the husband does not approach his wife during the fertile season, he becomes censurable. And if the son does not protect his mother after her husband has died, he would be reprehensible. (9.4)
Women must be protected especially from even the slightest of attachments;
for if they are not guarded, they will bring sorrow to both families. 9.5

"From even the slightest," etc.: Women must be protected especially from even minor bad associations that lead to immoral conduct, let alone from major ones; for if they are neglected in their protection, they will cause distress to both groups of fathers and husbands. (9.5)
For seeing this supreme dharma common to all castes, husbands strive to protect their wives, even if they are weak. (9.6)

Regarding the word "this": even those who are blind, lame, and so forth, knowing that the duty characterized by the protection of one's wife—pertaining to all classes such as the Brāhmaṇas—is superior to all other duties according to the manner of the verses to be cited, should strive to protect their wives. (9.6)
For by protecting his wife with diligence, he indeed protects his own offspring, his conduct, his lineage, himself, and his own dharma. (9.7)

"His own" (svām): because by protecting his wife, he protects—by means of procreating offspring that are unmixed and pure—his own lineage, as well as the conduct of the learned, the ancestral succession of father and grandfather, and himself through the attainment of the rewards for the afterlife resulting from a pure descent; and he also protects his own dharma, since only one with a pure wife is entitled to the rites of conception and so forth. Therefore, "he should strive to protect women"—this is the specific point of the preceding verse. (9.7)
The husband, having entered his wife, becomes an embryo and is born here;
for that indeed is the "wifehood" (jāyātva) of the wife, because he is born again from her. 9.8.

Regarding the term "husband" (*pati*): the husband, having entered his wife in the form of semen (*śukra*) and brought about a conception, is born from that wife in the form of a son. Thus says the Śruti: "Truly, you are the self (*ātman*) whose name is 'son'" (ĀśGṛ 1.15). It is precisely because the husband is born again from her that she possesses the status of a "wife" (*jāyā*). Accordingly, the Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇa states: "The husband enters the wife, becoming an embryo here in the mother;
having become new within her, he is born again in the tenth month."
She becomes his wife because he is born again from her.
And for this reason—that she must be protected—there is this etymological explanation of her name. 9.8.
For whatever kind of man a woman associates with, she gives birth to a son of that same kind;
therefore, for the sake of the purity of offspring, one should guard women with great effort. (9.9)

"Of what kind" means this: because whatever kind of man—whether enjoined or prohibited by the scriptures—a woman associates with, she gives birth to a son who is superior through associating with a man prescribed by the scriptures, or inferior through associating with a prohibited man. Therefore, for the sake of the purity of offspring, one should diligently protect one's wife. (9.9)
To the question "How is she to be protected? he says:
No one is able to protect a woman by force;
however, through the application of these means, they can be protected. (9.10)

"No," [he says]. No one is able to protect women even by forceful restraint and the like, for even in that case, infidelity is observed. However, they can be protected by the employment of these means of protection which are about to be described. (9.10)
He states those means:
"One should employ her in the gathering of wealth and in its expenditure, as well as in cleanliness, religious duty, the cooking of food, and the supervision of household utensils. (9.11)

"Of wealth" (arthasya): she should be employed in the accumulation and expenditure of riches; in the purification of household goods and the person; in service to the husband and the sacred fires; in the preparation of food; and in the supervision of domestic utensils such as beds, seats, bowls, and cooking pots. [The form "avekṣaṇe" is derived from *ava-īkṣ*, with the elision of the initial vowel. 9.11.
Those women who, though confined at home by trustworthy male guardians, protect themselves by their own selves, are well-protected. (9.12)

"Unprotected" means: even those who are trustworthy and obedient, if they are confined at home by such men, remain unprotected because they do not protect themselves due to their lack of virtue. However, those who protect themselves by their own selves through knowledge of the Dharma—they alone are well-protected. Therefore, this verse is intended to state the primary means of protection: that restraint must be exercised over them by instructing them on the fruits of dharma and adharma, such as the attainment of heaven or hell. 9.12.
Drinking, association with wicked people, separation from her husband, wandering about, sleeping, and living in another's house—these are the six things that corrupt women. 9.13.

"Drinking" refers to the drinking of intoxicants, association with wicked men, separation from her husband, wandering here and there, sleeping at improper times, and residing in the houses of others—these six things produce the fault known as infidelity in a woman. Therefore, she must be guarded against these. (9.13)
They do not examine his form, nor is there any regard for their own age; whether he is handsome or ugly, they enjoy him simply because he is a man. (9.14)

"Not these," [he says]. These women do not deliberate upon the beauty of form; nor do they have regard for age, such as youth and so forth. Rather, they enjoy him merely on the grounds that he is a man, whether handsome or ugly. (9.14)

"Because of their proclivity toward men, because of their fickle minds, and because of their natural lack of affection, these women act perversely toward their husbands even when guarded with great effort in this world. (9.15)

Regarding the phrase "due to their profligacy": because they are by nature inclined toward the desire for sexual enjoyment upon seeing men, because they lack stability of mind, and because they are naturally devoid of affection, these women—even when guarded with great effort in the world—undergo a change of heart toward their husbands by resorting to infidelity. (9.15)
Having thus understood their nature as born from the creation of Prajāpati, a man should exert the greatest effort toward their protection. (9.16)

"Thus. Having understood in this way the nature of these [qualities] as described in the two verses—nature produced at the time of Hiraṇyagarbha’s creation—a person should exert supreme effort for the sake of protection. (9.16)
Manu assigned to women the bed, the seat, ornaments, lust, anger, straightforwardness, malice, and bad conduct. (9.17)

Regarding the word "śayyā" (bed): From the beginning of creation, Manu ordained for women the habits of lying down, sitting, and adorning themselves, as well as lust, anger, lack of straightforwardness, injury to others, and reprehensible conduct. Therefore, they must be guarded with great effort. (9.17)
"There is no ritual action for women through mantras; such is the established rule in the Dharma.
For women are without [Vedic] authority and devoid of mantras; 'women are untruth'—this is the settled conclusion. (9.18)

"There is not. This is the established limit of the scriptures: that for women, rites such as the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*) and others do not exist when performed with mantras. Consequently, because they lack the collection of sacraments accompanied by mantras, their inner organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) are not purified of sin. Since the senses are the means of knowledge, and because they are devoid of the *śruti* and *smṛti* which are the authorities on *dharma*, they do not know *dharma*. Being "without mantras" means they are destitute of the recitation of mantras that remove sin; therefore, even if sin has arisen, they are incapable of its purification. "Women are impure like falsehood"—this is the limit of the scriptures. Therefore, the essential point here is that they must be protected with great effort. (9.18)
Likewise, many Vedic verses have been chanted even in the Nigamas;
listen now to their expiations for the purpose of examining their specific characteristics. 9.19.

"And so it is. It has been stated that the nature of women is to be prone to infidelity. In this regard, he cites scripture as authority. "In like manner," many scriptural passages—that is, numerous Vedic statements such as "We do not know this: whether we are Brahmins or non-Brahmins"—have been recited in the *Nigamas* to define their specific characteristics, namely their proneness to infidelity, for the purpose of recognizing them. Among those scriptures, listen to those which take the form of expiation (*niṣkṛti*), serving as penances for infidelity. Since only one scripture will be mentioned, the meaning is "listen to the scripture. The plural form is used for the singular accusative according to the rule *supāṃ supo bhavanti* (Pāṇini 7.1.39). || 9.19 ||
"Whatever my mother, wandering about unfaithful to her husband, lusted for—that seed let my father take up"; this is the illustration of that. (9.20)

Regarding the word "yat" (that which): a certain son, having perceived his mother’s mental transgression, says: "She who does not desire any man other than her husband through the actions of mind, speech, and body is a *pativratā* (faithful wife); any other than that is an *apativratā*. My mother is unfaithful and unchaste; she goes to the houses of others. That which she craved—that greed arose toward another man—may my father purify that seed in the form of the mother’s *rajas* (menstrual blood), which is defiled by the intention (*saṃkalpa*) for that man. These three lines of the mantra, ending with the particle "iti," serve as evidence for the woman's habit of sexual misconduct. And this mantra is employed in the *Cāturmāsya* and other rites. (9.20)
Now he states that this mantra serves as an expiation for mental transgression:
"Whatever undesirable thing one contemplates with the mind while grasping at living beings—the complete removal of such a transgression is here rightly declared. (9.21)

Regarding the phrase "she meditates": this mantra under discussion is declared by Manu and others to be a complete purifier of that mental transgression which a woman contemplates in her mind—namely, any act disagreeable to her husband, such as going to another man. Because of the mention of the word "mother," this mantra is of the nature of an expiation for the son alone, not for the mother. (9.21)
Whatever the qualities of the husband with whom a woman is united according to the prescribed rule, such qualities she acquires, just as a river does when it joins the ocean. (9.22)

"By whatever quality" means: in whatever form—whether good or bad—a woman is united with a husband through the rite of marriage, she comes to possess qualities similar to those of her husband. Just as a river, though possessing sweet water, becomes salty when joined with the ocean. This [verse] is intended to teach another method for protecting women, namely, the husband's self-respect. (9.22)
Regarding this, he states an example of excellence: "Akṣamālā, though born of a low womb, attained honor through union with Vasiṣṭha; Śāraṅgī reached a state of venerability through Mandapāla. (9.23)

Regarding "Akṣamālā": she who was known as Akṣamālā, born of a lowly womb, was married by Vasiṣṭha; likewise, Caṭakā, having united with the sage named Mandapāla, attained a state of venerability. (9.23)
These and other women in this world, though born of lowly origin, have attained eminence through their own respective auspicious qualities as wives. (9.24)

Regarding the word "these": although only two [types of women] are under discussion, the plural form "these" is used with the view that these two serve as illustrative examples. These and others, such as Satyavatī and the like, though born of low origins, attained preeminence in this world through the superior qualities of their husbands. (9.24)

Thus has been declared the auspicious conduct for men and women in their worldly life, which brings about happiness in this world and the next; now learn the duties regarding progeny that result in future well-being.

"This," [the author] says: "This conduct of the world regarding husband and wife has been declared as always auspicious. Now, hear the duties concerning progeny—such as 'Is the offspring of the owner of the field or of the sower?'—which are the causes of future welfare and happiness in this world and in the next. (9.25)
For the sake of the people, O highly fortunate ones, women are worthy of honor and are the lights of the home;
between them and the goddesses of fortune (Śrī) in households, there is no distinction whatsoever.

"Regarding the phrase 'for the sake of progeny': although faults have been mentioned for the purpose of guarding them, nevertheless, because they can be countered, there is no fault here. These women are of great benefit, being the vessels of much auspiciousness for the sake of producing offspring; they are worthy of equal treatment through the giving of clothing, ornaments, and so forth, and they bring beauty to their own home. Women are like the Goddess Śrī within houses; no distinction exists between the two. Just as a house does not shine when devoid of Śrī, so it is when devoid of women. (9.26)
Moreover:
"The procreation of offspring, the protection of those born, and the daily course of worldly life—women are the visible foundation for all this. (9.27)

Regarding "procreation": the birth of offspring, the nurturing of those born, and the daily worldly affairs such as the feeding of guests and friends—the wife alone is the manifest cause of all this. (9.27)
Offspring, religious duties, service, and supreme delight—these depend upon the wife; likewise, heaven for both one's ancestors and oneself depends upon her. (9.28)

Regarding the term "offspring": although the procreation of offspring has already been mentioned, it is stated again here for the purpose of making known its preeminent importance. Duties pertaining to dharma, such as the *agnihotra* and other rites; service; excellent sexual pleasure; and heaven for both the ancestors and oneself through the procreation of offspring and so forth—all this is dependent upon the wife. (9.28)
She who does not deceive her husband, being restrained in mind, speech, and body, attains the worlds of her husband and is called "virtuous" by the righteous. (9.29)

"Regarding the husband": by the force of employing the qualification "being self-restrained in mind, speech, and body," it follows that she who does not commit infidelity through mind, speech, or body alone attains the worlds such as heaven acquired together with her husband; and in this world, she is called a distinguished virtuous woman (sādhvī). 9.29.
But through infidelity with her husband, a woman incurs reproach in this world;
she enters the womb of a jackal and is tormented by sinful diseases. (9.30)

"Because of infidelity": through contact with another man, a woman incurs censure in this world and attains the species of a jackal in another birth; she is also afflicted by evil diseases and the like. Although these two verses were already stated in the fifth chapter under the duties of women (*strīdharma*), they are recited again here because they serve the great purpose of ensuring the birth of virtuous offspring. (9.30)
Listen to this meritorious discourse, beneficial to all people, which has been proclaimed by the virtuous and by the great seers of old concerning a son. (9.31)

"Regarding the son": listen to this deliberation concerning the son—which has been previously declared by the cultured ones such as Manu and by the great seers born of old—and which is for the benefit of all people, as it shall now be told. 9.32.

They recognize the son as belonging to the husband, yet there is a conflict of scriptural authorities regarding the husband; some say he is the progenitor, while others know him to be the owner of the field.

Regarding the word "of the husband" (*bhartuḥ*): the sages consider that he who is the husband's son becomes his son. Regarding the husband, there exists a twofold scriptural tradition (*śruti*). Some say that even one who has not wedded her, but is the biological progenitor, is the husband; by such a son, they declare him to be a father of a son. Others, however, say that the one who has wedded her is the husband, even if he is not the progenitor; by a son begotten by another, they declare him to be a father of a son. (9.32)
A woman is considered to be the field, and a man is considered to be the seed; from the union of the field and the seed arises the birth of all embodied beings. 9.33

Regarding the phrase "as a field": a field is the locus for the production of rice and other crops; women are remembered by the sages as being similar to that. And the man is remembered as being similar to the seed of rice and so forth. Although semen is the seed, nevertheless, because it is the substratum [of that seed], the man is designated as "the seed. From the union of the field and the seed, all living beings are produced. Thus, since the causality of both is indistinguishable, a conflict of views is logical: is the offspring of him to whom the field belongs, or of him whose seed it is? (9.33)
In some cases the seed is superior, while in others it is the female womb;
but where both are equal, that offspring is highly praised. (9.34)

Regarding the term "distinguished" (*viśiṣṭa*): in some cases, the seed (*bīja*) is predominant, as in the case of one born according to the principle stated in [Manu 9.160], "those who are begotten on an unauthorized woman," such as the wise Budha, who was the son of Soma; likewise, Vyāsa, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, and others are considered the sons of the seed-providers alone. In other cases, the field (*kṣetra*) is predominant, as he will state [in 9.167]: "he who is born from the bed of one who has died. For this very reason, although Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the others were produced by Brāhmaṇas, they became Kṣatriyas—the sons of the owner of the field—because they were born in the field of Vicitravīrya, who was a Kṣatriya. However, where there is equality between the seed and the womb, the offspring produced by the husband himself is considered praiseworthy; in that regard, they speak first with respect to the predominance of the seed.
Between the seed and the womb, the seed is said to be superior;
for the birth of all beings is indeed characterized by the nature of the seed. (9.35)

Regarding the phrase "of the seed": between the seed and the field, the seed is declared to be primary. For the origin of all things composed of the elements is seen to be characterized by the marks such as the color, form, and other qualities residing in the seed. (9.36)
Whatever kind of seed is sown in a field prepared at the proper time, such a crop grows there from that seed, manifested by its own inherent qualities. (9.36)

"Of whatever kind" means: whatever type of seed—such as rice and so forth—is sown in a field prepared by rain and other means during the summer season or other times, that very same type of seed, characterized by its own color and other qualities, grows in that field. (9.36)
Having thus demonstrated the predominance of the seed by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), he speaks in order to show it by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*):
"For this earth is called the eternal womb of beings;
yet the seed does not nourish any of the qualities of the womb during its growth. (9.37)

"This" (*iyam*)—the particle *hi* is used for emphasis. This very earth is said by all people to be the eternal womb, the cause, and the field-nature (*kṣetrātmaka*) of trees, shrubs, creepers, and so forth, which have originated from the elements. Furthermore, the seed does not partake of any of the properties of the womb called "earth"—such as its nature as clay and so on—during its own transformations in the stages of the sprout, the stalk, and so forth. Since the root *puṣ* has the sense of "to partake," it takes an object. Therefore, because there is no conformity to the qualities of the womb, the field is not predominant. (9.37)
Moreover:
Even in a single field on the earth, seeds sown at the proper time by farmers arise here in various forms according to their own nature. (9.38)

"Upon the earth": even in a single field on the earth, the various forms of rice, mung beans, and so forth, sown by farmers at the time of planting, arise according to the nature of the seeds themselves; they do not become uniform simply because the earth is one. (9.38)
For instance: rice, śāli paddy, mung beans, sesame, kidney beans, as well as barley, garlic, and sugarcane, sprout according to their respective seeds. (9.39)

Regarding the phrase "rice-grains": rice-grains such as the *ṣaṣṭika* variety, as well as *śāli* rice, *kalama* rice, and so forth, and likewise mung beans and other such things, arise in various forms without overstepping the inherent nature of their seeds. (9.39)
And this being so, it is not tenable that one thing is sown and another is born;
for whatever seed is sown, that very same thing sprouts forth. (9.40)

"Something else": it is not possible for rice sown to produce mung beans or other such crops; rather, whatever seed is sown, that very same thing is produced. Thus, because the qualities of the seed are followed and the characteristics of the field are not, the predominance of the seed applies even to rice and so forth among human beings. || 9.40 ||
Now he speaks of the preeminence of the field:
"Therefore, by a wise and disciplined man who understands both theoretical knowledge and practical realization, and who desires long life, seed must never be sown in another's wife. (9.41)

Regarding the word "that": that seed is the Veda, which is knowledge [taught] by fathers and others who possess innate wisdom (*sahajaprajñā*); likewise, specialized knowledge (*vijñāna*) refers to the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) and other treatises. One who knows this and desires long life must never sow it in the wife of another. 9.41.
Regarding this, those who know the past recite verses sung by Vāyu:
"Just as a seed should not be sown by a man in what belongs to another... (9.42)

Regarding this: in this matter, those who know the past recite verses proclaimed by Vāyu—sentences composed in specific meters—such as: "The seed must not be sown by one man in the wife of another. (9.42)
Just as an arrow, once shot, vanishes from the sight of one who continues to pierce the air where it was struck, so too does a seed sown in another's possession quickly perish. 9.43

"It perishes" means as follows: just as when a black antelope has been pierced by one [hunter], and another person subsequently shoots an arrow through that very same opening, the shot arrow becomes fruitless because it was already struck down by the first killer, who alone gains possession of that deer; in the same way, seed sown in another's wife quickly becomes fruitless, because the owner of the field immediately obtains the fruit upon the conception of the embryo. (9.43)
Those who know the past understand that even this earth was the wife of Pṛthu;
they say that a field belongs to him who clears away the stumps, and a deer to him who inflicts the arrow-wound. (9.44)

"Of Pṛthu": because this earth was formerly taken possession of by Pṛthu, people who know the past call her "the wife of Pṛthu," even though she has been connected with many kings. Therefore, there is the expression *sthāṇuccheda* ("cutting down a sacrificial post"); the suffix *aṇ* is used here in the sense of the object. They say that the field belongs to him alone by whom the sacrificial post was uprooted and the field cleared. Likewise, they call that deer "the arrow" (*śalya*) belonging to him by whom the arrow was first discharged at it when it was dead. And thus, since ownership belongs to the original taker, the offspring belongs only to the husband and not to the biological father. (9.44)
"The person is only this much: wife, self, and offspring—so the wise have said; likewise, he who is the husband is remembered as the woman. (9.45)

"To this extent" means that a person (*puruṣa*) is not merely one individual; rather, a person consists of this very measure: the wife, oneself, and the offspring. Thus says the Vājasaneyi Brāhmaṇa: "She is indeed half of one's own self; therefore, he who does not find a wife is not procreated, for until then he remains incomplete. But when he finds a wife, then he is procreated; then he becomes whole. And so the Brahmins who know the Vedas say: "He who is the husband is remembered as being the same as the wife."
And thus, the offspring produced in her belongs to the husband alone; for this reason, there is a unity between husband and wife. (9.45)
A wife is not released from her husband by means of sale or abandonment;
thus we know the law established of old by Prajāpati. (9.46)

"No," [it is argued]. "Purchase" (*niṣkraya*) means sale; "abandonment" (*visarga*) means relinquishment. A woman does not depart from her husband's status as wife through these two acts. Thus, we consider this to be the eternal duty (*nitya-karma*) remembered by Prajāpati in the past. And so, even if one has made another's wife one's own through purchase or other means, the offspring produced therein belongs only to the owner of the field (*kṣetrin*), not to the owner of the seed (*bījin*). (9.46)
A share of inheritance falls but once; a daughter is given in marriage but once;
"I give"—these three things are said but once by the virtuous. (9.47)

"Once," and so forth. The division of the father’s wealth and other property among brothers is performed once according to the law (*dharma*), and it is not done otherwise. Likewise, a maiden is given by her father and others once to one man, and she is not given again to another. Thus, even if she was previously given to one by another and later obtained by her father and others, the offspring born from her does not belong to the biological father (*bījī*). This is the purpose of this statement. Similarly, regarding things other than a maiden, such as cattle and the like, he says "I give once," meaning that it is not given again to another. These three things are done once by the virtuous (*sādhu*). Although the fact that the giving of a maiden is performed once is relevant to the present subject, nevertheless, the singularity of the division of shares is also mentioned incidentally. Even though the singleness of the maiden's gift is established by the very phrase "he says once, 'I give,'" it is mentioned separately precisely because it is relevant to the present context. (9.47)
Just as one who fathers offspring from cows, mares, camels, slave-women, buffaloes, goats, or sheep does not receive a share of their produce, so it is likewise with the wives of others. 9.48

"As follows": Just as one who produces a calf by separating his own bull from the cows of another does not share in that [calf], so too one who procreates upon the wives of another does not share in the offspring. 9.48.
Those who possess seeds but have no field, and sow them in another's field, never obtain any fruit of the crop that has grown. (9.49)

"Those who" refers to those who are not the owners of the field. Now, if those who are the owners of the seed sow that seed in another's field, they do not obtain anywhere in any region the fruit—such as grain and so forth—produced from that field; this is the illustration for the subject at hand.
If a bull were to sire a hundred calves upon the cows of another, those calves belong only to the owner of the cows; the bull's seed was spent in vain. (9.50)

"Regarding the phrase *yad anyeti*: if a bull were to sire even a hundred calves upon the cows belonging to another, all those calves would belong to the owner of the female cows (*strīgavī*) alone, and not to the owner of the bull. The emission of semen by the bull is entirely fruitless for the owner of the bull. By the verse *yathā go’śvoṣṭra-* (9.48), an example was given with the intent that the progenitor does not share in the offspring; this [verse], however, is intended to show that the owner of the field (*kṣetrasvāmin*) does share in the offspring. Therefore, there is no tautology. (9.50)
In the same way, those who possess no field but sow their seed in another's field benefit the owner of the field; the owner of the seed does not obtain the fruit. (9.51)

"In the same way": just as in the case of cows and other animals, so too those who, being themselves childless, sow their seed in the wife of another, produce for the owner of the field the result known as offspring; the sower of the seed, however, does not obtain the fruit called offspring. (9.51)
But when no fruit is intended for either the owner of the field or the sower, the benefit belongs clearly to the owner of the field; for the womb is more important than the seed. (9.52)

Regarding the phrase "the fruit": where no such agreement has been made—namely, that "whatever offspring shall be born of her shall belong to both of us"—there the offspring undoubtedly belongs to the owner of the field (*kṣetrin*). According to the reasoning stated, the field is more powerful than the seed. (9.52)
But when this [gift] is given for the sake of the seed because of an agreement regarding the labor, both the owner of the seed and the owner of the field are seen here as sharers in it. (9.53)

Regarding the term *kriyā*: when a field is delivered by its owner to a seed-sower under the stipulation, "Whatever offspring shall be born here shall belong to us both," both the seed-sower and the owner of the field are seen in the world to be the two sharers of that offspring.
The seed carried by a deceptive wind that sprouts in someone else’s field belongs to the owner of that field alone; the sower does not receive the fruit. (9.54)

"Or like a seed": when a seed is brought from another's field by the force of water or the wind and grows in a certain field, that seed belongs to the owner of that field alone; he who sowed the seed does not obtain its fruit. And thus, even if one goes to another man's wife under the delusion that she is one's own wife, and perceives, "This child shall be mine," it is shown by this [verse] that the offspring belongs to the owner of the field (the husband). (9.54)
This law regarding the offspring of cattle, horses, female slaves, camels, goats, sheep, birds, and buffaloes should be understood. (9.55)

"Regarding this": this very same rule is to be understood with respect to the offspring of cows, horses, and so forth; namely, that the owner of the field alone is the owner of the offspring of the cow or horse, but not the owner of the bull or stallion. However, when a formal agreement has been made, the ownership of the offspring belongs to these two [the owner of the field and the owner of the male animal] alone. (9.55)
Thus has been proclaimed to you the essential and the worthless nature of seed and womb;
hereafter, I shall declare the duty of women in times of distress. 9.56

"Regarding this": this predominance and non-predominance of the seed and the womb has been explained to you. Immediately following this, I shall state what must be done when women lack offspring. (9.56)
She who is the wife of an elder brother is the wife of a guru to the younger;
but she who is the wife of the younger brother is considered the daughter-in-law of the elder. (9.57)

"Of the brother": the wife of the elder brother is the teacher's wife for the younger brother; and the wife of the younger brother is recorded by the sages as the daughter-in-law of the elder brother. (9.57)

An elder brother who approaches the wife of his younger brother, or a younger brother who approaches the wife of his elder brother— even if they are authorized to do so— become outcasts, unless there be a time of distress.

Regarding the term "eldest": if an eldest and a youngest brother go to each other's wife—even if they were authorized [to do so]—they both become outcasts (*patita*), provided there is no lack of offspring [to be produced]. (9.58)
When the lineage is in danger of extinction, a woman who has been duly authorized by her husband or by a sapinda relative may obtain the desired offspring. (9.59)

Regarding the phrase “from the husband’s brother” (devarāt): in the absence of offspring, a woman authorized by her husband or other elders may procreate desired progeny by approaching—either the husband’s brother or another sapinda—another man who observes the rules to be described, such as being anointed with ghee and so forth. The use of the term “desired” (īpsitāḥ) implies that she may approach again for the purpose of producing a son capable of performing religious duties if the first son is incapable. (9.59)
But one appointed to a widow, being anointed with ghee and remaining silent, shall produce only one son at night, and never a second under any circumstances. (9.60)

Regarding the term "widow": this refers to the absence of offspring capable of producing further progeny. Even while her husband is still living, if she is appointed by her elders to produce offspring because she is otherwise incapable, she should—having anointed all her limbs with clarified butter and observing silence—give birth to one son at night, but never a second under any circumstances. (9.60)

Some who know the truth consider procreation with women to be the second [debt], seeing that the purpose of the appointment (niyoga) between those two has not yet been fulfilled according to dharma. (9.61)

"Second": other teachers, however, who understand the injunction for procreating a son, considering that the purpose of the *niyoga* is not yet fulfilled based on the saying of the learned, "one without a son has but one son," consider the procreation of a son with [another man's] wives to be the second [duty] according to dharma. (9.61)
But when the purpose of the appointment regarding the widow has been accomplished according to the rule, the two should behave toward each other like a father-in-law and a daughter-in-law. (9.62)

Regarding the phrase "in the case of a widow": when the purpose of the *niyoga*—namely, the conception of an offspring by a widow or similar woman—is accomplished in accordance with the scriptures, the eldest brother and the wife of the younger brother shall behave toward each other as a father-in-law and a daughter-in-law. (9.62)

If those two, being appointed, should act according to their own desire, setting aside the prescribed rule, they would both become outcasts, like one who violates his daughter-in-law or one who violates the bed of his teacher. (9.63)

"Regarding the phrase 'the two appointed': if the elder and younger brothers, having been appointed to each other's wife, should act according to their own will, abandoning the prescribed rule of being anointed with ghee and so forth, they both become outcasts (patita) for approaching their daughter-in-law and their teacher’s wife. (9.63)
Having thus stated the injunction, he speaks in order to refute it:
"A widow must not be appointed to another man by the twice-born;
for those who appoint her to another would destroy the eternal dharma. (9.64)

"Not with another" means that a widow must not be appointed by Brāhmaṇas and others to have sexual union with anyone other than her husband, such as a brother-in-law or similar relative. By appointing a woman to another man, they would destroy the dharma of women's having only one husband, which is established from time immemorial. (9.64)
Nowhere in the mantras pertaining to marriage is the practice of *niyoga* mentioned;
nor is the remarriage of a widow prescribed in the rules for wedding ceremonies. (9.65)

Regarding the phrase "not in those [mantras] pertaining to marriage": in mantras such as "Aryaman, the god... (ĀśGṛ 1.7) and others used for the purpose of marriage, the practice of *niyoga* is not mentioned in any branch of the Veda (*śākhā*). Furthermore, in the scriptures prescribing marriage, a remarriage with another man is nowhere stated. (9.65)
Indeed, this practice of treating humans like animals was censured by learned brahmins even while Vena was ruling the kingdom. (9.66)

"This" refers to the fact that this practice associated with cattle-keeping, which was declared as a duty to be performed by King Vena while he ruled—a king who was unrighteous—is censured even by learned men among humans. Therefore, because it originated starting from Vena, it is condemned as having a beginning. (9.66)
In former times, that most excellent of royal sages, while ruling over the entire earth,
brought about the intermixture of the social orders, his mind being struck down by lust.

"He [ruled] the earth": that Vena, while formerly protecting the entire earth, was thus the best of royal sages not by virtue of his righteousness, but because his intellect was impaired by lust; he initiated the confusion of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*) consisting of approaching the wives of his brothers.
From that time forward, the virtuous censure anyone who, out of delusion, employs a woman whose husband has died for the sake of obtaining offspring. (9.68)

Regarding the word "then" (*tataḥ*): from the time of Vena onwards, the virtuous invariably censure that man who, out of knowledge of the meaning of the scriptures, appoints a woman whose husband has died—or for whom he is otherwise ineligible—to have intercourse with a brother-in-law or similar relative for the sake of obtaining offspring. Furthermore, this prohibition of *niyoga* stated by himself refers specifically to the Kali Yuga. As Bṛhaspati says:
"The practice of *niyoga* was indeed taught by the Sage, but it was himself prohibited;
due to the succession of the ages, it is impossible for others to perform it according to the prescribed rules."
In the Kṛta and Tretā Yugas, men were endowed with austerity and knowledge;
however, in the Dvāpara and Kali Yugas, a decline in the power of men has indeed been ordained.
Sons have been produced in many ways by the ancient seers; they cannot be produced now by those of the present day who lack such power.

Therefore, we do not respect that which Govindarāja—unaware of the specific regulations for the different ages (yugas)—imagined by his own wit, namely that the position of non-appointment (*aniyoga*) is always superior to appointment (*niyoga*) in the absence of offspring; for this contradicts the explanations of the sages.
Indeed, in the majority of Manu’s verses, it is the interpretation of the sages alone [that is authoritative].
I am not at fault in the eyes of the learned; for where am I, a person of dull intellect, compared to those who know all things?
Since this is the section concerning *niyoga*, he states the specific rule regarding a maiden:
