"If the husband of a maiden dies after the verbal betrothal has been made, her own brother-in-law shall wed her according to this following procedure. (9.69)

Regarding the phrase "of whom": if the husband of a maiden should die after the betrothal has been performed, her brother from the same womb (uterine brother) shall marry her according to this procedure that is about to be described. (9.69)
Having approached her according to the prescribed rule—she who is clad in white garments and observes pure vows—he shall unite with her once in each fertile season until the birth of a child. (9.70)

"According to the prescribed rule": having accepted her through the marriage rite, that brother-in-law should approach her in private during each menstrual period until conception—provided she is dressed in white garments and possesses purity of body, speech, and mind—only once at a time. Thus, because this is the method of appointment (*niyoga*) for the maiden and because no formal marriage has been performed, the offspring belongs to the very man to whom she was verbally betrothed. (9.70)
A wise man, having given his daughter to one, should not give her again;
for by giving her away once more after she has been given, he incurs the sin of lying regarding a human being.

"Having not given": having verbally promised a maiden to someone, if that person dies, one who understands the merits and defects of giving should not give her to another. For by giving her to another after she has been given to one, one incurs the fault of a "lie regarding a man," as stated in the verse, "A thousandfold for a lie regarding a man" (8.98). This statement is made because, since the taking of the seven steps has not occurred, the status of wife is not yet established, and there might otherwise be a suspicion of her being given again. (9.71)
Even after accepting her according to the prescribed rites, one may abandon a bride who is blameworthy, diseased, corrupted, or one who was offered through deception. (9.72)

Regarding the phrase "according to the rule": even after accepting a girl in accordance with the injunctions beginning with "only with water [as the fee] for the foremost of the twice-born" (3.35), one may abandon her if she is found to possess the marks of widowhood, is diseased, is tainted by such curses as having had her virginity violated, or has been presented under the pretext of concealing a physical deformity such as an extra limb—provided this is known before the taking of the seven steps (*saptapadī*). Therefore, the purpose of this is that there is no fault in abandoning her once she is so discovered, not that she is to be abandoned as a matter of course. (9.72)
But if one should bestow a maiden who has defects without having disclosed them, he shall annul that gift of the evil-minded giver of the bride. (9.73)

"But he who," etc. Furthermore, if one gives away a girl who possesses defects without disclosing those defects, one should render void that gift by returning her to that evil-minded giver of the girl. This also is for the purpose of stating that there is no fault in such a renunciation.
A man who has business abroad should depart after providing for his wife's livelihood;
for a woman, even one of steadfast character, may fall into corruption when distressed by a lack of means. (9.74)

Regarding the phrase "having made provision": when there is a necessity, a man may go to another country after having provided for his wife’s food, clothing, and so forth. For, if she is distressed by the lack of food and other necessities, even a virtuous woman might seek contact with another man. (9.74)
If her husband has gone abroad after providing for her maintenance, she should live observing the prescribed rules;
but if he has gone abroad without providing for it, she should live by means of blameless crafts.

"Having provided," etc.: having given food, clothing, and so forth, she should live while avoiding adorning her body and going to another's house when her husband has gone to a foreign land. But if he has gone without providing these, she should live by blameless crafts such as weaving thread and the like. (9.75)
If he has gone abroad for the sake of dharma, he should be waited for eight years;
if for the sake of knowledge or fame, six years; but if for the sake of pleasure, three years. (9.76)

Regarding the term "gone abroad" (*proṣite*): if a husband has gone abroad for the sake of religious duties such as fulfilling his teacher’s commands, he should be waited for by his wife for eight years; beyond that, she may go to where her husband is. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "A wife whose husband has gone abroad shall wait for five years; after that, she may go to her husband's presence" (17.15). If he has gone abroad for the sake of learning, he should be waited for six years. If he has also gone abroad for the sake of fame through the distribution of his own knowledge, the husband should likewise be waited for six years. If he has gone for the purpose of enjoying another wife, [she should wait] three years. (9.76)
A husband should wait for one year for a wife who shows him hostility;
after a year, however, he may take back her property and cease to live with her.

"For a year" (9.77): A husband shall wait for one year for a wife who has conceived hatred toward him. Even after that period, he shall not approach her while she remains hostile, having confiscated the jewelry and other wealth he gave her; however, he must certainly provide her with food and clothing alone.
She who transgresses against one who is negligent, intoxicated, or even afflicted by illness,
shall be abandoned for three months, stripped of her ornaments and belongings.

Regarding the word *atīti*: if a woman, by failing to provide service and so forth, shows contempt for her husband who is negligent in gambling and such, intoxicated by drinks that produce madness, or afflicted by disease, she shall remain without ornaments, bedding, and other personal effects for three months and must not have sexual intercourse with him.
There is no abandonment of a wife who is insane, fallen [from caste], impotent, barren, or afflicted with a foul disease; nor is there any revocation of the inheritance for her. (9.79)

"Regarding the term *unmatta* (insane): one who has fallen from his natural state due to disturbances such as wind (*vāta*) and so forth, as will be described in the eleventh chapter; a *napuṃsaka* (impotent), meaning one devoid of seed due to lack of semen and the like; and one afflicted by leprosy and other diseases—if she does not attend to such a husband, she must neither abandon him nor take his property. (9.79)
A wife who drinks liquor, is of evil conduct, or is hostile; or one who is diseased, injurious, or always wastes wealth and the sacred fires—such a woman may indeed be superseded. 9.80.

"Addicted to liquor": she who is devoted to drinking forbidden intoxicants, who is of improper conduct, whose habit is to act in opposition to her husband, who is afflicted with diseases such as leprosy, who is prone to beating servants and others, and who is constantly extravagant—such a wife may be superseded; while she exists, another marriage should be performed. (9.80)
If she is barren, he may take another wife in the eighth year; if her children have died, in the tenth;
if she gives birth only to daughters, in the eleventh; but if she speaks unpleasantly, he may do so immediately.

Regarding the term *vandhyā*: a woman who has not given birth from the onset of her first menstrual period should be superseded by another wife (*adhivedanīyā*) in the eighth year; one whose children have died, in the tenth year; one who gives birth only to daughters, in the eleventh year; and one who speaks unpleasantly, immediately, provided she is childless. However, in the case of a wife who already has sons, supersession should not be performed because of the prohibition by Āpastamba: "One should not take another wife while his wife is endowed with both virtue and offspring; but he may do so when there is a deficiency in either" (ĀpDh 2.11.12–13). || 9.81 ||
But she who is sickly yet endowed with virtue and good character should be informed and may be superseded; she must never be treated with contempt. (9.82)

Furthermore, if a woman who is ill becomes compliant toward her husband and remains virtuous, he may marry another after having obtained her permission; however, she must never be treated with contempt. (9.82)
But a woman who, having been given in marriage, should depart from the house in anger, she must be restrained immediately or abandoned in the presence of the family. (9.83)

"Regarding 'one who has been superseded': if a woman who has already been superseded goes out in anger, she must be bound with a rope or similar means on that very day and kept confined until her anger subsides; or else she should be abandoned in the presence of her father’s family or other kin. (9.83)
If a woman, though forbidden, should nevertheless drink liquor even on festive occasions, or should go to a theatrical performance or a social gathering, she shall be fined six *kṛṣṇalas*. (9.84)

"Even though forbidden": furthermore, if a woman of the Kṣatriya or other castes, having been prohibited by her husband or others, should drink liquor—which is forbidden even at festivals such as weddings—or should go to a place of dancing and the like where crowds of people gather, she shall be fined six *kṛṣṇalas* of gold by the king according to the section on legal procedures (*vyavahāra-prakaraṇa*). (9.84)
If twice-born men should marry women both of their own class and of other classes, seniority, honor, and the right to the household shall belong to them according to the order of their castes. (9.85)

Regarding the word "yadi" (if): if women of the twice-born castes should marry men of their own caste or of a different caste, then, for the sake of granting them precedence according to the order of the twice-born castes, as well as honor and excellence in speech, respect, and the distribution of inheritance, seniority and honor shall belong to them, and the household shall be headed by the one [of the higher caste] through the giving of garments, ornaments, and so forth. (9.85)

The wife alone shall perform the service of her husband’s body and his daily religious duties for all [members of the family]; one who is not of the same caste shall never do so under any circumstances. (9.86)

Regarding the word "of the husband": the wife of the same caste (sajāti) alone—and never one of a different caste—shall perform for her husband the service of his body, such as providing food and so forth, as well as his religious duties (dharmakārya), such as the daily giving of alms, serving guests, and preparing materials for the fire-oblation (homa); this applies to all twice-born men. (9.86)
But he who, out of delusion, causes that [work] to be performed by another woman of the same caste while she is present, is just like the "Brāhmaṇa-Cāṇḍāla" previously described. (9.87)

"But he who... (9.87). Furthermore, if one should have bodily service and the like performed by a woman of a different caste when a woman of his own caste is available nearby due to folly, he is regarded as a *brāhmaṇacāṇḍāla*—born of a Śūdra man on a Brāhmaṇa woman—just as it was seen by the ancient seers; this is a restatement of what has been said before. 9.87.
To one who is eminent, handsome, excellent, and worthy, he should give his daughter according to the prescribed rite, even if she has not yet reached marriageable age. (9.88)

Regarding the phrase "to one who is distinguished": according to the *Dakṣasmṛti*, "One should marry off even a girl who has not reached the [marriageable] age to a bridegroom who is distinguished by his family conduct and other qualities and is handsome and of the same caste; thus the Dharma is not lost. Therefore, even before that time, one should give away the maiden according to the Brahma marriage rite. (9.88)
A maiden, even if she has reached puberty, may remain in her father's house at his pleasure until death;
yet he must never give her to one who is devoid of good qualities. (9.89)

Regarding the word *kāmam*: even if she has reached puberty (*saṃjātārtavā*), a maiden may rather remain in her father’s house until death; however, her father or others must never give her in marriage to one who is devoid of learning and virtue. (9.89)
A maiden who has reached puberty should wait for three years;
but after this period, she may seek a husband of equal status.

"Three": a maiden being given by her father or other guardians to a qualified suitor, once she has reached puberty, shall wait for three years. After those three years, however, if a suitor of superior quality is not obtained, she may herself choose a suitor of equal caste and quality.
If she should obtain a husband of her own accord when not being given away, she incurs no guilt whatsoever, nor does he whom she obtains. (9.91)

Regarding the phrase "adīyamānā" (not being given away): if a maiden, not being given away by her father or others, chooses a husband for herself at the time prescribed, then she incurs no sin whatsoever, nor does her husband incur any sin. || 9.91 ||
A maiden choosing her own husband shall not take for herself any jewelry belonging to her father, her mother, or given by her brothers; if she should take it, she would be a thief. (9.92)

"Enough. A maiden who has chosen her own husband shall return to him the ornaments given by her father, mother, or brothers prior to his acceptance; if she does not return them, she shall be considered a thief. 9.92.
One who takes a girl who has reached puberty should not pay a bride-price to her father;
for by obstructing her menses, he would be overstepping his rightful authority. (9.93)

"Not to the father. When a bridegroom marries a girl who has reached puberty, he should not pay a nuptial fee (*śulka*) to the father; for that father is deprived of his ownership of the girl due to his obstruction of the procreation of offspring during her fertile seasons. (9.93)
A man of thirty should marry a pleasing girl of twelve years; or one of twenty-four may marry an eight-year-old, if he is in haste to fulfill his religious duty. (9.94)

"Thirty years": a man of thirty years should marry a charming girl of twelve years; or one of twenty-four years, a girl of eight. He should be "hasty" in the duty of domestic life so as not to fall into decline. This is intended to indicate the appropriate time and is not for the purpose of a strict rule, for by approximately this much time one has usually mastered the Vedas. Furthermore, a girl who is a third of his age is suitable for a young bridegroom; and the meaning of "hasty" is that one who is a *brahmacārin* (a student who has mastered the Vedas) should not delay in entering the stage of the householder. 9.94.
A husband obtains his wife as a gift from the gods, not by his own will;
doing what is pleasing to the gods, he should always support that virtuous woman. 9.95.

"O God! [This is so] because of the indicative power (*liṅga*) of such mantras as: "The gods—Bhaga, Aryaman, Savitṛ, and Purandhi—have given you to me for the state of being a householder. Thus, the husband obtains that wife who was given by the gods, and not according to his own will. Being devoted to her, he should always support her with food, clothing, and so forth, even if she is possessed by hatred or other negative traits, so as to do what is pleasing to the gods. (9.95)

Women were created for the purpose of procreation, and men for the purpose of continuing the lineage; therefore, in the Veda, religious duty is declared to be common to both, performed together with the wife. 9.96.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of progeny": since women were created for the purpose of conceiving a fetus and men for the purpose of impregnation, the production of offspring is the primary duty of these two. Even duties such as the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*) are common to both husband and wife; this is declared in the Veda: "They two should establish the fires wearing linen garments," and so forth. Therefore, the statement "he shall support his wife" (9.95) is a supplement to what was previously mentioned. (9.96)
If the giver of the bride-price should die after the bride-price has been paid for a maiden,
she should be given to his brother-in-law, provided that the maiden consents.

Regarding the phrase "in the case of a maiden": when a maiden for whom the bride-price has been paid has not yet had her marriage performed, if the suitor who gave the price should die, then she must be given to his brother-in-law by her father or other relatives, provided that she accepts him. This refers to the subject of taking a bride-price, whereas the previously mentioned form of *niyoga* ("if [the husband] should die" at 9.69) pertains to a different context. (9.97)
Even a Śūdra, when giving away his daughter, must not take a bride-price;
for by accepting a bride-price, one effects a concealed sale of the daughter. (9.98)

"One should take [it]"—even a Śūdra who is ignorant of the scriptures, when giving away his daughter, should not accept a bride-price (*śulka*); how much less so a twice-born man learned in the scriptures? For by accepting a bride-price, one performs a concealed sale of one's daughter. Although the acceptance of a bride-price is prohibited by the verse "The father of a maiden... (3.51), since the acceptance of a price is observed even in the case of a maiden through the perception of scriptural injunctions, this prohibition is reiterated to eliminate any suspicion that such acceptance might be sanctioned by scripture. (9.98)
But this is what neither others have done nor any virtuous men have ever done:
that having made a promise to one, it is then given to another. (9.99)

Regarding this: furthermore, neither the cultured men of the past have ever done this, nor do those of the present time do it—namely, having accepted the daughter of one man, to give her again to another. And this refers to not giving away a girl for whom no bride-price (*śulka*) has been received; however, the rule cited as "in the case of a maiden" (9.97) concerns a case where the bride-price has been received. 9.99.
For we have never heard of such a thing, even in former births:
the sale of a daughter concealed under the name of a "bride-price. (9.100)

"No," [he says]. "We have perhaps never heard that even in previous kalpas this occurred—that some man, under the pretext of a 'bride-price' (śulka), secretly sold his daughter for a price. This is an explanatory passage (arthavāda) intended to prohibit the bride-price. (9.100)
Mutual fidelity until death—this, in brief, is the supreme duty of husband and wife. (9.101)

"Of each other": it should be understood that the preeminent duty of the woman and man, in brief, is that husband and wife should remain mutually unswerving in matters of dharma, artha, and kāma until death. (9.101)
And this being so:
"In that manner, once the rites have been performed, the man and woman should always strive so that, even when separated from one another, they do not violate their mutual fidelity. (9.102)

"So be it. Having performed the marriage ceremony, the woman and the man should always exert effort in such a way that, regarding the matters of dharma, artha, and kāma, they do not become separated from one another nor commit infidelity. 9.102.
This law concerning men and women, together with the rules for sexual pleasure, has been declared to you;
as well as the acquisition of offspring in times of distress. Now, learn the rules regarding the division of inheritance.

"This," he says: "This dharma, characterized by mutual affection between husband and wife, has been declared to you. Furthermore, the acquisition and non-acquisition of property in the absence of offspring have been explained. Now, listen to the rules for the partition of *dāya*—that is, the paternal estate and other wealth which is given (*dīyate*).

The brothers, having assembled after the death of the father, shall divide the paternal estate, and after the death of the mother, the maternal estate, making the portions equal. Since the special share (*uddhāra*) for the eldest will be described later, this rule of equal division is to be understood as applying when the eldest brother does not desire the special share. He states the cause for partition after the death of both parents: "After the death of the father and the mother, the brothers, having come together, shall divide the paternal inheritance equally; for they have no power over it while [the parents] are living. (9.104)

"Subsequently" means that those sons do not become owners of the father’s wealth while the parents are still living. Since the mother is also under discussion, the term "paternal" (*paitṛka*) includes her property as well. Furthermore, this division following the death of the father should be understood to apply when there is no wish of the father to live; however, by the father's own wish, a division may take place even while he is alive. Thus says Yājñavalkya:
"If the father should make a division, he may divide his sons according to his will. (YDh 2.114)
But when the eldest is righteous, then he alone shall take the paternal wealth in its entirety;
the remaining brothers shall depend upon him just as they did upon their father. (9.105)

Regarding the term "eldest": the eldest alone shall take the paternal wealth; the younger brothers, however, shall depend upon the eldest for food, clothing, and other necessities, just as they did upon their father. In this manner, all shall live together. 9.105.
By the mere birth of an eldest son, a man becomes a father of a son and is freed from his debt to the ancestors; therefore, he deserves everything. 9.106

Regarding the phrase "by the eldest": by the mere birth of the eldest son, even if he lacks formal sacraments (*saṃskāra*), a man becomes one who possesses a son. Consequently, there is an avoidance of the absence of the world of merit, based on the Vedic revelation: "There is no world for one who has no son. Likewise, based on the Vedic revelation: "By offspring [he pays the debt] to the ancestors," it is said: "By the mere birth of a son, he is free from debt to the ancestors. Therefore, the eldest alone is entitled to the entire estate; the younger brothers follow him under that same name. (9.106)
He through whom one pays off a debt and by whom one attains infinity—he alone is known as the son born of dharma; others they know as born of desire. (9.107)

Regarding the phrase "in whom": upon whose birth one pays off the debt; by whose birth one attains immortality. And so says the Śruti: "When a son is born, the father pays off his debt and attains immortality, provided he beholds the face of the living son. Thus it is said.

He alone becomes a son by virtue of the father’s dharma; for by him alone is the service of discharging the debt and so forth performed. But the sages know the others to be born of desire. And therefore, he alone may take the entire estate—this too is his specific distinction. (9.107)
The eldest brother should protect his younger brothers like a father protects his sons, and they should behave toward their eldest brother according to dharma as if he were a son. (9.108)

"Like a father": in the absence of partition, the eldest brother should support his younger brothers with food, clothing, and so forth, just like a father; and the younger brothers, like sons, should conduct themselves toward the eldest brother for the sake of dharma. (9.108)
The eldest son causes the family to prosper, or again, he causes it to perish;
the eldest is most worthy of honor in the world, and the eldest is not censured by the virtuous.

Regarding the word "eldest": if the eldest brother, who has not yet divided the inheritance, is righteous, then because his younger brothers also become righteous by following him, the eldest leads the family to prosperity. If he is unrighteous, then because his younger brothers also follow him and thus become unrighteous, the eldest destroys the family. Likewise, an eldest brother who possesses virtuous qualities becomes most worthy of honor in the world and is not censured by the virtuous. (9.109)
He who is the eldest and behaves as an elder is like a mother and like a father; but he who does not behave as an elder should be honored merely as a kinsman. (9.110)

"He who is the eldest": he who, among his younger brothers, conducts himself like a father, becomes as one not to be reviled, like a father or a mother. But he who does not conduct himself in that manner should be honored like a maternal uncle or other kinsmen. (9.110)
Thus they may dwell together or separately out of a desire for dharma; for dharma increases when they are separate, therefore separation is consistent with dharma. (9.111)

"Thus" means as follows: brothers who have not divided their property should live together; or, if they have divided it out of a desire for dharma (*dharmakāmanā*), they may live separately. Since their performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) and other duties increases when they reside separately, the act of partitioning is for the sake of dharma. And so Bṛhaspati says: "For those living under a single cooking fire, the worship of the ancestors, the gods, and the twice-born should be one; for those who are divided, that same worship should be performed in each individual house."

The eldest shall receive a twentieth part as his preferential share, and whatever is the best among all the goods; half of that shall belong to the middle son, but the youngest shall receive a fourth. (9.112)

Regarding the phrase "of the eldest": an *uddhāra* (preferential share) is that which is set aside; having extracted from the undivided common property a twentieth part for the eldest, as well as whatever is the best among all the goods, that should be given to him. To the middle son, a fortieth part should be given; furthermore, to the youngest, an eightieth part should be given. The remaining wealth, having been made equal, is to be divided. (9.112)
The eldest and the youngest shall take [their shares] as prescribed;
those others who are between the eldest and the youngest shall have the middle portion of the wealth. (9.113)

"And the eldest. The eldest and the youngest shall take the preferential share (*uddhāra*) as stated in the preceding verse. As for those who are middling, distinct from the eldest and the youngest, the aforementioned fortieth part of the estate is to be given to each of them, regardless of their internal status as elder or younger among themselves. This [rule] is intended to prevent inequality in the shares allotted to the elder and younger among the middling sons. (9.113)
The first-born son shall take the best of all kinds of property;
furthermore, he shall receive whatever is most excellent and one choice portion from each group of ten.

"Of all"—meaning, from among all types of property, the eldest shall take that which is the best wealth. This is stated to indicate the cumulative application of what was said in verse 9.112: "And whatever is the most excellent of all objects. Thus, even if there is only a single superior object, the eldest alone shall take it. Likewise, according to the traditional teaching of Gautama—"From among ten animals" (GDh 29.3)—the eldest receives the one best animal from among ten such as cows and the like. And this refers to the case where the eldest is virtuous while the others are devoid of merit. (9.114)

But when all possess equal merit—there is no preferential allotment among those accomplished in their own duties; however, something whatsoever should be given to the superior as an honor for increasing his dignity. (9.115)

Regarding the term "extra share" (*uddhāra*): this "extra share" which was mentioned [in verse 9.114]—namely, "he may receive a boon from each ten"—does not apply to the eldest brother among those brothers who are equally accomplished in their studies and other duties. Even in that case, "something should be given to him"; that is, property conducive to honor and prosperity should be given to the eldest. Thus, since a prohibition of the extra share is observed when qualities are equal, it should be understood that in the preceding case, the inequality of the extra share depends on the specific degree of excellence in qualities. (9.115)
In this way, when the preferential shares have been set aside, one should allot equal portions;
but if no preferential shares have been set aside, the allotment of shares for these [sons] shall be as follows. (9.116)

"Thus": in this manner, when the wealth has been set aside as an additional twentieth part, one should allot equal shares to the brothers; however, if the twentieth part and so forth have not been set aside, then this following method of allotting shares shall apply. (9.116)

The eldest son shall take one share in excess; the younger brother next to him shall take one and a half shares; and each of those younger than he shall take one share. Thus the law is established. (9.117)

"One share more" means one additional share—that is, two shares. The eldest son shall take them. He who is born immediately after the eldest shall take that additional portion, namely one and a half shares. Furthermore, the youngest sons shall each take one share; this is the established rule. However, this should be understood to apply when the eldest and his younger brother possess qualities such as learning, while the youngest sons are devoid of such qualities, since it is observed that an additional gift is given to the eldest and his younger brother. (9.117)
But the brothers shall give to their unmarried sisters portions from their own respective shares;
each shall give a fourth part of his own share, and those who refuse to give shall become outcasts.

"From their own" (*svebhyaḥ*). The four brothers—Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra—should give from their respective shares, as will be stated in the verse beginning with "The Brāhmaṇa shall take four shares" (9.153), a fourth part from each of their own portions to the unmarried sisters. Whichever sister is uterine to a brother, he should give that portion specifically for her *saṃskāra* (consecration). Thus they should give. In the absence of a uterine sister, she must certainly be consecrated by those born of other mothers, whether they be of higher or lower caste. And so says Yājñavalkya:
But those who have not been consecrated should be consecrated by their brothers who have already been consecrated;
and the sisters, having received a fourth part from their own share, [should likewise be consecrated].

If they do not wish to give a fourth part for the sake of the funeral rites of a sister, then they would become outcasts. By this, it should be understood that even when there are many half-brothers of the same caste and sisters, a fourth part must be given to the uterine sisters. 9.118.
One should never divide goats, sheep, and one-hoofed animals unequally;
however, it is ordained that goats and sheep may be divided unequally in favor of the eldest alone.

"Goats" (ajaiḥ). One-hoofed animals are horses and the like. At the time of partition, items such as goats and sheep that consist of single units and cannot be divided equally should not be partitioned; rather, they shall belong to the eldest alone. However, one should not equalize them by giving other property of equal value, nor should one sell them and divide the proceeds. The form "ajāvikam" is an optional singular compound (*ekavadbhāva*) formed from a dual of animal names. (9.119)
If a younger brother should beget a son upon the wife of the elder, the division of property in that case shall be equal; such is the established law. (9.120)

Regarding the term "the younger": if the youngest brother should, by means of *niyoga*, procreate a son upon the wife of his eldest brother, then that son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*) shall have an equal share with that paternal uncle; he does not receive an additional portion (*uddhāra*) as would be the case for a biological son of the father. Thus the rule for partition is fixed. He will state later that one born without *niyoga* has no share. Although it was stated [in verse 9.104] that "brothers, having come together, [shall divide] equally," nevertheless, from this very indicative mark, it is understood that even a grandson whose father is deceased has a share in his grandfather’s wealth, just like a paternal uncle. (9.120)

Having dispelled the doubt that even a son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*) of an elder brother ought to receive a preferential share (*uddhāra*) like a father, he confirms what was stated previously: "The subordinate cannot, according to dharma, take the place of the principal.
The father is the principal in procreation; therefore, one should deal with him [the *kṣetraja*] according to dharma. (9.121)

Regarding the term *upasarjana* (secondary): the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*) is secondary; he is not connected to the primary owner of the field (*kṣetrin*), the father, by means of the paternal right consisting of the taking of the preferential share (*uddhāra*). Even though the father is the owner of the field, he is primary only insofar as the offspring is produced through him. Therefore, the remainder of the preceding [verse] is that one should divide that *kṣetraja* son with the paternal uncle according to the very same rule previously stated, namely, the rule governing the arrangement of the partition. 9.121.
If a doubt should arise as to how the division of property should be made in a case where there is a younger son born of an elder wife and an elder son born of a younger wife: || 9.122 ||

Regarding the term "son": if a younger son is born of the first-married wife and an elder son is born later of a wife married subsequently, then if a doubt should arise as to how the division of property should be made—whether the seniority of the son follows the order of the mother's marriage or the order of his own birth—it is for this reason that [the author] says: 9.122.
The eldest son shall take one bull as his preferential share;
the others shall then take bulls of lesser size according to their respective mothers. (9.123)

"One" (*ekam*): "born earlier" (*pūrvaja*) means born before. The shortening [of the vowel] occurs according to Pāṇini 6.3.63: *ṅyāpoḥ saṃjñācchandasor bahulam*. Even he who is the youngest (*kaniṣṭha*) shall take one bull as his preferential share (*uddhāra*). Then, those other excellent bulls that remain after the best bull, they belong to each of the sons of the eldest sister (*jyaiṣṭhineya*), who are younger than him on their mother's side (*mātṛtaḥ*). Thus, seniority (*jyaiṣṭhya*) is determined by the order of their mothers' marriages. 9.123.
But the son born of the eldest wife shall take a bull as his sixteenth share;
thereafter, the remaining sons shall divide the rest according to their mothers—this is the settled rule. (9.124)

"Eldest": he who was born of the first-married wife and is senior by birth among his brothers shall take a bull as the sixteenth from among those cows; that is to say, fifteen cows and one bull. Thereafter, the others who were born of many wives shall divide the remaining shares and so forth according to their own mothers' portions, with due regard for the seniority of the wife from whom they were born—this is the settled rule.
Among sons born of wives of equal status, there is no seniority according to their mothers; rather, seniority is said to be determined by birth [from the father]. (9.125)

Regarding the word *sadṛśā* (equal): when sons born of women of the same caste (*samānajātīya*) lack any distinction based on their caste, seniority (*jyaiṣṭhya*) is not declared by the sages to follow the order of the mothers. However, for those who are senior by birth, the previously mentioned preferential share (*uddhāra*) of one-twentieth and so forth must be understood to apply. Thus, because seniority by mother is both prescribed and prohibited, there is an option (*vikalpa*), similar to the taking or not taking of the *ṣoḍaśī* cup. And this option is regulated according to whether the brothers possess qualities or are devoid of them, as it is understood that the gravity or lightness of the case depends on their virtues. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati and others state that the eldest by birth, if superior in learning and other qualities, shall receive three shares from the inheritance: "The eldest by birth, learning, or virtue shall obtain three shares of the estate. Furthermore, the rule "one bull for the one lacking qualities" refers to one with deficient qualities, while "sixteen bulls" refers to the preferential share based on maternal seniority. Medhātithi, however, stated that the injunction regarding maternal seniority is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*), whereas Govindarāja cited the opinion of others. (9.125)
Primogeniture by birth applies not only to the division of property, but also—in the *Subrahmaṇyā* liturgical formulas—it is recorded that the invocation is made by the one eldest by birth;
and even in the case of twins in the womb, seniority is recorded as being determined by birth. (9.126)

Regarding the word "birth" (*janman*): the mantra called *Subrahmaṇyā* is employed in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice for the purpose of summoning Indra. In that rite, the invocation is performed by the first-born son on behalf of his father, in the manner recorded by the seers: “The sacrificer is the father of so-and-so. Likewise, even in the case of twins whose embryos were infused at the same time, seniority is traditionally held to be determined solely by the order of birth. The plural number used in the phrase “among embryos” (*garbheṣu*) is intended to account for the possibility of multiple wives. (9.126)

A sonless man may, according to this rule, make a daughter an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), saying: "Whatever offspring may be born of her shall be the one who performs the *svadhā* offerings for me. (9.127)
"I will give you this sisterless maiden adorned with ornaments;
whatever son is born of her shall be my son.

Thus, thinking "I am sonless"—meaning that whatever offspring is born of her shall perform for me the *śrāddha* and other funeral rites—he may, at the time of giving the daughter away, make her a "son-like daughter" (*putrikā*) by means of an agreement with the bridegroom. (9.127)
In this regard, he states a restatement in the form of another’s understanding:
"By this method, the wise Prajāpati Dakṣa himself formerly fashioned those daughters for the sake of increasing his own lineage. (9.128)

"By this": Dakṣa Prajāpati, who was skilled and knowledgeable in the rules for procreating offspring, previously made all his daughters *putrikās* (appointed daughters) by means of this aforementioned procedure for the sake of increasing his own lineage. The word "atha" (then/now) implies completeness (*kārtsnye*).
With a joyful heart, he gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
and twenty-seven to King Soma, having honored them all.

"He gave," it is said. Dakṣa, his soul delighted by the prospect of obtaining sons through his daughters, honored them with ornaments and other gifts, and gave ten daughters to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa, and twenty-seven to Candra, the king of the twice-born and of the plants. The mention of "honoring" is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) that others also may act as fathers to their daughters; and the mention of "ten" and so forth indicates that one may have many daughters acting as *putrikās*. (9.129)
As is one's own self, so is a son; a daughter is equal to a son.
While she remains as one's very self, how could another take away the wealth? (9.130)

Regarding the phrase "just as": a son stands in the place of one's own self, based on the indicative mark of the mantra, "Thou art indeed the self, O son" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.15). A daughter is equal to him, because she too is produced from his limbs. Therefore, while that appointed daughter exists—who is the very nature of the father—how could any other person besides the daughter take the wealth of the deceased father who leaves no son? (9.130)

Whatever may be the mother’s separate property (yautaka), that indeed is the portion of the unmarried daughter; and the daughter’s son alone shall take the entire wealth of a woman who has no son. (9.131)

"Of the mother": whatever wealth belongs to the mother, when she has died, that shall be the share of the unmarried daughter alone; the sons have no share therein. And by "unmarried," an unmarriageable girl is intended. Likewise, Gautama states: "The property of a woman [belongs] to her daughters who are unmarried and not established [in life]. And for a maternal grandfather who has no son, the daughter's son—being the subject under discussion, namely the *pautrikeya*—shall take the entire inheritance. (9.131)
For the daughter’s son shall take the entire inheritance of his father who has no [other] son;
he alone shall offer two funeral cakes, one to his father and one to his maternal grandfather. (9.132)

Regarding the term *dauhitra* (daughter’s son): because of the context, it refers specifically to the *pautrikeya* (the son who makes the daughter’s lineage continue). For him, there is the taking of the maternal grandfather’s wealth as mentioned immediately prior, as well as the taking of the biological father’s wealth. This section is commenced for the purpose of prescribing the offering of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*), since the word "father" (*pitṛ*) is well-established in that very sense. The son of another man—that is, the *pautrikeya*—if he is without other sons, shall take the entire estate of his biological father. He alone shall offer two funeral cakes: one to his own father and one to his maternal grandfather. The mention of the offering of the funeral cake is intended to indicate the *śrāddha* rite in general. This statement is made to prevent confusion regarding the taking of the biological father’s wealth and the offering of the funeral cake on account of being a *pautrikeya*. (9.132)
In this world, according to the law of dharma, there is no distinction between a son’s son and a daughter’s son;
for both of them were produced from the very body of their parents. (9.133)

Regarding the term *pautra*: in the world, there is no distinction between a grandson (*pautra*) and a son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) in the performance of religious duties. Since the parents of both are born from his own body, this is merely a restatement of what was previously said. (9.133)
But if, after a daughter has been appointed, a son is subsequently born, the division of the estate shall be equal; for there is no right of primogeniture for a woman. (9.134)

Regarding the phrase "in the case of an appointed daughter" (*putrikāyām*): if, after an appointed daughter has been designated, a son is subsequently born to her father, then at the time of partition between those two, the division shall be equal; no preferential portion (*uddhāra*) is to be given to the appointed daughter. For, even in the case of that eldest daughter, her status as the eldest is not to be respected with respect to the preferential portion. (9.134)
But if the appointed daughter (putrikā) should somehow die without having borne a son,
the husband of that appointed daughter shall take her wealth without hesitation.

Regarding the phrase "in the case of one who has no son": if a daughter appointed as a son (*putrikā*) dies without having borne a son, her husband alone shall take her property without hesitation. This statement is intended to prevent the possibility that the father—who, being childless and lacking a wife, would otherwise inherit the wealth of his deceased son—might instead claim it, since the appointed daughter is equal to a son. (9.135)

Whether she was appointed or not, the maternal grandfather shall become the father of a grandson through the son whom she may bear from a husband of equal caste; he shall offer the funeral cake and inherit the wealth. (9.136)

Regarding the phrase *akṛtā* (unappointed): the two-fold classification of the appointed daughter (*putrikā*) is whether she is "unappointed" or "appointed. Among these, one who is made [an appointed daughter] at the time of giving the girl in marriage with the consent of the groom, after declaring, "Whatever offspring may be born of her, that shall be for my funeral rites (*svadhākara*)," is one who is "appointed merely by agreement," but not so by formal verbal transaction. Thus says Gautama: "According to some, [she becomes an appointed daughter] by mere agreement" (GDh 29.5). For this very reason, it was stated previously that she is ineligible for marriage due to the suspicion of being an appointed daughter (3.11). Whether appointed or unappointed, the appointed daughter (*putrikā*) shall produce a son from a husband of the same caste; because that grandson (*dauhitra*) performs the functions of a son (*pautra*), the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*) possesses a son's son (*pautrikeya*) and is thus "one who has a son's son. Accordingly, he shall offer the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) to him. Govindarāja, however, maintains that the term "unappointed" (*akṛtā*) refers to a daughter who is not an appointed daughter at all; thus, her son is entitled to the maternal grandfather’s wealth just like a *pautrikeya*, even when the mother or other female ancestors exist. This is incorrect, because since an appointed daughter is equal to a son, the son of an unappointed daughter and the son of an appointed daughter are not equal, and therefore it is inappropriate to treat their sons as equals. (9.136)
Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains infinity;
and through the grandson of a son, one reaches the realm of the Sun.

"By a son": by the birth of a son, one attains the worlds such as heaven; by a grandson, one remains in those very worlds for a long time; thereafter, by a great-grandson (*pautra*), one attains the world of the Sun (*ādityaloka*). And its mention here in the section on the partition of inheritance is for the purpose of making known the right of succession through the male line—namely, that even when the wife and others exist, the son has the right to the father's wealth, and in his absence, the grandson. (9.137)
Because a son saves his father from the hell named Put, he was therefore called "putra" by the Self-Existent One himself. (9.138)

Regarding the phrase "from one named Puṇya": because a son protects his father from the hell named Puṇya, he is called "putra" by Brahmā himself on account of that protection (*trāṇa*). Therefore, because of the great benefit conferred by a son, it is appropriate that his male descendants should be entitled to inherit; this [verse] is intended to reinforce what was stated previously. 9.138.
In this world, no distinction is found between a son’s son and a daughter’s son;
for even a daughter’s son delivers him to the next world, just like a son’s son. (9.139)

Regarding the term *pautra*: a *dauhitra* is the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*). In the world, no distinction whatsoever is conceived between a son and a daughter’s son, because even a daughter’s son rescues his maternal grandfather in the next world just like a son. And this is for the purpose of establishing the equality of the *pautrikeya* with a [legitimate] grandson, and for the purpose of making known that he shares an equal portion of the wealth together with a son born after the appointment of the daughter. (9.139)
The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā) should first offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his mother;
the second to her father, and the third to her father’s father. (9.140)

"Of the mother," and so forth. The son of an appointed daughter (*pautrikeya*) should first offer the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) to his mother, the second to his mother’s father, and the third to his mother’s grandfather. However, for the father and the others, since it has been stated [in verse 9.132], "To the father and to the maternal grandfather," the offering of the rice-balls follows the paternal order alone. (9.140)
But he whose adopted son is endowed with all good qualities shall indeed inherit that estate, even though he has come from another lineage. (9.141)

Regarding the term "one who has been received" (*upapanna*): the author will state that "sons are the inheritors of the father’s estate" (YDh 2.185), thereby declaring that inheritance belongs exclusively to the twelve types of sons. Furthermore, by the rule "but the other ten in order" (YDh 2.165), it follows as a matter of course that in the absence of an *aurasa* (legitimate) son or a *kṣetraja* (son born of the wife), the *dattaka* (adopted son) inherits his father's estate. Therefore, this present statement is intended to ensure that even when a legitimate son exists, the *dattaka*—provided he is endowed with all good qualities—is entitled to a share of the paternal inheritance. If a man has an adopted son who is endowed with all virtues such as Vedic study and the like, then even though he has come from another lineage (*gotra*), he shall receive a share of the paternal estate despite the existence of a legitimate son. Here, because the absolute superiority of the legitimate son is declared in the verse, "The legitimate son alone is the master of the paternal wealth" (YDh 2.163), it is not appropriate for him to have an equal share; rather, it is logical that he should receive only the sixth share prescribed for the *kṣetraja*. Govindarāja, however, stated: "This statement is for the purpose of granting a share of the paternal inheritance to an adopted son who is endowed with all virtues, specifically in the absence of both a legitimate and a *kṣetraja* son. That is incorrect, because while even the *kṛtrima* (artificially made) and other sons may inherit if they lack virtues, it would be illogical to restrict the inheritance of the *dattaka*—who is mentioned earlier in the sequence—to only those cases where he is endowed with all virtues.
An adopted son shall never take the family name or the inheritance of his biological father;
for the funeral cake follows the family name and inheritance, and the ancestral offering (svadhā) ceases for one who gives it away. 9.142.

Regarding the *gotra*: an adopted son (*dattaka*) can never obtain the wealth of the *gotra* belonging to his biological father. Furthermore, the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) follows the *gotra* and the inheritance; the *piṇḍa* is offered only to him whose *gotra* and inheritance one partakes of. Therefore, for the biological father who gives away his son, the ancestral offerings (*svadhā*), the *piṇḍa*, the *śrāddha*, and so forth, which were to be performed by that son, cease. (9.142)
Both the son of an unauthorized woman and the son obtained from the brother-in-law of a woman who already has a son are unworthy of a share; they are born of an adulterer and born of lust.

"Unappointed" (aniyuktā): he who is born without the authorization of the teacher or others, and he who is begotten by the husband's brother or another through lust—even though there was authorization for a woman who already has sons—both of these, being respectively born of an illicit lover or produced from a lustful desire, do not deserve a share of the wealth. (9.143)
Even if a man has begotten a son on a woman duly appointed, if it is done contrary to the prescribed rule,
that son is not entitled to the paternal inheritance, for he was procreated by one who has fallen from his status.

"Even when authorized" means that even if a son is born to a woman who has been authorized, provided he is born without the performance of the ritual procedure such as being anointed with clarified butter (*ghṛtābhyakta*), he is not entitled to receive the wealth of his biological father, the owner of the field (*kṣetrika*). This is because he was procreated by one who is fallen (*patita*), since it is stated that those who are "authorized but have abandoned the rule" (9.63) are fallen. 9.144.
A son born from a woman appointed for that purpose is, according to the law, just like a legitimate son (aurasa); for that seed belongs to the owner of the field, and so does the offspring. (9.145)

"He shall take" [the inheritance]. The son born of a woman appointed for that purpose is the *kṣetraja* son; he shall take the wealth just like a legitimate (*aurasa*) son. Because that seed, which is the cause of his birth, belongs to the owner of the field alone—since it produces its effect within that field—and because the offspring is also legally his by right, as stated in the verse: "If a younger brother should beget a son on the wife of the elder brother" (9.120), whereby it is declared that the *kṣetraja* son is entitled to an equal share of the grandfather's wealth along with his paternal uncle. This statement of equality with a legitimate son is intended to ensure that a virtuous *kṣetraja* son receives his own preferential share (*uddhāra*), just like a legitimate son. (9.145)
He who takes charge of the wealth and the widow of his deceased brother shall procreate an offspring for his brother and hand over that very wealth to him alone. (9.146)

Regarding the word "wealth": he who, by the law of *niyoga*, protects the movable and immovable property of a deceased brother that has been entrusted to him by a wife incapable of protecting it, and who maintains her, shall give [the estate] to the offspring of his brother begotten upon her. And this refers to the case of divided brothers, because of the statement, "he who shall maintain the wealth of the brother" (9.146), and because of the mention of equal shares in the verse, "the younger [brother] [begets] on the wife of the elder" (9.120). || 9.146 ||

If a woman, having been authorized by another, obtains a son from her husband's younger brother or a *devara*, they declare that son to be born of lust, excluded from inheritance, and procreated in vain. (9.147)

Furthermore: if a woman, authorized by her elders or others, or by her brother-in-law (*devara*) or another *sapiṇḍa*, should procreate a son, Manu and others declare that if he is born of desire (*kāmaja*), he is not an heir to the estate; only one born without desire (*akāmaja*) is an heir. And this has been stated by Nārada: "Avoiding mouth-to-mouth contact and not touching limb to limb, [he should procreate] for the sake of continuity in a family where only he remains, and not out of lust."
This rule for the division among those born of a single womb should be understood; now learn that which applies to those born of many wives of various kinds. (9.148)

"Regarding this": this rule for partition should be understood as applying to sons born of wives of the same caste by a single husband. Now, hear the rule for the partition of sons born of many wives belonging to different castes. (9.148)
If a Brāhmaṇa has four wives in the proper order of castes, this is the rule recorded for the division [of the estate] among the sons born of them. (9.149)

Regarding the phrase "of a Brāhmaṇa": if a Brāhmaṇa should have four wives in succession, beginning with a Brāhmaṇī, then this method of partition to be described hereafter has been declared by Manu and others regarding the sons born of them. (9.149)
A plowman, a bull, a vehicle, an ornament, and a house—these are to be given as the share of the eldest from the estate of a Brahmin, along with one principal portion. (9.150)

Regarding the term *kīnāśa*: a *kīnāśa* is a cultivator; a *vṛṣa* is a bull used for impregnating cows; a *yāna* is a vehicle such as a horse and so forth; an *alaṃkāra* is an ornament such as a ring and so forth; and a *veśma* is a house, which is the primary [item]. Among all the shares, that one share which is the principal is to be given as the *uddhāra* (preferential portion) for the son of the Brāhmaṇī wife. The remainder is to be divided according to the method to be described hereafter. (9.150)

From the inheritance, a Brāhmaṇa son shall take three shares; the son of a Kṣatriya woman shall take two shares; the son born of a Vaiśya woman shall take one and a half shares; and the son of a Śūdra woman shall take one share. (9.151)

"Three shares," and so forth. A Brāhmaṇa shall take three shares from the wealth; the son of a Kṣatriya woman, two; the son of a Vaiśya woman, one and a half; and the son of a Śūdra woman, one share. Thus, where only two sons exist—one from a Brāhmaṇa wife and one from a Kṣatriya wife—the wealth, divided into five parts, consists of three portions for the Brāhmaṇa and two for the Kṣatriya son. In this same manner, the calculation should be made for cases involving a Brāhmaṇa and a Vaiśya son, or when there are two or more sons [from different castes]. (9.151)

Or, having divided the entire collection of inherited property into ten parts, one who knows the Dharma should make a righteous distribution according to this rule: "Having divided the entire collection of inherited property into ten parts, one who knows the Dharma should make a righteous distribution according to this rule. (9.152)

"Everything" means that, having divided the entire estate—including all types of property from which the *uddhāra* (preferential shares) have not been extracted—into ten parts, one who knows the rules of partition should perform a division consistent with dharma according to the method to be described hereafter. || 9.152 ||
A Brahmin son shall take four shares; the son of a Kṣatriya woman, three shares;
the son of a Vaiśya woman shall take two shares; and the son of a Śūdra woman shall take one share. (9.153)

"Fourfold," etc.: a Brāhmaṇa son shall take four shares; a son of a Kṣatriya woman, three; a son of a Vaiśya woman, two; and one born of a Śūdra woman, one. Here too, when there is both a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya son, the estate being divided into seven parts, four shares go to the Brāhmaṇa and three to the Kṣatriya son. In this same manner, the calculation should be made for sons of a Brāhmaṇa and a Vaiśya woman, and so forth, as well as when there are two or many sons. (9.153)
Even if there be a legitimate son or even an illegitimate son,
one should not, according to the law, give more than a tenth part to the son of a Śūdra woman.

"Even if"—that is to say, even if a Brāhmaṇa has sons born of all the women of the twice-born castes, whether such sons exist or do not exist, nevertheless, he must not, according to the law, give more than a tenth part to the son of a Śūdra woman who is entitled to the inheritance immediately following them. And thus, because of this prohibition regarding the son of a Śūdra woman, the two sons of a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya woman shall take the entire estate when no son of the same caste exists. (9.154)
The son of a Śūdra woman by a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya does not inherit the estate;
whatever his father may give to him, that alone shall be his wealth. (9.155)

Regarding the term "Brāhmaṇa": the son of a Śūdra woman born to Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas does not become an inheritor of wealth; rather, whatever wealth his father may give to him, that alone shall be his. Thus, because of the prohibition of the previously mentioned division, there is an option (*vikalpa*), and that depends on whether the son is virtuous or lacking in virtue. Alternatively, this prohibition of the tenth share refers specifically to the case of a son by an unmarried Śūdra woman. (9.155)
Those sons of the twice-born who are born of wives of equal caste shall, after giving a preferential share to the eldest, divide the remainder equally among themselves. (9.156)

"Regarding those of equal caste": among the sons born of wives of the same caste as the twice-born, all of them, having given a preferential share (*uddhāra*) to the eldest, shall divide the remainder into equal portions and distribute it together with the eldest. (9.156)
For a Śūdra, however, only a wife of his own caste is ordained, and no other;
those born of her shall share equal portions, even if there be a hundred sons. (9.157)

Regarding the Śūdra: for a Śūdra, however, only a wife of the same caste is prescribed, neither one of higher nor lower caste. And those born of her—even if they number a hundred sons—shall have equal shares; therefore, no preferential portion (uddhāra) should be given to anyone. (9.157)
Svāyambhuva Manu has declared twelve kinds of sons for men;
among them, six are kinsmen and heirs, while six are kinsmen but not heirs. (9.158)

Regarding the term "sons": among those twelve sons whom Manu, the son of Hiranyagarbha, has mentioned, six are kinsmen (*bāndhava*) and heirs to the lineage (*gotra*). Therefore, by virtue of being kinsmen, they perform the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and water for the *sapiṇḍas* and *samānodakas*; and in the absence of others, they receive the inheritance of the lineage. This is because the right to inherit the father’s estate is stated [in verse 9.185] as belonging only to the twelve types of sons: "The sons are the heirs to the father's estate. The latter six are not heirs to the lineage or the wealth; however, they are kinsmen, and thus they perform the duties of kinship, such as the water-libation and other rites. Medhātithi, however, states that the latter group of six—beginning with "six are non-heirs and non-kinsmen"—are neither heirs nor kinsmen. That is incorrect, because Baudhāyana has declared their status as kinsmen. He says:

The son born of an unmarried girl (kānīna), the son received with a bride (sahoḍha), the purchased son (krīta), the son of a remarried woman (paunarbhava), the self-given son (svayaṃdatta), and the Niṣāda— these they declare to be sharers of the family name.

The legitimate son of the body, the son begotten on the wife, and the adopted son, as well as the son secretly born, the cast-off son, and the son purchased—these six are both heirs and kinsmen. (9.159)
Regarding the term "aurasa": the six types of sons beginning with the *aurasa*, which will be described hereafter, are both heirs to the estate and kinsmen. (9.159)
The son of an unmarried woman, the son received with a bride, the purchased son, the son of a remarried woman, the self-given son, and the Śūdra-born son— these six are kinsmen who do not inherit.

"And the son of an unmarried girl" (kānīna). It has been explained that the six types of sons beginning with the kānīna, whose characteristics will be described hereafter, do not inherit the family name (gotra) and do not take the property, but they are indeed kinsmen (bāndhava). || 9.160 ||
Since the *aurasa* (legitimate son) is mentioned alongside the *kṣetraja* (son born of the wife) and others, there might be a suspicion that they are equal; to dispel this, he says:
"As one obtains a result when crossing water with a leaky boat, so one obtains a result when crossing the darkness [of the afterlife] with bad sons. (9.161)

Regarding the phrase "of such a kind": just as one crossing water by means of a contemptible raft constructed of grass and other materials obtains a corresponding result, even so, through bad sons such as the *kṣetraja* and others, one encounters the difficult-to-overcome suffering of the next world. By this it is shown that the *kṣetraja* and other types of sons do not possess the capacity to fulfill the complete duties and functions in the same manner as a legitimate (*aurasa*) son. (9.161)
If there should be two sons who are co-heirs— one born of the wife and one born of a Kṣatriya woman—
each shall take that paternal inheritance which belongs to his own father, and not the other.
Regarding the word "yadi" (if):

"A son begotten by appointment upon the wife of another by one who is childless shall, according to dharma, be the heir to the estate and the offerer of the funeral cake for both. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.127)

Regarding this matter stated by Yājñavalkya: when an *aurasa* son is born after the *kṣetraja* son of a father who is a landowner (*kṣetrika*), then although both the *aurasa* and the *kṣetraja* are entitled to the inheritance of that same father and thus eligible for the estate, nevertheless, he [the *aurasa*] shall take only that which belongs to his own biological father, and not the property of the father from whose field he was born (*kṣetraja*). As for what will be stated later (9.164): "But when dividing the inheritance, the *aurasa* son shall give a sixth share of the paternal wealth to the *kṣetraja*."

Thus [is the rule] for one who has many sons. As for that which was stated by Yājñavalkya regarding the inheritance of the property belonging to both [the biological and the field-father], that should be understood to apply when the biological son (*aurasa*) of the field-father is absent. Medhātithi and Govindarāja, however, explain this verse with reference to the biological son and the son of an unauthorized woman (*aniyuktāputra*). That is not correct; for the son of an unauthorized woman is not a "field-born" son (*kṣetraja*), and because his exclusion from inheriting property is prohibited by the rule, "And the son of an unauthorized woman... (9.143), and because there would be no syntactic connection [with the phrase] "if they are co-heirs" (*yady ekarikthinau*). (9.162)
The son of the body alone is the master of the paternal wealth;
however, for the sake of kindness toward the others, he should provide them with a livelihood. 9.163.

"Only one": this is said when, due to illness or other causes, the legitimate son (*aurasa*) is initially absent and sons such as the *kṣetraja* have been appointed, but subsequently a legitimate son is born who is freed from illness by means of medicine and the like. The legitimate son alone is the owner of the father's wealth; for it will be stated later that the others—excluding the *kṣetraja*—are entitled to a sixth share and so forth, and therefore one should provide them with food and clothing merely to avoid the connection with sin. (9.163)
But when dividing the paternal inheritance, the legitimate son (aurasa) shall give a sixth share of the father's wealth to the son begotten on the wife (kṣetraja), or even a fifth share. (9.164)

"Sixth part": when a legitimate son (*aurasa*) divides the paternal inheritance, he shall give a sixth or a fifth share to the *kṣetraja* son. This option depends on whether the [other] son is devoid of qualities or possesses them. (9.164)
The son born of the wife and the son born of the self (aurasa) are both entitled to a share of the father's inheritance;
however, the other ten [types of sons] are, in due order, entitled to a share of the family lineage and the inheritance.

Regarding the term "aurasa": the *aurasa* and *kṣetraja* sons shall inherit the father’s wealth in the manner previously described. However, the other ten sons, beginning with the *dattaka*, become members of the lineage (*gotrabhāj*), and they are entitled to shares of the inheritance in this sequence, according to the rule: "In the absence of the preceding one, each subsequent one [inherits]" (YDh 3.132). || 9.165 ||
But that son whom one should procreate oneself in one's own wedded wife, who has been consecrated—that one should know as the legitimate (aurasa) son, designated as the first. (9.166)

Regarding the term "one's own field" (*svakṣetra*): one should know that the son whom a man himself begets upon his own wife—who has already undergone the sacramental rite of marriage while still in the state of maidenhood—is the primary *aurasa* (legitimate) son. This is because of Baudhāyana’s view: "One should know the son begotten on a woman of the same caste who has been consecrated by the rites as an *aurasa* son" (BDh 2.2.14). Thus, it should be understood that the *aurasa* son is one begotten by oneself upon a woman of the same caste. 9.166.
A son born on the bed of a man who has died, is impotent, or is diseased, from a woman duly authorized according to her own dharma, is known as a *kṣetraja* (son of the wife). 9.167.

"Who" refers to one who is born of the wife of a deceased man, of a eunuch, or of one afflicted by a disease incompatible with procreation, according to the rule of *niyoga*—such as being smeared with clarified butter—and when she has been authorized by her elders; he is remembered by Manu and others as the "son born of the field" (*kṣetraja*). (9.167)
If a mother or a father should give a son with water in times of distress—one who is similar [in status] and given with affection—he is to be known as a "given" (dattrima) son. (9.168)

Regarding the word "mother": according to the traditional teaching of Vasiṣṭha, "A person is born from semen and blood, having the mother and father as his cause; in the giving away, selling, or abandoning of him, the mother and father have authority" (VaDh 15.1). Therefore, when there is an occasion of distress caused by the absence of a son for the adopter, the mother or the father—with each other's consent—may, out of affection and not out of fear or the like, give a son of the same caste with a libation of water; he is to be known as the son called *dattrima* (the given-away son). 9.168.
But one whom he might make similar to himself, who is discerning of virtues and faults,
and who is endowed with the qualities of a son— such a son is not to be known as "artificial" (kṛtrima).

Regarding the term "similar": he who knows that the merits and defects of his parents depend on whether or not they perform the *śrāddha* and other rites for the sake of the next world for those of the same caste, and who, through the virtues of a son, is engaged in honoring his mother and father—he should be designated as a son called "artificial" (*kṛtrima*). (9.169)
He who is born in a house but whose father is not known is one born secretly in the house; he belongs to him by whom he was begotten on the bed. (9.170)

Regarding the phrase "is born": even when there is the knowledge that "this son belongs to the same caste as he whose wife was present in the house at the time of his birth," it may not be known from which specific man he was born; thus, he would be the son of that man from whose wife he was born, having been produced in the house in secret. (9.170)
One who takes in as his own a son abandoned by both his parents or by either one of them is called an *apaviddha* (abandoned) son. 9.171.

"By a mother": one should adopt a son who has been abandoned by both his mother and father, or abandoned by one of them due to the death of the other; such a son is called "the cast-off" (apaviddha). || 9.171 ||
If a maiden, however, should secretly give birth to a son in her father’s house, one should call him by the name Kānīna; he is born of the maiden, not of the husband. (9.172)
"In the father's house": whatever son a maiden may secretly bear in her father's home, one should call that son by the name *kānīna*, [belonging] to the one who marries the maiden. (9.172)
If a woman who is pregnant is married— whether her condition be known or unknown—
that child belongs to the man who marries her, and he is called a *sahoḍha* (one who marries a pregnant woman).

Moreover: "When a woman who is pregnant, whether her pregnancy be known or unknown, is married, the child born of her belongs to the man who marries her; he is designated as *sahoḍha* (one wedded while pregnant). (9.173)
If one should purchase from his mother and father a son for the sake of offspring, that son is his "bought" (krītaka) son, whether he be similar or dissimilar [in status]. (9.174)

"One should purchase [a son]" means that he whom one purchases from his mother and father for the sake of having a son is a *krītaka* (purchased) son; he becomes the son of the purchaser. He may be equal to or inferior to the purchaser in qualities, but in this matter, similarity or dissimilarity does not depend on caste (*jāti*). Since Yājñavalkya states, "This rule has been declared by me regarding sons of the same caste" (YDh 3.133), and because he thereby asserts that all sons are of the same caste as their progenitor, it should be understood—even according to Manu—that all sons other than the purchased son are of the same caste. (9.174)
She who, having been abandoned by her husband or being a widow, enters into marriage again of her own accord, is called a *paunarbhava* (a woman remarried). 9.175.

Moreover: "She who, having been abandoned by her husband or being one whose husband has died, becomes the wife of another of her own accord, and bears a son to him—that son is called the *paunarbhava* (son of a remarried woman) belonging to the progenitor. (9.175)
If she is still a virgin, or even if she has returned after having gone away,
she deserves to undergo the marriage rite again with her husband from a second marriage.

Regarding the phrase "sā cet" (if she): if that woman, while still a virgin (*akṣatayoni*), should resort to another man, then she deserves the sacrament known as remarriage with that husband taken from a second marriage (*paunarbhava*). Alternatively, if she has abandoned her childhood husband, resorted to another, and then returns to him again, she deserves the sacrament known as remarriage with that same childhood husband.
He who is deprived of his mother and father, or abandoned by them without cause, and who offers himself to someone else, is known as one who has given himself (svayaṃdatta). || 9.177 ||

Regarding the term "mother": he whose parents are deceased, or who, in the absence of any grounds for abandonment, is abandoned by them out of hatred or other such motives, and gives himself to someone—that son is known as *svayamdatta* (self-given) according to Manu and others. (9.177)
But the son whom a Brāhmaṇa may father out of lust upon a Śūdra woman is a corpse even while still alive; therefore, he is known as a Pāraśava. (9.178)

Regarding the word "yam": based on the observation of Yājñavalkya, who states, "This rule is prescribed for [daughters] born of [unmarried] women" (YDh 3.92), it is understood that when a Brāhmaṇa procreates a son with a married Śūdra woman for the sake of desire, that son is considered *pāraśava* even while living, as he is equal to a corpse (*śavatulya*). Although he indeed performs the *śrāddha* and other rites for the benefit of his father, he is designated as a "corpse" because he provides incomplete assistance. || 9.178 ||
If a son is born to a Śūdra by a female slave or by the female slave of a male slave, he shall, with permission, take a share; thus the law is settled. (9.179)

"Regarding 'in a slave woman': the scriptural rule is settled that the son born to a Śūdra from a slave woman—defined by the characteristics previously mentioned such as being acquired through purchase (*dhvajāhṛta*) or the like—or from a female slave belonging to a male slave, provided he has been permitted by his father with the words, 'May you be a sharer of equal portions with the sons of the wife legally married and permitted,' receives an equal share. (9.179)
The wise declare that these eleven sons, beginning with the son of the field (kṣetraja) as previously described, are substitutes for a son, intended to prevent the failure of religious rites.

Regarding the phrase "born of the field" (*kṣetrajātīn*): the sages have declared these eleven sons, beginning with the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), to be "substitutes for a son" (*putrapraticchandaka*) so that there may be no failure in the rite for procreating a son, nor any omission of the *śrāddha* and other duties to be performed by a son.
These sons born from the seed of others who have been mentioned incidentally belong to him from whose seed they were born, and not to anyone else. (9.181)

Regarding the word "these": those sons such as the *kṣetraja* and others, who were mentioned in connection with the *aurasa* son and are born from the seed of another, belong to the owner of that seed alone and not to the owner of the field (*kṣetrika*) and so forth. This is intended to mean that when there is a legitimate son (*aurasa*) and when there is an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), these other sons should not be adopted. The phrase "born from the seed of another" is used here as an illustration for all eleven types of sons. Even among those born from one's own seed, the *paunarbhava* and the *kānīna* (or *śaudra*) should not be adopted. For this very reason, the elder Bṛhaspati says: "Just as oil is considered by the virtuous to be a substitute for clarified butter (*ājya*) in its absence..."
Likewise, there are eleven types of sons, excluding those born of a daughter appointed as a son (putrikā) and the legitimate son of the body (aurasa).
Manu has declared that among brothers born of the same father, if even one should have a son, they all become possessed of sons through that son. (9.182)

Regarding the phrase "among brothers": among brothers who share the same mother and father, if one should have a son while the others are sonless, then Manu declares that by means of that single son, all the brothers become as if having sons. Consequently, while he exists, no other substitutes for a son should be appointed; it has been stated by this [text] that he alone is the one who offers the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and the inheritor of the share. And this is [consistent with]: "The wife, the daughters, the parents, the brothers, and likewise their sons... (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.135).
According to this statement of Yājñavalkya, it should be understood that [the right of inheritance] applies when there is an absence of heirs down to the brother. 9.182.
If among all the wives who have but one husband, one should have a son, Manu has declared that they are all possessed of sons by virtue of that son. (9.183)

Regarding the phrase "of all": Manu has stated that among all women who have but one husband, if even one should have a son, then by virtue of that son they are all considered to possess a son. Consequently, this verse is intended to show that when there is already a son from a co-wife, a woman must not adopt sons such as *dattaka* (given) and others. 9.183.
In the absence of a superior [heir], an inferior one is entitled to the inheritance;
however, if there are many of equal status, they all share the estate as co-heirs. (9.184)

Regarding the term "superior" (*śreyas*): Since all types of sons, beginning with the *aurasa*, are under discussion, Viṣṇu’s statement—"Among those beginning with the *aurasa*, each preceding one is superior; he alone is the taker of the inheritance, and he shall maintain the others"—establishes that in the absence of each preceding son among those beginning with the *aurasa*, each subsequent one is entitled to the estate. While the existence of the preceding one necessitates that he alone provide for the maintenance of the subsequent ones, this being established, the inclusion of the Śūdra son within the enumeration of the twelve sons serves as proof that he is ineligible for the wealth when sons such as the *kṣetraja* exist. Otherwise, like the sons of Kṣatriya or Vaiśya wives, since he is an *aurasa*, he would receive the wealth even when *kṣetraja* and other sons exist; furthermore, the rule that "the preceding one shall merely maintain the subsequent ones" should be understood to apply to cases other than those where an exception is made. This is because it is ordained that the *aurasa* son shall give a fifth or sixth share to the *kṣetraja* and the adopted (*dattaka*) son if they possess good qualities.
