However, if there are many sons of equal status, such as those born of remarried women (*paunarbhava*), then all of them shall divide and take the inheritance. (9.184)
Neither brothers nor fathers, nor sons are the heirs to the father's estate;
rather, the father shall take the inheritance of one who dies without a son, as shall his brothers. (9.185)

"No," [it is said]. It is not the uterine brothers, nor the fathers; rather, this is stated by this [verse] that in the absence of a legitimate son (*aurasa*), the secondary sons (*gauṇaputra*) such as the *kṣetraja* and others become the inheritors of the father's estate. For the case of the legitimate son is already established by the rule: "The legitimate son alone is the sole heir" (9.163). In the absence of a primary son, and for one who lacks a wife and daughters, the father shall take the wealth; and in the absence of those [father and mother], the brothers shall not take the wealth. This we shall explain in detail immediately hereafter. (9.185)
Now, in order to show that even those born of the field (kṣetraja) have a right to the wealth of a grandfather and others who have no son, he says:
Water must be offered for three; the funeral cake (piṇḍa) extends to three; the fourth is the giver of these; a fifth does not exist. (9.186)
The wives of the father who have no sons are declared to receive equal shares;
and all those paternal grandmothers are declared to be equivalent to mothers.

"Of three": the offering of water must be performed for three, namely the father and the others; and the funeral cake (piṇḍa) must be given to those same three. The fourth is the giver of both the cake and the water; there is no connection here with a fifth. Therefore, it is logical that the secondary grandson has a right of succession to the property of a sonless grandfather and the rest. Furthermore, regarding the biological son and grandson, their entitlement to the property of the grandfather and the rest is stated by this very verse: "Through a son, one conquers the worlds" (9.137). || 9.186 ||
The wealth of one who dies without an heir shall belong to his nearest *sapinda*;
after him, it shall go to a *sakulya*, or else to a teacher or a pupil. (9.187)

Regarding the term *anantara* ("immediate"): since this general statement would be redundant if it referred merely to the mass of the *aurasa* son and others already mentioned, it is intended to provide for the inheritance of wives and others not previously mentioned. Among the *sapiṇḍas*, whichever male or female *sapiṇḍa* is most closely related shall inherit the estate of the deceased. In that regard, because it has been stated that "the *aurasa* son alone [is the heir]" (YDh 2.132), he alone possesses the primary right to the estate of the deceased. However, to the *kṣetraja* and the qualified *dattaka*, one should give a fifth or sixth share as prescribed; for the *kṛtrima* and other types of sons, one should merely provide for their maintenance. In the absence of an *aurasa* son, the appointed daughter (*putrikā*) and her son [inherit], because it is stated: "The daughter's son alone shall take the entire estate of the childless man" (YDh 2.132); here, the term "childless" is intended to mean one who lacks an *aurasa* son. In his absence, the eleven types of sons beginning with the *kṣetraja* are entitled to the father’s wealth in their respective order. However, the son of a married Śūdra woman is entitled only to a tenth share, as it is stated: "One should not give more than a tenth part to the son of a Śūdra woman" (YDh 2.133). The remaining wealth, after the tenth share, shall be taken by the closest *sapiṇḍa*. In the absence of these thirteen kinds of sons, the wife inherits the entire estate of the husband. As Yājñavalkya says: [he provides the following verse].
The wife, daughters, parents, brothers, their sons,
a kinsman of the same lineage, a relative, a pupil, and fellow students [are the heirs in succession].
"In the absence of these [heirs], each subsequent one among the preceding groups is the heir to the wealth.
This rule applies to all castes regarding one who has died without a son.
Bṛhaspati also says:
In the Vedas, in the Smṛtis and Tantras, and in worldly custom,
the wise have declared that a wife is half of one's own body, sharing equally in the fruits of merit and demerit.
For one whose wife has not passed away, half of his body still lives;
but while half the body is living, how could another take possession of it as his own?
But when agnatic kinsmen (sakulyas)— those of the same lineage as the father or mother— are present,
the wife of a deceased man who leaves no son shall take his share.
When her husband has died, a devoted wife shall inherit his wealth, including the previously consecrated *agnihotra* fires; this is the eternal law.
Having taken movable and immovable property, gold, base metals, grain, and clothing, one should cause the śrāddha for the monthly, six-monthly, and other rites to be performed.

One should honor paternal uncles, preceptors, daughters' sons, the sons of a husband's sister, maternal uncles, elders, and guests— both men and women— with offerings to the ancestors (kavya) and works of public utility (pūrta).
If her sapindas or kinsmen should obstruct her or seize her property,
the king shall punish them with the same penalty as for theft.
Vṛddha-Manu: A sonless wife, preserving her husband’s bed and remaining steadfast in her vows,
shall herself offer his funeral cake and receive the entirety of his estate.

As for the statement, "But one should give a livelihood to women," which refers merely to their maintenance, that concerns wives who are immoral, unrighteous, afflicted by disease, or in the prime of youth. Therefore, what Medhātithi stated—prohibiting the wives' entitlement to a share—is incoherent.
The wives' entitlement to a share is agreed upon by Bṛhaspati and others;
by rejecting it, Medhātithi does not please the minds of the virtuous.

In the absence of a wife, the daughter who has no son [inherits]; in her absence, the father and mother; in their absence, a uterine brother; and in his absence, his sons—because it will be stated later: "And when the mother has passed away, the father’s mother shall take the wealth" (9.217). In the absence of the father's mother, another near *sapiṇḍa* should take the deceased's wealth. For example, if the lineage of the grandfather is non-existent, then the lineage of the great-grandfather [takes it]. That too is incorrect. Beyond this, in the absence of the *sapiṇḍa* lineage, the *samānodaka* kinsman, the teacher, and the pupil shall take the wealth in succession. (9.187)
But in the absence of all these, Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the three Vedas, pure, and self-controlled shall be the heirs; thus the Dharma is not violated. (9.188)

Regarding the phrase "of all": although it would have been sufficient to say "the absence of these," the expression "the absence of all" is used to include even fellow religious students (*sabrahmacārin*) and others as heirs to the wealth. In the absence of all [the aforementioned], Brāhmaṇas who have studied the three Vedas, who possess external and internal purity, and whose senses are subdued, become the heirs to the wealth; they alone are the offerers of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*). This being so, there is no loss of religious duties such as the *śrāddha* for the deceased owner of the property. (9.188)
The property of a Brāhmaṇa is always inviolable by the king; such is the settled rule. But in the case of the other castes, the king may take their property when no heirs exist. (9.189)

"Unseizable" means that the wealth belonging to a Brāhmaṇa must never be taken by the king; such is the boundary of the sacred law (*śāstra*). However, in the absence of a Brāhmaṇa possessing the aforementioned characteristics, it may be given even to Brāhmaṇas in general. On the other hand, the wealth of Kṣatriyas and others, in the absence of the previously mentioned heirs to the inheritance, the king may take for himself. (9.189)
For one who has died childless, one should obtain a son from a member of the same lineage; whatever wealth may have been produced by that [son] should be delivered to him. (9.190)

Regarding the phrase "of one who has passed away": when a man dies childless, his wife, being authorized by her elders, shall produce a son through the practice of *niyoga* from a man of the same lineage (*sagotra*). Upon that deceased man's death, whatever mass of wealth exists should be handed over to that son, because it has been stated [in verse 9.59]: "From a brother-in-law or from a sapinda. This [verse] is intended to show that a woman of the same lineage may be obtained for *niyoga*, and that the son born of her is entitled to a share of the inheritance. (9.190)
But if two [sons] should dispute over the wealth of their mother, both of whom were born from her, each shall take that which was his father's property, and not the other. (9.191)

"Two": This refers to the case where "if there should be two heirs to a single estate" (9.162), which was stated regarding the *aurasa* (legitimate son from the wife) and the *kṣetraja* (son begotten on the wife); however, this present rule concerns the *aurasa* and the *paunarbhava* (son born of a remarried woman). When, because her first husband who fathered an *aurasa* son has died, she takes possession of the husband's wealth while her child is still young, and subsequently bears another son to a *paunarbhava* husband; and when that *paunarbhava* husband also dies, she—having no other heir to the estate—takes the wealth; if those two sons born of the two different men should later dispute over the wealth held in the mother's hands, then whichever son belongs to whichever father shall take that very wealth, and not the son of one father the property of the other father. (9.191)
When the mother has passed away, all the uterine brothers and the uterine sisters shall divide the maternal inheritance equally. (9.192)

Regarding the phrase "in the case of the mother": when the mother has died, the uterine brothers and the uterine sisters who are unmarried shall divide the mother’s property equally and take it. However, those who are married receive honor proportionate to their wealth. As Bṛhaspati says: "The woman’s property shall belong to the offspring, and the daughter is entitled to a share thereof; but if she is unmarried and without [other] sons, she receives only honor."
And therefore, just as the paternal property is given to unmarried daughters, a fourth part of the mother's property must be given by the brother to the married daughters from his own share.
Whatever daughters they may have, from the maternal grandmother's wealth, something should also be given to them according to their merit and with affection. (9.193)

Regarding the word "yā" (those): among those daughters, to those who are unmarried daughters, something should also be given from the maternal grandmother's property out of affection, in such a way that their honor is maintained. (9.193)
That which is given before the nuptial fire, that which is received at the bridal procession, and that which is given as a token of affection;
that which is obtained from a brother, a mother, or a father—this is declared to be the sixfold property of a woman.

*Adhyagni*. By the rule *avyayaṃ vibhaktisamīpa-* (Pāṇini 2.1.6) and others, this is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of proximity. That which is given by the father and others at the time of marriage in the presence of the fire is *adhyagni* woman’s property (*strīdhana*). Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
“That which is indeed given to women at the time of marriage in the presence of the fire, that is proclaimed by the virtuous as *adhyagni*-made woman’s property.”

That which is obtained by a woman while being led from her father’s house to her husband’s house is called *adhyāvāhanika*. Thus says Kātyāyana: "Furthermore, whatever a woman receives while being led away from her father’s home is declared to be the woman's property known as *adhyāvāhanika*."

Furthermore, that which is given by a husband or others on the occasion of a marriage ceremony out of affection, as well as what is given by a father at another time—thus is the sixfold property of a woman traditionally recorded. (9.194)

That which was given as a subsequent gift (anvādheya), and that which was given by a husband who is well-pleased, shall belong to the offspring of a woman who has passed away while her husband is still living. (9.195)
Regarding "anvādheya": Kātyāyana has explained *anvādheya* as follows:
"Whatever is obtained by a woman from her husband's family after marriage, that is called *anvādheya*; likewise [what is obtained] from all her paternal kinsmen."

Whatever has been obtained by a woman after marriage, whether in her husband's family or her father's family, and whatever has been given by her affectionate husband, as well as the "adhyagni" and other types of property mentioned in the preceding verse—all that becomes the total wealth of the children of the woman who dies while her husband is still living. (9.195)

Whatever property exists in marriages contracted according to the Brahma, Daiva, Arsha, Gandharva, or Prajapatya rites, it is held that upon the death of a childless wife, it belongs to the husband alone. (9.196)

Regarding the term "Brahma": among the five forms of marriage beginning with the Brāhma, which have been described by their characteristics, the sixfold wealth that belongs to the wife is intended by Manu and others to go to the husband alone when she dies childless. || 9.196 ||
Whatever wealth may have been given to her in marriages such as the Āsura and others, it is ordained that upon her death childless, it shall belong to her mother and father. (9.197)

Regarding the word "yat" (which): furthermore, whatever sixfold wealth belongs to a woman in marriages characterized as those of the Asuras, Rākṣasas, or Paiśācas, that is also held to belong to her parents when she dies childless. (9.197)
Whatever may have been given to a woman by her father, or given to her in any manner whatsoever, that the Brāhmaṇī wife shall take; or it shall belong to her daughter or to her offspring. (9.198)

Regarding the term "in the case of a woman": when a Kṣatriya or other woman of a different caste belonging to a Brāhmaṇa has died childless and without a husband, her father-given property shall be taken by the Brāhmaṇa stepdaughter, even if there exist sons or daughters of the same or different castes from other co-wives. In the absence of her, that property shall belong to her offspring. (9.198)
Women should not carry out any acquisition from the midst of the many members of the household, nor even from their own wealth, without the permission of their husband. (9.199)

No. From the family wealth that is common to many, such as brothers and others, a wife or other women must not make a hoard of wealth for the sake of jewels, ornaments, and the like; nor should they do so even from the husband’s own property without his permission. Therefore, this is not [considered] "woman's property" (strīdhana). || 9.199 ||
Whatever ornaments may have been worn by women while their husband was alive, the heirs shall not divide them; those who do so fall from their status. (9.200)

Regarding the verse beginning with *patyau* and so forth: while the husband is alive, whatever ornament is worn by women with his consent, they shall not divide that at the time of partition once he has died. Those who do divide it become sinners. (9.200)
Those who have no share are the impotent, the outcaste, those born blind or deaf, as well as the insane, the idiotic, the mute, and whoever else is lacking in sense organs. (9.201)

"Those who have no share" means: eunuchs, those who have fallen [from caste], those born blind, those with defective hearing, the insane, the idiotic, the mute, and those with impaired faculties such as the crippled or the lame—they do not inherit the wealth of the father and others; rather, they are entitled only to food and clothing. (9.201)
He says that very thing:
"However, it is right for the wise man to give to all of them according to his ability food and clothing for as long as they live; for by not giving, he would become an outcast. (9.202)

"Of all" means that for all these individuals, beginning with the impotent, a kinsman who inherits their property and is learned in the scriptures must provide food and clothing according to his ability for as long as he lives. By failing to do so, he would become a sinner. (9.202)
If, however, there should somehow be a desire for wives on the part of eunuchs and others, their offspring, having produced progeny, shall be entitled to the inheritance. (9.203)

Regarding the word "yadi" (if): by the use of the expression "kathaṃcana" (in any way whatsoever), it is indicated that eunuchs and the like are unworthy of marriage. If, somehow, there should arise a desire for marriage among these [disqualified persons], then, when a son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*) is produced for the eunuch, the offspring of those others who have already produced offspring becomes the heir to the wealth. || 9.203 ||
Whatever property the eldest son acquires after the father has died,
a share of that belongs to the younger sons, provided they are observant of their studies.

Regarding the phrase "whatever [he may acquire]": when the father has died, the eldest brother who remains undivided with his brothers acquires some wealth through his own personal effort; from that wealth, a share belongs to the younger brothers who possess learning, but not to others. (9.204)
But if all those who were ignorant should acquire wealth through their own efforts, it is the settled rule that there should be an equal division of it, as it is not ancestral property. (9.205)

Regarding the phrase "of those who are ignorant": if all the brothers acquire wealth through activities such as agriculture or trade, then, in that wealth which is not ancestral but self-acquired, the division shall be equal; there is no special extra share (*uddhāra*) for the one who is not the father—this is the settled rule. (9.205)

Whatever constitutes the wealth of knowledge belongs to him alone; the same applies to gifts received through friendship, those given at marriage, and those presented with the honey-mixture (madhuparka). (9.206)

Regarding the phrase "wealth acquired through learning" (*vidyādhanam*): this refers specifically to that which is acquired through friendship or marriage, and that which is obtained as a guest-offering (*mādhuparkika*) at the time of the presentation of the *madhuparka*, by virtue of being worthy of honor. Having stated [in 9.204], "Whatever [is given] to the father," this is an exception to that rule. Furthermore, Kātyāyana has defined wealth acquired through learning: "When learning is obtained from another by means of providing him with food, and what is subsequently acquired by that learning according to the prescribed rule, that is called 'wealth acquired through learning.'"

Whatever is obtained through learning by means of a wager after it has been offered for instruction, that should be known as "learning-wealth" (vidyādhanam); it is not to be divided during a partition of inheritance.
That which is obtained from a disciple, from officiating as a priest, from questioning, from resolving a doubtful inquiry,
from praising one's own knowledge, from debate, and from thorough study;
But they say that the wealth of learning is not to be divided at the time of partition.

Therefore, that which was explained by Medhātithi and Govindarāja as the fee for officiating at the *madhuparka* ceremony is incorrect, because it is a form of wealth acquired through learning (*vidyādhanatvāt*). (9.206)
But he among brothers who, though capable through his own labor, does not desire wealth, shall be excluded from his share after being given something for his subsistence. (9.207)

Regarding the phrase "of the brothers": if one who is capable of acquiring wealth through such acts as following the king in service does not wish for the common property of the brothers, he should be separated from his brothers by giving them a small subsistence allowance from his own share; by this means, his sons will not dispute over that property at a later time. (9.207)
That which has been acquired through one's own labor without depleting the paternal estate, being obtained by one's own effort—that he need not give unless he so desires. (9.208)

"Without injuring" means that what one might acquire through the hardship of agriculture and so forth, without depleting the paternal estate, is obtained by one's own effort; one who does not wish to give it to his brothers is not required to do so. (9.208)
But if a father should acquire ancestral property that was previously unobtained, he need not share it with his sons against his own will, as it was acquired by himself. (9.209)

Regarding the phrase "paternal": furthermore, whatever wealth belongs to the father that was not acquired because it was neglected due to his incapacity, the son may obtain that by his own effort; however, he shall not divide with his sons that which he himself has acquired and does not wish to share. (9.209)
If those who were divided while living together should divide again, the division in that case shall be equal; there is no right of primogeniture therein. (9.210)

"Divided": if brothers who were previously divided—whether with a preferential share (*uddhāra*) or without one—later reunite their wealth and live together, and then divide it again, in that case an equal division must be made; no preferential share for the eldest is to be given. (9.211)
If the eldest or the youngest among them should be deprived of his share, or if either of them should die, his portion is not lost. (9.211)

Regarding the phrase "of those": among those brothers, if any one should be excluded from his own share at the time of partition due to renunciation or the like, or should die, his share shall not be lost. (9.211)
But rather—
those uterine brothers who have reunited, as well as the sisters of the same womb, shall assemble together and divide it equally. (9.212)

"Utterine brothers," and so forth. Utterine brothers, having come together and being joined with their uterine sisters, should divide that share equally. Among both the uterine and the half-brothers, those who are of one common interest because their wealth has been commingled should divide it; all the uterine brothers, or the uterine sister along with the half-brothers, should divide it equally. And this should be understood to apply in the absence of sons, wives, fathers, and mothers. (9.212)
If an eldest brother, out of greed, should defraud his younger brothers, he shall forfeit his status as the eldest, receive no share of the inheritance, and be restrained by the kings. (9.213)

"He who is the eldest": if an eldest brother, out of greed, should deceive his younger brothers, he shall be deprived of the honor due to an eldest brother, excluded from the additional share (*uddhāra*), and subject to royal punishment. (9.213)

All brothers who are engaged in improper occupations do not deserve to receive the wealth; nor should an elder brother make a separate acquisition for himself without having given a share to the younger brothers. (9.214)

"All indeed" means that even those brothers who have not fallen from their status, but are addicted to activities such as gambling or serving prostitutes, do not deserve the inheritance. Furthermore, the eldest brother must not, without making a provision for the younger brothers, convert common property into his own exclusive property.
If there should be a joint undertaking by brothers who have not divided their inheritance, the father must never, under any circumstances, give unequal shares to their sons. (9.215)

Regarding the phrase "of the brothers": if there should be a joint undertaking by brothers who live with their father and remain undivided for the purpose of acquiring wealth, then at the time of partition, the father shall never give more to any one son than to the others. (9.215)
But one who is born after the partition shall take the paternal wealth alone;
or, those who may have been reunited with him, he shall divide it together with them. (9.216)

"Subsequent" means: when a division has been made by the father while he is still living at his own will, then a son born after that division shall, upon the death of the father, take the paternal inheritance alone. Those who have already divided with the father and then reunited their wealth with him—along with them, he shall divide the estate when the father has died. (9.216)
The mother shall obtain the inheritance of a son who dies without offspring;
and when the mother has also passed away, the father’s mother shall take the wealth. (9.217)

Regarding the phrase "of one who has no offspring": the mother shall take the wealth of a sonless son. This is because it was previously stated, "The father shall take the inheritance of one who has no son" (9.185), whereas here Yājñavalkya uses the singular remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) in the term "the parents" (YDh 3.135). Furthermore, Viṣṇu employs the same singular remainder when stating: "The wealth of one who has no son goes to the wife; in her absence, to the daughter; in her absence, to the father. Therefore, the mother and father shall take the property by dividing it between them. When the mother has died and there is no wife, father, brother, or brother’s son, the father’s mother shall take the wealth. (9.217)
When all debts and assets have been distributed according to the rule, whatever may subsequently be discovered, all of that should be divided equally. 9.218

Regarding the term "debt" (*ṛṇa*): when a debt owed by the father or others has been settled, and all of that person's wealth has been divided according to the scriptures, if subsequently any paternal debt or wealth that was unknown at the time of partition is discovered, all of it must be divided equally; it is not to be deducted, nor is it to be taken [by one party], nor is a preferential share (*uddhāra*) to be given to the eldest son. (9.218)
Clothing, vehicles, ornaments, prepared food, water, women, security of possession, and pasture land are declared not to be subject to partition. (9.219)

"Garment" (*vastra*): A garment, a vehicle, or an ornament that was used by someone at the time of partition is not to be divided; it belongs to that very person alone. However, this applies only to items whose value is neither excessively low nor excessively high. But ornaments and the like of great value must certainly be divided. It is with reference to such cases that Bṛhaspati’s rule regarding division states: "Having sold the garments and ornaments... Cooked food, such as boiled rice or parched barley flour (*saktu*), is not to be divided. In that regard, if the parched barley flour or similar items are of very great value, they must indeed be divided by exchanging them for an amount of wealth equal to their value, according to Bṛhaspati’s statement: "Cooked food is to be divided after being exchanged for uncooked food. Water contained in wells and the like, being for the use of all, is not to be divided. Female slaves and others who do not receive equal shares are not to be divided, but rather should be made to perform equal labor. "Yogakṣema" refers to ministers, priests, and so forth, because they are the cause of security and prosperity. "Pasture" (*pracāra*) refers to the path for the grazing of cows and other animals. Manu and the other sages have declared all these things to be indivisible. (9.219)

This division of property for you and the rules for the performance of rites for the sons born of the wife and the others have been declared in due order; now learn the law concerning gambling. 9.220.

"This," [he says], "is the partition of inheritance for sons, beginning with the *kṣetraja* and others, in their respective order; this method of making the division has been declared to you. Now, listen to the rules regarding gambling. (9.220)
The king should prohibit gambling and betting within his kingdom;
these two vices bring about the end of kings who rule the earth. (9.221)

Regarding gambling: the king shall prohibit gambling and betting—which will have their definitions explained later—within his own kingdom, because these two vices cause the destruction of kings' realms. (9.221)
Gambling and betting are open forms of theft;
therefore, the king should always exert effort to suppress them. (9.222)
"Publicly" means openly; this gambling and betting is a manifest form of theft. Therefore, the king should always be diligent in his efforts to prevent it. (9.222)
That which is performed with inanimate objects is called gambling (dyūta) in the world;
but that which is performed with animate beings should be known as betting (samāhvaya). 9.223.

"By means of inanimate objects": that which is performed with inanimate things such as dice and stalks is called *dyūta* (gambling) in the world; whereas that which is performed with animate beings such as rams and cocks, preceded by a wager, should be known as *samāhvaya* (betting). Although these two are already well-known in the world, their definitions are stated here for the sake of providing a formal exclusion. (9.223)
The king shall cause to be executed all those who engage in gambling or betting, or cause others to do so, as well as Śūdras who assume the marks of the twice-born. (9.224)

Regarding gambling: if anyone should engage in gambling or betting, or if anyone should act as a master of the gaming house (*sabhika*), the king shall inflict upon them corporal punishment, such as the amputation of hands or execution, depending on the gravity of their offense. He shall put to death those Śūdras who wear the marks of the twice-born, such as the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). (9.224)
He shall quickly banish from the city gamblers, actors, cruel men, those belonging to heretical sects, men engaged in forbidden occupations, and liquor-sellers. 9.225.

"Gamblers": those who indulge in gambling and the like; dancers and singers; haters of the Vedas; those who observe vows contrary to the Śruti and Smṛti; those who, when not in times of distress, live by the labor of others; and vintners—those who produce liquor—the king shall quickly banish from the kingdom. By the mention of gamblers, others are also included. (9.225)
Regarding this, he states the reason:
"These, existing in the kingdom as the king's secret thieves, constantly harm the virtuous subjects through their improper actions. (9.226)
"These" refers to these gamblers and others, who are secret thieves living within the kingdom; they constantly afflict virtuous people through their deceitful activities. 9.226.
This gambling was seen in a former age to cause great enmity;
therefore, a wise person should not practice gambling, even for the sake of amusement. (9.227)

Regarding gambling: it is not only now, but even in a previous aeon (*kalpa*), this gambling was seen to cause excessive enmity; therefore, a wise person should not practice it, even for the sake of a joke. (9.227)
Whether it be done in secret or openly, whatever man should practice such [an act], there shall be a variety of punishments for him at the king's discretion. (9.228)

Now, regarding those who have been defeated but lack wealth, he says this: "But one born of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes, being unable to pay the fine, shall attain freedom from debt through labor; a Brāhmaṇa, however, should pay it gradually. (9.229)

Regarding the term "kṣatra": one born of the kṣatriya, vaiśya, or śūdra castes who, due to poverty, is unable to pay a fine, shall purify himself from that penalty by performing work appropriate to him. A Brāhmaṇa, however, should pay according to his means in due order; he must not be made to perform labor. (9.229)
For women, children, the insane, the elderly, the poor, and the sick, the king should administer punishment with whips, split bamboo, ropes, and the like. (9.230)
Regarding women: furthermore, the king should subdue women, children, and others by means of flogging with a whip, striking with bamboo leaves, binding with ropes, and so forth.
But those who, having been appointed to official duties, ruin the affairs of the litigants while being consumed by the heat of wealth—the king shall deprive them of their property. (9.231)

"But those who are appointed," etc.: those whom the king has appointed for tasks such as supervising legal proceedings, if they undergo a change of heart due to the power of bribery and should ruin the business of their masters and others, the king shall cause them to forfeit all their property. (9.231)
He shall put to death those who forge royal edicts, those who corrupt the subjects, those who kill women, children, or Brahmins, as well as those who serve his enemies. (9.232)

Regarding the word "kūṭa": the king shall put to death those who forge royal edicts and decrees, those who create dissension among ministers, those who kill women, children, or Brahmins, and those who serve the enemy. (9.232)
Whatever has been decided and adjudicated anywhere, one should know that to be established according to dharma; it shall not be overturned again. 9.233
“If one should think that a case has been decided or adjudicated through improper action, he should impose a double fine and have that matter reopened.

Regarding the word *tīritam*: in any legal proceeding such as the non-payment of debts (*ṛṇādāna*) and so forth, whatever matter has been decided according to the law—[the root] *pāra* and *tīra* are listed in the *curādi* group [of roots] with the meaning “to bring an action to completion”—it means determined by the established rules of the treatise. *Anuśiṣṭam* means it should have been brought to the point of a final sentence; once that is done, one should accept it and not reverse it. This applies when it was done without a valid reason. Therefore, if it was done for a valid reason, one must indeed reverse it. (9.233)
Whatever legal matter the ministers or the judge might decide incorrectly, the king himself shall settle that case and fine them one thousand [paṇas]. (9.234)

"Ministers": whether they be royal ministers or a judge appointed to oversee legal proceedings, if they should reach an improper decision in a lawsuit, the king himself shall make that decision and fine them one thousand paṇas. And this applies to cases other than the taking of bribes; for regarding the taking of bribes, it has already been stated [in verse 9.231]: "But those who are appointed... (9.231). || 9.234 ||

The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of spirituous liquor, the thief, and the violator of the guru’s bed—all these men are to be known individually as perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin). 9.235.

"Brahmaheti" refers to the following: a man who has killed a Brāhmaṇa is a "brahmahā"; a twice-born man who drinks liquor is a "surāpa"—meaning a Brāhmaṇa who drinks *paiṣṭī*, *mādhvī*, or *gauḍī* liquors; a "taskara" is a man who steals the gold of a Brāhmaṇa; and whoever approaches the wife of his guru—all these are to be understood as great sinners (*mahāpātakins*) individually. (9.235)
And for these four who do not perform expiation, he shall prescribe a lawful punishment consisting of both corporal and monetary fines. (9.236)

"Of the four": for all these four great sinners who do not perform expiation, one shall inflict corporal punishment and, by means of seizing their wealth, a punishment that is consistent with justice and not departing from dharma, as will be described below, in accordance with the nature of the offense. (9.236)

For violating the teacher's bed, the mark of a female organ shall be made; for drinking liquor, the sign of a tavern flag; for theft, the mark of a dog's foot; and for killing a Brahmin, the figure of a headless man.

Regarding the phrase "violation of the Guru’s bed" (*gurutalpa*): since it will be stated later [in verse 9.240], "They shall not be branded on the forehead by the king," it is understood that the forehead itself is the site of the branding. In that regard, for one who has had intercourse with the Guru’s wife, a mark of such intercourse in the form of a vulva must be made on the forehead with red-hot iron for as long as he lives. Likewise, when liquor has been drunk, a long sign in the shape of a liquor flag must be made on the drinker; when gold has been stolen, the thief must be marked with the form of a dog’s foot. In the case of a slayer of a Brahmin, he must be made into a headless trunk (*kabandha*). [9.237]
Indeed, being unfit to eat with, unfit to sacrifice for, unfit to study with, and unfit to marry into,
they shall wander the earth in misery, excluded from all religious duties.

"Unfit for social intercourse" means that these persons should not be fed with food and other provisions; they should not be employed as officiating priests (*yājya*), nor should they be taught the Vedas (*adhyāpanīya*); furthermore, no matrimonial alliance by the giving of a daughter should be entered into with them. And because they are destitute, being beset by the wretchedness of begging and the like, they shall wander the earth, excluded from all rites prescribed by the Śruti and other sacred texts. (9.238)
But these, having been marked with the brand, must be abandoned by their kinsmen and relatives; they are to be without compassion and without salutation—this is the instruction of Manu. (9.239)

Regarding the word "jñāti": these persons who have been branded should be abandoned by their kinsmen and relatives, such as maternal uncles and others; no compassion should be shown toward them, nor should they be saluted. This is the command of Manu. (9.239)
But when members of the higher castes perform the prescribed penance as declared, they shall not be branded on the forehead by the king; rather, they should be made to pay the highest fine. (9.240)

Regarding "atonement": when the three castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, perform again an atonement prescribed by the scriptures, they shall not be branded on the forehead by the king; however, they are to be punished with the highest fine. (9.240)
For offenses against a Brāhmaṇa, the middle amercement must be imposed; or he may be banished from the kingdom, along with his property and his belongings. (9.241)

Regarding the phrase "for offenses": the term "unintentionally" (*akāmataḥ*), which is heard in the subsequent verse, "But those others who have committed [offenses]" (9.242), should also be applied here. Therefore, for these offenses committed unintentionally, a middle amercement (*madhyama-sāhasa*) is to be imposed upon a virtuous Brāhmaṇa; however, the previously mentioned highest amercement (*uttama-sāhasa*) is to be understood as applying to one who lacks such virtues. If those offenses are committed intentionally, a Brāhmaṇa who possesses wealth, grain, and other belongings should be banished from the country. || 9.241 ||
But others who have committed these sins unintentionally deserve the confiscation of all their property; however, if they were committed intentionally, they deserve banishment. (9.242)

"Others" refers to those other than Brāhmaṇas—namely, Kṣatriyas and the rest—who, having committed these sins unintentionally, deserve the confiscation of all their property. And this confiscation of all property is to be determined in relation to the previously mentioned "highest fine" (uttamasāhasa), depending on the specific circumstances. However, if they commit these offenses intentionally, banishment or death shall be the penalty. Lexicographers record that the word *pravāsana* is a synonym for execution, citing such terms as "banishment," "driving away," "destruction," and "injury. (9.242)
A righteous king must not take the wealth of one who has committed a mortal sin;
for by taking it out of greed, he becomes tainted by that very guilt. (9.243)

"He shall not take" means that a righteous king must not accept wealth related to a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) as a form of punishment. However, by taking it out of greed, he becomes joined with the fault of a mortal sin. (9.243)
What, then, is the procedure for one who has paid the fine? To address this, he says: "Having cast that fine into the waters, he should offer it to Varuṇa;
or he should present it to a Brāhmaṇa endowed with learning and good conduct. (9.244)
"In the waters"—he should throw that staff and wealth into the water of a river or similar body of water, or he should give it to a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with learning and good conduct. (9.244)
Varuṇa is the lord of punishment, for he is the wielder of the rod over kings;
the Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas is the lord of the entire world. (9.245)

Regarding the word "Īśa": Varuṇa is the master of the fines for mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*) because he is the lord even over kings due to his role as the wielder of punishment. Likewise, a Brāhmaṇa who has studied the entirety of the Vedas is the master of the whole world. Therefore, by virtue of their lordship, those two are entitled to the fine money. (9.245)
Wherever a king avoids acquiring wealth from evildoers, there men are born in due time with long lives. (9.246)
And the crops of the people ripen individually according to how they were sown;
children do not die prematurely, nor is anything deformed born. (9.247)

"Where... and "are produced": in whatever region the king does not confiscate the wealth of those guilty of mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*), there humans are born complete and long-lived. And for the Vaiśyas, just as the crops such as grain are sown, so do they grow forth individually. Children do not die prematurely. Although it was already stated that they are "long-lived," children are mentioned again for the sake of emphasis. Furthermore, no being with a physical deformity is born. (9.246–247)
But if one born of a low caste should, out of desire, oppress Brāhmaṇas, the king shall slay him with various means of execution that cause them terror. (9.248)

Regarding the word "brāhmaṇān": if a Śūdra, through bodily affliction or the seizure of wealth and so forth, willfully oppresses Brāhmaṇas, the king shall slay him with executionary means that cause terror, such as mutilation and the like. (9.248)
As much demerit as there is in killing one who should not be killed, so much is found in a king who releases one who deserves death; but for him who restrains [the wicked], there is merit. (9.249)

"As great as" (yāvān): whatever unrighteousness (*adharma*) is known from the scripture to accrue to a king for the execution of one who should not be executed, exactly that much also accrues for the release of one who deserves execution. However, for one who inflicts punishment according to the scripture, there shall be righteousness (*dharma*); therefore, he should inflict it. 9.249.
Thus has been set forth in detail the determination of legal procedure for two parties disputing with one another in the eighteen titles of law. 9.250

Regarding the word "declared": this detailed exposition of the determination of legal cases for the plaintiff and defendant who are disputing with one another on the eighteen titles of law, beginning with the recovery of debts, has been stated. 9.250.
Thus, performing his duties in accordance with the Dharma correctly, the lord of the earth should seek to acquire territories not yet won and protect those already acquired. (9.251)

"Thus": by deciding legal cases in the manner described, the king, through the affection of the people, should desire to obtain territories not yet acquired and should properly protect those already obtained. In this way, it is stated that the purpose of correctly examining legal proceedings is the acquisition of territories not yet obtained. (9.251)
But having settled in a suitable location and constructed a fortress according to the treatises, he should constantly exert the greatest effort in the removal of thorns. (9.252)

Regarding the word "properly" (*samyak*): according to the manner stated in [verse] 7.69, "a region that is arid yet rich in crops," he should properly settle the territory and, having constructed fortifications there in the manner described in the seventh chapter, always exert supreme effort in eliminating thorns such as thieves and violent criminals. 9.252.
By protecting those of noble conduct and by clearing away thorns, kings who are devoted to the protection of their subjects go to the third heaven. 9.253.

"Because of protection": since kings who are intent on protecting their subjects go to heaven by virtue of protecting those of virtuous conduct and punishing thieves and others, they should therefore make an effort to remove the "thorns. (9.253)
But that king who collects taxes without punishing thieves, his kingdom becomes agitated and he falls away from heaven. (9.254)

"Regarding the phrase 'they did not govern': just as a king who does not suppress thieves and the like takes taxes such as the one-sixth share prescribed for him, the people dwelling in his realm become angry with him; even his attainment of heaven earned through other meritorious deeds is obstructed by this misconduct. (9.254)
But that kingdom which is fearless and relies upon the strength of its arms increases constantly, like a tree being watered. (9.255)

"Free from fear": when a kingdom, by relying on the prowess of its king's arms, becomes free from the fear of thieves and other dangers, it constantly prospers, just as a tree does through the sprinkling of water. (9.255)
The king, whose eyes are his spies, should recognize two kinds of thieves who steal the property of others: those who are open and those who are secret. (9.256)

"Of two kinds" means that the king—who possesses spies as his eyes because the spies themselves are the cause for knowing about thieves—should, by means of those very spies, lawfully identify those who seize the wealth of others through both open and secret methods. (9.256)
Those who live by various wares are open deceivers;
but those such as thieves and forest-dwellers are concealed deceivers. (9.257)

"Prakāśeti" [means]: furthermore, among those such as thieves and others, those who take the wealth of others through improper means—such as by using false scales, counterfeits, or adulteration—when selling commodities like gold, are "open cheats" (*prakāśavañcaka*). Those who take the wealth of others by breaking into houses, lurking in forests, and so forth, are "hidden cheats" (*pracchannavañcaka*). (9.257)
Moreover:
"Bribe-takers, those who use threats for gain, deceivers, gamblers, those who live by predicting auspicious events, fortune-tellers, along with diviners. (9.258)
And likewise, high ministers who act improperly, physicians,
those skilled in the practice of arts and crafts, and clever courtesans— || 9.259 ||
One should recognize such people as manifest thorns in the world, as well as others who move in secret—ignoble men wearing the outward marks of the noble. (9.260)

"Extortionists (*utkocaka*)," "those who act improperly," and "those who act in such a manner": Extortionists are those who, having taken money from litigants, perform improper legal acts. Those who live by means of wealth through the intimidation of fear are the "coercers" (*aupadhika*). Deceivers are those who, having received gold and other valuables, cheat by substituting inferior goods. Gamblers are those who play at dice or engage in betting matches. Those who subsist by predicting auspicious events such as the acquisition of wealth or sons are the "fortune-tellers" (*maṅgalādeśavṛtta*). The "auspicious ones" (*bhadra*) are those who accept wealth while concealing their wickedness behind a semblance of benevolence. Diviners (*īkṣaṇika*) are those who live by predicting good or bad fortune through the examination of hand-lines and so forth. Elephant trainers (*mahāmātra*) are those who live by the training of elephants. Physicians (*cikitsaka*) are those who live by medical treatment. The term "those who act improperly" (*asamyakkārin*) is an epithet for both the elephant trainers and the physicians. Artisans (*śilpopacārayukta*) are those who subsist on painting and the like; they too take money by inciting people to adopt crafts that do not provide a livelihood. One should discover through spies such public deceivers as courtesans (*paṇyastri*), who are skilled at bringing others under their influence, as well as others who move in disguise—such as Śūdras and others wearing the dress of Brāhmaṇas and the like—who seize wealth. (9.258–260)
Having identified them through secret agents who perform their duties with good conduct and by means of spies in various disguises, he should uproot them and bring them under his control. (9.261)

"Those" refers to those aforementioned deceivers whom the king should discover through spies stationed in various places—such as members of the assembly (*sabhyas*), secret agents who perform their specific duties, merchants engaged in theft, and other persons such as the *kāpaṭikas* taught in the seventh chapter—and having discovered them, he should suppress them and bring them under his control. (9.261)

Having publicly proclaimed their faults according to the truth in relation to each of their respective duties, the king should duly administer punishment based on the gravity of the offense and the strength of the offender. 9.262

"Of them" means: having made public in the world those ultimate faults—such as breaking into walls and so forth—which belong to those thieves, whether they be luminous or non-luminous, in their own work such as theft, the king shall inflict punishment in consideration of the wealth, body, and other resources of the offenders, as well as the nature of the offense. (9.262)
For indeed, without punishment, it is impossible to restrain the wickedness of thieves who possess evil intentions and move about secretly upon the earth. (9.263)

"No," [he says]. Because it is impossible to impose a restriction on the commission of evil deeds by thieves—who possess the intent to commit sin and wander the earth in disguised dress—without the application of punishment, one should therefore inflict punishment upon them. (9.263)
Assembly halls, water-stations, bakeries, taverns, and shops selling intoxicating foods; crossroads, sacred trees, public gatherings, and spectacles—(9.264)
Dilapidated gardens, forests, and the workshops of artisans; empty houses as well as woods and groves. 9.265.
The king should cause such regions to be patrolled by both stationary and mobile military outposts, as well as by spies, for the purpose of suppressing thieves. (9.266)

[The king] should cause [spies] to patrol. "Worn-out" means as follows: an assembly hall (*sabhā*)—a fixed place for gatherings of people in villages, cities, and so forth; a water-station (*prapā*)—a house for distributing water; a bakery; the house of a courtesan; places where liquor and food are sold; crossroads; the roots of famous trees; gathering places for crowds of people; dilapidated gardens; forests; craft-houses; empty houses; mango groves and the like; and artificial parks. In such locations, he should cause patrols consisting of troops, groups of infantry—both stationary and mobile—and others stationed in one place or wandering about—to patrol for the purpose of preventing thieves. For generally, in such places, thieves remain for the sake of seeking food, drink, women, sexual pleasure, sleep, weapons, and so forth. (9.264–266)
He should discover them through their companions who follow them and know their various activities, and he should eliminate them with the help of clever former thieves. (9.267)

Regarding the word "that": by means of former thieves who have become informants (*cāra*), who provide assistance to those [current thieves], who follow their conduct, who know how to carry out acts such as breaking into houses, and who are skilled in the arts of spying and deception, he should discover the robbers and eliminate them. (9.267)
Under the pretext of providing food and drink, by means of visiting Brahmins, and under the guise of discussing heroic deeds, they should bring about their meeting. (9.268)

"Regarding the word *bhakṣya* (edible): those former thieves, acting as spies, might say, 'Come, let us go to our house; there we shall eat sweetmeats, milk-rice, and other such things,' thus under the pretext of food and drink. Or they might say, 'In our country there is a Brahmin who knows how to accomplish one's desired goals; let us see him,' thus by means of visiting Brahmins. Or they might say, 'A certain man alone will fight against many; let us see him,' thus under the pretext of witnessing feats of valor. In these ways, the king’s law-enforcing officers should arrange a meeting with those thieves and cause them to be apprehended. (9.268)
Those who do not submit there, and those who are instigators from the root, the king should forcibly slay, along with their friends, kinsmen, and relatives. (9.269)

Regarding the word "those" (ye): those thieves who do not approach the food, drink, and other provisions there for fear of being apprehended, as well as those who associate with the group of old thieves appointed by the king at the base [of the operation] and remain vigilant—the king, having identified those thieves from them alone, should forcibly attack and slay them along with their friends, fathers, and other kinsmen and relatives who have joined them in that enterprise. (9.269)
A righteous king shall not execute a thief without the stolen goods; however, he may execute one caught with the goods along with the implements [of theft] without hesitation. (9.270)

"Not by suspicion. A righteous king shall not put to death one whose status as a thief is not established, except in cases involving stolen property, housebreaking, or the tools of the trade; rather, he shall execute one whose status as a thief is confirmed by the presence of stolen goods and the implements of theft, without further deliberation. (9.270)
Moreover, whoever in the villages provide food to thieves, or even give them space for their goods—all of those he should also cause to be executed. (9.271)

"In villages" means that even among those in villages and similar places, whoever—having recognized the thievery of thieves—provide food or give shelter for their goods and other items used in theft, they too the king should have executed, taking into account the degree of their offense, such as its continuity and so forth. (9.271)

He should swiftly punish those appointed to protect the realms and the vassal lords who have been exhorted [to act], if they remain indifferent during attacks, just as one would punish thieves. 9.272.

"In the realms" (rāṣṭreṣu): those who are appointed as guardians in the realms, and those who dwell on the borders—whether they be cruel men or those who remain neutral in the teaching of theft—the king should punish them swiftly like thieves. || 9.272 ||
And even one who lives by the Dharma, if he has fallen away from the covenant of the Dharma,
he should be scorched with punishment, for he has strayed from his own duty.

"And also he who... [refers to: A Brahmin who lives by means of officiating at sacrifices, receiving gifts, and so forth—having produced for others the merit (*dharma*) consisting of sacrifice, giving, and the like—is one who lives by *dharma*. Even such a person, if he has fallen from the boundary of *dharma*, one should cause him to suffer through punishment, having caused him to deviate from his own duty. (9.273)

Those who do not run to the aid of others to the best of their ability when a village is being plundered, when a dam is breached, or when a robbery is observed on the road, shall be banished along with their belongings. (9.274)

"Grāme" (in a village): when a village is being plundered by thieves and the like; "hitābhaṅge" (when a breach of embankments occurs), meaning when the destruction of water-dams has taken place—Medhātithi explains: "and when crops grown in the fields are destroyed, or when the means of livelihood is ruined. And on the road, those living nearby who do not provide protection to the best of their ability upon seeing a thief must be banished from the country along with their belongings, such as beds, cattle, horses, and other equipment.
He should cause those who steal the king's treasury, those who stand in opposition, and those who instigate enemies to be executed by various forms of punishment. (9.275)

"Of the king": the king shall cause those who seize the wealth from his treasury, as well as those who obstruct his commands, his enemies, and those who increase the enmity toward the king, to be executed by various forms of punishment—such as the cutting off of hands, feet, or tongues—in accordance with the nature of their offense. (9.275)
Those thieves who commit robbery at night by breaking through a wall—
the king, having cut off their hands, shall impale them upon a sharp stake.
Regarding "the breach": those thieves who, having made a breach at night, plunder the wealth of others—the king, having cut off both their hands, should impale them upon a sharp stake. (9.276)
In the first instance of breaking a seal, one should have the fingers of the thief cut off;
in the second, his hands and feet; in the third, he deserves the death penalty.

"Regarding the fingers": when a thief steals gold or other valuables situated at the edge of a cloth or similar object by untying the knot, he is a "knot-cutter" (*granthibheda*). Upon his first seizure of property, the king shall cause his fingers to be cut off. According to the statement of Yājñavalkya, "The pickpocket and the knot-cutter [shall have] their hands deprived of the thumb and forefinger" (YDh 3.274), those fingers to be cut are the thumb and the forefinger. Upon a second seizure, he shall have his hand and foot cut off. Upon a third seizure, he becomes liable to capital punishment. 9.277.
The king should punish those who provide fire, food, weapons, or shelter, as well as those who facilitate the theft, just as he would a thief. (9.278)

"Regarding 'those who provide fire': having identified those who commit acts such as breaking seals and the like, the king should seize as a thief those who provide fire, weapons, or places for concealment—these being the ones who facilitate the theft—and likewise those who deposit the stolen wealth of the thief. (9.278)
One who destroys a tank should be killed, or else executed by drowning in water;
or, if he should repair it, he must be made to pay the highest fine.

Regarding the verse beginning with *taḍāga*: one who destroys a tank that benefits the people through bathing, giving, and so forth—by breaking its embankment or other means—should be killed by drowning in water or by some other method. Alternatively, if he should restore the tank, he should be punished with the highest fine (*uttamasāhasa*). (9.279)
Those who break into storehouses, armories, or temples, as well as those who steal elephants, horses, or chariots, he shall surely put to death without hesitation. (9.280)

Regarding the word "storehouse" (koṣṭha): one should immediately execute those who destroy granaries and the like belonging to the king, as well as armories, weapon-sheds, and temples of deities—which require great expenditure of wealth—and those who steal elephants, horses, and chariots. As for the fine of five hundred [paṇas] which the author will later prescribe for those who break down bridges, flagstaffs, or images of deities, that should be understood here as referring to images of deities made of clay that have been worshipped and then discarded, since the death penalty has already been ordained here for the destroyer of a temple of a deity.
But he who diverts the water of a tank already established, or cuts off the inflow of waters, shall be made to pay the first amercement. (9.281)

"But he who... (verse 9.281). Furthermore, he who takes the water of a pond previously constructed by someone else for the sake of the public is subject to the following: for the destruction of the entire body of water in a pond, the death penalty was previously mentioned; likewise, he who destroys the water-course by means of a dam or similar works shall be fined the first amercement. || 9.281 ||
He who, without a valid reason, should discharge impurity upon the royal highway, shall pay two kārṣāpaṇas and must quickly clean away that impurity. (9.282)
"Should abandon": he who, being not afflicted by illness, voids excrement on the royal highways, shall pay a fine of two kārṣāpaṇas and must immediately remove that impurity. 9.282.

Furthermore, one who has fallen into calamity, or an elderly person, a pregnant woman, or even a child, deserve only a reprimand; and that [offense] must be cleared away—such is the settled rule. (9.283)

Those who are diseased, the elderly, pregnant women, and children are not to be punished; rather, they are to be admonished as to what they have done. Furthermore, they are to be cleansed of that impurity—such is the established rule of the scriptures. (9.283)
For all physicians who practice falsely, there shall be punishment:
the first amercement for offenses against non-human beings, but the middle amercement for those against human beings. 9.284.

Regarding "of physicians": a punishment must be imposed upon all those who practice difficult medical treatments, such as surgeons for bodily wounds and the like. In that regard, for difficult treatment involving cattle, horses, and so forth, the first amercement is the penalty; however, in the case of humans, it is the middle amercement. (9.284)
One who destroys the transition-arches, flagstaffs, or images shall repair all of that and pay five hundred [paṇas]. || 9.285 ||

"Saṃkrama" refers to a bridge or causeway for crossing over water, constructed of wood, stone, or similar materials; "dhvaja" is a banner or emblem at the gates of a royal palace and so forth; "yaṣṭi" is a pole or pillar at lotus ponds and the like; and "pratimās" are small images made of clay and other materials. One who destroys these shall pay a fine of five hundred paṇas, and he must restore everything that was destroyed to its original new state. (9.285)
For spoiling unadulterated goods, as well as for breaking them or boring gems in the wrong way, the punishment is the first amercement. (9.286)

Regarding the phrase "of those that are not defiled": when pure substances are defiled by the insertion of inferior substances; when gems such as rubies (*māṇikya*) and the like—which are indivisible—are split; and even when pearls and the like—which are pierceable—are pierced in a manner that causes instability, the punishment of the first *sāhasa* (lowest fine) shall be imposed. In all cases involving the destruction of another's property, the satisfaction of the owner must be secured through the delivery of another object or similar means. (9.286)
For if a man should act unfairly toward those who are equal, whether by means of the goods themselves or by the price, he shall incur the first or indeed the middle amercement. (9.287)

"By equals": with those who are equal, meaning those who pay the same price; he who deals unequally by giving goods of superior or inferior quality—giving a commodity of high value to one and a commodity of low value to another after having paid the same price—shall, depending on the specific circumstances, incur the first or middle amercement as punishment. (9.287)
And he should place all prisoners along the royal highway, so that those miserable, disfigured evildoers may be seen there. (9.288)
One who breaks down a wall, fills up a moat, or destroys a gate should be banished immediately. (9.289)

Regarding "imprisonment" and "fortifications": he should construct prisons on the royal highway where they are visible to all people, so that those who have committed evil deeds—bound in fetters and the like, overcome by hunger and thirst, with long hair, nails, and beards, and emaciated—may be seen by others for the purpose of deterring them from committing similar forbidden acts. Furthermore, the king should immediately banish from the country anyone who destroys the ramparts of his own houses or cities, or fills up their moats, or breaks down the gates situated therein. (9.288–289)
In all cases of malevolent magic, a fine of two hundred [paṇas] shall be imposed;
likewise for root-rites performed by those who are not authorized, and for various types of sorcery.

Regarding the phrase "in cases of malevolent magic" (*abhicāreṣu*): when rites such as oblations for malevolent purposes—whether scriptural means of killing or worldly methods such as burying roots, seizing dust from the footprints of an enemy, and so forth—are performed, but the result of death has not yet occurred, a fine consisting of the seizure of two hundred *paṇas* must be imposed. However, if death actually occurs, the punishment for killing a human being applies. Likewise, when others—distinct from one's mother, father, or wife—deceive one with falsehoods for the sake of seizing wealth and the like through subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), or when various kinds of sorcery (*kṛtyā*) are practiced for reasons such as eradication (*uccāṭana*) or causing paralysis (*pāṭava*), a fine of exactly two hundred *paṇas* must be imposed. (9.290)
One who sells seed that is unfit for sowing, one who steals such seed,
and likewise one who destroys a boundary marker, shall suffer the punishment of mutilation or death.

"Seedless," he says: one who sells rice or other grains that are seedless—meaning incapable of sprouting—as if they were capable of sprouting; likewise, one who sells inferior goods by mixing in a few superior ones, claiming "all this is of high quality"; and one who destroys the boundaries of villages, cities, and so forth—these shall suffer corporal punishment consisting of the mutilation of the nose, hands, feet, ears, and other limbs.
But the king shall have a goldsmith who is the most wicked of all thorns,
if he persists in unlawful conduct, cut into pieces with razors.

"Of all"—[this refers to] among all thorns (criminals), one who is most exceedingly wicked, such as a goldsmith engaged in the theft of gold and other precious metals by means of false scales, deceptive touchstones, the substitution of base materials, and so forth; him, according to the gravity of the offense, one should have his limbs severed in specific parts or have his entire body cut into pieces. 2.292.
In cases of the theft of land, goods, weapons, or medicine, the king, having considered the time and the nature of the deed, shall determine the punishment. (9.293)

Regarding the term *sītā*: when there is theft of agricultural implements such as ploughs and spades—along with weapons like swords and the like, or medicinal herbs and auspicious clarified butter (*kalyāṇaghṛta*)—the king shall impose punishment based on whether the act occurred at a time of utility or otherwise, and depending on the purpose served. (9.293)
The sovereign, the minister, the capital, the realm, the treasury, the army, and likewise the ally—these are the seven constituent elements; thus the kingdom is said to have seven limbs. 9.294.

Regarding the term *svāmī*: the sovereign (*svāmī*) is the king; the minister (*amātya*) is the counselor and so forth; the city (*pura*) is the capital where the king has established his fortress; the realm (*rāṣṭra*) is the country; the treasury (*kośa*) is the accumulation of wealth; the army (*daṇḍa*) consists of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry; and the ally (*mitra*) is of three kinds as described in the seventh chapter—these seven constituent elements (*prakṛti*) are the "limbs" (*aṅga*). This kingdom is said to possess these seven limbs. (9.294)
To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
"Among these seven constituent elements of sovereignty, one should know that, in their respective order, each preceding one is more serious and its misfortune greater. (9.295)

"Of the seven": regarding these seven constituent elements of sovereignty mentioned in their sequential order, one should understand that, with respect to the non-destruction of each subsequent element, there is a more serious calamity concerning the destruction of each preceding one. For instance: a calamity affecting the army is more serious than a calamity affecting the ally, because only one who possesses a powerful army has the capacity to favor an ally. Likewise, the treasury is more serious than the army, because if the treasury is destroyed, the army is also destroyed. The realm is more serious than the treasury, because if the realm is destroyed, from where would the treasury arise? Similarly, the destruction of the fort is more serious than the realm; for it is precisely from a fort well-supplied with fodder, fuel, and other necessities that the protection of the kingdom is accomplished. The minister is more serious than the fort, because if the principal minister is destroyed, all the constituent parts of the state become impaired. Even more so than the minister is the self (the king himself), because everything exists for the sake of the self. Therefore, one should protect each preceding element with effort in consideration of what follows it. (9.295)
In this world, of the sevenfold kingdom which is supported like a triple staff, nothing excels another because of the specific excellence of their mutual qualities. (9.296)

Regarding the phrase "of the seven-limbed": in this world, for a kingdom possessing the aforementioned seven limbs—which are interconnected like a triple-staff (*tridaṇḍa*) and provide distinct mutual assistance—not a single limb is superfluous. Although the preceding verse stated that each preceding limb is superior, nevertheless, among these limbs, no one limb can remedy the deficiency of another; therefore, even each subsequent limb must be relied upon. This negation of superiority is intended to convey this very point. In this context, the well-known triple-staff of an ascetic (*yati*) serves as the illustration. For that staff consists of three sticks bound together by a four-finger-width cord of cow-hair; they are mutually dependent, and within that system of holding the triple-staff according to scriptural injunction, no single stick is superfluous. (9.296)
In various specific tasks, however, this or that particular factor is distinguished;
whatever means accomplishes a given purpose is said to be the most excellent for that purpose. (9.297)

Regarding the phrase "in those": because in each of those various tasks to be accomplished, there exists a specific excellence (*atiśaya*) of its respective constituent part (*aṅga*), since that task cannot be performed by anything else; and thus, whichever constituent part accomplishes a particular task, that very part is called the primary factor (*pradhāna*) with respect to that task. Consequently, what was stated previously regarding the mutual distinction of qualities (*guṇaviśeṣa*) and so forth is clarified by this very point. (9.297)

Through the movement [of his spies], through the application of energy, and indeed through the performance of actions, the lord of the earth should constantly ascertain both his own power and the power of others. (9.298)

"By means of spies": the king should always know the state of his enemy and himself through the employment of spies such as the *kāpaṭika* and others mentioned in the seventh chapter, through the application of energy (*utsāha*) by the army, and through the execution of undertakings such as the capture of elephants and the opening of trade routes. (9.298)
Having reflected upon the gravity or lightness of all oppressions as well as calamities, one should then undertake the task. (9.299)

Regarding "afflictions" (*pīḍanāni*): afflictions are those arising from Mārakas and the like, born of desire and anger, as well as sufferings caused by one's own or an enemy's army; having carefully considered the relative gravity or lightness of these, one should undertake actions such as peace or war. || 9.299 ||
One should indeed undertake actions again and again, even when utterly exhausted; for prosperity attends the man who perseveres in his undertakings. 9.300

"One should begin. Even if a king, having undertaken actions for the sake of increasing his own kingdom and diminishing that of his enemies, should somehow encounter obstacles and think, "This has happened," he should, though personally distressed, begin those very tasks again and again. For Fortune intensely attends the man who undertakes his duties. Likewise, Fortune does not abide in one who is not a Brahmin nor in one who lacks a proper foundation; even if she has taken root, she withers away. Furthermore, since actions do not bear fruit merely by conforming to the age, the king must never remain indifferent. (9.300)
For it is said:
"The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages are all the conduct of the king; indeed, the king is called the age. (9.301)

Regarding the term *kṛta*: the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages are indeed specific manifestations of the king's own conduct, since it is through these very actions that the specific qualities such as truthfulness (*satya*) and so forth come into being. Therefore, the king alone is designated by the names of the Kṛta and other ages. (9.301)

To explain what kind of activity characterizes the Kṛta and other ages, he says: "Kali is when one is asleep; Dvāpara is when one is awake; Tretā is when one is intent upon actions; but Kṛta is when one is moving about [in virtue]. (9.302)

Regarding the term *kali*: when a king becomes inactive due to ignorance, laziness, and so forth, then it is the *kali* age. When he knows [his duty] but does not perform it, then it is the *dvāpara* age. When he is established in the performance of his duties, then it is the *tretā* age. But when he conducts himself performing actions according to the scriptures, then it is the *kṛta* age. Therefore, the essential point here is that the king must be intent upon the performance of his duties; it is not intended as a denial of the actual existence of the *kṛta* age and the others. (9.302)
A king should conduct himself with the same vigor as Indra, Arka, Vāyu, Yama, Varuṇa, Candra, Agni, and the Earth. (9.303)

"Of Indra," etc.: the king should emulate the conduct corresponding to the prowess associated with Indra and the other [deities]. And thus, by uprooting thorns [from his realm], the king shall be endowed with majesty and the affection [of his subjects]. (9.303)
To explain how one should emulate the conduct of Indra and others, he says:
"Just as Indra pours down rain during the four months of the rainy season, so should one who observes the vow of Indra shower his own kingdom with desired objects. (9.304)

Regarding the phrase "the rains": this is stated by relying on the perspective of the seasonal year (*ṛtusaṃvatsara*). Just as Indra rains for four months beginning with Śrāvaṇa for the sake of the growth of crops and so forth, so too the king, emulating the conduct of Indra, should satisfy the virtuous who have come from his own country with their desired objects. (9.304)
Just as the sun draws up water with its rays for eight months, so should he take taxes from the kingdom; for that is the constant vow of the sun. 9.305.

"Eight": Just as the sun draws up moisture little by little from the eight months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa with its rays through mild heat, so too should the king always take taxes from the realm without causing oppression; for this is his solar vow (arkavrata). 9.305.
Just as the wind enters all beings and moves through them, so too should one enter by means of spies; for this indeed is the "wind-like" vow.

"Having entered" means that just as the wind called *prāṇa* moves about after entering within all living beings, so too must one enter within the networks of one's own and others' maṇḍalas by way of the spy (*cāra*), for the purpose of knowing the intended object; for this is the movement of the wind. 9.306.
Just as Yama restrains both the beloved and the hated when the time has come, so too must subjects be restrained by the king; for that is the vow of Yama. 9.307

Regarding the word "yathā" (as): although Yama has neither enemies nor friends, nevertheless, just as Yama restrains both enemies and friends equally at the time of their death—those who revile him and those who worship him—so too must subjects be punished by the king at the time of their offense, having abandoned passion and hatred; for this is his vow as the son of Yama. 9.307.
Just as one who is bound by Varuṇa with his nooses is clearly seen, so should one restrain the wicked; for this is indeed the vow of Varuṇa. 9.308.

"O Varuṇa!"—just as one who is intended to be bound by Varuṇa’s ropes appears to be bound by those nooses even while remaining unsuspecting, so too should the king punish evildoers while they are still unsuspecting, before they have crossed over [to safety]. For this is his vow pertaining to Varuṇa. (9.308)
Just as men rejoice upon seeing the full moon, so do the subjects rejoice in that king who observes the lunar vow.

"Complete" means: just as people experience joy upon seeing the full moon, so too is that lord of men—who moves with the course of the moon—the one upon seeing whom ministers and others attain satisfaction. 9.309.
One who is endowed with majesty, radiant, always intent upon evil deeds,
and a destroyer of wicked vassals— that is remembered as the Agneya vow.

"Endowed with majesty," and so forth: he should be fierce and intolerant toward evildoers by always inflicting punishment; likewise, he should be habitually inclined to strike down hostile ministers. This is remembered as his vow pertaining to fire. (9.310)
Just as the earth supports all beings equally, so too is the vow of a king who sustains all beings. 9.311

"Yathā" means: just as the earth supports all things—high and low, stationary and moving, superior and inferior—making them equal, so too for one who supports equally through protection, the giving of wealth, and other means all beings, whether they be learned, wealthy, virtuous, or their opposites, including the poor, the helpless, and all others, there exists the vow pertaining to the earth. (9.311)
Employing these and other means, always untiring, the king should suppress thieves both within his own kingdom and in that of others. (9.312)

"By these" means: by these aforementioned means, as well as others not mentioned, a king who is diligent and employs his own intelligence should suppress both types of thieves—those who dwell within his own kingdom and those who dwell in foreign kingdoms and come to plunder that country. The fact that he possesses the nature of fire and wind was previously stated as an established truth in the verse beginning with "He becomes fire and wind" (7.7); here, however, it is made explicit by setting aside those specific qualities, and thus there is no tautology. 9.312.
Even when fallen into the greatest calamity, one should not provoke the Brāhmaṇas;
for if they are angered, they can instantly destroy him along with his army and his mounts. (9.313)
