"Even the highest" means that even if a king has fallen into extreme calamity due to the depletion of his treasury and so forth, he must not provoke the Brahmins; for if they are enraged, they could instantly destroy him, along with his army and vehicles, by means of curses and malevolent spells. (9.313)
For it is thus:
"By whom the fire was made all-consuming, the great ocean made undrinkable, and the moon made subject to waning and waxing—who would not perish by provoking them? (9.314)

"By whom": by which Brahmins fire was made to consume all things through their curse, the ocean was rendered unfit for drinking, and the moon, though subject to waning, was later filled back up—who would not perish after provoking them? (9.314)
Moreover:
"Who could prosper by harming those who, when provoked to anger, might create other worlds and world-protectors, or turn gods into non-gods? (9.315)

Regarding the word "worlds" (lokān): who could attain prosperity by oppressing those who are capable of creating other worlds such as heaven and so forth, as well as other world-protectors, and who turn gods into humans and the like through their curses? (9.315)
Moreover:
"Those upon whom the worlds and the gods always depend, for whom Brahman itself is wealth—who that desires to live would harm them? (9.316)

“Those whom... and so forth. Who indeed would wish to harm those Brāhmaṇas—those who perform sacrifices for themselves and officiate at the sacrifices of others—by depending upon whom, according to the principle that “the oblation cast into the fire [reaches the sun]” (3.176), the worlds beginning with the earth and the gods obtain their sustenance; and for whom the Veda alone is the means of prosperity through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and so forth, as well as the means of acquiring wealth? || 9.316 ||
If that is so, then one should serve only a learned Brāhmaṇa; to this he says:
"Both the ignorant and the learned Brāhmaṇa are a great divinity;
whether consecrated or unconsecrated, just as fire is a great divinity. (9.317)
"Regarding the term 'the ignorant': just as fire, whether enkindled or unenkindled, is a great deity, so too is a Brāhmaṇa, whether foolish or learned, a preeminent deity. (9.317)
Even in cremation grounds, the radiant fire is not defiled;
when offered oblations in sacrifices, it increases all the more. (9.318)

"In cremation grounds," and so forth. Just as fire, possessing great brilliance, though burning a corpse in a cremation ground during its task, is not at all defiled, but rather increases further when offered oblations in sacrifices. || 9.318 ||
Thus, even if they engage in all kinds of unworthy actions, Brahmins must always be honored, for they are indeed the supreme deity. (9.319)

"Even so" means this: even though Brāhmaṇas may engage in all kinds of contemptible actions, they must nevertheless be honored in every way. For that which is excellent is divine; and since this statement is intended as praise, one should not suspect a contradiction with the literal meaning of the words. (9.319)

When the Kṣatriya power has become excessively overbearing toward Brāhmaṇas in every respect, the Brāhmaṇical power alone should act as its restrainer; for the Kṣatriya is born from the Brāhmaṇa. (9.320)

Regarding the verse beginning with "kṣatrasya": for a Kṣatriya who in every way inflicts suffering upon Brāhmaṇas, the Brāhmaṇas alone are the proper restrainers by means of curses, malevolent rites, and so forth; because the Kṣatriya was born from the Brāhmaṇa, having been produced from the arms of the Brāhmaṇa. (9.320)
And so it is said:
"Fire arose from water, the Kṣatriya from the Brāhmaṇa, and iron from stone;
their all-pervading heat is extinguished within their own sources. (9.321)

Regarding the phrase "from the waters": fire, the Kṣatriya, and weapons are born from water, the Brāhmaṇa, and stone; their associated heat performs its function everywhere for the purpose of burning, overpowering, and cutting. Yet, within their own causes—namely water, the Brāhmaṇa, and stone—it does not perform the function consisting of burning, overpowering, and cutting. (9.321)

The spiritual power (brahman) does not prosper without the ruling power (kṣatra), nor does the ruling power increase without the spiritual power; when the spiritual power and the ruling power are united, they flourish both in this world and in the next. || 9.322 ||

"No," [the author replies]. A Kṣatriya devoid of Brāhmaṇas does not prosper, because he is deprived of the duties of performing rites for peace (*śāntika*), prosperity (*pauṣṭika*), legal proceedings, and supervision. Likewise, a Brāhmaṇa devoid of a Kṣatriya does not flourish, because sacrificial acts and the like cannot be accomplished without protection. However, it is only when the Brāhmaṇa and the Kṣatriya are mutually connected that they attain prosperity through the acquisition of virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), pleasure (*kāma*), and liberation (*mokṣa*) in this world and the next. Furthermore, this praise of Brāhmaṇas in the section on punishment is intended to establish the rule that even for Brāhmaṇas who are offenders, only a light penalty should be applied. (9.322)
But when, due to a specific vision [of one's end] or an incurable disease, death is imminent, then—
having given away all wealth arising from fines to the Brahmins and having entrusted the kingdom to his son— he should seek his departure in battle. (9.323)

"Having given," [means]: having given to the Brahmins all the wealth remaining after the fines have been paid, excluding that pertaining to those who have committed the great sins (mahāpātaka), and having entrusted the kingdom to his son, one whose death is imminent should sacrifice his life in battle for the sake of attaining an excellence of merit. If battle is not possible, however, he may do so even by means of fasting and the like. 9.323.
Acting thus, ever intent upon the duties of kingship and for the welfare of the world, the monarch should employ all his servants. 9.324

Thus: A king who conducts himself according to the duties of kings as set forth in these three chapters should always be diligent in the welfare of his subjects and employ all his servants accordingly. 9.324.
This eternal rule of action for the king has been declared in its entirety;
one should likewise know this rule of action for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra in due order. (9.325)

"Regarding this": this performance of duties by the king has been described as eternal and complete, having been handed down through tradition; now, one should understand that this performance of duties for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra is being stated in due order. 9.325.
But a Vaiśya, having undergone the purificatory rites and taken a wife, should be constantly engaged in agriculture and commerce, as well as in the protection of livestock. (9.326)

"But the Vaiśya," it is said. A Vaiśya who has undergone the sacraments up to and including initiation (upanayana), having performed marriage and other rites, should always be intent upon his livelihood as it will be described—upon activities such as agriculture and the tending of cattle. Although the protection of cattle is included within the category of "vocation" (vārtā), it is mentioned separately in order to emphasize its importance; thus, he demonstrates its preeminence in the two subsequent verses. 9.326.
For Prajāpati, having created cattle, entrusted them to the Vaiśya; and he entrusted all subjects to the Brāhmaṇa and the King. (9.327)

Regarding the term "Prajāpati": since Brahmā, having created the animals, gave them to the Vaiśya for the sake of protection, it is therefore stated as a restatement of what has been previously established that animals are to be protected by the Vaiśya. Furthermore, this is mentioned incidentally because [Prajāpati], having created all beings, gave them to the Brāhmaṇa and the King for the sake of protection. (9.327)
A Vaiśya should have no desire [to think], "I shall not tend cattle";
if the Vaiśya so desires, they must by no means be tended by anyone else. (9.328)

"Nor [should he say] 'I will not tend cattle. A Vaiśya must not entertain the desire, "I shall not perform the tending of cattle. Therefore, even when other means of livelihood such as agriculture are available, the tending of cattle must necessarily be performed by a Vaiśya. And while the Vaiśya is performing the tending of cattle, another person must be employed to perform the tending of cattle. (9.328)
Furthermore:
One should know the relative value and worth of gems, pearls, corals, metals, woven textiles, perfumes, and liquids. (9.329)

Regarding "gems" (maṇi): a Vaiśya should know the increase or decrease in value—based on place and time—of gems, pearls, coral, metals, and clothes; of fragrances such as camphor and the like; and of liquids such as salt and the like, whether they be of superior or middling quality. (9.329)

One should know the method of sowing seeds, as well as the defects and virtues of the field; one should understand the application of measures and all the applications of the scales in every respect. (9.330)

Regarding "of seeds": he should be one who knows the method of sowing all seeds—knowing that this seed, when gathered and sown at this particular time, will sprout in that place and not otherwise; likewise, he should know the defects and virtues of fields, such as "this is saline soil" or "this yields crops," and so forth. He should also truly understand all measures of capacity, such as the *prastha* and *droṇa*, and all methods of weighing, so that no other person may deceive him. (9.330)
He [should know] the value and worthlessness of goods, the merits and defects of regions, the profit and loss of merchandise, and the breeding of livestock. (9.331)

Regarding "the essential and the non-essential": he should know the distinction even among items of the same kind, such as "this is superior" and "that is inferior. Likewise, he should understand the merits and defects of regions—such as the east, west, and so forth—including where what is of little value and what is of great value. He should also know that for merchandise being sold, there is such an amount of decrease or increase within such a period of time. Furthermore, he should know that in this region, at this time, cattle flourish through such grass, water, barley, and so on, while they decline because of such other factors. (9.331)
He should know the wages of servants, the various languages of men, the methods of storing goods, and their buying and selling. (9.332)

Regarding "of servants": he should know the wages for cowherds, buffalo-herders, and others, which are to be given to them according to place, time, and the work performed. He should also know the various languages of men from Gauḍa, Dakṣiṇāpatha, and other regions, for the purpose of trade and so forth. Likewise, he should understand how this particular commodity is stored and that it remains for a long time when combined with this [other substance]; and he should also know how much of this commodity is sold in this region and at this time. (9.332)
One should exert the highest effort to increase one's wealth through righteous means, and one should diligently provide food for all living beings. (9.333)

"By means of dharma": he should exert great effort toward the increase of wealth through lawful means such as selling and so forth; and with regard to the giving of gold and other things, he should especially give food to living beings. (9.333)
For a Śūdra, however, the service of Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas, householders, and illustrious, is indeed the supreme dharma leading to the highest bliss. (9.334)

Regarding the word "of the Brahmins": for a Śūdra, however, the very service rendered to Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas, who are householders, and who are endowed with fame through the performance of their own duties, is that dharma which is the cause of the highest good, such as heaven. 9.334.
Pure, devoted to the highest service, gentle in speech, free from egoism, and always taking refuge in Brahmins and the like, one attains a superior birth. (9.335)

"Pure" means endowed with both external and internal purity; one who is habitually devoted to serving members of the twice-born castes superior to his own; who speaks without harshness; who is free from egoism; and who, primarily relying on Brāhmaṇas, or in their absence, even on Kṣatriyas or Vaiśyas, attains a caste superior to his own. (9.335)
This auspicious rule of action for the social classes in times of no distress has been declared;
now learn, in due order, that which pertains to them in times of distress. 9.336

"Regarding this": this rule of action for the four castes in times of non-distress has been declared as their *dharma*; now listen in due order to that *dharma* of theirs which applies even in times of distress, following the mention of the mixed castes. (9.336)
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Manvarthamuktāvalī, a commentary on the Code of Manu, composed by the illustrious Kullūkabhaṭṭa.
The tenth chapter:

The three twice-born castes, remaining steadfast in their own duties, may study; however, it is the settled rule that among them, only the Brāhmaṇa may expound [the Veda], and not the other two. 10.1.

“They should study. Since it was previously promised that “the origin of the mixed castes shall be described” (1.116) immediately after the duties of Vaiśyas and Śūdras, and since those mixed castes arise from the [four] primary castes, this verse restates the primary duty of study for the three twice-born castes and the teaching of the Veda for the Brāhmaṇa, in order to refer back to those castes. The three castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa—those who perform their own duties as experienced through study—should recite the Veda. Furthermore, among these, it is determined that only the Brāhmaṇa should perform the teaching, not the Kṣatriya or the Vaiśya. Although the prohibition against the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya teaching is already established by the statement “but the Brāhmaṇa should teach them,” the repeated prohibition “not the other two” is intended to indicate the severity of the penance required for such an act. 10.1.
Moreover:
A Brāhmaṇa should know the means of livelihood for all [classes] according to the rule;
he should declare them to the others, and he himself should likewise abide by them. (10.2)

"Of all"—a Brāhmaṇa should know the means of livelihood for all the social classes (varṇas) according to the scriptures, he should instruct them therein, and he himself should observe the prescribed rules as stated. 10.2.
On this point, there is a restatement:

"Due to his distinctiveness, the excellence of his origin, his adherence to the rules of discipline, and the particularity of his refinement, among the social classes, the Brāhmaṇa is the preeminent master. (10.3)

"Because of preeminence" (*vaiśeṣyāt*): because of the excellence of his birth; because of the excellence of his nature (*prakṛti*), which is the cause [of his status], namely the excellence of being the form of the head of Hiraṇyagarbha; and because he is "restrained by this," that is, the Veda—due to his superior retention of the Veda through its study, teaching, narration, and so forth. For this very reason, it was stated [in verse 1.93] that "by the retention of the Brahman alone" the excellence of the Brāhmaṇa is declared, referring specifically to the superior retention of the Veda. Govindarāja, however, explained it as "because of the observance of the vows of a *snātaka*. That is not correct, because such observances are common to Kṣatriyas and others as well. Since the initiation known as *upanayana* is established as primary for him compared to Kṣatriyas and others, and because of this distinction, the Brāhmaṇa alone is the master (*īśvara*) regarding the duties of teaching and instruction among the social classes (*varṇas*). 10.3.
The Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya—these three castes are twice-born;
the fourth is once-born, the Śūdra, but there is no fifth. (10.4)

"Brāhmaṇa," etc. The three castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa are the twice-born (*dvija*), because for them the rite of initiation (*upanayana*) is prescribed. The Śūdra, moreover, is the fourth caste and is "once-born" (*ekajāti*), due to the absence of initiation. Furthermore, there is no fifth caste. As for those of mixed castes (*saṃkīrṇajāti*), however, they do not possess the status of a caste (*varṇatva*) because, like a mule, they belong to a distinct intermediate caste different from the castes of their mother and father. And this instruction regarding these other castes is for the sake of conventional usage within the treatise. 10.4.
Among wives of equal caste who have not lost their virginity, those born in the direct order [of castes] are to be known as belonging to that same caste. (10.5)

Regarding the phrase "among all castes" (*sarvavarṇeṣu*): among the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, those born in direct order (*ānulomyena*)—that is, from a Brāhmaṇa by a Brāhmaṇī, from a Kṣatriya by a Kṣatriyā, and so forth—with women of the same caste who have been married according to the scriptures and whose virginity is intact, are to be known as belonging to that very caste, endowed with the caste of their mother and father. The mention of "direct order" here is of little utility, as it will be utilized in the following verse. Because there is no physical configuration of limbs that manifests the Brāhmaṇa caste—as there is in the case of cattle, horses, and the like—this definition of a Brāhmaṇa and so forth has been stated. Furthermore, because of the use of the term "wife" (*patnī*) here, those born of women other than the wife do not possess the caste of Brāhmaṇa and so on. Thus says Devala:
But he who is begotten by a father on a wife of his own caste through the second [form of marriage] is known as an Avavāṭa; by birth, he follows the dharma of a Śūdra.
Sons who are independent yet devoid of vows should not undergo the sacraments;
though begotten by a man of the same caste, they are excluded like outcasts (vrātyas).
Vyāsa says: "But those who are born of women of equal [caste] should be subject to the sacramental rites; otherwise, it is different. Yājñavalkya also [states this at 1.90].
"For from men of the same class, upon women of the same class, are born those of the same caste.
Having stated this, [he adds]:
"This rule is ordained for those who have been married. (1.92)
Speaking thus, he determined that the status of being born into the Brahmin and other castes belongs only to those produced by one's own wife. || 10.5 ||
Sons begotten by the twice-born upon women born immediately after them in the caste order are said to be equal [to their fathers], yet they are censured due to the defect of their mothers. (10.6)

Regarding the phrase "among women": those sons who are procreated by the twice-born (dvijāti) upon wives of the same caste as themselves in the direct order (*ānulomya*)—such as a Brāhmaṇa on a Kṣatriya woman, a Kṣatriya on a Vaiśya woman, and a Vaiśya on a Śūdra woman—are described by Manu and others as being censured due to the defect of the mother’s lower caste; they are said to resemble their fathers, but not to belong to the same caste as their fathers. Because of the mention of "resembling the father," it should be understood that they are superior to the mother's caste but inferior to the father's caste. The names of these [sons]—Mūrdhāvasikta, Māhiṣya, and Karaṇa—have been stated by Yājñavalkya and others, and their occupations have been stated by Uśanas:

Training in elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as the wielding of weapons, is for those consecrated as kings (*mūrdhābhiṣikta*); dancing, singing, astrology, and the protection of crops are for the *māhiṣyas*; and service to the twice-born, supervision of wealth and grain, service to the king, and the guarding of forts and the inner apartments are for the *pāraśavas* and *ugrakaraṇas*.
Such is the eternal rule for those born from women of the next lower caste.
One should know this to be the righteous rule for those born from women two or three castes below. (10.7)

"Regarding the term 'immediate' (anantarāsu): this eternal rule, handed down through tradition, has been declared for those born of wives belonging to the caste immediately following [one's own]. One should know that for those born of women separated by one or two castes—such as from a Brāhmaṇa with a Vaiśya woman, a Kṣatriya with a Śūdra woman, or a Brāhmaṇa with a Śūdra woman—there is this rule about to be described, which does not deviate from the Dharma. (10.7)
From a Brāhmaṇa and the daughter of a Vaiśya is born one named Ambaṣṭha;
from a Śūdra daughter is born a Niṣāda, who is also called a Pāraśava. (10.8)

Regarding the phrase "from a Brāhmaṇa": because of the mention of a "maiden," the word "when married" (*ūḍhāyām*) must be supplied here, as this has been made clear by Yājñavalkya (1.92): "This rule is prescribed for those who have been wedded. From a Brāhmaṇa, when a Vaiśya maiden is married, one born is called an Ambaṣṭha. When a Śūdra maiden is married, a Niṣāda is produced; he is also called a Pāraśava under another name. 10.8.
From a Kṣatriya man and a Śūdra woman is born a creature named Ugra, who possesses the physical form of both a Kṣatriya and a Śūdra and whose conduct and pastimes are cruel. (10.9)

"From a Kṣatriya": when a Kṣatriya fathers a son upon a married Śūdra maiden, a son is born who is called an Ugra; he possesses cruel behavior, delights in cruel deeds, and has the nature of both a Kṣatriya and a Śūdra. || 10.9 ||
These six are recorded as base-born (apasada): those born from a Brahmin in the three [lower] castes, from a Kshatriya in two castes, and from a Vaishya in one caste. || 10.10 ||

Regarding the verse beginning with "viprasya": among the three wives of the Brāhmaṇa—namely those of the Kṣatriya and other castes—the two wives of the Kṣatriya—namely those of the Vaiśya and other castes—and the Śūdra wife of the Vaiśya, these six sons of the three castes are *apasadas*, meaning they are degraded, fallen, and inferior when compared to the duties and status of sons born of wives of the same caste (*savarṇa*). || 10.10 ||
Having thus stated the [castes] in direct order, he speaks of those in reverse order:
"From a Kṣatriya and the daughter of a Brāhmaṇa is born a Sūta by birth;
from a Vaiśya are born a Māgadha and a Vaideha, who are the sons of a royal and a Brāhmaṇa woman respectively. (10.11)

Regarding the phrase "from a Kṣatriya": since marriage is impossible in this case, the mention of a "maiden" (kanyā) is intended to indicate any woman in general, as seen in this very verse where it says "the sons of the wives of kings and Brāhmaṇas. From a Kṣatriya father upon a Brāhmaṇī mother, a son is born by caste named a Sūta. From a Vaiśya father, sons known as Māgadha and Vaideha are born respectively from a Kṣatriya and a Brāhmaṇī mother. The occupations of these [mixed castes] will be described by Manu himself. (10.11)
From a Śūdra [beget] upon a Vaiśya woman an Āyogava; upon a Kṣatriya woman, a Kṣattṛ; and upon a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Caṇḍāla, the lowest of men.
Thus are born those of mixed caste from Vaiśya, Rājanya, and Brāhmaṇa women. || 10.12 ||

"From a Śūdra": from a Śūdra, upon women of the Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, and Brāhmaṇa castes respectively, are born the Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Nṛṇām-adhama (the lowest of men), and the Caṇḍāla; those among whom such offspring are to be produced are known as *varṇasaṃkaras* (those of mixed caste). || 10.12 ||
Just as the Ambaṣṭha and Ugra are traditionally held to arise from a one-interval union in the natural order,
so too do the Kṣattṛ and Vaidehaka arise from a one-interval union in the inverse order of birth.

Regarding the term "one degree apart" (*ekāntara*): even when a caste is one degree apart, from a Brāhmaṇa on a Vaiśya maiden an Ambaṣṭha is born, and from a Kṣatriya on a Śūdra maiden an Ugra is born; these two, being born in the natural order (*ānulomya*), are fit for physical contact and other such interactions. In the same way, when born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*) with a gap of one degree, from a Śūdra on a Kṣatriya woman a Kṣattṛ is born, and from a Vaiśya on a Brāhmaṇī woman a Vaideha is born; these two also should be understood as being fit for physical contact and so forth. Since those born with a gap of one degree are permitted physical contact and the like, it follows that those born with no gap at all—the Sūta, Māgadha, and Āyogava—are established as unfit for such contact. Therefore, the Caṇḍāla alone is excluded from physical contact and other interactions due to his inverse birth. || 10.13 ||

Those sons of the twice-born who are born of women immediately following [the wife of the same caste], as described in order, are designated by the name "anantara" (immediate) due to the defect of their mothers. || 10.14 ||

Regarding the term "sons": the mention of the phrase "due to the defect of the mother" as a reason is intended to include those born immediately after [the father], as well as to demonstrate those born one or two degrees removed. Those sons previously mentioned who were born in the direct order (*ānulomya*) from women of the twice-born castes who are immediate, one-removed, or two-removed in caste—these they call "defiled by the low caste of the mother," and they designate them by the name of the mother's caste. Even though these sons belong to mixed castes distinct from both the mother and the father, the statement that they are designated by the mother's caste is for the purpose of their obtaining the religious duties (*dharma*), such as the sacraments (*saṃskāra*), belonging to that mother's caste. (10.14)
From a Brāhmaṇa and the daughter of an Ugra is born one named Āvṛta; from the daughter of an Ambaṣṭha is born an Ābhīra, but from the daughter of an Āyogava is born a Dhigvaṇa. (10.15)

"From a Brāhmaṇa": from a Brāhmaṇa, upon an *ugrā*—an *ugrā* being a daughter born of a Kṣatriya man and a Śūdra woman—an offspring named *āvṛta* is born. From a Brāhmaṇa, upon an *ambaṣṭhā*—an *ambaṣṭhā* being a daughter born of a Brāhmaṇa man and a Vaiśya woman—an offspring called an *ābhīra* is born. From a Brāhmaṇa, upon an *āyogavī*—an *āyogavī* being a daughter born of a Śūdra man and a Vaiśya woman—an offspring called a *dhigaṇa* is born.
The Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla—the lowest of men—these three base-born sons (apasada) are born from a Śūdra by women of the higher castes in the reverse order of classes. 10.16.

"And the Āyogava. The Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla are the lowest among men; these three, born out of order from a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya, and a Brāhmaṇa woman respectively, are Śūdras who have fallen away from the duties of a son. They are mentioned again, despite having been previously described, for the purpose of demonstrating their unfitness for the duties of a son. The same applies to those mentioned in the following verse. 10.16.
From a Vaiśya, the Māgadha and Vaideha are born; from a Kṣatriya, however, the Sūta alone is born.
These others are also three base-born (apasada) castes, born in the inverse order.

"From a Vaiśya," and so forth. From a Kṣatriya father and a Brāhmaṇa mother are born the Māgadha and the Vaideha; from a Kṣatriya father and a Brāhmaṇa mother is born the Sūta. In this manner, three other base-born (apasada) sons are also produced through the reverse order (prātilomya) for the purpose of procreation. || 10.17 ||
One born from a Niṣāda father and a Śūdra mother is by birth a Pukkasa;
but one born from a Śūdra father and a Niṣāda mother is known as a Kukkuṭaka. || 10.18 ||
Regarding the term "born": one born from a Niṣāda father and a Śūdra mother becomes a Pukkasa by birth; however, one born from a Niṣāda woman by a Śūdra father is known as a Kukkuṭaka. || 10.18 ||
One born from a Kṣattṛ father and an Ugrā mother is known as a Śvapāka;
one begotten by a Vaidehaka on an Ambaṣṭhī woman is called a Veṇa.

Regarding the term *kṣattṛ*: one born of a Śūdra father and a Vaiśya mother is a *kṣattṛ*; one born of a Kṣatriya father and a Śūdra mother is an *ugrā*; and one born of that [ugrā] by him [the kṣattṛ] is called a *śvapāka*. One born of a Vaidehaka father and an Ambaṣṭhī mother—that is, by a Brāhmaṇa born of a Vaiśya woman—is termed a *veṇa*.
Those whom twice-born men beget on wives of equal caste, but who are devoid of sacred observances, one should designate as *vrātyas*, fallen from the *Sāvitrī*. (10.20)

Regarding the term "twice-born" (*dvijātayaḥ*): if the sons whom twice-born men procreate upon wives of their own caste (*savarṇā*) are devoid of the vow known as initiation (*upanayana*), then one should designate those who have not received initiation by the name *vrātya*. Although the definition of a *vrātya* was already stated [in verse 2.39] with the words, "From this point forward, these three also," it has been reiterated here in this section on mixed castes for the purpose of demonstrating that, like the sons born of women in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), they are likewise incapable of performing beneficial rites. 10.20.
From a Vrātya Brahmin is born the evil-natured Bhūrjakaṇṭaka,
as well as the Āvantya, the Vāṭadhāna, the Puṣpadha, and the Śaikha.

“From a Vrātya”: from a Brāhmaṇa Vrātya, by virtue of the continued application of the rule “in women of his own caste” (10.20), a Bhūrjakaṇṭaka of sinful nature is born from a Brāhmaṇī woman. Likewise, the Āvantyas, Vāṭadhānas, Puṣpadhas, and Śaikhās are born. These are the names of this single [caste], well known according to the distinctions of various regions. 10.21.
From a *rājanya* who has fallen from his caste (*vrātya*) are born the Jhalla, the Malla, and the Nicchivi;
as well as the Naṭa, the Karaṇa, the Khasa, and the Draviḍa. (10.22)

"Jhalla and Malla. From a *vrātya* Kṣatriya, on a woman of the same caste, are born those known as Jhallas, Mallas, Nichivis, Naṭas, Karaṇas, Khaśas, and Draviḍas; these are also merely different names for the same group. (10.22)
From a Vrātya Vaiśya are born the Sudhanvācārya, the Kāruṣa, the Vijanman, the Maitra, and the Sāttvata. (10.23)

"But from a Vaiśya," it is said. Furthermore, from a Vrātya of the Vaiśya caste, in union with a woman of his own caste, there are born those known as Sudhāvaka, Ācāryaka, Kāruṣa, Vijanman, Maitra, and Sāttvata; and these are also the names of a single individual. 10.23.
Through the violation of caste rules, through the marrying of those who should not be married, and through the abandonment of one's own duties, the intermixture of castes arises. (10.24)

"By transgression" means that through sexual intercourse with the wives of one another among the castes such as Brāhmaṇas and so forth, through marriage with women of the same lineage (*sagotra*) and the like, and through the abandonment of one's own duties in the form of the initiatory rite (*upanayana*), what is called "intermixture of castes" (*varṇasaṃkara*) arises. Therefore, it is appropriate that the *vrātyas* are mentioned in this section. 10.24.
But those of mixed origin who are born from inverse and natural orders,
and those who are mutually intermingled— I shall describe them in their entirety.

Regarding the term "intermixed": I shall specifically describe those of mixed origin who are born from mutual connections between those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*) and those born in the natural order (*anuloma*). || 10.25 ||
The Sūta, the Vaidehaka, and the Caṇḍāla, the lowest of men;
as well as the Māgadha, the Kṣattṛ caste, and likewise the Āyogava. || 10.26 ||
Regarding the word "sūta": these six, beginning with the *sūta*, whose characteristics have been stated, are restated in the second half [of the verse]. (10.26)
These six produce offspring of similar caste within their own wombs;
they also procreate children in wombs of superior castes, according to the mother's caste. (10.27)

"‘These’—these six previously mentioned *pratiloma* (inverse-caste) offspring produce sons in their own wombs (*svayoni*). For example, an Āyogava born of a Śūdra father and a Vaiśya mother [produces a son] in an Āyogava woman herself—that is, in a mother of his own caste—and in superior wombs, namely those of Kṣatriya and Brāhmaṇa; and by the word ‘and’ (*ca*), also in an inferior womb, namely in a woman of the Śūdra caste. In all these cases, they beget similar castes. This similarity is not with respect to the father, but rather because it will be stated later that from women of the four castes belonging to the mother’s lineage, a son more censurable than the father is produced; therefore, this verse prescribes only what was not previously established: that even in their own caste, they beget sons who are similar to them yet more censurable than the father. However, because they were begotten by a man of a lower caste upon women of a higher caste, the *pratiloma* offspring such as the Āyogava are corrupted in their ritual action (*kriyāduṣṭa*). And when an Āyogava son is begotten by parents who are both equally corrupted in their ritual action, he is rightly considered even more corrupt than one begotten by two Brahmin-slayers. But one begotten by a pure Brāhmaṇa of the same caste upon a pure Brāhmaṇa woman of the same caste is fit to be exactly equal to the father, and not one begotten by both parents who are corrupted in their ritual action. (10.27)
Just as for the three castes, a son is born from two [members] of one's own self,
so too, by immediate succession, is it produced among the outsiders according to their respective orders.

Regarding the word "yathā" (just as): Just as among the three castes—the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra—when a Brāhmaṇa approaches two of these castes, namely the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, he produces a twice-born (dvija) through the natural order (ānulomya), and a twice-born is likewise born from a woman of his own caste; so too, even among those outside [the fourfold system], there is an increase or decrease in status among those born from a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya father and a Vaiśya or Kṣatriya mother, or from a Kṣatriya or Brāhmaṇa father [and a Vaiśya or Śūdra mother]. This is intended to show the excellence of those born in the inverse order (pratiloma) from the twice-born and others, in comparison to those born in the inverse order from a Śūdra. Medhātithi, however, says that this statement establishing their status as twice-born is for the purpose of [authorizing] their initiation (upanayana). That is not correct, because Gautama prohibits such sacraments, stating: "But those born in the inverse order are devoid of dharma" (GDh 4.3).
And they also produce many outsiders, even more corrupted than themselves, who procreate upon one another's wives and are held in contempt. (10.29)

"And they too" means that these six, beginning with the Āyogava and others, procreate very many offspring who are even more degraded than themselves and excluded from social rites when uniting with wives of a different caste, even in the case of natural order (*ānulomya*). For example: an Āyogava begets upon the wife of a Kṣattṛ a son inferior to himself; likewise, a Kṣattṛ also begets upon an Āyogava woman a son inferior to himself. The same should be understood for the other cases of inverse order (*pratiloma*) as well. (10.29)
Just as a Śūdra begets an outcaste being upon a Brāhmaṇī woman, so does an outcaste beget one even more outcaste within the fourfold caste system. 10.30

"Just as" means: just as a Śūdra begets upon a Brāhmaṇī woman a degraded creature called a Caṇḍāla, even so an outcaste (bāhya) begets upon women of the four castes, beginning with the Caṇḍālas, a son who is even more degraded than those Caṇḍālas and the rest. || 10.30 ||
He elaborates on this very point:
"Acting in opposition [to their own kind], those of the outer castes produce even more outer ones; being inferior, they give birth to further inferior castes—indeed, fifteen in total. (10.31)

Regarding the term *pratikūlam* (contrary): here is the explanation of Medhātithi and Govindarāja—those outside the fourfold caste system (*cāturvarṇya*), namely the Caṇḍālas, Kṣattras, and Āyogavas, who originate from Śūdras, produce fifteen castes when they approach those within the fourfold system. Because they are born from mutually inferior and superior castes relative to one another, they produce these fifteen castes. For example: a Caṇḍāla begets upon a Śūdra woman a son inferior to himself but superior to those born of Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, and Brāhmaṇa women; likewise, upon a Vaiśya woman he begets one even more degraded than that; upon a Kṣatriya woman he begets one superior to the one born of a Brāhmaṇa woman, and upon a Brāhmaṇa woman he begets one inferior even to that. Similarly, the Kṣattra and the Āyogava each beget four sons upon each of the four castes. Thus, twelve sub-varieties arise from the Caṇḍālas, Kṣattras, and Āyogavas originating from Śūdras. Including themselves—the three being the Caṇḍāla, the Kṣattra, and the Āyogava—there are thus fifteen originating from Śūdras. Likewise, fifteen each arise originating from Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, and Brāhmaṇas. Thus, there are sixty varieties, which together with the fourfold caste system itself make sixty-four sub-divisions. These, through mutual intercourse, produce various further castes.

This is not compelling, because in the preceding verse the six *pratiloma* (inverse-caste) offspring were the subject under discussion, and this verse serves as an elaboration thereof. Furthermore, since the phrase "acting in opposition" (*pratikūlaṃ vartamānāḥ*) is employed here as well, this verse refers exclusively to those born of inverse unions and not to those born of natural order (*anuloma*). Consequently, the claim that fifteen each arise from women of the Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, and Brāhmaṇa castes—resulting in sixty—is inconsistent. Nor can it be argued that these sixty are mentioned merely as possibilities rather than as being inherently corrupt, or that only the three born of Śūdra women—the Āyogava, Kṣattṛ, and Caṇḍāla—are censured when they procreate within the four castes; for Manu himself has clearly stated immediately thereafter that "so too the one who is even more excluded (*bāhyatara*) is born from the excluded (*bāhya*) within the four castes" (10.30). Since you two have also explained it in this very way, the total of sixty-four (including the four castes themselves) is entirely irrelevant to the context. Indeed, counting the pure four castes is inappropriate in a section dealing with mixed castes (*saṃkīrṇa*). Moreover, after stating that "they produce fifteen castes," it is incorrect to say that the twelve *jāti*s mentioned, plus the three born of Śūdra women—the Caṇḍāla, Kṣattṛ, and Āyogava—make fifteen. Furthermore, the claim that they "produce fifteen including themselves" is untenable, as one cannot produce oneself. If one were to explain it as "fifteen are produced [by them]," the fault of supplying missing words (*adhyāhāra*) would remain. Therefore, it should be explained thus: those acting in opposition are the *pratiloma* outsiders (*bāhya*), because they are inferior to those born of the twice-born in the inverse order. The three born of Śūdra women—the Āyogava, Kṣattṛ, and Caṇḍāla—procreate fifteen sons each within their own species (*sajāti*) among the four castes mentioned in the preceding verse, since it was stated there that "these six [beget] similar [sons]" (10.27), implying that those born of the same species are censured relative to their fathers. Thus, the outsider Āyogava begets five sons inferior to himself upon women of the four castes, including an Āyogavī; likewise, the Kṣattṛ and the Caṇḍāla each beget five sons. In this way, the three outsiders produce fifteen sons each. Similarly, the three inferior ones born of Vaiśya and Kṣatriya fathers—the Māgadha, Vaideha, and Sūta—each beget five sons inferior to themselves upon women of the four castes, as before, within their own species; thus, though inferior, these three also produce fifteen sons each. These total thirty. Alternatively, the terms "outsider" (*bāhya*) and "inferior" (*hīna*) refer to only the six *pratiloma* castes. Here, the outsiders—the Caṇḍāla, Kṣattṛ, Āyogava, Vaideha, Māgadha, and Sūta—acting in the inverse order toward women, produce fifteen sons each who are even more excluded (*bāhyatara*) due to their progressive superiority. For example: the Caṇḍāla begets upon the five women beginning with the Kṣatriya; the Kṣattṛ upon the four beginning with the Āyogavī; the Āyogava upon the three beginning with the Vaidehī; the Vaideha upon the Māgadha and Sūta women; the Māgadha upon the Sūta woman; and the Sūta, due to the absence of further *pratiloma* unions, produces fifteen sons through the inverse order alone. By the use of the word "again" (*punar*), the inferiors—the Sūta and the others down to the Caṇḍāla—also, due to their progressive inferiority, produce fifteen sons each in the natural order (*ānulomya*) according to the method described for the inverse order, but inferior to themselves. Thus, these total thirty. (10.31)
From a Dasyu and an Ayogava woman is born a Sairandhra, who knows how to apply cosmetics and personal adornments, who is not a slave yet lives as one, and who subsists by means of nets.

Regarding the term *prasādhana*: grooming (*prasādhana*) refers to the arranging of hair and so forth; one skilled in such service, who is not a slave—that is, free from the duties of a slave such as eating leftovers—but who lives by the work of a slave such as massaging the limbs, and who earns a livelihood through another occupation known as the slaughter of deer and other animals by means of snares, is called a *sairindhra*. As will be stated in the verse beginning with “From the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet” (10.45), this *dasyu*—born from a Vaiśya woman by a Śūdra father in the *āyogava* female caste—begets [this offspring]. Furthermore, his killing of deer and other animals should be understood as being for the sake of the gods, the ancestors, or medicinal herbs. (10.32)
The Vaideha, however, procreates the Maitreyaka, who praises men incessantly and strikes a bell at the break of dawn. (10.33)

Regarding the term *maitreyaka*: from a Vaiśya father and a Brāhmaṇī mother who is not of the same caste (*prakṛtā*), a son called a Maitreya is born to an Āyogavī woman; he is sweet-spoken and, for the sake of his livelihood, constantly praises kings and others after striking a bell in the morning.
The Niṣāda begets the Mārgava, a slave who lives by the work of boats;
those who dwell in Āryāvarta call him a Kaivarta.

Regarding the Niṣāda: born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Śūdra mother, the Niṣāda begets upon the previously mentioned Āyogavī woman a Mārgava, also known as a Dāsa, who lives by the occupation of boatmen. Those dwelling in the land of Āryāvarta refer to him by the term *kaivarta* (fisherman). 10.34.
Among the Āyogavīs—who wear the clothes of the dead, are ignoble, and eat despised food—these three base-born castes arise separately. (10.35)

Regarding the word "mṛtā" (the dead): the three low-caste women—the Sairindhra, the Maitreyī, and the Mārgava—when they are Yogīs wearing the garments of the dead, cruel, and eating food consisting of leavings and the like, become divided due to their difference in fathers. || 10.35 ||
From a Niṣāda father and a Kārāvarī mother, a leather-worker (carmakāra) is born;
from a Vaidehaka father, the Andhra and Meda are born, both of whom have their dwellings outside the village.

Regarding the term *kārāvara*: since it is heard later [in verse 10.37] that "he is born from a Vaideha woman alone," that same [Vaideha woman] is connected here as well when there is doubt. Born from a Niṣāda on a Vaideha woman, one called a *kārāvara* is born, who works as a leather-cutter. For this very reason, in the *Auśanasa* [Smṛti], the practice of leather-cutting is stated to be the specific livelihood for *kārāvaras*. From a Vaidehaka, two types named Andhra and Meda are born, who dwell outside the village. Because of the intermediate mention [of the Vaideha woman], because it is appropriate that even a despised Vaidehaka born from a Vaidehaka on a Vaideha woman [be included], and because the *kārāvara* and *niṣāda* castes are mentioned together in this verse, he is born respectively from the women of the *kārāvara* and *niṣāda* castes. (10.36)
From a Caṇḍāla and a Vaidehī is born a Pāṇḍusopāka, who deals in bamboo; he is also called an Āhiṇḍika. (10.37)

"From a Caṇḍāla": from a Caṇḍāla and a Vaidehī is born one called Pāṇḍusopāka, who lives by the trade of making bamboo articles. And from a Niṣāda and a Vaidehī is born one called Āhiṇḍika; his livelihood is stated in the *Auśanasa* [treatise] to be the guarding of prisons and external [fortifications], hence he is called an Āhiṇḍika. Although they share the same parents, there is a difference in designation because a difference in livelihood is heard of for the Kārāvara and the Āhiṇḍika. (10.37)
But from a Caṇḍāla, by a Pukkasa woman, is born a sinful Sopāka, whose livelihood consists of the root of ruin and who is always censured by the virtuous. (10.38)

"By a Caṇḍāla": born of a Pukkasī woman—who herself was born of a Niṣāda man from a Śūdra woman—by a Caṇḍāla, there is one named Sopāka, a sinful soul who is always censured by the virtuous; he is fit to be killed for offenses deserving death, and his livelihood consists of that "misfortune," namely execution by royal decree. Thus he is born. (10.38)
But from a Caṇḍāla, a Niṣāda woman gives birth to a son called an Antyāvasāyin, who frequents cremation grounds and is despised even by those outside the caste system. (10.39)

Regarding the phrase "the Niṣāda woman": a Niṣāda woman, from a Caṇḍāla, gives birth to one known as an Antyāvasāyin—one who is even more wicked than the Caṇḍālas and others, a dweller in cremation grounds whose livelihood is that of such places. || 10.39 ||
These castes arising from intermixture, as indicated by their fathers and mothers—whether they be concealed or manifest—are to be known by their respective actions. (10.40)

Regarding the term "intermixture" (*saṃkara*): in the context of the intermixture of castes, these castes have been shown by first describing the father and mother—stating that "this woman is the mother of this one, and this man is the father of this one, and thus he belongs to such a caste. Likewise, whether they are hidden or manifest, they are to be known through the performance of the duties prescribed for those respective castes. || 10.40 ||
Six sons born in the direct order from wives of the same caste possess the dharma of the twice-born;
however, all those born from wives of lower castes are recorded as being of degraded status.

“Of the same class” (*sajātī*) means those born of women belonging to the same caste as the twice-born (*dvijāti*), as well as those produced through the natural order (*ānulomya*): namely, sons born of a Brāhmaṇa from a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya woman, and of a Kṣatriya from a Vaiśya woman. Thus, these six sons possess the status of the twice-born and are to be initiated. Regarding the statement, “But they [shall] have the names of the [immediate] next [caste]” (10.14), someone might mistakenly think that this is intended merely for the purpose of designating their caste and not for the purpose of their sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*). Therefore, this declaration is made for the sake of their initiation by the twice-born. However, as for others such as the Sūtas and so forth, who are born of the twice-born but through the inverse order (*pratiloma*), they follow the dharma of Śūdras; for them, there is no initiation. (10.41)
But by the power of the seeds of their asceticism, they undergo increase and decrease among human beings here, birth after birth, in age after age.

Regarding the word "tapaḥ" (austerity): those born of the same class or of an immediately lower class—through the power of austerity like Viśvāmitra, or through the power of their seed like Ṛṣyaśṛṅga and others—attain excellence of caste among humanity during the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages; and they undergo decline due to the causes that will be explained hereafter. || 10.42 ||
But through the gradual neglect of sacred rites and by the absence of Brāhmaṇas, these Kṣatriya lineages have become Śūdras in this world. (10.43)

"Gradually" means that these following Kṣatriya castes, due to the omission of rites such as the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), and because they lacked the visible purpose for officiating at sacrifices, teaching, or performing penances—which are duties of Brāhmaṇas—gradually attained the status of Śūdras in the world.
The Pauṇḍrakas, the Auḍras, the Draviḍas, the Kāmbojas, the Yavanas, the Śakas, the Pāradas, the Pahlavas, the Cīnas, the Kirātas, the Daradas, and the Khaśas. (10.44)
"Pauṇḍras" refers to those born in regions such as Pauṇḍra who, due to the neglect of ritual duties and other causes, have fallen into the status of Śūdras. 10.44.

Those castes in the world who are outside the lineages born from the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet—whether they speak the tongues of barbarians or the speech of the Aryans—are all remembered as Dasyus. (10.45)

Regarding the term *mukha*: those castes born outside [the fold] due to the omission of rites and so forth among Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—whether they employ the speech of Mlecchas or are endowed with Āryan speech—are all traditionally known as *dasyus*. (10.45)
Those who are considered the outcasts among the twice-born, as well as those born of degraded unions, should subsist by means of those despised occupations of the twice-born themselves. 10.46

Regarding the word "ya" (those): since those born of the twice-born in the direct order were previously designated by the term *apasada*—on account of their inferiority to their fathers—in the passage, "These six are declared to be *apasadās*" (10.10), they, being born of a degradation (*apadhvaṃsaja*), should live by the censured occupations to be described hereafter, which are intended solely for the service of the twice-born. 10.46.
The management of horses and charioteering for the Sūtas; medical practice for the Ambaṣṭhas; service to women for the Vaidehakas; and the trade of merchants for the Māgadhas. (10.47)

"Of the Sūtas": for the Sūtas, the livelihood consists of charioteering—such as breaking in horses and yoking them; for the Ambaṣṭhas, medical treatment such as the pacification of diseases; for the Vaidehakas, the protection of the inner apartments; and for the Māgadhas, trade by land routes. (10.47)
The killing of fish is the occupation of the Niṣādas, while that of the Āyogava is carpentry;
the Medas, Andhras, Cuñcus, and Madgus have the slaughter of wild animals as their livelihood.

Regarding "the killing of fish": for the aforementioned Niṣādas, it is the slaughter of fish; for the Āyogava, it is wood-carving; and for the Medas, Andhras, Cuñcus, and Madgus, it is the killing of wild animals. It should be understood that the Cuñcu and the Madgu were mentioned by Baudhāyana as being born from a Vaidehaka man and a female slave respectively. Furthermore, the "female slave" (bandhistrī) must be taken as one born from a Kṣatriya man and a Śūdra woman, who is an Ugrā. (10.48)
For the Kṣattrus, Ugras, and Pukkasas, however, there shall be dwelling in holes and the killing and binding [of animals];
for the Dhigvaṇas, the work of leather; and for the Veṇas, the playing of drums.

Regarding the term *kṣattrugra*: for the *kṣattras* and others, it consists of killing and binding creatures such as monitor lizards that dwell in holes; for the *dhigvaṇas*, it is leather-working—that is, the manufacture of leather goods and their sale—which constitutes the livelihood of the *dhigvaṇas*.

This is according to the view of Auśanas. For this very reason, their means of subsistence is cut off from the *kārāvaras*. For the *veṇas*, it is the playing of musical instruments such as gongs and drums. (10.49)
These learned ones, subsisting by their own prescribed duties, should dwell at shrines, under sacred trees, in cremation grounds, on mountains, and in groves.

Regarding the term *caitya*: a well-known tree near a village or similar location is a *caitya-tree*. At its base, as well as near cremation grounds, mountains, and forests, these [ascetics] should dwell, making themselves known through their own occupations. || 10.50 ||
The dwellings for Caṇḍālas and Śvapacas shall be outside the village;
they must be provided with broken vessels, and their wealth shall consist of dogs and donkeys.
Their garments are the clothes of the dead; their food is from broken vessels;
their ornament is black iron; and they must always maintain the life of a wandering mendicant.

"Caṇḍālas," "clothes," and "dwelling": a dwelling is a place of residence. However, the residence for Caṇḍālas and Śvapākas should be outside the village. They are to be deprived of [proper] vessels; wherever they have eaten from a vessel made of iron or other such materials, that vessel, even after being purified, must not be used again. Their wealth consists of dogs and donkeys, not bulls or similar animals; their clothes are the garments of the dead; they eat from broken bowls and the like; their ornaments are iron bracelets and so forth; and they are always by nature wanderers. (10.51–52)
A man practicing dharma should not seek association with them; their mutual dealings and marriages are only with their own equals. 10.53

"Nor with them": at the time of performing religious duties, one should not engage in social interactions such as looking at or conversing with *caṇḍālas* and *śvapākas*. Furthermore, their transactions involving the giving and receiving of debts, as well as marriage, should be conducted mutually among those of their own kind. (10.53)
Their food, dependent on others, should be given to them in separate vessels;
they must not wander about in villages or cities at night. (10.54)

"Food for them": their food is dependent on others; it should not be given to them directly, but must be given by servants in separate vessels. And they should not wander about at night in villages or cities. (10.54)
They should move about during the day for the sake of their business, marked by royal edicts; and they shall carry out the funeral of a corpse that has no kinsmen—such is the established rule.

"By day," it is said: by day, in villages and such places, they should wander about marked with signs by royal decree for the purpose of conducting business such as buying and selling; and they should carry out the corpses of those without protectors from the villages—such is the established rule of the scriptures. 10.55.
They shall constantly execute those deserving of death according to the scriptures and by the king's command;
they shall also take the clothes, beds, and ornaments of those condemned to die. (10.56)

"And those deserving of death": they should always execute those deserving of death by impalement on a stake or other such means, in accordance with the scriptures and by royal command; and they may seize their clothes, beds, and ornaments. || 10.56 ||
One should discern by their own actions a man who is devoid of proper caste, unknown, born of a defiled womb, and though appearing noble, is actually ignoble. (10.57)

"Devoid of caste" means one who has fallen away from the status of caste—a human being born of mixed parentage who is not recognized as such by the world, and who therefore resembles an Ārya in appearance but is in fact non-Āryan; one should determine this by his conduct, which is consistent with his censurable birth, as will be described hereafter. || 10.57 ||
Lack of nobility, harshness, cruelty, and a disposition toward inaction reveal in this world that a man is born from a defiled womb. (10.58)
"Un-Aryan-ness": cruelty, harsh speech, violence, and the failure to perform prescribed duties manifest one's status as being of mixed birth in this world. (10.58)
For this reason:
"A child inherits the character of the father, or of the mother, or of both;
however, one born of a low womb can never suppress his own innate nature. (10.59)

"Or paternal"—this one born of a mixture of castes, of corrupt origin, serves either the corrupt nature associated with his father, or that associated with his mother, or both; he can never conceal his own true cause. (10.59)
Even for one born into a preeminent family, if there should be a confusion of birth, that man surely adopts the conduct of those [of mixed origin], whether to a small or great extent. (10.60)

Regarding the word "family" (*kula*): even for one born of a great family, if there is a hidden confusion of birth (*yonisaṃkara*), that person will surely partake of the nature of his progenitor, whether to a small or a great degree. (10.60)
But in that country where these corrupters of the castes are born through promiscuity, that kingdom, along with its citizens, perishes very quickly. (10.61)

"In which [realm]" means: that kingdom in which these mixtures of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*), who are the defilers of the castes, are born, quickly goes to destruction along with its inhabitants. Therefore, the king must eliminate the mixing of castes.
The unconditioned sacrifice of one's body for the sake of a Brahmin or a cow, and for the protection of women and children, is the cause of success for those who follow external paths. 10.62

"For the sake of a Brahmin" means that the sacrifice of one's life, regardless of any malicious motive, for the purpose of protecting cows, Brahmins, women, or children—even if it concerns only one of these—is a cause for attaining heaven even for those born of inverse unions (pratiloma). 10.62.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, and restraint of the senses—Manu declared this to be the summary of dharma for the four social orders. 10.63.

"Non-violence," and so forth. Manu has thus briefly stated the dharma to be practiced by the four castes: the abandonment of violence, speaking the truth, not taking the property of others through unjust means, purification with earth, water, and so on, and restraint of the senses. By the force of the context, this dharma should be understood as applicable even to those of mixed caste. (10.63)

Now, in order to show that [the status of] Brāhmaṇa-hood and so forth exists even apart from the characteristics previously stated in the verse, "Among all castes, [if they are] equal" (10.5), he says:
"If one born of a Śūdra woman from a Brāhmaṇa procreates with a superior [man]..."
One who is inferior attains a superior birth for up to seven generations.

Regarding the phrase "in a Śūdra woman": by implication, the caste known as the Pāraśava, born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Śūdra mother, must be female. If she, being married by a Brāhmaṇa, gives birth, she produces only a daughter; and she too, being married by another Brāhmaṇa, produces only a daughter. In this very manner, at the seventh generation—that is, at the seventh birth—that caste called Pāraśava attains Brāhmaṇahood due to the predominance of the seed (*bīja*). Because of the expression "up to the seventh generation," the meaning is that he becomes a Brāhmaṇa at the seventh birth. (10.64)
A Śūdra attains the state of a Brāhmaṇa, and a Brāhmaṇa likewise descends to the state of a Śūdra; one should know that this is exactly the same for those born from a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya. 10.65.

Regarding the term *śūdra*: in the manner described in the preceding verse, a *śūdra* attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa, and a Brāhmaṇa likewise descends to the status of a *śūdra*. Here, the "Brāhmaṇa" should be understood as a *pāraśava*, born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Śūdra mother. If he, being a male, marries only a Śūdra woman and begets a male son upon her, and that son likewise marries only a Śūdra woman and begets another male, and that one does the same—then that original Brāhmaṇa, having reached his seventh birth, gradually attains the status of a pure Śūdra due to the degradation of the seed. One should understand the rise and fall in status in the same way for those born from a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother; however, this occurs through the degradation of the caste.
The elevation of caste is to be understood as occurring in the seventh or even the fifth generation. (YDh 1.96)

According to this view of Yājñavalkya, one should understand that for one born from a Kṣatriya woman, promotion and degradation occur in the fifth birth; for one born from a Vaiśya woman, they occur even later than that. Since Yājñavalkya includes an alternative view by means of the word "or" (vā), and following the interpretation of the elders, promotion and degradation should be known to occur in the third birth. By this same principle, for one born to a Brāhmaṇa from a Vaiśya woman, promotion and degradation occur in the fifth birth; for one born from a Kṣatriya woman, in the third; and for one born to a Kṣatriya from a Vaiśya woman, they should be understood to occur in the very third birth. (10.65)
If it should be asked: "Wherein lies the superiority between one born by chance from a Brāhmaṇa father upon a non-noble woman, and one born from a noble woman upon a non-noble father? (10.66)

Regarding the phrase "in a non-noble woman": one [son] is born from a Brāhmaṇa through a Śūdra woman who is not married to him by choice, and another is born from a Śūdra through a Brāhmaṇa woman. If a doubt should arise as to which of these two, born in such circumstances, possesses the superior status—the seed being the cause of doubt, just as in the case of the excellence of a seed—one might wonder: "Since a Śūdra born from a Brāhmaṇa through a Śūdra woman is virtuous, why should one born from a Śūdra through a Brāhmaṇa woman not likewise be a virtuous Śūdra, given the excellence of the field? (10.66)
Regarding this, he states the definitive conclusion:
"One born to a non-Aryan woman from an Aryan father may become an Aryan by his qualities; but one born to an Aryan woman from a non-Aryan father is a non-Aryan—this is the certainty. (10.67)

Regarding the phrase "one who is born": one born of a Brāhmaṇa from a Śūdra woman becomes praiseworthy when endowed with the qualities prescribed in the Smṛtis, such as the performance of *pākayajña* sacrifices and the like. On the other hand, one born of a Brāhmaṇa woman by a Śūdra, being produced through the inverse order (*pratiloma*), is not praiseworthy because he lacks even the entitlement to the duties of a Śūdra; this is the settled conclusion. Although the matter is established by logic, it is made known here by the authority of the scriptural statement. (10.67)
The law is established that both of these are ineligible for sacramental rites:
the former because of the deficiency of his birth, and the latter because he is born in the inverse order. (10.68)

"Both of them" refers to the Pāraśava and the Caṇḍāla; the established limit of the scriptures is that both are ineligible for initiation (*anupaneyau*). The former, the Pāraśava, is ineligible for initiation because of the deficiency of his caste, as he was born from a Śūdra woman [by a Brāhmaṇa]. The latter is ineligible for initiation because he was born in the reverse order (*prātilomyena*) from a Śūdra man by a Brāhmaṇa woman. (10.68)
Just as good seed grown in a fertile field comes to fruition, so too one born of a noble father from a noble mother is worthy of every refinement. 10.69

"Having good seed": just as a fine seed grown in a fertile field becomes abundant, so too one born from a twice-born man by a twice-born woman of the same caste, or by a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya woman in the direct order of castes, is entitled to all the sacraments of his own caste, as well as those of the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya—both those prescribed by the Śruti and those by the Smṛti. And the mention of the Pāraśava and the Caṇḍāla is for the purpose of reinforcing what was stated previously. (10.69)
To ensure the stability of the very meaning already stated, he says, citing other philosophical systems:
"Some wise men praise the seed, others the field; still others praise both the seed and the field. But in this matter, the established conclusion is as follows. (10.70)

Regarding the phrase "the seed": some scholars praise the seed, because they observe that those such as Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, who were born of deer and other animals, attained the status of Brahmanical sages. Others, however, praise the field, because they observe that one is seen to be the son of the master of the field. Still others praise both the seed and the field, because they observe that a good seed flourishes in a good field. Amidst this diversity of opinions, the following resolution should be understood as it will be explained below. (10.70)
Seed sown in a non-field perishes right there within;
likewise, a field without seed becomes merely a barren wasteland. (10.71)

Regarding the term "bad field": a seed sown in a saline wasteland fails to bear fruit and perishes in the interim. Even an excellent field, if devoid of seed, would be nothing more than bare ground, and no crop would grow there. Therefore, by criticizing each individually, the previously stated necessity of both—"good seed in a good field" (10.69)—is affirmed as essential.
Now, regarding the position that the seed is predominant, he states an illustration:
"Because by the power of the seed, those born as animals became sages, honored and praised; therefore, the seed is extolled. (10.72)

"Because"—that is to say, because even those born of animal species such as the female deer and others, like Ṛṣyaśṛṅga and his peers, attained the status of sages through the greatness of their seed (*bīja*); and because they were honored by being saluted and so forth, and praised with words for their knowledge of the Vedas and other qualities; therefore, the seed is introduced [as the primary factor]. This conclusion regarding the predominance of the seed should be understood as having the following intent: between the seed and the womb (*yoni*), the caste (*jāti*) derived from the seed is superior and thus the principal factor. (10.72)
Having carefully considered the non-noble who performs noble deeds and the noble who performs non-noble deeds, the Creator declared: "They are neither equal nor unequal. (10.73)

Regarding the term "un-Aryan" (*anārya*): Brahmā, having deliberated upon a Śūdra performing the duties of the twice-born (*dvijāti*) and a twice-born performing the duties of a Śūdra, declared, "They are neither equal nor unequal. For although a Śūdra performs the duties of the twice-born, he is not equal to a twice-born; because even by performing the duties of the twice-born, one who lacks the qualification for them cannot attain equality with them. Likewise, although a twice-born performs the duties of a Śūdra, he is not equal to a Śūdra; because by engaging in what is forbidden, the excellence of his caste is not lost. Nor are they unequal, because through the performance of forbidden acts, both have become equal. Therefore, whatever is censured for someone must not be done by him; such is the instruction on the duties of the castes, culminating in the prevention of social confusion (*saṃkara*).
Now, intending to set forth the duty of Brahmins in times of distress, he says this:
"Brahmins who abide in the source of the Veda and remain steadfast in their own duty should properly subsist by means of the six occupations in their proper order. (10.74)

Regarding the term "Brāhmaṇas": those Brāhmaṇas who are devoted to meditation on Brahman as the cause for attaining Brahman and are intent upon the performance of their own duties should duly carry out, in due order, the six duties to be described hereafter, beginning with teaching and so forth. 10.74.
He states those duties:
teaching, studying, sacrificing for oneself, officiating at sacrifices for others, as well as giving gifts and receiving them—these are the six duties of the first-born (the Brāhmaṇa). 10.75.

Regarding "teaching": teaching and studying the Veda along with its auxiliary sciences (aṅgas), as well as sacrificing for oneself and officiating at sacrifices for others, and giving and receiving gifts—these six duties are to be known as belonging to the Brāhmaṇa. (10.75)
Of his six duties, however, three are his means of livelihood:
officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and the acceptance of gifts from pure persons. (10.76)

Regarding the phrase "of the six": among these six activities of this Brāhmaṇa, beginning with teaching, namely sacrificing for others, teaching, and receiving gifts from pure sources—as indicated by the scriptural injunction, "A twice-born man should seek wealth from praiseworthy twice-born men"—it should be understood that these three activities, including receiving gifts from the twice-born, are for the purpose of livelihood. (10.76)
Three duties cease with respect to a Kṣatriya from a Brāhmaṇa:
teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and thirdly, the acceptance of gifts. (10.77)

"Three duties": with respect to a Brāhmaṇa, the three occupations of a Kṣatriya—namely teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts—which serve as means of livelihood, are excluded for him. However, study, sacrificing, and giving remain his duties as well. 10.77.
In the same way, these [prohibitions] shall cease with respect to the Vaiśya; such is the settled rule, for Prajāpati Manu did not prescribe those duties for them. 10.78

"Regarding the Vaiśya": Just as teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts are excluded for the Kṣatriya, so too are they for the Vaiśya; such is the established rule of the scriptures. Since Manu, the Lord of Creatures, did not prescribe those occupations for the sake of livelihood to the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, it follows that for the Vaiśya also, there exist the duties of study, sacrifice, and giving. 10.78.
Bearing weapons and missiles is the livelihood of the Kṣatriya; trade, cattle-rearing, and agriculture are those of the Vaiśya. But the duty [of all] is giving, study, and sacrifice. (10.79)

Regarding the phrase "weapons and missiles": weapons (*śastra*) are such as the sword and the like; missiles (*astra*) are such as the arrow and the like. The bearing of these is for the protection of the subjects and for the livelihood of the Kṣatriya. Trade, cattle-rearing, and agricultural work are the means of subsistence for the Vaiśya. Furthermore, for both of them, the purposes of Dharma consist of giving, study, and sacrifice. (10.79)
The study of the Vedas for the Brahmin, protection for the Kshatriya, and the occupation of trade for the Vaishya—these are the most distinguished among their respective duties. 10.80.

Regarding "the study of the Vedas": the study of the Vedas and the teaching of the Vedas are mentioned together with protection and commerce for the purpose of livelihood; these belong to the Brāhmaṇa. Protection of the subjects belongs to the Kṣatriya, and trade and cattle-rearing belong to the Vaiśya. These are the most excellent among the occupations intended for their livelihoods. 10.80.
Now he speaks of the duty in times of distress: "But if a Brāhmaṇa cannot subsist by his own aforementioned occupation, he may live by the dharma of a Kṣatriya, for that is the next in order. (10.81)

"Living not [by his own means]" means that if a Brāhmaṇa, while failing to live by his own duties such as teaching as previously described—namely, by performing his obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) while maintaining his family—he should live by the duty of a Kṣatriya, such as protecting villages and cities; for the duty of a Kṣatriya is his most proximate mode of livelihood. (10.82)
If, however, he cannot subsist by either of these two, how should it be?
He should live by adopting the livelihood of a Vaiśya, namely agriculture and cattle-rearing. (10.82)

"By both": if a Brāhmaṇa should have a doubt as to how he should conduct himself when unable to subsist by both his own duty and the duty of a Kṣatriya, then he should resort to agriculture and the protection of cattle, following the occupation of a Vaiśya. The mention of agriculture and cattle-rearing is intended to include trade, as the author will later specify items that may be sold. Furthermore, this practice of agriculture and so forth must be performed by the Brāhmaṇa himself; for that which is not performed by oneself is prescribed even in times of non-distress by the rule, "He should live by ṛta and amṛta" (4.4). 10.82.
Now he speaks of the relative strength and weakness of agriculture and other such occupations:
"Even if living by the occupation of a Vaiśya, a Brāhmaṇa or even a Kṣatriya should carefully avoid agriculture, which is mostly violent and dependent on others. (10.83)

Regarding the word *vaiśya*: whether he be a Brāhmaṇa or even a Kṣatriya, one who lives by the occupation of a Vaiśya should diligently avoid agriculture, which involves much injury to creatures dwelling in the earth and depends upon oxen and other animals. Therefore, it should be understood that agriculture is to be practiced only in the absence of animal husbandry and similar occupations. By the inclusion of the phrase “or even a Kṣatriya,” it is implied that the occupation of a Vaiśya is permissible for a Kṣatriya as well when his own specific duty is unavailable. (10.83)
They consider agriculture to be a good thing, yet that livelihood is censured by the virtuous;
for the iron-tipped wood destroys both the earth and those who dwell within it.

"Regarding agriculture": some consider agriculture to be a good way of life; however, that livelihood is censured by the virtuous because the wooden plowshare and other iron-tipped tools strike the earth and the creatures dwelling within it. (10.84)
But for one who, due to a deficiency in livelihood, abandons skill in the Dharma, this may be sold as merchandise to increase wealth—provided that the "choice portion" has been extracted. (10.85)

Regarding this [verse]: when a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya is unable to subsist by their own prescribed occupations, they may sell those articles that are fit for sale by a Vaiśya—provided they are excluded from those things forbidden to be sold—as mentioned in the context of dharma, in order to increase their wealth. (10.85)
He states those things which are to be avoided:
"One should exclude all savory juices, cooked food along with sesame seeds, stones, salt, as well as domestic animals and human beings. (10.86)

"Of all"—that is, he shall not sell any prohibited items (*adharmas*) that are not specifically mentioned, such as prepared food, sesame seeds, stones, salt, livestock, and human beings. Although the prohibition of salt is already established by its very nature as a *rasa* (liquid/flavor), its specific mention here is intended to indicate the gravity of the offense. This, in turn, serves to prescribe a more severe penance (*prāyaścitta*). In this same manner, the separate prohibition of other items should also be explained. (10.86)
And all woven cloth that is dyed, as well as garments made of hemp, linen, and wool—even if they should be undyed—as also fruits, roots, and medicinal herbs. (10.87)

"Everything": one should avoid all cloth made from threads that has been dyed with safflower or similar substances. Even if they are not red, one should not sell garments made from hemp, flax, or wool. Likewise, one should avoid fruits, roots, *guḍūcī*, and so forth. (10.87)
Water, weapons, poison, meat, soma, and all kinds of perfumes; milk, honey, curd, ghee, oil, liquor, molasses, and kuśa grass. (10.88)

Regarding the word "apa" (water): one should avoid water, iron, poison, meat, soma, milk, curd, clarified butter, oil, molasses, and *darbha* grass; likewise, all fragrant substances such as camphor and the like; honey (*kṣaudra*) meaning *mākṣika*; and beeswax (*madhu*), which Yājñavalkya has listed as "beeswax along with honey from bees" (*sabhrāmaramadhūcchiṣṭa*) in verse 1.33. || 10.88 ||
All wild animals, fanged beasts, and birds;
liquor, indigo, lac, and likewise all things that have a single owner. (10.89)

"Wild animals" means he shall not sell any wild beasts, such as elephants and the like; fanged creatures, such as lions and the like; likewise birds and aquatic animals; intoxicants and the like; and single-hoofed animals, such as horses and the like. || 10.89 ||
Having generated a desire for cultivation, the farmer himself may sell pure sesame seeds that have not long been stored, for the sake of dharma.

Regarding the word *kāmaṃ*: a cultivator, having himself produced sesame seeds by tilling, may sell them immediately after production without mixing them with other substances—not waiting for another time for the sake of profit—but he may do so for the purpose of *dharma*. This is a permission (*pratisrava*) for the sale of sesame, which is otherwise prohibited, when intended for religious merit. (10.90)
If one performs any act with sesame seeds other than giving them as food or as an ointment, he becomes a worm in a dog's excrement and sinks there together with his ancestors. (10.91)

Regarding the word "food": if one performs any other prohibited act concerning sesame seeds—such as selling them—apart from giving them as food or as an ointment, he, having attained the state of a worm along with his ancestors, sinks into the excrement of dogs. (10.91)
One falls immediately by selling meat, lac, or salt;
a Brāhmaṇa becomes a Śūdra within three days by selling milk. (10.92)

Regarding the word *sadyas* (immediately): this is stated for the purpose of declaring the gravity of the offense—that a Brāhmaṇa falls from his status at that very moment by selling meat, lac, or salt—since it will later be taught that there are only five causes for the loss of status among the great sinners (*mahāpātakin*). By selling milk, he attains the state of a Śūdra after three days; this too is for the purpose of declaring the gravity of the penance due to the gravity of the offense. (10.92)
But by intentionally selling other commodities here,
a Brāhmaṇa attains the status of a Vaiśya within seven nights.

"Of others": by selling for seven nights other forbidden commodities—besides meat and the rest mentioned in the case of a Brāhmaṇa—that are not mixed with other substances, and which he sells out of desire rather than through negligence, he attains the status of a Vaiśya. 10.93.
Flavors may be bartered for flavors, but salt must never be exchanged for other flavors;
prepared food may be exchanged for unprepared food, sesame seeds for grain, and these are considered equal. (10.94)

Regarding "flavors" (rasāḥ): flavors such as molasses and the like may be exchanged for other flavors such as ghee and the like. However, salt must not be exchanged for another flavor. Furthermore, prepared food may be exchanged for unprepared food; sesame seeds for grain, at the rate of one *prastha* of grain for one *prastha* of grain—in this manner, items of equal value may be exchanged. || 10.94 ||
A Kṣatriya who has fallen into misfortune may live by all these means;
however, he must never at any time take pride in a higher mode of livelihood.
