"He may live" means that a Kṣatriya who has fallen into distress may, having said "by this," live like a Vaiśya even by selling liquids and other forbidden items—since he has said "by everything"—even though such trade is prohibited for one whose sphere is the Brāhmaṇa; however, he must never resort to the livelihood of a Brāhmaṇa. Not only the Kṣatriya, but anyone else as well [may do so] like a Kṣatriya. 10.95.
If one who is base by birth should live by superior occupations out of greed, the king, having deprived him of his wealth, should banish him immediately. || 10.96 ||

"Whoever out of greed"—meaning, whoever, being of low birth, should live by means of actions prescribed for those of superior birth—the king, having confiscated all his property, should expel him from the country at that very moment. (10.96)
Better is one's own duty, though deficient, than the well-performed duty of another; for by living according to the duty of another, one immediately falls from one's caste. (10.97)

"Better," he says. It is right to perform even one's own duty imperfectly, but never that of another, even if it be complete; for by living on the work prescribed for another caste, one falls from one's own caste at that very moment—this is the fault that must be avoided. (10.97)
A Vaiśya who cannot subsist by his own duty may live even by the occupation of a Śūdra;
provided he does not perform forbidden acts and, being capable, he desists from them.

Regarding the word "vaiśya": a Vaiśya who is unable to subsist by his own occupation may live even by the occupation of a Śūdra; however, he should not perform service for the twice-born, nor eat the remains of their food, and so forth. Once he has crossed over the calamity, he should gradually desist from the occupation of a Śūdra. (10.98)
But a Śūdra who is unable to perform service for the twice-born, having fallen into distress regarding his children and wife, may live by the crafts of artisans. (10.99)

"Being unable" means that a Śūdra who is incapable of performing service for the twice-born, being distressed by hunger and lacking sons and a wife, should live by such occupations as those of a cook and the like. (10.99)
Those crafts and various arts by which, when practiced, the twice-born are served— these are the works of artisans.

Regarding the word "yair" (by which): this is for the purpose of specifying the particular crafts mentioned previously. He should perform those various kinds of works—such as carpentry and other such crafts (*takṣaṇādi*), as well as arts (*śilpa*) such as painting and so forth—by means of which, when performed, the twice-born are served.
A Brāhmaṇa who, remaining on his own path, does not adopt the livelihood of a Vaiśya, yet is distressed by a lack of means and is suffering, may practice this rule. 10.101.

Regarding the word *vaiśya*: a Brāhmaṇa, when oppressed by the lack of a means of livelihood and falling into distress, should not adopt the mode of life of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya; rather, because it has been stated that "one's own duty, even if defective, is better" (10.97), he should remain in his own duty and practice this livelihood about to be described. Therefore, it should be understood that recourse to the livelihood of another is permitted only when one's own duties, such as receiving gifts from improper persons, become impossible.
A Brahmin who has fallen into distress may accept gifts from anyone;
that a purifier should become defiled is not logically consistent with the Dharma. (10.102)

"From everyone" means that a Brāhmaṇa who has fallen into distress may accept gifts in due order even from those most censured. Here, there is a poetic figure called *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle): for it is not possible, according to the established tenets of the scriptures, that the Ganges or other sacred waters should be defiled by the water of a city street or the like. 10.102.
For this reason:
"Neither from teaching, nor from officiating at sacrifices, nor from accepting gifts—even if they are censurable—does any fault accrue to Brahmins; for they are like fire and water. (10.103)

"Nor from teaching": for Brahmins, in times of distress, there is no unrighteousness in teaching what is censurable, in officiating at sacrifices, or in accepting gifts; because by their very nature they are pure, equal to fire and water. 10.103.
He who, having fallen into a life-threatening situation, eats food from any source whatsoever, is not smeared by sin, just as the sky is not defiled by mud. (10.104)

Regarding "for the sake of life": he who, having reached a state where his life is at risk, eats the food of one born of an inverse union, is not tainted by sin, just as the atmosphere is not defiled by mud. 10.104.
In this regard, he states an explanatory passage (arthavāda) in the form of an account of another's action:
"Ajīgarta, being hungry, approached to kill his own son;
yet, while performing the remedy for hunger, he was not defiled by sin. (10.105)

Regarding the case of Ajīgarta: the seer named Ajīgarta, being afflicted by hunger, sold his own son named Śunaḥśepa. For the sake of obtaining a hundred cows at a sacrifice, he bound him to the sacrificial post, became a butcher, and proceeded to kill him; yet, though acting in this way for the purpose of counteracting his hunger, he was not defiled by sin. This is clearly stated in the *Bahvṛca-brāhmaṇa* within the narratives concerning Śunaḥśepa. (10.105)
Desiring to eat dog-meat when afflicted by hunger, Vāmadeva—who was discerning in matters of dharma and adharma—did not defile himself for the sake of preserving his life. (10.106)

"Regarding 'dog's flesh': the seer named Vāmadeva, who knew dharma and adharma, being afflicted by hunger and desiring to eat dog's flesh for the sake of preserving his life, was not tainted by fault. (10.106)
But Bharadvāja, a man of great asceticism, being afflicted by hunger in the lonely forest along with his sons,
accepted many cows from the carpenter Vṛdhu.
"Baradvāja": A sage named Bharadvāja, a man of great asceticism, having dwelt with his son in a lonely forest, was oppressed by hunger and accepted many cows from a carpenter named Vṛdhu. (10.107)
Afflicted by hunger, Viśvāmitra, who was discerning in matters of dharma and adharma, approached to eat the haunch of a dog, having taken it from the hand of a Caṇḍāla.
"Afflicted by hunger": the seer Viśvāmitra, who knew dharma and adharma, being tormented by hunger, took from the hand of a caṇḍāla the meat from the haunch of a dog and resolved to eat it. 10.108.
Whether from receiving gifts, officiating at sacrifices, or likewise from teaching, for a Brahmin, the acceptance of gifts is the lowest and is censured after death. (10.109)

Regarding the phrase "from accepting gifts": among the three censurable acts of teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and accepting gifts, for a Brāhmaṇa, accepting gifts from the unworthy is the most base and is a cause for hell in the next world. Therefore, in times of distress, one should first engage in the censured acts of teaching and officiating at sacrifices; only when those are impossible should one resort to accepting gifts from the unworthy—this is the intended meaning of this verse.
He states the reason for this:
"Sacrificing and teaching are always performed by those whose souls are purified;
however, the acceptance of gifts may be done even from a Śūdra of the lowest birth. (10.110)

Regarding the phrase "officiating at sacrifices": officiating at sacrifices and teaching are performed only for the twice-born whose souls have been refined by the initiation ceremony (upanayana), whether in times of distress or not. Receiving gifts, however, is performed even from a Śūdra of inferior birth; therefore, that [receiving of gifts] is censured in comparison to those two.

Sin committed through officiating at sacrifices or teaching is removed by recitation and burnt offerings; however, that caused by accepting gifts is removed only by renunciation and austerity. (10.111)

He causes [the sin] to be destroyed by recitation (*japa*). Because of the inclusion of the word "this" (*enaḥ*), whatever has been acquired through accepting gifts from the unworthy, officiating at sacrifices for the unworthy, or teaching the unworthy, is destroyed by means of *japa* and burnt offerings (*homa*) according to the sequence to be described in the section on penance (*prāyaścitta*). Furthermore, that which is produced by accepting gifts from the unworthy is removed by the renunciation of the accepted object and by the ascetic practices (*tapas*) to be described later, such as: "Having drunk milk in a cow-pen for a month" (11.193). 10.111.
A Brahmin who cannot subsist otherwise may gather grains from various sources;
gathering ears of grain (śila) is better than receiving gifts, and picking up individual grains (uñcha) is praised even more than that. (10.112)

Regarding the phrase "gleaning ears of grain" (*śiloñcha*): A Brāhmaṇa, subsisting by his own proper livelihood, may gather ears of grain (*śila*) from anywhere; however, when that is possible, he should not accept gifts from the unworthy (*asatpratigraha*). For gleaning (*śila*) is more praiseworthy than accepting gifts from the unworthy. *Śila* is the gathering of single grains from clusters of stalks; even better than that is *uñcha*. *Uñcha* is the picking up of individual grains and the like one by one. (10.112)
A lord of the earth should be entreated by Snātaka Brahmins who are sinking and desiring base metals or wealth; however, if he is unwilling to give, he deserves to be abandoned.

Regarding the phrase "by those who are sinking": when *snātaka* Brahmins, due to a lack of wealth, are falling into the ruin of their families for the sake of fulfilling their religious duties (*dharma*), they may beg from even a Kṣatriya who acts contrary to the scriptures for "wealth"—meaning base metals such as grain and clothing, as well as gold and silver used for sacrifices—since this falls under the section concerning times of distress (*āpad*). However, one who is determined to be miserly and does not wish to give should be abandoned; the meaning is that he should not be begged from. Medhātithi and Govindarāja, however, explain: "He deserves abandonment" means that one should not dwell in his country. (10.113)
From a cultivated field, one may take unprepared grain; likewise, cattle, goats, and sheep, gold, grain, and food—each preceding item is less blameworthy than the one following it. (10.114)

"And that which is unprepared": an unprepared field is one where no crop has been sown; accepting it from one who has sown a crop is free from fault. Likewise, among cows, goats, sheep, gold, grain, and cooked food, each preceding item is less objectionable than the one following it. Furthermore, in the absence of each preceding item, each subsequent one should be understood as permissible. (10.114)
There are seven righteous ways of acquiring wealth: inheritance, gain, purchase, victory, investment, professional labor, and the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous. 10.115

"Seven," etc. There are seven sources for the acquisition of wealth that are not contrary to *dharma*, according to the entitlement to property. Among these: *dāya* (inheritance) is wealth obtained through lineage; *lābha* (gain) refers to the discovery of buried treasure and so forth, as well as what is acquired through friendship and the like; *kraya* (purchase) is well known—these three are lawful (*dharmya*) for all four social classes (*varṇas*). *Jaya-dhana* (wealth from victory) is lawful for the Kṣatriya by virtue of his role as a conqueror; *prayoga* (investment) of money for interest and the like, and *karmayoga* (application to work) such as agriculture and trade—these two modes of livelihood are lawful for the Vaiśya; *sat-pratigraha* (receiving gifts from the virtuous) is lawful for the Brāhmaṇa. Thus, because these are declared to be lawful, in their absence one should resort to other means of subsistence that are prescribed for times of distress (*anāpad-vihita*). And in the absence of even those, one may resort to those prescribed for times of distress that have already been mentioned; it is for this purpose that this is stated here. (10.115)
Learning, craft, wages, service, cattle-rearing, trade, agriculture, contentment, begging, and usury—these are the ten means of livelihood. 10.116.

Regarding the term *vidyā*: because they are introduced as "means of livelihood" within the context of distress (*āpad-prakaraṇa*), among these [ten means], whichever occupation by which one's livelihood cannot be maintained in times of non-distress is permitted for that person in times of distress. For example, service for wages and the like for a Brāhmaṇa. The same should be understood regarding crafts and so forth. *Vidyā* refers to knowledge other than Vedic learning—such as medical science, logic, and the neutralization of poisons—and such knowledge, when used for the sake of livelihood in times of distress, is not blameworthy for anyone. *Śilpa* is the practice of perfumery and the like; *bhṛti* is receiving wages through the state of being a servant; *sevā* is carrying out the orders of another; *gorakṣya* is the tending of cattle; *vipaṇi* is trade; *kṛṣi* is agriculture performed by oneself; *dhṛti* is contentment, by virtue of which one can live even with very little; *bhaikṣya* is a collection of alms; and *kusīda* is the lending of money at interest, even if done by oneself. One must maintain one's life in times of distress by means of these ten. (10.116)
Neither a Brāhmaṇa nor a Kṣatriya should ever practice usury;
however, for the sake of dharma, one may at will give even a small amount to a person of evil character.

Regarding the term "Brāhmaṇa": whether he be a Brāhmaṇa or even a Kṣatriya, he should not lend money for interest even in times of distress; rather, for the sake of dharma, he may lend it through a lowly occupation at a very small rate of interest. 10.117.

Now he speaks of the duty of kings in times of distress: "Even when taking a fourth part as his share in times of distress, a Kṣatriya who protects his subjects to the best of his ability is released from sin. (10.118)

Regarding the phrase "the fourth part": although it has been stated that the king may take an eighth part of grain and other produce, and so forth, if he takes even a fourth part as tax during times of distress while protecting his subjects with the utmost effort, he does not incur the sin of collecting excessive taxes. (10.118)
But why is it said that even in times of distress the king must provide protection? Because: Victory is his own duty; he should not turn his back in battle.
Having protected the Vaiśyas with his weapons, he should collect the lawful tribute. (10.119)

Regarding "one's own duty" (*svadharma*): for a king, his own duty is the conquest of enemies; the meaning is that battle is the fruit of victory. If one who is engaged in protecting the subjects should experience fear from any source, he would then turn away from battle. And thus, having protected the Vaiśyas from robbers with weapons, he should cause them to pay tribute—which is not contrary to righteousness—through trustworthy men. (10.119)
"Who is this Bali? He replied:
"The eighth part of the grain is the tax for the people; for coins, it is one-twentieth, with a minimum of one kārṣāpaṇa.
Śūdras who provide services, as well as artisans and craftsmen, [pay no tax]. (10.120)

Regarding "grain": in the case of grain, when there is an increase [in yield], he should cause the Vaiśyas to pay a tax (*śulka*) of one-twentieth; however, one-twelfth of grains is also mentioned. This one-eighth is prescribed for times of distress (*āpad*). In extreme distress, the previously mentioned one-fourth should be understood to apply, yet even then, one-twentieth should be taken. Likewise, for gold and other items down to the *kārṣāpaṇa*, he should take one-twentieth as tax. Regarding that, it was stated in a non-distress situation: "The king should take a fiftieth part of cattle and gold" (7.130). In times of distress, this one-twentieth is prescribed. Similarly, Śūdras, artisans such as cooks and the like, and craftsmen such as carpenters and the like, serve through their labor alone; from them, no tax should be collected even in times of distress. (10.120)
But a Śūdra, desiring a livelihood, should serve a Kṣatriya;
or, having served a wealthy Vaiśya, a Śūdra may seek to live by that means. (10.121)

"But a Śūdra," [it is said]. A Śūdra who lives by serving Brāhmaṇas, if he should desire a livelihood, then he should live by serving a Kṣatriya; in the absence of that, by serving a wealthy Vaiśya. However, if he is incapable of serving the twice-born, he should perform the duties previously mentioned. (10.121)
For the sake of heaven, or for the sake of both worlds, he should propitiate the Brahmins;
for one who has acquired the title of "Brahmin," that indeed constitutes the fulfillment of his purpose.

"For the sake of heaven" means for the purpose of attaining heaven or for the purpose of seeking his own livelihood; a Śūdra should serve the Brāhmaṇas alone. Therefore, he is one who possesses the designation "one born from [the Brāhmaṇa]" and is dependent upon the Brāhmaṇa—a compound formed according to the *śākapārthiva* class of compounds. This is the fulfillment of duty for this Śūdra; by being designated as such, he becomes one who has accomplished his task. || 10.122 ||
Since this is so, therefore:
"Service to Brahmins alone is proclaimed as the distinguished duty of a Śūdra;
for whatever else he performs, that becomes fruitless for him. (10.123)

Regarding the word *vipra*: it is declared in the scripture that for a Śūdra, the service of Brāhmaṇas alone is the most excellent duty among all other duties. This is because whatever action he performs apart from this becomes fruitless for him; this is for the purpose of praising the former [duty], not for the purpose of excluding others, since *pākayajña* sacrifices and the like are also prescribed for him. (10.123)
He should provide for his livelihood from his own family estate as is appropriate, having regard for their capacity, their skill, and the number of dependents they maintain. (10.124)

"Having determined," [means]: having considered the capacity for service, the zeal for work, and the number of dependents such as sons and wives of that Śūdra servant, those Brāhmaṇas should provide him with a suitable livelihood from their own homes. (10.124)
Leftover food should be given, as well as worn-out garments, the dregs of grain, and old household utensils. (10.125)

Regarding the term "remnants" (*ucchiṣṭam*): the food remaining after a meal should be given by the Brahmins to that Śūdra who has sought refuge with them. In this way, the rule "one should not give advice to a Śūdra, nor his remnants" (4.80) remains applicable to a Śūdra who has not sought refuge. Likewise, worn-out clothes, coarse grain, and old beds and furnishings should be given to him. (10.125)
There is no sin for a Śūdra, nor does he deserve the purificatory rites (saṃskāra). He has no entitlement to dharma, yet there is no prohibition against him regarding dharma. (10.126)

"Not a Śūdra": by eating garlic and such things, no sin whatsoever accrues to a Śūdra; however, this does not apply even to [crimes such as] killing a Brahmin, because injunctions such as "non-violence and truth" (10.63) are prescribed as common to all four social orders (*cāturvarṇya*). Nor is he eligible for sacraments such as the initiation (*upanayana*); nor does he have the right to perform duties such as the *agnihotra*, because they are not prescribed for him. Furthermore, there is no prohibition against him regarding the duties prescribed for Śūdras, such as the *pākayajña* sacrifices. Thus, since all of this is already established, this verse is a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the sake of what follows. (10.126)
But those who desire dharma, who know dharma, and who practice the conduct of the virtuous, do not incur blame when acting except through counsel; rather, they receive praise. (10.127)

Regarding the phrase "those desiring dharma": furthermore, those Śūdras who know their own duty and desire the attainment of dharma, having resorted to the conduct of the three higher castes provided it is not forbidden, do not incur sin by performing the duties such as the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) with the mantra of salutation (*namaskāra*), devoid of other mantras, in accordance with the statement of Yājñavalkya: "One should not omit the five sacrifices by means of the mantra of salutation" (YDh 1.121). Moreover, they obtain renown in the world. 10.127.
For in whatever measure one who is free from malice abides in virtuous conduct, in that same measure he, being blameless, attains both this world and the world beyond. (10.128)

"As follows": Just as a Śūdra who censures the virtues of others, yet practices the conduct of the twice-born that is not forbidden, becomes increasingly free from reproach among people in this world and is remembered as superior, he attains the heavenly worlds and the like. || 10.128 ||
For even if he is capable, a Śūdra should not accumulate wealth;
for a Śūdra, having acquired wealth, oppresses the Brāhmaṇas themselves. (10.129)

"Even by one who is capable" means that even a Śūdra who is capable of acquiring wealth must not accumulate an excessive amount of money beyond what is required for supporting his dependents and performing the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*). This is a restatement of what was previously said: that a Śūdra, having acquired wealth, afflicts the Brāhmaṇas themselves because, being ignorant of the scriptures, he neither bestows that wealth [upon them] nor performs service for them. (10.129)
These duties in times of distress have been proclaimed for the four castes;
by performing them correctly, they attain the supreme goal. (10.130)

"These" refers to the duties prescribed for the four castes in times of distress, which have been declared. By practicing these correctly—through the performance of what is enjoined and the avoidance of what is forbidden—they become free from sin; and by attaining knowledge of Brahman, they reach the supreme goal characterized by liberation. (10.130)
This entire rule of dharma for the four castes has been proclaimed;
hereafter I shall declare the auspicious rule for expiation.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
"This," [it is said]: "this entire conduct of the four castes has been declared. Hereafter, I shall describe the auspicious performance of expiatory rites. (10.131)
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Manvarthamuktāvalī, a commentary on the Manu-smṛti composed by the illustrious Kullūkabhaṭṭa.

The eleventh chapter: One seeking to establish a lineage, one intending to perform a sacrifice, a traveler, one who has given away all his possessions, one seeking to support a teacher, one seeking to support parents, one seeking to study the Veda, and one who is afflicted by illness. (11.1)
One should know these nine types of *snātaka* Brāhmaṇas to be seekers of dharma; gifts should be given to them who possess nothing, according to the excellence of their learning. (11.2)

Regarding the phrase "to one who maintains the lineage" (*sāntānika*) and "these nine": surely, since it was previously promised that the rules for atonement (*prāyaścitta*) would be taught—specifically in the verse, "Henceforth I shall proclaim the auspicious rule for atonement" (10.131)—what is the relevance of the statement "it should be given to those who maintain the lineage and so forth"?

It is said: Since it was previously stated that "one [purifies] those who have committed forbidden acts by means of a gift" (5.107), and since it will be declared later that "one unable to perform the purification of killing for snakes and others through a gift... (11.139), etc., the presentation of the recipient for a gift—which consists of a superior expiation—is indeed relevant to the present topic. Furthermore, because this chapter aims to describe occasional duties (*naimittika-dharma*) such as expiations that are distinct from the duties pertaining to the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*), it is appropriate to introduce other occasional duties here as well. One should recognize these nine Brāhmaṇas—those who live on religious alms (*dharmabhikṣāśīla*) and are *snātakas*—as follows: one seeking progeny (*sāntānika*), one desiring marriage, one intending to sacrifice (*yakṣyamāṇa*), one wishing to perform the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices that must necessarily be performed, a traveler (*adhvaga*), one who has given away all his possessions in the *Viśvajit* sacrifice (*sarvavedasa*), one whose purpose is to provide food, clothing, and so forth for his teacher of knowledge (*gurvartha*), likewise those whose purpose is for their father or mother, a student (*brahmacārī*) seeking the means for clothing and so forth at the time of Vedic study (*svādhyāyārthī*), and one afflicted with disease (*upatāpī*). To these indigent persons, one should give gifts of cattle, gold, and so forth, according to the specific nature of their learning. (11.2)
For to these foremost of the twice-born, food together with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given;
for others, it is said that cooked food is to be given outside the sacrificial altar.

"From these": food together with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) is to be given within the sacrificial enclosure (antarvedi) to these nine most excellent Brāhmaṇas. To those other than these, however, cooked food (siddhānna) is prescribed as that which is to be given outside the sacrificial enclosure (bahirvedi). As for the gift of wealth, there is no fixed rule.
The king, however, should bestow all kinds of jewels according to their merit, as well as sacrificial fees for the sake of the sacrifice upon Brahmins learned in the Vedas. (11.4)

"Everything": furthermore, the king should cause the Brahmins who are knowers of the Vedas to accept all jewels, such as gems and pearls, as well as wealth suitable for sacrifice, for the purpose of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), in accordance with their learning. || 11.4 ||
If one who already has a wife obtains another wife by begging for her, his reward is merely sensual pleasure; however, the offspring belongs to the giver of the wealth. || 11.5 ||

Regarding the word *kṛtā*: for one who, while already having a wife, performs a marriage for the sake of progeny or other such reasons by begging for another wife from others—his fruit is merely sexual pleasure; however, for the giver of the wealth, there will be offspring born of that union. This is an extreme censure. Thus, one should not perform a marriage after begging for wealth in this manner, nor should one give wealth as a matter of rule to such a person. (11.5)
One should bestow wealth upon Brahmins according to one's ability—upon those learned in the Vedas and living in seclusion; thus, after death, one enjoys heaven.

"Riches" means that one should bestow riches—such as cattle, land, gold, and so forth—upon Brāhmaṇas who know the Vedas, provided they are secluded and not attached to sons, wives, and the like, without exceeding one's own capacity; and by virtue of that, the attainment of heaven occurs. || 11.6 ||
He who possesses enough food for three years to maintain his dependents,
or even more than that, is worthy to drink the Soma.

Regarding the phrase "of whom": he for whom there is sufficient food and so forth for three years—or more—intended for the maintenance of those who must necessarily be supported, is eligible to perform the optional *somayāga*. However, because the obligatory (*nitya*) sacrifice must be performed by all means whatsoever, this prohibition does not apply to it. For this very reason, [the author] stated that the rule "at the end of the year, with Soma sacrifices" (4.26) pertains to the obligatory category. 11.7.
Therefore, that twice-born man who drinks the Soma when the substance is very small, even if he has previously drunk the Soma, does not obtain its fruit.

Regarding the word "ataḥ" (therefore): when one possesses less wealth than what is required for three years' provisions, the first *somayāga* performed by such a person does not even fulfill its status as an obligatory (*nitya*) rite; how much more so, then, the second sacrifice, which is optional (*kāmya*)? 11.8.
One who is capable of giving to strangers while his own kin live in misery— this is a deceptive semblance of dharma, like honey at first taste but poison in its effect.

"Capable": one who, being wealthy and thus capable of giving, when his parents, relatives, and other kin who must necessarily be supported are beset by suffering due to poverty, gives to others for the sake of fame—this particular kind of giving is a mere semblance of dharma, not dharma itself. It is like the taste of honey at first, being sweet in its commencement because it initially brings fame; yet it has the taste of poison in the end, because its fruit is rebirth in hell. Therefore, this should not be done. (11.10)
Whatever one performs for the sake of the afterlife by causing distress to one's dependents results in unhappiness both while living and after death. || 11.10 ||

[“An aged mother and father, a virtuous wife, and an infant son—Manu has declared that these must be maintained even by performing a hundred improper acts. Regarding the phrase “of dependents”: when one performs acts such as giving gifts out of a sense of duty toward the next world (*pāralaukika-dharma-buddhi*) while causing suffering to those who must necessarily be supported, such as children and wives, that gift results in suffering for the donor both while living and after death. Thus, the previous prohibition concerned giving for the sake of visible ends such as fame; this, however, is a prohibition against giving for the sake of invisible (transcendental) ends. 11.10.
If a sacrifice of a sacrificer should be obstructed by even a single constituent part—
especially in the case of a Brāhmaṇa— while a righteous king is in power, [he must perform an expiation].
If there should be a Vaiśya who possesses many cattle but performs no sacrifices and does not drink the Soma juice,
one may take that wealth from his household for the sake of accomplishing a sacrifice.

"If there is a sacrifice" means: if for a Kṣatriya or other [caste] who is the sacrificer—and especially for a Brāhmaṇa—if the sacrifice should be incomplete due to the lack of even one subsidiary part despite the presence of other subsidiary parts, then one may take by force or by theft from the house of a Vaiśya who possesses much wealth such as cattle but is devoid of cooked sacrifices and the like, and is not a Soma-sacrificer, the substance appropriate for that missing part. And this must be done when the king is preoccupied with dharma; for he will not restrain one who is performing the purpose of the scriptures.
One may take three or two [grains] at will from the house of a Śūdra;
for a Śūdra has no entitlement to sacrificial rites. (11.13)

"Should take": when two or three components of the sacrifice are deficient, those three or two components he should take from the house of a Śūdra—provided a Vaiśya is unavailable—either by force or by theft, without hesitation; for a Śūdra has no connection whatsoever with the sacrifice. As for the forthcoming prohibition, "A Brāhmaṇa should not beg wealth from a Śūdra for the sake of a sacrifice" (11.24), this refers to begging from a Śūdra and not to taking it by force or other such means. 11.13.

If there is one who possesses a hundred cows but has not maintained the sacred fires, and another who possesses a thousand cows but does not perform sacrifices—one may take from the households of even these two without hesitation. (11.14)

Regarding the word "yaḥ" (who): one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) but possesses wealth amounting to a hundred cows, or one who has maintained the fires (*āhitāgni*) and performed the *Soma* sacrifice (*somayājī*) with wealth amounting to a thousand cows—from both these types of householders, a Brāhmaṇa should quickly procure the two or three aforementioned ritual components by means of two [messengers]. A Brāhmaṇa may also procure them from Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas. However, as in the case of the act of seizing property, the author will later prohibit a Brāhmaṇa from seizing the property of a Kṣatriya. (11.14)
One may take from a non-giver who is constantly taking [from others];
thus his fame spreads and his merit increases. (11.15)

"From one who is constantly engaged in taking" means: he whose constant practice of taking consists of receiving gifts and so forth, and the acquisition of wealth, is a Brāhmaṇa "constantly engaged in taking. From such a person—one devoid of the merit of sacrifices (*iṣṭa*) and charitable works (*pūrta*)—if a request is made for the sake of two or three components of a sacrifice, one should take [the property] by force or by theft if he does not give it. When this has been done, the fame of the seizer becomes manifest and his merit increases.
In the same way, having fasted for six meals during the seventh meal-time,
one may take food from a person of low conduct according to the rule of not providing for the morrow.

"In the same manner": because of the instruction to eat in the evening and morning, when the three-night fast has been completed, on the fourth day at dawn—during the seventh mealtime—one should steal by means of theft or other such methods an amount of wealth sufficient for one day, free from the performance of duties such as giving gifts. 11.16.
Whether from a threshing floor, a field, a house, or wherever it may be found—if he asks, one must tell that to him who asks. (11.17)

"From the threshing floor": from a place for threshing grain and so forth, or from a field, or from a house, or from whatever other location grain connected to a low-caste person is obtained, from there it should be taken. Or, if the owner of the wealth asks, "For what purpose was this done? and he asks thus, the motive—such as theft and so forth—should be stated. (11.17)
A Kṣatriya must never seize the property of a Brāhmaṇa; however, if he is unable to subsist, he may take it as his own for the purpose of ransoming himself from bandits. 11.18.

"Regarding 'the property of a Brāhmaṇa': even when the aforementioned causes for seizure exist, a Kṣatriya must not take the wealth of a Brāhmaṇa because he is inferior to him; however, by the same principle, he must not take it from those of a higher caste than himself, namely Vaiśyas and Śūdras. But in an extreme emergency, a Kṣatriya may take the property of both a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya who have committed forbidden acts or failed to perform prescribed duties. (11.18)
He who takes wealth from the wicked and bestows it upon the virtuous makes himself a raft and carries both of them across. 11.19

Regarding the phrase "to those who are not virtuous" (*asādhubhya*): he who, having performed the appropriate sacrificial implements and other requirements for those who are superior—such as those of inferior karma—and having given wealth to those who are virtuous and superior, such as the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), destroys the evil of the one from whom he takes it and removes the poverty designated as the suffering of the one to whom he gives it; thus, by making both of them his boat, he delivers them from suffering. (11.19)
The wise know that the wealth of those who habitually perform sacrifices is the property of the gods;
however, the property of those who do not sacrifice is said to be the property of the asuras.

Regarding the phrase "that which is wealth": the wise consider that wealth belonging to those who habitually perform sacrifices to be the property of the gods, because it is employed for sacrifices and other such rites. However, the property of those devoid of sacrifice and similar acts is called the property of the asuras, due to the absence of its application to dharma. Therefore, even by seizing that [wealth], one must make it the property of the gods through the performance of sacrifice. (11.20)
A righteous lord of the earth should not inflict punishment upon him;
for it is through the folly of a Kṣatriya that a Brāhmaṇa perishes from hunger. 11.21

"Not in that case" means: when the aforementioned cause for theft by force occurs, a king who prioritizes dharma should not inflict punishment; for, due to the king's folly, the Brahmin suffers the exhaustion of hunger. (11.21)
And therefore:

Having ascertained his circle of servants and his own family members, and having understood their learning and character, the lord of the earth should provide them with a righteous livelihood. (11.22)

Regarding the phrase "of him": having ascertained the class of dependents—such as sons and others—who must necessarily be supported by that Brahmin, the king shall provide from his own treasury a means of subsistence appropriate to those dependents and consistent with the Brahmin's learning and conduct. || 11.22 ||
Having provided for his livelihood, the king should protect him on all sides;
for from one who is thus protected, the king obtains a sixth part of the merit of dharma.

"Having provided for" means: having established a livelihood for this Brāhmaṇa, one should protect him from all sides against enemies, thieves, and the like; because from the Brāhmaṇa who has been protected, one obtains a sixth part of his merit (dharma). || 11.23 ||
A Brahmin should never beg for wealth from a Śūdra for the sake of a sacrifice;
for a sacrificer who has begged thus is born as a Caṇḍāla after death. (11.24)

"Not for the sake of sacrifice": a Brāhmaṇa should never beg wealth from a Śūdra for the successful completion of a sacrifice; for by performing a sacrifice after begging from a Śūdra, he becomes a Caṇḍāla upon death. Therefore, because of this prohibition against begging, it is not forbidden to accept what has been offered unasked from a Śūdra, even for the purpose of a sacrifice. (11.24)
That Brahmin who, having begged for wealth for the sake of a sacrifice, does not give it all away,
goes to the state of a crane or a crow for a hundred years.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of sacrifice": he who, having solicited wealth for the purpose of accomplishing a sacrifice, does not employ it all in that sacrifice, attains the state of a crane or a crow for a hundred years. (11.25)
He who, out of greed, seizes the property of the gods or the property of Brahmins,
that evil-souled man lives in this world on the leftovers of vultures.

"Property of the gods" refers to wealth dedicated for the sake of deities such as images; and he who, out of greed, seizes the property of Brahmins or the property of the gods, being of sinful nature, lives in another birth on the leftovers of vultures. 11.26.

At the end of each year, one should regularly perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice for the purpose of expiating the failure to perform the prescribed animal and Soma sacrifices when they cannot be performed. (11.27)

Regarding the term *iṣṭam*: when a year has concluded and the second year begins—that is, at the transition of the year (*abdaparyaya*), which is the commencement of the year starting with the bright fortnight of Caitra—one should always perform the *vaiśvānarī* sacrifice within that new year. This should be done by accepting wealth from Śūdras and others, even if a Soma sacrifice has been prescribed [but cannot be performed], for the purpose of removing the fault incurred by its non-performance. (11.27)

O twice-born ones, it has been determined that he who performs a religious rite by means of a substitute rule when no such occasion for substitution exists, does not obtain its fruit in the hereafter. (11.28)

Regarding the term "distress": it has been deliberated by Manu and others that if a twice-born man performs religious duties during times of non-distress according to the rules prescribed for times of distress, that act becomes fruitless in the next world. || 11.28 ||
By all the gods, the Sādhyas, the Brāhmaṇas, and the great Ṛṣis, fearing death in times of distress, a substitute for the sacred ordinance was established. (11.29)

Regarding the word "viśvaiḥ": by the Viśvedevas, the gods, the Sādhyas, as well as the great ṛṣis and Brāhmaṇas who were afraid of death, this substitute—such as the Vaiśvānarī sacrifice and others—was performed in place of the primary rite, such as the Soma sacrifice, during times of distress. This [substitute] should be employed when the primary rite is unavailable, but not when the primary rite is available. (11.29)
The lord of the primary rule who conducts himself according to a secondary rule—
no fruit pertaining to the next world exists for that person of evil intellect.

Regarding the word "prabhuḥ": for that foolish man who, despite being capable of performing the primary rite, performs it instead by means of a substitute prescribed for times of distress, there is neither the attainment of prosperity in the next world nor the fruit resulting from the avoidance of transgression. Although this was already stated in the verse, "He who [performs] dharma by way of a substitute in times of distress" (11.28), it is repeated here out of respect for the scripture. 11.30.
A Brahmin who knows the Dharma should not report anything to the king;
he should deal with those offending men, his own disciples, by his own power alone. (11.31)

"No. A Brahmin who knows the Dharma should not report even the slightest harm done to the king; rather, by his own power alone—through the malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) and so forth to be described hereafter—he should restrain those men who cause injury. Therefore, this passage intends to show that when one commits a minor offense due to a conflict with one's own duty, such acts as malevolent rites do not constitute a fault. It does not, however, enjoin malevolent rites, nor does it prohibit reporting [the crime] to the king. (11.31)
Between one's own effort and the effort of a king, one's own effort is more powerful;
therefore, a twice-born man should subdue his enemies by his own effort alone. (11.32)

"By his own prowess" means that since one's own capacity and the king's capacity are both at hand, one's own capacity is indeed stronger than the king's capacity which depends on others because it is under one's own control; therefore, a Brahmin should subdue his enemies by his own prowess alone. 11.32.
What, then, is one’s own power? He says:
"One should employ the *Atharva-Āṅgirasa* scriptures without hesitation;
for the word is indeed the weapon of a Brahmin, with which the twice-born may slay his enemies. (11.33)
"That weapon is irresistible by its power against all castes;

through the majesty of asceticism and heroism, it strikes down even those who are otherwise unslayable. Regarding the phrase "the *śrutīs*": one should perform the *āṅgirasa-śrutīs* of the Atharvaveda—the *śrutīs* concerning wicked sorcery—without hesitation. The meaning is that for that purpose, one should carry out the rite of sorcery (*abhicāra*). Since the speech of a Brāhmaṇa, consisting of the recitation of sorcery mantras, is a "weapon" because it performs the function of a weapon, a Brāhmaṇa may slay his enemies with it; however, a king should not be commanded to restrain his enemies.
A Kṣatriya should overcome his own misfortune through the strength of his arms;
for by doing so to the best of his ability, he attains the supreme goal.
A Vaiśya and a Śūdra should do so with wealth, while the best of the twice-born should do so through recitation and burnt offerings.

Regarding the term "kṣatriya": a kṣatriya should overcome the calamity that befalls him from an enemy in the form of humiliation by means of his own prowess; a vaiśya and a śūdra, however, by giving wealth to the retaliator; but a brāhmaṇa, by means of recitations and burnt offerings consisting of malevolent rites (abhicāra). (11.34)
One who is a provider, a teacher, a speaker, and friendly is called a brahmin;
one should not speak what is unwholesome to him, nor should one utter harsh words. 11.35.

Regarding the term *vidhātṛ*: one who performs prescribed duties, who instructs sons, disciples, and others, who explains the dharmas pertaining to expiation and wealth, and who is preeminent in friendliness toward all beings—such a person is called a Brāhmaṇa. To such a person, one should not speak what is undesirable, such as "Let him be restrained," nor should one utter against him speech consisting of verbal punishment (*vāgdaṇḍa*) or reprimand (*adhigdaṇḍa*). || 11.35 ||

Neither a maiden, nor a young woman, nor one of little learning, nor a fool; neither one who is afflicted by illness, nor likewise one who is uninitiated, should be the officiating priest (hotṛ) of the Agnihotra. 11.36.

"Va vā" means: an unmarried girl, a young woman even if married, as well as those who have studied little, the ignorant, those afflicted by disease and so forth, and those not initiated—these should not perform the Śrauta oblations of morning and evening. Since the performance [of the oblation] was previously established by the word "hāvayet" (he should cause to sacrifice), this is a prohibition specifically for the maiden and the others. (11.36)
For these fall into hell while offering oblations, as does he for whom they offer;
therefore, the officiating priest should be skilled in the sacrificial rites and one who has mastered the Vedas.

"Regarding 'hell': these [persons], such as virgins and others, go to hell if they perform the *homa*. He for whose sake they perform that *agnihotra* by way of substitution also goes to hell. Therefore, a *hotṛ* who is proficient in the Śrauta rites and has studied the entirety of the Vedas should be appointed. (11.37)

If a Brāhmaṇa, despite possessing the means, does not give a horse as the sacrificial fee for the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), he remains one who has not established the fires. (11.38)

Regarding the "Prājāpatya" [gift]: at the time of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), if a Brāhmaṇa has acquired wealth but does not give a horse dedicated to Prajāpati as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), even though the consecration has been performed, he remains one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) and does not obtain the fruit of the consecration. Therefore, at the fire-consecration, one should give a horse as the sacrificial fee. (11.38)
One who is faithful and has conquered the senses should perform other meritorious deeds;
however, one should never, under any circumstances, perform sacrifices here with meager sacrificial fees.

Regarding the term "meritorious acts": one who possesses faith, is self-controlled, and has conquered the senses should perform meritorious deeds such as pilgrimages and the like, apart from sacrifices; however, he should not perform sacrifices with insufficient sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) compared to those prescribed by the scriptures. Since the sacrificial fee exists for the sake of benefiting others, this statement is intended to prevent defects in the officiating priests and others, even when the fee is small. (11.39)

A sacrifice with meager sacrificial fees destroys one's senses, fame, heaven, longevity, renown, progeny, and cattle; therefore, one who possesses little wealth should not perform a sacrifice. (11.40)
"A sacrifice devoid of food burns the kingdom; one devoid of mantras burns the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*);

and one devoid of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) burns the initiated sacrificer. There is no enemy equal to a sacrifice. Regarding "the senses": a sacrifice with meager sacrificial fees destroys the senses—namely the eyes and so forth—of the living person; it destroys fame in the form of renown, heaven, and long life; and for the deceased, it destroys fame in the form of glory, as well as offspring and cattle. Therefore, one should not perform a sacrifice by giving meager sacrificial fees. (11.40)
If a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires should abandon those fires out of his own will, he must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for one month; for that act is equal to the killing of a hero.

Regarding the term *agnihotrī*: a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires (*agnihotrī*), having intentionally failed to perform the evening and morning oblations (*homa*) for a month, shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance. This is because it is equivalent to the "killing" (*hatyā*)—that is, the slaying—of his son, the hero (*vīra*). Thus says the Śruti: "He who allows the sacred fire to go out becomes a slayer of the hero among the gods. Others, however, support the view that he should abandon [the fires] for a month (*māsam apavidhya*). 11.41.
Those who, having acquired wealth from a Śūdra, maintain the Agnihotra sacrifice—they are indeed the officiating priests of Śūdras and are censured among those who discourse on Brahman. (11.42)

"Those [who act] from a Śūdra": those who, having obtained wealth from a Śūdra—either by receiving it directly or by accepting wealth through general entreaty—and having established the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) prior to performing the *agnihotra* sacrifice, as indicated by the forthcoming sign in verse 11.43, "from serving the fire of a Vṛṣala," they are the officiating priests for Śūdras alone; yet that fruit does not belong to them, and therefore they are censured among the exponents of the Vedas.
Treading with his foot upon the heads of those who are constantly ignorant and who serve the fire of the low-born (vṛṣala), the giver shall cross over all difficulties.

Regarding the phrase "of them": by placing his foot upon the heads of those fools—those who serve the wealth of Śūdras and maintain the sacred fires—the Śūdra constantly crosses over from sufferings in the next world through that gift; however, no fruit accrues to the sacrificers. (11.43)
A man who fails to perform prescribed duties, practices what is censured, and remains addicted to the objects of the senses, becomes liable to expiation. 11.44

Regarding the phrase "not performing": a person who fails to perform what is prescribed as obligatory (*nitya*), such as the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsanā*) and so forth, or what is prescribed as occasional (*naimittika*), such as bathing after touching a corpse; and likewise, one who practices what is forbidden, such as violence (*hiṃsā*) and so forth, or who displays excessive attachment to things neither prescribed nor forbidden—he, being merely a human being, deserves expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Now, an objection may be raised: since there is a prohibition in verse 4.16, "One should not become attached to any objects of the senses out of desire," the term "blameworthy" (*nindita*) already includes the case of "one who is attached to the objects of the senses. Therefore, this should not be stated separately.

It is said: because this [verse] is recited among the *snātaka* vows (*vrata*), and because it begins there with "One should observe these vows" (4.13), this is not a prohibition but rather an injunction regarding a vow. If it is argued that, since this is already established by the statement "By failing to perform the prescribed duty... (11.44), it need not be stated separately, we say no; for this [present verse] has its own scope, as it pertains to those other than the *snātaka*. 11.44.
The wise know that expiation is prescribed for a sin committed unintentionally;
however, some, citing the evidence of the Vedas, say it applies even to what is done intentionally.

"Unwillingly": the wise say that expiation exists for a sin committed unintentionally. However, some teachers say that expiation exists even for a sin committed intentionally. This separate mention is for the purpose of emphasizing the gravity of the expiation, based on the observation of the Vedic texts: "Indra gave the *yatīs* to the *sālāvṛkas*; a foul voice reproached him; he went to Prajāpati; [Prajāpati] gave this *upahavya* sacrifice to Indra. The meaning of this is: Indra intentionally gave the *yatīs* to the dogs; he approached Prajāpati for the sake of expiation; Prajāpati gave him the *upahavya* rite as expiation; therefore, there is expiation even for what is done intentionally. (11.45)
A sin committed unintentionally is purified by the study of the Vedas;
but that which is committed intentionally through delusion is purified by various kinds of expiatory rites.

Regarding the phrase "unwillingly" (*akāmataḥ*): sin committed unintentionally is purified—that is, destroyed—by the study of the Vedas (*vedābhyāsena*). The mention of "study of the Vedas" is intended as an illustration of a light penance (*laghu-prāyaścitta*) in comparison to the penances for sins committed intentionally (*kāma-kṛta*). Since other penances are also prescribed, this refers to heavy penance (*guru-prāyaścitta*), meaning that sin committed again unintentionally due to being deluded by passion, hatred, and so forth, is purified by various kinds of penances, such as knowledge, wealth, and austerity. Therefore, this is an explanation of what was stated previously. Although the determination of eligibility (*adhikāra-nirūpaṇa*) will be discussed immediately after the present penance, this is nonetheless a determination of eligibility in the sense that one who is eligible for a light penance due to ignorance is eligible for a heavy penance due to knowledge.

Having incurred the state of requiring expiation, whether by fate or by his own past actions, a twice-born man must not associate with the virtuous as long as the expiation has not been performed. (11.47)

"Prāya is said to be austerity (*tapas*), and *citta* is called mental resolve; that which is joined with the resolve for austerity is traditionally known as *prāyaścitta* (expiation). Regarding the phrase "one who requires expiation": due to fate, negligence, or misdeeds committed in another body during previous births—as indicated by diseases such as consumption—one becomes subject to expiation. Having incurred this state, until the expiation has been performed, one must not engage in association with virtuous people through activities such as officiating at sacrifices. (11.47)
In this world, certain evil-minded men undergo a transformation of their physical form due to their own misdeeds, as well as those committed in previous lives. (11.48)

"Here" means: in this very life, certain humans—possessing a corrupt nature due to prohibited actions committed in previous births—undergo deformities of form such as webbed fingers and the like. (11.48)
A thief of gold suffers from deformed nails; a drinker of liquor, black teeth;
a killer of a Brahmin, consumption; and one who violates the teacher’s bed, a skin disease.
A slanderer [attains] a putrid nose; a backbiter, a putrid mouth;
a stealer of grain, a deficiency of limbs; and one who adulterates [grain], an excess of limbs. (11.50)
The stealer of food suffers from disease; the stealer of speech suffers from dumbness;
the stealer of clothing suffers from leucoderma; and the stealer of horses suffers from lameness.
"One who steals a lamp becomes blind; one who extinguishes it becomes one-eyed.
Through violence there is an abundance of diseases, while through non-violence there is health.
Thus, by virtue of specific actions, people are born despised by the virtuous."
Those who are dull-witted, mute, blind, or deaf, as well as those of deformed appearance. || 11.52 ||

"Gold," "slanderer," "stealer of food"—thus [it is said]. A Brahmin who steals gold attains deformed nails; one who drinks forbidden liquor, black teeth; a killer of a Brahmin, consumption; one who approaches the wife of his guru, a protruding penis; a slanderer who reports existing faults, foul-smelling nostrils; one who reports non-existent faults, a foul-smelling mouth; a stealer of grain, a missing limb; one who mixes inferior substances with grain and the like, an extra limb; a stealer of food, weak digestion; one who studies without permission, dumbness; a stealer of clothing, white leprosy; a stealer of horses, lameness. Thus, those deficient in intellect, speech, sight, or hearing, those of deformed appearance, and those censured by the virtuous are born through the remainder of evil deeds acquired and experienced in previous lives.
One who steals a lamp becomes blind, and likewise one who extinguishes it becomes one-eyed;
one who delights in violence is always diseased, and an adulterer has wind-disorders in his limbs.

|| 11.49–52 || The king, having heard that speech, was filled with great joy; he spoke these words to his ministers: “Let the city be adorned today, for tomorrow the son of Daśaratha will enter it. Then, at the command of the king, the city was decorated like Amarāvatī by the gods; it was adorned with banners and flags, and strewn with flowers of every kind. The king’s wives, accompanied by their retinues, went out from the inner apartments to meet the prince; they were radiant, wearing ornaments and fine garments, and their eyes were moist with tears of joy. The citizens also came out from all sides, eager to see the son of Daśaratha, as people flock to see the rising moon. || 11.50–52 ||
Therefore, one must always perform expiation for the sake of purification;
for those who have not atoned for their sins are born endowed with censurable physical marks. (11.53)

"One must perform [expiation]. Because those by whom sin (*enas*) has not been expiated—that is, those whose sins have not been removed—meaning those who have not performed penance (*akṛtaprāyaścitta*), are born endowed with censurable physical marks such as deformed nails and the like, due to the remainder of their evil deeds (*duṣkṛta*) to be experienced in the next world; therefore, for the sake of purification—that is, for the removal of sin—penance must always be performed. Thus, unlike the case of "he offers when [the vessel] is broken," penance is not merely occasional (*naimittika*); rather, because of the inclusion of the phrase "those whose sins have not been expiated" and the instruction that "it must be performed for the sake of purification," only one who desires the destruction of sin has the qualification (*adhikāra*). For indeed, when there is an expectancy for a qualification regarding the injunction "penance must be performed," since only the result is mentioned, it is proper that the explicitly stated result—"for the sake of purification"—be understood as a qualification of the qualified person, according to the principle of the *Rātrisatra*. Yājñavalkya clarifies this very point in verse 3.219:
Through the non-performance of what is enjoined, through the performance of what is censured,
and through the lack of restraint of the senses, a man undergoes downfall.
Therefore, he must perform an expiation here for the sake of purification.
"Patana" means that he falls; it means he incurs sin. "For the sake of purification" means for the destruction of sin.

Having experienced many terrible hells for numerous groups of years, upon the exhaustion of that [sin], those who have committed the great sins (mahāpātakin) enter these transmigrations (saṃsāra): (12.54)

By such statements as these, he will describe the attainment of hell and other realms by those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin) and the like. It does not follow, therefore, that expiations (prāyaścitta) are merely occasional rites (naimittika). Consequently, it should be understood that only those who seek the destruction of the sin produced by killing a Brahmin and other such acts have the qualification for the injunction of expiation. 11.53
Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, and violating the teacher’s wife—these they call the great sins (mahāpātaka), as does association with those who commit them. 11.54.

Regarding the term *brahmahatyā*: the act that results in the separation of a Brāhmaṇa’s life-force is *brahmahatyā*. This occurs whether one acts directly or by appointing another; thus, even for one who performs an action for the sake of obtaining cattle, gold, or other such things, it constitutes *brahmahatyā* if a Brāhmaṇa dies with that [act] as its objective.

Now, if this were the case, would not the arrow-maker also incur *brahmahatyā* through the medium of producing the arrow, and likewise the victim [incur it] through the medium of generating anger in the killer?
It is said: according to the scriptures, only he who is recognized as the slayer of the Brāhmaṇa incurs *brahmahatyā*. For this very reason, Śātātapa says:
Whether it be for the sake of seizing cattle, land, or gold, or even for the sake of a marriage alliance with a woman,
he for whose sake one would give up one's life is called a slayer of a Brahmin.

In this manner, other scriptural grounds for the killing of a Brahmin should also be understood. Likewise: "He who, out of passion, hatred, or negligence—whether by his own hand or through another—causes a Brahmin to be killed, him they call a slayer of a Brahmin."

Thus, the status of being a killer belongs to the instigator as well, according to the scriptures. Likewise [include] the prohibited drinking of *surā* liquor, the theft of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold, and sexual intercourse with the wife of a guru—here, "guru" refers to the father, because he is designated as such by the rule beginning with "the rites beginning with conception" (2.142). Association with those who have committed these acts leads to a fall after one year; these they call "great sins" (*mahāpātakas*). This designation of "great sin" is for the purpose of distinguishing them from the lesser categories of sins, such as the minor sins (*upapātaka*), which will be described later. (11.54)
Falsehood regarding one's own excellence, malicious talebearing directed toward the king, and persistent deception of one's teacher are equal to the murder of a Brahmin. 11.55.

"Falsehood" refers to speaking of one's own excellence for the sake of gaining superiority over others by birth, such as when a non-Brāhmaṇa says, "I am a Brāhmaṇa"; or the accusation of a fault against a king that results in the death of others, such as thieves and the like; or the false accusation of a teacher. Thus says Gautama (GDh 22.3): "The false accusation of a teacher. These are equal to the great sins (*mahāpātaka*); that is, they are equal to the killing of a Brāhmaṇa. || 11.55 ||
Abandoning one's Veda, reviling the Vedas, giving false testimony, killing a friend, eating forbidden food or what should not be eaten—these six are equal to the drinking of spirituous liquor. 11.56.

"Abandoning the Veda" (*brahma-ujjhana*) means: the forgetting of the Veda already studied due to a lack of practice; the reviling of the Veda by resorting to false scriptures; giving false testimony; the killing of a friend who is not a Brahmin; the eating of forbidden things such as garlic and the like; and the consumption of inedible things such as excrement and the like. Medhātithi, however, explains that "inedible" refers to that which is eaten after having resolved, "I shall not eat. These [acts] are equal to the drinking of spirituous liquor. (11.56)
The misappropriation of a deposit, as well as the theft of men, horses, silver, land, clothing, and gems, is declared to be equal to the theft of gold.

Regarding "of a deposit": the theft of a deposit other than gold belonging to a Brāhmaṇa, as well as the theft of humans, horses, silver, land, diamonds, and gems, is equal to the theft of gold. (11.57)

They consider the emission of semen into women who are one's own sisters, virgins, or those born of the lowest castes, as well as into the wives of a friend or a son, to be equal to violating the bed of a guru. 11.58.

Regarding the phrase "the emission of semen": they say that the emission of semen into a uterine sister, an unmarried girl, a Caṇḍālī woman, or the wife of a friend is equal to approaching the wife of one's guru. This equalization by way of classification is for the purpose of [determining] the penance for that which has been equated with another. The fact that he will later prescribe the penance for killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) for both false testimony and the murder of a friend—both of which have been equated with drinking liquor—is for the sake of providing an option (*vikalpa*). Furthermore, the subsequent instruction regarding the penance for killing a Brahmin for falsely persisting against a guru—which has also been equated with killing a Brahmin—is for the purpose of making known that for those things equated [with a greater sin], there may be a lesser penance. Thus, in common worldly usage, when it is said, "the minister is equal to the king," the inferiority of the minister is understood. In this context, for those things equated [with a greater sin], the penance for those cases where the penance is extended by analogy (*ātideśika*) is less than the penances prescribed directly (*aupadeśika*).

Now he states the minor offenses (upapātakas): killing a cow, sacrificing for those unfit to sacrifice or for whom one should not sacrifice, adultery, selling oneself, abandoning one's teacher, mother, father, Vedic study, the sacred fires, or one's son. (11.59)
When a younger brother marries before his elder, that is *parivitta*; when an elder marries after his younger, that is *parivettṛ*.
Furthermore, there is the giving away of the girl to either of them, and officiating at their sacrifice. (11.60)
Defiling a maiden, usury, the violation of a vow, and the sale of a tank, a garden, a wife, or a child; 11.61.
The state of being a *vrātya*, abandoning kinsmen, teaching for wages, learning from one who teaches for wages, and the sale of goods that ought not to be sold. (11.62)

Exercising authority over all types of crafts, operating great machines, dealing in harmful medicinal herbs, living off women, performing malevolent magic, and performing root-rites (mūlakarma). 11.63.
Felling trees that are not yet dry for the sake of fuel, undertaking actions for one's own sake, and likewise eating food that is censured; || 11.64 ||
Not maintaining the sacred fires, theft, non-payment of debts, studying improper scriptures, and the practice of the arts of the stage. (11.65)

The theft of grain, base metals, or cattle; consorting with women who drink liquor; the killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya; and atheism—these constitute secondary sins (upapātaka). 11.66.

[The section] beginning with "killing a cow" (*govadha*) and ending with "grain and base metals" (*dhānyakupya*) [lists the minor sins]. Killing a cow; officiating at sacrifices for those defiled by birth or conduct; sexual intercourse with another’s wife; selling oneself; failing to perform service toward one's mother, father, or guru; the perpetual abandonment of the *brahmayajña* (Vedic study); and the forgetting of the Veda—this latter is not included because it was already mentioned under the term "neglecting the Veda" (*brahmojjhatā*, 11.56). Also, the abandonment of the domestic fire (*smārta-agni*), as opposed to the sacred fires (*śrauta-agni*), because it was stated: "one who maintains the *agnihotra* should not abandon the fires" (11.41); failing to perform the sacraments and maintenance of a son; becoming a *parivitti* (the elder brother whose younger brother marries first); and being a *parivettṛ* (the younger brother who marries before the elder)—as previously described in the verse beginning "marrying a wife and establishing the *agnihotra*" (3.171); giving a daughter in marriage to either of these two; acting as a priest (*ārtvijya*) for their wedding, *homa*, and other rites; defiling a maiden by inserting a finger or similar object, excluding actual sexual intercourse; sexual intercourse with one's own female relatives, virgins, or women of the lowest castes—which is forbidden by the rule: "emission of semen into one's own kin, virgins, or women of the lowest castes" (11.58); living off usury; sexual intercourse by a celibate student (*brahmacārin*); selling tanks, gardens, wives, or children; failing to undergo initiation (*upanayana*) at the proper time, which constitutes the state of a *vrātya*. As it has been said: "Beyond this, these three also, if not initiated at the proper time... (2.39). Failing to show deference to paternal uncles and other relatives; teaching for a fixed salary; studying for a fixed salary; selling items that should not be sold, such as sesame seeds; holding office by royal command over mines producing gold and other precious substances; constructing dams and the like which obstruct the flow of great rivers; and the destruction of plants merely for their species or similar reasons. This is because the penance is more severe when the act is committed intentionally and repeatedly. However, what will be stated later in the verse beginning "of cultivated plants" (11.144) refers to a single instance of destruction, as the penance is lighter there. Making one's wife or other women prostitutes and living off them; killing an innocent person through sacrifices such as the *śyena*; subjugating others by means of mantras or herbs; cutting down trees solely for visible purposes such as cooking; performing cooking and other acts without being ill and without dedicating them to the gods, ancestors, or others; eating once unintentionally garlic or other forbidden foods; but intentional and repeated consumption is forbidden by the rule: "eating forbidden food or drinking liquor" (11.56). Failing to establish the sacred fires despite having the qualification; stealing solid goods other than gold; failing to discharge debts—for a man is born burdened with three debts; teaching scriptures contrary to the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*; indulging in dancing, singing, and instrumental music; theft of grain, copper, iron, etc., or of animals; sexual intercourse with a twice-born woman who drinks liquor; killing a woman, a *Śūdra*, a *Vaiśya*, or a *Kṣatriya*; the belief that there is no efficacy to actions intended for transcendental results (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Each of these is a minor sin (*upapātaka*). Since the abandonment of one's mother and others is already covered by the phrase "abandoning relatives" (11.62), the separate mention here is for the sake of censure. While a penance is certainly required for abandoning paternal uncles and other relatives, it is less than the penance for abandoning one's mother and others. (11.59–66)
Causing pain to a Brāhmaṇa, smelling things that should not be smelled or drinking intoxicants, crookedness, and sexual intercourse with a male are recorded as acts that cause loss of caste. 11.67.

"Of a Brāhmaṇa": inflicting pain upon a Brāhmaṇa by means of a staff in hand or similar methods; smelling garlic, excrement, and so forth—which are unfit to be smelled due to their extreme foul odor—as well as liquor; crookedness or deceitfulness; and sexual intercourse with a male in the mouth or other such places: each of these is traditionally held to cause loss of caste. (11.67)

The killing of donkeys, horses, camels, deer, and elephants, as well as goats and sheep, and likewise of fish, snakes, and buffaloes, should be known as acts that cause loss of caste (saṃkarīkaraṇa). 11.68.

"Khara" means: the killing of each of the following—donkeys, horses, camels, deer, elephants, goats, sheep, fish, snakes, and buffaloes—is to be known as *saṃkarīkaraṇa* (an act that causes mixture of castes). || 11.68 ||
Accepting wealth from those who are censurable, engaging in trade, serving Śūdras, and speaking untruth—these should be known as acts that render one unworthy (apātrīkaraṇa). || 11.69 ||

"From those who are censured" means: accepting gifts from those whose wealth is not to be accepted, trade, service to a Śūdra, and speaking untruth—each of these should be known as an act that renders one unworthy (apātrīkaraṇa). || 11.69 ||
The killing of worms, insects, or birds; eating food mixed with intoxicants; stealing fruits, firewood, or flowers; and lack of fortitude—these bring about impurity. (11.70)

"Kṛmi" [means]: worms are small creatures; slightly larger than those are insects (*kīṭa*); their killing, as well as that of birds. "That which is accompanied by liquor" (*madyānugata*) refers to even edible food, such as vegetables and the like, which, having been placed together in a basket or similar vessel, is brought along with liquor and then eaten. Medhātithi, however, says it means "touched by liquor"; but that is not correct, because in that case the penance would be too severe. The theft of fruits, wood, and flowers—even when the loss is slight—causes extreme dejection. All of these, taken individually, are acts that cause impurity (*malinīkaraṇa*). (11.70)
Learn now correctly those various vows by which all these aforementioned sins, each individually, are expiated. (11.71)
"Regarding these": listen duly to those various vows in the form of expiations by which all these aforementioned sins, beginning with the killing of a Brahmin, are destroyed individually. 11.71.
A killer of a Brahmin shall dwell for twelve years in the forest, having built a hut,
subsisting on alms for the sake of self-purification, and carrying the skull of a corpse as his banner.

The *brahmaheti* (the weapon for killing a Brahmin): He who has killed a Brahmin should build a hut in the forest and, having made a mark from the skull of the slain person—or in its absence, from that of another—should dwell in the wilderness for twelve years, subsisting on alms, performing a vow to expiate his own sin. Regarding this, the author will later state: "Having shaved his head, he should dwell" (11.78). Furthermore, specific details mentioned by other sages are also to be adopted. Thus says Yama: "He should enter seven houses that have not been visited before and were not previously intended [for begging], slowly, when the smoke has ceased and the people have finished their meal."
"O killer of an embryo, give me alms; having made my sin public, I shall perform penance.
I shall go for alms at one time of day, and if that is not obtained, I shall drink water."

And this rule of twelve years applies to the killing of a Brāhmaṇa by another Brāhmaṇa who acted unknowingly, because it will be stated later: "This purification is declared for having unintentionally killed a twice-born man" (11.89). However, for Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, this twelve-year penance should be understood as being respectively double and triple. As it is said in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
"For Kṣatriyas, it is declared to be double; for Vaiśyas, triple;
and for Śūdras, fourfold—this is the assembly [of penances] prescribed for high-souled men."
The vow spoken for the assembly has been declared for the purification of those who have committed evil deeds.

The meaning is as follows: if the assembly (*sabhā*) of Brahmins consists of a certain number of Brahmins, the assembly of Kṣatriyas must consist of twice that number for the purpose of seeing the legal proceedings; likewise, for Vaiśyas it should be three times, and for Śūdras four times. Thus, by analogy with the assemblies, the penance (*vrata*) for the three classes beginning with the Kṣatriyas is also double, triple, and quadruple respectively. Furthermore, these statements regarding penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa spoken by Manu are explained in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* as referring to the killing of a Brāhmaṇa who is either virtuous or devoid of virtues.
O hero, if a virtuous man is slain, he is killed though he was unwilling; whereas one devoid of virtue is slain even when willing.
Having indeed performed the rites prescribed by Manu, one should perform the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha).
A killer of a Brahmin shall dwell in the forest for twelve years, having constructed a hut;
or he may go to the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) if the act was unintentional and the victim lacked merit.

Having ascertained the caste, capacity, and qualities [of the offender], as well as the nature of the connection [to the act] and so forth, one should prescribe the penance performed by a single act of cognition.

From this statement of Viśvāmitra, it should be inferred that the expiation is more severe [in the case of intentional killing]. However, for the intentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa, the expiation for killing a Brāhmaṇa is doubled, amounting to twenty-four years. Regarding this, Aṅgiras says:
"When a sin is committed unintentionally, there is expiation; not when it is intentional. But that which is committed unintentionally shall be doubled when done deliberately."
Or he may become a target for those who bear weapons, according to his own wish;
or he may cast himself headlong three times into a blazing fire. (11.73)

Regarding the term "target" (*lakṣyam*): for those bearing weapons such as bows and arrows who know that he has become a target for the purpose of destroying the sin of killing a Brahmin, he may remain at will as a target for arrows until he dies or becomes as good as dead, whereby he is purified. As Yājñavalkya says (YDh 3.248):
"Or, being killed in battle while serving as a target, he attains purification;
even if still living, he is purified when afflicted by mortal wounds."

Or, with his face turned downward, he should cast his body into a blazing fire three times; he should cast it in such a way that he dies, according to the statement of Āpastamba: "He should throw himself [into the fire] so that he may die. These two penances, as well as the one to be mentioned immediately hereafter—"or he should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha" (11.74)—constitute this triad of penances for a Kṣatriya who intentionally kills a Brāhmaṇa. Having cited the very verse of Manu, it is explained in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
"Or he may become a target for weapon-wielders at his own will, provided they are learned men."
Or he should throw himself three times head-first into a kindled fire.
Or a Kṣatriya who has killed a Brahmin should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha;
for these three are proclaimed as the expiations for a Kṣatriya.
O hero, having intentionally slain a virtuous Brāhmaṇa who is steadfast and has mastered the Vedas, a Kṣatriya must become a target for those who bear arms.
Having slain a wise Brāhmaṇa who knows the four Vedas and maintains the sacred fires,
out of lust, one should throw oneself headfirst into the fire.
O Guha, having intentionally killed a virtuous Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of qualities,
a Kṣatriya who is a lord of the earth may become pure by performing an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Or he should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha, the Svarjit, or the Gosava;
or with the Abhijit and Viśvajit, or even with the Trivṛt-Agniṣṭut.

"One should sacrifice. This has been explained immediately following the statement, "Or one should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha. One should cause [the sinner] to be sacrificed by means of the Svarjit—a specific sacrifice—or the Gosava, or the Abhijit, or the Viśvajit, or the Trivṛt-Agniṣṭut. These are the optional expiations for the unintentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa prescribed for a member of the three twice-born classes. As it is stated in the *Bhavishya Purāṇa*: "O Hero, Lord of Armies, the performance of these rites, such as the Svarjit and others, is indeed for the twice-born in the case of killing that was not preceded by intentional thought."
Or he may travel one hundred yojanas toward Japan or any other [sacred land],
