eating sparingly and with his senses restrained, for the sake of removing the sin of killing a Brahmin.

"Reciting" means that, reciting one of the Vedas from among them, eating very little, and with his senses restrained, he should travel a hundred *yojanas* in order to expiate the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa. This is the penance for a member of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) who kills a Brāhmaṇa by birth alone out of ignorance. To this effect, this very verse is read and explained in the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*: "When one should kill a Brāhmaṇa who is a mere matter of birth unintentionally, then this [penance] shall apply to him, provided he is a knower of the Vedas and a maintainer of the *agnihotra* sacrifice."
One should bestow one's entire property upon a Brahmin learned in the Vedas, or wealth sufficient for a livelihood, or a house together with its furnishings. (11.76)

"His entire property (*sarvasvam*). Or he should give his entire property to a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas; that is, as much wealth as is sufficient for his livelihood, or a house together with the wealth, grain, and other items necessary for a household. Therefore, he should give either his entire property or a house along with its furnishings. Because of the statement "sufficient for livelihood," he should give either his entire property or a house that is adequate for living, and not less than that. This is the expiation for a Brāhmaṇa who kills a Brāhmaṇa who is a mere member of the caste through ignorance. And so says the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*:
O Guha, when a Brāhmaṇa who is destitute of Vedic study, wealthy, and devoid of the sacred fires, should kill another Brāhmaṇa who is merely so by birth; [he incurs such sin].
Then one should perform this expiation for the purification of that sin:
either wealth sufficient for a livelihood, or a house together with its furnishings.
Or, eating only sacrificial food, he may follow the Sarasvatī river against its current;
or, with his diet restricted, he may recite the Saṃhitā of the Veda three times.

Regarding the term "haviṣya": one who eats sacrificial food such as *nīvāra* rice and the like should proceed along the Sarasvatī river toward its western ocean-flow, starting from the famous spring (*vikhyātaprasravaṇa*). This applies to the intentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa who is a Brāhmaṇa by birth alone. Thus, it is stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "O Lord of the Gods, when a Brāhmaṇa who is a Brāhmaṇa by birth alone is killed intentionally, and the killer is devoid of Vedic knowledge and has been maintained by wealth..."
In that case, one should perform this expiation; learn from me its atonement:
he should subsist on sacrificial food (haviṣya) and traverse the Sarasvatī river against the current.
Alternatively, one who has restricted his food may recite the Vedic Saṃhitā three times.
By the inclusion of the term "Saṃhitā," the *pada* and *krama* recensions are excluded. Here too, there is a specific rule from the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"If one should kill a Brāhmaṇa who possesses only his caste [status], unintentionally, then a Brāhmaṇa who is exceedingly virtuous should perform this [penance]."
Or, O best of gods, one who is restrained in diet should recite three times the Saṃhitā of the Veda—
the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman verses— which is known as the Traividya.

Now, following the instruction that "when the twelfth year is completed" (11.81), he states the specific details for the twelve-year penance: "Having shaved his head, he should dwell at the edge of a village, or in a cow-pen, or in a hermitage, or at the foot of a tree, devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins. (11.78)

Regarding the word *kṛtā*: having had his hair, nails, and beard shaved, devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins, and performing services for cows and Brahmins, he should dwell near a village at any one of the following places: a cow-pen, a sacred spot, or the foot of a tree. This [verse] is intended as an alternative to the rule "having built a hut in the forest" (11.72). || 11.78 ||
One who immediately gives up his life for the sake of a Brahmin or for the sake of a cow is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin, as is the protector of a cow or a Brahmin. (11.79)

"Regarding the purpose of a Brāhmaṇa": when the twelve-year penance has begun, one is released from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa by sacrificing one's life for the sake of protecting a Brāhmaṇa or a cow who is being attacked by fire, water, or a predator. Or, by rescuing a cow or a Brāhmaṇa from that danger, one is released even if one dies, and even if the twelve years have not been completed. (11.79)
Or he who repels [an attack] three times, or having conquered all his property, or when his life is lost for the sake of a Brahmin, is liberated [from that debt]. (11.80)

Regarding the phrase "three times": when the entire property of a Brāhmaṇa is being stolen by thieves and others, one who makes an honest effort according to his ability to recover it, engaging in battle there three times—even if he does not bring back the entire property—is liberated from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahatyā*). Alternatively, if on the very first occasion he defeats the thieves and restores the Brāhmaṇa’s entire property that was stolen, he is likewise liberated. Or, if the Brāhmaṇa himself proceeds toward death in battle because his wealth has been seized, then even if the rescuer restores him to life by giving back the stolen wealth, he is nonetheless liberated from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa due to the fact that the Brāhmaṇa’s life was saved for that purpose. This is distinct from the other method of protection mentioned in the verse, "The protector of a cow and of a Brāhmaṇa" (11.70), and thus there is no tautology. 11.80.
Thus, one who is firm in his vows, constantly chaste, and composed in mind,
removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin upon the completion of the twelfth year.

"Thus": in this manner, as described, one who is always constrained by the rules, free from sexual union with women and the like, and whose mind is restrained, destroys the sin of killing a Brahmin at the completion of the twelfth year. In this way, everything beginning with "for the sake of a Brahmin" (11.79) is to be understood as applying to the aforementioned twelve-year penance. 11.81.
Or, having confessed his own sin in an assembly of kings before the gods upon earth,
he is released from it after bathing in the final purificatory bath of a horse sacrifice.

"Having left behind," it says. In the Aśvamedha sacrifice, when Brāhmaṇas who are officiating priests and the Kṣatriya who is the sacrificer meet, one leaves behind—that is, announces—one's own sin of Brahmin-slaughter; having bathed at the final purificatory rite (*avabhṛtha*), one is released from the sin of Brahmin-slaughter. Because the twelve-year penance has already been mentioned [elsewhere], this is an independent expiation. And so it is stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "But when a virtuous Brāhmaṇa should unintentionally kill a Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of virtues, he should then go for the bath associated with the Aśvamedha."

Govindarāja, however, says: "By means of the intermediate *avabhṛtha* bath, there is purification for him through that very [act], from the remainder of all penances excluding the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), once this commenced twelve-year penance has been concluded. That is incorrect, because it contradicts the statement of the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*. 11.82.
The Brāhmaṇa is said to be the root of Dharma, and the Rājanya is its summit;
therefore, by confessing one's sin in their assembly, one becomes purified. (11.83)

Regarding the phrase "of Dharma": because the Brāhmaṇa is the cause of Dharma—since it is said by Manu and others that when instruction in Dharma has been given by a Brāhmaṇa, the King attains its highest point through the performance of Dharma—it is from these two, the Brāhmaṇa and the Kṣatriya, that the tree of Dharma, with its roots and its top, is produced. Therefore, this is the specific rule for them: "In the Aśvamedha sacrifice, having confessed his sin, he becomes pure after bathing at the final purificatory rite (avabhṛtha). (11.83)
By his very birth, the Brāhmaṇa is the deity even of the gods;
he is the authority for the world, for Brahmā himself is the cause in this matter.

Regarding the term "brāhmaṇa": by the mere fact of his birth, a brāhmaṇa is worthy of worship even by the gods, let alone by humans; he is an authority for the world as if through direct perception, because his instruction possesses validity. For in this matter, the Veda itself is the cause, since his instruction is rooted in the Veda. 11.84
Since this is so, therefore:
"Even all three of them should declare to those knowers of the Veda that their sin is well-expiated;
for that [declaration] shall serve as their purification, for the word of the learned is indeed purifying. (11.85)

"Of them": among those learned Brāhmaṇas, even three who know the Veda—how much more so if there are more—whatever penance they may prescribe for the removal of sin, that serves for the purification of the sinner. Since the speech of the learned is purifying, therefore, for the sake of a public penance, an assembly (*pariṣad*) of the learned must certainly be convened. However, this does not apply to secret penances, because that would contradict their very nature as being secret. (11.85)
Therefore, by adhering to any one of these rules with a concentrated mind, a Brahmin,
through self-mastery, removes the sin committed by killing a Brahmin.

"From this" means that by resorting to any one of these groups of penances with a restrained mind, a Brāhmaṇa or others remove the sin committed through the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, because it serves a praiseworthy purpose. Furthermore, this prescription for penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa and so forth applies to the case of committing the sin once; however, in the event of repetition of the sin, the penance must be repeated. This is because of the traditional teaching of Gautama: "In the case of a heavy sin, the penances are heavy; in the case of a light sin, they are light. Moreover, it is because a multiplicity of penances will be prescribed for multiple killings, as in: "When a cartload of boneless creatures has been killed, one should perform the vow [prescribed] for killing a Śūdra" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.265).
From this first rule, it is recorded that in the second [case] it is double,
and in the third it is declared to be triple.

Thus, according to the Smṛti of Gautama. However, regarding the simultaneous killing of several Brāhmaṇas by means such as setting a house on fire, there is a specific rule from the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "O Hero, having killed a Brāhmaṇa, or two Brāhmaṇas, or many Brāhmaṇas simultaneously, O Hero, one should perform a single penance that ends with death."
But if one should intentionally kill Brāhmaṇas, O best of gods, then one should burn oneself in fire according to the rite; listen to that.

And all of this refers exclusively to the domain of ignorance. Thus: "O Guha, if a Brāhmaṇa should kill other Brāhmaṇas unintentionally, he must dwell in a terrible forest until the exhaustion of his life."

And this [penance] applies to the killing of an ignorant person because that is the subject under discussion; however, regarding a killing carried out sequentially, there is a Vedic statement prescribing repetition: "From this first injunction... (11.86).

Having killed an embryo whose sex is unknown, one should observe this very same vow; as also in the case of killing a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who knows [the Veda], or a woman who is the wife of an Ātreya.

Regarding the word "having killed" (*hatvā*): because of the context, this refers to killing a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who has been engaged in a sacrifice and whose caste is unknown as being male, female, or neuter, as well as an *ātreyī* woman, that is, a Brāhmaṇa woman; for Yama records: "Likewise an *ātreyī*, a Brāhmaṇa woman. Having killed [these], one should perform the penance for the murder of a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahatyā*). An *ātreyī* is said to be a menstruating woman who has bathed after her menses, according to the Smṛti of Vasiṣṭha: "An *ātreyī* is a menstruating woman who has bathed after her menses" (VaDh 20.35). Thus, the killing of a Brāhmaṇa woman who is not an *ātreyī* constitutes a minor offense (*upapātaka*) requiring a three-year penance, as stated: "The killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya" (11.66). As for what is stated in the following verse, "and having committed the killing of a woman or a friend" (11.88), that refers to the wife of a Brāhmaṇa who is a Brāhmaṇa himself and maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*). So too says Aṅgiras.
Having killed the blameless wife of a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires, one should perform the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa; the same applies to the killer of an Ātreyī woman.
Having given false testimony, having obstructed a teacher, having misappropriated a deposit, and having committed the murder of a woman or a friend; 11.88.

Having said this: having spoken falsely in a legal testimony concerning gold, land, and so forth; having brought about a false accusation against a teacher; having embezzled a deposit—meaning property other than a Brāhmaṇa’s gold, such as silver and the like, or even gold itself from a Kṣatriya or others; and having committed the killing of a woman as previously explained, or having killed a non-Brāhmaṇa friend, one shall perform the penance for the murder of a Brāhmaṇa. (11.88)
This purification has been declared for killing a twice-born man unintentionally;
for the intentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa, no atonement is prescribed.

Regarding the phrase "this": this expiation has been prescribed for the unintentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa in the absence of a specific instruction. However, in the case of intentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa, this atonement does not apply; nor is this the expiation. Rather, it consists of performing double the penance and so forth, which serves to increase the gravity of the expiation and not to indicate its total absence, because that would contradict what was stated previously: "But that which is done intentionally out of delusion [is purified] by various kinds of expiations" (11.46). (11.89)
If a twice-born man, out of delusion, drinks liquor, he shall drink liquor that is the color of fire;
when his body has been consumed by it, he is then released from that sin.

Regarding the term *surā*: the word *surā* is primary (*mukhya*) only with respect to that made from flour (*paiṣṭī*), and not with respect to the three types—those made from molasses (*gauḍī*), honey (*mādhvī*), and flour—because there is no single form common to all three. Furthermore, if one were to postulate a separate denotative power (*śakti*) for each, it would entail the fault of over-complication (*gaurava*) by necessitating the postulation of three distinct powers. Moreover, the use of the word *surā* for liquors such as the *gauḍī* is justified through figurative application (*guṇavṛtti*). For this very reason, the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* states: "The *surā* made from flour is declared to be the primary [type]; the others are not equal to it.
Learn now the expiation for drinking these [other types] following the drinking of *paiṣṭī*."
O mighty-armed one, that which was spoken by Manu has been set forth through both concise and detailed methods.

The genitive case in the word *etāsām* is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). The meaning is: "Among these aforementioned [liquors]—Gauḍī, Mādhvī, and Paiṣṭī—learn the penance prescribed by Manu for drinking the *paiṣṭī*: 'Having drunk liquor through delusion, a twice-born [man]...'". Having drunk the primary *surā*, the *paiṣṭī*, a twice-born person—a Brāhmaṇa or others—out of infatuation with passion and so forth, should drink *surā* that is fire-colored. When his body has been consumed by that *surā*, the twice-born is liberated from that sin. And this refers to the intentional drinking of *surā*, because of its gravity. Thus says Bṛhaspati:
If the drinking of liquor was done intentionally, one should cast that blazing [iron ball] into his mouth;
having been consumed by it and thus died, he shall attain purification.
Or he should drink cow's urine that is the color of fire, or water alone;
or milk, or ghee, or the liquid from cow dung until death. (11.91)
Regarding "cow's urine": having brought any one of the substances—cow's urine, water, cow's milk, cow's curd, cow's ghee, or cow dung—into contact with fire, he should drink it until death. 11.91.
Or he may eat grains for a year, or consume oil-cake once at night;
wearing hair-cloth, with matted locks and carrying a skull-topped staff, in order to remove the sin of drinking liquor. (11.92)

"Or grains": alternatively, wearing garments made of cow-hair and the like, with matted locks and bearing the mark of a liquor-vessel, he should eat fine rice-particles or oil-extracted sesame seeds once a night for a period of one year, in order to destroy the sin of drinking liquor. This should be understood as an unintentional, secondary form of liquor-drinking; it is not an alternative [penance] involving the same qualities [as the primary penance], because it is lighter. (11.92)
Surā is indeed the dregs of food, and sin is called a dreg;
therefore, the Brāhmaṇa, the Rājanya, and the Vaiśya shall not drink surā. (11.93)

“Indeed. Because it is produced from the paste of rice, *surā* is the dregs (*mala*) of food; and by the word *mala*, sin is expressed. Therefore, since there is a prohibition stating that Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas shall not drink *surā* made from flour, the penance [prescribed] for its transgression is: “Having drunk *surā*” (11.90). Furthermore, because of the reference to the dregs of food, the prohibition of *surā* made from flour alone for the three castes has been clearly stated by Manu himself. (11.93)
Gauḍī, paiṣṭī, and mādhvī—liquor is to be known as being of these three kinds.
Just as one is so are all; they must not be drunk by the best of the twice-born.

Regarding the term *gauḍī*: that which is made from molasses (*guḍa*) is *gauḍī*; likewise, that made from flour (*piṣṭa*) is *paiṣṭī*; and that made from the flowers of the *madhuka* tree—which is honey—is *mādhvī*. Thus, three kinds of *surā* (liquor) are produced. This identification with the primary *surā* is intended to indicate that, compared to other types of liquor, the drinking of *gauḍī* and *mādhvī* by a Brāhmaṇa entails a heavier penance. Just as the single type of *paiṣṭī surā* is the primary one because it is prohibited for the three castes by the preceding statement, so too the aforementioned *gauḍī* and *mādhvī* must not be drunk by the best of the twice-born. (11.94)
Wine, meat, and spirituous liquors are the food of yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas;
that must not be consumed by a brāhmaṇa who partakes of the sacrificial oblation for the gods.

Regarding the term *yakṣa*: here, "intoxicant" (*madya*) should be understood as being of nine kinds, excluding the prohibited varieties made from flour (*paiṣṭī*), molasses (*gauḍī*), and honey (*mādhvī*). Pulastya states them as follows:
"Pānasa, drākṣa, mādhvīka, khārjūra, tāla, aikṣava, mādhvīka, ṭāṅka-mārdvīka, maireya, and that produced from coconut."
There are eleven kinds of intoxicants common to the twice-born;
however, the twelfth, the liquor of fermented rice (surā), is recorded as the lowest for all.

Meat is also forbidden, and three types of *surā* have been described. Regarding *āsava*, which is so called because it causes intoxication (*asūyate*), Pulastya has prescribed the following expiation:
"Having drunk the juice of grapes, sugarcane, *taṅka*, dates, jackfruit, and other such fruits immediately [after extraction], the best of the twice-born becomes pure after three days."

Thus, these four—liquor and the rest—are food belonging to the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas; therefore, they must not be consumed by a Brāhmaṇa who eats the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) of the gods. The mention of *surā* (liquor) here, though already prohibited, is for the purpose of censure by identifying it as the food of the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas. Regarding this, some say: "Because of the masculine designation in the phrase 'eats the oblation of the gods' (*devānām aśnatā haviḥ*), the prohibition of liquor applies only to the male Brāhmaṇa, not to the woman. That is incorrect.
"A Brahmin woman who drinks liquor does not go to the world of Brahmā;
even in this very world, she is reborn as a female dog, a vulture, or a sow. (YDh 3.256).
This is because [the proposed view] contradicts such Smṛti texts of Yājñavalkya and others. 11.95.
Intoxicated by liquor, a Brāhmaṇa might fall into impurity, or he might recite the Veda, or he might perform some other improper act, being deluded by intoxication. (11.96)

Regarding the term "impurity": it is a restatement of the previous point that a Brāhmaṇa, his intellect deluded by the intoxication of drinking liquor, might fall into impurity, utter Vedic words, or commit forbidden acts such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa; therefore, he must not drink liquor. (11.96)
He whose Brahmanical state, residing within his body, is once drenched by liquor—his status as a Brahmin departs and he becomes a Śūdra. (11.97)

Regarding the phrase "of whom": if the Veda, which is Brahman residing within the body of a Brāhmaṇa and exists in the form of sacred refinement (*saṃskāra*), is once drenched by liquor—since the individual soul and the body are one—then that Brāhmaṇa who drinks liquor even once loses his Brāhmaṇahood and attains the state of a Śūdra. Therefore, liquor must never be drunk under any circumstances. (11.97)
This manifold expiation for the drinking of spirituous liquor has been declared;
hereafter I shall proclaim the expiation for the theft of gold.

"Regarding this": these various kinds of expiations for the sin produced by drinking liquor have been declared. Beyond that, I shall now state the atonement for the sin of stealing the gold of a Brāhmaṇa. 11.98.
A Brahmin who has committed the theft of gold, having approached the king, should proclaim his own deed and say: "May Your Majesty punish me. (11.99)

Regarding the word "suvarṇa" [gold]: because of the traditional teaching of Śātātapa, "Having himself stolen the gold of a Brāhmaṇa," a Brāhmaṇa who is a thief of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold should go to the king, declare his own deed—the theft of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold—and say, "May you inflict punishment upon me. The mention of a "Brāhmaṇa" is intended to indicate any human being whatsoever, since the subject under discussion is "the man undergoes penance" (11.44), and no other specific penance has been prescribed for Kṣatriyas and others. (11.99)
Taking up a club, the king himself shall strike him once;
by this execution the thief is purified, or a Brāhmaṇa is purified by austerity alone.

Regarding the phrase "having taken": since it has been stated in the passage beginning with "taking a club upon his shoulder" (8.316), the king himself should strike once a man who has committed theft after taking the club or other implements offered by him. According to the legal tradition of Yājñavalkya, "He is pure whether killed or even released" (YDh 3.257), that thief—whether dead, or as good as dead from the blow of the club, or still living—is liberated from that sin. However, in the case of a Brāhmaṇa, because of the use of the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "or by austerity alone," he is purified by austerity alone; for it is said, "One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he stands guilty of every possible crime" (8.380). Therefore, in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa, which explains the meaning of Manu’s text:
O Hero, O Lord of the Gods, it is for this very reason— that the Brahmin speaks these words through asceticism alone— that the Brahmin is so designated, O Wise One.
By the phrase "by austerity alone," there is here a prohibition of killing.

The word "or" (*vā*) is intended to indicate that asceticism (*tapas*) is also an option for Kṣatriyas and others. For a Brāhmaṇa, however, there is the rule that asceticism alone [is his duty], but it does not mean that asceticism belongs to the Brāhmaṇa alone. Therefore, the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* states:
"O Lord, asceticism is not forbidden even for the others.

He states that very penance: "But a twice-born man who, desiring to remove the stain born of stealing gold, wears rags and shall perform in the forest the vow prescribed for a slayer of a Brahmin. (11.101)

Regarding the word *tapasā*: a twice-born man desiring to remove the sin arising from the theft of gold by means of austerity (*tapas*) should perform that vow which has been prescribed for the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa, because of its mention first [in the sequence] and because of the inclusion of the term "forest" (*araṇya*). And this twelve-year penance, due to its severity and because it is an alternative to death for Kṣatriyas and others, should be understood—when applied to the theft of gold belonging to a Brāhmaṇa—to refer to a quantity of gold defined as "a *māṣa* consists of five *kṛṣṇalas*, and sixteen of those make a *suvarṇa*" (MDh 8.134); it does not apply to less than that. For it is logical to adopt the measure stated by Manu in view of the specific quantity mentioned. As for the greater quantity heard in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*, that refers specifically to a case of theft characterized by such circumstances. Likewise, in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
If the three castes beginning with the Kṣatriya— who are indeed devoid of virtue and intent on evil—
should seize five gold coins from a Brāhmaṇa who is rich in virtues;
O hero, having likewise burnt eleven niṣkas of gold in the fire, they may be purified through death; for the purification of the self, one should practice the Brahma-vow.
By these vows, a twice-born man may remove the sin committed through theft;
however, he shall expel the sin of approaching the teacher's wife by means of these very vows.

"By these": a twice-born man shall remove the sin produced by stealing the gold of a Brāhmaṇa by means of these vows (*vrata*). Since both "vows" (*vrata*) and "austerities" (*tapas*) have been mentioned, the plural number in the word "by these" (*etair*) is used with reference to their connection; it is intended to indicate that even the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) prescribed by Manu should be devised [where appropriate]. Furthermore, the sin caused by approaching the wife of a guru shall be removed by the expiations that will be described hereafter. (11.102)
Having addressed the sin of violating the teacher’s bed, he should lie upon a heated iron bed, or embrace a blazing iron image; by death, he is purified. (11.103)

Regarding the word "guru": since it has been stated that "the rites beginning with the impregnation [are performed by him]" (2.142), the *guru* is the father; the *talpa* is the wife; thus, *gurutalpa* is the wife of the *guru*. One who approaches her—that is, one who commits the sin of violating the teacher's wife—should confess his crime and lie upon a heated bed of iron. Having fashioned an image of a woman out of iron, he becomes purified through death by embracing it while it is blazing. 11.103.
Or, having himself cut off his penis and testicles and placed them in his joined palms, he should walk straight toward the direction of Nirṛti until they fall. (11.104)

"Or himself" means that having himself cut off his own penis and testicles and placed them in his joined palms, he should go toward the south-western direction with straight gait until the fall of his body. Thus, these two prescribed penances, because of their severity, apply to the case of a wife of a guru of the same caste (*savarṇa*), and concern sexual intercourse resulting in the emission of semen when done intentionally. 11.104.
Carrying a skull-topped staff or clad in rags, with a beard and dwelling in a solitary forest,
he should perform the Prājāpatya penance for one year with a concentrated mind.

"Carrying a skull-topped staff," etc.: carrying a *khaṭvāṅga*, covered with a piece of cloth, with his hair, nails, body hair, and beard uncut, with a restrained mind, he should perform the *prājāpatya* vow for one year in a solitary forest. And because of the lightness of the penance to be described hereafter, this should be understood as applying to cases of ignorance, such as when one mistakes his own wife [for another]. (11.105)
Or, with his senses restrained, he should practice the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for three months,
subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya) or barley gruel (yavāgū), in order to expiate the sin of violating the Guru’s bed.

"Cāndrāyaṇa," and so forth. Alternatively, for the expiation of the sin of approaching the wife of a guru, one who has restrained his senses should perform Cāndrāyaṇa penances for three months, subsisting on sacrificial food such as fruits and roots, or on a gruel made of wild rice (nīvāra) and the like. This should be understood to apply to one who approaches a wife of the guru who is either unchaste or of a different caste, since this [penance] is lighter than the previously mentioned ones. 11.106.
By these vows, those who have committed mortal sins (mahāpātakin) may remove their impurity;
likewise, those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin) may do so by means of these various kinds of vows.

"By these vows," and so forth. By means of these aforementioned vows, those who have committed great sins such as the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) may remove their guilt. Furthermore, those who have committed secondary sins (*upapātaka*), such as the killing of a cow, may remove their sins through various forms of vows in the manner that will be described hereafter.
One who has committed the minor offense of killing a cow shall drink barley gruel for one month;
having shaved his head, he shall dwell in a cow-pen, covered with the hide of that very cow.
For two months, with his senses restrained, he should eat a measured amount of food, free from pungent seasonings and salt, at every fourth mealtime, and perform his bath using cow urine.
By day he should follow those cows, and while standing, he should inhale the dust raised by them;
having performed service and paid homage, he should remain in the vīrāsana posture at night.
While they stand, he should stand; while they walk, he should follow;
likewise, while they sit, he should sit—self-restrained and free from envy. (11.111)

Whether she is afflicted by illness or accused [of wrongdoing], or threatened by dangers such as thieves and tigers, or fallen or stuck in the mud—one should liberate her by every possible means. (11.112)
Whether it be hot, raining, cold, or when the wind blows violently, one should not seek protection for oneself without first doing so for the cow to the best of one's ability. (11.113)
Whether it be one's own or another's, one should not speak of a cow eating in a house, a field, or a threshing floor, nor of a calf drinking. (11.114)
But he who, following this rule, attends upon a cow, removes the sin committed by killing a cow within three months. (11.115)

Regarding the term *upapātaka* (minor offenses): starting from the verse “He who, by this rule... (11.115) and continuing through the entire section, [the following is prescribed]: A cow-killer guilty of a minor offense (*upapātaka*) shall first drink barley for one month in the form of a thin barley-gruel. Having shaved his head, leaving only the top-knot (*śikhā*), and having his beard clipped, he shall dwell for three months in a cow-pen with his body covered by the hide of a slain cow. With self-restrained senses, he shall perform his ablutions with cow urine. Having eaten sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) free from artificial salt for one day, he shall eat on the evening of the second day during the second and third months. For three months, he shall follow those cows in the morning during the daytime; standing, he shall inhale the dust raised above them by the striking of their hooves. He shall serve them by scratching them when they itch and so forth, and having bowed to them, he shall sit at night without encircling a wall or similar structure. Likewise, being pure and free from anger, he shall rise only after the cows have risen; he shall wander behind them as they roam in the forest, sit down when they sit down, and rescue a sick cow, or one attacked by thieves, tigers, and other dangers, or one fallen or stuck in mud, to the best of his ability. Similarly, when the sun is scorching hot, when clouds are raining, when cold has set in, or when the wind blows excessively, he shall not seek protection for himself without first providing protection for the cow to the best of his ability. Likewise, he shall not report to anyone else when she is eating grain and such in the house, field, or threshing floor of himself or others, nor when her calf is drinking milk. By this aforementioned procedure, the cow-killer who serves the cows removes the sin produced by the slaughter of a cow within three months. (11.108–115)
One who has successfully observed the vow should give ten cows and a bull;
if these are not available, he should offer his entire property to those learned in the Vedas.

"Eleven bulls": she for whom the bull is the eleventh—these he should give once the penance has been properly performed. If such wealth is not available, he should give his entire property to Brahmins learned in the Vedas. (11.116)

Twice-born men who have committed minor offenses (upapātaka), with the exception of one who has broken his vow of chastity (avakīrṇin), shall perform this very same penance for the sake of purification, or else the Cāndrāyaṇa.

"Exactly this. However, others maintain that those who have committed minor offenses (*upapātakin*), with the exception of the *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy) who will be mentioned later, should perform exactly this penance for killing a cow or the *cāndrāyaṇa* fast because of its lightness, in order to remove their sin. But the *cāndrāyaṇa* should be applied to a light minor offense after taking into account [the person's] caste, capacity, qualities, and so forth. (11.117)
But one who has spilled his seed shall, at night, sacrifice to Nirṛti at a crossroads with a one-eyed donkey, according to the procedure for a Pākayajña.

"But the *avakīrṇin*," it is said. The *avakīrṇin*, who will be described hereafter, shall sacrifice at night to the deity named Nirṛti at a crossroads with a one-eyed donkey, using the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of a *pākayajña*. (11.118)
Having performed the oblations in the fire according to the rule, and finally with the verse beginning "sam," he should offer oblations of clarified butter to Vāta, Indra, Guru, and Agni.

"Having offered," [it means]: then, having duly performed the offerings of the donkey's feet and so forth for Nirṛti at a crossroads, at the conclusion of that, one should offer oblations of clarified butter to the Maruts, Indra, Bṛhaspati, and Agni with this verse: "May the Maruts sprinkle me" (AV 7.33.1). || 11.119 ||
Because it is not well known, he states the definition of one who has broken his vow:
"The knowers of Dharma, the exponents of the Veda, declare that for a twice-born man established in his vows, the intentional emission of semen is a transgression of his vow. (11.120)

"Out of desire" means intentionally; for the twice-born student (*brahmacārī*), by having sexual intercourse with a woman, he becomes an *avakīrṇin*. As stated in the verse: "A twice-born man who, out of desire, has gone to a woman becomes an *avakīrṇin*" (YDh 3.281), all-knowing knowers of the Veda declare that the emission of semen into a female womb constitutes a transgression of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) known as *avakīrṇa*. || 11.120 ||
The fourfold Brahmanic splendor of one who has violated his vow approaches Māruta, Puruhūta, Guru, and Pāvaka.

Regarding the term *māruta*: the splendor (*tejas*) born from the observance of the rules for Vedic study belonging to one who observes a vow passes over to the four—Marut, Indra, Bṛhaspati, and Pāvaka—when he has become an *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy). Therefore, this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the offering of clarified butter (*ājyāhuti*), [prescribing] that one should offer oblations of clarified butter to them. (11.121)
When this offense has been committed, having worn the skin of a donkey,
he shall go for alms to seven houses, proclaiming his own deed.

Regarding the phrase "in this": when this sin known as *avakīrṇa* has arisen, having performed the previously mentioned rites such as the donkey sacrifice, and because of the traditional teaching of Hārīta stating, "having clothed himself in a donkey's hide," that *avakīrṇin*, covered by the hide belonging to a donkey and proclaiming his own deed by saying "I am an *avakīrṇin*," should go for alms to seven houses. (11.122)
Subsisting on alms obtained from them only once a day, and performing the ritual ablutions at the three periods of the day, he becomes purified in one year. (11.123)

"From them": by taking food only once a day from the alms obtained at those seven houses, and performing his ablutions in the evening, morning, and at midday, that one who has broken his vow of chastity is purified in exactly one year. 11.123.
Having intentionally committed any one of those acts that causes loss of caste, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra; if done unintentionally, one should perform the Prājāpatya.

Regarding the term "jāti" (caste): having intentionally committed any one of the specific acts that cause loss of caste, such as "causing injury to a Brāhmaṇa" (11.67) and so forth, which have been described, one should perform the *sāntapana* penance to be accomplished in seven days, as will be explained hereafter. However, having committed it unintentionally, one should perform the *prājāpatya* penance, as will be explained. 11.124.
For acts causing mixture of castes or unworthiness of receiving alms, purification is achieved by the lunar penance (*aindava*) for one month;
for acts causing defilement, one should subsist on hot barley-gruel for three days.

Regarding *saṃkara* (mixing): the acts that cause mixing (*saṃkarīkaraṇa*) have been described by the verse beginning with “A donkey, a horse, a camel... (11.68). The acts that render one unworthy of receiving gifts (*apātrīkaraṇa*) have been described by the verse beginning with “Accepting wealth from censurable persons... (11.69). Having intentionally committed any one of these, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for a month for purification. Regarding *malinīkaraṇa* (defiling acts): those have been described by the verse beginning with “Killing worms, insects, or birds... (11.70). Having intentionally committed any one of these, one should eat boiled barley-gruel for three nights. 11.125.
The fourth part of the penance for killing a Brahmin is prescribed for the murder of a Kṣatriya;
for a Vaiśya who abides by his duty, it is known to be one-eighth, while for a Śūdra, it should be understood as one-sixteenth.

Regarding the term "fourth": a fourth part of the penance for killing a Brahmin consists of three years, which is one-fourth of the twelve-year penance. And this expiation, prescribed as a minor offense (*upapātaka*) in the rule "the killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya" (11.66), should be understood as applying to the intentional killing of a Kṣatriya who is established in his duties (*vṛttastha*), because it is more serious than the [penance for] a three-year period. When a well-behaved (*sādhvācāra*) Vaiśya is killed intentionally, the penance is one-eighth part, a vow lasting one and a half years. When a Śūdra who is established in his duties is killed intentionally, it should be understood that the penance lasts nine months. (11.126)
But having unintentionally caused the death of a Kṣatriya, the best of the twice-born, having observed his vow well, should give a thousand cows and one bull.

"Unintentionally": furthermore, having killed a Kṣatriya unintentionally, one should give to Brāhmaṇas for the sake of one's own purification a thousand cows plus one bull—those cows of which there is one bull in excess over a thousand. 11.127.
Or, with his hair matted and self-restrained, he should perform for three years the penance for killing a Brahmin,
dwelling far from the village and making his home at the foot of a tree.

"Three years": Alternatively, one who is self-restrained, wearing matted hair (*jaṭā*), and having made his dwelling at the foot of a tree far removed from the village, should perform for three years that which was prescribed for the slayer of a Brahmin, beginning with "The slayer of a Brahmin [shall remain] for twelve years" (11.72). Nor should it be argued that this is a redundant repetition of the rule "A fourth part [is the penance] for the killing of a Brahmin" (11.126), because this text—by stating "wearing matted hair, [living] far from the village, with his abode at the root of a tree"—is intended to exclude all other duties such as carrying the skull-topped staff (*śavaśirodhvaja*) and so forth. Furthermore, since this pertains to the case of unintentional action (*akāmataḥ*), it is appropriate that there be a reduction in the severity of the limbs of the penance.
The best of the twice-born should perform this very same penance for one year after killing a Vaiśya who is established in his duty;
furthermore, he should give one hundred cows.

"Regarding this": a Brāhmaṇa or other [higher caste] shall perform this very same twelve-year vow for one year if he has unintentionally killed a Vaiśya who follows the conduct of the virtuous; or he may give one hundred and one cows. (11.129)
One who kills a Śūdra shall perform this entire vow for six months,
or else he should give ten white cows and a bull as the eleventh to a Brāhmaṇa.

Regarding this: even for this [offense], if committed unintentionally, the slayer of a Śūdra shall perform this very same vow for six months; he shall give to a Brāhmaṇa cows of white color, with a bull as the eleventh among them. || 11.130 ||
Having killed a cat, a mongoose, a blue jay,
or even a frog, as well as a dog, an iguana, an owl, or a crow, one should perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra.

Regarding the term *mārjāra*: having killed each of these—a cat, a mongoose, a blue jay, a frog, a dog, an iguana, a porcupine, or a crow—one should perform the vow for killing a Śūdra, namely the penance for a minor offense (*upapātaka*) prescribed in the rule "killing a woman or a Śūdra" (11.66), or the cow-killing vow, or the *cāndrāyaṇa*; however, one should not perform the penance prescribed in the rule "the Śūdra is to be known as the sixteenth [caste]" (11.126) and so forth, because the sin is lighter. Furthermore, this *cāndrāyaṇa* should be understood to apply to cases of intentional repetition and the like. (11.132)
One should drink milk for three nights, or travel a distance of one yojana, or bathe in a flowing river, or mutter the hymn dedicated to the waters (Ab-daivata Sūkta). || 11.132 ||

"Payah" (milk): In the case of killing a cat or similar animals unintentionally, one should drink milk for three nights. Now, if one is unable to travel a league (*yojana*) every three nights due to weak digestion or other reasons, being thus incapable, one should bathe in a river for three nights. If one is still unable even for that, one should mutter the hymn beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā" (RV 7.6.5) for three nights. Because each subsequent option is lighter, one should adopt each later alternative only when the preceding one is impossible; they are not merely optional alternatives. || 11.132 ||
Having killed a snake, the best of the twice-born should give an iron spade;
for killing a eunuch, a load of straw and one māṣa of lead.

Regarding the word "abhrim": having killed a snake, one should give a sharp-pointed iron rod to a Brāhmaṇa. Having killed a eunuch, one should give a load of straw and a māṣaka of lead to a Brāhmaṇa. || 11.133 ||
For killing a boar, one should give a jar of ghee; for a partridge, a drona of sesame seeds;
for a parrot, a two-year-old calf; and for killing a curlew, a three-year-old calf.

Regarding the word "ghṛta": when a pig is killed, one should give a jar filled with clarified butter to a Brāhmaṇa. When a bird known as a partridge is killed, one should give a quantity of sesame measuring four āḍhakas. When a parrot is killed, a two-year-old calf. Having killed a bird called a curlew (krauñca), one should give a three-year-old calf to a Brāhmaṇa. || 11.134 ||
Having killed a swan, a crane, a heron, or even a peacock, as well as a monkey,
a hawk, and a vulture, one should offer a cow to a Brāhmaṇa.
"Having killed" means: having killed any one of the birds known as the swan, crane, peacock, monkey, hawk, or vulture, one should give a cow to a Brāhmaṇa. 11.135.
Having killed a horse, one should give a garment; for killing an elephant, five dark-colored bulls; for killing a goat or a sheep, an ox; and for killing a donkey, a one-year-old calf.

Regarding the dwelling: having killed a horse, one should give a garment; having killed an elephant, one should give five dark-blue bulls; having killed a goat or a sheep individually, one should give a bull; having killed a donkey, one should give a calf one year old. || 11.136 ||
Having killed carnivorous wild animals, one should give a milch cow;
for non-carnivorous animals, a heifer; but having killed a camel, one should give a *kṛṣṇala* of gold.

Regarding the term "kravyādān" (meat-eaters): having killed wild animals such as tigers and others that consume raw flesh, one should give a cow yielding much milk. Having killed deer and others that eat raw flesh, one should give a mature heifer. Having killed a camel, one should give a *suvarṇa-kṛṣṇala*, that is, a *raktikā*. || 11.137 ||
For the purification of having slain women of unstable character belonging to any of the four castes, one should separately give a bow of Jina, a bull, and a horse. (11.138)

[“For killing a woman unintentionally, one should perform the penance for killing a Śūdra, provided she belongs to one of the three [higher] castes in their respective order and there is no distinction [of her virtue].

Regarding the word *jīne* (living): having killed women of the Brāhmaṇa and other castes who, out of greed, have committed adultery with superior or inferior men, one should give, in the order of the castes starting with the Brāhmaṇa, a leather bag, a bow, a goat, and a sheep, for the sake of purification. (11.138)

If a twice-born man is unable to expiate the killing of snakes and other such creatures through the giving of gifts, he shall perform a *kṛcchra* penance for each individual creature in order to remove his sin. (11.139)

Regarding the phrase "by means of a gift": since [the poor] lack such things as a spade, a Brāhmaṇa or others who are incapable of removing all sins through a gift must perform a *kṛcchra* penance for each killing; because it is the primary [prescribed penance], the twice-born should perform a *prājāpatya* for the sake of removing sin. And for those other than snakes, all those beginning from "one should give an iron spade" (11.133) up to this point are included. 11.139.
But for the killing of a thousand beings possessing bones,
or for a full cartload of boneless creatures, one should perform the penance prescribed for the murder of a Śūdra.

Regarding the phrase "of those possessing bones": because of their association with boneless creatures, for the killing of a thousand living beings possessing bones, such as lizards and the like, one should perform the penance prescribed for the killing of a Śūdra. And for the killing of boneless creatures, such as bedbugs and the like, when they amount to a cartload, one should perform that same penance. (11.140)
But for killing a vertebrate creature, one should give something to a Brahmin;
indeed, for the injury of boneless creatures, one is purified by a breath-control exercise (prāṇāyāma).

Regarding the phrase "something" (*kiṃcit*): for the killing of each individual small creature possessing bones, such as a chameleon and the like, one should give "something. Since Sumantu records that "for the killing of creatures with bones, a *paṇa* of gold should be given," it should be understood that "something" refers here to a *paṇa*. However, for the killing of each individual boneless creature, such as lice, bedbugs, and so forth, one becomes pure through a *prāṇāyāma*. And a *prāṇāyāma* is defined as follows: "One should recite three times the *Sāvitrī* together with the *Vyāhṛtis*, the *Praṇava*, and the *Śiras*, while holding the breath; that is called *prāṇāyāma*."
Thus, one possessing the characteristics described by Vasiṣṭha is to be accepted. 11.141
For cutting down fruit-bearing wolves (wild dogs), one hundred Ṛg-verses should be recited;
likewise for cutting down shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and flowering herbs.

Regarding the phrase "of fruit-bearing [plants]": for each instance of cutting fruit-bearing trees such as the mango, shrubs such as the *kubjaka*, creepers such as *guḍūcī*, climbing plants, and climbing vines—meaning those that cling to tree branches and bear flowers—as well as spreading herbs such as the pumpkin (*kūṣmāṇḍa*), one should recite a hundred verses beginning with the *Sāvitrī* for the sake of liberation from sin. This is because a heavy penance is prescribed for the act of felling green trees for fuel, which is enumerated among the minor sins (*upapātaka*) in the verse beginning, "Felling green trees for the sake of fuel" (11.64). It should be understood that this light penance for cutting fruit-bearing trees and the like applies to a single instance committed unintentionally. (11.142)
For beings born from food, those born from moisture,
and all those produced from fruits and flowers, the consumption of ghee is the complete purification.

Regarding the phrase "of those born from food and the like": for all living beings born from food and similar substances—those produced from juices such as molasses, those originating from fruits such as the *udumbara*, and those arising from flowers such as the *madhūka*—the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is the purification of the sin incurred by killing them. 11.143.
For the unauthorized cutting of cultivated plants or those grown spontaneously in the forest,
one should follow a cow for one day while subsisting on milk alone.

Regarding the phrase "of those grown by cultivation": for plants such as *ṣaṣṭika* rice that have grown after being ploughed, and for wild grains such as *nīvāra* that have arisen spontaneously in the forest, if one cuts them down without purpose, the penance is subsisting on milk. For these offenses, one should follow a cow for one day.
By these vows, indeed, the sin arising from violence—whether committed intentionally or unintentionally—is entirely removed; now hear [the rules] regarding the consumption of forbidden food.

"By these": indeed, by these aforementioned penances, the sin produced by violence—whether committed intentionally or unintentionally—is to be removed. Now, listen to the penance for eating forbidden food, which is about to be described. 11.145.

Having drunk *vāruṇī* through ignorance, one is purified by the sacramental rite alone; but for intentional drinking, it is beyond prescription—the established rule is that it ends with life. (11.146)

Regarding the phrase "through ignorance": because this statement is recorded after an interruption by the section on mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*), it does not concern the primary *paiṣṭī* liquor, but rather other types of intoxicants. In that regard, the statement "as is one, so are all" (YDh 11.94) indicates that the identification of *gauḍī* and *mādhvī* with the primary *surā* is intended to establish a greater severity of penance for a Brāhmaṇa compared to other liquors. Therefore, having unintentionally drunk *gauḍī* or *mādhvī*, one becomes pure only by performing the *taptakṛcchra* prescribed by Gautama followed by a re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*). Thus says Gautama: "For unintentional drinking of intoxicants, [one should consume] milk, clarified butter, water, or air daily for a *taptakṛcchra*; thereafter, his consecration [is performed]" (GDh 24.1). This very point has been explained in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
O lord of men, if one drinks liquor made from molasses or honey unintentionally,
the performance of the *taptakṛcchra* penance shall be as prescribed by Gautama.

However, regarding the intentional drinking of liquor made from flour (*paiṣṭī*) or other types of intoxicants, the limit of the scriptural law is that "it is incurable even unto death. Likewise, because the drinking of *gauḍī* and *mādhvī* liquors when done knowingly is forbidden as leading to death and because they are more serious than other intoxicants, Manu himself has prescribed the penance: "Or he may eat grain-particles for a year" (11.92). For this very reason, in the case of the intentional drinking of *gauḍī* and *mādhvī*, the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* states: "Or, in this very matter, one should apply the rule of Manu:
'Or he may eat grain-particles for a year, or [eat] oil-cake once at night.'"
"Clad in hair-cloth, with matted locks and carrying a banner, for the purpose of removing the sin of drinking *surā*.

Regarding the drinking of each of the nine types of intoxicants mentioned by Pulastya—excluding *vaiṣṭī*, *gauḍī*, and *mādhvī*—such as *pānasā* and so forth, because they are minor offenses, it is appropriate for a Brāhmaṇa to perform only a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) or some other light expiation. However, in the case of intentionally drinking *pānasā* or similar intoxicants, [the rule is]:
"O Guha, when drinking *surā* is performed intentionally and with full knowledge..."
The Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra penances are indeed required for the rite of re-consecration.
Thus ends the [account] from the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa; other various [details] have been stated by other sages. 11.146.
Having drunk water that has been kept in a vessel for *surā* or likewise in a container for intoxicants,
one should drink milk infused with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for five nights.

Regarding the term *apaḥ*: having drunk water that is free from the taste and smell of liquor, which has been placed in a vessel for *paiṣṭī* liquor or in a vessel for other types of intoxicants, one should consume milk boiled with the herb called *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, but not water. This is because of the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) of Baudhāyana: "One should subsist for three days on milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī*"; [according to this, one should drink it] for five nights. Since heavy and light penances are prescribed everywhere for both *surā* and *madya*, the application of these rules here must be reconciled according to distinctions such as whether the act was intentional or unintentional. Medhātithi says: "The penance must be determined exactly as stated in the scriptural injunction."
Having touched or given liquor, or having accepted it according to rule,
and having drunk water left over by a Śūdra, one should drink water infused with Kuśa grass for three days.

"Having touched," etc. Having touched *surā*, having given [it], and having accepted [it] after first reciting the *svastivācana* blessing, as well as having drunk water left over by a Śūdra—because of the inclusion of the word "having accepted"—a Brāhmaṇa shall drink water boiled with *darbha* grass for three days. (11.148)
But a Brāhmaṇa who has drunk Soma, having smelled the breath of one who has drunk liquor, becomes purified by suppressing his breath three times in water and consuming clarified butter. 11.149.

"But a Brāhmaṇa," and so forth. Furthermore, a Brāhmaṇa who has performed the Soma sacrifice, having smelled the odor associated with the mouth of a liquor-drinker, becomes purified by performing three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) while immersed in water and consuming clarified butter.
Having unintentionally swallowed feces, urine, or anything touched by liquor, the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the rite of regeneration again. (11.150)

"Out of ignorance": since pigs and other such animals will be mentioned later (11.154), if the three twice-born castes unintentionally consume human urine or feces, or food and other liquids that have come into contact with *madya* or *surā* liquor, they deserve to undergo re-initiation (*punar-upanayana*). 11.150.
Shaving the head, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the religious observances—
all these are dispensed with for the twice-born upon the performance of the rite of re-consecration.

Regarding "shaving": shaving the head, wearing a girdle, carrying a staff, and the various vows consisting of begging for alms—all these penances involving the avoidance of honey, meat, and women, do not apply to the twice-born during a second initiation. || 11.151 ||
But having eaten the food of those whose food should not be eaten, or the leavings of women and Śūdras,
or having consumed forbidden meat, one should drink barley-gruel for seven nights.

Regarding the phrase "of those whose food is not to be eaten": having eaten the food of those described as "one should not eat at the sacrifice of one who is not a Śrotriya" (4.205) and so forth, one should drink barley—having rendered it fit for drinking in the form of groats mixed with water or in the form of gruel—for seven nights. In this very same context, an expiation has been stated in the fourth chapter: "Having eaten intentionally, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance" (4.222); this [present rule] is an alternative to that. And the choice between alternatives depends on the capacity of the agent. Likewise, having eaten the leavings of women of the twice-born castes or the leavings of a Śūdra, one should do exactly this. Similarly, having eaten forbidden meat, one should do this very thing, rather than the specific expiation prescribed by the verse beginning "of carnivorous beasts, pigs, and camels" (11.153). 11.152.
Even after drinking fermented acids and astringent decoctions, though they are purifying, a twice-born man remains impure as long as he has not passed wind. (11.153)

Regarding the term "sour things" (*śuktāni*): those substances which are naturally sweet or of other tastes, but through the influence of time and the transformation by water and so forth, attain a state of acidity—these are "sour things. As for astringent decoctions such as those of *vibhītaka* and others, even though they are not specifically prohibited, a person remains impure as long as he has drunk them and they have not yet been digested. (11.153)
Having consumed the urine or excrement of a village pig, a donkey, a camel, a jackal, a monkey, or a crow, a twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

Regarding the term *viḍvarāha* (village-pig): if a twice-born man eats the urine or excrement of a village pig, a donkey, a camel, a jackal, a monkey, or a crow, he should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance as a means of purification. As for the rule stating, "A mushroom and a village-pig" (5.19), which prescribes the Taptakṛcchra for the intentional consumption of a village-pig or a village-cock, there is no contradiction, as they refer to different cases. (11.154)
Having eaten dried meats, mushrooms growing from the earth,
or any meat from a slaughterhouse that was not known [to be pure], one should observe this very same vow.

Regarding the term "dried up": one should recognize as slayers of Brahmins those who, having eaten flesh dried by wind and other elements, eat mushrooms produced from the earth and so forth— those who consume mushrooms whether they grow from the ground or from trees.

Thus, because even the meat of a tree-dweller (a deer) is prohibited by Yama; or, that which was not known as edible or non-edible—such as the meat of a deer or the meat of a donkey—and likewise that which has been brought from a slaughterhouse (*sūnā*), a place of violence: having eaten such, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance alone. (11.155)
For eating the flesh of carnivorous animals, pigs, camels, and cocks, as well as that of humans,
crows, and donkeys, the *taptakṛcchra* penance is the means of purification.

Regarding the term *kravyāda* ("flesh-eater"): for those who eat raw meat—namely, the village pig, the camel, and the village cock, as well as humans, crows, and donkeys—the penance for intentionally eating their flesh is the *taptakṛcchra*, which will be described later. As for the village pig and the cock, their consumption through intentional repetition is stated in the fifth chapter to result in loss of caste (*pātitya*); that has been explained as referring to the case of habitual practice. This present rule, however, concerns the *taptakṛcchra* for a single instance and not for habitual practice; thus there is no contradiction. (11.156)
If a twice-born man who has not yet returned home from his teacher's house should eat food given on the monthly śrāddha occasion,
he shall fast for three days and remain in water for one day.

"Monthly food": if a Brahmin student (brahmacārī) eats food related to a monthly śrāddha—this being an indication for the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha performed prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*—he shall fast for three nights. During those three nights, he should stay in water on one day. (11.157)
But a student who should eat honey or meat in any way whatsoever, having performed the ordinary Kṛcchra penance, shall complete the remainder of his vow. || 11.158 ||

Regarding the student (*brahmacārī*): if a student should, out of necessity or in times of distress, eat honey or meat against his will, he shall perform a *prājāpatya* penance and then complete the remainder of the vow of studentship he had undertaken. (11.158)
Having eaten the leavings of a cat, a crow, or a rat, or those of a dog or a mongoose, or food contaminated by hair or insects, one should drink the *brahmasuvarcalā* plant.

Regarding the term *biḍāla*: having learned that food has been defiled by contact with the leavings of a cat, a crow, a mouse, a dog, or a mongoose, or by contact with hair or insects, one should purify it by throwing earth upon it; then, after eating it, one should drink water boiled with *brahmasuvarcalā*.
One who desires purity for oneself must not eat food that is unfit to be consumed.
However, if it has been eaten unknowingly, it should be vomited up or quickly purified by means of purificatory rites. (11.160)

"Unfit for consumption": one who desires his own purity must not eat food that is forbidden. If, however, it has been eaten through negligence, it must be vomited up. If that is impossible, he must quickly purify himself through penances (*prāyaścitta*). In the case of vomiting, the penance is indeed light; but if it was done intentionally, the previously mentioned penance applies. (11.161)
This has been declared as the various rules for the vows regarding the abstention from eating;
now hear the rule for those vows that remove the fault of theft.

"This refers to the following: those penances which are prescribed for eating forbidden food have been declared in various ways. Now, let the rule for those who remove the sin of theft be heard. (11.161)
Having committed thefts of grain, food, or wealth out of desire from the house of one of his own caste, the best of the twice-born is purified by performing the Kṛcchra penance for one year.

Regarding the word "grain": if a Brāhmaṇa, having intentionally committed thefts of wealth from a Brāhmaṇa’s house in the form of grain, cooked food, or other types of sustenance—yet not out of a delusion that they were his own property—and has carried them away, he becomes purified after one year by performing the prescribed penance. This [duration] should be understood as depending on the magnitude [of the act], which in turn depends on factors such as the place, time, quantity of the substance, the status of the owner, and so forth. The same applies in subsequent cases as well.
But for the abduction of human women, as well as fields, houses, wells, tanks, and water, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is prescribed as the purification. (11.163)

Regarding the phrase "of men": for the theft of any one of the following—a man, a woman, a field, or a house—or for the theft of all the water of a well or a pond, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance has been prescribed by Manu and others as the expiation. 11.163.
Having stolen articles of small value from another's house, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance for the sake of self-purification after returning that property. 11.164.

Regarding the phrase "of substances": having committed theft from another's house of substances such as tin, lead, and so forth—which are of little value, of little utility, and for which no specific penance has been mentioned—one should restore that stolen substance to its owner and perform the *sāntapana-kṛcchra* penance to be described hereafter for the sake of self-purification. "The stolen substance must be returned to the owner" is a rule that applies as a supplement to all penances for theft. (11.164)

For the theft of food that is chewed or eaten, as well as vehicles, beds, and seats, and for flowers, roots, and fruits, the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is the means of purification.

Regarding the phrase "having consumed": for the theft of each of the following—edibles such as sweetmeats (*modaka*), foods such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*), vehicles such as carts (*śakaṭa*), beds, seats, and flowers, roots, and fruits—the drinking of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) is the purification.
For grass, wood, trees, dried food, molasses,
clothing, leather, and meat, there shall be a fast of three nights.

Regarding the word "tṛṇa" (grass): upon stealing even one of these—grass, wood, trees, dry food such as rice and the like, or cloth, leather, or meat—one should observe a fast for three nights. (11.166)
For gems, pearls, corals, copper, silver, iron,
bell-metal, and stones, one should subsist on grains for twelve days.

Regarding "gems" (maṇi): for the theft of each of the following—gems, pearls, coral, copper, silver, iron, bronze, and stones—one should subsist on grains of rice for twelve days. In all these cases, one must effect an equalization of the offense by considering the capacity [of the perpetrator] and the relative excellence or inferiority of the object stolen, taking into account factors such as whether the act was a first-time occurrence or a repetition, the place and time, the nature of the substance, and the status of the owner. 11.167.
For cotton, silk, wool, animals with cloven hooves, and those with uncloven hooves, for birds, perfumes, medicinal herbs, and rope, one must subsist on milk alone for three days.

Regarding the verse beginning with *kārpāsa*: for stealing garments made of cotton, silk, or wool; for two-hoofed or single-hoofed animals such as cows, horses, and the like; for birds such as parrots and others; for fragrant substances such as sandalwood and the like; and for ropes—for the theft of each of these, one shall subsist on milk for three days. Here too, as before, the avoidance of inequality in the subject matter is achieved by the fact that the penance remains uniform despite the superior or inferior nature of the items stolen, and because of the scriptural injunction regarding the restoration of the property to its owner. (11.168)
By these vows, a twice-born man may remove the sin committed through theft;
however, he shall expel the sin of approaching those who should not be approached by means of these same vows.

"By these": by these aforementioned penances, a twice-born man shall remove the sin produced by theft; however, he shall expiate the sin caused by approaching those who should not be approached by means of the vows that will be described hereafter. 11.169.

Having emitted semen into women of his own lineage, into the wives of a friend or a son, or into virgins and women of the lowest castes, he shall perform the vow for violating the Guru’s bed. (11.170)

Regarding the vow for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpavrata*): having discharged semen into each of the following—women of one's own kin (sisters born of the same womb), wives of friends, wives of sons, virgins, and *caṇḍāla* women—one must perform the penance prescribed for approaching the Guru’s wife. In these cases as well, depending on factors such as the presence of knowledge, repetition, and other attendant circumstances, the penance may culminate in death. Therefore, it is said:
"Having discharged semen into virgins, *caṇḍāla* women, and women of other castes, as well as into the children or wives of one's *sapiṇḍa* relatives, the abandonment of life is ordained."
Thus was that vow, ending in death, taught by Yama out of ignorance. 11.170.
Having approached a daughter of his father’s sister, a daughter of his mother’s sister, or a daughter of his mother’s brother, he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (11.171)

Regarding the term *paitṛṣvaseyīm*: having approached the daughter of one's father’s sister or mother’s sister—that is, a paternal aunt or maternal aunt—as well as the daughter of one’s mother’s uterine brother, who is like a sister, and for whom intercourse is forbidden, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; this applies to a single instance of unintentional transgression, as the offense is minor. (11.171)
A wise man, however, should not take these three as wives; they are not to be approached because of their kinship, for by marrying them he falls low. (11.172)

"These women" refers to these three, beginning with the daughter of one's father's sister, whom a wise man should not marry for the purpose of taking her as a wife. Because they are kinswomen and blood relatives, they should not be approached. For by approaching—meaning by marrying—these women, one goes to hell. Although the prohibition is already established by the rule "she who is not a sapinda of the mother" (3.5), this statement is repeated to strengthen the prohibition in view of the customs observed among the people of the South. 11.172.
Having discharged semen into non-human females, into a woman in her courses, into those who are not the proper womb, or indeed into water, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance. (11.173)

"Regarding non-human females": this refers to mares and the like, but not to cows, because Śaṅkha, Likhita, and others have prescribed a heavy penance for one who has "emitted semen among cows," stating that he must perform the *pāyāpatya* penance for a year. Likewise, having discharged semen into a woman during her menstrual period, or into a woman other than through the vagina, or by discharging semen into water, a man shall perform the *sāntapana* *kṛcchra*. (11.173)
But having engaged in sexual intercourse with a man or a woman, a twice-born man shall perform a bath with his clothes on in a bullock cart, in water, or during the daytime. (11.174)

Regarding the term *maithunam*: having engaged in sexual intercourse with a woman in any place whatsoever, or having engaged in sexual intercourse with a woman while in a cow-drawn vehicle, a cart, or the like, or in water, or during the daytime, one should bathe while still wearing one's clothes. (11.174)

By approaching women of the Caṇḍāla or other lowest castes, or by eating their food, or by accepting gifts from them, a Brahmin falls [from his status] through ignorance; but through knowledge, he becomes equal [to them]. (11.175)

Regarding the term *caṇḍāla*: if a Brāhmaṇa, out of ignorance, approaches the women of Caṇḍālas, of those born of the lowest castes (*antyaja*), or of Mlecchas and similar groups, eats their food, or accepts gifts from them, he falls from his status (*patati*). For one who has fallen, he must perform penance (*prāyaścitta*). This [penance] applies to cases of eating and accepting gifts when the act is repeated or involves a heavy offense. However, if he intentionally approaches their women, he attains equality with them. This [latter statement] is intended to emphasize the severity of the penance. (11.175)
A husband shall confine a corrupt wife in a single room;
she must perform that same penance which is prescribed for a man regarding another's wife.

"Vipraduṣṭām" means one who is especially corrupted; that is to say, one who has committed adultery intentionally. The husband shall restrain his wife—having turned her away from her duties—he should keep her in a single house as if she were bound in fetters. And whatever penance is prescribed for a man for approaching the wife of another of his own caste, that very same he shall cause her to perform. Consequently, the statement made by Vasiṣṭha and others, that "half [of the penance] should be assigned to women," must be applied in cases of adultery committed unintentionally. (11.176)
If, however, she should become corrupted again while being restrained by a husband of equal status,
the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances are prescribed for her purification.

Regarding the phrase "if she": if that woman, having once committed adultery with a man of her own caste and performed the penance, should again engage in intercourse with him when solicited by him, then for her, Manu and others have prescribed the Prājāpatya, the Kṛcchra, and the Cāndrāyaṇa as penances. (11.177)
Whatever sin a twice-born man incurs by consorting with a Vṛṣalī for a single night, he removes that by subsisting on alms and constantly reciting prayers for three years. (11.178)

Regarding the word "yad" (which): here, "vṛṣalī" refers to a Caṇḍālī woman, due to the severity of the penance. Whatever sin a Brāhmaṇa incurs by approaching a Caṇḍālī woman in a single night, he removes that by subsisting on alms and constantly reciting the Sāvitrī and other mantras for three years. Thus says Āpastamba: "The dark-complexioned Brāhmaṇa who serves a [Caṇḍālī] woman incurs through her the same sin that he would incur in a single night. By eating at every fourth mealtime, reciting sacred texts, and living on alms, he dispels that sin in three years. (ĀpDh 1.27.11)
Medhātithi, however, has explained it in this very manner; Govindarāja, on the other hand, states that this is the penance for approaching a Śūdra woman whom one married out of order. 11.178.
This expiation has been declared for all four types of evildoers;
now hear these expiations for those who have associated with the outcasts. || 11.179 ||

"This" refers to the purification declared for these four types of evildoers: those who commit violence, eat forbidden food, steal, or have sexual intercourse with women who should not be approached. Now, listen to these purifications that will be described for those who associate directly with such evildoers. 11.179.
One becomes an outcast by associating with an outcast for a year through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, or marriage; but not by sharing a vehicle, a seat, or food.

"By a year": one who practices association with an outcaste—practicing associations consisting of traveling in the same vehicle, sitting on the same seat, or eating in the same row—falls [from his caste] after a year. However, he does not fall from his caste by officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*), teaching (*adhyāpana*), or matrimonial alliance (*yauna*) after a year; rather, the meaning is that he falls immediately. Here, "teaching" refers to the instruction of the *Sāvitrī* following the initiation (*upanayana*). And Devala (34) states that officiating at sacrifices and so forth cause immediate loss of caste: "Officiating at sacrifices, matrimonial alliance, Vedic study, and eating together..."
Having done so, these fall immediately with the outcast; of this there is no doubt.
Viṣṇu:
One who associates with an outcast for a year becomes an outcast;
however, through the habitual practice of sharing a vehicle or a seat, or through marriage, one indeed becomes so immediately.
Baudhāyana says:
"One falls by associating with a fallen person for a year;
[one does not fall] immediately through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, or marriage, but not through sharing a bed or a seat."

Govindarāja, however, explains that while the three acts beginning with officiating at sacrifices cause loss of caste (*pātitya*) within one year, sitting on the same seat and so forth are minor offenses; therefore, they do not result in loss of caste after one year, but rather after that period has elapsed.
Our own commentary on the *Manu-smṛti* follows the interpretation of the sages;
we do not conform to this construction of Govindarāja.
Whichever of these [sinners] a man associates with by falling in with him, he must perform that very person's vow for the sake of purification from that association. (11.181)

Regarding the phrase "whoever with whom": this word *patita* refers to those who have committed sins, as it is applied without distinction to all sinners. Among these fallen persons, whoever enters into the aforementioned association with whichever sinner, he shall perform that very person's vow-like expiation (*prāyaścitta*), but not the penance ending in death (*maraṇāntika*). Furthermore, even that vow being performed by the associate must be carried out without the [original] sin, such as "the slayer of a Brahmin for twelve years" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.172). And thus Vyāsa says: "Whoever associates with another for a year, he too shall attain equality with him."
That twice-born man shall also perform the specific vow for each of those offenses, reduced by one quarter.

The sapinda relatives and kinsmen must perform the water-libation for one who has fallen from his caste outside the village on an inauspicious day, in the evening, in the presence of his agnates, officiating priests, and teachers. (11.182)

Regarding the phrase "of one who has fallen": for an outcaste (mahāpātakin) who has died while still alive, the water-rite (udakakriyā) must be performed outside the village by the sapindas and samānodakas in the presence of kinsmen, officiating priests, and teachers, on the ninth lunar day—which is empty—at the end of the day, according to the method to be described hereafter. 11.182.
A female slave should overturn a water-pot full of water with her foot as if for a dead person;
the impurity shall last for a day and a night along with the kinsmen.

"A female slave" (dāsī): A female slave employed by a sapinda or a samānodaka shall, facing south, kick with her foot a water-filled jar so that it becomes empty of water, as if for a deceased person. Thereafter, those sapindas, together with the samānodakas, shall observe impurity (aśauca) for one day and night. || 11.183 ||

From that point on, however, they should desist from conversing with him or sitting together with him, as well as from the granting of his inheritance and even ordinary social intercourse. || 11.184 ||

"They shall cease": therefore, for those who are sapinda relations of one who has fallen (patita), conversation with him, sitting together on the same seat, the giving of his inheritance, and worldly dealings such as invitations to annual rites and the like—these shall cease. 11.184.
The status of being the eldest shall cease, as well as the wealth obtainable by the eldest;
