however, the younger brother who is superior in virtue shall receive the portion of the eldest. (11.185)

Regarding the phrase "the status of the eldest": that duty which belongs to the eldest, such as rising from one's seat to greet him, is not to be performed by him; nor is the wealth obtainable by the eldest—such as the twentieth part of the estate as an extra share (*uddhāra*)—to be given to him. Although the prohibition of the extra share is already established by the very prohibition of giving the inheritance, it is restated here so that the younger brother may obtain it. That wealth belonging to the eldest, including the portion of the extra share, is obtained by the younger brother if he is superior in virtue. (11.185)
But when the penance has been performed, they should bathe in a sacred body of water and together with him cast a new jar full of water into it.

Regarding the term *prāyaścitta*: once the penance has been performed by the outcaste, his *sapiṇḍas* and *samānodakas* shall bathe together with him—now that he has completed the penance—in a pure reservoir of water and then cast a new jar filled with water [into it]. Here, because of the mention of a "new jar," it is understood that this is not the same jar used for the purpose mentioned in verse 11.183, "A female slave [carrying] a jar. (11.186)
Having thrown that jar into the water and entered his own home,
he should perform all the ancestral rites for his kinsmen as he did before.

"He, however" means: he who has performed the penance, having thrown that previously mentioned jar into the midst of water and then entered his own home, should perform all the ancestral rites for his kin as before. || 11.187 ||
In this very same manner, one should act toward women who have fallen from their status;
however, clothing, food, and drink must be given to them, and they should dwell near the house. 11.188.

"In this same manner": even in the case of women who have become outcasts (*patita*), the group of *sapiṇḍas* and *samānodakas* beginning with the husband should perform the same ritual injunctions, such as "the water-libation for the outcast must be performed" (11.182). Furthermore, food and clothing should be given to them, and they should provide a small hut near their house for their residence. (11.188)
One should not associate in any way with those who have committed sins and have not been purified; yet, once they have undergone purification, one should never despise them. (11.189)

"With those who have committed sins" means that one should not perform any activity, such as giving gifts or receiving them, together with evildoers who have not performed expiation. One should never revile those who have performed expiation on account of their previous sins; rather, one should deal with them as before. (11.189)

He states an exception to this: "One should not live together with those who kill children, those who are ungrateful, even if they are pure according to the Dharma, nor with those who kill one who has sought refuge, nor with those who kill women. (11.190)

"Killers of children": one who has killed a child; one who, by committing an injury, has destroyed someone who had previously rendered assistance; one who has killed someone who came for the sake of protecting his life; and one who has caused the death of a woman—one should not dwell in association with these, even if they have duly performed their penance. (11.190)
Those twice-born men for whom the Sāvitrī has not been recited according to the rule,
one should cause them to perform three Kṛcchra penances and then initiate them according to the rule.

Regarding the phrase "of those": for those Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas whose initiation (*upanayana*) was not performed according to the scriptures during the prescribed secondary period (*ānukalpika-kāla*), one should have them perform three *prājāpatya* penances and then initiate them according to the scriptures. As for the expiations such as the *vrātyastoma* sacrifice mentioned by Yājñavalkya and others, one should consider this [present rule] alongside them, weighing their relative severity and lightness, and understand that there is an option depending on factors such as caste and capability. (11.191)
This same penance one should prescribe even for those twice-born men who, having engaged in forbidden acts and being abandoned by the Veda, desire to perform expiation. (11.192)

Regarding the penance: those twice-born men who have served forbidden Śūdras—even if they have been initiated but have not studied the Veda—if they desire to perform a penance, for them also one should prescribe these three [penances] beginning with the Prājāpatya. (11.192)
Whatever wealth Brāhmaṇas acquire through a censurable act, they become purified by its renunciation, as well as by the recitation of sacred texts and by austerity. (11.193)

Regarding the word "yat" (which): by the renunciation of that wealth which Brāhmaṇas acquire through censurable acts—such as forbidden or improper acceptance of gifts—they are purified by means of recitation (*japa*) and austerity (*tapas*), which will be described hereafter. Since the rule for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is prescribed through the renunciation of wealth, it is logical that the same expiation is declared whether one has accepted something of great value, such as an elephant or a horse, or something of little value, such as iron and the like. The same applies to the sale of items that should not be sold. (11.193)
Having recited three thousand repetitions of the Sāvitrī mantra with a concentrated mind,
and having drunk only milk for a month in a cow-pen, they are liberated from the sin of accepting improper gifts.

Regarding the phrase "having muttered": having muttered three thousand repetitions of the Sāvitrī, one becomes freed from the sin produced by accepting gifts from the unworthy while subsisting on milk for a month in a cow-pen. This same penance applies even to the acceptance of gifts from a Śūdra and so forth, because there is no difference in the censurability of the acceptance itself, whether due to the defect of the object or the defect of the giver. (11.194)
But when he has returned from the cow-pasture, emaciated by his fasts and bowing before them, they should ask him: "O gentle one, do you desire equanimity? (11.195)

Regarding "fasting": when he has returned from the cow-pen with an emaciated body due to subsisting solely on milk and abstaining from other food, and is bowed down—having become humble—the Brāhmaṇas should question him regarding the Dharma, saying: "Do you desire equality with us? Will you no longer accept improper gifts? || 11.195 ||
Having spoken the truth before the Brahmins, he should scatter fodder for the cows;
when the ford has been established by the cows, they should perform his formal reception there.

"Truth," he says: "This is true; furthermore, I shall not accept gifts from the wicked. Having spoken thus to the Brāhmaṇas, he should give fodder to the cows. Since that place where the grass is being eaten has been purified by the cows, it becomes a sacred site (*tīrtha*); thereupon, the Brāhmaṇas may accept his transactions. (11.196)

Having performed a sacrifice for Vratyas, or having performed the funeral rites for others, or having practiced malevolent magic (abhicāra) or the Ahīna sacrifice, one removes that sin by means of three Kṛcchra penances.

Regarding the phrase "of the Vrātyas": having performed the *vrātyastoma* and other sacrifices for those Vrātyas who have been described as "these three [classes] from this point forward" (2.39); and having performed the cremation and *śrāddha* rites—which are otherwise forbidden—for those other than one's father, teacher, and so forth; and having performed malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) such as the *śyena* sacrifice; and having performed the *ahīna* sacrifice—a specific type of sacrifice, since the scripture states, "Performing the *ahīna* makes one impure"—or having performed its sacrifice for three nights and so forth, one is purified by three *kṛcchra* penances. || 11.197 ||
Having abandoned one who has sought refuge or having caused the Veda to be corrupted, a twice-born man removes that sin by subsisting on barley for one year.

"Regarding 'one who has come for refuge': if a twice-born man, being capable, neglects one who has approached him for protection, he incurs the sin of not teaching the Veda; and that sin he removes by subsisting on barley for one year. (11.198)
One who has been bitten by a dog, a jackal, or a donkey, or by domestic carnivorous animals,
as well as by humans, horses, camels, or pigs, becomes pure through breath control (prāṇāyāma).

[For that which has been smelled by a dog, licked, torn by teeth, or washed with water, purification by fire is prescribed. Regarding "by dogs, jackals, etc.": one who has been bitten by domestic animals such as dogs, jackals, donkeys, humans, horses, boars, and the like, or by wild animals such as cats and so forth, is purified by breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*). 11.199.
Eating only at the sixth mealtime for a month, or the constant recitation of the *Saṃhitā*,
as well as daily *Śākala* oblations, are the means of purification for those excluded from the company at meals (*apāṅktyas*).

Regarding the phrase "not from the sixth": those who are excluded from the company at meals (*apāṅktya*), such as those mentioned in the verse beginning "those who are thieves, outcasts, or eunuchs" (3.150), for whom no specific penance has been prescribed, must perform the following: for one month, they should eat only on the third day, eating only in the evening; they must recite the Vedic *saṃhitā*; and they must perform oblations (*homa*) with each of the mantras beginning with "Thou art the expiation for the sin committed against the gods" (VS 8.13). This is what is designated as purification through giving (*dānaśodhana*). || 11.200 ||
Having mounted a camel-carriage or, out of desire, a donkey-carriage,
a Brahmin who is naked after bathing becomes pure through breath control (prāṇāyāma).

"Camel-vehicle" refers to a cart or similar conveyance yoked with camels; the same applies to a donkey-vehicle. Having intentionally mounted such a vehicle without any intervening interval, one becomes purified by many breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*); likewise, having intentionally bathed while naked, one becomes pure through breath-restraint. (11.201)
If one is afflicted while away from water or even within water, one becomes pure by arranging the bodily excretions, then bathing outside with one's clothes on and touching a cow. 11.202.

He shall undergo purification. Having voided urine or feces in water that lacks living beings, or in the midst of water while overcome by urgency, he becomes pure by bathing outside the village with his clothes on in a river or similar body of water, and by touching a cow. (11.202)
In the event of transgressing the duties prescribed by the Vedas, or in the case of violating the vows of a *snātaka*, the penance is fasting. (11.203)

He experiences [the consequences]. When there is an omission of Vedic rites such as the Agnihotra and others for which no specific expiation has been prescribed, or when there is a transgression of the Snātaka vows mentioned in the fourth chapter, one should perform a fast for one day as the expiation.
Having addressed a Brāhmaṇa with "huṃ" or an elder with "thou," one should bathe and, fasting for the remainder of the day, seek their favor by offering salutations.

Regarding the word *huṃkāram*: having issued the challenge to the Brahmin with the sound "Huṃ! Be silent!", and having addressed one who is superior in learning with the term "thou," he should, from the time of the greeting until the end of the day, appease his anger by bathing, refraining from food, and clasping the [teacher's] feet. 11.204.
Having struck him even with a blade of grass, or having bound him by the neck with a cloth,
or having defeated him in a dispute, one should propitiate him by bowing down.

"Having struck," etc.: Having struck even a common Brahmin with a blade of grass, or having bound him by the neck or with a cloth, or having defeated him in a verbal dispute, one should propitiate him by prostrating. 11.205.
Having merely threatened a Brahmin, one enters hell for a hundred years; having struck him, for a thousand years; and by the mere intent to kill a Brahmin, one likewise falls into hell. || 11.206 ||

Regarding the term "having threatened": by raising a staff with the intent to kill a Brāhmaṇa, one attains hell for a hundred years; but by striking him again with that staff or similar weapon, one attains hell for a thousand years. (11.205)
For as many particles of dust as the blood collects upon the surface of the earth,
for that many thousands of years shall the perpetrator dwell in hell.

Regarding "blood": for as many particles of dust as one collects from the ground after striking a Brahmin and causing his blood to flow, for that many thousands of years shall the shedder of that blood dwell in hell. (11.207)
Having threatened [a Brahmin], one should perform the Kṛcchra penance; for striking him down, the Atikṛcchra.
Having caused blood to flow from a Brahmin, one should perform both the Kṛcchra and the Atikṛcchra.

He understands: if one raises a staff or similar weapon with the intent to kill a Brāhmaṇa, he shall perform a *kṛcchra* penance; if a blow with a staff or the like has been dealt, he shall perform an *atikṛcchra*, as will be described; and having caused blood to flow, he shall perform both a *kṛcchra* and an *atikṛcchra*. (11.208)
But for the removal of sins for which no expiation has been stated, one should prescribe an atonement after considering both the capacity [of the offender] and the nature of the sin. (11.209)

Regarding the phrase "unspoken": for those cases where no expiation has been specifically mentioned—such as the killing of those born in the inverse order (pratiloma) and so forth—one should determine the expiation by considering the body and wealth of the perpetrator according to his capacity, and by discerning the nature of the sin in terms of whether it was intentional or unintentional, whether it was a single occurrence or repeated, and its attendant circumstances. || 11.209 ||
I shall describe to you those means, practiced by gods, sages, and ancestors, by which a human being removes his sins. 11.210
"By which"—I shall tell you those causes for the destruction of sin, by which causes a human being dispels evil deeds, and which have been practiced by the gods, sages, and ancestors. 11.210.

For three days he should eat in the morning, for three days in the evening, for three days he should eat food given unasked, and for the next three days he should not eat at all; thus a twice-born man performs the Prājāpatya penance. (11.211)

Regarding the phrase "for three days": a twice-born person performing the *kṛcchra* penance known as *prājāpatya* should eat only in the morning for the first three days. This term "morning" (*prātaḥ*) refers to the time of day appropriate for meals. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha states: "He eats during the day for three days, eats at night for three days, and observes the vow of not begging for food for three days; thus is the *kṛcchra*. Āpastamba also says: "He eats only at night for three days, then eats only during the day for three days, observes the vow of not begging for food for three days, and does not eat anything at all for three days"; such is the rule for the twelve-night *kṛcchra*. Furthermore, for another three days he should eat after the evening twilight has passed. For the next three days he should eat only food that is unasked for. And for the remaining three days he should not eat anything at all. Regarding the required number of mouthfuls (*grāsa*) here, Parāśara says:
In the evening, thirty-two mouthfuls; likewise, twenty-six in the morning;
twenty-four when food is unasked for; and fasting thereafter is prescribed as the highest.
One should know that a mouthful (grāsa) is the size of a hen’s egg, or as much as can enter the mouth; this is the purification of the mouthful for the sake of purity.
He should eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) both by night and by day,
taking three mouthfuls at a time for three days, as prescribed by the scriptures.
Likewise, one should eat only what is unasked for; this constitutes a three-day fast.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass, followed by a fast for one night—this is known as the *sāntapana* penance. (11.212)

Regarding the term *gomūtra*: having combined cow’s urine and the other substances, one should consume them on each successive day and eat nothing else; on the following day there is a fast—this is known as the *sāntapana* penance. However, when one consumes each of the six substances, beginning with cow’s urine, for six days respectively and observes a fast on the seventh day, then it becomes the *mahāsāntapana*. Thus says Yājñavalkya: "Having consumed water boiled with *kuśa* grass, cow’s milk, curd, urine, dung, and ghee, one should fast on the next day while performing the *sāntapana* penance."

"A six-day period with each of the *sāntapana* substances separately, followed by a day of fasting— this seven-day rite is known as the *mahāsāntapana*. (YDh 3.314) One should eat a single morsel for three three-day periods, as previously described.
And while performing the Atikṛcchra penance, the twice-born man should fast for the final three days.

"Each single one": while performing the *atikṛcchra* penance, a twice-born man should consume one morsel each in the morning, evening, and as an unasked meal (*ayācita*), three times for three days each as before; furthermore, for another three days he should not eat anything at all. (11.213)
A Brahmin performing the *taptakṛcchra* penance should drink hot water, milk, ghee, and air, each for three days, bathing once daily and remaining composed. (11.214)

Regarding the term *taptā*: while performing the *taptakṛcchra* penance, a twice-born person, being self-restrained and bathing only once a day, should drink hot water for three days, hot milk for three days, hot clarified butter for three days, and [inhale] hot air for three days. In this regard, there is a specific detail stated by Parāśara: "One should drink six *palas* of water, three *palas* of milk, and one *pala* of clarified butter; this is prescribed as the *taptakṛcchra*."
For one who is self-restrained and vigilant, fasting for twelve days is this penance called Parāka, which removes all sins. (11.215)

Regarding the phrase "of one who has restrained the self": for one whose lack of attentiveness has departed and whose senses are controlled, fasting for twelve days is the penance known as *parāka*; through its repetition in varying degrees, it removes sins that yield heavy, light, or middling fruits.
One should decrease the morsel by one each day during the dark fortnight and increase it during the bright fortnight;
touching water at the three periods of the day, this is known as the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.

"One by one" means: performing his ablutions at dawn, noon, and dusk, he should eat fifteen morsels on the full moon day; thereafter, he should decrease the morsels one by one in the sequence of the first day of the dark fortnight, so that on the fourteenth day there remains only one morsel. Then, having fasted on the new moon day, he should increase the morsels one by one starting from the first day of the bright fortnight. Thus, fifteen morsels are completed on the full moon day. This is known as the *cāndrāyaṇa* called "ant-like" (*pipīlikāmadhya*). (11.216)
One who performs the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, being self-restrained from the beginning of the bright fortnight, should carry out this entire procedure in its entirety during the Yavamadhyama variety. (11.217)

"Etam" (this): one who has controlled the senses, performing the Cāndrāyaṇa, should practice this very rule consisting of the reduction and increase of morsels and bathing at the three periods of the day in the Cāndrāyaṇa known as *yavamadhya* (barley-shaped). Starting from the first day of the bright fortnight, he should increase the morsels by one each day; thus, on the full moon day, fifteen mouthfuls are reached. Then, starting from the first day of the dark fortnight, he should decrease the morsels by one each day, so that there is a fast on the new moon day. (11.217)
Restraining his self and eating sacrificial food, one performing the Yati-Cāndrāyaṇa should eat eight morsels when the sun has reached midday. (11.218)

"Eight": one performing the *yaticāndrāyaṇa* vow, having restrained his senses, should eat eight mouthfuls at midday every day for one month, beginning either with the bright fortnight or the dark fortnight. The term "at midday" is intended to exclude evening meals for householders and students (*brahmacārin*). (11.218)
A Brahmin, with a concentrated mind, should eat four morsels in the morning and four when the sun has set;
this is known as the Śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa.
"Four": one should eat four mouthfuls in the morning, and one should consume four mouthfuls when the sun has set; this is known as the *śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa* by the sages. (11.219)
By eating, with a concentrated mind, three hundred and eighty mouthfuls of sacrificial food (haviṣya) in any manner whatsoever during a month, one attains the same world as Candra.

Regarding the word "yathā" (as): one who, for the duration of a month, eats with self-restraint two hundred and forty mouthfuls of sacrificial food such as wild rice (*nīvāra*) and the like—whether ten, five, sixteen, or even by fasting at times—in whatever manner and without fixed rule, attains the same world as the Moon. This has been stated for the purpose of destroying sin and for the sake of spiritual prosperity; therefore, Yājñavalkya says:
"He who performs this for the sake of dharma attains the same world as the Moon."
But one who performs the Kṛcchra-cāndrāyaṇa with the desire for merit shall attain great prosperity.
Therefore, Yājñavalkya has stated that even the *prājāpatya* and other *kṛcchra* penances yield the fruit of prosperity. 11.220.
The Rudras, as well as the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Maruts, together with the great seers, observed this vow for the sake of liberation from all that is unwholesome.

Regarding the word "this": this vow known as Cāndrāyaṇa was performed by the Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, and Maruts, together with the great seers, for the destruction of all sins, according to the manner of single or repeated performance in consideration of whether the sin was heavy or light. 11.221.
One should personally perform the fire-oblation every day with the Mahāvyāhṛtis;
one should practice non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and straightforwardness. (11.222)

“With the great *vyāhṛtis*”: that is, with these great *vyāhṛtis*, namely *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*. According to the statement in the *Pariśiṣṭa*, “In oblations where no material is specified, clarified butter (*ājya*) is prescribed as the offering,” one should perform the daily oblation with clarified butter. One should also practice non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and freedom from crookedness. Although these are prescribed as duties for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), this instruction is given here as an integral part of the vow (*vrata*). (11.222)
Three times during the day and three times at night, he should enter the water with his clothes on;
nor should he ever speak to women, Śūdras, or outcasts.

"Three times": he should enter the water of a river or other body of water with his clothes on for the purpose of bathing at the beginning, middle, and end of the day and night. This applies to the *pipīlikā-madhya* and *yava-madhya* forms of the *cāndrāyaṇa*, as well as other types of *cāndrāyaṇa*; for regarding those two, it has been stated: "He should perform ritual ablutions three times a day" (6.24). Furthermore, he should never engage in conversation with women, Śūdras, or outcasts for as long as his vow lasts. (11.223)
He should spend his time standing or sitting; if unable, he may lie down on the ground.
He should remain celibate and observant of vows, worshipping his guru, the gods, and the twice-born. || 11.224 ||

Regarding the word "place" (*sthāne*): during the day and at night, he should remain standing or sitting, but not lying down. However, if he lacks the physical strength, he may lie down on the bare ground (*sthaṇḍila*), but not on a bed or similar furniture. He should be a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), observing the vow of abstaining from sexual union with women. He should be one who observes the vows (*vratī*), equipped with the girdle of muñja grass, the staff, and so forth, for Yama’s legal tradition states:
"He should carry a staff made of *pālāśa* wood, and, being pure, wear a girdle of muñja grass. Furthermore, he should be a worshiper of his guru, the gods, and Brahmins. (11.224)
And he should daily recite the Sāvitrī and purificatory texts according to his ability;
in all such vows, he should thus be diligent for the sake of expiation. (11.225)

Regarding the *sāvitrī*: he should always mutter the *sāvitrī*. He should also mutter purificatory texts (*pavitra*), such as the *aghamarṣaṇa* and others, according to his ability. And just as in the *cāndrāyaṇa*, so too in the *prājāpatya* and other *kṛcchra* penances, he should diligently perform these for the sake of expiation.
The twice-born whose sins have been made public shall be purified by these vows;
however, those whose sins have not been made public, one should purify with mantras and burnt offerings. 11.226.

Regarding the word "by these": the twice-born whose sins are known to the world are to be purified by the aforementioned penances through an assembly (pariṣad) that will be described hereafter. However, the assembly itself should purify those men whose sins are not publicly known by means of mantras and burnt offerings (homas). Although the secrecy of the sin is lost when it is reported to the assembly, there is no contradiction in the case of a general inquiry such as, "If a certain sin has been committed by someone without being known by anyone in the world, what would be the appropriate penance? (11.226)
A doer of evil is released from that evil by confession, by remorse, by austerity, and by study; likewise, in times of distress, by giving.

Regarding the phrase "by confession": a man who has committed evil in this world is purified by confessing his own sin and through remorse, thinking, "Fie upon me, a perpetrator of great evil! He is also released from sins by means of severe penance (*tapas*), such as the recitation of the *Sāvitrī* mantra, and so forth. One who is unable to perform penance becomes freed from sins through giving (*dāna*). This confession is a constituent part of public penance (*prakāśaprāyaścitta*) and not a part of secret penance (*rahasyaprāyaścitta*), because that would entail the loss of its secret character. Remorse likewise is a constituent of both public and secret penances. Regarding "through giving," since the *Prājāpatya* vow prescribes one cow, and a cow is worth five or three *purāṇas*, it follows that for the twelve-year vow occasioned by the murder of a Brahmin, there are thirty cows per year—calculated on the basis of two and a half *Prājāpatyas* per month—and thus over twelve years, there are three hundred and sixty cows. (11.227)
To the extent that a man, having himself committed an unrighteous act, confesses it, to that same extent he is freed from that unrighteousness, just as a snake is freed from its skin. || 11.228 ||

"Yathā" means: just as a man, having himself committed a sin, speaks of it and makes it known in the world, so by that very act of confession he is freed from the sin, like a snake shedding its worn-out skin; this is a restatement (anuvāda) of the rule for confession. 11.228.
To the extent that his mind reproaches the evil deed he has committed,
to that same extent is his body released from that unrighteousness.
"Yathā" means: just as the mind of that evildoer censures his evil deed, so too is the body—the living self—liberated from that unrighteousness. This is a restatement of remorse. 11.229.
For by repenting after having committed a sin, one is indeed released from that sin; however, one is purified through desisting with the thought, "I shall not do this again. (11.230)

Regarding the phrase "having done": it has been stated that after committing a sin, one is released from that sin by feeling remorse; this is restated here as "I shall not do so again. However, when remorse results in a resolution (*saṃkalpa*) characterized by cessation—namely, "I will never do this again"—then one becomes even more thoroughly purified from that sin. And this is for the purpose of prescribing both manifest and unmanifest expiations as ancillaries (*aṅga*) to that resolution of cessation. (11.230)
Having thus reflected in his mind upon the arising of the fruits of action after death, he should constantly perform virtuous deeds through his mind, speech, and body. (11.231)

"Thus" means as follows: having reflected with the mind upon how pure and impure actions yield desirable and undesirable fruits in the next world, one should perform only every kind of pure action through mind, speech, and body, because they have desirable fruits; not impure action, because it is the cause of suffering in hell and other realms. (11.231)
Whether through ignorance or through knowledge, having performed a censurable deed, one who seeks liberation from it should not commit it a second time. (11.232)

Regarding the phrase "due to ignorance": having performed a prohibited act through negligence or intentionally, one who desires liberation from that sin should not perform it again. This [prohibition against repetition] is for the purpose of increasing the severity of the penance (*prāyaścitta*) upon such repetition. For this very reason, Devala states: "From this first rule, in the case of a second [offense], it shall be double."
In whatever action he has performed that causes unease of mind, he should perform penance for it until it becomes a source of satisfaction. (11.233)

Regarding the phrase "in which": if, when a particular rite called *prāyaścitta* (expiation) has been performed, there is no satisfaction of the mind for this evildoer, he should repeat that very same expiation until there is satisfaction—that is, clarity—of the mind. (11.233)
All this happiness of gods and men has austerity as its root;
it has been declared by the wise who have seen the Vedas that austerity is its middle and austerity its end.

Regarding "asceticism" (*tapas*): all this happiness belonging to both gods and humans has asceticism as its cause; indeed, its maintenance is through asceticism alone. Asceticism is a fixed internal rule (*pratiniyatavidhi*), so it is declared by those who know the meaning of the Vedas, because the happiness of the gods and others is produced by asceticism. This refers to the asceticism consisting of penances such as the *prājāpatya*, which have been mentioned. And in this context, there is an incidental explanation of the greatness of all forms of asceticism, as well as that which is yet to be described. (11.234)
The austerity of a Brahmin is knowledge; the austerity of a Kshatriya is protection;
the austerity of a Vaishya is trade and agriculture; and the austerity of a Shudra is service. (11.235)

"Of the Brāhmaṇa," etc. For the Brāhmaṇa, the realization of the Vedānta through celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is austerity; for the Kṣatriya, protection is austerity; for the Vaiśya, agriculture, trade, animal husbandry, and so forth, are austerity; and for the Śūdra, service to the Brāhmaṇas is austerity—this is stated for the purpose of indicating excellence according to the specific castes. (11.235)
Sages who have restrained their selves, subsisting on fruits, roots, and air,
behold the three worlds with all that is mobile and immobile through austerity alone.

Regarding the word "sages" (ṛṣayaḥ): Sages are those endowed with the restraint of speech, mind, and body, subsisting on fruits, roots, and air; by means of austerity alone, while remaining in a single location, they clearly perceive the three worlds—consisting of the earth, the intermediate space, and heaven, together with all moving and stationary beings—their internal organs being purified of sin. 11.236.
Medicines, antidotes, knowledge, and the various states of divine power—all these are accomplished through austerity alone; for austerity is their means of attainment.

Regarding "medicines": medicines are the causes for the alleviation of disease. *Agada* is the absence of disease, that is to say, health. *Vidyā* is the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas, consisting of the practice of Brahman and Dharma, as well as various forms of existence in heaven and other realms related to the Vedas; all these are obtained through austerity alone, because austerity is the cause for their attainment. 11.237.

Whatever is difficult to cross, whatever is difficult to attain, whatever is difficult to traverse, and whatever is difficult to accomplish—all that can be achieved through austerity, for austerity is indeed hard to surpass. (11.238)

Regarding the word "yat" (that which): that which is crossed over with difficulty, such as calamities indicated by the influence of planetary afflictions; that which is attained with difficulty, such as the status of a Brahmin by a Kṣatriya and others, as was achieved by Viśvāmitra with that very same body; that which is reached with difficulty, such as the summit of Mount Meru; and that which is performed with difficulty, such as the giving of abundant gifts of cows—all that can be accomplished through austerity (*tapas*). For everything that involves performing extremely difficult tasks is accomplished by austerity; austerity possesses the power to overcome what is otherwise insurmountable. (11.238)
Even those who have committed great sins, as well as others who have performed improper acts, are liberated from that defilement by means of well-performed austerity alone. (11.239)

"Great" (mahat): those who have committed great sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, as well as others who have performed secondary sins (upapātaka) and other improper acts, are liberated from that sin by means of penance performed in the manner described. The repetition of what has already been stated is for the purpose of praising the expiation (prāyaścitta). || 11.239 ||
Insects, snakes, moths, beasts, birds,
and even stationary beings go to heaven by the power of austerity.

"Regarding 'insects' (kīṭāḥ): insects, snakes, locusts, beasts, birds, and stationary beings such as trees and shrubs go to heaven by the greatness of their asceticism (tapas). In the Itihāsas and other texts, in stories such as that of the pigeon, it is heard that even birds perform ascetic penances such as entering the fire. Whatever suffering is innate to the species of insects, that itself is their asceticism; and with their impurities destroyed by that, remaining unchanging, they go to heaven through the merit performed in previous births. (11.240)
Whatever sin people commit through mind, speech, or body, those whose wealth is austerity quickly consume it all by means of austerity alone. (11.241)

"Whatever little... means that whatever small amount of evil humans commit through mind, speech, or body, they burn away all that evil by austerity alone. "Those whose wealth is austerity" (*tapodhana*) refers to those for whom austerity itself is like wealth—something to be protected.
For a Brahmin purified by austerity alone, the denizens of heaven accept his offerings and fulfill his desires. (11.242)

"By austerity alone": the gods accept the sacrificial offerings at the sacrifice of a Brahmin whose sins have been destroyed by the austerity of expiation (prāyaścitta), and they bestow upon him the objects he desires. || 11.242 ||
The Lord Prajāpati created this scripture through austerity alone;
likewise, the seers attained the Vedas through austerity alone.

Regarding the term "Prajāpati": Hiraṇyagarbha, the Lord of the origin, maintenance, and dissolution of all worlds, composed this very text preceded by the performance of austerity. Likewise, the sages such as Vasiṣṭha and others obtained the Vedas, consisting of Mantras and Brāhmaṇas, through austerity alone. 11.243.
Thus the gods proclaim this great majesty of austerity,
perceiving the supreme merit of all this austerity.
“Celibacy, austerity, burnt offerings, eating pure and little food at the proper time, and freedom from passion, hatred, and greed—this is called austerity by the Self-Existent One.

Thus it is said. Seeing that for every living being birth is difficult to obtain through the power of austerity, the gods proclaim the greatness of austerity, beginning with the words: “All this has austerity as its root” (11.234). 11.244.
The daily study of the Vedas according to one's ability, the performance of the great sacrifices, and forbearance quickly destroy even those sins born of the most heinous crimes. (11.245)

Regarding "the study of the Vedas": daily Vedic study according to one's ability, the performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), and forbearance toward offenses—these quickly destroy even those sins produced by mortal transgressions (*mahāpātaka*), let alone others.
Just as fire, by its heat, consumes whatever fuel it encounters in an instant, so does the knower of the Vedas burn away all evil with the fire of knowledge. 11.246

"Yathā" (as): just as fire, by its very heat, completely consumes pieces of wood that have been brought near in a mere moment, so too does the Brāhmaṇa who knows the meaning of the Vedas destroy all evil by the fire of knowledge. This is stated for the purpose of making known the excellence of this supreme self-knowledge in terms of the destruction of evil. 11.246.
Thus has the expiation for these offenses been declared according to the rule;
hereafter, learn the expiation for secret sins.

"Thus this" means: thus has the expiation for public sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa been declared according to the rule. Hereafter, hear the expiation for secret sins. This verse was not written by Govindarāja, but it was indeed written by Medhātithi. (11.247)
Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), accompanied by the Vyahṛtis and the Praṇava, performed day after day, purify even the killer of a learned Brāhmaṇa within a month. (11.248)

"Accompanied by the *vyāhṛtis*": sixteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāmas*) performed daily—consisting of inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*) according to the prescribed method, along with the *Sāvitrī*, the *Śiras*, and the *praṇava*—purify even a slayer of a Brahmin of his sin after one month. By the use of the word "even," it is implied that this applies even to one who is subject to the penance for killing a Brahmin as extended by analogy. Furthermore, this expiation is intended only for the twice-born (*dvijāti*), and not for women, *śūdras*, and others, because they lack the entitlement to use sacred mantras. (11.248)

Having recited the *Kautsa* hymn beginning with "apaḥ," the *Vāsiṣṭha* verse beginning with "pratīcī," the *Māhitra*, and the *Śuddhavatī* verses, even a drinker of spirituous liquor is purified. (11.249)

"Kautsa": the seer Kautsa saw this hymn, "May our sin be burnt away like water" (*RV* 1.7.5); the seer Vasiṣṭha saw this verse, "The Vasiṣṭhas [praise] Uṣas with their hymns" (*RV* 5.5.27); the Māhitra hymn, "May there be the protection of the great ones" (*RV* 8.8.43); and the Śuddhavatī verses, these three verses beginning with "Come, let us praise Indra, the pure one" (*RV* 6.6.31). Having recited these every day for the month under discussion, even a drinker of *surā* becomes purified. By the use of the word "even" (*api*), it is implied that even one who is subject to the penance for drinking *surā* by extension is included. (11.249)
By reciting the Āsyavāmīya and the Śivasaṃkalpa even once,
one who has stolen gold becomes stainless in an instant.

Regarding the word "once": having stolen gold, a Brāhmaṇa should recite this hymn, "Of this lovely, grey-haired one" (RV 2.3.14), once daily for one month because it is the subject at hand; and having recited the Śivasaṃkalpa, which is read in the Vājasaneyaka as "That which [is far from] the waking state" (VS 34.1), he becomes instantly free from sin after having stolen the gold. || 11.250 ||
Having repeatedly recited the *Haviṣpāntīya* and the hymn beginning with "na taṃ ha," and having chanted the *Puruṣasūkta*, one who has violated the Guru's bed is liberated from that sin.

Regarding the *Haviṣpāntīya*: one should recite nineteen verses beginning with “*haviṣpāntam ajaraṃ svarvidi*” (RV 8.4.10), eight verses beginning with “*na tam aṃho na duritam*” (RV 2.6.29), the hymn known as the *Śivasankalpa* beginning with “*iti vā iti me manaḥ*” (RV 8.6.26), and this sixteen-verse hymn beginning with “*sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ*” (RV 10.90.1). Since there is a scriptural injunction that one should practice these daily for one month, and because they are the subject under discussion, by reciting them sixteen times, even a violator of his teacher’s wife is liberated from that sin. (11.251)
Desiring to remove gross and subtle sins, one should recite for a year either the verse beginning with "aveti" or the verse beginning with "yat kiṃcedam. (11.252)

Regarding the phrase "enasām" (of sins): desiring to effect the removal of gross sins, namely the great transgressions (*mahāpātaka*), as well as subtle ones such as the minor offenses (*upapātaka*), one should mutter daily for one year—once per day—the verse beginning with "ava te heḷo varuṇa namobhiḥ" (RV 1.2.15), the verse beginning with "yat kiṃcedaṃ varuṇa daivye jane" (RV 5.6.11), and the hymn (*sūkta*) beginning with "iti vā iti me manaḥ" (RV 8.6.26). || 11.252 ||
Having accepted what should not be accepted, or having eaten food that is censured,
a man is purified in three days by reciting the *Taratsamandīya* hymn.

"Having accepted," etc.: having accepted food that is unfit to be accepted—either by its very nature or because it is the wealth of a great sinner—and having eaten food defiled by its inherent nature, the time of its acquisition, the act of acceptance, or contact with the impure, a man becomes purified from that sin after reciting these four *ṛc* verses beginning with "The slow one crosses over" (*tarat sa mandī dhāvati*, RV 7.1.15) for three days. 11.253.
But by practicing the Soma-Raudra rite for many nights for a month, one is purified;
likewise by performing the ritual bath in a flowing river while reciting the verse beginning with "aryamṇām. (11.254)

"Somārudrā dharayethām asuryam" (RV 5.1.18)—these four verses; and "Aryamaṇaṃ varuṇaṃ mitraṃ ca" (RV 3.4.16)—these three ṛks. Having bathed in a river and practiced each of these for one month, one who has committed many sins is purified. This is an indicator that even when there are many sins, a single expiation may be performed by way of a collective application (*tantra*). 11.254.

One who has committed an offense should mutter the seven verses beginning with "abdārdham indram" [RV 8.61.7–13]; but having performed an act that is not praiseworthy, he should subsist on alms for a month while remaining in water.

Regarding the phrase "half a year": because of the specific mention of "the sinner" (*enasvī*), for all sins whatsoever, one should mutter these seven verses beginning with "Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni" (RV 2.3.22) for six months. Having performed an improper act, such as the voiding of urine or excrement in water, one should subsist on food fit for consumption for one month. (11.255)

Having offered clarified butter for a year with the mantras used for the *śakala-homa*, a twice-born man destroys even the most grievous sin; or he does so by reciting the verse beginning with "namaḥ. (11.256)

Regarding the phrase "with mantras": by performing oblations of clarified butter for one year with the Śākala-homa mantras beginning with "devakṛtasya" (VS 8.13), or by muttering for one year this verse beginning with "nama indraś ca," a twice-born man destroys even the sin of a mortal transgression (mahāpātaka). || 11.256 ||
One who is joined with a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) shall follow cows with a concentrated mind;
by practicing the Pāvamānī verses for a year while subsisting on alms, he becomes purified.

Regarding the term *mahāpātaka*: one who is afflicted by a great sin (*mahāpātaka*) such as the killing of a Brahmin, subsisting on food obtained through alms, with his senses restrained, and following behind cows for one year, becomes purified from that sin by reciting daily with repetition the verses beginning with "He who studies the *Pāvamānī*s" (RV 9.67.22). || 11.257 ||
Or, having recited the Vedic Saṃhitā three times in the forest while purified, one who has been cleansed by three *parāka* penances is released from all sins. (11.258)

"In the forest": having purified himself with three *parāka* penances and having recited the Vedic collection consisting of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas three times in the forest, or being self-restrained and endowed with external and internal purity, he is released from all mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*). || 11.258 ||
One who, being self-controlled, fasts for three days and approaches the water three times a day,
is released from all sins by reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times.

"Tryaham" means: fasting for three nights while remaining self-restrained, performing ablutions every day in the morning, at midday, and in the evening; having immersed himself in water precisely at the times of the three daily baths and recited the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn, "Ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca" (RV 8.8.48), three times, he is released from all sins. In this matter, the repetition [of the rite] should be adjusted according to the gravity or lightness of the sin and according to the individual's capacity and other factors. (11.259)
Just as the horse-sacrifice, the king of rituals, is the remover of all sins,
so too is the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn the remover of all sins.

Regarding the word "yathā" (just as): just as the Aśvamedha sacrifice is the best of all sacrifices and the cause for the destruction of all sins, so too is the Aghamarṣaṇa Sūkta the cause for the destruction of all sins; such is the excellence of the Aghamarṣaṇa Sūkta. || 11.260 ||
Even having slain these three worlds and eating [their inhabitants] from here and there, a Brahmin who maintains the Ṛgveda incurs no sin whatsoever. (11.261)

"Having slain" means that even after slaying the three worlds beginning with the earth, a Brahmin or others who eat the food of those guilty of mortal sins and the like, while upholding the Ṛgveda, does not incur any sin. || 11.261 ||

The *Ṛgveda* was taught for the purpose of secret expiation; therefore, when a secret sin has been committed, one should study the *Ṛksaṃhitā*, which consists of both mantra and brāhmaṇa. Regarding this, it is said:
"Having studied the *Ṛksaṃhitā* three times, or the *Yajus* with a concentrated mind, or the *Sāmans* together with their secret portions (*rahasya*), one is liberated from all sins. (11.262)

"Ṛk"—that is, having practiced three times the *Ṛksaṃhitā*, consisting of both mantra and brāhmaṇa (and not merely the mantras alone), as is indicated by the subsequent reference to "the threefold Veda" (11.263); or the *saṃhitā* of the *Yajus* mantras and brāhmaṇas; or that of the *Sāmans* together with their brāhmaṇas and upaniṣads—one becomes liberated from all sins. 11.262.
Just as a clod of earth thrown into a great lake perishes,
so does all evil conduct sink away when immersed in the threefold Veda.

"Yathā" (as): It is called *trivṛt* because it revolves three times in the form of the *Ṛg* and other Vedas. Just as a clod of earth is shattered upon entering a great lake, so too does all evil conduct perish within the *Trivṛt* Veda. 11.263.
He explains its threefold nature:
"The Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, and various other Sāman-chants—this is to be known as the threefold Veda; he who knows this is a knower of the Veda. (11.264)

Regarding the term *ṛc*: the *ṛcs* are the *ṛg-mantras*, the *yajūṃṣi* are the *yajur-mantras*, and the *sāmāni* are the various types such as the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara*. One should know that this threefold Veda (*trivṛdveda*) consists of the *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa* portions of each of these three separately; he who knows this becomes a knower of the Veda. 11.264.
That which is the primordial Brahman of three syllables, in which the triple Veda is established—
that other secret threefold Veda, he who knows it is a knower of the Vedas.

[For that Veda is traditionally held to be threefold, consisting of the separate Brāhmaṇas and Kalpas. O connoisseurs of merit, accept as the true exposition of the sages' words that which I have spoken after reflecting upon the opinions of many regarding expiation (prāyaścitta).
Neither Medhātithi nor Govindarāja has stated this, nor have other commentators proclaimed it; therefore, it is difficult for you to obtain from elsewhere.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the *Mānava Dharmaśāstra*, in the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Chapter Twelve.
O sinless one, you have declared this entire dharma of the four social orders.
Now tell us truly the supreme outcome of the fruits of actions.

"Regarding the four castes": "O sinless one, this dharma for the four castes—beginning with the Brāhmaṇas—who have their origins in successive births, has been declared by you. Now, tell us about the supreme attainment of the fruits of good and evil actions, which arises in future births and consists of ultimate goals. Thus the great sages spoke to Bhṛgu. (12.1)
That righteous-souled Bhṛgu, the son of Manu, said to those great seers:
"Hear the definitive conclusion regarding this entire yoga of action. (12.2)
"Listen to them," he said—Bhṛgu, the son of Manu, whose very self was dharma, spoke thus to those great seers regarding the determination of the fruits of this entire connection with action. (12.2)
Action, arising from mind, speech, and body, bears fruit that is auspicious or inauspicious;
the destinies of men—whether superior, inferior, or middling—are born of action. (12.3)

Regarding the word "auspicious" (*śubha*): action (*karman*) caused by mind, speech, and body, consisting of that which is enjoined or prohibited, has happiness and suffering as its fruit. From that very [action] arise the destinies (*gati*)—the attainments of future births—as humans, animals, and so forth, categorized as superior, middling, or inferior according to their relative status. Furthermore, the word *karman* here does not refer solely to physical movement; rather, it applies to every form of activity, including the mere mental resolve such as "this is mine," as well as the practice of yoga, meditation, and the like. (12.3)
One should know that for this embodied being— whether of these three types, having three bases, and endowed with ten characteristics— it is the mind that is the instigator.

Regarding the word "of that": one should know that the mind alone is the instigator of that action belonging to the embodied being—action which is of three kinds (superior, middling, and inferior), which rests upon mind, speech, and body, and which is endowed with the ten characteristics to be described hereafter. For it is by the mind that one intends, and then speaks and acts. Thus, in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad: "Therefore, what a person reaches with the mind, that he speaks with speech; that he performs with action. (12.4)
To demonstrate those ten types of actions, he says:
Coveting the property of others, thinking of what is undesirable with the mind, and false attachment—these are the threefold mental action. (12.5)

"Regarding the property of others": how one thinks, "How may I seize another's wealth unjustly?"; the mental longing for prohibited acts such as the killing of a Brahmin; and the adherence to such views as "there is no other world" and "the body alone is the self"—this threefold mental action has inauspicious results. Furthermore, the opposite cognition regarding these three is the threefold mental action with auspicious results; for both types have been introduced [in the verse] as "action having auspicious and inauspicious results" (12.3). || 12.5 ||
Harshness, falsehood, slander in every form, and incoherent prattle—these constitute the fourfold nature of speech. (12.6)

Regarding "harshness" (*pāruṣya*): verbal action that bears inauspicious fruit is of four kinds—speaking what is unpleasant, speaking untruths, speaking of others' faults in their absence, and the useless description of even true matters such as news concerning kings, countries, or townspeople. The opposite of this—speaking what is pleasant and true, and recounting the virtues of others or the histories of kings and so forth found in the *Śruti*, *Purāṇas*, and other texts—is of auspicious fruit. (12.6)
Taking what has not been given, violence contrary to the rules, and consorting with another's wife—this is remembered as the threefold bodily [evil]. (12.7)

"Of things not given" means that bodily action of three kinds—unjust seizure of another's property, unscriptural violence, and sexual intercourse with another's wife—has an inauspicious fruit. The opposite of these three has an auspicious fruit. (12.7)
This person experiences the auspicious and inauspicious results of mental action by means of the mind alone;
likewise, verbal action is experienced through speech, and bodily action through the body itself.
One should abandon the ten paths of unrighteous action: threefold action by means of the body, fourfold by means of speech, and threefold by means of the mind.

Regarding the phrase "mental": whatever action—whether good or evil—is performed by the mind, its fruit, in the form of pleasure or pain, this person experiences through the mind alone, either in this life or in another birth. Likewise, one experiences the auspicious or inauspicious results of speech through the medium of speech, such as speaking sweetly or with a faltering voice; and the auspicious or inauspicious results of the body through the medium of the body, such as the enjoyment of pleasant things like garlands and sandalwood paste, or the state of being afflicted by disease. Therefore, with great effort, one should avoid and not perform those actions of body, mind, and speech that are devoid of dharma. 12.8
Through the defects of actions born of the body, a man goes to the state of an immobile being;
through those of speech, to the state of a bird or a beast; and through those of the mind, to the status of an outcaste.
Through auspicious applications one becomes a deity; through mixed ones, a human;
and through exclusively inauspicious ones, one is born among the animal wombs.
The punishment of speech destroys wisdom; the punishment of the mind destroys the supreme goal;
but the punishment of action, if left unguarded, destroys the three worlds.
The restraint of speech is silence, while the restraint of mind is fasting;
for the restraint of the body, breath control (prāṇāyāma) is prescribed.

Regarding the word "body" (*śarīra*): although for the most wicked only three types of sin—bodily, verbal, and mental—are possible, it is nevertheless explained that if one predominantly practices unrighteousness (*adharma*) while practicing righteousness (*dharma*) only to a small extent, then by virtue of this predominance, a human being attains the state of an immobile being (*sthāvara*) through sins born of bodily actions; through predominance of those committed by speech, the state of a bird or a beast; and through predominance of those committed mentally, the state of a *caṇḍāla* or similar low-born being. (12.9)
"The staff of speech, the staff of mind, and likewise the staff of body—he in whose intellect these are firmly established is called a *tridaṇḍin* (one who possesses the triple staff). (12.10)

Regarding the term *vāgdaṇḍa*: *daṇḍa* means restraint (*damana*). The restraints of speech, mind, and body consist in the abandonment of prohibited utterances, intentions, and forbidden activities, remaining established within the intellect; one who possesses these is called a *tridaṇḍin*. It is not merely by carrying three physical staffs that one is so designated; thus, this is a praise of the three internal restraints. (12.10)
Having laid down this triple staff among all beings, and having restrained desire and anger, a person then attains perfection.

Regarding the term "tridaṇḍa" (the triple staff): having thus performed the subduing of speech and other faculties so that they do not range over all beings, and having restrained desire and anger for the very purpose of that subduing, a person then attains success characterized by the attainment of liberation. || 12.11 ||
Who is it that attains perfection? To this he says:
"That which is the cause of this self's activity, they call the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña);
but that which performs actions is called the elemental self (bhūtātman) by the wise. (12.12)

Regarding the word "ya" (who): the wise call that "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña) who, because he assists this self known as the body well-established in the world, impels it toward actions. On the other hand, that which performs these activities—the one called the body—is said by the wise to be merely the "self of the elements" (bhūtātman), since it is composed of the elements such as earth and the rest. 12.12
There is another inner self, known as the *jīva*, which is innate to all embodied beings;
by means of it, one experiences all pleasure and pain throughout successive births.

Regarding the term "designated as the *jīva*": this word *jīva* refers to the Great One (*mahat*), because of the use of the instrumental case in the word "by which" (*yena*), and because in the following verse, "Both of these, conjoined with the elements—the Great One and the Knower of the Field" (12.24)—it is referred back by the pronoun "those two. Thus, distinct from the embodied Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), it is the one called the Self (*ātman*) within the body; it is known as the *jīva*, the innate Self of all Knowers of the Field. Its application is through those [elements] for the sake of attaining that [state], by means of which—having transformed into the form of ego and the senses and serving as the cause—the Knower of the Field experiences pleasure and pain in every birth. (12.13)
Both of these—the Great One (Mahat) and the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña)—are joined with the elements;
they remain pervading that which abides within high and low beings.

"Those two"—that is, those two great knowers of the field (kṣetrajña), conjoined with the five elements beginning with earth, abide by taking refuge in the Supreme Self (paramātman), who is designated as "Him" because He is well-known from all the worlds, Vedas, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and so forth, and who is established among beings of superior and inferior natures. 12.14.
Innumerable forms issue forth from his body, which constantly set various beings in motion. (12.15)

"Innumerable" means that from the body of that Supreme Self, innumerable forms—the individual souls (*jīvas*)—which were just mentioned by the term "knower of the field" (*kṣetrajña*), emerge like sparks from fire according to the manner described in the Vedānta, being delimited by subtle bodies (*liṅgaśarīra*). Those forms, having transformed into the nature of superior and inferior beings, such as gods and fires, constantly impel [beings] toward their actions. (12.15)
After death, for men who have committed evil deeds, another body certainly arises from those very five elements for the purpose of undergoing torment.

"From the five" means that for humans who have committed evil deeds, a body capable of enduring suffering—one distinct from the womb-born (*jarāyuja*) and other types of bodies—is produced in the next world, caused by the experience of torment arising precisely from the five elements, beginning with earth. 12.16.
Having experienced those torments of Yama with this very body,
they dissolve part by part back into those same elemental constituents.

"By that" means: by that body which has gone forth, those torments (*yātanā*) were caused to be experienced; when the gross bodies—though previously experienced subtly—are destroyed, those wicked living beings dissolve respectively into those very constituent portions of the elements (*bhūta*). The meaning is that they remain having become conjoined with them. (12.17)
Having experienced those faults born of attachment to sense objects, which result in future suffering,
he approaches those two of great luster with his impurities removed.

"He experiences," it is said. Having experienced the suffering of the world of Yama and other such things produced by the enjoyment of prohibited objects—namely sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—he who is embodied and delimited by the subtle body consisting of the subtle elements and so forth, becomes free from sin after that experience, and then resorts to those very two, the Great One and the Supreme Self, who possess great power. 12.18.
Together with him, they tirelessly observe his merit and his evil;
joined with these, he attains happiness or misery both here and after death in the realm of Yama.

"Those two" refers to Mahat and the Supreme Self (Paramātman). Being tireless, they deliberate together upon the merit and the remaining sin of that living being (jīva). Joined with his righteousness and unrighteousness, the jīva experiences happiness and suffering in both the next world and this world. (12.19)
If one practices dharma for the most part and unrighteousness only slightly,
being enveloped by those very elements, he enjoys happiness in heaven.

Regarding the word "yadi" (if): if that individual soul (*jīva*), during its human state, predominantly practices dharma and only slightly practices adharma, then, joined with those very elements—earth and the others—which have transformed into the form of a gross body, it experiences the bliss of heaven.
But if one mostly practices unrighteousness and only rarely practices righteousness,
abandoned by those very beings, he undergoes the torments of Yama.

Regarding the word "yadi" (if): if, moreover, that *jīva* predominantly practices sin and only slightly merit during its human state, then, having been abandoned by those very elements (*bhūta*) which had transformed into the form of the human body, it dies; immediately thereafter, in the manner described in the verse, "From the five elements alone" (12.16), it acquires a coarse body suitable for experiencing torment and undergoes the agonies of Yama.
Having undergone those torments in the Yāmis, that living being, freed from defilement,
returns once again to those very five elements, each according to its own portion.

"Yāmīḥ" means: that living soul (jīva), having experienced those torments inflicted by Yama with that coarse body, is then—its impurities (pāpman) removed through that experience—presides over those five elemental portions (bhūta-bhāga), such as earth and the rest, which initiate the formation of bodies born from a womb and so forth; the meaning is that it takes on a human or other kind of body. || 12.22 ||
Having observed these destinies of the living being by means of his own mind— both those resulting from righteousness and those from unrighteousness— one should always fix the mind upon them.

"These" refers to the following: having understood within the internal organ that these attainments of bodies—agreeable or disagreeable, fit for the experience of heaven, hell, and so forth, caused by merit and demerit—belong to this living being (jīva), one should always keep the mind intent upon the practice of dharma. 12.23.
One should know that *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are the three qualities (*guṇa*) of the Self;
pervaded by these, the Great One (*mahat*) abides in all these states without exception. (12.24)

Regarding the word "sattva": one should understand that *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—the three whose characteristics as qualities (*guṇa*) will be described—are the qualities of the Great Self (*mahat*), because they serve its purpose. Pervaded by these, the Great One remains having completely permeated all these objects in the form of both the stationary and the moving. 12.24.
Whichever of these qualities predominates entirely within the body at any given time,
it then makes that embodied being consist primarily of that quality.

Regarding the word "ya" (which): although all this indeed consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), nevertheless, in whichever body whichever quality among them becomes entirely predominant at any given time, it then makes that embodied being (*dehin*) abundant in the characteristics of that particular quality. 12.25.
Now he states the characteristics of *sattva* and the others:
"Sattva is knowledge; *tamas* is ignorance; passion and hatred are known as *rajas*.
This is their pervasive nature, which rests within all beings. (12.26)

Regarding *sattva*: knowledge (*jñāna*), which is the appearance of things as they truly are, is the characteristic of *sattva*. Its opposite, ignorance (*ajñāna*), is the characteristic of *tamas*. Despair and longing, which are mental effects, are the characteristic of *rajas*. As for the essential nature of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, it consists of joy, aversion, and despair. Thus they recite: "The *guṇas* consist of joy, despair, and [inertia]; their purposes are illumination, activity, and restraint; and their functions consist of mutual suppression, production, and coexistence. He will explain this essential nature of these [qualities] in the three subsequent verses. This aforementioned characteristic—knowledge and so forth—is that which pervades all living beings belonging to the qualities of *sattva* and the rest. (12.26)
In that regard, whatever he perceives within himself as associated with joy—
tranquil and radiant like purity— he should understand that to be the quality of sattva.
Regarding the word "therein": one should know that *sattva* to be that experience within that self which is associated with joy, free from afflictions, and of the nature of luminosity. 12.27.
But that which is joined with suffering and is disagreeable to oneself, know that to be *rajas*, which is constantly carrying away embodied beings against their will. (12.28)

As for the phrase "but that which": furthermore, one should know that *rajas* is that perception which is permeated by suffering, and for that very reason does not produce joy in the pure being or the self; it is that which always generates a craving for sense objects in embodied beings and serves as the adversary to the truth-revealing [sattva]. 12.28.
But that which is joined with delusion, unmanifest, consisting of sense objects, beyond reasoning, and unknowable—one should understand that to be darkness (tamas). || 12.29 ||

Regarding the phrase "but that which": one should know that *tamas* is that which is devoid of the discrimination between the existent and the non-existent, whose nature is an indistinct form of objects, whose essence is inconceivable, and which is difficult to perceive by means of either the internal or external organs. The purpose of this description of the essential natures of these qualities is so that one may strive to remain established in the functioning of *sattva*. 12.29.
And I shall explain in its entirety the arising of the fruit for each of these three qualities— whether it be superior, middling, or inferior.
"Of the three": I shall specifically explain that which, among these three qualities—sattva and the others—produces fruit in the form of superior, middling, and inferior, respectively. 12.30.

The study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, purity, restraint of the senses, performance of righteous deeds, and contemplation of the Self—these are the characteristics of the quality of goodness (sattva). 12.31.

Regarding "the study of the Vedas": the study of the Vedas, the performance of rites such as the Prājāpatya, comprehension of the meaning of the scriptures, purity through clay, water, and so forth, restraint of the senses, the practice of duties such as charity, and devotion to meditation on the Self—this is the effect of the quality known as *sattva*. (12.31)

Delight in undertaking new projects, lack of steadfastness, embracing what is not beneficial, and the constant pursuit of sensual objects—these are the characteristics of the quality of passion (rājasa). 12.32.

"Initiative" (ārambha) means the habit of performing actions for the sake of results, agitation even over a trivial matter, the performance of prohibited acts, and the constant enjoyment of objects such as sound and the rest; this is the effect of the quality designated as rajas. 12.32.
Greed, sleepiness, lack of fortitude, cruelty, atheism, deviation from right conduct, a habit of begging, and negligence— these are the characteristics of the quality of darkness (tamas).

"Greed," and so forth. An excessive longing for wealth, a state of constant sleepiness, cowardice, backbiting, the conviction that there is no other world, the neglect of proper conduct, a habit of begging, and a lack of attention toward dharma and other duties even when they are possible—this is the definition of the quality designated as *tāmasa*. 12.33.
And for these three qualities as they abide in the three [states], this should be known as the concise definition of their characteristics in their respective order. || 12.34 ||

"Of the three" means that for these three qualities (*guṇa*), such as *sattva* and the others, which exist throughout the three times—past, future, and present—one should understand, in their respective order, the definition of each quality as it will be explained below with its necessary correlative. (12.34)

Whatever action one feels ashamed of after having done it, while doing it, or even when intending to do it—that should be known by the wise as entirely characterized by the quality of darkness (tamas). || 12.35 ||

Regarding the word "yat" (which): that action which, having been performed, being performed, or about to be performed, causes one to feel shame—whether in all three times or in two of them—that is intended here. Because it is an effect of *tamas*, it is designated as *tamas*; this definition of the quality (*guṇa*) is to be understood by the knower of the scriptures.
That action by which one desires abundant fame in this world,
yet does not grieve over its failure to be accomplished— that should be known as rajasic.

Regarding the word "by which": that action which one performs solely for the purpose of attaining great renown in this world—neither for the sake of the next world nor because one becomes distressed by the non-attainment of the fruit of that action—is to be known as characterized by the quality of *rajas*, because it is the effect of *rajas*. (12.36)
That which one desires to know in its entirety, that which one does not feel ashamed to practice,
and that by which one’s own self is satisfied— this is the defining characteristic of the quality of a virtuous being.

Regarding the word "that" (yat): that action which one desires to know as the meaning of the Veda with one's whole being, and that action which one does not feel shame for even when performing it throughout the three periods of time, and by whatever action satisfaction arises within one’s self—that is to be known as the characteristic of the quality called *sattva*.
Desire is said to be the characteristic of *tamas*, while purpose is said to be that of *rajas*;
the characteristic of *sattva* is righteousness (*dharma*). Among these, each succeeding one is superior.

Regarding the verse beginning with *tamasah*: the defining characteristic of *tamas* is the predominance of desire (*kāma*); that of *rajas*, the pursuit of material objects (*artha*); and that of *sattva*, the predominance of virtue (*dharma*). Among these—desire and the others—the subsequent one is superior to the preceding: material wealth is better than desire, because desire is rooted in material wealth; and virtue is better than both of those, because they are rooted in virtue. (12.38)
I shall now describe, in brief and in their proper order, those qualities by which each of these beings enters into various states of existence.

"By which," and so forth. Among these qualities, such as *sattva* and the rest, I shall describe in brief and in due order all those states of existence which the individual soul (*jīva*) attains through whichever quality serves as its own effect within this entire world. || 12.39 ||
Those characterized by sattva attain the state of gods; those characterized by rajas, the state of humans;
and those characterized by tamas, the state of animals perpetually—such is this threefold destiny.

"Regarding the state of divinity": those who abide in the mode of goodness (sattva-vṛtti) attain the state of gods; those who abide in the mode of passion (rajas-vṛtti) attain the state of humans; and those who abide in the mode of darkness (tamas-vṛtti) attain the state of animals—this is the threefold attainment of birth. 12.40.
This secondary course of existence should be understood as being threefold and of three kinds:
inferior, middling, and superior, according to the distinction of action and knowledge. (12.41)

Regarding the phrase "of three kinds": that threefold attainment of another birth which was described as being caused by the three qualities (guṇas) such as *sattva* and so forth, should further be understood as being of three types—namely inferior, middling, and superior—due to the distinctions of place, time, and so on, as well as the distinctions among the karmas that cause *saṃsāra* and the distinctions among [types of] knowledge. || 12.41 ||
Immovable beings, worms, insects, fish, snakes along with tortoises,
domestic animals, and wild beasts— this is the lowest state, characterized by darkness (tāmasī gati).

Regarding the term "stationary beings" (*sthāvara*): stationary beings are trees and the like; worms are minute living creatures; insects are slightly larger than those; and likewise fish, snakes, tortoises, domestic animals, and wild beasts—this is the lowest state of existence, caused by *tamas*. 12.42.
Elephants, horses, Śūdras, and despised Mlecchas;
lions, tigers, and boars—these constitute the middling state of darkness (tāmasī gati). || 12.43 ||

"And elephants" refers to the fact that elephants, horses, Śūdras, Mlecchas, lions, tigers, and boars constitute the intermediate state of existence caused by the quality of darkness (tamas). The term "despised" is a restatement of the essential nature of the Mlecchas. 12.43.
Cāraṇas, Suparṇas, and deceitful men, as well as Rākṣasas and Piśācas—these are the highest destination among those in the quality of darkness (tamas). || 12.44 ||

And the *cāraṇas*. The *cāraṇas* are actors and the like; the *suparṇas* are birds; those who act through deception are men; as well as *rākṣasas* and *piśācas*—this is the highest destination among those belonging to *tamas*. (12.44)
Jhallas, Mallas, and Naṭas, as well as men who live by the sword, those addicted to gambling and drinking, and those of the lowest sort—this is the rājasic destiny. 12.45.

Regarding the term *jhallāḥ*: the *jhallas* and *mallas* are those born from a *vrātya* Kṣatriya father and a woman of the same caste; they are to be understood as described in the tenth chapter. Among them, the *jhallas* are those who strike with clubs, while the *mallas* are wrestlers. Furthermore, actors (*naṭas*) who descend onto the stage, as well as men addicted to weapons, gambling, and drinking, are to be known as the lowest state belonging to *rajas*. 12.45.
Kings, Kṣatriyas, and the domestic priests of kings,
as well as those for whom battle is their primary concern— this is the intermediate Rājasa path.

"Kings" means kings who have been consecrated as lords of the realm; likewise, kṣatriyas and royal chaplains who take pleasure in disputes over the meaning of the scriptures—this is to be understood as the middling *rājasī* state. || 12.46 ||
The Gandharvas, Guhyakas, Yakṣas, and those who are followers of the gods,
as well as all the Apsarases— this is the highest destination among those belonging to the Rajas quality.

"Gandharvas" refers to the Gandharvas, Guhyakas, and Yakṣas—specific classes of beings well-known from the Purāṇas and other sources—as well as those such as the Vidyādharas who follow the gods, and all the Apsarases, the celestial courtesans; this is the most excellent state within the intermediate Rājasa realm. (12.47)
Ascetics, yogis, brahmins, and the hosts of celestial beings in their vimānas,
as well as the stars and the daityas— this is the first, sattvic destination.

"Ascetics" refers to forest-dwellers (*vānaprasthas*), mendicants (*bhikṣukas*), and Brahmins; those who travel in celestial chariots such as the Puṣpaka but are distinct from Apsarases; the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*); and the Daityas—this is the lowest state, caused by the quality of *sattva*. (12.48)
Sacrificers, seers, gods, the Vedas, the luminaries, the years, the ancestors, and the Sādhyas— this is the second, sattvic goal.

"Performers of sacrifice" means those whose nature is to perform sacrifices; likewise the ṛṣis, the gods, and the deities presiding over the Vedas who are known from the Itihāsas as possessing physical forms; the luminaries such as Dhruva and others; the years, which according to the perspective of the Itihāsas possess physical forms; the ancestors, such as the Somapas and others; and the Sādhyas, who are a specific class of divine beings—this is the intermediate state caused by the quality of *sattva*. (12.49)
Brahmā, the creators of the universe, Dharma, Mahat, and the Unmanifest—these the wise declare to be the highest state characterized by sattva. || 12.50 ||

"Brahman" refers to the four-faced one (Brahmā), the creators of the universe such as Marīci and others, Dharma personified, Mahat, and the Unmanifest—the two principles well-known in Sāṃkhya; it is these two presiding deities that are intended here, for it is impossible for the mere non-conscious triad of qualities alone to constitute the highest state of being characterized by goodness (sattva). The wise declare this superior goal, consisting of the four-faced one and the rest, to be caused by sattva. (12.50)
Thus has been fully described this entire transmigratory existence, consisting of all elemental beings, which is threefold in its three types of action and itself of three kinds.

"This" refers to the entirety of the specific destinies pertaining to all living beings, which is described in its totality. This [destiny] is threefold according to the division of action into the three types—mental, vocal, and physical; it is again threefold according to the division of the qualities (guṇas) into sattva, rajas, and tamas; and it is further threefold according to the division into low, middling, and superior.
