Because of the designation "belonging to all beings" (*sārvabhautika*), those destinies not explicitly mentioned here are also to be understood as included; the destinies already mentioned, however, serve merely as illustrations. 12.51.
Through attachment to the senses and by not practicing the Dharma, the ignorant and lowest of men go to sinful states of existence. 12.52

"Of the senses": through attachment to the objects of the senses and by practicing what is forbidden, as well as by failing to perform duties such as expiatory rites, deluded men—the lowest of humanity—attain contemptible states of existence. 12.52.
Learn now all that specific womb into which this living being enters in this world, and by what particular karma, in due succession. (12.53)
"Whichever...": Listen now in due order to all those various births which this individual soul (jīva) attains in this world as a result of whatever sinful karma he has committed. 12.53.
Having endured terrible hells for many series of years, upon their exhaustion,
those who have committed great sins enter these transmigrations.

"Many" means that those who commit great sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, having reached terrifying hells for many collections of years, obtain—upon the exhaustion of their experience there—the specific types of births to be described here due to the remainder of their evil deeds. || 12.54 ||
The killer of a Brahmin enters the womb of a dog, a pig, a donkey, or a camel; or that of a cow, a goat, a sheep, a deer, or a bird; or even that of a Caṇḍāla or a Pukkasa. || 12.55 ||

"Śveta": The killer of a Brahmin attains the birth associated with dogs, pigs, donkeys, camels, goats, sheep, wild animals, birds, Cāṇḍālas, and Pukkasas born of Niṣādas from Śūdra women; in this regard, it should be understood that he undergoes birth in all these species sequentially, depending on the relative gravity or lightness of the remaining sin. The same applies in subsequent cases as well. (12.55)
A Brahmin who drinks liquor shall go among worms, insects, moths, birds that feed on excrement, and indeed among predatory creatures.
"Kṛmi": A Brāhmaṇa who drinks liquor goes to the species of worms, insects, and locusts; of birds that feed on excrement; and of predatory creatures such as tigers and the like. (12.56)
A Brahmin who is a thief [becomes] thousands of times a spider, a snake, a lizard, aquatic animals, predatory beasts, and Piśācas. (12.57)

Regarding the phrase "spiders and snakes": a Brāhmaṇa who steals gold undergoes birth a thousand times among spiders, cobras, lizards, aquatic animals such as crocodiles and the like, and among those species whose nature is to do harm. 12.57.
The violator of his teacher's bed is reborn as grasses, shrubs, and creepers, as well as as carnivorous animals with fangs, and even as those who perform cruel deeds by the hundreds.

"Grass," etc.: one who has sexual intercourse with the wife of his guru attains birth a hundred times among grasses such as *dūrvā*, shrubs (*gulma*) such as those without trunks, creepers (*latā*) such as *guḍūcī*, scavengers of raw flesh such as vultures, fanged creatures such as lions, and those characterized by cruel deeds and a habit of killing such as tigers. (12.58)
They become carnivorous beasts of prey, worms that eat what is unfit for food, thieves who devour one another, and ghosts who consort with women of the lowest castes. (12.59)

Regarding the word *hiṃsrāḥ*: those who are habituated to killing living beings become cats and other such creatures that eat raw meat (*āmamāṃsāśinaḥ*). Those who eat what is forbidden to eat are born as worms. Thieves, excluding those guilty of the great sins (*mahāpātaka*), become eaters of one another’s flesh. And those who have sexual intercourse with women of the *caṇḍāla* caste and so forth are born as specific types of beings called *preta*s. This is because the *Smṛti* texts share the same metrical form as Vedic *chandas*, according to the rule: "All rules [of grammar] are optional in *chandas*" (Kātyāyana’s *Paribhāṣāsūtra* 36); thus, there is either the elision of the *visarga* or the lengthening by *savarṇadīrgha* following the elision of *ya*. (12.59)
By entering into union with outcasts, by approaching the wife of another,
and by stealing the property of a Brahmin, one becomes a Brahmarākṣasa.

Regarding the phrase "by association": for as long as one remains associated with those who have fallen, for that duration of time, having engaged in social intercourse with the four types beginning with the slayer of a Brahmin, having approached the wives of others, and having stolen gold other than that of a Brahmin—one becomes a *brahmarākṣasa*, a particular kind of spirit, by the commission of each of these individual sins. (12.60)
Having stolen gems, pearls, corals, and various other jewels out of greed, a man is born among those who work with gold.

Regarding the word *maṇī*: having stolen with greed gems such as rubies (*māṇikya*) and others, as well as pearls and coral, and various kinds of jewels such as lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*) and diamonds, one is born in the womb of a goldsmith, except through the delusion that [the act] was one's own. Some, however, call it the "goldsmith-bird. (12.61)

By stealing grain one becomes a rat; by stealing bell-metal, a swan; by stealing water, a water-fowl; by stealing honey, a gadfly; by stealing milk, a crow; by stealing savory food, a dog; and by stealing ghee, a mongoose. (12.62)

Regarding "grain": having stolen grain, one becomes a mouse; having stolen bell-metal, a swan; having stolen water, a bird called a *plava*; having stolen honey, a gadfly; having stolen milk, a crow; and having stolen the juice of sugarcane and so forth—excluding specifically mentioned items such as molasses and salt—one becomes a dog. Having stolen clarified butter (*ghṛta*), one becomes a mongoose. (12.62)
The vulture [eats] flesh, the cormorant the fat, the oil-drinking bird the oil,
the cricket the salt, and the crane the curd.

Regarding "meat": having stolen meat, one becomes a vulture; having stolen fat, one becomes an aquatic creature named *madgu*; having stolen oil, one is born as a bird called *tailapāyika*; having stolen salt, one becomes a loud-sounding insect called *cīra*; and having stolen curd, one is born as a bird called *balākā*. (12.63)
Having stolen silk, a partridge [is reborn as such]; having stolen linen, a frog; having stolen cotton cloth, a curlew; for stealing a cow, an iguana; and for stealing molasses, a guḍa-insect.

Regarding "kauśeya": having stolen cloth made from the cocoon of a silkworm, one becomes a bird named *tittiri*. Having stolen cloth made of linen (*kṣauma*), one becomes a frog; having stolen a garment made of cotton (*kārpāsa*), one becomes a creature called a *krauñca*; having stolen a cow, one becomes a monitor lizard (*godhā*); and having stolen molasses (*guḍa*), one becomes a bird named *vāgguda*. (12.64)
The muskrat [eats] auspicious fragrances, while the peacock [eats] leaf-vegetables;
the porcupine [eats] various kinds of prepared food, while the hedgehog [eats] unprepared food.

Regarding the musk-rat (*chucchundari*): by stealing fragrant substances, one becomes a musk-rat. By stealing leaf-vegetables such as *vāstūka* and the like, one becomes a peacock. By stealing various kinds of prepared food, such as boiled rice, parched grain, and so forth, one is born as a creature called a porcupine (*śvāvidh*). However, by stealing unprepared food, such as rice, barley, and the like, one is born as a porcupine (*śalyaka*). (12.65)
By stealing fire, one becomes a crane; by stealing household utensils, a house-builder;
and by stealing dyed garments, one is born as a jīvajīvaka bird.

Regarding the crane (*baka*): having stolen fire, one is born as a bird called a crane. Having stolen household implements such as winnowing baskets and pestles, one becomes a winged insect that builds dwellings out of clay and the like upon walls and other structures. Having stolen garments dyed with safflower and similar colors, one is born as a bird called a *cakora*. (12.66)
A wolf [seizes] a deer; a tiger, a horse; a monkey, fruit and roots; a bear, a woman; a cuckoo, water; a camel, vehicles; and a goat, livestock. || 12.67 ||

Regarding "a wolf": having stolen a deer or an elephant, one becomes a predatory animal known as a wolf. Having stolen a horse, one becomes a tiger. Having stolen fruits or roots, one becomes a monkey. Having stolen a woman, one becomes a bear. Having stolen water for drinking, one becomes the bird called a *cātaka*. Having stolen vehicles such as carts and the like, one becomes a camel. Having stolen other animals not mentioned, one becomes a goat. (12.67)
Whatever another's property it may be, having forcibly seized it, a man inevitably goes to the state of an animal, as does one who has consumed an oblation that was not consecrated.

Or else: whatever unsubstantial property belonging to another a man may take by his own desire, having consumed an unoffered oblation such as the *puroḍāśa* cake and so forth, he certainly attains the state of an animal. (12.68)
Women also, by taking [property] according to this same rule, incur guilt;
they become wives of these very same creatures. (12.69)
"Women also"—women likewise, by this same manner, having stolen the property of others out of desire, incur sin; through that sin, they become the wives of the aforementioned creatures. (12.69)
Having thus described the fruits of performing prohibited actions, he now states the ripening of the fruit resulting from the non-performance of prescribed duties:
"For the social classes (varṇas), when they deviate from their respective duties in times of no distress, having wandered through miserable transmigrations, go to servitude among enemies. (12.70)

Regarding the phrase "to their own": the four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, if they abandon the performance of the five sacrifices and other duties without being in distress, will—after falling into the contemptible wombs mentioned below—attain the state of being slaves to their enemies in a future birth. (12.70)
A Brahmin fallen from his own dharma becomes a preta with a mouth like a firebrand who eats what has been vomited;
and a Kṣatriya becomes a kaṭapūtana who eats impure matter and corpses.

"One who eats vomit" means that a Brāhmaṇa who has fallen from his own duty becomes a *charditabhuk* (one who eats what has been vomited), a specific kind of *preta* named *Jvālāmukha*. Furthermore, a Kṣatriya whose duty has perished becomes a specific kind of *preta* called *Kaṭapūtana*, one who feeds on excrement and corpses. (12.71)
A Vaiśya who has fallen from his own dharma becomes a preta named Maitrākṣajyotika who feeds on pus;
and a Śūdra, having fallen from his own dharma, becomes a Cailāśaka.

Regarding the term *maitra*: a Vaiśya who has fallen from his duty becomes a *preta* named Maitrākṣajyotika, whose food is pus. He is called *maitra* because Mitra is his presiding deity (*devatā*). The anus is that very "eye" (*akṣa*), which is an organ of action; he whose light (*jyotis*) is there is *maitrākṣajyotika*. The change from *jyotis* to *jyotika* occurs according to the rule for words like *pṛṣodara*, involving the elision of the letter *ṣ*. Furthermore, a Śūdra who has fallen from his duty becomes a *preta* known as Celāśaka. He is called *celāśaka* because he eats (*aśnāti*) lice (*yūkā*) associated with clothing (*cela*, i.e., cloth). Govindarāja, however, says that a creature called Celāśaka is a type of insect (*kīṭa*) found in cloth, and that he becomes one who feeds on such. That is incorrect, because the context concerns a specific class of beings known as *pretas*. (12.72)
To whatever extent those whose nature is the objects of sense indulge in those objects, to that same extent skillfulness arises in them regarding them. 12.73
"Yathā" means: just as those who are greedy for sense objects excessively indulge in objects such as sound and the rest, so too does their proficiency in those very objects increase. || 12.73 ||
Then— due to the repetition of those sinful deeds, those of small intelligence undergo sufferings in various wombs here in this world. (12.74)

"Those" refers to those of dull intellect who, due to the intensity of their habitual attachment to the enjoyment of sense objects, experience suffering in various births among animals and other such states—some contemptible, some more contemptible, and some most contemptible. (12.74)
There is the tossing about in the fierce hells such as Tāmisra,
as well as the forests of sword-leaves and the severing of bonds.

Regarding the phrase "in Tāmisra and the others": the word "they attain" (*saṃprāpnuvanti*) from the preceding verse (12.74) is carried over here and into the subsequent one. They undergo the experience of suffering in the terrible hells such as Tāmisra mentioned in the fourth chapter; likewise, they attain hells consisting of binding and cutting, such as the Forest of Sword-Leaves (*asipatravana*). 12.75.
And various torments indeed, such as being devoured by crows and owls,
the heat of sand heated like parched grain, and the dreadful Kumbhīpāka hells.

"Various" means that they undergo various torments, such as being devoured by crows and other scavengers, and they reach the dreadful hells such as *taptavāluka* (heated sands) and *kumbhīpāka* (the boiling pot). || 12.76 ||
And he constantly experienced births in various wombs that were mostly full of suffering,
as well as the afflictions of cold and heat and manifold fears.

"And regarding 'origination' (saṃbhava)": they undergo origination—that is, birth—among the various classes of beings such as animals, which are characterized by constant and abundant suffering. Therein, they encounter afflictions such as cold and heat, as well as various other forms of misery. (12.77)
Repeatedly dwelling in the womb and undergoing dreadful births, as well as painful bondages and even the state of being a servant to others. (12.78)

"Repeatedly" means that they dwell again and again in the locations of the womb and undergo birth, which brings suffering through the pressure of the birth canal and other such means; and once born, they experience the pain of being bound with chains and the like, and they fall into a state of servitude to others.
The separation from kinsmen and loved ones, as well as dwelling with wicked people; the acquisition of wealth and its loss, and the gaining of friends and enemies. (12.79)

"Beloved by kinsmen": due to separation from relatives and friends, dwelling together with wicked people, the exertion of acquiring wealth, the loss of wealth, the difficulty of winning friends, and the emergence of enemies—these they encounter. 12.79.
And [he saw] old age, which is beyond remedy, and the torment of diseases,
various kinds of afflictions, and death itself, which is difficult to overcome.

Regarding "old age": they encounter old age for which there is no remedy, the affliction of diseases, various kinds of sufferings such as hunger and thirst, and death, which is difficult to ward off. || 12.80 ||
With whatever disposition one performs any particular action, with a body corresponding to that very disposition, one experiences its respective fruit. (12.81)

"By whatever kind [of mind]" means: by whatever sort of mind—whether characterized by *sattva*, *rajas*, or *tamas*—one performs any particular action such as bathing, giving, or yoga, one experiences the corresponding fruit, such as a particular state of existence, with a body of that very same nature: whether *sāttvika*, dominated by *rajas*, or dominated by *tamas*. (12.81)
This entire arising of the fruits of your actions has been fully described;
now learn this action which brings about the supreme good for a Brahmin.

"This" refers to this: all the arising of fruits for your prescribed and prohibited actions has been declared. Now, listen to this performance of action which is beneficial for the supreme good and liberation of a Brāhmaṇa. 12.82.
The study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, restraint of the senses, non-violence, and service to the guru are the supreme means for attaining the highest good. 12.83.

"Study of the Vedas" means the repeated recitation of the Veda, beginning with the Upaniṣads, both in terms of its text and its meaning; austerity refers to the Kṛcchra and other such penances; knowledge is that which has Brahman as its object; mastery over the senses; avoidance of unenjoined violence; and service to the teacher—this is the preeminent means for attaining liberation. 12.83.
And among all these auspicious actions here, some particular action has been declared to be more conducive to welfare for a person. (12.84)

"Of all"—this refers to the doubt that among all these auspicious actions, such as the study of the Vedas and so forth, some particular action might, by its excellence, be the means to liberation. Because of the sages' specific desire to know, he states the conclusion in the following verse. || 12.84 ||
And for all of these, knowledge of the Self is remembered as supreme; for that is the foremost of all sciences, since through it immortality is attained. (12.85)

"Of all these": among all these, such as the study of the Vedas and so forth, the knowledge of the supreme reality taught in the Upaniṣads is traditionally held to be the most excellent, because it is the foremost of all branches of knowledge. He states the reason for this here: "because from this alone is liberation attained. (12.85)
Of these six aforementioned types of action, it should be known that the Vedic rite is always more conducive to welfare, both in this world and after death.

Regarding the word "of the six": among these aforementioned six activities, beginning with the study of the Vedas, Vedic action (*vaidika-karma*)—which is knowledge of the supreme reality—is to be known as that which more effectively brings about welfare both in this world and the next. There is no redundancy here, because in the previous verse the status of self-knowledge as the cause of liberation was stated, whereas here its status as the cause of other forms of welfare in this world and the next is being declared. To illustrate: regarding the meditations on symbols (*pratīkopāsanā*), the arising of doubt is shown by the text: "He who meditates on Name as Brahman has free movement as far as Name extends. Govindarāja, however, has explained: "Among these six activities mentioned in the previous verse, beginning with the study of the Vedas, Vedic action is to be known as superior to Smārta (tradition-based) action; it is the means for attaining fame, heaven, and the supreme good with greater excellence throughout all bodies and in the next world. That is incorrect, because each of the six, including the study of the Vedas, is prescribed individually by the Śruti. Among them, it is not possible that some are thus [superior] while others are not, in comparison to Smārta action. Consequently, how could the genitive case be used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*)? Therefore, the explanation is exactly as stated above. (12.86)
Now he clarifies that the knowledge of the Self alone is the means for attaining excellence both in this world and the next:
"But in the Vedic path of action, all these [means] without exception are included, respectively, within each specific injunction for ritual performance. (12.87)

Regarding the word *vaidake*: furthermore, in the Vedic application of action consisting of the worship of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), all these aforementioned means for attaining welfare in this world and the next occur sequentially within that rite of worship. Alternatively, the phrase "all these" refers specifically to the study of the Vedas and so forth; for in the knowledge of the Supreme Self, the study of the Vedas and other such practices are included as constituent parts (*aṅga*) prescribed by the scripture: "The Brahmins seek to know Him through the recitation of the Vedas, through sacrifice, through giving, through austerity, and through fasting" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22). || 12.87 ||

Vedic action is of two kinds: that which leads to worldly prosperity and that which leads to the supreme good; it is also twofold, consisting of the path of active engagement and the path of withdrawal.

Regarding the word "sukha" (happiness): here, Vedic action (*karma*) is understood to include both rites such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and meditations on symbols (*pratīkopāsana*). Vedic action is called "active" (*pravṛtta*) because it is the cause for engaging in *saṃsāra* that leads to the attainment of happiness such as heaven; likewise, "liberation" (*niḥśreyasa*) is *mokṣa*, and action for that purpose is "conducive to liberation" (*naiḥśreyasika*), being the cause for the cessation of *saṃsāra* and thus termed "withdrawn" (*nivṛtta*). In this way, Vedic action should be known to be of two kinds. (12.88)
He clarifies this very point:
"In this world or the next, action performed with desire is called 'pravṛtta' (active);
but that which is free from desire and preceded by knowledge is taught as 'nivṛtta' (withdrawn). (12.89)

[Action performed without desire is ordained as *nivṛtta* (withdrawn), while action performed out of desire is taught as *pravṛtta* (engaged). Regarding the word "here" (*iha*): here, rites such as sacrifice which are means for achieving desired ends—such as bringing about rain—and elsewhere, rites such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* which are means for achieving results such as heaven, when performed out of desire, are called *pravṛtta* because they are the cause of engagement in *saṃsāra*. On the other hand, that which is devoid of desire for seen or unseen fruits, and is preceded by the practice of the knowledge of Brahman, is called *nivṛtta* because it is the cause of the cessation of *saṃsāra*. (12.89)
By practicing active (pravṛtta) karma, one attains equality with the gods;
but by practicing renunciate (nivṛtta) action, one indeed transcends the five elements.

"Engaged" (*pravṛtta*) means that through the practice of engaged action (*pravṛttakarman*), one attains a state equal to the gods as its fruit; this is mentioned for the sake of illustration, for by means of any other engaged action, one may also attain another fruit. On the other hand, through the practice of disengaged action (*nivṛttakarman*), one transcends the five elements that initiate the body; the meaning is that one attains liberation (*mokṣa*). || 12.90 ||
Seeing the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self, he who sacrifices to the Self attains self-sovereignty. 12.91

"Regarding the word *sarva* (all): knowing in a general sense that "I alone exist in all beings—both stationary and moving—in the form of the Self, and all beings, established as transformations of the Supreme Self, abide in Me alone, the Supreme Self," the *ātmayājī* (one who sacrifices for the Self), performing the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites according to the principle of offering to Brahman (*brahmārpaṇa*), shines by himself and is thus manifest; hence he is a *svarāṭ* (self-ruler). He attains the state of being a *svarāṭ*, which is *svārājya* (sovereignty), namely, the state of Brahman. The meaning is that he attains liberation. And so says the Śruti (ChU 3.14.1): "All this, indeed, is Brahman, born from it, dissolved in it, and breathing in it; one should meditate on it with a peaceful mind. Likewise, there is a mantra of the Yajurveda:"
But he who perceives all beings in the Self alone,
and the Self in all beings, does not feel aversion toward anything thereafter.
Having abandoned the aforementioned activities, the best of the twice-born should be diligent in self-knowledge, tranquility, and the study of the Vedas.

Regarding the word "yathā" (as): even having abandoned ritual acts such as the *agnihotra* enjoined by the scriptures, a Brahmin should apply effort to the study of the Vedas, including the meditation on Brahman, the conquest of the senses, the *praṇava*, the *Upaniṣads*, and so forth. And this is stated for the purpose of demonstrating that these are internal means to liberation, but it is not said with the intent of advocating the total abandonment of the *agnihotra* and other rites.
For this indeed is the fulfillment of birth, especially for a brahmin;
having attained this, the twice-born becomes one who has accomplished his purpose, and not otherwise.

"Regarding this": this—namely, knowledge of the Self, the study of the Vedas, and so forth—brings about the fulfillment of birth for the twice-born; thus, it is especially the fulfillment of birth for the Brāhmaṇa. For, having attained this, the twice-born becomes one who has accomplished his purpose, and not by any other means.
Now, in order to demonstrate that Brahman must be known from the Veda alone, he speaks in praise of the Veda:
"The Veda is the eternal eye of the ancestors, the gods, and human beings;
the scripture of the Veda is impossible to master and immeasurable—such is the established rule. (12.94)

Regarding the phrase "the gods of the ancestors" (*pitṛdeva*): among the offerings of *havya* (oblations to the gods), *kavya* (oblations to the ancestors), and food for humans, the Veda alone is like an eye—an imperishable eye—because it is the authoritative standard (*pramāṇa*). This is because in matters such as the giving of *kavya*, whose fruits are not perceptible, there is no room for other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*). Furthermore, the Vedic scripture cannot be composed [by anyone]. By this, its non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatā*) is stated. It is also "unmeasurable" (*aprameya*), meaning that its objects of knowledge are not understood independently of the logic of Mīmāṃsā and other systems; such is the established rule. Consequently, it is settled that one should come to know the entire meaning of the Veda—which has Brahman as its self—through Mīmāṃsā and the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) such as grammar. 12.94.
Whatever Smṛtis are outside the Veda, and whatever false doctrines there may be—all those are fruitless after death, for they are said to be grounded in darkness. (12.95)

"Those which are outside the Vedas" refers to those *smṛtis* which do not have the Veda as their source, such as statements concerning perceptible matters like "Heaven results from worshipping a *caitya*," and those based on fallacious reasoning (*asattarka*), such as the Cārvāka systems which consist of the negation of deities, *apūrva*, and so forth, and which contradict the Veda—all these are fruitless regarding the next world; for Manu and others have recorded that they result in hell. (12.95)
He clarifies this very point:
"Whatever other things there may be besides these, which arise and perish, they are fruitless and false because they belong to the past. (12.96)

Regarding the phrase "they arise": those various treatises other than the Veda which arise from sources other than it, because they are of human origin, arise and likewise perish quickly. And because they are recent, they are fruitless and unreal in nature; however, the Smṛtis and other such works possess authority precisely because they are rooted in the Veda. 12.96.
The four castes, the three worlds, and the four stages of life in their distinctness—the past, the present, and the future—all are established through the Veda. (12.97)

Regarding the "fourfold caste system" (*cāturvarṇya*): the fourfold caste system is established from the Veda itself, such as in the passage, “The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth” (RV 10.90.12). Since the status of being born of a mother and father who have become Brāhmaṇas depends upon that [Vedic authority], even the worlds such as heaven are established from the Veda alone. Likewise, the four stages of life (*āśrama*), beginning with studentship (*brahmacarya*), are established from the Veda alone because they are rooted in the Veda. What need is there for more? Whatever has passed, exists now, or will be in the future—all that is established from the Veda alone, according to the principle stated in [Manu Smṛti 3.76]: “An oblation properly cast into the fire... and so forth. 12.97.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—
these are produced from the Veda alone, according to their specific origins, qualities, and functions.

Regarding the word "sound" (*śabda*): those objects such as sound and the rest which are produced and employed here in this world and in the next world—being thus "produced" (*prasūta*)—as well as the "productions" (*prasūtayaḥ*), namely the *guṇas* consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, become established through the Veda alone, because they are the cause of the Vedic rites based upon them. (12.98)
The eternal Vedic scripture sustains all beings;
therefore, I consider this to be the supreme means for the accomplishment of a living being.

"It sustains": the Vedic scripture constantly supports all living beings. And so it is said in the Brāhmaṇa: "The oblation is offered into the fire; that fire ascends to the sun; the sun rains down through its rays; by that, food comes into being; and thus here occurs the birth and maintenance of living beings, for from food, the oblation is produced. Therefore, they know that the Vedic scripture is the supreme means for achieving the goals of human life for this creature—a person entitled to perform Vedic rites. 12.99

One who is learned in the Vedic scriptures is worthy of the command of an army, the sovereignty of a kingdom, the leadership of the rod of punishment, and even the lordship over all the worlds. (12.100)

Regarding the term "commandership": commandership, sovereignty, the authority to administer punishment, lordship over the entire earth, and so forth—all these aforementioned functions can be attained only by one who knows the scriptures whose essence is the Veda. (12.100)
Just as a fire that has gained strength consumes even moist trees, so does one who knows the Vedas burn away the defects of his own actions born of karma. 12.100
"One should not take pleasure in evil deeds by relying on the power of the Veda;
for it is through ignorance and negligence that one is consumed by karma, and not otherwise.

As for "just as": just as a great fire burns even moist trees, so too one who knows the Veda both in its letter and its meaning destroys the evil produced by the performance of prohibited acts and the like. And thus it is shown that the Veda is not merely the cause of heaven and liberation, but also the cause of the cessation of what is harmful. (12.101)
One who knows the true meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras, dwelling in whatever stage of life he may be,
becomes fit for union with Brahman even while remaining in this very world.

Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the Veda and the scriptures": he who knows in reality the Veda, its meaning, and the ritual action as being of the nature of Brahman—he, established in the stages of life (āśrama) such as celibacy (brahmacarya), by means of the knowledge of Brahman supported by obligatory and occasional rites, becomes fit for Brahmanhood while remaining in this very world. 12.102.

Those who possess the texts are superior to the ignorant; those who retain them are better than those who merely possess the texts; those who possess knowledge are superior to those who merely retain them; and those who act with resolve are superior to those who merely possess knowledge. (12.103)

Regarding the phrase "to the ignorant": since both [the ignorant and the learned] are praiseworthy, when one wishes to express the superiority of one over the other, the suffix *iṣṭhan* is prescribed in the sense of "most excellent" (*śreṣṭha*). Thus, those who have studied only slightly are "ignorant"; compared to them, those who have studied the entire text are more excellent. Compared to them, those capable of retaining the text they have studied are more excellent. By this, the term *granthin* (those possessing the text) should be understood as those who have studied but forgotten the text. Compared to those who merely retain [the text], those who know the meaning of the text they have studied are superior; and compared to them, those who practice [the teachings] are most excellent. (12.103)
Austerity and knowledge are the supreme means for a Brahmin to attain the highest good;
by austerity he destroys sin, and by knowledge he partakes of immortality.

Regarding "austerity" (*tapas*): according to the *Bhārata*, "austerity is the performance of one's own duty. Thus, for a Brahmin, the action prescribed for his stage of life (*āśrama*) and the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*) are the means to liberation. In this regard, he states the intermediate operation of austerity: "By austerity one destroys evil; by the knowledge of Brahman one attains liberation. And so says the Śruti: "He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together—having crossed over death by means of ignorance, he enjoys immortality through knowledge."

Ignorance is that which is other than knowledge; it is "death" because it is a means of suffering, like death itself, and it is "evil. This very meaning of the Vedic revelation has been explained and stated by Manu [in verse 12.104].
Perception, inference, and scripture consisting of various traditions—these three must be well understood by one who desires the purification of dharma. (12.105)

Regarding "perception" (pratyakṣa): by one who desires the realization of the true nature of dharma, perception and inference must be well-understood for the sake of knowing the reality of the substances, qualities, and genera that serve as the means of accomplishing dharma; and the scripture rooted in the Veda, in the form of the Smṛtis and so forth, must be well-understood for the sake of discerning the various forms of dharma. And these three alone are the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) favored by Manu. Analogy, presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), and the rest are included within inference. 12.105.
He who examines the instruction on dharma given by the seers with reasoning that does not contradict the Vedas and the scriptures—he, and no other, knows dharma. (12.106)

Regarding the term *ārṣa*: because it was seen by the seers (*ṛṣi*), the Veda and the instruction on Dharma based upon it—such as the Smṛtis—are called *ārṣa*. He who investigates these through the logic of Mīmāṃsā and other systems that are not in conflict with them knows Dharma; however, one who is ignorant of Mīmāṃsā does not. In this regard, the Veda is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for Dharma, while Mīmāṃsā occupies the position of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). As it has been stated by the author of the Bhaṭṭavārttika:
"When Dharma is being cognized by means of the Veda acting as the instrument, Mīmāṃsā shall fulfill the portion consisting of the procedure."
This action leading to the supreme good has been declared in its entirety; now the secret of this treatise on the Laws of Manu is being taught. 12.107

"Regarding the term *naiḥśreyasa*: this action, which is the means for attaining the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), has been declared in its entirety and exactly as it is. Hereafter, listen to this secret of the *Mānava-śāstra*, which is to be kept hidden, that is about to be spoken. (12.107)
Anticipating the objection that this treatise does not mention all dharmas, he makes known its status as a teacher of the complete range of dharmas through this general statement:
"If it be asked how it should be regarding those dharmas not mentioned here, let it be so:
whatever learned Brāhmaṇas declare, that shall be the dharma, free from doubt. (12.108)

Regarding the phrase "in cases not specifically mentioned": if a doubt should arise as to how one ought to act in matters that fall under general injunctions but have not been taught with specific detail, then whatever dharma learned Brahmins—possessing the characteristics to be described hereafter—should declare, that shall be the settled dharma in that case. 12.108.

But those by whom the Veda, together with its supplements, has been mastered according to the Law—they are to be known as the cultured Brahmins, the authorities for the Vedas and direct perception. (12.109)

"By means of dharma": by means of the dharma consisting of the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and so forth. Those Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Veda augmented by the *Aṅgas*, *Mīmāṃsā*, *Dharmaśāstra*, *Purāṇas*, and so on, are the causes for the direct perception of the Śruti; those who, having studied the Śruti, teach its meaning are to be known as the *Śiṣṭas* (the cultured). 12.109.
Whatever dharma an assembly of at least ten, or even three, who are established in virtuous conduct, should determine, one should not deviate from that dharma. (12.110)
"The Purāṇas, the Law of Manu, the medical science with its limbs and sub-limbs, and the four [Vedas] established by authority—these four are not to be undermined by reasoning.

Regarding the word "ten": if many virtuous men are not available, then that assembly (*pariṣad*) which has at least ten members—or, as will be defined later, one with at least three—is the one; in the absence of such, an assembly with at least three members may determine what is Dharma through their conduct of the virtuous, and one should accept that as Dharma and not contradict it. (12.110)
One who possesses the three Vedas, a logician, a dialectician, an etymologist, a reciter of the Dharma,
and the first three classes of ascetics— this assembly shall consist of at least ten members.

Regarding the term "one learned in the three Vedas" (*traividya*): one who studies the three branches (*śākhā*) related to the three Vedas; one who knows the treatises on logic (*nyāya-śāstra*) not contradicted by *Śruti* and *Smṛti*; one who understands the reasoning (*tarka*) consisting of *Mīmāṃsā*; one who knows *Nirukta*; one who knows the law-books (*dharma-śāstra*) such as that of Manu; a student (*brahmacārin*); a householder (*gṛhastha*); and a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). This shall constitute an assembly of at least ten members. (12.111)

One who knows the Ṛgveda, one who knows the Yajurveda, and likewise one who knows the Sāmaveda—this assembly of at least three is to be known as the authority for resolving doubts regarding dharma. (12.112)

Regarding the term "knower of the Ṛgveda": those who have studied the branches of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as those who know their meaning—these three constitute the assembly (pariṣad) consisting of at least three members, which should be understood as intended for the purpose of resolving doubts concerning dharma. (12.112)

In their absence—even a single best of the twice-born who knows the Veda, whatever dharma he may determine, that should be known as the supreme dharma; not that which is proclaimed by tens of thousands of ignorant men. (12.113)

"Even a single person": even a single individual who knows the Dharma that is the meaning of the Vedas, whatever Dharma he may determine, that should be understood as the preeminent Dharma; it is not [the Dharma] spoken by ten thousand who are ignorant of the Vedas. This term "knower of the Veda" (vedavid) refers to one who knows the Dharma that is the meaning of the Vedas. And this is an indication of excellence; one who knows the Smṛtis, Purāṇas, Mīmāṃsā, and Nyāya-śāstra, as well as one who possesses the instruction of the lineage of gurus, should also be known [as such]. Likewise: "A definitive conclusion must not be made by relying on the scriptures alone; for in an investigation devoid of reasoning, the loss of Dharma arises."

Therefore, even if one who possesses great knowledge of the scriptures understands the law of penance correctly, then by him alone has the Dharma been spoken; that Dharma is to be known as the excellent Dharma. For this very reason, Yama says: "Whether one, two, or even three reciters of the Dharma should speak, that is to be known as the Dharma, and not that of thousands of others."
Among those who lack vows, who lack mantras, and who subsist merely by birth—even if they have gathered by the thousands—the status of an assembly does not exist. (12.114)

Regarding the phrase "of those who do not observe vows": for those devoid of the vows of a *brahmacārin* such as the *Sāvitrī* and others; for those lacking the study of mantras and the Vedas; and for those who merely bear the Brāhmaṇa caste—even if many are assembled together—they possess no status as an assembly (*pariṣad*), because they lack the capacity to determine the Dharma. (12.114)
Whatever those who are shrouded in darkness, the fools who do not know the Dharma, declare to be the Dharma—that sin becomes tenfold and follows after those who spoke it. (12.115)

Regarding the phrase "whom they declare": fools who abound in the quality of darkness (*tamas*), being ignorant of the Vedic meanings that are the authority for *dharma* and consequently unacquainted with the specific *dharma* under discussion, teach a person a rule of expiation or the like; the sin of that person becomes a hundredfold and falls upon the many speakers. (12.115)
All this has been declared to you, which brings about the supreme good;
the Brahmin who does not fall away from this attains the highest goal.

"‘This indeed’—all this, beginning with dharma, which is the preeminent means for achieving the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), has been declared to you. By practicing this, a *brāhmaṇa* or any other [twice-born] attains the highest goal, consisting of heaven and liberation. (12.116)
Thus that Blessed One, the God, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
has told me all this, the supreme secret of the Dharma.

"So be it. Thus the Blessed One—the Lord (deva) endowed with sovereignty and other attributes, who is so called because of his radiance—Manu, in the manner described, spoke all this, which is not to be concealed, concerning the ultimate truth of Dharma for the sake of disciples desiring to hear it, out of a desire for the welfare of the world; thus Bhṛgu said to the great seers. 12.117.
Having thus concluded what was spoken for the benefit of the great seers, he sets aside that [teaching] on self-knowledge—which, while excellent, is an auxiliary to liberation—and says:
"Composed, one should perceive everything, both the existent and the non-existent, within the Self.
For by perceiving everything within the Self, one does not direct the mind toward unrighteousness. (12.118)

"Everything": a Brahmin, knowing both existence and non-existence as "everything," should—through the excellence of meditation with an undistracted mind—directly realize the nature of Brahman established within himself as being of that very essence. For, seeing everything as the Self, his mind does not engage in unrighteousness due to the absence of attachment and aversion. (12.118)
He clarifies this very point:
"The Self alone is all the deities; everything is established within the Self.
For the Self indeed produces the connection with action for these embodied beings. (12.119)

"It is the Self alone. Indra and all other deities are indeed the Supreme Self, because the Supreme Self is the self of all. The entire world is situated within the Self alone, because it is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the Supreme Self. The particle *hi* serves to emphasize. The Supreme Self alone brings about the connection with karma for these [beings], such as the individual knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*). And so says the Śruti (Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa): "For He alone causes him whom He wishes to lead upward to perform good deeds; He alone causes him whom He wishes to lead downward to perform evil deeds. 12.119

Now, for the sake of the specific meditation on Brahman that will be described, he explains the dissolution of the external ether and other elements into the ether and other elements within the body: "One should dissolve the ether into the [bodily] spaces, and the wind into the functions of movement and touch."
The supreme light resides in the digestive fire and the eyes; water in oily substances; and earth in solid forms.
One should meditate on the Moon in the mind, the Quarters in the ears, Viṣṇu in the stride, Hara in strength, Agni in speech, Mitra in excretion, and Prajāpati in procreation.

"Kham" means "in the mind. One should contemplate the external ether as merged in oneness within the spaces of the body delimited by the belly and other cavities. Likewise, one should meditate upon the external air as merged in the bodily air which is the cause of movement and touch; the preeminent light of the two fires—the digestive fire and the solar light—in the internal heat and the visual light; the external waters in the bodily fluids; the external earth and other elements in the earthly portions of the body; the moon in the mind; the quarters of space in the sense of hearing; Viṣṇu in the organ of the feet; Hara in strength; Agni in the organ of speech; Mitra in the organ of excretion; and Prajāpati in the organ of generation—all as merged in oneness. (12.120–121)
Having thus meditated upon the internal elements and so forth as merged into oneness—
one should know that Supreme Person, the ruler of all, subtler even than the subtle, golden-hued, and accessible to the intellect through dream-consciousness. (12.122)

"Of the Ruler" means the Controller, the Restrainer, of the entire range of sentient and insentient beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass. That which is this fixed order of heat in fire and other elements, the fixed order of revolution in the sun and other celestial bodies, and the fixed distribution of fruits according to actions—all this is dependent upon the Supreme Self. Thus say the Upaniṣads: "Under the command of this very Imperishable, O Gārgī," and so forth;
likewise: "From fear of Him the fire burns, from fear the sun shines."
“Out of fear of Him, Indra and Vāyu run, and Death as the fifth.
Likewise: “Smaller than the smallest,” because He is the Self of all. And so says the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: “Of the hundredth part of the tip of a hair divided a hundredfold...”
That portion should be known as "jīva," and it leads to infinity.

"Having the luster of gold. Although the Upaniṣads—such as "without sound, without touch, without form, immutable" (Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad 1.3.15)—deny that the Supreme Self possesses form, nevertheless, for the sake of a particular mode of meditation, He has the luster of pure gold. For this very reason, the Chāndogya Upaniṣad states, "He who is within the sun, golden" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.6). This is an illustration accessible to the cognition of a dream; that is, graspable by a knowledge similar to dream-cognition. Just as dream-cognition is produced by the mind alone when the external senses such as the eyes have ceased their activity, so too is the cognition of the Self. Therefore, Vyāsa says:
It cannot be grasped by the eye, nor even by the other remaining sense organs;
however, it is perceived by those who see the subtle with a serene mind.
One should contemplate the Supreme Self in this manner.
Some call him Agni, others Manu, others Prajāpati; some Indra, others Prāṇa, and still others the eternal Brahman. (12.123)

"Regarding this": some ritualists worship this Supreme Self as the Fire (*agni*). Likewise, the Adhvaryu priests worship "that one Fire. Others, however, because of His role as the Creator, worship Him in the form of Prajāpati, known as the Creator. Still others, on account of His possession of sovereignty, worship Him in the form of Indra. Yet others worship Him as the Vital Breath (*prāṇa*), based on the observation of such scriptural passages as: "All these beings, beginning with the earth, enter into the Vital Breath alone, and from the Vital Breath they emerge. Furthermore, others worship the Supreme Self whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*) and who is devoid of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Indeed, all these forms of worship are well-established in the Śruti regarding Brahman, which possesses both a manifest (*mūrta*) and an unmanifest (*amūrta*) nature. (12.123)
Pervading all beings with its five forms, this [Self] perpetually causes them to revolve like a wheel through birth, growth, and decay. (12.124)

"This" refers to this Self (ātman). Having encompassed all living beings with the five great elements—earth and the others—which initiate the body, it causes them to transmigrate until liberation, undergoing repeated cycles of birth, existence, and destruction according to the karma acquired in previous lives, like the wheels of a chariot and so forth. || 12.124 ||
Now, concluding that the vision of the Supreme Self in all things is what must be practiced because it is the excellence among all dharmas described as liberation, [the text] says:
"Thus, he who perceives the Self by means of the self within all beings, having attained equanimity toward all, reaches Brahman, the supreme state. (12.125)
[“By the retention of this scripture, one gains merit equal to that of the four Vedas, or even greater; it is a great expiation for sins.

Thus, “in all beings... and so forth. In this manner, according to the method stated in “and the Self in all beings” (12.9), he who perceives by means of his own self the Self abiding in all beings attains the supreme, most excellent state or station, which is Brahman. The meaning is that he merges completely therein and becomes liberated. 12.125.
Thus, by reciting this Mānava Śāstra proclaimed by Bhṛgu, a twice-born man becomes eternally possessed of right conduct and shall attain his desired goal. (12.126)
The divine Manu Svāyambhuva, who had reached the further shore of the meaning of all scriptures,
having deliberated upon the Dharma that issued from his mouth in great detail, [taught it].
"Those twice-born who recite this, which grants the pacification of all sins, go to the supreme station, the eternal abode of Brahmā.
Thus ends the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra.

The Twelfth Chapter. Regarding the phrase "ity etat" (thus this): the word "iti" signifies completion. This treatise on *smṛti* was proclaimed with excellence by Bhṛgu; by reciting it, a twice-born man becomes possessed of right conduct (*sadācāra*) through the performance of prescribed duties and the avoidance of prohibited ones. Furthermore, he shall attain the goal as desired, whether it be heaven, liberation (*apavarga*), or other states. (12.126)
In the art of elaborating upon words of essential and non-essential meaning, Medhātithi possesses great skill;
Govindarāja has expressed a subtle matter with few words.
In this work of Dharaṇīdhara, there is much independence; such is the extent of it.
This effort has been made to clearly explain the entire essential truth regarding human affairs. ||1||
This [work] explains the meaning of the *Manusmṛti* as it has been mostly elucidated by the sages;
a commentary consisting of seventeen thousand verses has been composed [by me]. (2)
Thus has this exposition on the *Mānavadharmaśāstra* been composed by me for the benefit of the learned;
through it, may the Lord of the worlds grant me the destruction of the sins arising from the difficulty of understanding [the text]. (3)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Manvarthamuktāvalī, a commentary on the Laws of Manu, composed by the illustrious Kullūkabhaṭṭa, son of Divākara, a resident of Varendrinandana.
Thus ends the *Manvarthamuktāvalī* composed by the illustrious Kullūkabhaṭṭa.
